en.title: 1895: Cinema Becomes Public Entertainment
en.summary: The Lumières turned projection into a ticket, a seat, and a shared audience. Cinema moved from technical demo to public time.
en.html:
Home/History & Literacy/1895: Cinema Becomes Public Entertainment

History / Cinema

1895: Cinema Becomes Public Entertainment

The Lumières turned projection into a ticket, a seat, and a shared audience. Cinema moved from technical demo to public time.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 08Edited 2026-11

The Lumières turned projection into a ticket, a seat, and a shared audience. Cinema moved from technical demo to public time.

The first public screening

In December 1895, the Lumière brothers held a ticketed screening in a Paris café basement. An audience sat in the dark and watched moving images on a screen together.

It was not the first film, but it was the first time “going to the movies” became a repeatable public event: buy a ticket, enter, sit, laugh together, leave together.

Duration and audience

Early films ran only tens of seconds, often “a train arriving” or “workers leaving.” Audiences came not for a story but to see a real place.

Once projection became a program, editing, music, narration, and audience reaction began to shape one another. Cinema was not just an image; it was a room.

Today

Today we watch on phones, but “sit down and watch together” still has power. When you make a short, decide whether you want a swipe or sixty seconds of attention.

The two goals need different openings, rhythms, and endings. Do not use a cinema trailer grammar for a feed video that will be swiped away with sound off.

Three checks

  • You can explain why the 1895 screening marks public entertainment.
  • You can distinguish a technical demo from a program.
  • You can choose “swipe” or “stay” for a specific film.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: exhibition and audience history

1895 is not a single point called “the invention of cinema”; it is the start of cinema as public entertainment. The Lumière screenings had a venue, tickets, a programme and an audience; the audience was not passive, they laughed, flinched and talked. Cinema was collective viewing from the beginning.

Treating 1895 as a technical miracle misses the business conditions: projector, film, venue, distribution, audience flow. Technology offers possibility; business turns it into a habit. Understand that and you understand later cinema, television and feeds.

Condition B: production and technology history

From production history, 1895 films are short because film loads were limited; the camera is fixed because it was heavy; the subject is daily life because sets and actors were not needed. Creators did not choose shortness; equipment did. Technical limits shaped early grammar.

Today's short video returns to “short, fixed, daily”, not because history repeats but because conditions rhyme: low barrier, fragmented viewing, platform distribution. Compare the two eras by who shoots, who watches and how it is distributed, not by length alone.

Counterexample: one film changed the world

The popular story is “the train arrival frightened the audience, so cinema was born”. It is a good story that flattens complex history into a moment. The audience may have flinched, but the screening also needed a venue, tickets, a programme and word of mouth; without them, a film is only a novelty.

The fix is not denying the story; put it back into conditions: technology, exhibition, audience and business all had to align for cinema to become public entertainment. Tell the story, but do not mistake it for cause.

Reusable model

Technology → exhibition → audience → business. Read the four lines together and history is not “who invented what”. Technology gives possibility, exhibition gives a place, audience gives meaning, business gives persistence.

For any image change, ask four questions: what technology changed, where it was watched, who watched and who paid. All four answers make a change; only one is usually a lab event.

en.title: Animation History: From Cels to 3D
en.summary: Paper, cels, polygons: the tools changed. Animators still face the same daily problem: how to make a still thing look like it wants to move.
en.html:
Home/History & Literacy/Animation History: From Cels to 3D

History / Animation

Animation History: From Cels to 3D

Paper, cels, polygons: the tools changed. Animators still face the same daily problem: how to make a still thing look like it wants to move.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 08Edited 2026-11

Animation is not a style; it is a method for controlling time frame by frame. The medium moved from paper to cels to polygons; the problem stayed.

Frame by frame

The core of early animation was not realistic drawing; it was making still images produce motion. Twelve or twenty-four drawings per second turned action into units of time.

That is the fundamental difference from live action: live action records motion that already happened; animation has to decide how motion happens.

Cel animation

Cel animation separated character, foreground, and background so one background could be reused. Layering saved money and built an industrial method for putting a character in space.

The logic survives: character layer, background layer, effects layer, text layer. The software changed; the layer thinking did not.

3D

3D turned “what do I draw in each frame” into “what is in the scene, where is the camera, where is the light.” Control moved from line to space, but timing remained central.

Do not chase realism. Audiences remember weight and rhythm, not polygon count. Block out a readable action first, then talk about materials.

Three checks

  • You can explain the difference between animation and live action in the source of motion.
  • You can explain why cel layering was an industrial method.
  • You block out in 3D before doing materials.

en.html:
Home/History & Literacy/Media Literacy: Five Questions for Any Video

Literacy / Media

Media Literacy: Five Questions for Any Video

Do not start with “is it real.” Start with: who made it, what was cut, what context, and why it reached me now.

2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 08Edited 2026-11DEEP / 7 MIN

Do not start with “is it real.” Start with: who made it, what was cut, what context, and why it reached me now.

Five questions

Source: who shot it, who paid, who is spreading it. Edit: what was removed before and after. Context: do title, music, and subtitles change the meaning. AI: are there generation traces. Copyright: can I use it, and how.

You do not need to answer all five. If one cannot be answered, pause before sharing.

How editing changes meaning

The same footage becomes comedy with a laugh track and tragedy with a pause. Editing creates cause and effect by what it removes and what it places next to what.

When a video makes you feel strongly, find the cut: when did it make you laugh or get angry. That timing is the author’s hand.

AI traces

Hands, text, physics, reflections, and repeated textures are common generation traces. But traces do not prove the whole is fake, and no traces do not prove it is real.

Treat AI traces as an entry point for questions, not a verdict. Source and context matter more: who has a motive to make this video.

Three checks

  • You can ask at least three source questions about a video.
  • You can find a key cut in a video.
  • You do not treat an AI trace as a truth verdict.

Boundary

en.title: Three Acts: Put the Character Against a Wall
en.summary: Act one gives a goal, act two applies pressure, act three forces a choice. Each act does one job.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Three Acts: Put the Character Against a Wall

Story / Structure

Three Acts: Put the Character Against a Wall

Act one gives a goal, act two applies pressure, act three forces a choice. Each act does one job.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Act one only gets the character moving

Act one does not need a world bible. It needs three things: what this person wants, what blocks them, and what they decide to do. End on an action, not an explanation.

A short film should finish this in its first quarter. If the audience still does not know the want halfway through, later beauty is just pictures.

Act two applies pressure, not complication

Act two is where most short films break: new characters, new subplots, new twists. A short does not need more stuff; it needs the same obstacle to get harder to avoid.

The midpoint changes the method: ask for help, lie, compromise, fight back. When the method changes, the pressure actually rises.

Act three answers one question

Act three answers one question: what is he willing to pay. Do not introduce new information, characters, or locations. The ending can be a win or a loss, but not a blur.

End after the choice, without a voice-over summary. The sentence the audience supplies is stronger than the one you write.

Three checks

  • You can state the want and the obstacle in one sentence.
  • The method changes at the midpoint, not the goal.
  • Act three introduces no new character or rule.

en.title: Composition: Tell the Eye Where to Look
en.summary: Who should the eye hit first, and where does it go second? Composition is that order. Set the subject, then the layers.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Composition: Tell the Eye Where to Look

Shooting / Composition

Composition: Tell the Eye Where to Look

Who should the eye hit first, and where does it go second? Composition is that order. Set the subject, then the layers.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN Tech DeskEdited 2026-11

One frame, one subject

The eye lands in one place first. Use the brightest, sharpest, most central element to say who matters; everything else supports it.

If the face and the background fight, darken the background, move the clutter, or step closer. Composition is subtraction first.

Foreground, middle, background

Foreground sets space, middle ground holds the person, background carries information. All three layers give depth; if all three compete, the frame becomes noise.

With no foreground, find a leaf, a door frame, a shoulder. It does not need to matter; it only needs to separate the space.

Leave room for gaze and movement

If the person looks right, leave space on the right; if they walk left, leave a path on the left. Negative space is not waste; it lets the audience anticipate the next second.

Landscape and vertical need different lead room. In vertical, keep the face in the safe area first, then talk about side space.

Three checks

  • Pause the frame; you can name the subject in three seconds.
  • The frame has at least two layers of space.
  • There is lead room in the direction of the gaze.

Intent split: this page covers the practical details of “Composition: Tell the Eye Where to Look”; start with Camera Height: Lower Before You Change Lenses for the cluster-level judgement, then return here.

Boundary

This page only covers “Composition: Tell the Eye Where to Look”; it does not replace Coverage: Do Not Shoot One Angle, Camera move: handheld, stabiliser, coverage, Color: Match First, Style Second. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Deep dive

About 8 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: wide or environmental composition

Wide composition is not “fit everything in”; it is “show where the person is in the space”. Set three lines first: horizon, wall line and eyeline; do not let them fight. Placing the person on a third is not a rule; it gives the space room to breathe.

Wide lenses distort edges; keep important faces inside the central sixty percent and leave the edge to environment. The audience looks at the face, then the space; reverse the order and the person becomes a dot in a landscape.

Condition B: close or two-shot composition

Close composition starts with where the eyes sit, then where the shoulders are cut. Do not cut on a joint; cut at the chest or upper arm. Put the eyes on the upper third and leave room under the chin. In a two-shot, do not make both people the same size unless you mean “they are equal”; one larger gives the relationship a direction.

Simplify the close background, do not just blur it. Blur hides things and information; if a detail matters, keep it instead of wiping it with a wide aperture.

Counterexample: correct composition, nobody looks

A frame follows the rule of thirds, the person sits on a power point, the background has leading lines and the colours match. But the audience looks at the lamp in the background, not the person, because the person has no action and the background is brighter.

The fix is not moving the person to the centre; give them an action and bring the background down a stop. Composition ends at “the audience knows where to look”, not “the rules are met”. Ask who is brightest, who moves and who has eyes; if the three answers differ, the frame is scattered.

Reusable model

Eyes → weight → edges → background. Set where the person looks, then visual weight, then check edge distractions, then decide what the background keeps. Follow the order; do not start with the rule of thirds.

After the take, watch three seconds on monitor: where the eye lands first, what it sees second, whether a third thing distracts. If three seconds cannot answer, move the camera, not the lens.

en.title: Color: Match First, Style Second
en.summary: Fix white balance, exposure, and shot matching before LUTs and looks. If shots do not match, more style only makes it messier.
en.html:
Home/Post/Color: Match First, Style Second

Post / Color

Color: Match First, Style Second

Fix white balance, exposure, and shot matching before LUTs and looks. If shots do not match, more style only makes it messier.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 03Edited 2026-11

Match the shots first

In one scene, shots may come from different times, lenses, and white balance. View them side by side and bring exposure, temperature, and contrast close before anything else.

Matching does not mean identical; it means the cut is invisible. Half a stop of face brightness makes the audience feel a jump.

Skin is the anchor

Audiences are most sensitive to skin. Keep faces from going green, gray, or too red before choosing an overall warm or cool look. The skin line on a scope is more reliable than mood.

A look can lean, but skin must stay consistent within a scene. Ads can be cool, docs can be warm, but one film cannot have two skin tones.

One direction of style

Style is not maxing every tool. Pick one direction: low saturation, high contrast, cool shadows, warm highlights, or the reverse. Let the other controls serve it.

A LUT is a starting point, not a finish. After applying it, return to primary correction and check crushed shadows and clipped highlights.

Three checks

  • Face brightness and temperature match within a scene.
  • White objects read neutral.
  • The look has one main direction, not a new one per shot.

en.title: The 3D Pipeline: Blockout to Render
en.summary: 3D does not start with animation after modeling. Blockout sets timing, then layout, animation, lighting, and render, each step reversible.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Intermediate
en.html:
Home/Animation/The 3D Pipeline: Blockout to Render

Animation / 3D

The 3D Pipeline: Blockout to Render

3D does not start with animation after modeling. Blockout sets timing, then layout, animation, lighting, and render, each step reversible.

2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · IntermediateTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11DEEP / 7 MIN

Blockout sets timing

Use simple cubes and spheres to lay out timing and camera. No modeling or texturing yet; only answer when things happen and where the camera is.

Do not move on until blockout works. If the rhythm is wrong here, detail makes it harder to fix later.

Layout locks the camera before animation

Layout sets framing, focal length, and camera path. If the camera is not locked, animators perform inside the wrong frame and everything gets redone.

Make a playblast with no detail and confirm the cut points. Once shot length is fixed, allocate animation time.

Lighting and render are separate checks

Lighting checks separation: subject, background, environment. Render checks output: noise, samples, passes, and compositing.

Do not treat “fix it in render” as a workflow. Preview lighting at low samples to confirm mood; only then raise samples.

Three checks

  • Blockout timing and cut points are approved.
  • Cameras are locked before animation starts.
  • Lighting preview and final render are reviewed separately.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. The 3D pipeline is not a software menu. It is a chain where every step can go back one step; skip blockout and you rebuild structure forever.

Blockout before modeling

Block with boxes and cylinders for proportion, camera, and blocking. Confirm what the shot can see before modeling detail. If the blockout fails, more detail is more waste.

Put the camera in the scene first and check composition at the real focal length. Do not model first and look for a camera later; by then it cannot change.

Rig and animation handoff

Set joint count and naming before rigging. Animators need a rig that bends, turns, and carries weight, not a pile of controls. Record a test action at handoff.

Animate on the low model first to confirm timing and center of gravity, then move to high. Animating heavy geometry slows both the viewport and your judgment.

Lighting, render, and rollback

Light the gray model first to confirm the key direction. Do not load full materials at the start; read the value structure first. Render low resolution and low samples to confirm motion and composition.

Save a version at every stage with date and content in the name. Rolling back is part of the pipeline, not a failure. Without versions, rollback means redo.

Five-minute drill: one shot through the pipeline

Take a simple scene through blockout, low model, rig test, low-model animation, gray lighting, low-res render. Ten minutes per step; no detail chasing.

Save a version each step, then roll back to the blockout and check the camera. If it moved, you changed structure later without admitting it.

When a 3D shot is done

From blockout to final render: the camera did not secretly move, proportions held, the rig did not break, light direction matches, and the low-res test and final share composition. All five pass.

If the final composition differs from the blockout, roll back and check. Do not hide it with a post crop. The expensive 3D problems are decisions changed late.

Ten 3D pipeline checks

  • Blockout before modeling
  • Boxes and cylinders in blockout
  • Camera placed first
  • Composition at real focal length
  • Joints and naming before rig
  • Test action recorded at handoff
  • Animation on low model
  • Gray-model lighting first
  • Low-res, low-sample test render
  • Version saved at every stage

The way to save time in 3D is not skipping a step. It is making every step able to go back one.

en.title: Brand Film: Make Them Believe One Sentence
en.summary: A brand film does not explain specs; it leaves one attitude. The product is evidence, not the protagonist.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Intermediate
en.html:
Home/Formats/Brand Film: Make Them Believe One Sentence

Formats / Brand Film

Brand Film: Make Them Believe One Sentence

A brand film does not explain specs; it leaves one attitude. The product is evidence, not the protagonist.

2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · IntermediateTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11DEEP / 7 MIN

Write one stance first

The first line is not “founded in 1998”; it is an attitude someone could disagree with. For example, “slow down, and you can see.”

The more specific the stance, the easier the images. Vague “craft” and “passion” all look the same on screen.

Prove it with one person

Do not prove the brand with a crowd of smiles. Choose one person doing one concrete thing, and let the product be a tool in their hand, not an icon.

The less the product appears, the more weight each appearance has. A brand film is not a long product ad.

End on an action

Do not end with “this is our brand.” End on an action: close the door, leave, turn back, keep working. Let the audience say the attitude themselves.

A brand film can have no voice-over, but it cannot have no stance. Without a stance, it is just a more expensive promo.

Three checks

  • You can state the stance in one arguable sentence.
  • The product is evidence, not the hero of every shot.
  • The ending lands on an action, not a slogan.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. A brand film is not a company profile. It is one stance, proved by one person doing one thing.

Write a stance someone could argue with

Do not write “innovation, quality, care.” Anyone can use those. Write a stance someone might disagree with, such as “slower is the only way to finish.”

The stance must become an action: waiting, redoing, refusing an order, turning the light off. Only action proves it; a slogan cannot.

Prove it with one person

Choose one employee, customer, or founder and let them do something in a real situation that embodies the stance. Do not have them recite company values to camera.

The product is evidence, not the hero. Show it being used, repaired, refused. A hand, a desk, a workbench is more useful than a building.

The landing

Return to the opening action at the end and let the viewer see the cost or result. No drone shot with a subtitle summary. Keep it ninety to one hundred eighty seconds, few subtitles, room for silence.

If the film still works with the brand name removed, the stance is real. If nothing remains without the name, rewrite it.

Five-minute drill: remove the brand name

Write a stance someone could argue with, then shoot one twenty-second action: what a person did extra, or gave up, for that sentence. No office, no logo.

Remove every brand name and show it to someone who does not know the client. If they can still name the stance, it works. If not, rewrite the stance; do not add a subtitle explanation.

When it is done

Remove the brand name, logo, and product name, then show it to a stranger. If they can still say in one sentence what these people believe, the film is done. If they only say “nice shots,” rewrite the stance. Do not add a narration summary.

Ten brand-film checks

  • The stance can be argued with
  • The stance becomes an action
  • One main person
  • The person acts in a real situation
  • No recited values
  • Product is evidence, not hero
  • Show use, repair, or refusal
  • End returns to the opening action
  • It works without the brand name
  • No drone-and-subtitle summary

A brand film does not say who you are; it shows what you are willing to pay for.

en.title: Media Management: Back Up Today, Name for Finding
en.summary: Back up before wrap. Put date, scene, and camera in the filename. Footage you cannot find was never shot.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Beginner
en.html:
Home/Tools/Media Management: Back Up Today, Name for Finding

Tools / Media

Media Management: Back Up Today, Name for Finding

Back up before wrap. Put date, scene, and camera in the filename. Footage you cannot find was never shot.

2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11DEEP / 7 MIN

The 3-2-1 rule

At least three copies: camera card, portable drive, another drive or cloud. Keep two in different places and one offline. Do it the same day, not after the edit.

Verify, do not just copy. Open a few files at random and confirm they play, have the right duration, and are not zero bytes.

Naming rules

Use date_project_scene_camera_card: 20261120_coffee_S01_A_001. Do not use IMG_0001, and never name anything “final”.

Same day, same scene: S01, S02. Different cameras in one scene: A, B. Avoid spaces in names for cross-platform safety.

Project archive

Archiving is not dumping footage into one folder. Use footage, audio, graphics, project, and export, plus a README explaining versions.

AI projects also store prompts, seeds, references, and generation logs. Otherwise you cannot reproduce or prove provenance three months later.

Three checks

  • Two independent copies exist the same day and play on spot check.
  • Any shot can be found within a minute.
  • AI projects keep prompts, seeds, and references.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. Storage is not buying one big drive. It is keeping the same material in three places and knowing which copy is newest.

Three copies

One on the card, one on a portable drive, one on another drive or cloud. Do not carry all three in the same bag. Back up the day you shoot, not the day you edit.

Verify after copying: open three random files and play them, check sizes and file counts. A progress bar at 100% is not verification.

A folder structure you can read

Sort by project, date, camera, scene. File names carry date and version; never “final” and “final2.” Keep camera original, proxies, exports, audio, and graphics separate.

Write a README: which folder is camera original, which is proxy, which is final export. You should still find it in three months.

Calculate capacity

Calculate from bitrate: megabytes per minute equals bitrate times sixty divided by eight. Multiply by minutes, cameras, and copies. Leave twenty percent headroom.

Card speed matters too: sustained write below the codec drops frames. Do not trust peak numbers. Check the camera's recommended card list.

Five-minute drill: one project storage sheet

Write a three-day project: minutes per day, cameras, bitrate, copies. Calculate total capacity and how many drives.

Show the sheet to your editor and ask if it is enough. If not, add a copy now; do not buy when the drive is full.

When storage is safe

Storage is safe when three copies exist, verification playback passed, the folder structure is readable, headroom is over twenty percent, and old projects are archived. Five pass.

Two copies are not a backup; they are “not lost yet.” Add the third before editing.

Check the third copy again

Unplug two drives and open the project from the third alone: can you find the originals, play them, rebuild the folder? The third copy is not “for later”; it is the one that can revive the project by itself right now.

Ten storage checks

  • One copy on card
  • One on portable drive
  • Third off-site or cloud
  • Three copies not in one bag
  • Back up the day you shoot
  • Play three random files to verify
  • File names carry date and version
  • Originals, proxies, exports separate
  • Capacity from bitrate with twenty percent headroom
  • Sustained write speed sufficient

Storage safety does not come from drive size. It comes from being able to say where all three copies are.

en.title: Rights: Check Five Things Before Publishing
en.summary: Footage, music, fonts, likeness, and location are five separate permissions. CC is not a commercial license.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 8 min deep read · Beginner
en.html:
Home/History & Literacy/Rights: Check Five Things Before Publishing

History / Rights

Rights: Check Five Things Before Publishing

Footage, music, fonts, likeness, and location are five separate permissions. CC is not a commercial license.

2 min quick read + 8 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 08Edited 2026-11DEEP / 8 MIN

The five-item list

Footage: did you shoot it, or is it stock? Music: platform library, CC, or purchased? Fonts: personal free or commercial license?

Likeness: did the on-camera person sign? Location: does the mall, subway, or restaurant allow filming and publishing? One missing item can get the video pulled.

CC is not free commercial use

CC BY requires credit; CC BY-SA requires derivatives to share alike; CC BY-NC forbids commercial use; CC BY-ND forbids adaptations. These conditions often combine.

“Findable online” does not mean “licensed for commercial use.” For commercial work, buy a clear license or use only what you shot or made.

Platform rules and disclosure

Each platform has separate rules for music, ads, AI-generated content, health, and finance. Read the creator policy before publishing, not just other people’s videos.

Label AI generation, digital humans, and synthetic voice as required. Disclosure is not an apology; it tells the audience what they are watching.

Three checks

  • All five permissions have records or clear sources.
  • Commercial scope for music and fonts is written down.
  • AI generation or synthetic voice is labeled per platform.

DEEP DIVE / 08 MIN

Go deeper: for people already shooting

Copyright protects expression, not ideas. You can take the same subject; you cannot copy the specific expression.

en.title: Six Things to Write Down Before Your First Shoot Day
en.summary: First shoots fall apart around time, place, ownership, shot order, backups, and when to stop. Put all six on one page.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Six Things to Write Down Before Your First Shoot Day

Production / First Day

Six Things to Write Down Before Your First Shoot Day

First shoots fall apart around time, place, ownership, shot order, backups, and when to stop. Put all six on one page.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11

A call sheet that fits on one page

A call sheet is not paperwork for the crew. It forces you to name what you are unsure about: call time, address, contact, lunch, parking, and the latest wrap time. Six lines will do. If you cannot write a street number, you have not scouted the location.

Photograph it, send it to the group, and ask everyone to reply “in.” Anyone who does not reply is assumed absent. Calling them on the day is usually too late.

Shoot the light before the scene

Natural light will not wait. Shoot the window side, the backlight, and the dusk first; the sun moves every day. Dialogue you can pick up later goes in the afternoon. The sky you cannot recreate goes in the morning.

Order shots by light and by the actor’s condition, not by script page. New directors often shoot scene one through the end in order, then discover the best dusk light has ten minutes left.

Give each department one concrete question

Camera: does this shot move? Sound: did we get room tone? Producer: when is lunch, and where do cars park? The director answers “what,” not every “how.”

Keep ten minutes before wrap: play back the last take, make one backup, confirm tomorrow’s call time. Skip those ten minutes and you will likely reshoot the next day.

Three checks

  • A driver can navigate to the address on the call sheet.
  • The irreplaceable light is shot within two hours of rolling.
  • Before wrap, the footage opens from a second drive.

Boundary

This page only covers “Six Things to Write Down Before Your First Shoot Day”; it does not replace Fluid Head: Pan and Tilt Need Drag, Follow Focus: One Hand Can Follow, Composition: Tell the Eye Where to Look. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Three failures

The three common first-shoot-day failures happen before the first take:

  • 1. Batteries and cards are not labelled. You discover both batteries are flat and the card still holds last week's footage; label one battery and one card per body.
  • 2. Shooting the hardest shot first. You block the actor and props while the good light goes; shoot the natural-light-dependent shots first, then the controllable pickups.
  • 3. Recording only the on-camera mic. No independent audio, no room tone, no second backup; when the dialogue is unusable in post, there is no rescue material.

en.title: Directing Non-Actors: Give Them a Task, Not a Performance
en.summary: The more you tell a real person to act natural, the stiffer they get. Give them a task, their own words, and a little more distance.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Directing Non-Actors: Give Them a Task, Not a Performance

Directing / Non-actors

Directing Non-Actors: Give Them a Task, Not a Performance

The more you tell a real person to act natural, the stiffer they get. Give them a task, their own words, and a little more distance.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 01Edited 2026-11

Give an action, not an emotion

Wipe a cup, find a key, lift a box onto the table. When the hands have a job, the face stops thinking “I am being filmed.” Emotion comes from the task, not from an instruction.

If they are nervous, ask them to walk you through their daily route. Moving helps people relax more than sitting down.

Put the line in their words

Write the meaning, not a word-for-word script. Let them say it their way. If they stall, ask “what were you thinking then?” Do not correct grammar mid-sentence, and do not make them repeat until it sounds like a broadcast.

The first pass is usually the truest; by the third, it sounds memorized. If you need more, ask about one detail instead of restarting the whole answer.

Move the camera back and hold the cut

Start on a medium or wide shot so the camera becomes normal. A lens in someone’s face makes a non-actor perform “serious.”

Keep rolling for ten seconds after “cut.” People often say the most human line when they think the take is over.

Three checks

  • The subject has a concrete task, not just sitting still.
  • The words sound like theirs, not a script.
  • At least one usable moment happens after “cut.”

en.title: Pacing Is Not Speed; It Is When They Want the Next Line
en.summary: Fast cuts do not make a film good. Cut the explanation, land cuts on movement, then decide where silence belongs.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Beginner
en.html:
Home/Post/Pacing Is Not Speed; It Is When They Want the Next Line

Post / Pacing

Pacing Is Not Speed; It Is When They Want the Next Line

Fast cuts do not make a film good. Cut the explanation, land cuts on movement, then decide where silence belongs.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 03Edited 2026-11DEEP / 6 MIN

Cut the explanation first

Watch it with the voice-over muted. If the action still reads, the narration is doing too much. The audience does not need to be told “he is sad”; they need to see him put the chopsticks down.

Cutting one line of explanation usually opens two seconds. Do not fill those two seconds with music right away. Let the image carry them.

Cut on movement, not after it

A hand reaching for a handle, a foot leaving frame, a head turning: these are cut points. Cut late and the audience waits; cut early and the action never completes.

Dialogue can enter before the picture and leave after it. Hear the next line while the previous face is still on screen; the audience will bridge the two spaces.

Silence is pacing too

Not every gap needs music. Five seconds of two people not talking can be tenser than a drum cue. Let room tone hold the scene before the score enters.

If a scene feels long no matter what, check whether it delivers new information. Without new information, even a short shot drags; with it, a long take can hold.

Three checks

  • The story reads with the voice-over muted.
  • At least three cuts land on movement.
  • One silent beat is left without music.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Pace is not cutting fast. It is making the audience want the next line at the right moment.

Pace lives in the information gap

At the end of a shot, leave a small question in the audience’s mind: will he come in? did she hear it? The next shot answers it. Answer too fast and there is no wait; too slow and attention is gone.

Link scenes as question, answer, new question, not as one long acceleration. If everything is fast, nothing has pace.

Keep one main question per scene. Sub-questions can coexist, but do not ask them all in the same second.

Alternate long and short shots

Three shots of the same length feel flat; hold one two seconds longer, shorten the other two, and the scene breathes.

Action can use short shots, but after every three or four, leave a slightly longer reaction or the audience only feels dizziness.

A long shot is not slow; it gives the audience time to finish an action. A short shot is not fast; it gives them no time to think. Each should explain the other.

A music hit is not a cut point

Do not cut on every drumbeat. Music is background; picture has its own cause and effect. Cut the action first, then align the music; reverse it and the track drags the scene.

Leave at least one two-second passage without music so the audience hears the room. Silence makes the next passage push.

If a sequence only works with music, ask whether it has any action. Music cannot make a decision for the character.

Five-minute drill: one long, two short

Take thirty seconds of footage and cut three shots of equal length, then recut as two short and one long. Compare both and ask which makes you want the next line sooner.

Do not add music; watch picture only. If the pace is wrong, music only covers it. Make a third version with one shot removed and see whether the story still stands.

Ten pacing checks

  • Ask what the scene wants the audience to wait for
  • Leave one question at each cut
  • Do not answer too early
  • Alternate long and short shots
  • After three or four shorts, hold a reaction
  • Cut action before music
  • Do not cut on every beat
  • Keep one two-second silence
  • Cut repeated information
  • Watch once on a phone speaker

Pace is not making the picture faster; it is making the audience want to keep watching.

en.title: How to Use One Window as Your Key Light
en.summary: You do not need a lighting kit for a face: set the direction, add a little bounce, then bring the background down.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/How to Use One Window as Your Key Light

Shooting / Available Light

How to Use One Window as Your Key Light

You do not need a lighting kit for a face: set the direction, add a little bounce, then bring the background down.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 02Edited 2026-11

Turn the face, not the window

Ask the subject to turn slowly toward the window until the nose shadow falls on one cheek. Facing the window flat is boring; facing away is dark. Thirty to forty-five degrees is the reliable zone.

Direct sun is too hard; add a sheer curtain or a white cloth. An overcast window is often easier: soft face, still some background separation.

Keep the bounce low

Bounce from chest height and the shadow softens; hold it above the head and the face gets two top lights. A white wall, paper, or foam board works; you do not need a professional reflector.

Fill only the shadow side, and do not bring it up to the bright side. One stop of difference keeps the face dimensional.

Take the background one stop down

Close the curtain behind the subject or kill the overhead light in the background. A bright face against a darker background creates depth; equal brightness makes the person look pasted on.

If the background cannot change, choose a darker angle or move the subject half a meter forward. With available light, moving the person is easier than moving the light.

Three checks

  • The nose shadow falls on one side only.
  • The shadow side has detail without matching the bright side.
  • The background is darker than the face, so the subject separates.

Boundary

This page only covers “How to Use One Window as Your Key Light”; it does not replace Wireless Lav: Hide It, Back It Up, Cross the Line and the Room Disappears, Color: Match First, Style Second. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: one window, small room

In a one-window room, first decide which side the window is on. Forty-five degrees side-front is the safest, side-back is more dramatic, side-on gives volume. Do not face the person into the window; the face flattens and the eye socket loses shadow. Let the window hit the nose bridge and one cheek, then lift the other side half a stop with a reflector.

Do not put the reflector directly opposite the face; it creates a second catchlight. Put it on the shadow side, angled up. Closer is softer, farther is harder; try three positions and compare ten seconds.

Condition B: mixed light or overcast

In mixed light, decide which source is key. Cool window and warm room lamp: pick one as key and the other as fill; do not let both be key. If the window is key, turn off or match the room lamp; if the lamp is key, curtain the window to reduce its strength.

Overcast window light is soft but directionless; flag one side with black to create direction. The flag is not to darken the frame; it is to give the face contrast. On an overcast day, contrast matters more than brightness.

Counterexample: the window behind the subject

To show “the city outside”, the camera faces the window and the person sits with their back to it. The window is beautiful, the face is black; brightening in post clips the background and adds noise to the face. The audience watches the city, not the person.

The fix is not losing the window; change the relationship. Turn the person sideways to the window and shoot from the side, leaving the window at the edge. It is still the background, but the face has light; the city does not need the whole frame, a corner is enough.

Reusable model

Direction → ratio → colour → background. Give the person an angle to the window, control face-to-background contrast, match colour, then decide how much window is in frame. Follow the order; do not start by closing the curtain.

Every camera move redoes direction; window light does not follow the camera. A new angle can turn side light into backlight; without redoing it, the scene breaks.

en.title: From Daguerreotype to Phone: Five Turns in Photography
en.summary: In 1839 you sat still for dozens of seconds. In 1888 Kodak handed the camera to ordinary people. In 1975 a sensor turned light into a file. In 2007 the phone made photographing the default.
en.html:
Home/History & Literacy/From Daguerreotype to Phone: Five Turns in Photography

History / Photography

From Daguerreotype to Phone: Five Turns in Photography

In 1839 you sat still for dozens of seconds. In 1888 Kodak handed the camera to ordinary people. In 1975 a sensor turned light into a file. In 2007 the phone made photographing the default.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 08Edited 2026-11

1839: Make people believe the photograph

Exposures ran for dozens of seconds; sitters used braces to stay still. A photograph was closer to a unique object than to today’s infinite copy.

That is also when photographs became “evidence.” People quickly learned to pose and retouch, so proof and performance arrived together.

1888: The camera leaves the studio

Kodak’s roll film and “you press the button, we do the rest” turned photography into a daily act. You no longer needed to mix chemicals or calculate exposure.

As cameras shrank, the world inside photographs changed: streets, trips, and family gatherings entered ordinary people’s own albums.

1925: A small camera that moves with people

The 35mm camera let reporters carry a machine into a crowd, and photojournalism began to catch people mid-action. Smaller gear made a bigger world fit in the frame.

Cartier-Bresson’s generation did more than compose: they proved the “decisive moment” could happen in the street, not only in a studio setup.

1975: Light becomes a file

A Kodak engineer built the first digital camera prototype; at the time, few believed it would replace film. Then the cost curve made the decision for everyone.

From that point, photographs could be copied without loss, transmitted instantly, and tracked through metadata. The time sense of photography shifted from “develop” to “upload.”

2007: The phone makes photographing the default

After the iPhone, the camera stopped being a destination and became part of speech. Computational photography made “sharp” the default, and “processed” the default too.

Everyone now carries a camera that shoots, edits, and publishes immediately. Photography history did not end; it moved into everyone else’s hands.

Three checks

  • You can say what happened in 1839, 1888, 1925, 1975, and 2007.
  • You can explain why “photographs are evidence” was unstable from the start.
  • You know phones changed not only gear but publishing speed.

Boundary

This page only covers “From Daguerreotype to Phone: Five Turns in Photography”; it does not replace Platform Rules: What Gets Throttled, Likeness, Location, and Minors: What a Release Must Say, Documentary Template: One Person, One Thing, One Change. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Three failures

The three common failures in photography-history writing are not just “wrong date”:

  • 1. Giving the invention to one person. The 1839 announcement sits on different lines of work by Daguerre, Niépce and Talbot; one name turns technical competition into a hero story.
  • 2. Judging early processes by today's sharpness. Daguerreotype, calotype and wet plate each had material and exposure limits; modern pixel standards hide the real constraints.
  • 3. Listing dates without materials or circulation. A process works only through its sensitive material, exposure time, viewing method and reproduction cost; drop one and the timeline becomes an empty shell.

en.title: Twelve Checks Before Publishing: Do Not Lose the Last Hour
en.summary: Three groups of checks: rights, technical, and publishing. Each takes ten minutes; do not discover a black frame or a typo after upload.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Beginner
en.html:
Home/Tools/Twelve Checks Before Publishing: Do Not Lose the Last Hour

Delivery / Publishing

Twelve Checks Before Publishing: Do Not Lose the Last Hour

Three groups of checks: rights, technical, and publishing. Each takes ten minutes; do not discover a black frame or a typo after upload.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11DEEP / 6 MIN

Check rights first

Music, fonts, likeness, location, and AI disclosure: five separate checks. A platform music library is not a commercial license; a verbal yes is not a likeness release.

Keep the paperwork in one folder named for the project and date. If a complaint arrives after publishing, you can find it in ten minutes instead of pulling the whole film.

Then check the file

Ratio, bitrate, loudness, subtitles, black frames, and file name. Watch the film from start to finish, not on the timeline; the timeline will not tell you the dialogue is muddy on a phone speaker.

Proofread subtitles by reading them aloud, not just scanning the screen. Check names, numbers, and place names separately; those are the three most common mistakes.

Finally, check the publishing

Title, cover, platform rules, backup, and schedule. Can you see the face at thumbnail size? Does the title promise something the film does not deliver?

Do not close the laptop right after uploading. Open it on your phone once, confirm ratio, subtitles, and sound, then shut down.

Three checks

  • All five permissions can be found within ten minutes.
  • The film has been watched once on a phone speaker.
  • The subject reads at thumbnail size.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Publishing is not pressing upload. It is closing rights, subtitles, cover, backup, and version on the same day.

Clear rights first

Check music, fonts, footage, likeness, and location one by one. If there is no written permission, do not use it. Free download does not mean commercial use.

Label AI-generated material and read both platform rules and local law; do not trust a single tutorial.

Keep the permission files in the project archive, named by asset and expiry. Someone will ask again in six months.

Technical delivery

Play the export yourself: opening, ending, subtitles, sound, black frames. Do not trust the progress bar. Name the file with date, project, version, platform.

One wrong subtitle character is remembered; one wrong cover ratio is cropped by the platform.

Use the platform’s current bitrate, resolution, and loudness spec, not a blog post from three years ago; platforms change requirements.

The first 24 hours

Check for platform compression, cropping, and lip-sync drift first, then read comments for misunderstanding. Log the issues for the next version.

Back up the original project and export. Do not overwrite the published version; keep a read-only archive.

Write the actual spec into the project README so the next release does not start from trial and error.

One page before publishing

Put platform, resolution, bitrate, loudness, cover ratio, and subtitle language on one sheet and tick each item at release.

Archive the sheet after publishing; the next release on the same platform starts from it instead of trial and error.

When the platform changes a spec, change the sheet first, then the export preset. Do not fix one file and forget the next.

Ten checks before publishing

  • Written permission for music, fonts, footage
  • Likeness and location releases complete
  • AI material labeled
  • Subtitles proofread character by character
  • Opening and ending complete
  • Loudness and bitrate match the platform
  • Cover survives all three ratios
  • Filename has date, project, version, platform
  • Project and export backed up
  • Published version kept read-only

Publishing is not the end; it turns this version into the foundation for the next.

en.title: Stop Asking “How Did You Feel”: Ask for an Action
en.summary: People rarely remember a feeling. They remember which foot they moved first. Specific questions get human answers.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Stop Asking “How Did You Feel”: Ask for an Action

Story / Interview

Stop Asking “How Did You Feel”: Ask for an Action

People rarely remember a feeling. They remember which foot they moved first. Specific questions get human answers.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 01Edited 2026-11

Ask what happened that day

Ask ten people “how did you feel” and eight will say “terrible” or “happy.” They are not stonewalling; the question is too big. Ask what time they left the house and where they went first, and they start looking for keys and bus cards. The words come with the actions.

I watched a reporter spend twenty minutes asking a market vendor whether the work was hard. He kept saying “it’s okay.” Then she asked what time he arrives and what he does first. He talked for half an hour about laying ice and keeping the scale from getting knocked. The audience remembers the ice, not the word “hard.”

Leave three seconds of silence

When they stop talking, do not jump in. A lot of the truth arrives around second three. Nod, look at your notes, wait. They often add, “Actually, there is one more thing.”

That gap is not dead footage. In the edit, those three seconds are often where the audience enters the person. If the interviewer grabs the turn back, the subject returns to “being interviewed.”

Check names and numbers before wrap

Read names, places, ages, and amounts back to them before you pack up. “Wang” and “Wong,” “fourteen” and “forty” sound alike on a recording and look wrong once subtitled.

Then ask what cannot be published. Someone may be willing to talk but not willing to be seen by their employer. Draw that line now; it is cheaper than taking the film down later.

Three checks

  • The first three questions can be answered in one sentence and contain an action.
  • At least one silence longer than three seconds survived the edit.
  • Names, places, and numbers were checked on site.

en.title: Cross the Line and the Room Disappears
en.summary: Move the camera to the other side of a conversation and the audience thinks the people swapped seats. Pick a line before you cross it.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Cross the Line and the Room Disappears

Shooting / Camera

Cross the Line and the Room Disappears

Move the camera to the other side of a conversation and the audience thinks the people swapped seats. Pick a line before you cross it.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 02Edited 2026-11

Draw the line first

Two people face each other. Treat the line between them as a border. Keep the main shot on one side and the reverse shot on the same side, and the audience knows who is left and who is right. The rule is not magic; it protects the map of the room in their head.

Before rolling, take a wide shot on your phone and look at it. A is on the left, B is on the right. Check every later setup against that frame instead of trusting your memory on set.

When crossing is allowed

If someone walks across the room, if the camera follows them through, or if you insert a neutral shot, the audience can accept the change. A neutral shot can be hands, a glass of water, a doorway. It just cannot belong to either side.

The hard cut with no reason is the problem. A is left, then A is right, and the audience spends two seconds relocating. Whatever was said in those two seconds is gone.

Shoot clean singles

With one camera, shoot a clean single of A, then a clean single of B, then pick up hands and objects. Clean singles let you reorder the scene in the edit without using a line cross for “cinematic” texture.

Refocus and re-white-balance every time you move. Dialogue scenes usually fail on matching color between two setups, not on the acting.

Three checks

  • The wide shot makes left and right obvious.
  • Every line cross has a walk, a move, or a neutral shot to justify it.
  • The two reverse angles match in color temperature and exposure.

en.title: Timing in Animation: The Weight Lives Between Two Keys
en.summary: A ball falls off a table. How many in-betweens you draw, and how far apart they sit, tells the audience whether it is a ping-pong ball or a shot put.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Beginner
en.html:
Home/Animation/Timing in Animation: The Weight Lives Between Two Keys

Animation / Timing

Timing in Animation: The Weight Lives Between Two Keys

A ball falls off a table. How many in-betweens you draw, and how far apart they sit, tells the audience whether it is a ping-pong ball or a shot put.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 05Edited 2026-11DEEP / 6 MIN

Decide the weight first

The same move from A to B reads as a steady slide when the in-betweens are evenly spaced. Pack them near the start and end and spread them in the middle, and you get acceleration and deceleration. That is what animators mean by spacing.

Before drawing, ask: is it thrown, or does it walk? Does it bounce, and how many times? Once those answers are fixed, the in-betweens mostly place themselves.

Test at 12, finish at 24

Do not animate every frame in the rough pass. Test the timing on twos at 12 fps; a wrong action is obvious there. Once the rhythm works, fill in to 24. Otherwise you spend hours polishing a move that was wrong to begin with.

Shoot live-action reference when you can, especially for lifting, sitting, and turning. Real bodies do not move at a constant speed. The most common animation mistake is being too smooth.

Judge a loop by its ends

When a cycle is done, put the first and last frame side by side. If they do not line up, the loop will pop. Fix the ends before touching the middle; doing it the other way wastes ten passes.

For a walk, watch the feet. If the planted foot slides, the character looks like they are on ice. Holding the contact frame one extra beat often does more than adding more in-betweens.

Three checks

  • You can say whether the action is heavy or light, and why.
  • The action reads clearly in the 12 fps test.
  • The first and last frames of the loop connect without a pop.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Animation timing is not constant speed. It is acceleration, deceleration, holds, and suddenness; those four create weight.

Spacing decides speed

Between two keys, inbetweens close to the start read as a slow launch; close to the end read as a fast drop. Even spacing is constant speed, usually the fakest. Adjust spacing before curves.

One action needs at least two speeds: slow start, fast middle, held landing. All constant speed makes objects float.

A hold is also action

A hold is not missing drawings; it lets the audience read the last one. Two frames before a turn, three before a line, four after a landing. The right hold gives action cause and effect.

Too long breaks the flow, too short blurs it. Watch frame by frame on the phone and find the longest hold the eye can still read.

Easing is not universal

Heavy objects launch slow and land fast; light objects launch fast and settle slow. Elastic things rebound; machines move linear. Easing everything makes the frame look like jelly.

Ask how heavy it is, who pushes it, what it hits. The answer decides the curve, not the software default.

Five-minute drill: one action, three timings

Animate a hand picking up a cup three ways: constant, slow start fast landing, fast start slow settle. Change only spacing, not drawings. Play them in sequence and see which reads as a cup, which as a balloon.

Show the three to one person and ask how heavy the cup is. The more specific the answer, the better the timing.

When the timing is right

Cover the image and watch only motion: you can feel the weight. Slow it by half: you still see launch, travel, landing. Mute it: the action still has rhythm. All three pass.

If only sound effects give weight, the visual timing is not there yet. Adjust spacing and holds before adding music.

Watch the landing again

Slow the four frames around the landing: if there is no hold at contact, the weight is not there yet. Add one hold frame and remove one rebound frame; that is usually enough. Timing is not about smoothness; it is about daring to stop.

Ten timing checks

  • Spacing adjusted first
  • At least two speeds per action
  • Slow start, fast middle, held landing
  • Constant speed only for machines
  • Hold lets the last drawing read
  • Hold length checked frame by frame
  • Heavy: slow launch, fast landing
  • Light: fast launch, slow settle
  • Elastic rebounds
  • Curve decided by weight

Right timing makes an audience believe a ball has weight. Wrong timing makes the finest drawing look like paper.

DEEP DIVE / 06 MIN

en.title: Hold Ten Percent for the Unexpected
en.summary: Weather, overtime, reshoots, and last-minute hires happen on almost every shoot. If they are not in the budget, the overrun steals from somewhere else.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Hold Ten Percent for the Unexpected

Producing / Budget

Hold Ten Percent for the Unexpected

Weather, overtime, reshoots, and last-minute hires happen on almost every shoot. If they are not in the budget, the overrun steals from somewhere else.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11

List the four likely surprises

Exteriors depend on weather. Interiors depend on when the location closes. Cast depends on availability. Gear depends on whether there is a backup. Write one worst case for each, multiply by a number you can survive, and put it in the budget.

I watched a two-day shoot lose an afternoon to rain. The crew waited three hours. Because the budget held money for another day of rent, they picked up the missing scenes the next morning. A crew without that line would have moved a night scene to daylight and changed the mood of the whole film.

Hold ten percent, with a rule

Ten percent is not “we will figure it out.” It is three rules written in advance: weather overtime comes from this line; cast reshoots do not; gear damage can use half. With the rules on paper, spending it does not require an argument.

If you spend it, cut the same amount somewhere else. Otherwise it is not a buffer. It is a quieter budget increase.

Keep overruns on one page

Before wrap each day, write three lines: what you spent, how far over plan it is, and what is due tomorrow. Do not wait until the shoot ends to total it; by then nothing can change.

The client version can be one page. You still need to know why each line moved. Next time you quote, those numbers are your footing.

Three checks

  • The budget has a separate contingency line of at least ten percent.
  • The rules for using it were written before the first day.
  • At every wrap, you can say how much today went over and why.

en.title: Write a Shot List Someone Else Can Run
en.summary: A shot list says what comes first, how long it takes, and what happens if it fails. A wish list says everything at once.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Write a Shot List Someone Else Can Run

Shooting / On Set

Write a Shot List Someone Else Can Run

A shot list says what comes first, how long it takes, and what happens if it fails. A wish list says everything at once.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 02Edited 2026-11

The first shot list usually follows the script: scene one, scene two. Then you get to set and the lights have to move, the wardrobe has to change, and the sun is already gone.

Order by camera and light

Order by camera and light instead. Keep shots facing the same way and using the same kit together. Put wardrobe continuity and the location’s time window in the header.

I write three lines at the top: three shots we must get today, three we can push, three we can lose. With those lines on the page, the day can fall apart and we still know where the floor is.

Give every row a fallback

Add a fallback column to every row: reverse, close-up, insert, sound. When the master shot gets stuck, the whole crew should not stand around. If the dolly cannot get in, go handheld and follow the action. If the wide is impossible, take the doorway insert and a bed of room tone.

The ten extra seconds you grab on the day are what save you in the edit. A shot list is not there to fill the schedule. It is there to get the few pieces that cut into a film.

Check the list before wrap

After a scene, stand at the monitor and strike the rows. Do not work from memory; memory loses things between card changes, battery swaps, and wardrobe. Strike the rows before you move on, and you avoid a pickup day.

Leave one blank page at the end for what you find on set. The unplanned shots are often the ones that survive the final cut.

Checks

  • The list is grouped by camera and light, not script pages.
  • Every essential shot has a fallback.
  • At wrap, you can point to the rows you did not get.

Boundary

en.title: B-roll: Give the Sentence a Picture
en.summary: When someone says “I set up at five every morning” and the camera stays on their face, the audience can only listen. B-roll turns that line into something visible.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Beginner
en.html:
Home/Shooting/B-roll: Give the Sentence a Picture

Shooting / Coverage

B-roll: Give the Sentence a Picture

When someone says “I set up at five every morning” and the camera stays on their face, the audience can only listen. B-roll turns that line into something visible.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 02Edited 2026-11DEEP / 5 MIN

List the nouns before you leave

Circle the concrete nouns in the interview: the scale, the old bicycle, the cash tin, the alley before dawn. For each noun, shoot three things: the whole, the detail, the action. If you wait until you are on location to “find the feeling,” you usually find nothing.

The more specific the noun, the easier the edit. You cannot shoot “life.” You can shoot a man flattening bills one at a time.

Hands, feet, back

Hands working, feet walking, a back leaving. Faces carry feeling; hands and feet carry life. Hold ten seconds before and after each action so the edit has room to cut.

Do not come back with only mediums. A wide says where he is, a close-up says how he does it, and you still need one shot that shows the action from start to finish. With all three, a sentence can breathe.

Room tone is picture too

Do not mute the location. The scale hitting the counter, the roller shutter, a radio in the distance: those sounds hold the picture up. At every new place, record thirty seconds of clean room tone. It patches more holes than you expect.

Play it back in the car before you leave. If something is missing, go back while you are still on the street. Finding out at the edit that you never shot a hand is too late.

Checks

  • Every concrete noun has a wide, a detail, and an action.
  • Every action has ten seconds of handle on both sides.
  • Every location has thirty seconds of room tone.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. B-roll is not filler. It gives the main story something to cut to and details that make it credible.

Shoot hands, feet, and backs first

Before a character enters, shoot the hand pushing the door, the foot crossing the threshold, the back pausing. These let the edit cut anywhere in the main action.

Do not shoot only faces. A face is emotion; hands and feet are action. Action footage cuts more easily.

Get two takes per action: one complete, one detail only. The detail take gives the edit room.

Every b-roll shot answers something

Ask of every b-roll shot: what does it answer? Environment, action, time, relationship. If nothing, it is a pretty outtake.

Shoot at least three groups per location: establishing space, human detail, environmental change. Two takes each so they can be joined.

B-roll needs a beginning and an end; a middle fragment alone gives the editor no in-point or out-point.

Do not let b-roll steal the scene

Keep b-roll shorter than the main shot unless it carries a turn; past three seconds, the audience assumes it is the point.

If the color, movement, or sound in the b-roll is stronger than the main story, cut it; it will pull attention away.

More is not better. Two or three usable details per scene beat twenty beautiful shots.

Pickup list: three lines

For every main location, list three lines: space, action, environmental change. Strike them out when shot; do not rely on memory.

Do not shoot ten b-roll shots at once. Get three usable ones, confirm an in-point and an out-point, then add a second take.

With five minutes left, shoot hands and feet before faces; a face can act again, hands and feet cannot.

Ten b-roll checks

  • Shoot hands, feet, backs first
  • Every action has a full and a detail take
  • Every b-roll shot answers a question
  • One group each for space, detail, change
  • At least two takes per group
  • B-roll has an in and an out
  • Keep each shot under three seconds
  • Color and movement do not overpower the story
  • Sound does not bury dialogue
  • Pick up missing details before wrap

B-roll is not extra; it is the edit’s way out.

Boundary

This page only covers “B-roll: Give the Sentence a Picture”; it does not replace Blocking: Let the Body Tell the Story, Boom Operator: Follow the Action, Not the Line, Color: Match First, Style Second. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

en.title: Fix the Noise Before You Build a Mood
en.summary: When a film sounds uncomfortable, the audience rarely says “the sound is bad.” They just stop watching. Fix noise, levels, and sync before reaching for music.
en.html:
Home/Post/Fix the Noise Before You Build a Mood

Post / Sound

Fix the Noise Before You Build a Mood

When a film sounds uncomfortable, the audience rarely says “the sound is bad.” They just stop watching. Fix noise, levels, and sync before reaching for music.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 03Edited 2026-11

Listen three times before touching anything

First pass for the whole thing. Second pass for voices only. Third pass with the picture off, listening to the room. Write the problems down: hiss, clipping, echo, level jumps between shots. Do not start pulling faders while you listen; you will forget what the original sounded like.

Once the list is clear, decide what to fix and what to re-record. Re-recording one line is often cheaper than ten minutes of repair.

Do not over-clean the noise

Push noise reduction too far and voices turn to plastic. Start with constant sounds: air conditioning, a fridge, a ballast. For intermittent noise like fans and traffic, change the shot or re-record. Keep a little room tone so the ear believes the space is real.

If a passage cannot be saved, shorten it. The most effective move in sound post is often a cut, not a plug-in.

Dialogue first, music last

Keep dialogue peaks between -6 and -3 dB, with room tone 12 to 18 dB below. Add music last. Then listen with the picture off and make sure the voice is still on top. A line buried under music does not get replayed; the viewer leaves.

Do not sync by eye. Clap at the head of every take and match the waveform. Without a clap, find a door close, a cup set down, a footstep, and match the transient.

Checks

  • The problem list separates hiss, clipping, echo, and level jumps.
  • Dialogue peaks sit between -6 and -3 dB, room tone 12 to 18 dB below.
  • With the picture off, the voice is still clear.

en.title: Does the Cover Still Read at 200 Pixels?
en.summary: On a phone, a cover is the size of a thumb. Secure one face, one action, one contrast before adding type.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Beginner
en.html:
Home/Formats/Does the Cover Still Read at 200 Pixels?

Publishing / Cover

Does the Cover Still Read at 200 Pixels?

On a phone, a cover is the size of a thumb. Secure one face, one action, one contrast before adding type.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11DEEP / 5 MIN

Make a black-and-white proof at thumb size

Turn the frame black and white, then shrink it to 200 pixels wide. If the subject disappears, reshoot or recrop. Color and type cannot rescue composition. Plenty of covers look fine at 1080 and turn into a color smudge in a phone list.

The black-and-white proof also forces you to see the face, the action, and the light instead of falling for a grade.

One face, one action, one contrast

A face reads faster than a landscape. An action reads faster than a pose. A strong light-dark contrast reads faster than detail. With three or more people, the viewer does not know where to look. Keep one clear center and let everything else fall back.

If there is no face, show something happening: a hand entering frame, a door pushed open, an object falling. A still empty scene usually needs type to hold it up.

Keep the words to three or five

Cover type is a road sign, not a title. “She left” does more than “a story about leaving.” Small type turns into a line at phone size, especially over a bright background.

Make three covers for the same film and test them in the feed. Do not ask a colleague which one looks better. Data is faster than taste, and more honest.

Checks

  • The subject still reads in a 200-pixel black-and-white proof.
  • There is one clear center.
  • Cover type is five words or fewer and stays legible on a phone.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. A thumbnail is not a shrunken poster. It is one image that has to be recognized in a phone list within two seconds.

Recognize the person, then the event

At thumb size, first check whether there is a face or an action; if not, only text remains. A face should occupy at least a third of the frame, eyes to camera or to the key object.

The title should not repeat the image; the image gives emotion, the title gives information.

With two subjects, the audience looks for the face first. Blur or crop the secondary person so they do not steal focus.

Contrast and breathing room

The thumbnail needs light-dark or warm-cool contrast, a clean background, and at least eight percent margin around the subject. Do not put type over the face or key action where the platform UI will cover it.

Check three crops: 16:9, 1:1, and 9:16. If the subject survives the crop, it is a thumbnail.

Two lines of type at most: the first line asks, the second delivers. Do not write a promise the film cannot keep.

Test it, do not guess

Make three versions: face, action, object. Put them in a phone list and ask five people what they saw within two seconds. If they cannot say, redo it.

Do not use click-through as the only measure; the film must deliver what the cover promises. Disappointment makes the next cover fail.

Compare the three on a real phone, not on a 27-inch monitor pretending to be thumb size.

Three-cover test

Make three covers for one film: face, action, object. Put them in a phone list and ask five people what they saw in two seconds; write down their first word.

If the first words disagree, the image has no claim. Remove decoration and keep one subject.

Export at the platform’s real size and do not judge on a desktop enlargement; thumb size is the test.

Ten thumbnail checks

  • Readable at thumb size
  • A face or an action is visible
  • Face fills at least a third
  • Title does not repeat the image
  • Clean background
  • Eight percent margin around the subject
  • Two lines of type at most
  • Subject survives 16:9, 1:1, and 9:16
  • Test on a phone with five people
  • The film delivers the promise

The cover only makes people stop; the film makes them stay.

en.title: Compositing: Make Both Layers Believe the Same Light
en.summary: A clean key is not a composite. Match direction, softness, color temperature, and contact shadow before touching the edge.
en.html:
Home/Post/Compositing: Make Both Layers Believe the Same Light

Post / Compositing

Compositing: Make Both Layers Believe the Same Light

A clean key is not a composite. Match direction, softness, color temperature, and contact shadow before touching the edge.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 03Edited 2026-11

Drop the foreground in and turn off edge checking for a minute. See where the key comes from, where the shadow falls, and whether the background is hard sun or overcast. If the direction is wrong, a perfect edge still looks like a sticker.

Then match softness and color temperature. Window light is soft; noon sun is hard; a warm room pushes skin toward orange. Put both layers in the same light before discussing the edge.

Contact shadow saves more than the edge

If a person stands on a floor, the area under the feet needs to go darker. If a hand rests on a table, the table needs a small shadow. Without contact, the subject floats. Follow the key direction; do not paint a black ring around everything.

Reflective surfaces also need a little bounce: a table throws shirt color up to the chin, glass throws window light onto a cheek. It does not need much. Direction is enough.

Grain, flare, and lens share the room

A clean foreground over a grainy background gives itself away. Add grain in the same direction, then a little highlight bloom and slight dispersion so the edge belongs to the same lens. A hard key edge is often not a mask problem; the light and grain do not match.

Do a ten-second test: one turn, one occlusion, one highlight pass. If ten seconds hold, comp the shot. Finding the problem after the full shot costs days.

Checks

  • You can name the key direction in both layers, and they agree.
  • Feet and hands have contact shadows; the subject does not float.
  • The ten-second test has no obvious sticker edge.
