en.title: The Walk Cycle: The Foot Plant
en.summary: Walks look hard because feet slide, weight is wrong, and limbs move together. Lock the four poses first, then talk style.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Beginner
en.html:
Home/Animation/The Walk Cycle: The Foot Plant

Animation / Cycle

The Walk Cycle: The Foot Plant

Walks look hard because feet slide, weight is wrong, and limbs move together. Lock the four poses first, then talk style.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 05Edited 2026-11DEEP / 6 MIN

Lock the four poses

Block a walk with four poses: contact, down, passing, up. Contact is the front heel down and the back toe still on the ground. Down is the lowest point of the hips. Passing is the back leg under the body. Up is the highest point before the front foot leaves.

Stand the four poses up before adding in-betweens. A floaty walk usually has bad weight in the poses, not too few drawings.

The planted foot cannot slide

Once a foot lands, it should look pinned to the screen. The body can pass over it; the foot cannot drift with it. Lock the foot, then move the hips and shoulders past. A sliding foot makes the character walk on ice.

The hips need to go up and down. Every step has a low point and a high point; the body does not travel on a flat line. Hold the down pose one extra frame and weight appears.

Let hands and head lag; judge the loop by its ends

Do not move arms and head on the same frame as the hips. Hips first, arms one or two frames later, head a little after that. That is what makes a walk feel weighted instead of translated. Arms swing opposite the same-side leg; do not move hand and foot together.

When the cycle is done, put the first and last frames side by side. If they do not match, it pops. Fix the ends before the middle; doing it backwards wastes ten passes.

Checks

  • All four poses carry weight.
  • The planted foot does not slide; hips and shoulders pass over it.
  • First and last frames connect without a pop.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. A walk is not legs alternating. It is weight falling, one foot supporting, then the other foot catching.

Four poses

Contact, down, passing, up: four drawings make half a step. Contact is the widest stride; down is the lowest center; passing is the straight support leg; up is the highest body.

Draw the pelvis and ribcage up and down first, then the legs. Without that bounce, correct legs still slide.

The planted foot cannot slide

The support foot must stay planted on screen while the body moves forward. Check by lining up the background with the foot and watching frame by frame for drift.

Heel contacts, foot rolls, toe leaves. Three clear points give the push. Do not slap the whole foot down flat.

Arm and head lag

Arms swing opposite the legs but one or two frames later; the head lags the ribcage by one. If everything arrives together, the walk looks robotic.

A tired walk adds a drag: shorter support, deeper down, head lowering first. Do not just slow the playback.

Five-minute drill: eight-drawing cycle

Draw an eight-drawing walk: left contact, left down, left passing, left up, right contact, right down, right passing, right up. Side view only, no background.

Play the loop. Check foot slide first, then the vertical bounce, then arm lag. When all three work, add cloth and hair.

When the walk is right

Line the background to the foot and check the plant does not drift; the pelvis bounces, the head lags, the arms swing opposite; the loop returns to the first drawing without a jump. All three pass.

If the foot slides, check the plant before changing the upper body. If it looks robotic, add lag before adding inbetweens.

Watch the pelvis again

Cover the legs and watch only the pelvis: no side shift makes it march in place; too much makes it dance. Set the side shift to half a foot, then animate the legs.

Ten walk-cycle checks

  • Four poses per half step
  • Pelvis and ribcage first
  • Widest stride at contact
  • Lowest center at down
  • Straight support leg at passing
  • Planted foot does not slide
  • Heel, ball, toe clear
  • Arms opposite and lagging
  • Head one frame behind ribcage
  • Fatigue adds drag, not slow motion

Every walk-cycle problem comes back to two places: does the center bounce, and does the planted foot slide?

en.title: Dialogue: Let Them Fight with Words, Not Explain
en.summary: Dialogue stalls when the writer says everything the character is thinking. Good lines fight for something, the listener reacts, and the backstory stays on screen.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Dialogue: Let Them Fight with Words, Not Explain

Story / Dialogue

Dialogue: Let Them Fight with Words, Not Explain

Dialogue stalls when the writer says everything the character is thinking. Good lines fight for something, the listener reacts, and the backstory stays on screen.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 01Edited 2026-11

Every line is after something

Before writing a line, mark the action underneath it: he wants the other person to admit it, apologize, stay, shut up, pay, or just let the room go quiet. If you cannot name the action, the line is probably filler.

Two people want the same thing and the scene has tension. One asks, “Did you eat?” The other hears, “Why did you leave without me?” The words are about food. The fight is about who left first.

Cut the manual

“You know, when I was a kid…” is an explanation for the audience, not something a person would say in that moment. People in an argument do not pause to brief each other. They go for the sore spot.

Put the backstory into objects and actions: a photo left behind, a suitcase still by the door, a cigarette pressed into an unwashed plate. Once the audience sees it, you do not have to say it.

If you must explain, let it slip out during the fight. A slip costs something. A summary costs nothing.

The listener carries the scene

Dialogue is not a relay of lines. The reaction after a line is the temperature of the scene: how long the other person waits, whether they look away, what their hand does on the table.

Shoot a separate angle on the listener. Even with no line, the audience reads how much the last sentence landed.

Silence is dialogue too. If the expected answer does not come, the audience supplies it. Cutting away there is stronger than adding one more explanation.

Checks

  • You can name the action under every line.
  • Explanatory lines are gone; objects or actions carry the backstory.
  • The listener has a reaction shot, and the silence does something.

Intent split: this page covers the practical details of “Dialogue: Let Them Fight with Words, Not Explain”; start with Want and Stakes: What Does Losing Cost? for the cluster-level judgement, then return here.

Boundary

This page only covers “Dialogue: Let Them Fight with Words, Not Explain”; it does not replace Directing Debut: Protect Performance Before Coverage, Directing Non-Actors: Give Them a Task, Not a Performance, Composition: Tell the Eye Where to Look. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Deep dive

About 8 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: subtext scene

Subtext is not “saying the opposite”; it is a want that cannot be spoken. Before dialogue, write two notes: what A wants and what B wants; they cannot be the same. The lines talk about a third thing: ordering food, finding keys, closing a window; the want leaks through action.

Leave a moment of “not understanding”: one person says a true thing, the other answers with an unrelated word. The audience hears the mismatch and knows the relationship is off.

Condition B: exposition or debate

Exposition also needs a want, or the lines become data. One person wants to persuade, the other wants to end it; every explanation carries a purpose. A debate is not an exchange of views; two people fight for the same conclusion. The scene moves when someone concedes.

Split exposition into action, reaction and cost: a piece of information is spoken, the listener does something, the speaker pays something. Information is not delivered in one block; it is forced out by reactions.

Counterexample: every line is clever

Every line in a scene is a killer line. The audience enjoys it, but nobody changes, because every line performs cleverness and nobody wants anything. Cut any line and the scene still works; that means no line carries a turn.

The fix is not removing the clever lines; give them a cost. The person who wins the line loses the relationship; the next line must be slower and truer. Cleverness needs a consequence, or it is only line performance.

Reusable model

Two wants → a third subject → mismatch → cost. Two people want different things, the talk is about a third subject, at least one moment is misunderstood, and one person pays. With all four, lines have subtext.

At the read, ask only three questions: who wants what, who blocks it, who changes after the lines. If the three cannot be answered, the dialogue needs work.

en.title: Camera Movement: Ask Why Before How
en.summary: Moving the camera is easy. Keeping the audience from noticing the machine is the work. Write down what they should follow, discover, or feel before you move.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Camera Movement: Ask Why Before How

Shoot / Camera movement

Camera Movement: Ask Why Before How

Moving the camera is easy. Keeping the audience from noticing the machine is the work. Write down what they should follow, discover, or feel before you move.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 02Edited 2026-11

Write the reason on the shot list

Next to every moving shot, write one sentence: why does the camera move? To follow someone, to reveal what they cannot see, or to make them feel cornered. If you cannot write the reason, lock the camera off first.

Movement is not a story. Motivation is. The audience will not care that the dolly runs smooth; they forget the machine only when they are being taken somewhere.

Three moves, one per shot

  • Follow. Keep the subject at roughly the same size in frame and let the audience walk with them. Good for travel, presence, and long takes. Match the operator’s pace to the subject’s; do not let the stabilizer arrive first.
  • Reveal. Start on a detail, then pan or boom out to the larger space. Good for information gaps: a hand first, then the knife on the table. Move slowly enough for the eye to read.
  • Pressure. Push in slowly, or hold the subject still and let the background recede. Good for the seconds before a decision. Push fast and the scene becomes a thriller.

Pick one primary move per shot. Follow and pan and push in the same shot, and the audience stops knowing where to look.

Stop after the move

Most shots do not need more movement. They need stillness. When the camera reaches its new position, hold on the face or on the empty space and let the audience digest what they just saw.

The cut often lives in that stop. If you never settle, the edit has to cut from a frame that is still moving.

Checks

  • Every moving shot has a written reason.
  • One primary movement per shot.
  • The move ends with a hold long enough to read.

en.title: Let Sound Cross the Cut: J-cuts and L-cuts
en.summary: Picture does not have to cut at the same time as sound. Let the next scene arrive early, or the last one linger, and the cut stops hitting the audience.
en.html:
Home/Post/Let Sound Cross the Cut: J-cuts and L-cuts

Post / Editing

Let Sound Cross the Cut: J-cuts and L-cuts

Picture does not have to cut at the same time as sound. Let the next scene arrive early, or the last one linger, and the cut stops hitting the audience.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 03Edited 2026-11

Decide whose ear leads

A cut is not only a picture change. It is a change of attention. Before the cut, ask what the audience needs to hear first. If the next scene’s sound can build the space early, let it cross the cut.

Sound arriving half a beat ahead keeps the audience from feeling pushed. Picture and sound slamming together at the same frame feels like a door shutting.

J-cut: the next scene speaks first

The picture is still in the previous scene, but the next scene’s room tone or line has already entered. Hear the market before you see it; hear the voice on the phone before cutting to the person holding it. The audience enters the next scene early, so the picture cut does not feel like a gap.

Method: drag the next scene’s audio 12–24 frames left. Try one second first. Dialogue scenes can go longer, but do not let the next line steal focus while the previous character is still speaking.

L-cut: the last scene stays in the ear

The picture has cut to the listener, but the previous voice continues. A character lands a hard line; we cut to the other face and the sentence is still in the air. The audience uses that gap to think about what was just said.

Method: drag the previous audio right so it covers the first one or two seconds of the new picture. Give the new frame an action that can stand on its own; do not leave the audience watching a static face.

Do not use sound to hide a bad cut

J-cuts and L-cuts are bridges, not bandages. If the picture has a continuity error, a crossed line, or a broken performance, covering it with sound does not fix it. Make the picture cut work first, then use sound to make it smoother.

Checks

  • For every J-cut or L-cut, you can say what the audience hears first and sees second.
  • The audio overlap stays under two seconds unless there is a deliberate design.
  • Watch it muted. The picture still works.

Boundary

This page only covers “Let Sound Cross the Cut: J-cuts and L-cuts”; it does not replace Fix the Noise Before You Build a Mood, Sound Post: The Order from Dialogue to Final Mix, Cross the Line and the Room Disappears. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: between scenes

A sound bridge between scenes is not “bring the next room tone in early”; it is “carry the feeling of the previous scene into the next”. The tail of a line, a door, footsteps can enter the next scene before the picture cuts. Sound leads, and the audience does not feel the jump.

Length follows information: if the next scene must establish place immediately, bring room tone in 0.5–1 second early; if it continues emotion, two to three seconds. Do not use the same bridge on every transition; the audience hears the template.

Condition B: inside a scene

J-cut and L-cut inside a scene are not tricks; they let the audience hear a reaction first. A line ends, sound cuts to the listener while picture stays on the speaker; the audience hears “mm” before seeing the face, and the reaction has weight. An L-cut keeps the previous line while picture moves ahead.

Internal bridges follow the eyeline: whoever looks at whom gets the sound first. Do not J-cut every edit point; too many make the dialogue feel ungrounded.

Counterexample: a J-cut on every transition

A ten-minute film brings the next scene's sound one second early on every transition. It feels smooth at first; by the fourth transition the audience expects “hear first, see second”, and the bridge becomes a pattern. The more bridges, the fewer bridges.

The fix is not removing all bridges; use them only where the hard cut fails. Cut hard first and see whether the audience loses place; add a bridge only then. A bridge is medicine, not food.

Reusable model

Hard cut first → find the lost point → add sound → test again. Start without a bridge and find where place or emotion is lost; add sound only there; test again. A bridge is not a default; it is a repair.

A bridge carries one thing: place, emotion or information. Bridge three at once and the audience is lost. Decide what this cut must carry, then choose the sound.

en.title: Let the Room Speak First
en.summary: Before anyone speaks, the room is already talking: shoes at the door, two cups on the table, one lamp left on. Set dressing is the first line.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Let the Room Speak First

Shoot / Production design

Let the Room Speak First

Before anyone speaks, the room is already talking: shoes at the door, two cups on the table, one lamp left on. Set dressing is the first line.

3 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 02Edited 2026-11

Before anyone speaks, the room is already talking. Set dressing is the first line.

Decide who has lived here

Before asking how to make a room look good, write three lines: who lives here, what they just did, and what they do not want anyone to see. If you cannot write those lines, the room is only a backdrop.

Take a shared flat: two pairs of shoes at the door, one lined up, one kicked over; a bowl left in the sink for three days; a tie hanging on the bedroom handle, never given away. The audience reads two people living at different speeds without a word of explanation.

Props need a use and a before/after

Props are not decoration. They should be picked up, put down, knocked over, hidden. Before the shoot, give every key prop a state: full, empty, clean, used. The audience reads the change of state, not the object.

Three things at the entry: keys, mail, shoes. Three on the table: a cup, pills, bills. One thing in the corner: what he does not want seen. Three groups are enough. More and the room becomes a prop warehouse.

Then make one thing wrong. A chair facing the door. An expired train ticket on the fridge. A bunch of flowers still wrapped in the bin. The audience asks why, and the scene starts.

The light belongs to the room too

If the room has only a ceiling light, people look like they are in an office. If there is one table lamp, they sit toward it. The position of light decides whether the character wants to be seen.

Find the sources already in the room: window, table lamp, fridge door, hallway light. Give each one a reason: it is not dark yet, he is waiting, she forgot to turn it off. Add a reflector or a sheet of white paper to open the shadow; do not light the whole room.

Before shooting, walk from the door to the window with a phone. What the eye sees first and second is often not what looked good on the floor plan.

Checks

  • You can name who lived here, what just happened, and what is hidden.
  • Key props carry wear or a change of state.
  • The light comes from the room, and one thing is wrong enough to make the audience ask why.

en.title: Lip Sync: Close on Consonants, Open on Vowels
en.summary: Lip sync is not a drawing for every word. Land the closed consonants, open on the vowels, let the expression arrive late, and the audience believes the voice.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Lip Sync: Close on Consonants, Open on Vowels

Animation / Lip sync

Lip Sync: Close on Consonants, Open on Vowels

Lip sync is not a drawing for every word. Land the closed consonants, open on the vowels, let the expression arrive late, and the audience believes the voice.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 05Edited 2026-11

Lip sync is not a drawing for every word. The audience watches the closure, not the lip detail.

Sort the voice into four mouths

You do not need the full phoneme chart. Start with four mouth groups: closed (m, b, p), open (a), round (o, u), wide (e, i). Most dialogue needs no more than these.

Draw one clear profile or front view for each group and pin it beside the lightbox. Do not invent a fifth mouth mid-scene. The more consistent the set, the more the audience believes one person is speaking.

If the design is simple, use fewer shapes. Closed and open can carry a scene. Timing of the closure matters more than lip detail.

The closed frame matters more than the open one

The audience decides “is he speaking” on the consonant closure. On m, b, and p, the lips actually meet, even for a single frame. A mouth left half open reads as dubbing no matter how good the track is.

Listen once, mark the closed-lip sounds on the waveform, put the closed shape one or two frames before each mark, then move into the vowel. Do not cut a shape for every letter. A five-second line needs five to eight mouth shapes.

Keep the closure clean. Too many in-betweens make the mouth look like it is chewing.

Let the expression lag; stop nodding

Do not land eyes and brows on the same frame as the mouth. Let the eyes arrive two to four frames late, the head a little after that. The audience hears the stress first and sees the reaction second; that is where believability comes from.

The head can move on a stressed word. At the end of a line, stop the mouth first and let the eyes settle. The worst habit is a nod on every word, like keeping time. One sentence needs one main action: look away, lower the head, blink, take a breath.

Checks

  • Four mouth shapes cover the whole line.
  • Every closed consonant actually closes for at least one frame.
  • Eyes and head arrive after the mouth; the mouth stops first at the end.

Boundary

en.title: Vertical Drama: A Want in the First Three Seconds
en.summary: Vertical drama has no time for a world. Put a want in the first frame, an obstacle by the third second, and leave one question unanswered.

Home/Formats/Vertical Drama: A Want in the First Three Seconds

Format / Vertical drama

Vertical Drama: A Want in the First Three Seconds

Vertical drama has no time for a world. Put a want in the first frame, an obstacle by the third second, and leave one question unanswered.

3 min quick read + 6 min deep read · IntermediateTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11DEEP / 6 MIN

Vertical drama has no time for a world. The first frame has to put a want on screen.

One person, one want in the first frame

A vertical screen cannot hold environment, two people, subtitles, and mood at once. The first frame should hold one person, one want, one obstacle. She wants in; the door is locked. He needs a signature; the pen is dry. She came to return the key; he thinks she came back.

Do not open on an empty city shot. A viewer swiping a vertical feed asks, “Is this about me?” One person staring at one object builds that faster than ten seconds of scenery.

The want has to be visible: a door, a contract, a phone, a key, a pregnancy test. Do not let a voice-over announce “I have to get the money today.” Show the payment notice in her hand; that lands harder than saying it.

One information gap per scene

Short drama runs on an information gap, not an argument. One person knows; the other does not. She knows the contract is fake; he is still counting his commission. He knows the child is not his; she is still choosing a name.

One gap per scene, one turn. Add a second and third reversal and the audience gets tired and stops believing. One scene written through beats five twists.

Turn on an action, not a line like “I knew all along.” Push the contract back, put the key on the table, turn the phone screen around.

Vertical framing: face high, hands low

The most useful vertical frame is “face in the upper third, hands or object in the lower third.” The audience reads expression first, action second. For a confrontation, do not force a two-shot. Cut between close-ups; the faces get bigger and the pressure rises.

Vertical movement works better than horizontal blocking: entering, going downstairs, sitting, standing up. A sideways pan in vertical easily throws the subject out of frame. Mount the phone vertically; do not shoot wide and crop later, or you lose heads and hands.

Keep subtitles in the bottom safe area, off the mouth and hands. Platform UI covers the bottom, so lift important action a little.

Checks

  • In the first three seconds, you can name the want and the obstacle.
  • One information gap per scene, one turn.
  • Face high, hands low, and one question left unanswered.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Vertical drama is not a long show cut short. It builds a want, hides information, and turns once in thirty seconds.

A want in three seconds

In the first second, someone wants something concrete: money, keys, a signature, an admission. In the second, show who blocks it. No company, job title, or backstory first.

An information gap drives the form: the audience knows something the character does not, or the character knows something we do not. Either one pulls the viewer forward.

One room, two people, one turn

One location is enough: a front desk, a car, a table, an elevator. Two people are enough: the one who wants and the one who blocks. A third person only splits attention.

Offer a false answer so the viewer thinks the problem will resolve one way; then turn it with an action or a line. The turn must change the relationship, not just swap a sentence.

Vertical performance and coverage

Use medium and close shots; the face should fill about a third of the frame. Do not place two people too far apart or the expressions vanish. Keep lines short, under twelve characters, and leave the pauses.

Do not use a three-shot montage for backstory. Hide it in a prop, a form of address, an action. End on a hook: a new problem, threat, or secret. No moral summary.

Five-minute drill: one room, one turn

Write a thirty-second scene: one person wants, one blocks, one prop decides what is true. Give a false answer in the first fifteen seconds, then turn it with an action in the last fifteen.

Shoot vertical medium shots, lines under twelve characters. Show it to someone new and ask who ended up with power. If they cannot answer, the turn changed a line, not the relationship.

When it is done

Show it to someone new and ask who ended up with power and which line changed the relationship. If both answers are clear, the scene is done. If they only say “there was a twist” but cannot name the change, the turn is still only in the dialogue.

Ten vertical-drama checks

  • A concrete want in second one
  • The blocker visible in second two
  • An information gap exists
  • One location only
  • Two main characters only
  • False answer and turn
  • The turn changes the relationship
  • Medium or close framing
  • Lines under twelve characters
  • A new question at the end

Short drama is not short. It is every second changing the distance between two people.

en.title: Conflict: Both Sides Need a Point
en.summary: An argument is not conflict. Real conflict is two valid wants that cannot both win. The audience has to understand both sides before it can hurt.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Conflict: Both Sides Need a Point

Story / Conflict

Conflict: Both Sides Need a Point

An argument is not conflict. Real conflict is two valid wants that cannot both win. The audience has to understand both sides before it can hurt.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 01Edited 2026-11

An argument is not conflict. Real conflict is two valid wants that cannot both win.

Give both sides a reason they could say out loud

A villain is easy to write and easy to forget. If both people are only out for themselves, the scene is a tug of war. If both are trying to protect someone else, the audience gets caught in the middle.

Example: she wants to move her father into care, because she cannot keep caring for him alone and is about to lose her job. He wants to bring his father home, because he promised not to send him away. Both reasons hold. Either way, someone loses something.

Give each person a sentence they could say to a friend without shame. A reason that cannot be said out loud is usually a reason the writer forced in.

Conflict is not volume; it is fewer options

Louder is not escalation. Real escalation is the same decision getting harder to postpone: first it can be discussed, then it must be settled tonight, then the signature cannot be taken back.

Apply pressure with time, money, or a third person. Do not keep adding characters. Each turn removes an option: cannot wait, cannot lie, cannot go back. The fewer choices they have, the more the audience feels it.

If the two still have a third way out, the conflict has not arrived yet.

Someone has to pay at the end

When the conflict ends, someone has to pay. Show what the winner lost and what the loser kept. A crying scene is not a cost. If nothing changes after the tears, the audience will not remember it.

One last action is enough: sign the form, close the door, put the key on the table, return the shoe to the cupboard. The audience reads who won from that action, and who did not.

Checks

  • Both reasons fit in one sentence and both hold.
  • Each turn removes an option instead of raising the volume.
  • Someone pays a visible cost at the end.

en.title: Subtitles: Help Them Read, Not Just Transcribe
en.summary: Subtitles are not a transcript. They have to land the meaning before the eye gives up: short lines, breaks at the right place, numbers and names that read at a glance.
en.html:
Home/Post/Subtitles: Help Them Read, Not Just Transcribe

Post / Subtitles

Subtitles: Help Them Read, Not Just Transcribe

Subtitles are not a transcript. They have to land the meaning before the eye gives up: short lines, breaks at the right place, numbers and names that read at a glance.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 03Edited 2026-11

Subtitles are not a copy of the dialogue. They are the rail the audience grabs when the ear cannot keep up.

Decide what must be read

Subtitles are not a full transcript. Drop filler, repetitions, and vocal tics. Keep names, numbers, negations, and turns. The eye should catch the meaning in one pass; if it has to go back, the scene is broken.

Compress the sentence into one readable thought before breaking it. Never split “not” from “agree” across two lines; the viewer may read only half.

Subtitles are a guardrail for the ear, not a word-for-word record. Fill in what is hard to hear; do not fight what is already clear.

Break by meaning, not by character count

Chinese: 12–16 characters per line. English: 32–42 characters. Two lines maximum, never three. Keep numbers with their units, names with their titles, and negations with the word they modify.

If a sentence is too long, cut it before shrinking the type. Smaller type makes the viewer lean in, and the picture loses.

Break before a clause or a turn, not after a connector like “and” or “but.” The eye needs to breathe at the line end, not fall off it.

Timing and placement are grammar too

Subtitles should arrive with the voice, not ahead of it and not late. Hold a short line for at least one second; keep a long one under four to six seconds. If it cannot be read, merge or cut, do not speed it up.

On vertical video, place subtitles above the bottom safe area, off the mouth and hands. Do not rely on color alone to mark a speaker; add a name or a position. Color fails for color-blind viewers.

Leave a little margin on both ends. Arriving too early spoils the line; staying too long holds the next one hostage.

Checks

  • Chinese lines stay under 16 characters, English under 42, with two lines maximum.
  • Numbers, names, and negations survive unbroken.
  • Subtitles stay off the mouth and hands, inside the vertical safe area.

en.title: Location: Five Questions Before You Unpack
en.summary: A location is not a place that looks right. Who can say yes, who will complain, where the power comes from, what the sound does, and who pays for damage: miss one and the day stops.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Location: Five Questions Before You Unpack

Tools / Location

Location: Five Questions Before You Unpack

A location is not a place that looks right. Who can say yes, who will complain, where the power comes from, what the sound does, and who pays for damage: miss one and the day stops.

3 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11

A location is not a place that looks right. Answer five questions before you move the gear in.

Who can actually say yes

A location is not a place that looks right. Ask who owns it, who manages it, and who can open the door on the day. If the owner, tenant, building manager, or landlord has not agreed, the shoot can stop.

A verbal yes is not permission. Put the date, hours, crew size, equipment, power, noise, parking, bathrooms, and cleanup in writing. The person who signs must be able to stand behind it, not an intermediary who “thinks it should be fine.”

If the shoot blocks a door, takes a public way, or affects neighbors, check the local rules. Do not treat “nobody will notice” as a permit.

Can the room actually work

Do not scout only for the frame. Walk the carry route: is the door wide enough, can the stairs take the cases, does the elevator need booking, can you park nearby. Then check power: where the outlets are, how far they run, what the total load is. Do not discover on the day that you need three extension runs.

Listen to the room: HVAC, fridge, street traffic, a neighbor’s renovation. Record a thirty-second test and play it back for the noise floor. You can add light; you cannot add silence.

Finally, check time: when the window light arrives and leaves, when the owner closes, when the neighbors sleep. The room’s light and business hours will rewrite your schedule.

Put the trouble in the plan

For public space, check the local filming permit. For homes and shops, talk to the neighbors before the crew arrives. Carry insurance for gear and third-party damage. Ask how damage is assessed before paying a deposit.

Have a backup location, even if you never use it. Put the location contact on the first line of the call sheet. Restore the room before wrap, let the owner inspect it, then settle the deposit. Do not promise “we will be back” unless you mean it.

The relationship is a long-term asset. A clean wrap makes the next door, outlet, and quiet hour much easier to borrow.

Checks

  • Written permission covers dates, hours, crew, power, and cleanup.
  • Carry route, power, and noise floor are tested on site.
  • Permit, insurance, and a backup location are arranged.

en.title: Why Faces Got Closer: Cinema to Phone
en.summary: Faces did not get closer because directors fell in love with close-ups. The screen changed. Cinema could hold a face; TV gave it a living room; the phone gives it a thumb.
en.html:
Home/History & Literacy/Why Faces Got Closer: Cinema to Phone

Context / Viewing

Why Faces Got Closer: Cinema to Phone

Faces did not get closer because directors fell in love with close-ups. The screen changed. Cinema could hold a face; TV gave it a living room; the phone gives it a thumb.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 08Edited 2026-11

Shot size did not change because directors fell in love with close-ups. The screen and the viewing distance changed together.

Cinema: the wide shot is the default

The cinema screen is large, the audience sits in the dark, and the eye can scan the whole frame. A wide shot can hold the room, the people, and the background without losing information. A face can be small because the screen is half a wall.

This is not “directors used to be better.” The viewing conditions allowed them to spread information out. The audience had no phone and no pause button; it followed the frame.

TV: the medium shot becomes living-room language

Television moved into the living room. The screen shrank to 4:3 and the viewing distance became a few meters. A face in a wide shot turned into a dot, so shows moved to medium and close shots. Sitcoms, talk shows, and news all held the viewer with one face and one line.

A smaller screen pulls the framing closer. That is reading conditions, not taste. TV composition also became more centered, because the edges were often blocked by furniture.

Phone: one face, one action

A vertical phone is a thumb wide, and the viewer is thirty centimeters away. A wide shot reads as a pile of small people and background; the space is gone. The most useful frame is “face high, hands or object low,” one action per shot.

For the same scene, a cinema version can establish the room with a wide. The phone version has to be re-cut from close shots and inserts. Do not crop a landscape frame into vertical; decide again who the audience sees first.

Vertical is not a smaller movie. It has its own shot sizes, pace, and viewing distance. Shooting for the phone beats cropping for it.

Checks

  • You can explain why a wide shot fails on a phone.
  • The same scene has cinema, TV, and phone framing plans.
  • The phone version holds one face and one action per scene.

en.title: Continuity: Every Take Has to Cut
en.summary: Continuity is not timecode. It is what the audience will notice: a cup switching hands, a button undone, sunlight jumping to the other side. One extra note on set saves a day in the edit.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Continuity: Every Take Has to Cut

Shoot / Continuity

Continuity: Every Take Has to Cut

Continuity is not timecode. It is what the audience will notice: a cup switching hands, a button undone, sunlight jumping to the other side. One extra note on set saves a day in the edit.

3 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 02Edited 2026-11

Continuity is not the person behind the monitor calling out timecode. It is one job: make every take cut with the next.

Track the three things that will drift

Wardrobe, props, and physical state drift quietly between takes. The second button comes undone, the cup moves from the right hand to the left, the actor cried in the last scene and still has swollen eyes. The audience may not name it, but it reads as fake.

At every new setup, take a continuity still on your phone. The frame should hold the full figure, the key prop, and the background. Use notes only for what the photo cannot show: the coat is wet, the cup is half full, his left hand is injured.

Do not write “wardrobe same as before.” The person doing continuity may not know which “before.” Write “blue coat, second button open, wet cuff.” That is when the note starts working.

Give every take a handle

Roll three seconds before the action and hold three seconds after. The edit needs material to grab: room to cut in early or stay late. A shot with no handles cuts like hitting a wall.

For any important action, shoot it at least three ways: the full action, the first half, the second half. Use the wide for the whole and the close for the pieces. Do not count on one take, and do not let the actor get faster and faster inside the same action.

After each take, write one line about what was best. Not a score: an entrance for the editor. “She paused before setting the cup down.” “He looked at her before opening the door.” That line beats ten OKs.

Write it on set, not from memory

Keep a three-column sheet: setup, take, note. Notes stay concrete; “felt good” is not a note. Hand the sheet and the photos to the editor before wrap, not the next morning.

Continuity is not the police. Do not chase every background mismatch. Protect what the audience will see: faces, hands, key props, direction of light. An extra chair in the background may pass; the key in the hero’s other hand will not.

Checks

  • Every setup has a continuity still with the key prop and wardrobe visible.
  • Every take has handles, and important actions have a wide and a close.
  • The sheet names the best take and why it is best.

en.title: Cut Points: Action, Eye Line, Sound
en.summary: A scene that will not cut usually has the wrong cut point, not too little footage. At every cut, the eye, the ear, or an action needs somewhere to land.
en.html:
Home/Post/Cut Points: Action, Eye Line, Sound

Post / Editing

Cut Points: Action, Eye Line, Sound

A scene that will not cut usually has the wrong cut point, not too little footage. At every cut, the eye, the ear, or an action needs somewhere to land.

3 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 03Edited 2026-11

A scene that will not cut usually has the wrong cut point, not too little footage.

Cut on action: move through the seam

Cut while the hand is reaching, the door is half open, the body is mid-turn. The action covers the seam. The eye is following the hand and does not notice the frame changed.

Do not wait for the action to finish. Once it stops, the cut lands with a thud. Put the cut while motion is still running, and start the next shot in the second half of the same action. The viewer reads one continuous move.

Action cuts are the most reliable and the cheapest. If there is no action, make one: set the cup down, pull the door open, turn the page. A hand with a job gives the cut somewhere to hide.

Cut on eye line: let the viewer follow the look

A looks offscreen; cut to B’s reaction. The viewer follows the gaze. This is not an editing trick; it is the order in which people look: first who is looking, then what they see.

Match the direction. If A looks frame right, B should look back from frame left. Reverse it and the two stop sharing a room. Most axis problems show up here.

Do not cut while the viewer is still searching. If the previous shot has no landing point, give it one: the photo on the table, the person in the doorway, the phone in hand. Once the eye has a target, the cut holds.

Cut on sound: let the next line arrive early

Bring the next scene’s sound in before its picture: a J-cut. Let the previous scene’s sound run into the new one: an L-cut. Sound is freer than picture. It covers the jump and builds the next place early.

Sound cuts matter most in dialogue. The last line is still running when the next face appears, and the viewer does not feel the jump because the ear is still following the line. Do not bury it under music; the moment the music swells, the audience knows you are hiding.

A cut point is not a frame number; it is a handoff of attention. Ask at every cut: what is the viewer watching, hearing, or waiting for? One answer and the cut holds. No answer, and the perfect frame will not save it.

Checks

  • You can name the action, eye line, or sound carrying each cut.
  • Action cuts land mid-motion, not after the action stops.
  • Sound bridges do not step on dialogue or hide under music.

en.title: Call Sheet: One Page, One Plan
en.summary: A call sheet is not paperwork. It decides who arrives when, where, with what, and whom to call. If it is vague, the set fills with phone calls and the day slows down.
en.meta: 3 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Beginner
en.html:
Home/Tools/Call Sheet: One Page, One Plan

Tools / Producing

Call Sheet: One Page, One Plan

A call sheet is not paperwork. It decides who arrives when, where, with what, and whom to call. If it is vague, the set fills with phone calls and the day slows down.

3 min quick read + 7 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11DEEP / 7 MIN

A call sheet is not a form for the producer. It is the one version the whole crew shares on the day: who arrives when, where, with what, and whom to call when something goes wrong.

The first line is call time, not roll time

Call time and roll time are different. Call is when people arrive, eat, and change. Roll is when the first frame turns over. Put both at the same time and someone will be late, while someone else stands around.

Write an address that navigation can find. “The noodle place in the old town” is not an address. Add the entrance, parking, the freight elevator, and which door to use. A driver or a first-timer should be able to arrive from the first line alone.

Put a mobile number for the on-site contact, not “ask in the group chat.” Add the weather and the backup plan: move inside if it rains, or push the day. The worst thing on a shoot is not rain; it is the whole crew waiting for one person to decide.

Schedule by the hour, not by department

Do not write “interiors in the morning, exteriors after lunch.” Every department will prepare against a different idea of that. Write times: 6:30 call, 7:00 lighting, 8:00 first take, 12:30 lunch, 13:30 move.

After each slot, name who does what and what they need. “7:00 camera enters the kitchen, set the window light; sound measures the fridge hum; art swaps the bill on the table for version two.” One line and three departments know their next move.

Leave buffers. Moving, card offloads, makeup, waiting for light all take time. A full day breaks at the first delay.

Keep changes on paper

Number the version and date it. When V1 changes, say “read V2” in the group; do not let people guess which one is live. Mark on-set changes with a highlighter, and send the next day’s sheet before wrap.

Verbal updates disappear in the wind. A changed time, a new location, an extra wardrobe piece: put it back on the page. The set is already loud; do not add memory work.

The sheet does not need to be beautiful. It needs to be executable. One clear A4 beats a polished shared doc nobody can find on the day.

Checks

  • The first line has call time, a navigable address, and an on-site phone number.
  • The schedule runs by the hour, with who does what in each slot.
  • Version, date, and changes are marked, and the next sheet goes out before wrap.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. A call sheet is not a table for the producer. It is how the whole crew believes the same thing on the same morning: when, where, what.

The call sheet is the day's single source of truth

The most expensive thing on set is not gear; it is fifteen people each believing a different plan. A call sheet must have one version: the filename carries the date and version number, and you confirm everyone received the same one. “Check the latest” in a group chat means nothing; everyone's “latest” differs.

Also state the release time: first version at noon the day before, confirmed version before wrap for the next day. For changes, start with “V2 replaces V1” and do not bury the change in chat history. The sheet does not need to be beautiful, but the call time, address, and contact must be findable at a glance on a phone.

Six fields, one time block per row

The minimum executable call sheet has six columns: time, scene, cast and props, owner, contact, notes. Each row is a time block, not a department block such as “camera” or “sound.” Department blocks let each group prepare by its own reading; time blocks align everyone.

Example: 07:30 meet at the river, 08:00 first wide, 09:30 close-up, 11:00 move to the cafe, 12:30 lunch. Put an owner and a phone number on each row; never “ask in the group.” Who opens the door, who handles parking, who brings the permit copy: all in notes, not in someone's head.

Write an address people can navigate to, not a city

“The noodle place in the old town” is not an address. Write the street number, entrance, floor, freight elevator, which door opens, where to park, the nearest subway exit. A first-timer should arrive from this row alone; the driver should not need to call for directions.

Add four location facts: nearest toilet, route to the nearest hospital, where to buy water, whether there is signal at the set. They look trivial, but each saves ten minutes at the worst moment. The address is not for the producer; it is for the person who left at five in the morning and has never been there.

Put the time budget in the sheet

Do not write “morning: exteriors.” Write call, lighting, roll, first shot, move, lunch, wrap; leave fifteen to thirty minutes of buffer after each stage. Moves, card changes, makeup, and waiting for light all take time. A packed schedule fails at the first item.

Work backward from sunset: the last exterior must be done forty minutes before sunset, leaving time for pickups and gear. Do not start looking for a restaurant at 12:30; state who buys lunch, when it arrives, where people eat. A schedule is not a wish; it is a budget. If it overruns, cut shots, not safety.

Change control: verbal notes disappear

On-set changes have only three legitimate forms: highlight it on paper, post “V2 replaces V1” in the group, or send the confirmed next-day version before wrap. Saying “we move to three” does not count; someone did not hear, and someone heard two.

Every change states three things: what changed, why, and who is affected. A location change means resending the address and parking; a time change means reworking lunch and transport; a shot change means confirming props and cast are still there. A change is not a message; it is a realignment.

The next version after wrap

Spend ten minutes before wrap writing the “as-built” version: which shot overran, which one was skipped, what is first tomorrow, who needs to arrive early. Write actual times back into the sheet; tomorrow's schedule needs evidence. Do not re-plan from memory; memory keeps only the smoothest or the worst part.

The call sheet is not finished when it is sent. It is finished when it is useful after wrap. Tomorrow's version carries today's lesson: if lighting always overruns, move lighting earlier; if the move always hits traffic, change the meeting point. A sheet is worth it when the same mistake happens only once.

Ten call-sheet checks

  • Filename has date and version
  • Call time separate from roll time
  • Each row is a time block
  • Six columns complete: time, scene, cast, owner, phone, notes
  • Address includes street number and entrance
  • Parking, toilet, hospital stated
  • Buffer after every stage
  • Exteriors scheduled backward from sunset
  • Change states what, why, who
  • Next-day confirmed version sent before wrap

If the call sheet is unclear, the set spends phone-call time making decisions that ten minutes of writing could have settled.

DEEP DIVE / 07 MIN

en.title: Talking Head: Write for the Ear
en.summary: A talking-head piece is not an article read aloud. The viewer cannot hear punctuation, only meaning. Keep sentences short, turn early, use concrete examples; if it cannot be said in one breath, split it.
en.meta: 3 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Beginner
en.html:
Home/Formats/Talking Head: Write for the Ear

Format / Talking Head

Talking Head: Write for the Ear

A talking-head piece is not an article read aloud. The viewer cannot hear punctuation, only meaning. Keep sentences short, turn early, use concrete examples; if it cannot be said in one breath, split it.

3 min quick read + 6 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11DEEP / 6 MIN

A talking-head piece is not an article read aloud. The viewer cannot see punctuation or paragraphs, only whether a sentence lands.

Write sentences you can say

Cut “therefore,” “in conclusion,” and “it is worth noting.” They connect paragraphs on paper and tie the tongue on camera. One sentence does one job: give the point, give the example, make the turn. Finish one, then start the next.

Lead with the conclusion, not the background. The viewer is scrolling; if the first three seconds do not answer “what is this to me,” they are gone. The conclusion can be rough, but it must be clear: “The problem with talking heads is not your accent; it is your sentence length.”

Say “you,” not “the user.” “The user should note” belongs in a report. “You need to watch this” puts someone across the table. The distance closes in one word.

Land something every thirty seconds

With no pictures to help, attention rides on information. Every twenty or thirty seconds, give something concrete: an example, a number, a question, a scene the viewer can see. Three abstract nouns in a row and the ear goes numb.

Keep examples small. Not “many people struggle when shooting,” but “you shoot in the living room, turn off the lamp, and your face goes black.” Small enough that the viewer sees themselves, and the line lands.

Turn early. Do not spend forty seconds setting up a “but.” Put the turn in the first ten seconds, then use the rest to explain why. The rhythm is not steady; it comes in blocks, and each block stops before the next.

The body is also dialogue

Do not memorize a word-for-word script. Memorized eyes look up, the mouth outruns the brain, and it sounds like reading. Compress the script to three keyword cards: opening, example, close. The middle comes out the way you talk to a friend.

Look at the lens, not the screen. The lens is the person’s eye; the screen is your own face. Looking into the lens takes ten tries to feel natural. Looking at the screen makes the viewer think you are talking to someone else.

Keep your hands visible. Rest them on the table, at chest height, or at your sides; do not hide them under the desk. When you say “this big” or “this long,” your hands do the talking. If you flub a line, stop for one second and say it again. Do not fill with “um”; the filler cannot be cut.

Checks

  • Every sentence can be said in one breath, with no written connectives.
  • Something concrete lands every thirty seconds.
  • The cards hold keywords, not a script; the eyes stay on the lens.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Talking head is not reading a script smoothly. It is giving the viewer something new every ten seconds.

Write for the ear first

Write for the ear: clear subject, verb, object; one idea per sentence. Put numbers, examples, and action words first; adjectives and backstory later. The viewer needs something new every ten seconds, or the thumb moves.

Open with a judgment or a conflict in the first three seconds. No self-introduction, no “today I want to talk about.” Put the most counterintuitive line first, then support it with three reasons.

Three shot types keep attention

The main shot is a half-body at eye level, with hands in frame. When you give a concrete example, cut to hands, product, screen, or the room. Use jump cuts to remove pauses, not every two seconds.

Change the information form every twenty to thirty seconds: talking head, insert, screen recording, empty frame. Cuts should follow the sentence, not decorate it. Keep subtitles to two lines; clarity beats bold keywords.

Record one complete take, then add proof

Record one complete take first and make sure the logic holds. Then add examples, a counterexample, and a closing question. Do not polish wording before the structure exists, or you will never finish take one.

Before delivery, watch on a phone: is there a conclusion in three seconds, new information every ten, and a real question at the end? Put one short line on the cover, not three.

Five-minute drill: one point only

Record sixty seconds on your phone with one judgment and three examples. No self-introduction, no backstory. Delete every “I think,” “actually,” and “you know,” then cut the first polite sentence.

Watch on a phone: conclusion in three seconds, new information every ten, a question at the end. If one is missing, record again. Do not fix it with subtitles.

Ten talking-head checks

  • Judgment or conflict in three seconds
  • One idea per sentence
  • Something new every ten seconds
  • At least three concrete examples or numbers
  • Eye-level half-body as the main shot
  • Hands or product visible
  • Change form every twenty to thirty seconds
  • Jump cuts remove pauses only
  • Two subtitle lines max
  • A real question at the end

Talking head is not reading. It is cutting one argument into pieces the viewer can swallow.

en.title: Character Arc: Not Better, Different Choices
en.summary: An arc is not a character turning good. Under the same pressure, they first choose safety and finally choose the cost. The audience sees the choice change, not a new personality label.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Character Arc: Not Better, Different Choices

Story / Character

Character Arc: Not Better, Different Choices

An arc is not a character turning good. Under the same pressure, they first choose safety and finally choose the cost. The audience sees the choice change, not a new personality label.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 01Edited 2026-11

A character arc is not “she became braver.” It is the same pressure returning, and she makes a different choice, then pays for it.

Give the character a default reaction

When pressure arrives, what do they do first: run, please, control, go silent, make a joke. That is the starting point. You do not need a biography; write three scenes with the same kind of pressure and show how they respond each time.

The first time, let them use the familiar move, even if it makes things worse. The audience has to know the old habit before the change can mean anything.

Do not move the arc with adjectives. Not “she gradually becomes steady,” but she stops in the doorway, pushes the suitcase back inside, apologizes for the first time or refuses to. When the action changes, the person changes.

The middle has to fail once

Change is not one decision. At the midpoint, let them try the new choice, fail, and fall back into the old habit. That is what makes the audience believe it.

Example: she speaks up in a meeting for the first time and is shut down in front of everyone. In the next scene, she is quiet again. The retreat is not repetition; it shows how heavy the old habit is.

An arc is not a straight line. It steps back before it steps forward. Without the failure, the final choice feels like a prize from the writer, not something the character earned.

The final choice has to cost

When they choose the new road, they must lose something old: safety, a relationship, face, a job. Do not give them a speech, and do not let others praise how much they have changed. Settle it with an action: leave the key, push the contract back, carry the suitcase inside, sign the name.

The audience reads the change from the cost, not the line. The more concrete the cost, the more believable the arc.

Checks

  • The character has a default reaction that can repeat.
  • The change fails once at the midpoint, and the old habit returns.
  • The final choice costs something visible, without a speech explaining it.

en.title: Camera Height: Lower Before You Change Lenses
en.summary: The same face at one inch lower reads as a different person. Height sets the power relationship before the shot size; a new lens cannot fix standing in the wrong place.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Camera Height: Lower Before You Change Lenses

Shoot / Camera

Camera Height: Lower Before You Change Lenses

The same face at one inch lower reads as a different person. Height sets the power relationship before the shot size; a new lens cannot fix standing in the wrong place.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 02Edited 2026-11

The same face, one inch lower, reads as a different person. Height sets the relationship before it sets the shot size. A new lens cannot fix standing in the wrong place.

High presses down, low lifts up

Camera above the subject's eyes: the person gets smaller, floor fills the frame, and the audience reads them as passive or watched. Camera below: the person gets bigger, ceiling enters the frame, and they seem to press forward.

This is not “the cooler the better.” Use one clear high or low angle in a scene, and the change means something. Stay low the whole time and the audience just gets tired.

Start at eye level, then decide to move

Dialogue defaults to level. If the subject sits, put the camera at their eye height. Do not stand and shoot down at them unless you want the scene to feel like an interrogation.

The most common phone mistake is standing with the phone at your chest, pointing down. Squat until the lens is at the other person's eyes. Their face changes at once. A small tripod and a stack of books is cheaper than a new lens.

Height follows action

When power shifts, lower the camera: he stands, the lens goes low; she sits, the lens comes back to level. If height follows the body, the audience feels the relationship change without naming it.

Do not stay low for the whole film to look “cinematic.” Height is a sentence, not an accent. One per scene.

Checks

  • Is the default height level, or is the high/low angle a deliberate choice?
  • For a seated interview, is the lens also seated at eye height?
  • Does the height change land on a stand, sit, step in, or step back?

en.title: Mixing: Land the Dialogue Before the Music
en.summary: The audience can ignore the music; they cannot afford to miss the line. Level the dialogue first, then push the music down. Music is background, not a cover-up.
en.html:
Home/Post/Mixing: Land the Dialogue Before the Music

Post / Sound

Mixing: Land the Dialogue Before the Music

The audience can ignore the music; they cannot afford to miss the line. Level the dialogue first, then push the music down. Music is background, not a cover-up.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 03Edited 2026-11

The audience can ignore the music. They cannot afford to miss the line. Level the dialogue first, then push the music down. Music is background, not a cover-up.

Level the dialogue first

Listen line by line. Remove pops, mouth noise, and obvious room tone; match every take and every microphone to the same level. Do not ride one master track: pull it up for the quiet line and the next line will blow out.

Play the dialogue track alone, without picture. Listen for clarity, not beauty. Mark every word you cannot hear and fix it in the cut or with an alternate take.

Make music give way

Duck music 6–10 dB under dialogue. Do not start at full and stay there. Use sidechain or manual keyframes: drop when the line enters, come back when it leaves.

Music should enter for a reason: an action, a turn, a scene change, a jump in time. Do not lay it under everything or the audience hears “this is the part where I should feel something” before they hear the story.

Silence is part of the mix

Not every minute needs music. Leave half a second of quiet before or after an important line so it can land. Keep room tone underneath; do not create a vacuum. A fridge hum or distant traffic is more real than total silence.

At the end, let the music leave before the picture does. The last bit of quiet is what people remember.

Checks

  • Every line is clear without relying on subtitles.
  • Music clearly gives way under dialogue, not just turned down once.
  • There is at least one deliberate pause that is not filled with music.

en.title: Budget: Four Buckets, One Decision
en.summary: A budget is not a column of numbers. It is four buckets: what must be paid, what will be seen, what can be swapped, and what will blow up. Keep the film shootable before you make it pretty.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Budget: Four Buckets, One Decision

Producing / Budget

Budget: Four Buckets, One Decision

A budget is not a column of numbers. It is four buckets: what must be paid, what will be seen, what can be swapped, and what will blow up. Keep the film shootable before you make it pretty.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11

A budget is not a column of numbers. It is four buckets. Keep the film shootable before you make it pretty.

Four buckets: must-pay, on-screen, swappable, buffer

Must-pay: people, location, insurance, meals, transport. If this stops, the shoot stops. On-screen: art, wardrobe, gear, props. What the audience actually sees. Swappable: what can be borrowed, rented, simplified, or cut. Buffer: 10–15%, and do not touch it.

Set the proportions before you fill in the details. Do not start with “what I want to buy.” Start with “which bucket cannot stop.”

Spend inside the frame and inside the ear

The audience will not notice the extra assistant. They will notice the lead's coat and hear the dialogue. Protect what is on screen and what is in the ear. A great location beats expensive gear; a good microphone in a quiet room beats a fancy one in a bad room.

If it can be borrowed, write borrowed. If it can be rented, write rented. If it is yours, write yours. A zero still needs a reason, or it becomes a new cost on set.

Every line gets a fallback

Add a “cheaper option” column to every expense: borrow, rent, reduce, replace, cut. Update the sheet as reality changes, one change at a time, and leave the buffer alone. Reconcile at wrap each day, not after the money is gone.

A budget is not for the accountant. It is for the decisions on set. Write down which line can be cut on the day and which line stops the shoot if cut.

Checks

  • The four buckets have proportions, and the buffer has not been raided.
  • Every line has a cheaper option, not just a total.
  • Actuals are updated daily, so overspend is visible before it happens.

en.title: Focal Length: Decide How Close the Audience Stands
en.summary: Wide is not “fit everything in,” and long is not “shoot far away.” Focal length decides how close the audience stands before it decides how the face and background stack. Walk the scene first, then change the lens.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Focal Length: Decide How Close the Audience Stands

Shoot / Lens

Focal Length: Decide How Close the Audience Stands

Wide is not “fit everything in,” and long is not “shoot far away.” Focal length decides how close the audience stands before it decides how the face and background stack. Walk the scene first, then change the lens.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 02Edited 2026-11

Focal length is not “wide” versus “far.” It first decides where the audience stands to look at the person, then how the face and background stack.

Wide opens the room and pushes the person away

A wide lens fits the whole room and pulls foreground and background apart. Put it close to a face and the nose grows, the background drops back, and the viewer feels shoved in front of the subject. It is right for corridors, cars, tight rooms, or making two people look far apart.

Do not open the zoom to its widest just to “get it all in.” Ask first: in this room, does the audience stand at the door or sit at the table? At the door, go wide. At the table, step back and use something longer.

Long presses the person into the background

A long lens pulls the far thing closer and flattens the person against the background. The subject floats out of the room. It is right for watching, for looking without being seen, for finding one face in a crowd. The viewer stands across the street, not disturbing anything, but seeing clearly.

Press too hard and the space becomes a sheet of paper; the viewer no longer knows where anyone is. Keep a piece of foreground: a railing, a shoulder, leaves. Let them know what they are standing behind.

Pick the distance before the lens

If you can move, move. Two steps forward or one step back is cheaper than a lens and faster. Zoom is a compromise: the wall, the crowd, or the clock has blocked the position.

Do not change focal length in a scene just to make it “rich.” Wide establishes the relationship; long delivers a judgment. Between the two, the audience's position has to make sense.

Checks

  • When the wide lens is close to a face, is the distortion what you want?
  • Has the long lens flattened the space into paper? Does the viewer still know where the person is?
  • Before changing lenses, did you try the position your feet can reach?

en.title: Stripboard: Turn the Script into Shootable Days
en.summary: Scheduling is not filling the calendar in script order. Break the script into strips by location and cast, then group them into days: one company move, one actor call. The schedule protects the performance, not just the progress.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Stripboard: Turn the Script into Shootable Days

Producing / Schedule

Stripboard: Turn the Script into Shootable Days

Scheduling is not filling the calendar in script order. Break the script into strips by location and cast, then group them into days: one company move, one actor call. The schedule protects the performance, not just the progress.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11

Scheduling is not filling the calendar in script order. Break the script into strips, then group them. One company move a day, one actor call. The schedule protects the performance, not just the progress.

Strip first, dates later

One strip per scene: location, day or night, cast, page count, props, special needs. Color every strip at the same location the same color; put strips that share an actor next to each other. Do this before dates and you will see “three company moves today” before noon, not after.

Write the reason a scene cannot move: daylight, shop hours, actor availability, a special prop. If you cannot name the reason, it can move.

Group by location and cast

Keep one location per day when you can. A company move is not ten minutes; it is unloading, parking, relighting, waiting for keys. Half a day is gone. If an actor is available for one day only, put all their scenes on that day, even if the script separates them by ten pages.

Do not force day and night into the same day. Switching to night means waiting for the sun while the whole crew costs money. Better to add a shoot day than ask an actor to play a clear-headed scene at three in the morning.

Start easy, end with the shot you need

Put the simplest scene on day one and let the crew find its rhythm. Start each day with a shot that can stand alone; end with the shot you must have. If weather turns, shoot interiors first, then go outside.

The board is not a contract. It is the thing you make decisions against. When it changes, write the change on the call sheet; do not leave it in a group chat.

Checks

  • Every strip carries location, day or night, cast, pages, and special needs.
  • Does the day hold one location where possible, and one actor call?
  • Does each day have an easy start and a must-get ending?

en.title: Room Tone: Do Not Let the Picture Live in a Vacuum
en.summary: The room's sound is not noise; it is the space. In every location, record thirty seconds of nothing: no voices, no movement, just the room. When the dialogue stops, room tone takes over, and the cut stops sounding like a cut.
en.html:
Home/Post/Room Tone: Do Not Let the Picture Live in a Vacuum

Post / Sound

Room Tone: Do Not Let the Picture Live in a Vacuum

The room's sound is not noise; it is the space. In every location, record thirty seconds of nothing: no voices, no movement, just the room. When the dialogue stops, room tone takes over, and the cut stops sounding like a cut.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 03Edited 2026-11

The room's sound is not noise; it is the space. In every location, record thirty seconds of nothing: no voices, no movement, just the room. When the dialogue stops, room tone takes over, and the cut stops sounding like a cut.

Thirty seconds in every space

Before recording, ask everyone to stop: no walking, no paper, no light adjustments. Put the microphone where the dialogue mic was and roll thirty seconds. Name the file with location and date, something like “kitchen_1120_room.” In the edit, those thirty seconds are worth more than a cue.

If the room has a fridge, an AC, or a fluorescent hum, record one pass normal and one with them off. Do not quietly kill the room on the day. The silence the audience hears still contains those sounds.

Room tone is the glue

When dialogue drops between two shots, room tone fills the hole and the ear stops hearing a gap. It does not need to be loud; it needs to be there. A low bed of room under the line goes unnoticed until it is removed, and then everything sounds fake.

Match the tone to the space. A living room and a hallway are two different rooms; one generic bed cannot run under the whole film. Across a cut, the room tone has to continue, or the sound jumps before the picture does.

Do not cover a dead room with music

If the room sounds wrong, fix the room: close the window, turn off the fridge, lower the AC, move the table. Music cannot cover a dead room; it only tells the audience “do not notice this.”

Music is allowed, but room tone is the floor. Lay the room first, then add music. Reverse the order and post becomes a permanent hole-patching job.

Checks

  • Every location has thirty seconds of room tone, findable by filename?
  • Does room tone run continuously under the cuts without jumping?
  • Was the dead room fixed, or covered with music?

en.title: Transitions: Mark Time, Do Not Hide It
en.summary: A dissolve, a fade, a wipe is not decoration. Every transition answers: how long, where, and who is still here. If it cannot answer, hard cut.
en.html:
Home/Post/Transitions: Mark Time, Do Not Hide It

Post / Editing

Transitions: Mark Time, Do Not Hide It

A dissolve, a fade, a wipe is not decoration. Every transition answers: how long, where, and who is still here. If it cannot answer, hard cut.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 03Edited 2026-11

A dissolve, a fade, a wipe is not decoration. Every transition answers three questions: how long, where, and who is still here. If it cannot answer, hard cut.

Hard cut is the default

Time and place continue: cut. The audience does not need to be told “this is another shot.” A hard cut is the fastest and least distracting. Most films should be ninety percent hard cuts.

Do not use a fancy transition to cover a scene you failed to shoot clearly. The audience sees a dissolve and does not think time passed; they think “something is being hidden.”

Dissolve only when time stretches

A dissolve says time has passed, places have merged, a state has changed. The two images need to share composition, action, or color, or it reads as an accident. If the person sits in the same place and the light goes from day to dusk, the dissolve holds.

Do not dissolve between every scene. The first one tells the audience years passed; the third one starts a slideshow. One or two in a short film is enough.

Sound can cross first

The picture is still in the old room, but the sound has entered the new one: a doorbell, traffic, the next scene's dialogue. The audience hears the new space before seeing it, and the transition softens.

The reverse works too: the picture has cut to the new scene while the old room's sound stays half a second. One sound stitches two spaces together, cheaper than an effect and more believable.

Checks

  • Does this transition answer “how long, where”?
  • If it were a hard cut, would the audience misunderstand? If not, cut.
  • Do the two images share composition, action, or sound?

en.title: Shot Size: Decide How Much the Audience Sees
en.summary: Shot size is not a vocabulary list of wide, medium, and close. It sets the distance between the audience and the person: do they see where he stands, or only an eye? Ask what this cut needs before moving the camera back.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Shot Size: Decide How Much the Audience Sees

Shoot / Shot Size

Shot Size: Decide How Much the Audience Sees

Shot size is not a vocabulary list of wide, medium, and close. It sets the distance between the audience and the person: do they see where he stands, or only an eye? Ask what this cut needs before moving the camera back.

2 min read · BeginnerTVCN / 02Edited 2026-11

Wide: show where he is

In a wide shot the person is small and the place is large. The audience sees the door, the road, the wall, the awning, then the person. It is not a landscape photograph; it describes the relationship between a person and a situation: how big the place is, how far the exit, whether anyone else is near.

If the person is too small to recognize, the audience sees only a place, not a person. A wide shot can open or close a scene, but three wides in a row and the viewer loses a handhold.

Full and medium: action and relationship

A full shot shows the whole body: what he is doing, where he stands, how far he is from the next person. A medium shot cuts at the waist, so the hands can still work and the face still reads. For dialogue, medium is the workhorse: both people are in frame, and a step forward is visible.

Do not stay in medium for the sake of “cinematic.” The audience forgets the room and where the character came from. Medium is a working size, not a default aesthetic.

Close and detail: one piece of information

A close shot cuts at the chest; the face starts to matter. A close-up on the face, an eye, or a hand leaves one piece of information. It is a promise: something will happen next. Do not spend a close-up on a throwaway line, and do not ask the viewer to watch the eyes, the background, and the subtitle at once.

Do not change size just for variety. Too many jumps in one scene and the viewer tires. Hold one main size to establish the relationship, then change once on the action that matters.

Checks

  • Does this size show the one thing this cut needs?
  • In the wide, is the person still recognizable? In the medium, does the room still exist?
  • After the close-up, does something happen that deserves the size?

en.title: Casting: Can They Stand in the Room Before They Can Act?
en.summary: Casting is not finding the best actor. It is finding the person who fits this relationship. Check whether the look and voice hold, then whether two people have something between them, and only then the lines. Give an action in the audition, not a monologue.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Casting: Can They Stand in the Room Before They Can Act?

Producing / Casting

Casting: Can They Stand in the Room Before They Can Act?

Casting is not finding the best actor. It is finding the person who fits this relationship. Check whether the look and voice hold, then whether two people have something between them, and only then the lines. Give an action in the audition, not a monologue.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11

Write what they do, not what they are like

Before casting, turn the character into actions: when he wakes up, how he opens a door, where his hands go while he waits, where he looks when he lies. Do not write “gentle,” “repressed,” or “has a past.” An actor can only guess at adjectives.

Then list three things you cannot replace: voice, walk, and the way they look at people. A face can be dressed; a coat can be changed; those three are hard to swap. Age, stamina, accent, and the marks of a job: if one is wrong, the audience leaves the room on the first look.

Audition: give an action, not a monologue

Ask the actor to do one concrete thing: wait for someone, open a door, hide an object, push a cup away. The line is part of the action, not the whole performance. Watch how they breathe inside it, where they pause, how they avoid the lens.

Do not ask for “sad.” Ask them to hold back something they need to say; the audience will fill it in. Record the audition. On playback, mute it and watch whether they are waiting or performing waiting.

Two people in a room make a relationship

Being good alone does not count. Put two actors across from each other and watch height, tempo, who blinks first, who listens while the other talks. If each is good and nothing happens between them, cast someone else.

Do not only read the most heated scene. Read a meal, a search for keys, a call where neither wants to hang up first. Ordinary scenes reveal whether they are family, coworkers, or ex-lovers.

Availability and backup matter as much as the performance

Confirm how many days they can work, whether they can stay late, and whether they have stage or camera experience. If one actor cannot come, the whole schedule moves; keep a backup for every lead.

After you cast, send the character notes, script, and shoot dates together. Do not send “you got it” and let them arrive on set without knowing the part.

Checks

  • Is the character note built from actions, not adjectives?
  • Did the audition give an action rather than a monologue?
  • With two actors in the room, does something happen between them?
  • Are availability, backup, and character materials written down?
