en.title: Voice-Over: Do Not Summarize What the Picture Already Says
en.summary: Voice-over is not the picture read aloud. It either gives information the picture cannot, or gives one person's judgment. If you can shoot it, do not say it. If you must say it, keep it short, concrete, and biased.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Voice-Over: Do Not Summarize What the Picture Already Says

Story / Voice-Over

Voice-Over: Do Not Summarize What the Picture Already Says

Voice-over is not the picture read aloud. It either gives information the picture cannot, or gives one person's judgment. If you can shoot it, do not say it. If you must say it, keep it short, concrete, and biased.

2 min read · IntermediateTVCN / 01Edited 2026-11

Three kinds of voice-over, three jobs

Expository VO gives context: the time, the place, how one event led to the next. First-person VO gives bias: how this person sees others, how they fool themselves. Inner VO gives the line the character cannot say out loud.

You can mix all three, but know who is speaking. If the last line was the author explaining the world and the next is the character's private complaint, the audience does not know which ear to trust.

Write for the ear, not the eye

Short sentences. Concrete nouns. Few adjectives. Do not write “we can see” or “the next thing that happens”; the audience can see it. Each line does one job: a fact or a judgment.

Read it aloud and listen for where the tongue trips. The problem is the sentence, not the voice. Delete the first line and the last line; what remains is often the real text.

When to shut up

If the picture already says it, do not repeat it. The character pushes the door open; the audience knows he is leaving. Do not say “he decides to leave.” Let the action happen. Leave half a second before the VO enters and half a second after it leaves.

Do not name the emotion. Do not say “he regrets it.” Let him pause at the door; let his hand slide off the handle. VO supplies facts and bias. The face and the action supply the feeling.

Do not record it in a bedroom

Find a quiet room. Turn off the AC, the fridge, the window. Put the mic a fist away from the mouth, not against it. Record three passes: normal, lower, a little faster. Start with normal; do not begin with “voice-of-god.”

Keep the breath. Do not cut every pause flat. VO is not a commercial; it should sound like a person standing nearby.

Checks

  • Does this line add information the picture cannot, or repeat what is already there?
  • Whose voice is it: the author, the character, or the character's inner voice?
  • Read aloud, does it trip or sound like an essay?
  • Does the VO cover the action at its entrance or exit?

en.title: Delivery: Find the Wrong Export Before the Last Hour
en.summary: Delivery is not hitting export. Ask what the platform needs: ratio, resolution, frame rate, bitrate, color, channels, filename. Build a template you can repeat, then watch the file from start to finish.
en.meta: 3 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Beginner
en.html:
Home/Tools/Delivery: Find the Wrong Export Before the Last Hour

Tools / Delivery

Delivery: Find the Wrong Export Before the Last Hour

Delivery is not hitting export. Ask what the platform needs: ratio, resolution, frame rate, bitrate, color, channels, filename. Build a template you can repeat, then watch the file from start to finish.

3 min quick read + 7 min deep read · BeginnerTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11DEEP / 7 MIN

Get the spec before you export

Ask about four destinations: the platform, the client, a cinema or event, and your own archive. Each wants different things: ratio, resolution, frame rate, codec, bitrate, color, audio channels, subtitles, filename.

Write them into one sheet. Do not keep it in your head. Platform notes change; old tutorials do not remind you. If the client says “whatever,” write down a default and have them confirm it. Do not guess.

Picture: size, frame rate, bitrate

Deliver the resolution you shot, not a 1080p file forced into 4K. Keep one frame rate for the whole film; 23.976, 25, and 29.97 each have uses, but mixing them makes the opening stutter.

Favor compatibility: H.264 plays almost everywhere, H.265 is smaller but some older devices choke, ProRes is right for archive and regrading. Do not use the lowest bitrate. The platform will compress it again; give it too little and shadows and motion go first.

Color follows the destination. Most web platforms want Rec.709 SDR. Do not label an SDR grade as HDR. Check the scopes before export: are the blacks and whites crushed?

Sound and subtitles: do not let the ear take the blame

Use 48 kHz audio and the channel layout the platform asks for: stereo is the safe default; 5.1 only when someone explicitly needs it. Dialogue must be clear and music must not eat the words. Hit the platform's loudness target; if there is none, avoid clipping and avoid level jumps.

Subtitles come in two forms: burned-in and sidecar. Deliver the one they asked for, not both. For sidecar, check encoding, timing, and punctuation. For burned-in, check the safe area so the platform UI does not cover the words.

Play the file from start to finish

Do not trust the progress bar. Watch on a phone, on a computer, and on a TV if you can. Listen to the first ten seconds, the last ten, and every transition. Confirm sync, and confirm subtitles are neither early nor late.

Name the file with project, version, date, and resolution, like “project_v3_20261120_1080p.” Send a short note: which file is the master, which is the subtitle, which is the cover. Do not dump ten files into a zip and call it delivery.

Checks

  • Does the spec sheet list ratio, resolution, frame rate, codec, bitrate, color, audio, and subtitles?
  • Is the frame rate consistent, with no 1080p file forced into 4K?
  • Have you watched the whole file on a phone and a computer, with sync and subtitles correct?
  • Can the client find the master from the filename and delivery note?

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. Delivery is not exporting a file. It is making the film open on the right device, at the right spec, for the right person.

Ask where it goes before asking what spec

One film has four destinations: platform, client, cinema or event, and your archive. Each needs something different: the platform needs ratio, bitrate, subtitles; the client needs a downloadable master and cover; cinema needs a DCP or high-bitrate ProRes; the archive needs something you can grade again.

Do not make one file serve all four. Make a destination-spec-owner table, one row per destination. If the client says “whatever,” write your default spec and get confirmation. Confirmed text is more reliable than memory and cheaper than an argument later.

Seven specs, none guessed

Write all seven: ratio, resolution, frame rate, codec, bitrate, color, audio channels. Ratio includes the platform safe area, not just 16:9. Resolution matches what you shot and deliver; do not stretch 1080p into 4K. One frame rate for the whole film; mixed rates make the opening stutter.

Favor compatibility: H.264 is safest, H.265 is smaller but older devices may refuse it, ProRes is for archive and regrading. Do not use the lowest bitrate; the platform compresses again, and shadows and motion fail first. Color follows the target: most online platforms want Rec.709 SDR; do not label an SDR film as HDR.

Filenames and versions that survive three months

A filename states four things: project, version, date, spec. Example: “riverside_v3_20261120_1080p_zh-sub.” Never “final,” “final2,” “really final.” Version numbers only increase and do not need explanation. Master, subtitles, and covers share a prefix so they pair at a glance.

Name the folders too: 01_master, 02_subs, 03_covers, 04_vertical. The client does not need to understand your edit project, but must know what to open first. The filename is not for you; it is for whoever inherits the project in three months, possibly the client, possibly you.

Sound and subtitles: do not make the ears pay for the picture

Use 48 kHz audio. Channels follow the platform: stereo is the safe default; 5.1 only when explicitly requested. Dialogue must be clear and music must not cover words. Hit the platform loudness target; if none, at least avoid clipping and level jumps. Before export, listen to the first ten seconds, the last ten, and every transition.

Subtitles are either burned in or sidecar; deliver the one requested, not both. For sidecar, check encoding, timing, and punctuation. For burned-in, check the safe area so platform UI does not cover them. Subtitles are not decoration; they are a second audio track that must tell the story when dialogue is unclear.

Before delivery, play it on three devices

Do not trust the progress bar. Play it on a phone, a computer, and a TV if possible. Check audio-video sync, subtitle lead or lag, crushed blacks, clipped highlights. Phone speakers expose unclear dialogue; a TV exposes compression blocks.

Write problems down: timecode, device, symptom. Fix what you can; document what you cannot. Delivery is not “the file is sent.” It is “what they see when they open it is what you saw.”

The delivery package and receipt

The package contains only what the recipient needs now: master, subtitles, covers, vertical cuts, and a readme. The readme states what each file is, which is the master, how to load subtitles, and the cover ratio. Do not include project files, raw footage, and old versions; that is moving house, not delivery.

Ask for a receipt: can they open it, is there sound, do subtitles match? No receipt means no delivery. A receipt is not politeness; it is the last acceptance step that turns “I thought” into “confirmed.”

Ten delivery checks

  • One row per destination
  • Ratio, resolution, frame rate stated
  • Codec and bitrate stated
  • Color labeled Rec.709 or HDR
  • Channels and loudness stated
  • Filename has project, version, date, spec
  • One subtitle type, not both
  • Played on phone, computer, TV
  • Package contains only what is needed now
  • Delivery is done only after a receipt

Delivery does not end when the file uploads. It ends when the other person opens it and sees the film you saw.

DEEP DIVE / 07 MIN

Go deeper: for people already shooting

Delivery is not exporting a file. It is making the film open on the right device, at the right spec, for the right person.

en.title: Blocking: Let the Body Tell the Story
en.summary: Blocking is not pretty placement; it makes relationships visible in space: who approaches, who retreats, who blocks whom.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Blocking: Let the Body Tell the Story

Shooting / Blocking

Blocking: Let the Body Tell the Story

Blocking is not pretty placement; it makes relationships visible in space: who approaches, who retreats, who blocks whom.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Tech DeskEdited 2026-11

Blocking is not pretty placement; it turns who approaches, who retreats and who blocks whom into visible information. Tape the door, chair and camera on the floor, then let one action carry the actor across that distance.

Make the relationship spatial

Shoot a wide and play it back: if the bodies alone tell you who holds power, the blocking works. If a line has to explain it, re-block.

Limits

Do not pose people into a poster. If the body does not move, the relationship does not move either.

On set

Tape the door, the chair, and the camera on the floor. Walk the actor from the door to the chair, stopping two seconds in front of the camera. Shoot one wide and check who blocks whom.

Do this

Mark the positions, move the actor through the space with one action, then check the relationship in a wide.

  1. Tape the door, chair, and camera positions on the floor.
  2. Walk the actor from the door to the chair, stopping two seconds in frame, without lines.
  3. Shoot a wide first and review who blocks whom and whether the distance reads.

Avoid

Do not pose people like a poster; a false body makes a false relationship.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. In the wide, you can see who approaches, who retreats, and who blocks whom without dialogue.
  • 2. The actor takes an action path, not a pose; start, turn, and end are visible in frame.
  • 3. A blocking diagram or phone video lets another person walk the same path.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“In the wide, you can see who approaches, who r…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The actor takes an action path, not a pose; st…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not pose people like a poster; a false body makes a false relationship.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Tape the door, chair, and camera positions on”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • In the wide, you can see who approaches, who retreats, and who blocks whom without dialogue.
  • The actor takes an action path, not a pose; start, turn, and end are visible in frame.
  • A blocking diagram or phone video lets another person walk the same path.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Blocking lets the body speak first and the camera record second. Put an actor in the wrong place and no lens can save it.

Block first, place the camera second

Walk the actors through the space without lines, only action. Tape the turn, the stop, the prop touch.

Find the camera from the blocking; do not lay track first and squeeze the actors into it. Track serves blocking that already works, it does not force performance.

Distance is relationship

Stand two people close and the audience feels intimacy or pressure; put a table between them and the relationship cools. Height speaks too: a low camera gives power, a high camera diminishes.

A doorframe, table edge, or corridor as foreground creates space better than a filter. Foreground is not decoration; it says “we are watching from outside.”

Change blocking and camera together

If blocking hides a face, change the lens or move the camera; do not ask the actor to twist. An uncomfortable body makes false dialogue.

Shoot a wide during rehearsal, play it back to see who is blocked and who leaves frame, then set the final camera. The wide is not for the film; it is a blocking check.

Draw a blocking diagram

Draw the room from above: doors, windows, tables, actor starts and ends. Arrows for direction, numbers for order.

The diagram need not be beautiful, only readable to script and camera. On the next setup, the diagram is more reliable than memory.

Blocking a group scene

In a group scene, assign roles: who decides, who resists, who only watches. Give each person an action instead of letting them stand and wait for lines.

Use triangular positions instead of a straight line. Shoot from one side and the foreground and background separate naturally.

Ten blocking checks

  • Walk the scene without lines first
  • Tape start, end, and turn points
  • Find the camera from blocking, do not lay track first
  • Distance matches the relationship
  • Height matches the power dynamic
  • Use a doorframe or table edge as foreground
  • Shoot a rehearsal wide and play it back
  • If blocked, change lens or move camera first
  • Keep one main blocking pattern per scene
  • Photograph the blocking diagram for the file

Blocking is not arranging actors to look nice; it lets space speak before the audience understands.

When you have five minutes

  • Walk it once without lines
  • Mark start, end, and turns
  • Test sitting and standing
  • Confirm the key light does not hide the face
  • Give every group actor one action
  • Photograph the blocking diagram

Right blocking gives dialogue a place to land; wrong blocking makes actors carry it with their faces.

en.title: Coverage: Do Not Shoot One Angle
en.summary: Coverage is not more takes; it gives the edit different information: wide, close, insert, reverse.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Coverage: Do Not Shoot One Angle

Shooting / Coverage

Coverage: Do Not Shoot One Angle

Coverage is not more takes; it gives the edit different information: wide, close, insert, reverse.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Tech DeskEdited 2026-11

Every scene needs at least three kinds of material: a safe master that explains the space, a reverse or over-the-shoulder, and two or three insertable action details. The edit uses them to change pace, hide cheats and rescue performance.

Coverage gives the edit choices

Before the shoot, list coverage as master–reverse–insert, and write what must be captured to pass. Do not shoot whatever looks interesting on the day.

Limits

More angles do not equal an editable scene. Every angle must share the same action line; if the actor does something different in each take, more coverage makes the cut harder.

On set

Shoot four pieces of one scene: a wide for space, a medium for relationships, a close for reaction, and a hand insert for information. Get at least two takes of each and play them in order on the monitor.

Do this

Coverage is not shooting one angle ten times; it gives the edit different information: a wide for space, a medium for relationship, a close-up for reaction, an insert for detail.

  1. Shoot a wide that explains the whole scene, at least two takes.
  2. Add medium, close-up, and hand inserts, at least two takes per size.
  3. Shoot reverse angles and transitions, then review in order to confirm every beat has an alternative.

Avoid

Do not shoot the whole scene in one size; that is repetition, not coverage.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Wide, medium, close-up, and insert all have at least one usable take.
  • 2. The hand or prop insert carries a story beat without voice-over.
  • 3. Every information beat has two usable sizes on the timeline; a missing one triggers a pickup.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Wide, medium, close-up, and insert all have at…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The hand or prop insert carries a story beat w…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not shoot the whole scene in one size; that is repetition, not coverage.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Shoot a wide that explains the whole scene,”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • Wide, medium, close-up, and insert all have at least one usable take.
  • The hand or prop insert carries a story beat without voice-over.
  • Every information beat has two usable sizes on the timeline; a missing one triggers a pickup.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Coverage is not shooting every angle. It is giving the edit a choice at the decisive moment. Miss the reverse and the scene becomes a radio play.

Protect the full action, then add angles

Let the master cover the scene from entrance to sitting. The emotional floor is there; every other angle is lifted out of it.

If there is time for only two passes, protect the master and the reverse. A reverse is not the whole shot-reverse-shot, but without it dialogue can only cut one way.

Four shot sizes, four jobs

A wide establishes space and relationships, a medium protects performance, a close protects emotion, an insert protects the cut. Get at least two of each so panic has an alternative.

Do not use movement as coverage. Movement looks good but leaves no still point; the audience tires and the editor has nowhere to cut.

When you can shoot less

A ten-second short does not need eight angles. One main view, one detail, one reverse is enough to land a single idea.

Long dialogue needs reverses and reactions. Ask who the scene wants the audience to watch, then assign cameras; not every character needs equal coverage.

Coverage has a priority order

With limited time and money, the order is full master, reverse, key insert, atmosphere. The first three protect the story; the last protects texture.

Do not shoot beauty plates first. A beautiful plate that cannot cut into dialogue is wasted; a missing master leaves the scene broken.

The cost of one missing angle

On set you think “we will pick it up later,” but later the wardrobe changed, the light moved, the set is gone. A pickup costs three times a set shot.

Go through the sheet before wrap and get the missing reverse and insert now. Half an hour late is better than a reshoot three months later.

Ten checks after coverage

  • Master covers the whole action
  • Every group has wide, medium, close, insert
  • At least two takes per angle
  • Reverse and reaction shots listed separately
  • Movement did not replace coverage
  • Check whether actors are blocked by foreground
  • Log actual takes per shot
  • Pick up missing inserts before wrap
  • Photograph the sheet and send it to edit
  • Confirm backup before formatting cards

Coverage is not shooting more; it is shooting complete. The take the edit needs is often one angle you skipped.

en.title: Treatment: Make the Film Visible on Paper
en.summary: A treatment does not decorate a script; it lets the client see the film's shape, tone, and limits before the shoot.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Treatment: Make the Film Visible on Paper

Tools / Treatment

Treatment: Make the Film Visible on Paper

A treatment does not decorate a script; it lets the client see the film's shape, tone, and limits before the shoot.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

One page: who the audience follows, what blocks them, and what change is visible at the end. No shot list, no director's statement; those belong to later steps.

A one-page treatment answers three questions

One page: who the audience follows, what blocks them, and what change is visible at the end. No shot list, no director's statement; those belong to later steps.

Write in the present tense, one action per paragraph. The treatment passes when the client can retell the story after one page.

Limits

A treatment is not literature. More adjectives leave the client less certain of what you will shoot; replace “warm” and “premium” with visible places and actions.

On set

Use twelve pages: one sentence, three reference frames, the shooting plan, and delivery limits. One idea per page so the client can see the film.

Do this

A treatment is not a script rewritten in fancy words; it lets the client see the film's look, tone, and boundary before the shoot.

  1. Use twelve pages: one sentence, three reference frames, shooting plan, delivery boundary.
  2. One idea per page.
  3. By the last page the client can say what the film looks like, what is delivered, and what is excluded.

Avoid

Do not use “premium, cinematic” as the plan; the client cannot see those words.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Each of twelve pages carries one topic without text piles.
  • 2. Three reference frames show look and tone.
  • 3. The client can repeat deliverables, dates, price, and exclusions.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Each of twelve pages carries one topic without…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Three reference frames show look and tone”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use “premium, cinematic” as the plan; the client cannot see those words.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Use twelve pages: one sentence, three reference frames,”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Each of twelve pages carries one topic without text piles.
  • Three reference frames show look and tone.
  • The client can repeat deliverables, dates, price, and exclusions.

en.title: Title Design: Readable Before Cool
en.summary: Title design must be readable before it is cool; if the name is missed, the style is wasted.
en.html:
Home/Post/Title Design: Readable Before Cool

Post / Titles

Title Design: Readable Before Cool

Title design must be readable before it is cool; if the name is missed, the style is wasted.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

A good title tells the right viewer in half a second what the film is and what it does for them. Write one “content title” and one “hook title,” then merge. Do not start with trending words.

A title explains first, then attracts

Every promise in the title must be paid in the film. A mismatch costs not only this view but the next trust.

Limits

Do not replace content with bait. Exaggeration is allowed; lying is not. Swap “shocking” for a concrete result; clicks may drop, completion rises.

On set

Set the title in lines of two or three characters and test the longest line at phone width. Start with white on black; add style only after it reads.

Do this

Title design starts with legibility, then style. If the audience cannot read the title, the design failed.

  1. Keep two or three characters per line and measure the longest line at phone width.
  2. Start with white type on black; add font, texture, and motion only after it reads.
  3. Watch it on a phone without zooming and confirm it stays inside the safe area.

Avoid

Do not pair a thin typeface with a busy background; unreadable is failed.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The title reads on a phone without zoom and the longest line stays in frame.
  • 2. The white-on-black version works first and the styled version does not shrink the type.
  • 3. Three screenshots and a type-size sheet show the minimum size and safe area.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The title reads on a phone without zoom and th…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The white-on-black version works first and the…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not pair a thin typeface with a busy background; unreadable is failed.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Keep two or three characters per line and”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • The title reads on a phone without zoom and the longest line stays in frame.
  • The white-on-black version works first and the styled version does not shrink the type.
  • Three screenshots and a type-size sheet show the minimum size and safe area.

en.title: Want and Stakes: What Does Losing Cost?
en.summary: What a character wants matters less than what losing it costs.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Want and Stakes: What Does Losing Cost?

Story & Screenwriting / Story

Want and Stakes: What Does Losing Cost?

What a character wants matters less than what losing it costs.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

“Wants recognition” is abstract; “needs that signature by Friday” is playable. Loss must also be concrete: the job, the apartment, someone's trust. Abstract desire cannot drive action; specific loss can.

Make the want concrete and the loss visible

“Wants recognition” is abstract; “needs that signature by Friday” is playable. Loss must also be concrete: the job, the apartment, someone's trust. Abstract desire cannot drive action; specific loss can.

Write three columns: what they want, what they lose if they fail, what they will pay. All three must be playable in the same scene.

Limits

Bigger stakes are not better. An ordinary person losing a job holds the audience more than a superhero losing Earth; scale must match the character.

On set

Before writing a scene, fill two boxes: the concrete thing they want, a key or a signature, and the concrete cost of losing it, no bed tonight or a lost job. Both must be nouns and actions, not dignity or security.

Do this

What the character wants matters less than what losing it costs. Write a concrete object, then a concrete cost.

  1. Write the specific thing they want in this scene: a key, a signature, one sentence.
  2. Write the specific cost of losing it: no bed tonight, a lost job, a missed person.
  3. Keep both boxes to nouns and actions, not dignity or security.

Avoid

Do not replace the scene with a character biography; the audience sees only now.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Both boxes hold filmable nouns and actions, not abstractions like dignity or security.
  • 2. The want and the cost happen in the same scene without voice-over.
  • 3. Another reader can name exactly what the character fears losing.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Both boxes hold filmable nouns and actions, no…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The want and the cost happen in the same scene…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not replace the scene with a character biography; the audience sees only now.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Write the specific thing they want in this” and “Write the specific cost of losing it: no”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Both boxes hold filmable nouns and actions, not abstractions like dignity or security.
  • The want and the cost happen in the same scene without voice-over.
  • Another reader can name exactly what the character fears losing.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Want and stakes are not a character bio. The audience needs to know what it costs to fail.

Make the want concrete

Do not write “wants to succeed.” Write “wants his daughter in a room with a window before school starts.” A concrete goal becomes action.

The want must be filmable: moving boxes, signing, handing over keys, not “becoming better.”

Make the stake visible

Name what is lost: money, a relationship, status, time. Show the cost in the first scene, not in the last line.

A stake does not have to be life or death. A mother missing a parent-teacher meeting can be the heaviest thing in her year.

Escalate the pressure

The same wall closes in: late once, then fired, then a custody hearing. Each turn must change the character’s choice.

Escalation is not repeating the same bad luck; each beat forces a new method at a higher price.

Put the stake into an action

Do not let the character say “I cannot lose you.” Let them transfer the last money or hand over the keys; an action makes the stake visible.

At the end of every scene ask: what did he just lose, or nearly lose? If there is no answer, the scene may be information only.

The stake must be seen by another character; knowing it only as the audience is not enough pressure. When the opponent knows the cost, the conflict becomes real; when they do not, it goes soft.

Do not explain the stake at the end; let the choice speak. If the audience cannot name what he fears losing, cut the premise and add an action.

The one-sentence check

Ask a friend who has not read the story to repeat one sentence: “He wants ____, and if he fails, he loses ____.” If both blanks are concrete, the story stands.

If the friend asks why he cannot simply choose another goal, the stake is not painful enough. Raise the cost until he cannot walk away.

Ten checks before the story works

  • The want is filmable
  • The goal has a deadline
  • The cost appears in the first scene
  • The stake is money, a relationship, or status
  • The opposition wants the opposite
  • Every escalation changes the choice
  • The hero cannot win by luck
  • Each failure costs more
  • The ending stops after a choice
  • The audience can name what he fears losing

The audience is not tense about a premise; it is tense about what a person is about to lose.

en.title: Scene Description: Only What the Camera Can See
en.summary: Describe only what the camera can see: light, action, objects, sound. Leave inner life to the actor.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Scene Description: Only What the Camera Can See

Story & Screenwriting / Screenplay

Scene Description: Only What the Camera Can See

Describe only what the camera can see: light, action, objects, sound. Leave inner life to the actor.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Scene description is not novelistic atmosphere. Write “one unwashed cup on the table, another soaking in the sink,” not “she feels her life out of control.” The first can be shot; the second can only be acted.

Write only what the camera can see and hear

Keep each paragraph to one or two actions and leave room for the director and art department; do not decide wallpaper or focal length for them.

Limits

Shootable is not a list. Every object must do something—advance action, show relationship or block it. Purely decorative props go.

On set

Rewrite one page as only what can be seen and heard: who sits where, what is in hand, what sound comes through the window. Delete he is anxious; let the actor show it by bouncing a knee or checking a watch.

Do this

Scene description writes only what the camera can see and the mic can hear: light, action, objects, sound. Psychology belongs to the actor.

  1. Rewrite one page to visible and audible facts: who sits where, what is in hand, what sounds outside.
  2. Delete “he is anxious” and replace it with an action: bouncing a leg, checking the door.
  3. Read it once and confirm every line can be captured by camera or recorder.

Avoid

Do not let the character speak the theme; once spoken, the scene dies.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Every description can be shot or recorded; no interior monologue remains.
  • 2. States like anxiety or hesitation are replaced with concrete actions.
  • 3. A DP and a sound recordist can mark setups and sounds from one page.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Every description can be shot or recorded; no…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“States like anxiety or hesitation are replaced…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not let the character speak the theme; once spoken, the scene dies.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Rewrite one page to visible and audible facts:” and “Delete “he is anxious” and replace it with”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Every description can be shot or recorded; no interior monologue remains.
  • States like anxiety or hesitation are replaced with concrete actions.
  • A DP and a sound recordist can mark setups and sounds from one page.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. A scene description writes only what the camera can see. What the audience sees is what the script actually says.

Cut the inner adjectives

Do not write “she is anxious.” Write “she opens the bottle, closes it again, and never drinks.” Action gives the actor something to play and the camera something to see.

Do not write “an oppressive mood.” Write “the window is shut; two cups on the table, one still steaming.”

Write space and props

Two cups, a half-open box, a dent in the sofa: these do more than “the room is messy.” A prop must be visible to the camera and touchable by the actor.

A prop should do work the first time it appears. If it is only background, cut it; do not make art department build furniture for nothing.

One action per paragraph

Opening the door, sitting, speaking: three paragraphs. Put three actions in one and the actor rushes while the edit finds no cut point.

Leave a blank line between actions so the director and actor can both see the breath.

Make it readable for the actor

Read your own page and answer three questions: where are the hands, where do the feet go, who does the eyes look at? If you cannot answer, the actor will guess on set.

Replace abstractions with filmable nouns and verbs: cup, door gap, corridor, put down, hold for two seconds.

If a description runs past three lines, it usually holds two actions; split it so each paragraph has one. State where a prop is and what it is doing: on the table, in the hand, on the floor. The actor should not have to ask art department.

Rewrite light and sound at every new location; do not save words with “same as above.” When director and camera disagree, fix the description instead of arguing on set.

The three-line check

Read three lines per paragraph: does the first have action, the second space, the third sound or light? If none, the paragraph is only explanation.

Cut “then” and “begins”; actions happen in order by themselves. Leave a blank line so the editor and actor can breathe.

Ten scene-description checks

  • One action per paragraph
  • No inner adjectives
  • No empty mood words
  • Every action is filmable
  • Props do work on first appearance
  • Space relationships are clear
  • Light and sound are visible or audible
  • Blank lines between actions
  • Full name on first appearance
  • Read it once; the actor knows where the hands go

A scene description is not prose; it is a construction drawing for the camera and the actor.

en.title: Shot Sheet: Number, Framing, Action, Duration
en.summary: Four columns are enough: number, framing, action, duration. If these are vague, the set will be chaos.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Shot Sheet: Number, Framing, Action, Duration

Story & Screenwriting / Storyboard

Shot Sheet: Number, Framing, Action, Duration

Four columns are enough: number, framing, action, duration. If these are vague, the set will be chaos.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Each row: shot number, framing, camera position, action, line, duration, props, sound. Miss one and the set stops to ask. A shot sheet is not a substitute for the board; it is the board made executable.

A shot sheet must be executable on set

Order by shoot sequence, not edit sequence, grouping the same camera and light to reduce moves.

Limits

The sheet can change, but every change goes to camera, sound and script supervisor. Three people with three versions is worse than no sheet.

On set

Fill shots 1, 3, and 5 first: one verb and one duration each. Read the sheet before rolling; if a shot runs past 8 seconds or has no action, cut it or split it.

Do this

A shot sheet needs four columns: number, size, action, duration. If these are unclear, the set will be chaos.

  1. Fill shots 1, 3, and 5 first, each with one verb and one duration.
  2. Cut or split any shot over eight seconds or without an action.
  3. Read it aloud before rolling so camera and edit can repeat the order.

Avoid

Do not draw what the camera cannot shoot; a board is not an illustration.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Every shot has number, size, action, and seconds; no column is missing.
  • 2. No shot runs over eight seconds without an action.
  • 3. A third person can repeat the shooting order from the sheet.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Every shot has number, size, action, and secon…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“No shot runs over eight seconds without an act…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not draw what the camera cannot shoot; a board is not an illustration.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Fill shots 1, 3, and 5 first, each” and “Cut or split any shot over eight seconds”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Every shot has number, size, action, and seconds; no column is missing.
  • No shot runs over eight seconds without an action.
  • A third person can repeat the shooting order from the sheet.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. A shot sheet is not a second storyboard. It decides what gets shot first, how many takes, and when the day can wrap.

A shot sheet is not a storyboard

A storyboard shows what the frame looks like; a shot sheet shows how the day runs. Five columns are enough: number, size, action, camera position, duration. One main action per row; do not put opening a door, sitting, and talking in one box.

Schedule the safety shots first: a wide for space, a medium for performance, a close for emotion, an insert for the cut. Get at least two takes of each, or panic will leave you with no alternative.

Three rules for changing the sheet on set

First, change the order, not the numbers. Second, pickups get letter suffixes instead of being inserted back into old numbers. Third, photograph the completed sheet before wrap and send copies to script supervisor and editor. Paper dies from rain, coffee, and hands; a photo does not.

If a scene runs past twelve shots, split it into morning and afternoon blocks. When people tire, the first things lost are inserts and reactions, not the main angle.

Schedule by setup, not by story order

Shoot everything that fits one setup together; what you save is moving lights, track, and focus. Story order belongs to the edit; set order belongs to the camera.

Draw a line on the sheet at every setup change and write “move / est. 20 min.” That twenty minutes is the most underestimated part of the day.

The last three minutes before wrap

Go back through the sheet and confirm every action has a wide, a close, and an insert. Pick up the missing one now; tomorrow it is gone. Letter the pickups, do not memorize them.

Photograph the completed sheet and one wide of the set. Send copies to script, edit, and director so nobody relies on memory tomorrow.

Ten things your shot sheet needs before call time

  • One main action per row
  • Five columns: number, size, action, position, duration
  • Every group has wide, medium, close, and insert
  • Group by setup, not story order
  • Draw a line and estimate time at every setup change
  • Letter pickups instead of reusing old numbers
  • Note props needed for each shot
  • Mark blocking and eyeline
  • Leave a column for actual takes
  • Photograph it at wrap and send to script and edit

The sheet is not for other people; it is for tomorrow’s you, who will not remember why one shot was skipped.

en.title: Rehearsal: Block First, Lines Later
en.summary: Block first, scripts in hand. Once the body is in the right place, the lines have somewhere to land.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Rehearsal: Block First, Lines Later

Story & Screenwriting / Directing

Rehearsal: Block First, Lines Later

Block first, scripts in hand. Once the body is in the right place, the lines have somewhere to land.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

On-set rehearsal does three things: blocking, prop handoffs, cue points. Do not perform the scene start to finish and spend the emotion; save it for the take.

Rehearse blocking, not the whole performance

Walk camera and sound through too, checking positions, mic and light. Space problems found in rehearsal are worth more than performance notes.

Limits

Rehearsal is not a take. Do not use it as footage; the actor knows it is a rehearsal, and attention changes.

On set

Spend the first 20 minutes on blocking only: tape the door, the chair, and the camera. Walk it three times without lines; add lines on the third pass.

Do this

Rehearsal blocks first; lines can stay in hand. Once the body is in place, words have somewhere to land.

  1. Spend the first twenty minutes on blocking only, taping door, chair, and camera.
  2. Walk the actor through three times without lines, only action and pauses.
  3. Add lines on the third pass and confirm they land on established positions.

Avoid

Do not shout “be natural” from behind the monitor; the actor cannot execute that.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The first two passes have no lines, only positions and actions.
  • 2. On the third pass, pauses still land on actions.
  • 3. The actor can state what they want throughout the scene.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The first two passes have no lines, only posit…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“On the third pass, pauses still land on action…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not shout “be natural” from behind the monitor; the actor cannot execute that.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Spend the first twenty minutes on blocking only,” and “Walk the actor through three times without lines,”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • The first two passes have no lines, only positions and actions.
  • On the third pass, pauses still land on actions.
  • The actor can state what they want throughout the scene.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. Rehearsal is not line practice. It lets the body learn the space and the action first.

Block first, lines later

Walk the scene without lines and mark the start, turn, sit, and prop touch. When the body knows where it goes, the line has somewhere to land.

Do not film the first pass. Let the actor find the rhythm; a recording is reference, not performance.

Give verbs only

Do not say “be sadder.” Say “put the cup down and leave your hand on the table for two seconds.” An executable action gives the performance a base.

Change one action at a time. Change three and the actor will not know which one is right.

Shoot a rehearsal wide

Shoot one wide and play it back to check blocking, exits, and repeated paths. The wide is not for the film; it is a checking tool.

Run the last pass from the final camera position without rolling. Let the actor see where the camera is, instead of discovering it on set.

Rehearsal is not a performance for the director

Talk less in rehearsal. Let the actor walk it twice, then give one verb on the third pass. A body memory the actor finds is more reliable than a director’s instruction.

Put the phone away and do not record every pass; too much filming makes the actor play for the lens.

Run the last pass from the final camera position without makeup or rolling. Let the actor see where the camera is so they do not hide on the take. End with three notes: who is blocked, who exits frame, which action still feels unsafe.

If the actor asks what emotion to play, give an action, not an adjective.

The last action of rehearsal

Ask the actor to repeat the opening action without lines, body only. Then ask where the hands want to be. Their answer is usually more accurate than your diagram.

Write it on the blocking sheet; do not keep it in your head. On a new location the next day, half the body memory is gone.

Ten checks after rehearsal

  • Walked once without lines
  • Marked start, end, and turns
  • Tested sitting and standing
  • Touched every prop once
  • Gave verbs, not adjectives
  • Changed one action at a time
  • Checked blocking on the wide
  • Confirmed nobody exits frame
  • Ran the last pass from the final camera
  • Photographed the blocking diagram

Rehearsal keeps surprises in rehearsal and out of the first take.

en.title: Sensor Size: What the Frame Really Changes
en.summary: Sensor size changes angle, depth, and low light, not "cinematic feel" by itself.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Sensor Size: What the Frame Really Changes

Shooting / Camera

Sensor Size: What the Frame Really Changes

Sensor size changes angle, depth, and low light, not "cinematic feel" by itself.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

A larger sensor needs a longer lens for the same angle, gives shallower depth and usually better low light. It does not automatically buy better color, codec or latitude. Choose the format from working distance and depth, then look at the processor and recording specs.

It sets angle, depth and low light, not “image quality”

Crop modes change the real angle: the same lens becomes longer and depth changes with it. Calculate with the actual readout width, not the full-frame claim.

Limits

Do not sacrifice focus, cooling and lens cost for “full frame.” A small sensor with good light can be steadier than a large one with the wrong glass.

On set

Put the same lens on M4/3, S35, and full-frame bodies and shoot the same half-body frame. Keep the framing equal, compare background compression and shadow noise, then choose the body for the project.

Do this

Sensor size changes angle of view, depth of field, and low-light response, not “cinematic look” by itself. Compare the same lens and framing across formats before paying for the difference.

  1. Mount the same lens on M4/3, S35, and full-frame bodies and keep the same half-body framing.
  2. Compare background compression, depth of field, and shadow noise, not resolution alone.
  3. Choose the body for the project, then check mount, recording format, and heat.

Avoid

Do not sell sensor size as a “cinematic” parameter; the look comes from light, lens, and blocking.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The three half-body frames match closely enough to compare side by side.
  • 2. You can name the difference in compression, depth of field, and shadow noise instead of saying “more cinematic.”
  • 3. The chosen body covers eighty percent of the project without adapter workarounds.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The three half-body frames match closely enoug…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“You can name the difference in compression, de…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not sell sensor size as a “cinematic” parameter; the look comes from light, lens, and blocking.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Mount the same lens on M4/3, S35, and”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • The three half-body frames match closely enough to compare side by side.
  • You can name the difference in compression, depth of field, and shadow noise instead of saying “more cinematic.”
  • The chosen body covers eighty percent of the project without adapter workarounds.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. Sensor size is not a rank. It changes field of view, depth of field, and weight before it changes the look.

One lens, a different view per format

A 50mm lens is 50mm on full frame, roughly 70mm on S35, and 100mm on M4/3. Calculate the equivalent before asking whether a lens is wide enough.

Do not assume a full-frame wide works on a small sensor; an 18mm on M4/3 is a 36mm, and the room suddenly gets tight.

Compare depth at the same framing

At the same framing and aperture, full frame has less depth of field; a smaller sensor needs one or two stops wider to approach the same separation. That also changes exposure, so shutter and ND need a new calculation.

If two people must both stay in focus, a smaller sensor is easier. If the face must lift off the background, full frame helps, but focus errors show sooner.

Weight and runtime are part of the format

Full-frame bodies, lenses, batteries, and ND filters weigh more; a full day handheld will find your shoulder first. Smaller sensors suit travel, events, documentary, and tight rooms; full frame suits low light, shallow depth, and wide angles.

Ask how long you shoot, how far you walk, and who carries the bag before choosing a format. A spec sheet will not carry the camera for you.

Borrow one for a real day

Do not judge from a spec sheet. Borrow or rent the target format and shoot a real day: walking, handheld, lens changes, low light, ingest, edit. Log when your shoulder starts to ache, how many batteries you change, whether the wide is wide enough, and whether shadow noise is acceptable.

Shoot the same day on a smaller format and cut the two together. Many “must be full frame” needs are only a cleaner shadow; many “lightweight” needs turn out to be lens-kit weight.

Test with the same lens on both bodies, or you are comparing lenses, not formats.

Ten checks before choosing a format

  • Calculate equivalent focal length
  • Compare depth at the same framing
  • Check noise in low light
  • Include lens, battery, and ND weight
  • Confirm continuous record time
  • Test wide-angle edges
  • Recalculate ND and shutter
  • Check cards and backup
  • Shoot one test in three kinds of light
  • Ask whether the format is enough last

Format is a constraint, not a rank. Fit the camera to the day first, then to your taste.

en.title: Waveform: Exposure You Can Measure
en.summary: The waveform measures brightness, not beauty. Protect highlights first, then decide how much shadow to keep.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Waveform: Exposure You Can Measure

Shooting / Exposure

Waveform: Exposure You Can Measure

The waveform measures brightness, not beauty. Protect highlights first, then decide how much shadow to keep.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

A waveform shows where brightness sits: black on the left, white on the right. Check whether skin sits slightly above the middle, then whether highlights touch the top and shadows pile at the bottom. A shot can average correctly and still leave the face in black.

Read the distribution, not one peak

Use waveform with zebras and vectorscope: waveform for luma, vector for color, zebra for a specific highlight range.

Limits

The waveform is not a judge of composition or performance. Backlit silhouettes, night scenes and stylized low contrast can look “wrong” on the scope and still work. Play it back.

On set

Put the face at 55 to 65 IRE and keep the sky under 95. If the trace hits the top, cut a stop of light or add ND instead of fixing it in post.

Do this

A waveform shows luminance distribution. Protect highlights first, then decide how much shadow to keep. Put skin at 55 to 65 IRE and sky below 95; if the trace hits the ceiling, cut light or add ND.

  1. Place the face between 55 and 65 IRE.
  2. Bring the sky or window below 95 IRE so detail survives.
  3. If the trace still clips, cut a stop of light or add ND; do not plan to recover it in post.

Avoid

Do not let the waveform clip and plan to recover it later; clipped highlights are gone.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Skin sits between 55 and 65 IRE with no flat white patch.
  • 2. Sky or window still holds detail and the trace does not sit on the ceiling.
  • 3. When exposure clips, light or ND changes first; ISO is not pushed to compensate.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Skin sits between 55 and 65 IRE with no flat w…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Sky or window still holds detail and the trace…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not let the waveform clip and plan to recover it later; clipped highlights are gone.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Place the face between 55 and 65 IRE.”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • Skin sits between 55 and 65 IRE with no flat white patch.
  • Sky or window still holds detail and the trace does not sit on the ceiling.
  • When exposure clips, light or ND changes first; ISO is not pushed to compensate.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. A waveform is not decoration. It turns “looks about right” into whether highlights clip and where skin sits.

Brighter is not better

When the waveform touches 100, the white is gone; post cannot bring it back. Log footage sits lower by design, so do not push it as if it were Rec.709. Check clipping first, skin placement second, overall brightness last.

Exposure must match within a scene. Recheck the waveform after every setup and lens change; background brightness may shift, the face should not.

When you have no waveform

Turn on zebras at 95 percent; if both face and window stripe, stop down. If you have false color, watch purple or red for highlights. If you have neither, shoot a test and read the histogram. Do not trust the viewfinder; ambient light lies to it.

Carry white paper or a gray card and shoot three seconds at the start. At least post will know how white looked, especially under mixed light.

Leave headroom on log footage

Log looks flat; that is not a instruction to brighten it on set. Keep highlights under the top of the waveform and leave a stop for post. Noisy shadows can be helped; clipped highlights cannot.

Shoot a gray card at the start of a scene and match every shot to it in post. Without a card, use a white wall or paper, but keep it from specular clipping.

Three kinds of light that lie

A window behind the subject, a practical on the table, and a white wall all make the viewfinder look brighter than the file. Read the waveform, not the screen; read highlights, not overall brightness.

Without a waveform, shoot a test and look at the right edge of the histogram. If it is pinned, the white is gone; stop down and shoot again.

Ten exposure checks before you roll

  • Check whether highlights touch the top of the waveform
  • Then check where skin sits
  • Read overall brightness last
  • Match exposure across the whole scene
  • Recheck after every camera move
  • Recheck after every lens change
  • Without a waveform, set zebras to ninety-five
  • With false color, watch purple or red for highlights
  • Shoot three seconds of gray card or white paper first
  • Play back and check the right edge of the histogram

The waveform is not there to make you a technician; it is there so playback does not make you curse. One look on set saves an hour in post.

en.title: Lighting Style: Soft, Hard, Natural
en.summary: Pick one direction first: soft, hard, or natural. All three at once means no attitude.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Lighting Style: Soft, Hard, Natural

Shooting / Lighting

Lighting Style: Soft, Hard, Natural

Pick one direction first: soft, hard, or natural. All three at once means no attitude.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Tech DeskEdited 2026-11

Lighting style is not a preset. Set the ratio—how many stops between face highlight and shadow; then direction—where the key comes from; then color—warm, cool or mixed. With those three, the style repeats.

Style starts with ratio, then color

Read references for direction, shadow hardness and face brightness, not only tone. Tone can be graded; position cannot.

Limits

Style is not a new look every scene. The film needs one ratio through-line; changing every scene reads as chaos.

On set

Pick one reference: soft, hard, or window light. Use one direction and shoot three versions at different strengths; choose the take where the face has the most shape.

Do this

Pick one lighting direction first: soft, hard, or natural. Then adjust brightness. Wanting all three leaves the face without an attitude.

  1. Choose one reference: soft source, hard source, or window light, and use one direction only.
  2. Shoot three intensities from that direction and compare facial structure.
  3. Pick the take with the clearest structure, then decide whether the shadow needs fill.

Avoid

Do not open three lamps at once; without direction, three lamps only make it brighter.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. All three stills share one key direction; three styles are not mixed on one face.
  • 2. You can name the intensity with the clearest facial structure and say why.
  • 3. Shadows keep detail without being flattened by fill.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“All three stills share one key direction; thre…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“You can name the intensity with the clearest f…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not open three lamps at once; without direction, three lamps only make it brighter.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Choose one reference: soft source, hard source, or”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • All three stills share one key direction; three styles are not mixed on one face.
  • You can name the intensity with the clearest facial structure and say why.
  • Shadows keep detail without being flattened by fill.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Soft, hard, and natural are not three filters. They are three choices of source size, distance, and direction.

Softness is relative size

The larger the source and the closer it sits, the softer the shadow edge; a 120cm softbox at 1.5m is softer than a 60cm at 2m.

Soft light does not mean no shadow; it means a shadow with a transition. No shadow at all flattens the face.

Hard light is not a mistake

Hard light gives nose shadow, cheekbone, and a shadow on the wall; it suits genre, dance, and product. Control the angle so the nose shadow does not cut the upper lip, and add a bounce for the dark side.

The worst hard light is half-hard: lamp too far, diffusion too small, shadow edge dirty. Commit to harder or softer.

Find the direction in natural light

A north window, an overcast sky, and a white wall are free soft sources. At noon, move the face into shade or use diffusion. In a mixed-light room, turn off unneeded lamps before adding anything.

Natural light changes; shoot a frame at the start and another ten minutes later. Do not let a scene begin overcast and end in sun.

Three layers for one face

The key sets the shadow direction, the bounce decides how dark the shadow side goes, and the background light decides where the person stands. All three can be measured; do not rely on “it feels right.”

Turn off every light and keep only the key. If the face reads, add the bounce. If the background is too bright, flag it or kill the background lamp. Play back after each layer.

Softbox and window light can mix if their color temperature is close; a big mismatch cannot be fixed later. If three layers still fail, move the source before buying another lamp.

Five-minute drill: one face, two sources

Take one desk lamp and a sheet of white paper, stand 1.5 meters away: light the face directly, then through the paper, and compare the shadow edge. Move the lamp forty-five degrees to the side and watch where the nose shadow lands.

Do not add a second lamp yet. Learn one direction first; if the direction is wrong, a second lamp only hides the problem.

Ten checks before lighting

  • Decide how long the shadow should be
  • Judge softness by relative source size
  • Move the softbox closer for softer light
  • Control the nose shadow with hard light
  • Bounce into the dark side
  • Find the window and shade first
  • Turn off unneeded mixed sources
  • Shoot one frame before and after
  • Check skin against background
  • Avoid half-hard light

Decide how long the shadow should be before deciding which lamp to buy.

en.title: Set Safety: Cables, Heights, Roads
en.summary: Cables, heights, traffic: check those three before anything else on set.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Set Safety: Cables, Heights, Roads

Shooting / Safety

Set Safety: Cables, Heights, Roads

Cables, heights, traffic: check those three before anything else on set.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Tech DeskEdited 2026-11

Walk the set before rolling: cable paths that trip, stands without sandbags, heights without tie-offs, roads without closure and hi-vis. Give every risk an owner and a stop-work condition.

People before the shot

Put the must-get list and the safety list on the same call sheet. If any safety condition fails, stop first; do not “finish the shot and deal with it later.”

Limits

Safety is not paperwork, and it is not a reason to let untrained people take risks. Use qualified electricians, traffic control or riggers. “We always did it this way” is not a permit.

On set

Walk the set before rolling: tape cables flat across walkways, sandbag every stand, put a hand on high rigs, and wear a reflective vest near roads.

Do this

Check three things before rolling: cables that trip, heights that fall, and roads with traffic. Walk the set and fix the risk, not just write it down.

  1. Tape cables flat across walkways and sandbag every light stand.
  2. Put a person on high stands and wear hi-vis near roads.
  3. Put the nearest hospital, assembly point, and contact in the call sheet and read them to the crew.

Avoid

Do not let one person carry a light stand; if it falls, nobody catches it.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. No cable crosses a walkway untaped and every stand is sandbagged.
  • 2. High stands have a spotter and everyone near the road wears hi-vis.
  • 3. Any crew member can name the nearest hospital, assembly point, and on-set contact.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“No cable crosses a walkway untaped and every s…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“High stands have a spotter and everyone near t…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not let one person carry a light stand; if it falls, nobody catches it.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Tape cables flat across walkways and sandbag every”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • No cable crosses a walkway untaped and every stand is sandbagged.
  • High stands have a spotter and everyone near the road wears hi-vis.
  • Any crew member can name the nearest hospital, assembly point, and on-set contact.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. Set safety is not a disclaimer. It is checking cables, heights, and roads before the first take.

Tape the cables first

Tape every cable to the edge and keep a walking path clear. Do not use a chair as a light stand, and do not chain too many power strips.

Clear the path people actually walk, then place stands outside the frame. One trip can cost both the gear and the person.

Someone holds the ladder

Someone holds the ladder, tools are tethered, nobody stands on a railing, and tripods get sandbags.

Look up for cables before lifting a light overhead. Outdoors, check the wind first; a softbox becomes a sail.

Roads and weather

Wear high-visibility clothing at the roadside, set cones, check weather and sunset, and never stand in traffic for a shot.

Post the emergency contact, nearest hospital, and meeting point in the group chat before rolling. In an emergency nobody has time to scroll back.

The ten minutes before rolling

Divide the set into three lines: where people walk, where power runs, and where gear stands. Keep them from crossing and you remove half the trips and kicked stands.

Weight every stand, tripod, and track. Outdoors, every tall object gets one more tie-down.

Write the nearest hospital, emergency contact, and meeting point on paper and tape it by the monitor; it works when a phone dies. Wrap in the same three lines: power off, small items first, lights last. Do not make people cross lines in the dark.

The last thing before wrap

Cut the main power, pack small items, move the lights last, and never make anyone cross cables in the dark. Put cones and high-vis vests back in one box so the next shoot does not hunt for them.

Look at the floor once more: tape, screws, lens caps. Pick up everything; otherwise your foot will find it on the next shoot.

Ten safety checks before rolling

  • Tape every cable
  • Keep the walkway clear
  • No chairs as stands
  • Do not overload power strips
  • Someone holds the ladder
  • Tether tools
  • Sandbag the tripods
  • Look up before lifting a light
  • High-vis and cones at the road
  • Post emergency contacts

Safety is not shooting slower; it is making sure everyone can shoot the next take.

en.title: Proxy Workflow: Cut First, Quality Later
en.summary: Proxies do not lower the final quality; they let the edit move. Keep the originals untouched.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Post/Proxy Workflow: Cut First, Quality Later

Post / Editing

Proxy Workflow: Cut First, Quality Later

Proxies do not lower the final quality; they let the edit move. Keep the originals untouched.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Proxies solve “the machine cannot cut the originals,” not “quality can drop.” Keep the original filename, timecode and reel name, finish the cut, relink to the originals, then export the master.

A proxy is an editing copy, not a delivery file

Choose proxy resolution from timeline needs, not always the smallest. On multicam, test how many streams one machine can play before choosing a bitrate.

Limits

Every proxy must map to one original. Renaming, dropping timecode or mixing frame rates turns relinking into manual file hunting. Before delivery, confirm the master points at originals, not proxies.

On set

Use ProRes Proxy or quarter-resolution proxies on a separate SSD. Lock the originals as read-only, edit only proxies, and relink before delivery.

Do this

Proxies do not lower delivery quality; they let the edit run. Originals stay untouched beside them.

  1. Generate ProRes Proxy or quarter-resolution files on a separate SSD.
  2. Set the originals to read-only and edit only against proxies.
  3. Relink to originals before delivery and confirm no proxy slipped into the master.

Avoid

Do not treat proxies as masters; deliver before relinking and the quality shows.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Proxies and originals live on separate drives and the originals are read-only.
  • 2. The timeline references proxies only, with one-to-one names and paths.
  • 3. After relinking, three random shots return to original resolution and detail.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Proxies and originals live on separate drives…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The timeline references proxies only, with one…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not treat proxies as masters; deliver before relinking and the quality shows.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Generate ProRes Proxy or quarter-resolution files on a”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Proxies and originals live on separate drives and the originals are read-only.
  • The timeline references proxies only, with one-to-one names and paths.
  • After relinking, three random shots return to original resolution and detail.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. A proxy is not a quality downgrade; it makes the edit run. The original stays untouched; the proxy only buys responsiveness.

When you need proxies

Above 4K, multicam, or an older machine: if playback stutters, make proxies. A smooth 1080 single track does not need them; do not add process for its own sake.

Set proxy resolution to the timeline. Do not make a proxy larger than the timeline; 1080 proxies are enough for a 1080 cut.

How to generate proxies

Keep filename, timecode, and reel name identical; put them in a separate Proxy folder. Never overwrite the originals or change their folder structure.

Spot-check three shots after generating; confirm audio and color survived. A proxy can be soft, but it cannot lose sound.

Relink and export

Lock the cut before relinking to originals. After relink, check speed changes, captions, and transitions; proxy and original can differ by a frame.

Always export from the originals; proxies stay in the project. Treat a proxy as a master and quality drops exactly when it matters.

Proxy naming and folders

Originals in Camera, proxies in Proxy, projects in Project. Keep the three folders separate.

Add _proxy to the proxy filename so relink is obvious. Never rename the originals.

Multicam proxies

Make multicam proxies at the same resolution and frame rate, or the timeline refuses them.

Sync once after generating and confirm audio and camera mapping before editing.

Ten proxy-workflow checks

  • Only for high resolution or multicam
  • Proxy filenames match originals
  • Proxies in a separate folder
  • Never overwrite originals
  • Keep timecode and reel names
  • Spot-check three shots after generating
  • Edit with proxies
  • Lock the cut before relinking
  • Check speed and captions after relink
  • Export from originals

A proxy is scaffolding, not the building. Take it down after the cut; do not deliver from inside it.

When you have five minutes

  • Only for high resolution or multicam
  • Proxy names match originals
  • Keep proxies in a separate folder
  • Spot-check three shots
  • Lock before relinking
  • Export from originals

Proxies let the edit run; originals let the film stand at the end. A broken proxy can be rebuilt; a lost original has no second take.

en.title: Primary Correction: Exposure and White Balance
en.summary: Primary correction fixes exposure and white balance first. Do not hide technical problems under a look.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Post/Primary Correction: Exposure and White Balance

Post / Color

Primary Correction: Exposure and White Balance

Primary correction fixes exposure and white balance first. Do not hide technical problems under a look.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Primary correction only unifies exposure, white balance and contrast: align black, white and skin on every shot before discussing a look. Use scopes, not guesswork in a dark room.

Bring every shot to the same start line

Order: normalize exposure, normalize white balance, normalize contrast, then check shot-to-shot jumps. If one step is skipped, the secondary grade locks the cast in.

Limits

Primary is not “make every shot equally bright.” Different shot sizes and lighting may differ; unify the reference, not the emotion.

On set

Shoot a grey or color card first: set black to 0 to 5 and white below 100. Match every shot in the scene, then check the skin line.

Do this

Primary correction fixes exposure and white balance before style.

  1. Shoot a gray or color chart; set black to 0 to 5 and white below 100.
  2. Match every shot in the scene for exposure and white balance, then check the skin line.
  3. Add contrast and style only after the technical problems are gone.

Avoid

Do not use a LUT to hide technical problems; it makes them look prettier.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Black and white levels match across the scene and cuts do not jump.
  • 2. Skin sits on the same vector line with no green or red drift between shots.
  • 3. Turn off the style LUT and the image still holds technically.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Black and white levels match across the scene…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Skin sits on the same vector line with no gree…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use a LUT to hide technical problems; it makes them look prettier.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Shoot a gray or color chart; set black”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Black and white levels match across the scene and cuts do not jump.
  • Skin sits on the same vector line with no green or red drift between shots.
  • Turn off the style LUT and the image still holds technically.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Primary correction does three things: match exposure, unify white balance, restore contrast. Do not build a look here.

Match first, grade later

Choose the most accurate shot in the scene as reference and bring the others to it. Read the waveform, not your eye; the eye is fooled by neighboring shots.

Grade interior and exterior separately; do not pull the window to the same brightness as the room. The audience knows outside is brighter, and flattening it looks false.

White balance on neutral gray

A white wall carries a cast; a gray card is truer. Without one, use white paper but do not overexpose it; clipped paper is no longer white.

Under mixed light there is no absolute correct. Choose one dominant source and let other colors remain. Pull everything to white and the room dies.

Do not crush the contrast

Lifting blacks makes them milky; crushing them loses detail. Read the scope before deciding; black is not a grade contest.

Put the LUT after primary. Do not use a LUT to hide exposure errors; if primary is wrong, every later node patches the wrong image.

The order of shot matching

Exposure first, white balance second, contrast third, skin last. Reverse the order and every adjustment undoes the one before.

After a scene, play three shots before moving on and confirm there is no jump.

Skin and memory colors

Sky, grass, and skin are memory colors; the audience notices a small shift. Protect skin before sky.

Do not grade every face to the same brightness. Different people have different skin, and unifying it looks false.

Ten primary-correction checks

  • Choose one reference shot per scene
  • Match exposure first
  • Then white balance
  • Then skin tone
  • Then black level
  • Then highlights
  • Keep ambient color under mixed light
  • Place the LUT after primary
  • Check on the scopes
  • Play the whole scene back

Primary correction is not about looking good; it is about making the seams between shots disappear.

When you have five minutes

  • Choose one reference per scene
  • Match exposure
  • Then white balance
  • Then skin
  • Check black and highlight
  • Place the LUT after primary

Primary correction is the foundation for any look; if it is crooked, every later grade looks false. Make the faces in one scene look like the same person before you talk about style. The face must stay the same person across the scene, not two color temperatures.
