en.title: Short-Film Economy: Cut What You Cannot Shoot
en.summary: Cut what you cannot shoot, then make what remains more specific.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Short-Film Economy: Cut What You Cannot Shoot

Story & Screenwriting / Story

Short-Film Economy: Cut What You Cannot Shoot

Cut what you cannot shoot, then make what remains more specific.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Every extra location, actor and VFX shot adds coordination, transport and a failure point. Compress to one main location, two actors, one time block; put the savings into sound and rehearsal.

Short-film savings come from fewer variables

Use staging instead of coverage: play a scene in one space with blocking and framing changes. It is cheaper than ten locations and more coherent.

Limits

Savings are not a shorter film. The necessary change cannot be cut; remove the story and the saved budget cannot buy it back.

On set

Cross out the three most expensive scenes: crowds, night exteriors, vehicles. Rewrite with one room, two people, one prop, and keep the conflict working.

Do this

Short films cut what they cannot afford, then make what remains more specific.

  1. Strike the three most expensive scenes: crowd, night exterior, vehicles.
  2. Rewrite with one room, two people, one prop.
  3. Confirm the conflict still holds, then add detail instead of scale.

Avoid

Do not hide an empty script behind scale; an unaffordable scene also hides the character.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The three costliest scenes are gone and the script stands without them.
  • 2. The rewrite uses one room, two people, and one prop.
  • 3. The conflict stays clear and the character becomes more specific, not smaller.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The three costliest scenes are gone and the sc…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The rewrite uses one room, two people, and one…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not hide an empty script behind scale; an unaffordable scene also hides the character.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Strike the three most expensive scenes: crowd, night” and “Rewrite with one room, two people, one prop.”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • The three costliest scenes are gone and the script stands without them.
  • The rewrite uses one room, two people, and one prop.
  • The conflict stays clear and the character becomes more specific, not smaller.

en.title: Script Format: Make the Whole Crew Read It the Same Way
en.summary: Script format is not for a literary prize; it helps camera, sound, and edit find information at a glance.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Script Format: Make the Whole Crew Read It the Same Way

Story & Screenwriting / Screenplay

Script Format: Make the Whole Crew Read It the Same Way

Script format is not for a literary prize; it helps camera, sound, and edit find information at a glance.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Format exists so the director, camera, sound and editor can find scene, action, dialogue and time on the same page. The slug line states location and time; action describes only what the camera can see; the character name sits above the line.

A script is a working document

Do not put unfilmable psychology in dialogue. Change “she is hesitant” into “she picks up the keys, then puts them back.”

Limits

A short film script does not need every shot, but every scene needs a want, an obstacle and a turn. Pretty format cannot save a scene with none of the three.

On set

Start each scene with interior or exterior, location, and time. Keep action blocks under four lines and capitalize a character name on first appearance. The sound team needs to know when the door opens.

Do this

  1. Open every scene with interior or exterior, location, and time.
  2. Keep action blocks under four lines; capitalize a character name on first appearance.
  3. Put door, phone, and footstep cues into the action so sound knows what to capture.

Avoid

Do not write a novel; if the crew cannot find scene numbers and sound cues, the set will miss them.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Contracts, tax, insurance and consent rules differ by market; use the local currency and local counsel before signing or invoicing.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Every scene has interior or exterior, location, and time with continuous numbering.
  • 2. Action blocks stay under four lines and first character names are capitalized.
  • 3. Sound can mark at least three cues to record from the script.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Every scene has interior or exterior, location…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Action blocks stay under four lines and first…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not write a novel; if the crew cannot find scene numbers and sound cues, the set will miss them.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Open every scene with interior or exterior, location,” and “Keep action blocks under four lines; capitalize a”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Every scene has interior or exterior, location, and time with continuous numbering.
  • Action blocks stay under four lines and first character names are capitalized.
  • Sound can mark at least three cues to record from the script.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. The field note tells you how to write. This layer is about one page that lets five people start work at once, and which words to cut when you rewrite.

One page, five people using it at once

The director looks for action, the camera department for space, sound for lines, art for props, and the editor for scenes. A script is not literature; it is a work order five people can read at once.

A scene heading carries four facts: interior or exterior, location, time. Action describes only what the camera can see, and a character name is capitalized on first appearance. Keep each dialogue line under roughly thirty-five Chinese characters; long lines make actors gasp and subtitles overflow.

INT. KITCHEN — NIGHT
The kettle whistles. She kills the flame, picks up her phone, and deletes the message she just wrote.

Rewrite only three kinds of words

Cut explanatory adjectives, repeated names, and inner states the actor can play. Change “she angrily slams the door” to “she slams the door; it bounces back once.” Precise action gives the actor something to do.

Solve one class of problem per pass: one pass removes explanation, the next fixes pace, the next rewrites lines. Change three things at once and tomorrow you will not know who wrote which line.

Do not drop scene headings; the edit finds footage by them

Scene numbers are not for the director; they let script supervisors, editors, and post find footage. Start a new scene whenever time or place changes. Never replace a heading with “later.”

Separate day and night inside the same location. An editor looking for “kitchen night” does not want to read a page of prose.

Page count and shoot days

A page is roughly a minute on screen, but takes one to three hours on set depending on setups, cast, and weather. Three pages of dialogue are not automatically one day.

Schedule by pages times difficulty, not by scene count. Ten empty shots can take half a day; one crowd scene can take two.

Ten checks before you print

  • Scene heading names interior or exterior, place, and time
  • Action describes only what the camera can see
  • Capitalize a character name on first appearance
  • Keep each dialogue line under thirty-five characters
  • Give each scene one turn, not two
  • Delete explanatory adjectives
  • Turn inner states into playable action
  • Keep scene numbers continuous from first to last
  • Mark pickups and flashbacks separately
  • Leave a notes column for the script supervisor

If two of these ten fail, do not start a new scene. Make this page shootable; that is worth more than three more pages.

en.title: Rewrite: Delete the Explanation, Add the Action
en.summary: In a rewrite, delete the explanation and add a visible action; often they are the same fix.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Rewrite: Delete the Explanation, Add the Action

Story & Screenwriting / Screenplay

Rewrite: Delete the Explanation, Add the Action

In a rewrite, delete the explanation and add a visible action; often they are the same fix.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Rewrite by deleting explanation first, then adding one visible action; often they are the same fix.

On set

Search the draft for because, so, and felt. Replace each with an action or an object; keep at most one explanatory sentence per page.

Do this

  1. Search for “because,” “so,” and “feels”; delete every hit.
  2. Replace the deleted information with an action or object.
  3. Keep at most one explanatory line per page and let the image carry the rest.

Avoid

Do not patch holes with explanation; more explanation means fewer actions.

Three causes

For “Rewrite: Delete the Explanation, Add the Action”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Explaining themeA character says “I learned to let go” and the scene diesTurn theme into action and cost
Repeated informationThe same fact arrives three times and the audience leaves earlyOne new fact per scene
No actionThe page talks and nobody does anythingAt least one action changes the relationship

On-set diagnosis

  1. Mark “says” and “does” on every page; a page of pure talk gets cut or changed.
  2. Write the change of each scene in one sentence; if you cannot, there is no change.
  3. Delete the last line and see whether the previous line still stands.

Fix

A rewrite is not a word-count cut; every page must produce a change. Remove explanation first, then hide information in action.

  1. Cut lines where a character explains why they are like this.
  2. Put backstory in a prop, space or action: an old photo, a locked door.
  3. End each scene with a change in relationship or information; do not return to neutral.
  4. Save the theme for the final action; do not let a character state it.

Failure cases

With “Rewrite: Delete the Explanation, Add the Action”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Cut words onlyThe page is shorter and still unchangedCheck change per scene
Add more eventsEvents pile up but nobody choosesEvery event must force a choice
Turn explanation into voice-overThe information survives with a new mouthMake it visible action

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
Change per sceneEvery scene has a from-X-to-Y sentenceScene table
Say/do ratioAt least one action per pagePage marks
ExplanationCharacters do not explain their psychologySearch “because/actually”
EndingThe last action carries the themeRead the final three pages

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The page has no “because,” “so,” or “feels” explaining the action.
  • 2. Deleted information now appears as a filmable action or object.
  • 3. At most one explanatory line remains per page; the image carries the rest.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The page has no “because,” “so,” or “feels” ex…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Deleted information now appears as a filmable…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not patch holes with explanation; more explanation means fewer actions.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Search for “because,” “so,” and “feels”; delete every” and “Replace the deleted information with an action or”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • The page has no “because,” “so,” or “feels” explaining the action.
  • Deleted information now appears as a filmable action or object.
  • At most one explanatory line remains per page; the image carries the rest.

Boundary

This page only covers “Rewrite: Delete the Explanation, Add the Action”; it does not replace Scene Description: Only What the Camera Can See, A Sequence: Three Scenes, One Change, Composition: Tell the Eye Where to Look. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

en.title: Subtext: The Thing Under the Line
en.summary: Subtext is saying A while needing B; the director's job is to let the audience see the B.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Subtext: The Thing Under the Line

Story & Screenwriting / Screenplay

Subtext: The Thing Under the Line

Subtext is saying A while needing B; the director's job is to let the audience see the B.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Subtext is saying A while wanting B; the director makes B visible.

On set

Give every line a hidden action: she says whatever, but closes the menu. Direct the hand, not the line.

Do this

  1. Give each line a hidden action: she says “whatever” and closes the menu.
  2. Let the actor play the hand, not the line.
  3. Review that line and action contradict each other and B reads.

Avoid

Do not let the line speak the subtext; once said, it is no longer subtext.

Three causes

For “Subtext: The Thing Under the Line”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Lines state itA character says “I want you to stay” and the scene is overHide the want in action and other words
No hidden goalThe character only completes the surface task and wants nothing from the other personGive every character an unspeakable aim
No pressureThe other person agrees too easily, so subtext has nothing to pushLet them refuse or misunderstand

On-set diagnosis

  1. Write one line of what each character really wants; keep it out of the script.
  2. Ask the actor what they lose if this line fails.
  3. Play the scene as action without lines and see whether the relationship still reads.

Fix

Subtext is not an explanation hidden under the line; it is the detour a character takes to get something. Give them a reason not to say it, then let them say something else.

  1. Give each character an aim they cannot state: fear of rejection, loss of face, refusal to admit.
  2. Make lines do actions: probe, deflect, threaten, appease; not state.
  3. Let the scene partner resist so the subtext has pressure.
  4. Hold a pause at the key moment so the audience feels the unsaid line.

Failure cases

With “Subtext: The Thing Under the Line”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Let the character say the subtextThe moment the thought is spoken, subtext disappearsKeep the truth in action
Add musicThe score feels for the audience and the lines get flatterChange the line and resistance first
Hide everythingThe scene becomes a puzzleKeep the surface task clear

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
Surface taskEach scene has a clear surface goalWrite it per scene
Hidden aimEach character has an unspeakable aimCharacter notes
ResistanceThe partner does not cooperateWatch the exchange
PauseA key unsaid pause existsPlayback

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Every key line has a contradicting or offsetting action.
  • 2. The actor plays the hand and body, not the hidden line aloud.
  • 3. The audience can name what is said and what is actually wanted.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Every key line has a contradicting or offsetti…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The actor plays the hand and body, not the hid…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not let the line speak the subtext; once said, it is no longer subtext.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Give each line a hidden action: she says” and “Let the actor play the hand, not the”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Every key line has a contradicting or offsetting action.
  • The actor plays the hand and body, not the hidden line aloud.
  • The audience can name what is said and what is actually wanted.

en.title: Monologue: Give It a Listener and a Block
en.summary: A monologue needs a listener who cannot easily leave and does not quite want to hear it.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Monologue: Give It a Listener and a Block

Story & Screenwriting / Screenplay

Monologue: Give It a Listener and a Block

A monologue needs a listener who cannot easily leave and does not quite want to hear it.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

One person talking to camera most easily becomes recitation. Give them a listener—someone absent, the mirror, an object—and an action: packing, writing, driving. The action interrupts the speech so the audience sees thinking, not memorizing.

A monologue needs a listener and an action

Save the most important line for after an action. Start with the ordinary, then leak the truth; it is more believable than starting at full emotion.

Limits

A monologue is not a plot explanation. Cut every “because” and “so”; let pauses and actions carry cause.

On set

Before the monologue, place a listener: someone packing, a child facing away. Give the speaker a task that keeps interrupting the speech.

Do this

A monologue is not a speech to air; it needs a listener who does not want to hear but cannot leave.

  1. Place a listener: someone packing, a child with their back turned.
  2. Give the speaker an action that interrupts the speech.
  3. Keep the listener's reaction in frame; they are not background.

Avoid

Do not play the monologue to a mirror or empty air; without a listener it feels false.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. A listener is trapped in frame and their reaction is visible.
  • 2. The speaker does an action that interrupts the speech.
  • 3. Remove the listener and the monologue weakens, proving the relationship matters.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“A listener is trapped in frame and their react…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The speaker does an action that interrupts the…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not play the monologue to a mirror or empty air; without a listener it feels false.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Place a listener: someone packing, a child with” and “Give the speaker an action that interrupts the”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • A listener is trapped in frame and their reaction is visible.
  • The speaker does an action that interrupts the speech.
  • Remove the listener and the monologue weakens, proving the relationship matters.

en.title: Short Drama: A Hook Every Thirty Seconds
en.summary: Short drama runs on hook, turn, cliff: every thirty seconds something must change the board.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Short Drama: A Hook Every Thirty Seconds

Story & Screenwriting / Screenplay

Short Drama: A Hook Every Thirty Seconds

Short drama runs on hook, turn, cliff: every thirty seconds something must change the board.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Short drama scripts run hook, reversal, cliffhanger, with a situation change every thirty seconds.

On set

List a turn every 30 seconds: an identity exposed, money taken, a door locked. Write the turn as an image, not as explanation.

Do this

  1. List one situation change every thirty seconds: identity exposed, money taken, door locked.
  2. Write the change as an image, not a character explaining it.
  3. End on an unanswered question, not a summary, so the next episode can connect.

Avoid

Do not let a character explain the reversal; it must happen on screen.

Three causes

For “Short Drama: A Hook Every Thirty Seconds”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
No conflict in the first three secondsThe opening is scenery or narration and the viewer swipes awayPut goal and obstacle in the first line
Hook arrives lateThe first turn lands after forty seconds; the first thirty have no changeMove the turn inside ten seconds
No question at the endEach episode ends on an answer, so there is no reason to open the nextEnd on an unresolved problem

On-set diagnosis

  1. Write what happens in 0–3, 3–10 and 10–30 seconds.
  2. Count information changes in thirty seconds; fewer than two means rewrite.
  3. Look at the last frame: does the viewer know what will happen next?

Fix

Short drama is not a long drama shortened; it delivers one promise and one new question every thirty seconds. Conflict first, turn second, hook last.

  1. Put person, goal and obstacle in the first line; do not open on scenery.
  2. Deliver the first turn within ten seconds and a second small change within thirty.
  3. End each episode on a choice that creates a new problem.
  4. Remove explanation; push with action and props.

Failure cases

With “Short Drama: A Hook Every Thirty Seconds”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Hook with musicThe music is loud but nothing happensWrite the event first
Turn every episodeThe audience tires and turns lose weightAlternate small changes and big turns
Summarise at the endNarration explains the next episodeStop on the question

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
First 3 secondsA goal, obstacle or anomalySecond-by-second marks
10 secondsThe first turn has happenedTime it
30 secondsAt least two information changesCount them
EndingOne unresolved problem remainsInspect the last frame

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Every thirty seconds has a situation change that can be played as an image.
  • 2. The reversal is visible without a character explaining it.
  • 3. The ending stops on an unanswered question with no summary.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Every thirty seconds has a situation change th…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The reversal is visible without a character ex…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not let a character explain the reversal; it must happen on screen.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “List one situation change every thirty seconds: identity” and “Write the change as an image, not a”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Every thirty seconds has a situation change that can be played as an image.
  • The reversal is visible without a character explaining it.
  • The ending stops on an unanswered question with no summary.

en.title: Adaptation: From Real Event to Shootable Scene
en.summary: Adaptation is not retelling an event; it is finding a conflict that can be shot within two hours.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Adaptation: From Real Event to Shootable Scene

Story & Screenwriting / Screenplay

Adaptation: From Real Event to Shootable Scene

Adaptation is not retelling an event; it is finding a conflict that can be shot within two hours.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Prose enters the mind through narration; film can only show action and sound. First translate “what he thinks” into “what he does,” then decide which line to cut.

Adaptation changes the medium, not reads the novel aloud

Choose one action that carries the theme and rebuild events around it. Do not distribute every chapter evenly across every character.

Limits

Faithful does not mean line-by-line. Keep the author's judgment and change events; losing the judgment while keeping the plot is the real betrayal.

On set

Take one shootable core from the real event: one person makes one decision in one room. Compress time to 24 hours and cut the years you cannot shoot.

Do this

Adaptation is not retelling events; it finds one conflict that can be shot in two hours.

  1. Take one filmable core from the real event: one person, one room, one decision.
  2. Compress time to twenty-four hours and cut years of unfilmable backstory.
  3. Build the film on one character, one space, one choice.

Avoid

Do not retell the event as a timeline; the audience needs a conflict, not an archive.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The adaptation keeps one core event and one character's decision.
  • 2. Time is compressed to twenty-four hours and years of backstory are gone.
  • 3. The film can be described with one person, one space, and one choice.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The adaptation keeps one core event and one ch…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Time is compressed to twenty-four hours and ye…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not retell the event as a timeline; the audience needs a conflict, not an archive.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Take one filmable core from the real event:” and “Compress time to twenty-four hours and cut years”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • The adaptation keeps one core event and one character's decision.
  • Time is compressed to twenty-four hours and years of backstory are gone.
  • The film can be described with one person, one space, and one choice.

en.title: Table Read: Listen for Three Problems Only
en.summary: A table read tracks three problems only: unclear, boring, out of character. Do not turn it into a seminar.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Table Read: Listen for Three Problems Only

Story & Screenwriting / Screenplay

Table Read: Listen for Three Problems Only

A table read tracks three problems only: unclear, boring, out of character. Do not turn it into a seminar.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Bring two people who do not know the story, read it start to finish without interruption. Log three columns: unclear, boring, unbelievable. Do not log “add a shot here”; that is the next pass.

A table read logs three kinds of problem

After the read ask what they think the character wants, then which line felt most false. Those answers beat praise.

Limits

A table read is not a performance review. Do not rewrite a line because someone read it flat; first decide whether the line or the reading is the problem.

On set

Hand out three colors: blue for confusing, red for boring, yellow for false character. Discuss at most three notes per act; do not rewrite line by line.

Do this

A table read logs three problems: confusing, boring, out of character. It is not a script seminar.

  1. Use three sticky notes: blue for confusing, red for boring, yellow for out of character.
  2. Discuss at most three notes per act; do not rewrite every line.
  3. After the read, fix only the repeat note and log the rest for the next round.

Avoid

Do not turn the read into a line-by-line rewrite; ten pages changed overnight collapse the next day.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Three problem types are separated by color and not mixed in discussion.
  • 2. No act discusses more than three notes and no line-by-line rewrite happens.
  • 3. Only one repeated problem is changed after the read; the rest are logged.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Three problem types are separated by color and…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“No act discusses more than three notes and no…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not turn the read into a line-by-line rewrite; ten pages changed overnight collapse the next day.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Use three sticky notes: blue for confusing, red” and “Discuss at most three notes per act; do”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Three problem types are separated by color and not mixed in discussion.
  • No act discusses more than three notes and no line-by-line rewrite happens.
  • Only one repeated problem is changed after the read; the rest are logged.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: pre-casting read

A pre-casting read is not a performance; it is listening for structure. Let different actors read the same scene and hear who gives the lines a want; do not listen for who sounds like the character. Note only three questions: which line is unclear, which scene has no change, whose decision comes too late.

Do not direct and do not give emotion; let actors sit and read the words. Sitting exposes the writing; standing performance covers structure.

Condition B: full-crew read before shooting

The full-crew read is not for memorising lines; it lets departments hear where money, time or space is needed. Camera hears blocking, sound hears unclear lines, art hears props, producing hears scene count. After the read each department names one thing that must be prepared in advance, not ten.

Read in shooting order, not script order, to catch too many company moves in one day, costume changes that cannot happen and repeated props. The read is not a creative meeting; it is a risk meeting.

Counterexample: the read becomes a performance

At a read, actors stand and perform, the director gives emotion, everyone applauds. The room is lively, but nobody notices scene two and scene five say the same thing. After two shoot days, the edit reveals the repetition.

Split the read: first sitting, structure only; then standing, action only. Structure before performance, not performance first. Keep music off during the sitting read; do not let mood cover the problem.

Reusable model

Three questions → one risk sheet → one advance action. The read records three questions; each department writes one risk sheet; each department takes one advance action. The value is not applause; it is one less stop on set.

Send the three questions to the writer and the risk sheets to the producer the same day. Do not wait for the shoot. Problems are cheaper early.

en.title: Scene Transitions: Carry an Action Across the Cut
en.summary: Carry an action, a sound, or an object across the cut instead of using a title card to explain time.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Scene Transitions: Carry an Action Across the Cut

Story & Screenwriting / Screenplay

Scene Transitions: Carry an Action Across the Cut

Carry an action, a sound, or an object across the cut instead of using a title card to explain time.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

A scene change is not “then he went to the office.” Write what the last action left behind: he slams the door and it is still ringing; she sets down a cup and someone else holds it. Consequence connects the spaces.

Write the consequence of an action, not “then”

End each scene on an unfinished action and catch it at the next opening; the audience fills in time.

Limits

A transition is not a title card. “Three days later” is weaker than stubble, light or wardrobe; titles are the last resort.

On set

Find a shared action between scenes: close a door, then open one; pick up a cup, then put it down. Let action carry the time jump.

Do this

Connect scenes with action, sound, or an object, not a title card saying “three days later.”

  1. Find a shared action: door closes in one scene, opens in the next.
  2. Or a shared object: cup picked up, then set down.
  3. Use sound arriving early or late to bridge the spaces without a card.

Avoid

Do not use a title card for time; if an action can bridge it, do not write it.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Adjacent scenes share at least one action, object, or sound.
  • 2. The time jump reads without a title card.
  • 3. Remove the card and the audience can still say how much time passed or where they are.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Adjacent scenes share at least one action, obj…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The time jump reads without a title card”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use a title card for time; if an action can bridge it, do not write it.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Find a shared action: door closes in one” and “Or a shared object: cup picked up, then”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Adjacent scenes share at least one action, object, or sound.
  • The time jump reads without a title card.
  • Remove the card and the audience can still say how much time passed or where they are.

en.title: Comedy: Build the Expectation, Then Break It
en.summary: Comedy lets the audience predict the next beat, then removes one crucial condition.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Comedy: Build the Expectation, Then Break It

Story & Screenwriting / Screenplay

Comedy: Build the Expectation, Then Break It

Comedy lets the audience predict the next beat, then removes one crucial condition.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Comedy lets the audience predict the next beat, then removes one key condition.

On set

Write the three steps the audience expects, then replace the second with something plausible but wrong. Do not explain the joke; let the character stay serious.

Do this

  1. Write the three steps the audience expects.
  2. Replace step two with something logical but wrong.
  3. Do not explain the joke; let the character keep treating it seriously.

Avoid

Do not explain the joke; when the character laughs, the audience stops.

Three causes

For “Comedy: Build the Expectation, Then Break It”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
No expectationThe audience does not know what the character believes, so the joke has no targetWrite one false belief the character trusts
Character is too cleverIf the character knows it is funny, the audience does not laughLet them take a small thing seriously
Too slowThe setup runs long and attention leaves before the payoffCompress the setup to three beats

On-set diagnosis

  1. Mark setup and payoff. If the pattern is not repeated before the payoff, expectation is missing.
  2. Ask someone who has not seen it whether they expected that; if not, the setup is too thin.
  3. Cut half the lines before the joke and see whether it still works.

Fix

Comedy is not telling jokes; it is letting someone take an unwise task seriously. Build expectation, then let it fail in a concrete way.

  1. Use three beats: establish the rule, repeat it, break it.
  2. Give the character a wrong method for a concrete problem: wrong key, wrong jacket.
  3. Land the joke on an action or prop, not an explanation.
  4. Put the second laugh on a reaction, not a line.

Failure cases

With “Comedy: Build the Expectation, Then Break It”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Explain the jokeTelling the audience it is funny kills the laughRemove explanation and keep the action
Character performs funnyThe audience watches the performance, not the personLet them be serious
Long setupAttention is gone by the payoffDeliver the first change within three beats

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
ExpectationSetup and payoff are identifiableMark each beat
SeriousnessThe character does not know they are funnyReview with the actor
RhythmFirst change within three beatsTime it
ReactionA reaction shot follows the jokePlayback

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The first two steps set a clear expectation and the third is predictable.
  • 2. Only one condition breaks; the rest stays logical.
  • 3. The character neither explains nor laughs and keeps treating the error seriously.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The first two steps set a clear expectation an…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Only one condition breaks; the rest stays logi…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not explain the joke; when the character laughs, the audience stops.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Write the three steps the audience expects.” and “Replace step two with something logical but wrong.”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • The first two steps set a clear expectation and the third is predictable.
  • Only one condition breaks; the rest stays logical.
  • The character neither explains nor laughs and keeps treating the error seriously.

en.summary: An insert can replace a line: a shaking hand, a cup rim, an open door.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Insert Shot: One Detail Beats One Line

Story & Screenwriting / Storyboard

Insert Shot: One Detail Beats One Line

An insert can replace a line: a shaking hand, a cup rim, an open door.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Prepare two or three inserts per scene: hand action, prop state, environment detail. They must cut anywhere into the master and help hide jumps, pace the scene or add information.

Inserts are the edit's breath, not random scenery

Shoot five seconds of head and tail around the action; one second at the center leaves no room.

Limits

Inserts cannot replace a missing master. If the space is unclear, ten close-ups will not explain it; protect the master first.

On set

List three shootable details per scene: fingers, a cup rim, a door gap. Cut to one for 1 to 2 seconds before the key line, with no explanation.

Do this

An insert can replace a line: a shaking hand, a cup rim, an unclosed door says more than explanation.

  1. List three filmable details per scene: fingers, cup rim, door gap.
  2. Cut one in one to two seconds before the key line.
  3. Do not add explanation; let the detail speak.

Avoid

Do not use an insert as decoration; if it carries no information, cut it.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The insert carries a specific piece of information, not just beauty.
  • 2. It runs one to two seconds and cuts before the key line.
  • 3. Remove it and information goes missing, proving it replaced a line.

Failures

  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“It runs one to two seconds and cuts before the…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.

Extend

en.title: Sequence Board: Shoot the Scene, Not the Script
en.summary: A sequence board does not illustrate every line; it decides what the audience sees first.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Sequence Board: Shoot the Scene, Not the Script

Story & Screenwriting / Storyboard

Sequence Board: Shoot the Scene, Not the Script

A sequence board does not illustrate every line; it decides what the audience sees first.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

A sequence board is not a spread of beautiful panels. First decide how the previous shot ends and how the next begins. Each cut names the match—action, gaze or sound—then the panels fill in.

Lay out the cuts before drawing panels

Use a landscape sheet: shot number on the left, cut logic on the right. If two panels do not connect, fix the cut before the drawing.

Limits

Panels do not need finish, but each must answer why it sits here rather than before or after.

On set

Draw three panels for one scene: what the audience sees first, what is hidden, what is revealed last. Then fill the middle; do not illustrate every line.

Do this

  1. Draw three panels: what to show first, what to hide, what to reveal last.
  2. Fill the middle shots so information releases in order.
  3. Board information, not one panel per line.

Avoid

Do not draw one panel per line; a board is information order, not illustration.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The first three panels show what is shown, hidden, and revealed last.
  • 2. Middle shots fill by information order, not line count.
  • 3. A third person can repeat the release order from the board.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The first three panels show what is shown, hid…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Middle shots fill by information order, not li…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not draw one panel per line; a board is information order, not illustration.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Draw three panels: what to show first, what” and “Fill the middle shots so information releases in”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • The first three panels show what is shown, hidden, and revealed last.
  • Middle shots fill by information order, not line count.
  • A third person can repeat the release order from the board.

en.title: Animatic: Time the Scene Before You Draw It
en.summary: An animatic fixes shot length and cut points first; rough drawings are fine, wrong rhythm is not.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Animatic: Time the Scene Before You Draw It

Story & Screenwriting / Storyboard

Animatic: Time the Scene Before You Draw It

An animatic fixes shot length and cut points first; rough drawings are fine, wrong rhythm is not.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

The first job is timing, not drawing. Mark seconds per shot and record voice first; let sound length set the shot. Do not draw everything then add voice; pacing will be wrong.

Animatic sets shot length first

Use simple lines and temp sound to test whether actions connect; if not, return to the board, not effects.

Limits

An animatic is not a final. It can be rough, but order, duration and action direction must be locked; changing them later is a rebuild.

On set

Record the lines on a phone and time them at real speed. Put each shot's duration into the board before drawing; keep the total under 110 percent of the target length.

Do this

An animatic fixes shot duration and cut points first; rough drawings are fine, wrong rhythm is not.

  1. Record the dialogue on a phone and time it at real speaking speed.
  2. Write seconds into every panel, then draw.
  3. Keep total length within 110 percent of the target.

Avoid

Do not draw pretty frames before timing; wrong rhythm forces a redraw.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Every shot duration comes from recorded speech at real speed, not a guess.
  • 2. Each panel has a duration and total length stays within 110 percent of target.
  • 3. Playback at those seconds lines up with the intended cut points.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Every shot duration comes from recorded speech…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Each panel has a duration and total length sta…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not draw pretty frames before timing; wrong rhythm forces a redraw.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Record the dialogue on a phone and time” and “Write seconds into every panel, then draw.”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Every shot duration comes from recorded speech at real speed, not a guess.
  • Each panel has a duration and total length stays within 110 percent of target.
  • Playback at those seconds lines up with the intended cut points.

en.title: Board Review: Let Camera and Edit Find the Gaps
en.summary: In a board review, camera finds positions, edit finds gaps, and the director chooses three panels to fix.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Board Review: Let Camera and Edit Find the Gaps

Story & Screenwriting / Storyboard

Board Review: Let Camera and Edit Find the Gaps

In a board review, camera finds positions, edit finds gaps, and the director chooses three panels to fix.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Go through four columns: who acts, where the camera is, what is needed, and how long. A beautiful panel with no camera position still cannot be shot.

Review the board for shootability, not drawing quality

Ask camera and edit each for one “how I would shoot/cut this” question. Specific questions expose gaps early.

Limits

A review is not a vote. Do not reject a panel with “it feels wrong”; name whether action, space or time is unclear.

On set

Before the review, give the DP a camera-question list and the editor a gap list. Change only three panels in the meeting; log the rest for the next pass.

Do this

Board review lets camera flag setups and edit flag gaps; the director then changes three panels.

  1. Give the DP a setup question list and the editor a gap list.
  2. Change only three panels in the meeting; log the rest for next round.
  3. The director decides last; nobody redraws the whole board at once.

Avoid

Do not redraw the whole board in review; three panels per round is what ships.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Camera and edit each arrive with a question list.
  • 2. Only three panels change in the meeting and the rest are logged.
  • 3. After the three changes, setups and edit gaps improve concretely.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Camera and edit each arrive with a question li…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Only three panels change in the meeting and th…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not redraw the whole board in review; three panels per round is what ships.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Give the DP a setup question list and” and “Change only three panels in the meeting; log”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Camera and edit each arrive with a question list.
  • Only three panels change in the meeting and the rest are logged.
  • After the three changes, setups and edit gaps improve concretely.

en.title: Adjusting Actors: Give Verbs, Not Adjectives
en.summary: Give actors verbs: slower, hold the anger, do not touch her. Never "be more natural."
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Adjusting Actors: Give Verbs, Not Adjectives

Story & Screenwriting / Directing

Adjusting Actors: Give Verbs, Not Adjectives

Give actors verbs: slower, hold the anger, do not touch her. Never "be more natural."

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

“Be sadder” rarely works. Replace it with a playable action: push the cup to the edge, glance then look down, stop mid-sentence. Change the action and the feeling follows.

Give an action, not an emotion adjective

Adjust one action at a time. Three notes at once split attention and leave only “acting.”

Limits

Do not perform it for them. A demonstration is allowed, but they must then do it their way; a copy puts a second director in the frame.

On set

Give one verb at a time, then watch the take. If it is still wrong, change the verb, not the adjective. When the actor asks why, say do it first, we will talk after.

Do this

Give the actor a verb: walk slower, hold the anger, do not touch her. Never “be more natural.”

  1. Give one verb at a time, then watch playback.
  2. If it is still wrong, change the verb, not the adjective.
  3. If the actor asks why, say “do it first, we'll explain after.”

Avoid

Do not give three adjectives at once; the actor plays “confused,” not the character.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Each adjustment gives one verb with no adjective stack.
  • 2. Two takes differ by one variable and the difference can be named.
  • 3. The actor can repeat their next action.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Each adjustment gives one verb with no adjecti…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Two takes differ by one variable and the diffe…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not give three adjectives at once; the actor plays “confused,” not the character.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Give one verb at a time, then watch” and “If it is still wrong, change the verb,”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Each adjustment gives one verb with no adjective stack.
  • Two takes differ by one variable and the difference can be named.
  • The actor can repeat their next action.

en.title: Ensemble Scene: Give Everyone a Task
en.summary: In an ensemble scene everyone has a task; only then does the space feel real instead of a row of waiting actors.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Ensemble Scene: Give Everyone a Task

Story & Screenwriting / Directing

Ensemble Scene: Give Everyone a Task

In an ensemble scene everyone has a task; only then does the space feel real instead of a row of waiting actors.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

A group scene is chaotic not because there are many people but because power is unclear. Draw a gaze map: who wants to speak, who blocks, who watches. Every position and look answers those three questions.

Ensemble scenes start with who watches whom

Give each person a continuous action—pour water, collect cups, flick a lighter. Actions layer the scene without everyone speaking.

Limits

Ensemble is not equal dialogue. Someone can be silent the whole scene, but their reaction must change the pressure.

On set

In an ensemble scene, give everyone an action and an objective: one looks for keys, one avoids a call, one waits for someone. Fill a page before rolling.

Do this

In an ensemble scene everyone has something to do; otherwise it is a row waiting for lines.

  1. Give each person an action and a goal: find keys, avoid a call, wait for someone.
  2. Fill one page before rolling so nobody stands empty in the background.
  3. Let the actions interfere so relationships appear.

Avoid

Do not line up extras waiting for lines; an empty background makes the space fake.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Everyone in frame has an action and a goal; nobody stands empty.
  • 2. At least two actions interfere and a relationship becomes visible.
  • 3. Remove any one action and the space visibly empties.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Everyone in frame has an action and a goal; no…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“At least two actions interfere and a relations…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not line up extras waiting for lines; an empty background makes the space fake.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Give each person an action and a goal:” and “Fill one page before rolling so nobody stands”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Everyone in frame has an action and a goal; nobody stands empty.
  • At least two actions interfere and a relationship becomes visible.
  • Remove any one action and the space visibly empties.

en.title: Performance Scale: Closer Camera, Smaller Action
en.summary: The closer the camera, the smaller the action; a gesture that works wide looks acted in a close-up.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Performance Scale: Closer Camera, Smaller Action

Story & Screenwriting / Directing

Performance Scale: Closer Camera, Smaller Action

The closer the camera, the smaller the action; a gesture that works wide looks acted in a close-up.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Small action is invisible in a wide; exaggeration looks false in a close-up. Lock the framing, then the scale: wides use body and blocking, closes use breath, eyes and fingers.

Framing sets the size of performance

When a scene has both, let the actor play two scales. Do not use one scale for every shot size.

Limits

“Cinematic” does not mean permanently restrained. What should be big must read in a wide; what should be small must not mug in a close.

On set

Rehearse the wide with large gestures, then halve them for the close-up. Before the close-up, shoot a hand insert to check the action does not look performed.

Do this

The closer the shot, the smaller the action; a gesture that works wide looks theatrical close.

  1. Rehearse the wide with larger actions so spatial relationships read.
  2. Before the close-up, ask the actor to halve the action.
  3. Shoot a hand close-up first and confirm it does not look performed.

Avoid

Do not use one performance scale for every size; the close-up magnifies acting.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Wide and close actions differ visibly, with the close halved.
  • 2. The hand close-up looks natural in joints and pressure.
  • 3. Put the close action back into the wide and it feels too small, proving the scale.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Wide and close actions differ visibly, with th…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The hand close-up looks natural in joints and…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use one performance scale for every size; the close-up magnifies acting.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Rehearse the wide with larger actions so spatial” and “Before the close-up, ask the actor to halve”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Wide and close actions differ visibly, with the close halved.
  • The hand close-up looks natural in joints and pressure.
  • Put the close action back into the wide and it feels too small, proving the scale.

en.title: Callback: Compare the Same Action
en.summary: In a callback, do not give a new scene; give the same action and compare.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Callback: Compare the Same Action

Story & Screenwriting / Directing

Callback: Compare the Same Action

In a callback, do not give a new scene; give the same action and compare.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Callbacks should compare the same action, not new monologues.

On set

Callback with the same 30-second action: enter, search, notice something wrong. Use the same camera and lines for both actors, then compare the takes.

Do this

  1. Give the same thirty-second task: enter, search, notice something wrong.
  2. Use the same camera position and same lines for both actors.
  3. Compare reactions on playback, not who is more likable.

Avoid

Do not give each actor a different scene; different material makes comparison useless.

Three causes

For “Callback: Compare the Same Action”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Reading onlyThe callback repeats the first-round scene and the director sees no changeUse the same scene with two different intentions
No contrastBoth versions are identical, so range is invisibleAsk for one restrained and one outgoing version
No adjustmentThe actor can only perform the prepared versionGive one new action and watch the response

On-set diagnosis

  1. Prepare a 30-second action, not just lines.
  2. Ask for one version that wants to stay and one that wants to leave; compare the body.
  3. Give one new instruction: put the cup down before answering. See whether the actor can absorb it.

Fix

A callback is not another first-round read; it tests whether the actor can change under pressure. Use the same material so range becomes visible.

  1. Fix one action and two lines; every candidate uses the same material.
  2. Ask for two different intentions, not two different tones.
  3. Give one adjustment and log how quickly the actor takes it.
  4. Shoot one wide and one close; check that the performance holds at both sizes.

Failure cases

With “Callback: Compare the Same Action”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Repeat the same versionYou see polish, not rangeRequire a second intention
Talk onlyThe callback becomes an interview and never tests the frameShoot at least one take
Abstract direction“More sincere” is not executableGive an action and an object

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
Same materialEvery candidate uses the same action and linesCallback sheet
Two versionsThe intentions differ and the body shows itCompare playback
AdjustmentThe actor changes after one noteLog on set
SizesOne usable wide and closeReview footage

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Both actors perform the same thirty-second task with identical lines.
  • 2. Camera, lens, and light match so the takes can play side by side.
  • 3. Comparison addresses reaction and action, not likability.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Both actors perform the same thirty-second tas…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Camera, lens, and light match so the takes can…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not give each actor a different scene; different material makes comparison useless.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Give the same thirty-second task: enter, search, notice” and “Use the same camera position and same lines”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Both actors perform the same thirty-second task with identical lines.
  • Camera, lens, and light match so the takes can play side by side.
  • Comparison addresses reaction and action, not likability.

Boundary

This page only covers “Callback: Compare the Same Action”; it does not replace Character Arc: Not Better, Different Choices, Directing Children: Give a Task, Not a Line Reading, Composition: Tell the Eye Where to Look. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

en.title: Directing Children: Give a Task, Not a Line Reading
en.summary: With children, give a task, not an instruction: hand me the cup beats "look sad."
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Directing Children: Give a Task, Not a Line Reading

Story & Screenwriting / Directing

Directing Children: Give a Task, Not a Line Reading

With children, give a task, not an instruction: hand me the cup beats "look sad."

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

Put child-actor rules on the call sheet: maximum hours, breaks and meals, guardian always present, no closed room alone, no dangerous action.

Protect rest and guardianship before performance

Explain any content the child should not see in advance. Direct through games and concrete actions, not emotional manipulation like “imagine your mother died.”

Limits

A child's nod is not consent. The guardian can stop at any time; if the child becomes distressed later, delete the footage.

On set

Give the child a concrete task and a time limit: put three things from the table into a bag in 30 seconds. Never say act natural.

Do this

Direct children with tasks, not instructions: hand me the cup works better than “look sad.”

  1. Give a concrete task and a time limit: put three things in a bag in thirty seconds.
  2. Do not say “act natural”; state the task and the boundary.
  3. Give feedback right after the take and do not leave the child waiting.

Avoid

Do not ask a child to perform an emotion; a clear task produces the reaction.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The child receives a concrete task and time limit, not an emotion direction.
  • 2. Nobody says “be natural” or “look sad” during the take.
  • 3. Feedback arrives right after the task and the child is not left waiting.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The child receives a concrete task and time li…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Nobody says “be natural” or “look sad” during…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not ask a child to perform an emotion; a clear task produces the reaction.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Give a concrete task and a time limit:” and “Do not say “act natural”; state the task”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • The child receives a concrete task and time limit, not an emotion direction.
  • Nobody says “be natural” or “look sad” during the take.
  • Feedback arrives right after the task and the child is not left waiting.

Author and test note

2026-11-25
Author

TVCN Story Desk

Review

en.title: Directing Debut: Protect Performance Before Coverage
en.summary: On a first directing job, protect the performance and the scene before chasing more coverage.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Directing Debut: Protect Performance Before Coverage

Story & Screenwriting / Directing

Directing Debut: Protect Performance Before Coverage

On a first directing job, protect the performance and the scene before chasing more coverage.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

First-time directors overestimate three things: shoot days, actor availability and post patience. Write three to five scenes, two to three characters, one main location. Every extra location adds a permit, a move and weather risk.

Your first feature should be the one you can finish

Compress the must-get list to one page and delete every “nice to have” shot before rolling.

Limits

Low budget is not an excuse. Fewer locations is not less content; spend the saved time on rehearsal and sound, not extra shots.

On set

On day one, stage one scene only. Shoot a wide and two close-ups; simplify light and camera so the actor gets full performance time.

Do this

On a first directing job, protect the actor and one scene before adding setups.

  1. Schedule only one scene on day one.
  2. Shoot a wide and two close-ups so a full performance exists.
  3. Simplify light and camera and leave time for rehearsal and another take.

Avoid

Do not schedule ten scenes on day one; more setups mean no complete performance.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Day one has one scene and the actor gets full rehearsal time.
  • 2. A wide and two close-ups exist, so more than one complete performance is usable.
  • 3. Light and setup count stay low enough to wrap on time.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Day one has one scene and the actor gets full…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“A wide and two close-ups exist, so more than o…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not schedule ten scenes on day one; more setups mean no complete performance.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Schedule only one scene on day one.” and “Shoot a wide and two close-ups so a”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Day one has one scene and the actor gets full rehearsal time.
  • A wide and two close-ups exist, so more than one complete performance is usable.
  • Light and setup count stay low enough to wrap on time.

en.title: Notes to Actors: One Executable Sentence
en.summary: One executable sentence is enough for an actor; three suggestions add up to none.
en.html:
Home/Story & Screenwriting/Notes to Actors: One Executable Sentence

Story & Screenwriting / Directing

Notes to Actors: One Executable Sentence

One executable sentence is enough for an actor; three suggestions add up to none.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN Story DeskEdited 2026-11

One executable note is enough; three suggestions equal none.

On set

Write the note as one change for the next take: walk half a beat slower, look at the cup before the person. Say it, let them do it, and stop talking.

Do this

  1. Write the next take as one change: walk half a beat slower.
  2. Or eyes go to the cup first, then the person.
  3. Say it, let the actor do it, and stop adding explanation.

Avoid

Do not give three notes at once; the actor can execute one.

Three causes

For “Notes to Actors: One Executable Sentence”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Too many adjectives“More natural” or “more pain” leaves the actor guessingReplace with one verb and one object
Three notes at onceThe actor fixes one and loses the othersGive one note, shoot, then give the next
Negative notes“Don’t do that” does not say what to doSay what to do instead

On-set diagnosis

  1. Ask the actor to repeat the note; if they cannot, it is too abstract.
  2. In playback, ask what they were doing before giving the note.
  3. Compress the note into one verb sentence: put the cup down, then look at him.

Fix

A note to an actor is not a review of performance; it is the next action. One executable sentence beats five feelings.

  1. Use verb + object + timing: hold half a beat before the door, then look.
  2. Give one note at a time: shoot, review, then the next.
  3. Name what works before the adjustment; do not restart from zero.
  4. Ask the actor to repeat the note so you can hear whether it landed as action.

Failure cases

With “Notes to Actors: One Executable Sentence”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Say “be more natural”The actor does not know natural toward whatGive a concrete action
Give five notesOnly the last one survivesOne at a time
Criticise in front of the crewThe actor defends and tightensGive notes privately

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
ExecutableThe note is an action, not an adjectiveActor repeats it
CountOne note at a timeSet log
EffectThe next take shows a visible changeCompare playback
RespectThe note addresses the work, not the personActor feedback

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Each note contains one executable action.
  • 2. The actor can do it immediately without asking “how exactly.”
  • 3. The next take changes only that one thing and holds the rest.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Each note contains one executable action”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The actor can do it immediately without asking…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not give three notes at once; the actor can execute one.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Write one 30-second scene with only “Write the next take as one change: walk” and “Or eyes go to the cup first, then”. Cut every explanation and ask one person to retell what the character wants.

Check

  • Each note contains one executable action.
  • The actor can do it immediately without asking “how exactly.”
  • The next take changes only that one thing and holds the rest.

en.title: Frame Rate: Motion and Slow Motion
en.summary: Frame rate sets how motion feels; high speed does not slow time, it lets the eye study a moment.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Frame Rate: Motion and Slow Motion

Shooting / Camera

Frame Rate: Motion and Slow Motion

Frame rate sets how motion feels; high speed does not slow time, it lets the eye study a moment.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

Project frame rate drives sound, captions and platform compatibility; slow motion is a capture rate. 24/25/30 is the narrative base, 60/120 for later slowdown. Do not mix base rates in one project.

Set the project rate before slow motion

Choose capture rate by the slowdown: 2x needs 48/50/60; 4x needs 96/100/120.

Limits

High frame rate is not more cinematic. It makes action too smooth and weightless; narrative usually stays at 24/25, with slow motion only where needed.

On set

Shoot 25p for a 25p project. For a two-times slow motion, shoot 50p at 1/100 shutter and play back to check for flicker.

Do this

Frame rate decides how action feels in time. High-speed is not “slow”; it lets the audience see one instant. Decide the timeline and slow-motion factor before rolling.

  1. Shoot 25p for a 25p project; keep footage and timeline matched.
  2. For two-times slow motion, shoot 50p at 1/100 shutter.
  3. Review for flicker and decide which second the slow-motion beat belongs to.

Avoid

Do not treat high-speed as a post slap-on; decide at the shoot, because stretching later stutters.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Timeline and footage frame rates match; 50p is not dropped onto a 25p timeline as normal speed.
  • 2. The slow-motion shot uses 50p at 1/100 and shows no flicker.
  • 3. Slow motion is used only where the instant matters, not as decoration.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Timeline and footage frame rates match; 50p is…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The slow-motion shot uses 50p at 1/100 and sho…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not treat high-speed as a post slap-on; decide at the shoot, because stretching later stutters.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Shoot 25p for a 25p project; keep footage”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • Timeline and footage frame rates match; 50p is not dropped onto a 25p timeline as normal speed.
  • The slow-motion shot uses 50p at 1/100 and shows no flicker.
  • Slow motion is used only where the instant matters, not as decoration.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. Frame rate changes the feel of time. 24 looks like cinema, 50 like television, 120 exists to pull action apart.

Set the project rate first

Narrative uses 24 or 25; news and events use 25 or 30. Keep one rate for the whole piece, not one rate per shot.

Shutter is twice the frame rate: 1/48 or 1/50 at 24. Higher shutter makes motion look brittle.

Do the slow-motion math

120 fps on a 24 fps timeline is five times slow. Decide the multiplier before you shoot, or you will discover it is either not enough or unwatchable.

Slow motion needs more light and a higher shutter; meter indoors before committing. Do not use slow motion to rescue action that was never designed.

The mixed-rate trap

Mix 24 and 60 in one scene and playback stutters. Use one rate for the whole block and conform in the edit; do not cut 24 into 60.

Do not record sync sound for slow motion; dub the dialogue later. On-set audio is a reference, not a timeline track.

When slow motion earns its place

Slow motion is for one turn: a jump, an impact, a look back. Slow the whole film and nothing is emphasized.

Before high-speed, ask what the audience needs to see. If the answer is nothing, do not slow it.

Mark the frame rate on set

Write the frame rate on the slate and say it on the audio. Post should not guess whether the file is 24 or 120.

Put different rates in different folders and add fps to the filename. It saves one mistake at relink.

Ten frame-rate checks before rolling

  • One frame rate for the whole piece
  • Shutter is twice the frame rate
  • Calculate the slow-motion multiplier first
  • Confirm enough light before high-speed
  • Record separate reference audio for slow motion
  • Mixed rates only within one block
  • Timeline rate matches the footage
  • Check whether motion blur looks natural
  • Write the frame rate on the slate
  • Play the whole piece before export

Higher frame rate is not better. The audience wants the right sense of time, not the biggest number.

When you have five minutes

  • Set one rate for the piece
  • Shutter at twice the rate
  • Calculate the slow-motion factor
  • Confirm light before high-speed
  • Separate folders by rate
  • Write the rate on the slate

Frame rate is discipline before style; break the discipline and style becomes an accident. Check the project rate before the first slate; do not let the first take be wrong.
