en.title: Shutter Angle: The Amount of Blur
en.summary: Shutter angle controls motion blur. 180 degrees is a default, not a rule.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Shutter Angle: The Amount of Blur

Shooting / Camera

Shutter Angle: The Amount of Blur

Shutter angle controls motion blur. 180 degrees is a default, not a rule.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

1/50 at 25p or 1/48 at 24p approximates 180 degrees and film-like motion. A faster shutter sharpens the instant; a slower one lengthens blur but risks flicker and skew.

180 degrees is a start, not a law

Match mains: in 50Hz regions use 1/50 or 1/100, not 1/60, to avoid rolling bands.

Limits

Shutter is not an exposure tool. If light is low, add light or open the iris; slow shutter turns action to mud.

On set

At 25p use a 180-degree shutter, which is 1/50. Use 90 degrees for crisper action or 360 for more blur, but never fight the mains frequency.

Do this

Shutter angle controls motion blur. 180 degrees is a default, not the only answer. Calculate shutter from frame rate, then choose crisp or smeared.

  1. At 25p, use 180 degrees, which is 1/50.
  2. Use 90 degrees for crisper action or 360 degrees for more smear.
  3. Test under 50Hz lights and confirm there is no flicker or banding.

Avoid

Do not use 180 degrees for every action, and do not let shutter fight 50Hz lighting.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Shutter is calculated from frame rate and angle, not guessed.
  • 2. Motion blur matches the choice: crisp action or softer smear.
  • 3. Playback under location lights shows no flicker, banding, or rolling bars.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Shutter is calculated from frame rate and angl…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Motion blur matches the choice: crisp action o…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use 180 degrees for every action, and do not let shutter fight 50Hz lighting.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “At 25p, use 180 degrees, which is 1/50.”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • Shutter is calculated from frame rate and angle, not guessed.
  • Motion blur matches the choice: crisp action or softer smear.
  • Playback under location lights shows no flicker, banding, or rolling bars.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. Shutter angle decides motion blur. Make movement look natural before you make it look like a style.

Start at 180 degrees

Use 1/48 or 1/50 at 24 fps, 1/50 at 25, 1/60 at 30, 1/100 at 50, and 1/240 at 120. That 180-degree shutter gives motion a natural trail; it is not a cinematic ornament.

If the project is 25 fps, do not copy 1/48 from a 24 fps job; the difference shows in a fast pan.

The amount of blur is information

A hand passing, a car crossing, a head turning: 180 degrees gives the audience direction. To freeze motion, go to 1/250 or 1/500; the action turns brittle. For more smear, drop to 1/25, but lights may flicker.

In 50Hz countries use 1/50 or 1/100 under fluorescents; in 60Hz use 1/60 or 1/120. Shoot a test and play it back; do not guess.

Slow motion needs light

At 120 fps, a 180-degree shutter is 1/240, more than two stops less light; add a lamp indoors or open the aperture. LEDs can flicker too, so shoot a slow-motion test and look for rolling bands.

Do not use slow motion to rescue action that was never designed. Slowing it down only makes the emptiness clearer.

Shoot three tests before you commit

Shoot the first at 180 degrees, the second one stop faster, the third one stop slower; repeat the same action and compare smear and flicker on playback.

If the frame has a screen, LED, or car light, check for rolling bands and flicker first. Shutter is not the only variable; lights and frame rate change the result too.

Write the chosen value on the shot sheet and do not change it by feel at the next setup. One shutter change on set means another motion match in post.

Ten shutter checks

  • Confirm the project frame rate
  • Set shutter at twice the rate
  • Use 1/50 or 1/100 under 50Hz light
  • Use 1/60 or 1/120 under 60Hz light
  • Play back a fast-action test
  • Calculate light loss before high-speed
  • Confirm the lights do not flicker
  • Recalculate ND and aperture together
  • Keep some blur in action
  • Do not hide bad action behind a high shutter

Shutter serves movement first and style second; if the action is unclear, style is just noise.

en.title: ND Filter: Wide Open in Daylight
en.summary: An ND filter does not darken a picture; it lets you stay wide open in daylight and keep your depth.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/ND Filter: Wide Open in Daylight

Shooting / Camera

ND Filter: Wide Open in Daylight

An ND filter does not darken a picture; it lets you stay wide open in daylight and keep your depth.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

ND restores a cinematic shutter without overexposure. Calculate the gap from target aperture, 1/50 shutter and current ISO, then choose the filter; do not guess by “it looks dark.”

Calculate ND stops, then check IR

Strong ND can cause IR cast, turning black fabric purple. Use IR-suppressed ND or shoot a color chart comparison.

Limits

ND is not a substitute for stopping down. It matters when you need F1.4; at F8, stop the lens first and then consider ND.

On set

At noon, f/2.8, ISO 100, start with a 6-stop ND. If the shutter is still above 1/50, add 3 stops. On a variable ND, twist to the lightest setting first to avoid the cross pattern.

Do this

ND is not about darkening the image; it lets you hold a wide aperture and shallow depth in daylight. Set shutter and aperture first, then calculate the stops.

  1. At noon, f/2.8, ISO 100, start with a 6-stop ND.
  2. If shutter is still above 1/50, add 3 stops until it returns to target.
  3. With a variable ND, start at the lightest setting and increase gradually to avoid cross patterns.

Avoid

Do not add ND and leave aperture or shutter uncorrected; do not crank a variable ND to its darkest setting.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. At wide aperture in daylight, shutter stays near 1/50 and depth of field is not sacrificed.
  • 2. The variable ND shows no cross pattern or color shift.
  • 3. Highlights are protected without underexposing the whole frame.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“At wide aperture in daylight, shutter stays ne…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The variable ND shows no cross pattern or colo…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not add ND and leave aperture or shutter uncorrected; do not crank a variable ND to its darkest setting.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “At noon, f/2.8, ISO 100, start with a”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • At wide aperture in daylight, shutter stays near 1/50 and depth of field is not sacrificed.
  • The variable ND shows no cross pattern or color shift.
  • Highlights are protected without underexposing the whole frame.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. ND is daylight aperture insurance. Without it you either overexpose or stop down until the depth of field disappears.

Shutter first, aperture second

Outside in daylight, set a 180-degree shutter; if you want a wide aperture, you need ND. Calculate total light first, then choose the strength; do not buy a filter and look for an exposure afterward.

Do not use a high shutter to control exposure; motion turns brittle. ND returns the shutter to its natural place; it is not decoration.

How the stops add up

One stop halves the light; two stops cut three quarters. On a variable ND, screw to maximum density first, then back to the target, to avoid the cross shadow.

Minimum density differs by lens, and wides vignette sooner. Test every lens before the shoot, not on location.

Color cast and infrared

Cheap ND goes green or magenta, and white balance cannot fully save it. Shoot a gray card and correct later; if it is severe, change the filter.

Black synthetics turn purple in strong sun from infrared pollution. Add an IR cut or change the filter; do not force the blacks in post.

ND and polarizers are different

ND cuts all light; a polarizer cuts reflections. Water and glass need a polarizer; a wide aperture needs ND.

Stack ND first, then the polarizer; reverse the order and you get vignetting.

Recheck after a lens change

The same ND passes different light on different lenses, especially fast ones. Meter again after a lens change.

A zoom can differ from wide to long end; test one frame at each before the take.

Ten checks before adding ND

  • Set shutter before aperture
  • Calculate total light
  • Remember one stop halves the light
  • Screw variable ND to maximum first
  • Test wides for vignetting
  • Shoot a gray card
  • Check for green or magenta
  • Check black synthetics for infrared
  • Clean both sides of the filter
  • Meter again after a lens change

Use ND well and the audience sees shallow depth; use it badly and they see a color cast and vignette.

When you have five minutes

  • Shutter first, aperture second
  • Calculate total light
  • Screw variable ND to maximum
  • Test wides for vignetting
  • Shoot a gray card
  • Clean both sides of the filter

ND returns the image to natural exposure; it is not a decoration that makes the frame darker. Price is not the test; first confirm no color cast and no vignette. Look again before and after a lens change.

en.title: False Color: Find the Clip at a Glance
en.summary: False color turns brightness into bands, so clipped skin or a dead sky is obvious at a glance.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/False Color: Find the Clip at a Glance

Shooting / Exposure

False Color: Find the Clip at a Glance

False color turns brightness into bands, so clipped skin or a dead sky is obvious at a glance.

3 min read · Exposure toolTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

False color maps luminance into color blocks, so overexposed skin or a dead sky is obvious. Check skin first, then highlights.

On set

Put the face in the skin patch and keep the sky out of red. Change the light first, not the ISO.

Do this

  1. Put the face in the skin-tone zone with no red warning.
  2. Keep the sky out of red so highlight detail survives.
  3. Change light or add ND first; do not raise ISO to compensate.

Avoid

Do not treat false color as a look; red is a warning, not a style.

Calibrate the monitor first

False colour is not a universal standard: brands map 70–90% luminance to different colours. Confirm the skin-tone band, highlight warning and overexposure red on your monitor. Never judge from the camera LCD.

Set zebra to 95%: false colour shows distribution, the waveform shows values. When they disagree, trust the waveform and the Log/Raw headroom. False colour is a locator, not a meter.

Lighting order

  1. Set the key light first and put the face in the skin-tone band. Do not raise ISO to brighten the background.
  2. Then treat windows and practicals: add ND, change bulbs or draw curtains so highlights leave the red.
  3. Check the shadows last: keep some texture in black clothing; do not crush the dark side to save the highlight.

Without ND, change the light position or camera angle first. ISO is for the last third of a stop, not for rescuing three stops of overexposure.

False-colour misreads

  1. Treating red as a look: red is a warning, not a LUT. Lower the highlight first, then talk about tone.
  2. Checking the face but not the window: the face is fine, the window is pure white and cannot be recovered.
  3. Judging on the camera LCD: its brightness changes with the room. Use an external monitor or the waveform.
  4. Assuming every camera maps colour the same: confirm each body’s false-colour scale.

Exposure acceptance log

  • The face sits in the skin-tone band with no red patch; nose and forehead are not the first to clip.
  • Windows, bulbs and white walls retain layers; highlights are not a flat white block.
  • Black clothing still shows folds; shadows are not a single black mass.
  • Log EI, ND setting, light position and monitor model; recheck after a lens change.

Exposure log

One line per setup: body, EI, ND, key position, monitor model, brightest window reading and the face’s false-colour band. Recheck after a lens or window change; do not reuse the previous setup’s exposure.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The face sits in the skin zone with no red patch.
  • 2. Sky and windows are not red and highlights retain gradation.
  • 3. The fix came from light or ND, not from pushing ISO.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The face sits in the skin zone with no red pat…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Sky and windows are not red and highlights ret…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not treat false color as a look; red is a warning, not a style.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Put the face in the skin-tone zone with”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • The face sits in the skin zone with no red patch.
  • Sky and windows are not red and highlights retain gradation.
  • The fix came from light or ND, not from pushing ISO.

en.title: Log Footage: Shoot for the Grade
en.summary: Log is not "flat looks pro"; it preserves highlights and shadows for post, if exposure and color are handled.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Log Footage: Shoot for the Grade

Shooting / Exposure

Log Footage: Shoot for the Grade

Log is not "flat looks pro"; it preserves highlights and shadows for post, if exposure and color are handled.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

Log is not “brighter is better.” Expose with one to one-and-a-half stops of highlight headroom, midtones in the middle of the waveform; shadows may underexpose but must not crush. Use false color or zebra, not the monitor LUT.

Log protects highlights, then midtones

Apply the conversion LUT first, then primary and look. Do not use one LUT across different cameras and ISOs.

Limits

Log is not free latitude. Noise still exists at high ISO; light the scene rather than lifting in post.

On set

Expose the face slightly above middle grey and use the waveform to keep highlights off the ceiling. Shoot a color chart before the take so post has a reference.

Do this

Log is not a “flat look”; it reserves highlight and shadow range for post, provided exposure and color management are right. Shoot for the grade.

  1. Expose the face slightly above middle gray and confirm on the waveform.
  2. Keep highlights below the ceiling; do not blow the sky for a brighter face.
  3. Shoot a color chart before rolling to give post a transform reference.

Avoid

Do not treat a flat image as a style; without correct exposure and color management, Log is harder to rescue.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Skin sits slightly above middle gray, shadows are not crushed, and highlights are unclipped.
  • 2. A color chart was shot for every setup and post can apply one transform.
  • 3. You can state the exposure intent of the Log take instead of “we'll fix it later.”

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Skin sits slightly above middle gray, shadows…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“A color chart was shot for every setup and pos…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not treat a flat image as a style; without correct exposure and color management, Log is harder to rescue.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Expose the face slightly above middle gray and”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • Skin sits slightly above middle gray, shadows are not crushed, and highlights are unclipped.
  • A color chart was shot for every setup and post can apply one transform.
  • You can state the exposure intent of the Log take instead of “we'll fix it later.”

en.title: Night Interior: One Practical Can Carry a Room
en.summary: Find a practical light the room can believe, then add one small face light. Do not flatten the whole room.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Night Interior: One Practical Can Carry a Room

Shooting / Lighting

Night Interior: One Practical Can Carry a Room

Find a practical light the room can believe, then add one small face light. Do not flatten the whole room.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

At least one practical must motivate the light: lamp, window, TV, hallway. Fill the face from that direction, not flat from camera. Protect the shade and window; keep some shadow detail.

Interior night needs one believable source

Turn off all off-screen sources to avoid mixed color and flicker; darken windows with curtains if needed.

Limits

Night is not blue moonlight. Interior night can mix warm lamps and cool windows; one uniform blue looks fake.

On set

Let one practical lamp or wall light sit in frame as the motive. Add a small light at 45 degrees for the face and leave the background dark; do not turn on the ceiling.

Do this

A night interior needs a practical light the audience believes, then one small lamp on the face. Do not flatten the room.

  1. Let a practical lamp or wall sconce motivate the scene and actually stay on.
  2. Add a small light at 45 degrees to the face for an eye light and nose shape.
  3. Keep the background dark and leave the ceiling light off so bright and dark zones separate.

Avoid

Do not turn on the ceiling light and flatten the room; night is not daylight dimmed down.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The practical is visibly on and motivates why the face is lit.
  • 2. The face has a nose shadow and an eye light, not a flat frontal wash.
  • 3. The background sits at least a stop darker than the face and keeps shadow detail.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The practical is visibly on and motivates why…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The face has a nose shadow and an eye light, n…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not turn on the ceiling light and flatten the room; night is not daylight dimmed down.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Let a practical lamp or wall sconce motivate”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • The practical is visibly on and motivates why the face is lit.
  • The face has a nose shadow and an eye light, not a flat frontal wash.
  • The background sits at least a stop darker than the face and keeps shadow detail.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. A night interior is not all lights on. It is one motivated source, then a face that survives.

Find one practical first

A table lamp, a fridge, a sign outside, a hallway light: all are sources the audience can see. Choose it first, then add light; the audience needs a reason why this place is lit.

Without a practical, use cold window light and one warm table lamp. Cold for space, warm for the person.

Even one lamp needs three layers

Key the face, bounce the shadows, flag the background. Three layers are not three lights; they are three controls: lift the face, keep shadow detail, push the background back.

One stop over the background is enough; do not turn night into day. Leave a little window frame or wall reflection so the space is not a black hole.

Black level and noise

Do not underexpose log; lifting shadows creates noise. Protect the face first, then let blacks fall. A style with an unusable face is just an excuse.

Pure black can lack detail, but do not crush it into a single hole. Keep an edge light so the audience knows the room still has walls.

Treating the window

The window should sit two or three stops over the room to read as night. The frame can clip, but the face cannot go black.

Blinds, sheers, and tree shadows break up the outside. A pure white window looks like a studio, not night.

Keep the skin alive

Night skin tends toward cyan. Warm the key a little or isolate skin in post.

Do not push every shadow blue. The audience believes night because the face still looks human.

Ten night-interior checks

  • Find the practical in frame first
  • Face one stop over background
  • Use soft key light
  • Bounce into the shadows
  • Flag the background down
  • Do not lift the whole room into day
  • Do not underexpose log
  • Shoot three seconds of gray card or white paper
  • Check window and lamp color
  • Play back and inspect shadow noise

Night is not hard because it is dark; it is hard to make the audience believe someone is there in the dark.

When you have five minutes

  • Find one practical in frame
  • Window three stops over the room
  • Face one stop over background
  • Flag the background down
  • Do not underexpose log
  • Play back for shadow noise

Night needs a reason before a mood: the reason is one lamp, the mood is a visible face.

en.title: Mixed Light: Keep the Two Temperatures
en.summary: Do not white-balance mixed light into one color; keep the cool window and warm bulb for depth.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Mixed Light: Keep the Two Temperatures

Shooting / Lighting

Mixed Light: Keep the Two Temperatures

Do not white-balance mixed light into one color; keep the cool window and warm bulb for depth.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

With window, lamp and neon together, decide the dominant temperature: daylight leans to window, night to lamp. Use gel or fill to bring others closer; do not neutralize everything to white and lose the place.

Choose one dominant temperature in mixed light

Shoot a chart and balance to the dominant source; keep secondary color as layering.

Limits

Mixed light is not “bad white balance.” A warm-cool contrast can be the point; if skin is acceptable, do not unify every lamp.

On set

With 5600K daylight outside and 3200K bulbs inside, do not force one white. Keep the window cool, the bulb warm, and the face in between.

Do this

Do not white-balance mixed light into one flat white; keep the cool window and warm bulb so the room has depth. Decide which source leads, then place the face between them.

  1. With 5600K daylight outside and 3200K bulbs inside, do not force one white balance.
  2. Let the window stay cool and the bulb stay warm.
  3. Balance the face in between so skin does not follow the background.

Avoid

Do not white-balance every source to white; fighting temperatures flatten the room.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The frame shows a cool window and a warm bulb as an intentional contrast.
  • 2. Skin stays neutral without a green or yellow cast on one side.
  • 3. One white balance was not used to erase both sources into one color.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The frame shows a cool window and a warm bulb…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Skin stays neutral without a green or yellow c…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not white-balance every source to white; fighting temperatures flatten the room.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “With 5600K daylight outside and 3200K bulbs inside,”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • The frame shows a cool window and a warm bulb as an intentional contrast.
  • Skin stays neutral without a green or yellow cast on one side.
  • One white balance was not used to erase both sources into one color.

en.title: Hard Light: The Shadow Is the Shape
en.summary: Hard light is not ugly; shadows shape the space. The problem is usually that the shadow lands in the wrong place.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Hard Light: The Shadow Is the Shape

Shooting / Lighting

Hard Light: The Shadow Is the Shape

Hard light is not ugly; shadows shape the space. The problem is usually that the shadow lands in the wrong place.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

Hard light has a crisp shadow edge and high contrast. Use a small source, bare lamp or distant sun; to keep it hard without clipping, lower output or add ND, not a big softbox.

Hard light is read at the shadow edge

Hard light suits power, conflict and texture. On faces, watch nose and eye-socket shadows; use a small bounce if needed.

Limits

Hard is not “no lighting.” It needs more precise placement and control; a wrong shadow direction looks like an accident.

On set

Use the hard source as a side light and watch where the shadow lands. If it cuts across an eye or the mouth, move the lamp or the actor by ten centimeters.

Do this

Hard light is not “ugly”; it divides space with shadow. The usual problem is a shadow in the wrong place. Use it as side light and watch the edge.

  1. Place the hard source to the side so the shadow falls on the wall or background.
  2. Watch whether the shadow cuts across an eye or the mouth.
  3. If it hits a feature, move the lamp or actor ten centimeters and shoot again.

Avoid

Do not fire hard light straight into the face; the shadow becomes a stain on the skin.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The shadow falls on the background or wall and becomes part of the composition.
  • 2. Eyes and mouth are not cut by shadow and features remain readable.
  • 3. The fix moved the lamp or actor ten centimeters instead of swapping in a softbox.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The shadow falls on the background or wall and…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Eyes and mouth are not cut by shadow and featu…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not fire hard light straight into the face; the shadow becomes a stain on the skin.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Place the hard source to the side so”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • The shadow falls on the background or wall and becomes part of the composition.
  • Eyes and mouth are not cut by shadow and features remain readable.
  • The fix moved the lamp or actor ten centimeters instead of swapping in a softbox.

en.title: Practical Light: Use the Lamp in the Frame
en.summary: A lamp in frame must actually turn on, off, or flicker, but it motivates light rather than lighting the face.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Practical Light: Use the Lamp in the Frame

Shooting / Lighting

Practical Light: Use the Lamp in the Frame

A lamp in frame must actually turn on, off, or flicker, but it motivates light rather than lighting the face.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

Lamps, windows and neon can be in frame, but confirm color, output and flicker. Swap bulbs for adjustable temperature, add diffusion or dimmers; do not let a practical blow out the face.

Practicals must be believable and controllable

Check flicker with phone slow motion; rolling bands mean change the lamp or shutter.

Limits

A practical is not a key light. It motivates and fills the background; the face still needs separate fill, or shadows go muddy.

On set

Let the lamp in frame actually glow, but dim it to 20 or 30 percent. Light the face with a separate small source; do not treat the practical as the key.

Do this

A practical must really be on, off, or flicker, but it is motivation, not a key light. The face needs a separate small source.

  1. Keep the practical visibly on but dim it to 20 or 30 percent.
  2. Light the face with a separate small lamp; the practical motivates the background.
  3. Check that the bulb does not clip and does not light the whole room.

Avoid

Do not make the visible bulb the only key; it cannot light the face and will clip.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The practical is visibly on without clipping into a white block.
  • 2. A separate lamp shapes the face while the practical motivates the background.
  • 3. Turn the practical off and the face is still supported by its key.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The practical is visibly on without clipping i…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“A separate lamp shapes the face while the prac…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not make the visible bulb the only key; it cannot light the face and will clip.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Keep the practical visibly on but dim it”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • The practical is visibly on without clipping into a white block.
  • A separate lamp shapes the face while the practical motivates the background.
  • Turn the practical off and the face is still supported by its key.

en.title: Wireless Lav: Hide It, Back It Up
en.summary: Hide the lav, secure it, and record a backup track before worrying about brand.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Wireless Lav: Hide It, Back It Up

Shooting / Sound

Wireless Lav: Hide It, Back It Up

Hide the lav, secure it, and record a backup track before worrying about brand.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

Scan the room, avoid TV and crowded Wi-Fi bands; keep the transmitter on the body, receiver above the crowd, antennas off metal. Every wireless pair needs a wired backup to camera or a second recorder.

Scan frequencies before discussing range

Walk the actor through the whole space and listen for dropouts, static and cloth noise; do not test only at the mark.

Limits

Wireless is not cable-free. Batteries, blocking and body absorption drop signal; critical dialogue needs a second recording.

On set

Hide the capsule ten centimeters below the collar and tape it with medical tape. Put the transmitter at the back waist, record a backup track, and listen for thirty seconds before rolling.

Do this

A lav is first about hiding and backup: under the collar, in the hair, taped down, plus a second track. A clean hide still fails if cloth rubs the capsule.

  1. Hide the capsule ten centimeters below the collar and secure it with medical tape.
  2. Put the transmitter at the lower back and record a backup track.
  3. Listen for thirty seconds before rolling and check rub, AC, and plosives.

Avoid

Do not drop the transmitter in a pocket or record one track; rub and loss have no second chance.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The thirty-second test has no cloth rub, AC hum, or plosive.
  • 2. The transmitter is not in a pocket, the cable has slack, and the mic does not swing when the actor walks.
  • 3. The backup track recorded alongside the main and can be switched in playback.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The thirty-second test has no cloth rub, AC hu…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The transmitter is not in a pocket, the cable…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not drop the transmitter in a pocket or record one track; rub and loss have no second chance.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Hide the capsule ten centimeters below the collar”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • The thirty-second test has no cloth rub, AC hum, or plosive.
  • The transmitter is not in a pocket, the cable has slack, and the mic does not swing when the actor walks.
  • The backup track recorded alongside the main and can be switched in playback.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. A lav is not hard to buy. It is hard to hide, to keep from rustling, and to back up.

Four places to hide a lav

A palm below the collar is safest, unless the collar is stiff. Hair works for suits and shirts but hurts on removal. A chest pocket must clear fabric, and a prop only suits short lines because low end gets muffled.

Tape the clothes first, then the skin, and leave a slack fold. Test sitting, turning, and raising a hand; if you hear cloth, move the mic.

Backup and monitoring

Record on the transmitter, feed the receiver to camera, and run a phone backup; at least two of the three must be usable. Wear headphones on set, not in post. Capture ten seconds of room tone before each scene for patch work.

If the performer sings or shouts, do not raise gain; leave headroom and lift later. A clipped take cannot be saved by a backup.

Wardrobe decides where the mic goes

On a stiff collar, place the mic below the points; on a sweater, use a furry wind cover at the chest; on silk, keep it off skin because it slides and rustles. Read the wardrobe before taping.

Make the performer sit, stand, and cross their arms in every position. Cloth noise is invisible on a monitor and loud as a drum in headphones.

Choosing among three tracks

Record transmitter, camera, and phone. Do not choose on set; choose in post. On set, only confirm that a second usable track exists, and never kill one because another sounds good.

Before wrap, listen ten seconds to each and note clipping or rustle. That note is worth more than another take.

Ten steps before you hide the lav

  • Read the fabric before choosing a position
  • On a stiff collar, place the mic a palm below
  • Use a furry cover on a sweater, not bare skin
  • Keep silk off skin; it slips and rustles
  • Tape the clothes first, then the skin
  • Leave a slack fold; never stretch the cable
  • Test sitting
  • Test turning
  • Test crossed arms
  • Record on the transmitter and keep camera and phone backups

The expensive part of a lav is not the gear; it is discovering the rustle after the performance is over. Listen ten seconds to each of the three tracks before wrap and write down the unusable one; do not wait for post.

en.summary: The boom follows action, not lines. Lines stop; bodies keep moving.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Boom Operator: Follow the Action, Not the Line

Shooting / Sound

Boom Operator: Follow the Action, Not the Line

The boom follows action, not lines. Lines stop; bodies keep moving.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

It is not holding the pole high. Listen to breath and footsteps, anticipate the next line and action; the tip follows action, not dialogue. When the actor stops, the pole stops; when they turn, go around the outside.

Boom operating is listening before lifting

Record ten seconds of room tone and a boom test each scene; confirm no lamp hit, shadow or cloth rub.

Limits

Longer is not better. A long pole hits walls and tires arms in tight spaces; use the shortest that works. Protect the line over the pose.

On set

Follow the actor's hands and steps, not the lines. Stop when they stop; when they turn, keep the tip above and outside the frame.

Do this

The boom follows action, not lines; lines stop, bodies do not. Keep the tip above frame.

  1. Follow the actor's hands and footsteps instead of swinging on every line.
  2. Stop when the actor stops and keep the tip above the head through turns.
  3. Review for the boom entering frame and dialogue masked by cloth or breath.

Avoid

Do not swing the boom on every line; the tip will enter frame and the sound will shift.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The boom tip never enters frame and casts no edge shadow.
  • 2. Dialogue level stays stable as the actor walks and turns.
  • 3. The pole does not pump on every line and the voice does not shift direction.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The boom tip never enters frame and casts no e…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Dialogue level stays stable as the actor walks…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not swing the boom on every line; the tip will enter frame and the sound will shift.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Follow the actor's hands and footsteps instead of”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • The boom tip never enters frame and casts no edge shadow.
  • Dialogue level stays stable as the actor walks and turns.
  • The pole does not pump on every line and the voice does not shift direction.

en.title: Dual-System Sound: Slate and Timecode
en.summary: Sync dual-system sound with a clap or timecode. With neither, post is guessing.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Dual-System Sound: Slate and Timecode

Shooting / Sound

Dual-System Sound: Slate and Timecode

Sync dual-system sound with a clap or timecode. With neither, post is guessing.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

The camera mic is scratch; the external recorder captures clean dialogue. Clap or slate before rolling so both files share a sync point; do not align by camera audio alone.

Dual system records scratch and clean sound

Record 48 kHz/24-bit, keep raw WAV; no denoise or compression on set.

Limits

Dual system is not “two copies of sound.” If the lav is misplaced or gain is wrong, the clean track is also ruined; monitor on set.

On set

Clap three times at the head, or sync the recorder to timecode. Announce the scene number at the end of every take so post never has to guess.

Do this

Dual-system sound needs a clap or timecode; without either, post is guessing. Leave a sync mark at the head and tail.

  1. Clap three times at the head so camera and recorder both capture it.
  2. Jam timecode or announce the scene and take at the end of each run.
  3. Sync on the clap frame or timecode in post, then check each take for drift.

Avoid

Do not rely on waveform auto-align; without a clap or timecode, drift grows as you fix it.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Every take starts with three claps visible and audible.
  • 2. Timecode or slate notes are complete enough for post to match audio by scene.
  • 3. After sync, playback stays in lip-sync from head to tail.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Every take starts with three claps visible and…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Timecode or slate notes are complete enough fo…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not rely on waveform auto-align; without a clap or timecode, drift grows as you fix it.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Clap three times at the head so camera”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • Every take starts with three claps visible and audible.
  • Timecode or slate notes are complete enough for post to match audio by scene.
  • After sync, playback stays in lip-sync from head to tail.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. The real cost of dual-system sound is not the recorder; it is sync. If sync is wrong, the sound does not count.

Shoot three things before syncing

At every setup, shoot a clap, a slate, and the timecode on camera; without timecode, the clap must be sharp and close to the mic. Write scene, shot, and take on the slate, not just the date.

Always run the camera scratch mic, even if it sounds bad. It is the last rescue track for lip sync.

Sync without timecode

Find the waveform spike, listen for the plosive, then check the lips; one or two frames of disagreement is fine. Sync the primary audio first, then attach the other angles. On long takes, check drift every ten minutes.

Spot-check three clips after syncing: one dialogue, one action, one ambience. If all three hold, start editing; if not, go back to the script supervisor’s log.

Timecode is not magic

Timecode saves sync time, but a battery, frame rate, or cable can make it fail quietly. Slate again after every card or battery change.

Check drift every ten minutes on long takes. Sound half a frame early makes lips look odd; half a frame late makes the gear look broken.

Sync order for multiple cameras

Sync the primary audio first, attach camera A, then B and C. Do not sync three cameras at once or you will not know where the error started.

Rename every track scene_shot_camera_take. The editor should open the timeline and use it without guessing what “Audio 3” is.

Ten checks before dual-system sound rolls

  • At a new setup, clap first: sharp and close to the mic
  • Then slate so the words are readable
  • Then shoot the timecode on camera
  • Write scene, shot, and take on the slate
  • Always run the camera scratch mic
  • Leave headroom on the recorder
  • Sync primary audio first on multicam
  • Find the waveform spike first
  • Then the plosive, then the lips
  • Check drift every ten minutes on long takes

Bad sync turns the best performance into a dubbing exercise. Ten seconds on set, ten hours in post. After syncing, listen to three random transitions with five seconds on each side before you continue editing. Listen first, then cut; never sync and cut at the same time.

en.title: Handheld: Let Breathing Into the Frame
en.summary: Handheld is not random shake; it turns the operator's breath into rhythm. Steady the feet first.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Handheld: Let Breathing Into the Frame

Shooting / Movement

Handheld: Let Breathing Into the Frame

Handheld is not random shake; it turns the operator's breath into rhythm. Steady the feet first.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

Handheld is not random shake; it turns the operator's breath into rhythm. Stabilize the feet first, then allow movement.

On set

Stand with feet shoulder-width, elbows against the ribs, and breathe between takes. Walk three steps in ten seconds and play it back: it should feel like breathing, not an earthquake.

Do this

Handheld is not random shake; it turns the operator's breath into rhythm. Stabilize the feet first, then allow movement.

  1. Stand feet shoulder-width apart and keep elbows against the ribs; breathe between takes.
  2. Walk three steps in ten seconds and let the body carry the camera, not the arms.
  3. Review: it should feel like breathing, not an earthquake.

Avoid

Do not shake for style; movement without reason steals the performance.

When not to handhold

Handheld works for walking with a subject, tight spaces and reactive coverage. It does not work for long lenses, low light, repeatable track moves, or product close-ups where the viewer must read small text.

Three hard limits: focal length over 85mm, shutter slower than 1/50, or a shot that must hold readable text. If any applies, use a tripod, slider or gimbal. “Breathing” is not an excuse for shake.

Stance and settings

Use 24–50mm, 1/50 at 25p; do not go below 1/50 if you want natural motion blur. Set stabilisation to standard; for a pan, switch to vertical-only so it does not fight your horizontal move.

  1. Feet shoulder-width, left foot slightly forward, knees soft. Wrap the strap around your wrist; right hand on the grip, left hand under the lens.
  2. Stand still for 10 seconds and find the steadiest part of your breath. Roll at half-exhale, not at the top of an inhale.
  3. Walk three steps and pause. Land heel first; let the body carry the camera. Turn the foot first, then the waist; do not swing the arms.

Moves that ruin the take

  1. Arm swing: the frame sways and the subject looks seasick. Move the weight instead.
  2. Walking too fast: steps outrun the breath and the frame bobs. Stretch three steps over 10 seconds.
  3. Holding the breath: hands shake and the take ends with a gasp. Breathe normally, just smaller.
  4. Never stopping: no pause means no edit point. Leave one steady beat every three steps.

If the shot follows a running actor, shoot a locked-off reference first. Do not use handheld to rescue blocking.

Handheld acceptance log

  • Shoot 10-second three-step takes at 24mm and 50mm; horizon drift under 2% of frame height.
  • Keep the head near the upper third; vertical drift under 2% of frame height.
  • Breath cycle every 3–4 seconds; no unexplained stop or acceleration.
  • Log body, lens, focal length, frame rate, shutter and stabilisation mode; another operator can repeat the rhythm.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Three steps in ten seconds stays even with no sudden vertical jump.
  • 2. The breath comes from the body, not from arm shaking.
  • 3. The horizon and the actor's head do not drift continuously.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Three steps in ten seconds stays even with no…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The breath comes from the body, not from arm s…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not shake for style; movement without reason steals the performance.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Stand feet shoulder-width apart and keep elbows against”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • Three steps in ten seconds stays even with no sudden vertical jump.
  • The breath comes from the body, not from arm shaking.
  • The horizon and the actor's head do not drift continuously.

en.title: Stabilizer: Walk Like You Mean It
en.summary: Gimbals hate tiny steps. Soft knees, heel-first, even speed.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Stabilizer: Walk Like You Mean It

Shooting / Movement

Stabilizer: Walk Like You Mean It

Gimbals hate tiny steps. Soft knees, heel-first, even speed.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

Post stabilization zooms and cuts edges. Confirm the frame has margin; without it you get black or soft edges. Handheld wide is easier to rescue than long lens.

Check room to crop before stabilizing

Order: lens correction, stabilization, then reframe. Do not crop before stabilizing.

Limits

Stabilization cannot fix motion blur or rolling shutter. Slow shutter and heavy skew become more visible; fix them on set.

On set

Bend the knees slightly, land on the heels, and walk a straight line. Practice twenty meters empty before mounting the camera. Slow down for turns; do not twist at the waist.

Do this

A gimbal hates small choppy steps. Bend the knees, land on the heel, and keep an even speed.

  1. Bend the knees, land heel first, and walk a straight line.
  2. Walk twenty meters without the rig to find an even pace.
  3. Turn slowly with the feet, not by twisting the waist.

Avoid

Do not take tiny steps or twist the waist; a gimbal smooths micro-jitter, not footstep bounce.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The frame does not bounce with each footstep on a straight walk.
  • 2. Turns stay even with no sudden whip or lateral snap.
  • 3. The twenty-meter empty walk and the rig walk share the same rhythm.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The frame does not bounce with each footstep o…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Turns stay even with no sudden whip or lateral…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not take tiny steps or twist the waist; a gimbal smooths micro-jitter, not footstep bounce.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Bend the knees, land heel first, and walk”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • The frame does not bounce with each footstep on a straight walk.
  • Turns stay even with no sudden whip or lateral snap.
  • The twenty-meter empty walk and the rig walk share the same rhythm.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. A gimbal is not stable because it is on. Walking, grip, and center of gravity decide the shot.

Three points for walking

Bend the knees, land on the heel first, and stop bouncing; walk about thirty percent slower than usual. Look ahead, not at the screen.

Walk the same path backward and play it back for vertical breathing. If it bobs, slow down again.

Balance and modes

Balance all three axes before powering up and check that the motors stay cool. Follow mode suits walking; lock mode suits a fixed position. Do not use full follow in strong wind.

Balance is not a level reading; it means the head stays put at any angle. A small error makes the motors fight all day.

Common bad habits

Straight arms, a death grip, and twisting the waist to turn are the usual failures. Keep the arm against the body, the gimbal near your center of gravity, and turn with your feet.

Invert the head for low angles and raise the column for high angles; do not hunch over to reach the frame.

Find a ten-meter path

Find a ten-meter corridor or sidewalk and walk it three times: normal, thirty percent slower, then slower again. Play each back for vertical breathing and side sway.

Then practice walking backward, sidestepping, and orbiting a person half a turn; two passes each, and notice which part of your body tires first.

Walk the path empty before shooting and check for thresholds, cables, and wet patches. A gimbal fears a sudden stop more than shake. If the path includes stairs, decide whether to carry the rig or break it down before you reach the steps.

Five-minute drill: orbit a cup

Put a cup on the floor and walk a full circle around it while keeping the rim in the same frame position. Do three circles, reversing direction each time. Play back for side drift and vertical breathing.

Then replace the cup with a person at two meters and practice a half orbit; a person will not wait like a cup, so agree on the blocking first.

Ten gimbal checks before rolling

  • Balance three axes before power
  • Motors stay cool
  • Battery and card seated
  • Choose follow or lock mode
  • Keep the arm against the body
  • Walk thirty percent slower
  • Land on the heel
  • Look ahead
  • Turn with the feet, not the waist
  • Play back for vertical bob

Gimbal stability starts in the body, then in the machine.

en.summary: Set dressing is not shopping for pretty objects; each prop answers why this person kept it.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Set Dressing: Props Tell the Character

Shooting / Art

Set Dressing: Props Tell the Character

Set dressing is not shopping for pretty objects; each prop answers why this person kept it.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

Props are not abundance. Write three habits: where shoes go, where the cup sits, what stays on the wall. Each habit leaves a visible trace; the audience reads life from traces, not quantity.

Dressing answers who lives here

Keep one foreground object for blocking and one empty background area to breathe; the person belongs in between.

Limits

Dressing must not steal performance. Too much color or pattern and the audience watches the wall; calm the background first.

On set

Write one origin line for every prop: who bought it, how long it has been used, why it was kept. Shoot a wide before the take and check it after wrap.

Do this

Set dressing is not a pile of nice objects; every prop answers why this person kept it.

  1. Write one origin line per prop: who bought it, how long they kept it, why it stayed.
  2. Shoot a wide plus details of the table, hands, and wardrobe before rolling.
  3. Remove props that neither move the action nor explain the character.

Avoid

Do not turn the set into a junk shop; too much information means none.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Every prop left in frame has an origin line you can say aloud.
  • 2. Wide and detail photos match and props do not drift between setups.
  • 3. At least one non-action decoration was removed so the frame reads more clearly.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Every prop left in frame has an origin line yo…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Wide and detail photos match and props do not…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not turn the set into a junk shop; too much information means none.

Extend

Prop Continuity: Photograph the Table

Continuity lives in photos: shoot the table, hands, and wardrobe before and after the take.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

Photograph the full prop layout before each scene: position, count, state—water level, ash, papers, wounds. Reset against the photo before every setup; do not rely on actor or script-supervisor memory.

Prop continuity uses photos and a sheet, not memory

Keep doubles of consumables: food, drinks, cigarettes, breakables. Every take starts from the same state.

Limits

Continuity is not OCD. The audience will not count water level, but they feel “that changed.” Protect only what they notice.

On set

Photograph the tabletop, the hands, and the wardrobe before rolling. Repeat at the end of every scene, including which way the cup handle faces.

Do this

Prop continuity lives in photos: shoot the table, hands, and wardrobe before rolling and again at wrap.

  1. Photograph the table, hands, and wardrobe before the take, noting the cup handle direction.
  2. Shoot the same frames at the end of each scene and compare side by side.
  3. If something moved, reset it or shoot an insert that hides the break.

Avoid

Do not trust memory for cups and wardrobe; photos are more reliable.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Cup handle, collar, and table objects face the same way across cuts.
  • 2. Every scene has before-and-after continuity photos.
  • 3. A break is either reset or covered by an insert, not ignored.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Cup handle, collar, and table objects face the…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Every scene has before-and-after continuity ph…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not trust memory for cups and wardrobe; photos are more reliable.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Photograph the table, hands, and wardrobe before the”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • Cup handle, collar, and table objects face the same way across cuts.
  • Every scene has before-and-after continuity photos.
  • A break is either reset or covered by an insert, not ignored.

en.title: Multicam Sync: Timecode and a Camera Map
en.summary: Draw the camera map, then sync timecode. The edit must know which camera stood where.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Multicam Sync: Timecode and a Camera Map

Shooting / Multicam

Multicam Sync: Timecode and a Camera Map

Draw the camera map, then sync timecode. The edit must know which camera stood where.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

With timecode, jam sync; without it, use a shared clap or flash. Every camera must see the same event and align by audio waveform; do not guess from picture.

Unify the time base before multicam

Match frame rate, shutter, white balance and audio sample rate. Color can be matched later; mixed frame rates cannot sync losslessly.

Limits

Sync is not one-time. Long records drift; realign every twenty to thirty minutes, and use a timecode generator for critical scenes.

On set

Draw a top-down camera map and mark what A, B, and C cover. Sync by timecode or a clap; the editor uses the map to find the take.

Do this

Multicam starts with a camera map, then timecode. The edit must know where each camera stood. Two cameras on the same size is repetition, not coverage.

  1. Draw a top-down map and label what size A, B, and C shoot.
  2. Sync by timecode or clap and confirm all three angles align.
  3. Check that each camera contributes different information, not the same size.

Avoid

Do not put two cameras on the same size; multicam is not duplicate cam.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The map shows what A, B, and C each cover with no duplicate size.
  • 2. All three angles align frame-accurately on the timeline.
  • 3. Each angle offers different information, so cuts have a reason.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The map shows what A, B, and C each cover with…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“All three angles align frame-accurately on the…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not put two cameras on the same size; multicam is not duplicate cam.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Draw a top-down map and label what size”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • The map shows what A, B, and C each cover with no duplicate size.
  • All three angles align frame-accurately on the timeline.
  • Each angle offers different information, so cuts have a reason.

en.title: LED Volume: Track First, Light Second
en.summary: In LED volume work, lock tracking before lighting. If tracking drifts, no background will stick.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/LED Volume: Track First, Light Second

Shooting / Virtual production

LED Volume: Track First, Light Second

In LED volume work, lock tracking before lighting. If tracking drifts, no background will stick.

4 min read · Virtual productionTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

LED volume work starts with tracking, then light. If tracking drifts, a beautiful background will not stick.

On set

Shoot a pan and a push-in first and check background tracking. Match set light to the background direction, then grade.

Do this

  1. Shoot a pan and a push-in to check background tracking and latency.
  2. Match the on-set light direction to the background source before brightness.
  3. Grade last and confirm no scan lines, drift, or color shift in the background.

Avoid

Do not build the pretty background first; if tracking drifts, all of it is wasted.

Boot order and tracking

Match the LED wall refresh to the camera shutter before judging the image. At 24p/25p, 1/50 or 1/60 is common. If scan lines appear, change shutter or wall refresh first, not the grade.

  1. Run a pan, a push-in and a half-circle around the subject with a tracking chart; watch the background edge for lag.
  2. Put tracking latency, genlock and lens-distortion calibration on the boot checklist. Recalibrate after a lens change.
  3. Shoot a test with no subject, only wall and floor, to confirm perspective and horizon.

Wall light and colour temperature

The wall is background, not key light. Keep the key on the front side; run the wall 1–2 stops below the key so green/blue bounce does not tint the face.

Put wall and practicals on the same side of 5600K or 3200K; do not mix warm and cool. Keep the actor at least 1.5m from the wall to reduce spill and moiré.

Virtual-production failures

  1. Tracking drift: the background looks like a sticker and slips when the actor moves. Recalibrate; do not fix it with post tracking.
  2. Scan lines or moiré: shutter and refresh disagree. Change shutter or shooting distance.
  3. Wall bounce: the face turns green. Lower wall brightness; add negative fill or a black flag.
  4. Wrong perspective: horizon and floor do not meet. Adjust camera height and lens; do not stretch the background.

Tracking acceptance log

  • Ten-second pan and push-in: no lag, drift or frame jump at the background edge.
  • Actor at 1.5m from the wall: no visible green/blue spill on the face.
  • No scan lines or moiré at delivery size; artefacts visible only at 100% are not a failure.
  • Log refresh rate, shutter, lens, tracking software version and calibration date.

Boot log

Log wall refresh, shutter, genlock state, tracking software version, lens-distortion calibration date and actor distance. If any one changes, retest tracking and colour; do not reuse the previous setup.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The background does not lag or drift during the pan and push-in.
  • 2. Light direction on the subject matches the source inside the background.
  • 3. At delivery size there are no scan lines, moire, or obvious color shift.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The background does not lag or drift during th…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Light direction on the subject matches the sou…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not build the pretty background first; if tracking drifts, all of it is wasted.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Shoot a pan and a push-in to check”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • The background does not lag or drift during the pan and push-in.
  • Light direction on the subject matches the source inside the background.
  • At delivery size there are no scan lines, moire, or obvious color shift.

Boundary

This page only covers “LED Volume: Track First, Light Second”; it does not replace Focal Length: Decide How Close the Audience Stands, Lighting Style: Soft, Hard, Natural, Color: Match First, Style Second. en.title: Live Encoding: Bitrate, Uplink, Backup
en.summary: Calculate uplink before bitrate, and always keep a local recording as backup.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Live Encoding: Bitrate, Uplink, Backup

Shooting / Live

Live Encoding: Bitrate, Uplink, Backup

Calculate uplink before bitrate, and always keep a local recording as backup.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

Set bitrate at 70% of upload, keyframe every two seconds, audio 128–192 kbps. High resolution without bitrate turns motion into blocks; stable 720p beats stuttering 4K.

Live starts with staying up, then looking good

Test ten minutes before: dropped frames, latency, audio sync, backup network. Do not discover upload limits after going live.

Limits

Live is not recorded. Post cannot fix it; state information once, prepare captions and graphics in advance.

On set

Measure upload speed first: you need 1.5 times the target bitrate for headroom. Set a primary stream and a hotspot backup, and record a local high-bitrate copy.

Do this

Live encoding starts with uplink bandwidth, then bitrate. Always keep a local recording as backup.

  1. Measure upload speed; 1.5 times the target bitrate is the safe margin.
  2. Set a primary stream, a hotspot backup, and a high-bitrate local recording.
  3. Rehearse a disconnection and record the dropout time and recovery steps.

Avoid

Do not run one path or treat the stream as one-shot; a dropout kills more than soft image quality.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Uplink is at least 1.5 times the target bitrate and the margin is recorded.
  • 2. When the primary drops, the hotspot backup and local recording still run.
  • 3. The rehearsal log shows the dropout time, cause, and recovery duration.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Uplink is at least 1.5 times the target bitrat…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“When the primary drops, the hotspot backup and…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not run one path or treat the stream as one-shot; a dropout kills more than soft image quality.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Measure upload speed; 1.5 times the target bitrate”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • Uplink is at least 1.5 times the target bitrate and the margin is recorded.
  • When the primary drops, the hotspot backup and local recording still run.
  • The rehearsal log shows the dropout time, cause, and recovery duration.

en.title: Permits: Parks, Transit, Shops
en.summary: A permit is not paper; it decides whether you can stand a light, block a walkway, or frame a sign.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Permits: Parks, Transit, Shops

Shooting / Safety

Permits: Parks, Transit, Shops

A permit is not paper; it decides whether you can stand a light, block a walkway, or frame a sign.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

Permits have three layers: private property needs the owner; public space may need city or police permission; special areas—airport, subway, park, historic building—have their own authority. Call first; do not gamble on the day.

Ask whose ground, road and air first

Put permit number, contact, valid window and restrictions on the call sheet so everyone knows what not to touch.

Limits

A small crew is not a waiver. Fewer people and a small camera may lower the approval level, but do not remove it; enforcement varies by city.

On set

Ask three questions: can you rig lights, can you block the sidewalk, can you show the storefront? Put the permit contact on the call sheet.

Do this

A permit is not a piece of paper; it decides whether you can light, block a walkway, or show a storefront. Ask three questions before choosing the shot.

  1. Ask: can we set a light, can we block the pavement, can we show the storefront?
  2. Put the answers and permit contact in the call sheet and mark restricted areas.
  3. If one answer is unclear, change the shot or the plan; do not wing it on the day.

Avoid

Do not treat “we'll shoot quickly and leave” as permission; security can stop both the camera and the footage.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Lighting, pavement, and storefront questions all have clear answers.
  • 2. The call sheet lists the permit contact, valid hours, and restricted areas.
  • 3. If one item was denied, the shot or plan changed instead of being forced on location.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Lighting, pavement, and storefront questions a…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The call sheet lists the permit contact, valid…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not treat “we'll shoot quickly and leave” as permission; security can stop both the camera and the footage.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Ask: can we set a light, can we”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • Lighting, pavement, and storefront questions all have clear answers.
  • The call sheet lists the permit contact, valid hours, and restricted areas.
  • If one item was denied, the shot or plan changed instead of being forced on location.

en.title: Risk Assessment: Fill One Page Before You Roll
en.summary: One page before rolling: who can get hurt, what can fall, who is in charge, and where the nearest hospital is.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Risk Assessment: Fill One Page Before You Roll

Shooting / Safety

Risk Assessment: Fill One Page Before You Roll

One page before rolling: who can get hurt, what can fall, who is in charge, and where the nearest hospital is.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Shoot DeskEdited 2026-11

A risk sheet is not every possible bad thing; it is the three to five that would make today unshootable: weather, key person absent, gear failure, location refused, transport cut. For each, write trigger, backup and decision time.

Name the item that would stop the shoot

Put the latest decision moment on the call sheet: if it is not solved by then, switch to Plan B without an on-set debate.

Limits

A risk sheet is not insurance. It cannot remove risk, only decide earlier; real safety still needs an on-set owner with stop-work authority.

On set

Fill one page with four boxes: who can get hurt, what can fall, who is responsible, and the nearest hospital. Read it to the crew before rolling.

Do this

A risk assessment is one page: who can get hurt, what can fall, who is responsible, and where the nearest hospital is. Read it to the crew.

  1. Fill four boxes: who can be hurt, what can fall, who owns the risk, and the nearest hospital.
  2. Read it aloud before rolling and assign an owner to each risk.
  3. Update it when the set changes and confirm at wrap that nothing was missed.

Avoid

Do not fill the form and lock it in a drawer; if nobody heard it, it was not done.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. All four boxes contain specifics, not “be careful.”
  • 2. Every risk has a named owner and crew can state their own item.
  • 3. The sheet was updated after set changes and checked again at wrap.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“All four boxes contain specifics, not “be care…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Every risk has a named owner and crew can stat…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not fill the form and lock it in a drawer; if nobody heard it, it was not done.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Shoot three 10-second takes by the same window, changing only “Fill four boxes: who can be hurt, what”. Compare highlights, skin and background; keep the one that is editable.

Check

  • All four boxes contain specifics, not “be careful.”
  • Every risk has a named owner and crew can state their own item.
  • The sheet was updated after set changes and checked again at wrap.

en.title: Fine Cut: Remove the Rough Edges
en.summary: Fine cutting is not adding effects; it smooths every cut, breath, and extra half-second.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Post/Fine Cut: Remove the Rough Edges

Post / Editing

Fine Cut: Remove the Rough Edges

Fine cutting is not adding effects; it smooths every cut, breath, and extra half-second.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

A fine cut does three things: remove the extra half second around each shot, align action cuts, and drop reactions the performance does not need. Structural problems go back to the rough cut; do not hide them with transitions here.

Fine cut trims edges, not structure

After every cut ask what the audience knows less. If cause and effect survive, the cut works. If a caption must explain it, go back to the rough cut.

Limits

Shorter is not automatically better. Remove every breath and pause and the character becomes a machine; keep the pauses that carry relationship.

On set

Find three rough edges per scene: a cut half a frame early, overlapping breaths, an extra second of air. Then let a stranger watch and note when they check their phone.

Do this

Fine cut is not adding effects; it smooths every cut, breath, and extra half-second.

  1. Find three burrs per scene: a cut half a frame early, overlapping breath, an empty shot one second long.
  2. Fix only those three categories without adding shots.
  3. Show a stranger and note when they check their phone; fix that second.

Avoid

Do not hide structure problems with fancy transitions; a wipe cannot save a drag.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Each scene loses at least three specific burrs and cuts no longer bite.
  • 2. Breaths and pauses connect without a line being cut in half.
  • 3. The stranger checks the phone less, or you can name why the drag remains.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Each scene loses at least three specific burrs…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Breaths and pauses connect without a line bein…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not hide structure problems with fancy transitions; a wipe cannot save a drag.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Find three burrs per scene: a cut half”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Each scene loses at least three specific burrs and cuts no longer bite.
  • Breaths and pauses connect without a line being cut in half.
  • The stranger checks the phone less, or you can name why the drag remains.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. The rough cut answers “is it clear?” The fine cut answers “does it flow, does it sting, and is anything extra?”

Fix four kinds of cut first

Cut on action halfway through a reach; cut on eyeline between looker and looked-at; cut on sound by letting a line tail cover the picture change; cut on shape by aligning a door, table edge, or shoulder across frames.

These are not tricks; they keep the audience from noticing the cut. If a join still fights you after three passes, the problem is usually missing coverage, not the edit.

Cut three things

Cut repeated information, cut the full walk from sofa to door, and cut reactions that change nothing. The audience does not need the transit; start with the character already at the door.

After every deletion, ask what the character loses. If the answer is nothing, the scene was filler.

Pace is change, not speed

Three shots of the same length in a row lose attention; three progressively shorter shots build pressure. Pace is alternation, not cutting everything faster.

Leave one shot that holds for two seconds so the audience can breathe. Without a pause, the later break has nothing to contrast against.

Cut a scene in half

Take a three-minute scene and keep only three beats: arrival, turn, decision. Cut everything else. The scene will still read, often better.

Add back one necessary reaction. Do this three times and you will see which shots were habit, not story.

Ten joins to fix in the first fine-cut pass

  • Cut halfway through a reach
  • Cut between the looker and the looked-at
  • Let a line tail cover the picture change
  • Align a door, table edge, or shoulder across the cut
  • Delete repeated information
  • Delete the full walk from sofa to door
  • Delete reactions that change nothing
  • Leave one two-second pause in every scene
  • Break three same-length shots in a row
  • After every deletion, ask what the character loses

Fine-cutting is not beautifying frames; it is finding the places that are almost right. Do it ten times and you will start trusting your discomfort. After every cut, play five seconds on each side; pace lives in the relationship, not the cut point alone.

en.title: Parallel Editing: When Do Two Lines Meet?
en.summary: Parallel editing is not back-and-forth; it makes the audience ask when the two lines will collide.
en.html:
Home/Post/Parallel Editing: When Do Two Lines Meet?

Post / Editing

Parallel Editing: When Do Two Lines Meet?

Parallel editing is not back-and-forth; it makes the audience ask when the two lines will collide.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Two lines intercut because they share a question: the same time, the same money, the same person. Every return must tighten the question, not just change location.

Parallel editing needs a shared problem, not constant switching

Give the lines different rhythms—one slow, one fast—and connect on action, sound or graphic match so the viewer does not get lost.

Limits

More intercutting is not more tension. Without a meeting point, fast switching is two films taking turns.

On set

Give each line a countdown: A has ten minutes left, B has three. Cross them when the audience starts doing the math.

Do this

Parallel editing is not constant cutting; it makes the audience ask when the two lines will collide.

  1. Give each line a countdown: A has ten minutes, B has three.
  2. Cross when the audience starts calculating, not every ten seconds.
  3. After the cross, let the lines share an object, sound, or action.

Avoid

Do not cut back and forth for technique; without a countdown, the cross has no pressure.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Each line has a readable countdown so the audience can calculate who arrives first.
  • 2. The cross happens at rising pressure, not at even intervals.
  • 3. After the cross, the lines share an element instead of running separately.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Each line has a readable countdown so the audi…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The cross happens at rising pressure, not at e…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not cut back and forth for technique; without a countdown, the cross has no pressure.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Give each line a countdown: A has ten”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Each line has a readable countdown so the audience can calculate who arrives first.
  • The cross happens at rising pressure, not at even intervals.
  • After the cross, the lines share an element instead of running separately.
