en.title: Versioning: Never Name It Final
en.summary: Name versions by date, platform, duration, and change reason. Never "final final."
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Post/Versioning: Never Name It Final

Post / Editing

Versioning: Never Name It Final

Name versions by date, platform, duration, and change reason. Never "final final."

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Use v001, v002, never “final” or “final2.” Every export gets one line: which scene, which shot, why. Without a note, a version number is just a number.

Version numbers only go up, with a change note

Keep current and previous in the working folder, archive older ones. State which version is the master at delivery so the client opens the right file.

Limits

More versions is not better. One purpose per pass, name it immediately; ten versions a day means no version control.

On set

Name files date_platform_duration_v3 and log every change: what changed, why, and who approved it.

Do this

Version names carry date, platform, duration, and reason, never “final really final.”

  1. Name files date_platform_duration_v3, e.g. 20261122_web_60s_v3.
  2. Log what changed, why, and who approved it.
  3. Keep one current delivery and archive the rest; do not rely on memory.

Avoid

Do not use “latest” as a filename; in three months nobody knows what it is latest over.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The filename contains date, platform, duration, and version and sorts cleanly.
  • 2. The log shows why each change happened and who approved it.
  • 3. Pick an old version and you can state how it differs from the current one.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The filename contains date, platform, duration…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The log shows why each change happened and who…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use “latest” as a filename; in three months nobody knows what it is latest over.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Name files date_platform_duration_v3, e.g. 20261122_web_60s_v3.”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • The filename contains date, platform, duration, and version and sorts cleanly.
  • The log shows why each change happened and who approved it.
  • Pick an old version and you can state how it differs from the current one.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. Version control is not saving more files; it is knowing three months later which one can ship and which was a draft.

Set the naming rule first

Project_date_version_status: tvcn_20261121_v03_review. Never use final, final2, or really-final; those words lie eventually.

Multiple versions in one day get letters, v03a and v03b, and never overwrite. Overwrite once and the client’s “previous version” is gone forever.

Lock and change

After picture lock, every change goes into a change log: who asked, what changes, which shots are affected. A verbal change becomes triple work in post.

Put client approval in email or a document, not just a call. A record is not distrust; it makes everyone responsible to the same version.

The delivery package

The package includes master, textless, captions, cover, and project archive. Miss one and you rebuild next time; rebuilding always costs more than archiving.

Open the project once before archiving and confirm no media is offline. The file exists but the link is broken, which means nothing was saved.

Writing the change sheet

Five columns: date, requester, change, affected shots, status. One row per change, no prose.

Keep the sheet at the project root so everyone reads the same one. A “change this” in chat is not a record.

The archive structure

Archive by media, projects, exports, documents. One folder per type, no more than three levels deep.

Put a README at the root with software versions, plug-ins, and restore steps. Three months later you will need it.

Ten version checks before delivery

  • Filename has project, date, version, status
  • No final or final2
  • Same-day versions use letters
  • Picture is locked
  • Changes logged in a change sheet
  • Client approval kept in writing
  • Delivery package has a checklist
  • Master, textless, and captions all present
  • Project archived
  • Open the archive and check media before closing

With version control, delivery is not luck; it is opening the right folder.

When you have five minutes

  • Filename has project, date, version, status
  • No final or final2
  • Lock picture before delivery
  • Log changes in a change sheet
  • Delivery package has a checklist
  • Open the archive before closing

Version control is not for tidiness; it is so the previous version can actually be found.

en.title: Color Management: Put the LUT in the Right Place
en.summary: Color management is not applying a cinematic LUT. It answers what the source space is, what the monitor is, and what delivery needs, then puts the transform on the right node.
en.html:
Home/Post/Color Management: Put the LUT in the Right Place

Post / Color management

Color Management: Put the LUT in the Right Place

Color management is not applying a cinematic LUT. It answers what the source space is, what the monitor is, and what delivery needs, then puts the transform on the right node.

4 min read · AdvancedTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Separate the four spaces

A film has at least four spaces: capture (S-Log3, LogC, RAW), working (ACES or DaVinci Wide Gamut), display (Rec.709, P3, HDR PQ), and delivery (platform Rec.709, HLG, PQ). Mix them and the LUT becomes a guess.

Match each source to the correct input transform: camera, gamut, gamma, matrix. If it is missing, shoot a grey card or color chart and build it manually; do not use a “close enough” LUT.

Where the LUT goes: three nodes, no stacking

The input transform creates the working space; the creative LUT sits inside it; the display transform sits before the monitor; the delivery transform sits before output. A common error is putting a Rec.709 look LUT on Log footage, then another display LUT, crushing highlights twice.

Each LUT answers one question: transform, look, or calibration. If it cannot answer, do not stack it. Name nodes input/look/display/delivery so the next artist can read the tree.

Monitor and calibration: trust the screen before the eye

Calibrate the monitor before grading: white point, gamma, gamut, luminance. Without calibration, every decision is true on this screen and false elsewhere. Check black, white, and skin with a grey ramp and color chart.

Do not judge on an office monitor; its contrast and gamut flatten shadows. Client review must use the same display transform, or “the client sees it differently” is usually a different screen, not a bad grade.

Handoff: deliver LUT, node tree, and references together

The handoff includes project file, LUTs, input-transform notes, display-transform notes, reference frames, and a limit list. Sending one LUT without its position is sending nothing.

Mark each reference “light” or “color”: light means direction, softness, ratio; color means white point, skin, saturation. Mixed references make the colorist guess.

Failure case: one LUT on every camera

A three-camera interview used three camera models and one “film LUT” on all sources. A went green in skin, B went grey in highlights, C went red in shadows. The colorist blamed the lighting until realizing the input transforms were never separated.

The fix is per-camera input transforms into one working space, then one creative LUT. Multicam starts with correct transforms, not “looks the same.”

Cost and acceptance

Low: input-transform cleanup and one display calibration, ¥2,000–6,000. Mid: full color management, node tree, handoff pack, ¥6,000–20,000. High: ACES pipeline, dual HDR versions, on-set DIT, ¥20,000–60,000+.

Check

  • Every source has a named input transform.
  • Working, display, and delivery spaces are written separately.
  • One creative LUT sits on the correct node.
  • Monitor is calibrated; grey ramp and color chart pass.
  • References are marked light or color.
  • Handoff includes LUTs, node tree, and limits.

en.title: Secondary Correction: Change One Area
en.summary: Secondary correction changes one area: skin, sky, wardrobe. More areas, more fake.
en.html:
Home/Post/Secondary Correction: Change One Area

Post / Color

Secondary Correction: Change One Area

Secondary correction changes one area: skin, sky, wardrobe. More areas, more fake.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Use masks, HSL or qualifiers to move one range: sky, skin, clothing or background. Primary first, secondary second; without a primary, secondary locks the cast in.

Secondary only changes the selected area

One node, one purpose, named clearly. With too many nodes, disable all and re-enable one by one to find what actually works.

Limits

Secondary is not a local filter. Feather the edge and track motion; hard edges and drifting masks read as fake immediately.

On set

Pick one area: face or sky. Feather the qualifier 10 to 20 pixels, keep the change under five percent, and toggle it off to check.

Do this

Secondary correction changes one region: face, sky, or clothing. The more regions, the faker it looks.

  1. Choose one region: face or sky.
  2. Feather the qualifier 10 to 20 pixels and keep the change under five percent.
  3. Toggle the node and check for halo or color patch at the edge.

Avoid

Do not change five regions at once; every edge leaves a trace.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Only one region moved and neighboring colors are untouched.
  • 2. Feathering looks natural with no halo, jagged edge, or patch.
  • 3. With the node off, the audience cannot tell which area was isolated.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Only one region moved and neighboring colors a…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Feathering looks natural with no halo, jagged…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not change five regions at once; every edge leaves a trace.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Choose one region: face or sky.”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Only one region moved and neighboring colors are untouched.
  • Feathering looks natural with no halo, jagged edge, or patch.
  • With the node off, the audience cannot tell which area was isolated.

en.title: LUT: A Starting Point, Not a Finish
en.summary: A LUT is a start, not a finish. Return to primary correction and check blacks and highlights.
en.html:
Home/Post/LUT: A Starting Point, Not a Finish

Post / Color

LUT: A Starting Point, Not a Finish

A LUT is a start, not a finish. Return to primary correction and check blacks and highlights.

4 min read · Grading handbookTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

A LUT is a starting point, not a finish. After applying it, return to primary correction for blacks and highlights.

On set

Balance exposure and white balance before the LUT. After applying it, check for lifted blacks and stained highlights, then return to primary.

Do this

  1. Balance exposure and white balance before the LUT.
  2. Check whether blacks lifted or highlights picked up a cast.
  3. Fix in primary and then decide how much LUT strength to keep.

Avoid

Do not use a LUT as a repair; it only tints the problem one color.

Kinds of LUT

Separate three kinds: technical LUT (Log→Rec.709, colour-space conversion), creative LUT (a look) and calibration LUT (monitor or printer). A technical LUT belongs at the front of colour management; a creative LUT comes after the primary grade. Do not stack all three in one node.

Confirm the LUT’s input colour space and cube size. Put a Rec.709 LUT on Log footage and black level and highlights will be wrong.

Node order

  1. Convert to the working colour space first; do not apply a creative LUT to camera-native Log.
  2. Do the primary grade: exposure, white balance and black level. Bring the plate back to neutral.
  3. Apply the LUT at controlled strength; then fix black level, highlights and skin with curves or wheels.
  4. Finish with output transform and legalisation; check the waveform and scopes.

LUT misuse

  1. Using a LUT to fix exposure: on a blown plate it only tints the highlight; detail does not return.
  2. Running the LUT at 100%: blacks lift and skin turns orange. Drop to 50–70% and see if it still works.
  3. Applying one LUT across lenses without matching: each lens has its own cast. Match first.
  4. Treating a creative LUT as a technical transform: the colour space is wrong, so everything after is wrong.

Grade acceptance log

  • Before the LUT: exposure is correct and white balance neutral; black level neither lifts nor crushes on the waveform.
  • After the LUT: highlights are not visibly tinted and skin has not gone uniformly orange or green.
  • At 50% LUT strength the image still holds; that proves the base grade is right.
  • Log LUT name, input colour space, strength and node order; check once in Rec.709 before delivery.

Grade log

Log LUT name, input colour space, strength, node position, output transform and viewing standard. Watch the whole timeline in Rec.709 before delivery, not a single frame.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The footage is correctly exposed and neutral before the LUT.
  • 2. After the LUT, blacks are not lifted and highlights show no obvious cast.
  • 3. Lower the LUT strength and the image still returns to a deliverable state.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The footage is correctly exposed and neutral b…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“After the LUT, blacks are not lifted and highl…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use a LUT as a repair; it only tints the problem one color.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Balance exposure and white balance before the LUT.”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • The footage is correctly exposed and neutral before the LUT.
  • After the LUT, blacks are not lifted and highlights show no obvious cast.
  • Lower the LUT strength and the image still returns to a deliverable state.

Boundary

This page only covers “LUT: A Starting Point, Not a Finish”; it does not replace Mastering: One File to Rule the Delivery, Mixing: Land the Dialogue Before the Music, Composition: Tell the Eye Where to Look. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

en.title: HDR: You Need HDR on Set and in the Room
en.summary: HDR is not a brighter SDR; capture, monitoring, and delivery must all support it.
en.html:
Home/Post/HDR: You Need HDR on Set and in the Room

Post / Color

HDR: You Need HDR on Set and in the Room

HDR is not a brighter SDR; capture, monitoring, and delivery must all support it.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

HDR is not lifting shadows infinitely; it preserves information from window to dark corner. Expose so highlights just avoid clipping, confirmed with false color or waveform; leave noise room in shadows and decide later how far to push.

HDR protects highlights before brightness

Check on the target display before delivery: an HDR master can look gray on a normal screen. Make a separate SDR version; do not post one master everywhere.

Limits

HDR is not a look filter. Without an HDR display and correct metadata, the audience may see worse than SDR. Confirm the delivery chain before shooting.

HDR needs a monitor before it needs a delivery spec

Grading HDR without an HDR monitor is grading blind. Confirm the chain: camera log → HDR monitor → PQ/HLG delivery. If any link is SDR, you are guessing.

  1. Set monitor luminance to the delivery standard, not the TV's “vivid” mode; keep room light low.
  2. Grade highlights in PQ first, then make the SDR trim. Do not reverse-engineer HDR from SDR.
  3. Watch the SDR version on a normal TV before delivery; highlights should not glare and shadows should not crush.

Acceptance: both HDR and SDR versions, skin consistent and highlights detailed. If only one works, the conversion is not reversible.

On set

Confirm the monitor supports HDR and the footage is 10-bit Log. Deliver HDR10 or HLG as its own pass; do not stretch an SDR grade.

Do this

HDR is not a brightened SDR image; capture, monitoring, and delivery must all support HDR.

  1. Confirm the monitor supports HDR and the footage is 10-bit Log.
  2. Make a separate pass for HDR10 or HLG delivery.
  3. Do not lift an SDR version; preserve HDR highlights and shadows.

Avoid

Do not call a lifted SDR image HDR; the highlights are fake and shadows carry no information.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Footage is 10-bit Log and the monitoring chain truly supports HDR.
  • 2. The HDR pass is separate, not an SDR lift.
  • 3. Watch both HDR and SDR versions; each holds its own highlights and shadows.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Footage is 10-bit Log and the monitoring chain…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The HDR pass is separate, not an SDR lift”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not call a lifted SDR image HDR; the highlights are fake and shadows carry no information.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Confirm the monitor supports HDR and the footage”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Footage is 10-bit Log and the monitoring chain truly supports HDR.
  • The HDR pass is separate, not an SDR lift.
  • Watch both HDR and SDR versions; each holds its own highlights and shadows.

en.title: Scopes: Black, White, Skin
en.summary: Scopes answer three things: dead blacks, clipped whites, and skin line drift.
en.html:
Home/Post/Scopes: Black, White, Skin

Post / Color

Scopes: Black, White, Skin

Scopes answer three things: dead blacks, clipped whites, and skin line drift.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Waveform shows overall brightness and clipped highlights; vector shows saturation and hue; RGB parade shows channel alignment. Use all three to separate “bright” from “cast.”

Waveform for luma, vector for color, parade for separation

Check parade black and white balance, then vector skin line, then waveform highlights; do not conclude from one scope.

Limits

Scopes are not creative judges. Stylized low contrast, night and backlight can look “wrong”; set intention before reading them.

On set

Keep black above 0 and white below 100. Put the skin line in the skin patch on the vectorscope; if it drifts red, lower saturation or fix white balance.

Do this

Scopes answer three things: are blacks crushed, are whites clipped, is skin off.

  1. Keep black at or above 0 and white at or below 100.
  2. Put the skin line inside the vector scope's skin zone.
  3. If it skews red, lower saturation or adjust white balance; do not guess by eye.

Avoid

Do not replace scopes with your eyes; an uncalibrated monitor lies too.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Black does not go below 0 and white does not exceed 100.
  • 2. The skin line sits in the skin zone without a red or green shift.
  • 3. Before-and-after scope grabs show a change that maps to a specific parameter.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Black does not go below 0 and white does not e…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The skin line sits in the skin zone without a…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not replace scopes with your eyes; an uncalibrated monitor lies too.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Keep black at or above 0 and white”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Black does not go below 0 and white does not exceed 100.
  • The skin line sits in the skin zone without a red or green shift.
  • Before-and-after scope grabs show a change that maps to a specific parameter.

en.title: Foley: Steps, Cloth, Doors
en.summary: Foley does not add ambience; it rebuilds the sound of visible action: steps, cloth, handles.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Post/Foley: Steps, Cloth, Doors

Post / Sound

Foley: Steps, Cloth, Doors

Foley does not add ambience; it rebuilds the sound of visible action: steps, cloth, handles.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Foley passes first on sync: the frame the foot lands, cloth rubs, cup meets table. Match the action, then add weight and material; out-of-sync Foley is worse than none.

Sync to action before getting creative

Layer contact, movement and ambience separately and mix them independently; do not put everything on one track.

Limits

Foley is not “more sound equals richer.” Do not add actions the picture does not show; the audience feels the separation.

Foley in three layers: feet, cloth, props

Foley is not “add sound effects”; it makes on-screen action carry audible weight. Feet first, cloth second, prop contact last. Record them separately so post can adjust.

  1. Feet by surface: wood, concrete, carpet. Record one foot at a time, not both.
  2. Cloth only on visible movement, never a continuous bed; keep it 12–18dB under dialogue.
  3. Door handles, cups and paper on a close mic, dry. Leave reverb to the mix.

Acceptance: with music off, Foley and dialogue alone should tell you body weight and surface. If not, add feet first.

On set

Record footsteps, cloth rustle, and a door handle after the shoot. Match them in silence, then mix under room tone without covering dialogue.

Do this

Foley is not background sound; it rebuilds the action in the frame: steps, cloth, door handles.

  1. Record footsteps, cloth rub, and door handles after the shoot.
  2. Mute the picture and sync each sound to the action.
  3. Mix under ambience and dialogue; Foley must not mask words.

Avoid

Do not fill every quiet beat with Foley; silence has weight too.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Footsteps, cloth, and door handles each land on a specific action.
  • 2. With the picture muted, every action has a sound and none arrives half a frame early.
  • 3. Under dialogue, words stay clear and Foley does not fight the midrange.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Footsteps, cloth, and door handles each land o…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“With the picture muted, every action has a sou…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not fill every quiet beat with Foley; silence has weight too.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Record footsteps, cloth rub, and door handles after”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Footsteps, cloth, and door handles each land on a specific action.
  • With the picture muted, every action has a sound and none arrives half a frame early.
  • Under dialogue, words stay clear and Foley does not fight the midrange.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Foley is not filling in footsteps; it gives the picture weight. What the audience hears is often not the action but what the action lands on.

Lay the room tone first

Record thirty seconds of empty room per scene and fill the floor under dialogue. Without room tone, cuts sound like vacuum and the picture appears to jump.

Room tone must match the location; kitchen and bedroom cannot share. Size, surface softness, and distant noise all have to agree.

Footsteps and cloth

Footsteps have three layers: sole, surface, cadence. Wood, concrete, and carpet sound different; read the picture before choosing.

Rub a small cloth near the mic for fabric instead of pasting a library effect. A library cloth always sounds like someone else’s coat.

Sync is not one frame

Match the start of the action, then listen for weight. Two frames off feels light; five frames off feels fake. Numerical sync is not felt sync.

Watch the picture while recording, not just the waveform; Foley is performance. Get the performance right and the waveform follows.

How to record Foley

Keep the mic twenty to thirty centimeters from the source: closer clips, farther sounds like a library.

Record each pass three times: normal, light, heavy. The edit needs weight variation.

Ambience versus Foley

Ambience lays the bed; Foley makes the points. Too thick a bed hides the points; too thin a bed makes them stick to the picture.

Lay the bed, add the points, and solo after every layer.

Ten Foley checks

  • Record thirty seconds of room tone
  • Footsteps split into sole, surface, cadence
  • Record cloth separately
  • Record props separately
  • Watch the performance while recording
  • Match the start of the action
  • Keep error within two frames
  • Change the room tone per location
  • Do not use only library effects
  • Solo each layer before mixing

Good Foley goes unnoticed; bad Foley makes the actor look like they are walking on air.

When you have five minutes

  • Record room tone first
  • Footsteps split into sole, surface, cadence
  • Record cloth separately
  • Watch the picture while recording
  • Match the action start
  • Solo before mixing

Foley is not a library; it is the weight a body leaves when the actor is no longer there. Land the foot first, then make it sound good. The foot lands first.

en.title: Music Editing: Let the Music Follow the Action
en.summary: Music does not run wall to wall; it enters, exits, and leaves space at the turn.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Post/Music Editing: Let the Music Follow the Action

Post / Sound

Music Editing: Let the Music Follow the Action

Music does not run wall to wall; it enters, exits, and leaves space at the turn.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Do not cut picture to the beat from the start. Make the story work, then lay the music; move the track's sections when needed instead of chopping picture to fit.

Cut the story first, then the music

Do not cut picture to the beat from the start. Make the story work, then lay the music; move the track's sections when needed instead of chopping picture to fit.

Use phrases and rests as transitions: half a beat before the chorus, pull music before the bridge. Do not cut on every beat.

Limits

Music is not emotional glue. If the picture does not change, louder music is only noise; make the action work first.

On set

Mark the action beats: door opens, turn, sit. Bring music in on the first, change it on the second, and take it out on the third.

Do this

Music is not wall-to-wall; it enters, changes, and exits at action turns.

  1. Mark action points: door opens, turn, sit down.
  2. Bring music in at the first point, change at the second, and exit at the third.
  3. Leave one breath without music and let ambience take over.

Avoid

Do not fill every gap with music; without an exit, the entrance has no power.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Music has at least one clear entrance, change, and exit.
  • 2. The three action points line up with musical changes instead of arbitrary beats.
  • 3. The silent passage works on ambience alone and does not feel like a dropout.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Music has at least one clear entrance, change…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The three action points line up with musical c…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not fill every gap with music; without an exit, the entrance has no power.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Mark action points: door opens, turn, sit down.”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Music has at least one clear entrance, change, and exit.
  • The three action points line up with musical changes instead of arbitrary beats.
  • The silent passage works on ambience alone and does not feel like a dropout.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. Music is not wallpaper; it breathes with the action. When it enters and leaves matters more than the track itself.

Find the accents first

Lay the music on the timeline and mark the hits, rests, and chorus. Major picture actions should land on accents so the audience feels the lock.

Music without accents does not support hard cuts; use ambience or silence instead. Not every track has to serve the edit; some just need to exist.

Dialogue comes first

When dialogue enters, bring the music down. Not a little; enough to make the line clear. Expensive music that hides a line is worthless.

Do not push music over dialogue and pull it back; the audience hears the fight. Lose two bars before losing a sentence.

Endings and silence

Leave two seconds after the last line before the music leaves. The audience needs time to react; cut the music too soon and the emotion is guillotined.

Be silent when silence is right. Silence is not absence; it returns attention to the picture. Constant music tires an audience.

Temp track versus final score

Use a temp track to find rhythm in the rough cut, then replace it after lock. Never deliver the temp.

Keep the accent positions when swapping cues, or the whole section needs re-cutting.

Licensing and replacement

Confirm the license scope before release: platform, territory, term. A “in-video use” license may not cover advertising.

Export a music-free version before replacing the cue; do not layer the new track over the old.

Ten music-edit checks

  • Mark the musical accents first
  • Land major actions on accents
  • Drop music when dialogue enters
  • Do not fill the whole film with music
  • Leave a breath at transitions
  • Hold two seconds at the end
  • Be silent when silence is right
  • Check that bass does not mask dialogue
  • Listen on a phone speaker
  • Solo dialogue before delivery

Music is not there to make the film look expensive; it is there to let the audience breathe when they should.

When you have five minutes

  • Mark the musical accents
  • Drop music under dialogue
  • Leave a breath at transitions
  • Hold two seconds at the end
  • Be silent when silence is right
  • Listen on a phone speaker

Music enters to push, and leaves so the audience can take a step alone. It does not fill silence; it decides where silence belongs. Silence is part of the score; let the last beat land on the picture before it leaves.

en.title: Keying: Edge First, Color Second
en.summary: Keying checks edges before color. If the edge is mush, grading cannot save it.
en.html:
Home/Post/Keying: Edge First, Color Second

Post / VFX

Keying: Edge First, Color Second

Keying checks edges before color. If the edge is mush, grading cannot save it.

4 min read · Post handbookTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Keying starts with the edge, then color. If the edge is mushy, grading cannot save it.

On set

Check the edge first: hair, fingers, a clear cup. Key coarse then fine, feather one or two pixels, and fix spill last.

Do this

  1. Check hair, fingers, and a transparent glass edge.
  2. Do a rough and then a fine pass, adding one to two pixels of feather.
  3. Fix spill and review at delivery size, not at 400 percent.

Avoid

Do not fix flaws at 400 percent that nobody sees at delivery size.

Get it right on set

Light the green screen evenly. Keep the subject 1.5–2m from it and keep shadows off the screen. Light the background first, then the subject; add an edge or rim light to separate hair and shoulders.

Do not push the shutter too high: 1/50 keeps natural motion blur. For heavy keying, 1/100 reduces edge smear but hardens motion. Test one take before committing; do not use one setting for the whole day.

Keying node order

  1. Do a primary grade first and even out the screen’s brightness and colour cast. Do not key a badly underexposed plate.
  2. Key coarse to fine: get the large matte, then fix edges, hair and transparent objects.
  3. Add 1–2px edge blur, then spill suppression; finish with light wrap so background light returns to the edge.

Do not force one keyer on glass, gauze and smoke. Split layers; keep the practical element when you can.

Edge failures

  1. Hair becomes a hard block: raise matte detail, do not just lower tolerance; roto the fine strands separately.
  2. Edges chatter in motion: check shutter and motion blur; fix per frame, not with overall blur.
  3. Green spill on the face: lower screen brightness first, then suppress spill; do not desaturate the whole face.
  4. Transparent objects vanish: split the layer and keep refraction and edge highlights.

Keying acceptance log

  • At delivery size, hair, fingers and transparent objects have no hard cut, jagged edge or black line.
  • Edges track the subject in motion; no frame jumps or sticks.
  • No green bounce on face and shoulders; a white collar stays white.
  • Log keyer, node order, edge blur and spill strength; redo after a lens or screen change.

Keying log

For every green-screen setup log screen type, subject distance, shutter, ISO, edge-light position, keyer and edge blur. After a screen or lens change, shoot a 10-second test before the take.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Hair, fingers, and transparent edges show no hard cut or jagged line.
  • 2. The edge tracks through motion without jitter or drift.
  • 3. At delivery size there is no green spill or black fringe.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Hair, fingers, and transparent edges show no h…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The edge tracks through motion without jitter…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not fix flaws at 400 percent that nobody sees at delivery size.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Check hair, fingers, and a transparent glass edge.”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Hair, fingers, and transparent edges show no hard cut or jagged line.
  • The edge tracks through motion without jitter or drift.
  • At delivery size there is no green spill or black fringe.

en.title: Tracking: Put the Point on Something Real
en.summary: Put tracking points on real, textured, unoccluded surfaces; a flat wall will drift.
en.html:
Home/Post/Tracking: Put the Point on Something Real

Post / VFX

Tracking: Put the Point on Something Real

Put tracking points on real, textured, unoccluded surfaces; a flat wall will drift.

4 min read · Post handbookTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Tracking points belong on real, textured, unobstructed surfaces; a flat wall will drift.

On set

Place three tracking points: a textured corner, a high-contrast mark, and a backup. If one gets blocked, switch to manual keyframes.

Do this

  1. Place three points: a textured corner, a high-contrast mark, and a backup.
  2. Switch to manual keys when a point is occluded.
  3. Play the whole shot and check for drift or sliding.

Avoid

Do not put points on a flat wall or mirror; the tracker has nothing to grab.

How to choose points

Choose textured, high-contrast, non-repeating features: a wall corner, label, screw or floor pattern. Do not put points on a flat wall, a mirror, a fast-moving hand or an ear that hair will cover.

Use at least three points for planar tracking and six at different depths for 3D. More is not better; a point that survives occlusion is.

Solve order

  1. Set origin and scale before solving. Do not change lens distortion while solving.
  2. Solve translation/rotation/scale first, then perspective. If the error is large, go back to manual keys.
  3. Check reprojection: stick a test grid to the plate; the edge must not slide.

For motion-blurred shots, compensate or key manually first. Do not make the tracker guess.

Tracking failures

  1. Flat wall: no texture, so the tracker drifts. Add temporary marks or key manually.
  2. Reflective or transparent surface: the point moves and the solve scales. Move to nearby real texture.
  3. Rolling shutter: fast pans warp the plate. Undistort first or change the lens.
  4. Occlusion: points disappear and do not recover. Place backup points and switch to manual keys.

Solve acceptance log

  • Reprojection error at delivery size is 1–2px or less; no slide at 200%.
  • Play the full shot: no scale drift, foot slide or sudden point jump.
  • Occlusion sections have manual keys and no hard transition.
  • Log tracking software, version, lens, focal length, solve error and manual key count.

Solve log

Log lens, focal length, tracking software version, solve error, manual key count and occlusion sections. When the error grows, check these fields before re-solving the whole shot.

Check before re-solving

Check lens-distortion calibration and focal length first, then whether points were occluded. Do not re-solve the whole shot immediately. Save the previous solve so you can roll back.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. At least two of three points stay visible and textured through the shot.
  • 2. When occlusion happens, manual keys take over with no hard jump.
  • 3. On full playback the tracked surface shows no slide or scale drift.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“At least two of three points stay visible and…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“When occlusion happens, manual keys take over…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not put points on a flat wall or mirror; the tracker has nothing to grab.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Place three points: a textured corner, a high-contrast”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • At least two of three points stay visible and textured through the shot.
  • When occlusion happens, manual keys take over with no hard jump.
  • On full playback the tracked surface shows no slide or scale drift.

en.summary: Rotoscoping is not one drag. Hair, fingers, and transparency need frame-by-frame work.
en.html:
Home/Post/Rotoscoping: One Frame at a Time

Post / VFX

Rotoscoping: One Frame at a Time

Rotoscoping is not one drag. Hair, fingers, and transparency need frame-by-frame work.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Rotoscoping is not tracing. Mark joints and motion direction first, then the outline; correct joints give the shape volume. Check every five to ten frames and fix keys on drift.

Mark joints before outlines

Edge hardness follows the plate: live action has motion blur, so keep some; hard edges look like cut paper.

Limits

Rotoscoping cannot replace performance. If the action is unclear, accurate tracing copies the confusion; shoot it clearly first.

On set

Test five frames first: hair, fingers, and something transparent. Check the edge every frame; do not wait 200 frames to notice drift.

Do this

A mask is not one drag; hair, fingers, and transparent edges need frame-by-frame work.

  1. Test five frames: hair, fingers, and a transparent object.
  2. Check each edge and confirm the mask does not eat the subject.
  3. Only then cover the full shot; do not discover drift at frame 200.

Avoid

Do not use one mask for the whole shot; once the edge fails, every later frame needs rework.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. In the five-frame test, hair, fingers, and transparent edges are clean.
  • 2. The mask neither eats the subject nor leaves background on the edge.
  • 3. After covering the shot, three random frames show no sudden warp or drift.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“In the five-frame test, hair, fingers, and tra…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The mask neither eats the subject nor leaves b…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use one mask for the whole shot; once the edge fails, every later frame needs rework.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Test five frames: hair, fingers, and a transparent”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • In the five-frame test, hair, fingers, and transparent edges are clean.
  • The mask neither eats the subject nor leaves background on the edge.
  • After covering the shot, three random frames show no sudden warp or drift.

en.title: Cleanup: Remove the Mistake, Keep the Information
en.summary: Cleanup removes the mistake, not the information the audience needs.
en.html:
Home/Post/Cleanup: Remove the Mistake, Keep the Information

Post / VFX

Cleanup: Remove the Mistake, Keep the Information

Cleanup removes the mistake, not the information the audience needs.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Before removing a cable, mic or stand, read the background: a plain wall is easy; foliage, crowds and texture are not. Shoot a clean plate or empty frame so post has a source.

Ask what the background contains before erasing

Match grain, noise and motion blur. A clean still that falls apart in motion is the usual failure.

Limits

Do not erase story information. Removing a key prop or sign can change how the audience reads the space; confirm it is not load-bearing.

On set

List what must survive: faces, text, actions. Remove only the mistake, then check at 100 and 50 percent.

Do this

Cleanup removes the wrong thing, not everything; keep the information the audience needs.

  1. List what must stay: faces, text, action.
  2. Erase only the error object, not the background texture.
  3. Review at 100 and 50 percent to confirm the patch disappears.

Avoid

Do not erase information for cleanliness; lose a face or text and the shot is useless.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Faces, text, and action remain; only the error object is gone.
  • 2. The patch disappears at 100 and 50 percent and texture connects.
  • 3. A before-and-after shows what was removed rather than a full repaint.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Faces, text, and action remain; only the error…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The patch disappears at 100 and 50 percent and…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not erase information for cleanliness; lose a face or text and the shot is useless.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “List what must stay: faces, text, action.”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Faces, text, and action remain; only the error object is gone.
  • The patch disappears at 100 and 50 percent and texture connects.
  • A before-and-after shows what was removed rather than a full repaint.

en.title: CG Integration: Match Light, Shadow, Atmosphere
en.summary: CG integration matches light direction, shadow softness, and atmosphere before detail.
en.html:
Home/Post/CG Integration: Match Light, Shadow, Atmosphere

Post / VFX

CG Integration: Match Light, Shadow, Atmosphere

CG integration matches light direction, shadow softness, and atmosphere before detail.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

CG-live integration fails at light direction and lens distortion. Record the live key position, color temperature, focal length and aperture, then render CG with the same set. Color can be graded; light position cannot.

Share light and lens before color

Compare a gray ball and chart before comp; match CG reflection, shadow and grain to the plate.

Limits

CG cannot save a bad plate. Wrong motion blur or perspective makes effects look worse; shoot it right first.

On set

Match three things first: key direction, shadow softness, and atmospheric haze. Then grain and lens distortion; detail comes last.

Do this

CG integration matches light direction, shadow softness, and haze before detail.

  1. Match the key direction so CG and live plate receive the same light.
  2. Match shadow softness and atmospheric haze to set depth.
  3. Match grain and lens distortion last, then add detail.

Avoid

Do not start with detail; if light and shadow are wrong, more detail looks faker.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. CG and plate share the key direction and shadows fall on the same side.
  • 2. Shadow softness and haze match so the layers do not look pasted.
  • 3. Grain and distortion align and the CG boundary disappears at delivery size.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“CG and plate share the key direction and shado…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Shadow softness and haze match so the layers d…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not start with detail; if light and shadow are wrong, more detail looks faker.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Match the key direction so CG and live”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • CG and plate share the key direction and shadows fall on the same side.
  • Shadow softness and haze match so the layers do not look pasted.
  • Grain and distortion align and the CG boundary disappears at delivery size.

en.summary: SDH names speakers, ambience, and important effects; it does not just transcribe dialogue.
en.html:
Home/Post/SDH: More Than Dialogue

Post / Accessibility

SDH: More Than Dialogue

SDH names speakers, ambience, and important effects; it does not just transcribe dialogue.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

SDH is not only dialogue; it names sound events: door, footsteps, phone, music mood. Mark speaker changes by name or position; overlap gets “together.”

SDH writes what is heard

Describe music in brackets by style and feeling, not just “music.” Key plot sounds include direction: approaching from back left.

Limits

SDH is not a full sound list. Caption only what drives understanding or emotion; labeling every sound buries the image.

On set

Mark the speaker: male, female, phone. Write [door] or [rain] for effects and [music] for score; do not just transcribe dialogue.

Do this

SDH captions name the speaker, ambience, and key effects, not just dialogue.

  1. Label speakers: male, female, phone.
  2. Write ambience as [door], [rain], and music as [music].
  3. Check placement and reading speed; captions never cover mouths or hands.

Avoid

Do not place captions over mouths or hands; the audience needs the performance.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Each caption identifies the speaker and distinguishes phone or off-screen voice.
  • 2. Door, rain, music, and other key sounds appear in the captions.
  • 3. Captions stay off mouths and hands, within two lines, and read at pace.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Each caption identifies the speaker and distin…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Door, rain, music, and other key sounds appear…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not place captions over mouths or hands; the audience needs the performance.

Extend

Check

  • Each caption identifies the speaker and distinguishes phone or off-screen voice.
  • Door, rain, music, and other key sounds appear in the captions.

en.title: Audio Description: Say What Matters
en.summary: Audio description says what is invisible but necessary: who moves, where, and what they hold.
en.html:
Home/Post/Audio Description: Say What Matters

Post / Accessibility

Audio Description: Say What Matters

Audio description says what is invisible but necessary: who moves, where, and what they hold.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Audio description is not narrating every image. Write three kinds: who does what, spatial relations, on-screen text. Do not repeat what characters already say.

Describe what is unseen but necessary

Fit description into dialogue gaps and never cover a line. Time it first; if too long, cut adjectives, keep action and direction.

Limits

Description is not commentary. Do not write “she is sad”; write “she looks down and turns the photo over.” Let the listener judge.

Audio description: who and where first, then what happens

Audio description is not shot-by-shot narration. It fills the gaps between dialogue with what cannot be seen. Order: who, where, doing what. Do not describe camera movement first.

  1. One information point per gap; prioritize relationships, spatial position and key action.
  2. Avoid dialogue and important sound. Speak 10% slower and leave a one-second margin.
  3. Do not judge or spoil. Not “he looks sad”; write “he lowers his head, hand stops on the door handle.”

Acceptance: with the picture off, the story is still followable; with it on, the description does not fight the dialogue. Both must pass.

On set

Leave a gap every 20 to 30 seconds and say who moves, where they go, and what is in hand. Do not describe feelings.

Do this

Audio description says only what cannot be seen but must be known: who moves, where, and what is in hand.

  1. Leave a gap every 20 to 30 seconds and never cover dialogue.
  2. Say who moves, where they go, and what they hold.
  3. Do not describe emotions; let performance and sound carry them.

Avoid

Do not say “he is sad”; let action and sound say it.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Description lands in dialogue gaps and never covers a key line.
  • 2. Each passage names who moves, where, and what is held.
  • 3. No emotion is interpreted; the listener can judge from action and sound.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Description lands in dialogue gaps and never c…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Each passage names who moves, where, and what…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not say “he is sad”; let action and sound say it.

Extend

Check

  • Description lands in dialogue gaps and never covers a key line.

  • No emotion is interpreted; the listener can judge from action and sound.

en.title: Multilingual Subtitles: One Language at a Time
en.summary: Do not stack two languages in one line; switch tracks or deliver separate versions.
en.html:
Home/Post/Multilingual Subtitles: One Language at a Time

Post / Accessibility

Multilingual Subtitles: One Language at a Time

Do not stack two languages in one line; switch tracks or deliver separate versions.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Deliver multilingual captions as separate tracks: one language each, aligned timecode, separate styles. Do not stack Chinese and English on one line; mobile collapses and neither can be turned off.

One track per language, never mixed

Check line breaks per track: about 16–18 Chinese characters or 42 Latin characters per line. The languages need different breaks, not shared ones.

Limits

Translation is not word replacement. Place names, terms and tone follow the target language; one wrong character makes the audience doubt the whole film.

On set

One language per line. Use separate subtitle tracks or two versions; do not squeeze two languages into small type.

Do this

Do not stack two languages on one line; switch subtitle tracks or deliver separate versions.

  1. One language per line.
  2. Use selectable tracks or two independent versions.
  3. Check type size and line count; do not squeeze bilingual text into two tiny lines.

Avoid

Do not squeeze bilingual text into two small lines; neither reads.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Contracts, tax, insurance and consent rules differ by market; use the local currency and local counsel before signing or invoicing.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Each line holds one language with no stacked bilingual text.
  • 2. Tracks switch independently, or each version is complete on its own.
  • 3. Type size and line count remain readable on a phone without shrinking for both languages.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Each line holds one language with no stacked b…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Tracks switch independently, or each version i…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not squeeze bilingual text into two small lines; neither reads.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “One language per line.”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Each line holds one language with no stacked bilingual text.
  • Tracks switch independently, or each version is complete on its own.

en.title: Mastering: One File to Rule the Delivery
en.summary: The master is the single trusted source; platform, vertical, and subtitled versions derive from it.
en.html:
Home/Post/Mastering: One File to Rule the Delivery

Post / Delivery

Mastering: One File to Rule the Delivery

The master is the single trusted source; platform, vertical, and subtitled versions derive from it.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

The master is the single high-quality file: max resolution, max bitrate, no burned-in captions or separate tracks. Platform versions export from it; never re-compress a platform file.

Master once; platform cuts derive from it

Name it with date, version and project; keep two copies, one offline. Re-releases, caption changes and compilations all start here.

Limits

A master is not “the biggest file.” Bitrate beyond platform and display needs only costs storage; the goal is no visible compression, not the largest number.

On set

Make the master in high-quality ProRes or DNxHR and name it master. Derive the platform, vertical, and subtitled versions from it.

Do this

The master is the only trusted delivery source; platform, vertical, and subtitled versions derive from it.

  1. Make the master in the highest-quality ProRes or DNxHR and name it master.
  2. Derive platform, vertical, and subtitle versions from it; never edit backward.
  3. Confirm the master opens, plays, and relinks before delivery.

Avoid

Do not use “latest” as the filename; delivery must be traceable.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The master is the highest-quality format and its filename says master.
  • 2. Every platform version traces back to the same master with no backward overwrite.
  • 3. The master opens, plays, and relinks on a clean machine.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The master is the highest-quality format and i…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Every platform version traces back to the same…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use “latest” as the filename; delivery must be traceable.

Extend

Check

en.title: Archive: Open It in Three Years
en.summary: Archiving is not dragging files to a drive; it means findable, openable, and editable in three years.
en.html:
Home/Post/Archive: Open It in Three Years

Post / Delivery

Archive: Open It in Three Years

Archiving is not dragging files to a drive; it means findable, openable, and editable in three years.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

The package includes final project, originals or proxies, fonts, LUTs, music licenses, captions, delivery files and a one-page note. Missing fonts and LUTs means a wall of errors next time.

Archiving is not zipping; it is opening next time

Generate a checksum manifest, keep two copies, one offline; restore-test one package a year.

Limits

Archiving is not every version. Keep the final project and necessary media; store old versions separately or the package becomes too big to open.

On set

Archive three things: media, project file, and a readme. The readme lists software versions, plugins, LUTs, and restore steps; test one restore.

Do this

Archiving is not dragging files onto a drive; it means finding, opening, and editing them in three years.

  1. Archive three things: media, project files, and documentation.
  2. Document software versions, plugins, LUTs, and recovery steps.
  3. Restore one random file to another machine and open it.

Avoid

Do not archive media without the project; in three years you have a pile of unopenable cards.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Media, project files, and documentation are all present with matching paths.
  • 2. The notes list software, plugins, LUTs, and recovery steps.
  • 3. A random file restores on another machine and opens successfully.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Media, project files, and documentation are al…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The notes list software, plugins, LUTs, and re…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not archive media without the project; in three years you have a pile of unopenable cards.

Extend

Check

en.title: QC: Black Frames, Frozen Frames, Dead Audio
en.summary: QC follows a list: black frames, freezes, audio drops, subtitle overflow, channel swaps.
en.html:
Home/Post/QC: Black Frames, Frozen Frames, Dead Audio

Post / Delivery

QC: Black Frames, Frozen Frames, Dead Audio

QC follows a list: black frames, freezes, audio drops, subtitle overflow, channel swaps.

3 min read · Delivery QCTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

QC runs a checklist: black frames, freeze, audio dropout, subtitle overflow, channel swap.

On set

Run the checklist: black frames, freeze frames, audio drops, subtitles outside safe area, channel swap. Judge on a calibrated monitor, not laptop speakers.

Do this

  1. Check black frames, freeze, audio dropouts, subtitle overflow, and left-right channels.
  2. Use a calibrated monitor and headphones, not laptop speakers.
  3. Mark problems with timecode and fix the master, not the platform copy.

Avoid

Do not judge sound on laptop speakers; you will miss low end and dropouts.

QC checklist

Check the delivery spec: resolution, frame rate, duration, channels, loudness, subtitles, safe area and file naming. Do not only look at picture; sound and subtitles are the two easiest misses.

  1. Black frames and freezes: watch from head to tail at 1x and log timecode.
  2. Dropouts and peaks: listen with headphones, not just the waveform; check left/right and phase.
  3. Subtitles: check safe area, typos, line breaks, timing and forced subtitles.

Pass order

  1. Conform first and confirm the timeline matches the master. Do not QC a platform-compressed version.
  2. Play the whole film at 1x and log timecode and frame number at the moment you see a problem.
  3. Recheck with scopes, a calibrated monitor and headphones; laptop speakers are reference only.

QC is a full pass, not a spot check. Watch 10 minutes, rest, then continue; attention fatigue hides errors.

What gets missed

  1. Laptop speakers hide low end and dropouts. Use headphones or a monitor.
  2. Checking only the platform preview hides problems; the platform re-encodes.
  3. Checking only the first subtitle screen misses later safe-area, typo and timing issues.
  4. Swapped channels can sound fine in headphones. Check phase or mono.

QC log

  • Every issue has timecode, frame, type and fix status; recheck the same spot after the fix.
  • Black frame, freeze, dropout, subtitle, channel and loudness all have pass/fail.
  • Final check uses a calibrated monitor and headphones, not laptop speakers.
  • Log master filename, delivery version, QC operator and date; the platform copy never replaces the master.

Delivery log

Before delivery log master filename, duration, resolution, frame rate, loudness, subtitle version, QC operator and date. Keep the platform upload separate; fix problems in the master.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Black frames, freeze, and audio dropouts are timecoded and fixed.
  • 2. Subtitles stay in frame and left-right channels are correct.
  • 3. Review uses a calibrated monitor and headphones, not laptop speakers.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Black frames, freeze, and audio dropouts are t…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Subtitles stay in frame and left-right channel…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not judge sound on laptop speakers; you will miss low end and dropouts.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Check black frames, freeze, audio dropouts, subtitle overflow,”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • Black frames, freeze, and audio dropouts are timecoded and fixed.
  • Subtitles stay in frame and left-right channels are correct.
  • Review uses a calibrated monitor and headphones, not laptop speakers.

Boundary

en.title: Project Structure: Folders Beat Software
en.summary: Set folders and naming before software; if the app changes, the media still makes sense.
en.html:
Home/Post/Project Structure: Folders Beat Software

Post / Assets

Project Structure: Folders Beat Software

Set folders and naming before software; if the app changes, the media still makes sense.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

The project root holds only three things: 01_media, 02_project, 03_delivery. Media sorts by date and scene; project by edit, grade and sound; delivery by platform and date. Every path should tell you which stage a file belongs to.

Three folders before any naming debate

Name files date_scene_shot_version, never “final” or “revised.” Version numbers only go up, so even the trash shows order.

Limits

Structure is not decoration. The test is whether someone with the drive can find the original media and the latest project in five minutes.

On set

Create 01_media, 02_project, 03_exports, and 04_docs at the root. Name files date_scene_camera; never final version.

Do this

Project structure fixes folders and names so the media survives a software change.

  1. Create 01_media, 02_project, 03_exports, and 04_docs at the root.
  2. Name files date_scene_camera, never “final”.
  3. Keep proxies and originals separate and back up the same day.

Avoid

Do not leave media on the desktop; a system reinstall erases it.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The four root folders exist and media, project, exports, and docs each live in place.
  • 2. Filenames carry date, scene, and camera and sort cleanly.
  • 3. On another machine or app, the path still leads to the original media.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The four root folders exist and media, project…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Filenames carry date, scene, and camera and so…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not leave media on the desktop; a system reinstall erases it.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Take 30 seconds of footage and make an A/B, changing only “Create 01_media, 02_project, 03_exports, and 04_docs at the”. Note one timecode and one difference before keeping it.

Check

  • The four root folders exist and media, project, exports, and docs each live in place.
  • Filenames carry date, scene, and camera and sort cleanly.
  • On another machine or app, the path still leads to the original media.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: solo project

Solo projects easily become “desktop is the project”: footage in Downloads, project on the desktop, exports on another drive. Three days later you cannot find anything. Solo structure does not need complexity; it needs three things: one project root, four fixed subfolders and one version rule.

The four: 01_footage, 02_project, 03_audio, 04_export. Everything goes into these four; no more “New Folder”. Version by date plus sequence, never final. Back up even a solo project, at least one copy on another drive.

Condition B: team or handoff

The first rule of a team project is “someone else can take over”. Use English or numeric folder names, not personal initials; put a README in each folder with source, frame rate, colour, proxies, timecode and contacts. Hand over the README before the project.

Team versions need a lock folder: every approved version goes into 05_lock and others read only. Do not keep editing the lock; copy to 06_rev, change, then lock again. The lock gives “which version was approved” an answer.

Counterexample: a folder called final

A project has final, final2, final_ok, final_really and final_to_client. Two months later the client wants one word changed; the team opens five finals and cannot tell which is the master. They reverse-engineer from a compressed platform download.

The fix is not final_final; use date plus state: 20261126_lock, 20261127_rev, 20261128_client. Date shows order, state shows responsibility. Final is an adjective, not a version name.

Reusable model

Root → four folders → README → lock. The root makes the project independent, four folders give files a home, README explains handover, lock answers approval. With all four, the project does not leave when the person does.

Run a stranger test every quarter: someone uninvolved finds the master, proxies and delivery files using only folders and README. If they cannot, the structure needs work.

en.title: Proxy and Cache: Do Not Fill the Drive First
en.summary: Keep proxies and cache on a separate drive; a full edit drive drops frames.
en.html:
Home/Post/Proxy and Cache: Do Not Fill the Drive First

Post / Assets

Proxy and Cache: Do Not Fill the Drive First

Keep proxies and cache on a separate drive; a full edit drive drops frames.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

A proxy is a low-resolution copy for editing; a cache is a preview file generated for playback. Deleting cache does not lose media; deleting proxies takes the timeline offline. Keep them in separate folders.

Proxies and cache are different things

Put proxies in a Proxy folder and cache in the software's cache directory; clean cache only.

Limits

Do not let a cleaner app delete “media cache” in one click. It may sweep proxies and originals. Confirm the path before deleting.

On set

Put proxies and cache on a second SSD and keep 20 percent free on the system drive. When the edit drive fills, clear cache, not originals.

Do this

Proxies and cache belong on a separate drive; a full edit drive drops frames.

  1. Put proxies and cache on a second SSD.
  2. Keep twenty percent free on the system drive and never let the edit drive go red.
  3. When space runs out, clear cache first; never delete originals.

Avoid

Do not delete originals for space; cache can be rebuilt, media cannot.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Proxies and cache sit on the second drive and the edit drive still has free space.
  • 2. The system drive keeps at least twenty percent free with no red warning.
  • 3. After clearing cache, the project rebuilds and every original remains.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Proxies and cache sit on the second drive and…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The system drive keeps at least twenty percent…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not delete originals for space; cache can be rebuilt, media cannot.

Extend

Check

en.title: Backup Recovery: Rehearse One Restore
en.summary: Backup is not finished when the copy ends; restore one random file to prove it.
en.html:
Home/Post/Backup Recovery: Rehearse One Restore

Post / Assets

Backup Recovery: Rehearse One Restore

Backup is not finished when the copy ends; restore one random file to prove it.

3 min read · Data safetyTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

A backup is not done until a random file restores. Test recovery, not just copying.

On set

Use 3-2-1: three copies, two media types, one offsite. Restore one random file to another machine and open it.

Do this

  1. Follow 3-2-1: three copies, two media types, one off-site.
  2. Restore one random file to another machine.
  3. Open it, confirm playback or relink, and record the recovery time.

Avoid

Do not copy without restoring; a failing drive does not warn you.

Put 3-2-1 on the desk

Three copies: card/in-camera, on-set SSD and backup drive. Two media types: SSD/HDD or LTO. One offsite: cloud or another building. RAID is not backup; it survives a dead drive, not deletion, ransomware or fire.

  1. Checksum the card copy before formatting. Do not wipe the card until two readable copies exist.
  2. Power and carry the on-set SSD and backup drive separately; never in the same bag.
  3. Check the backup log at wrap. Rerun a failed job immediately; do not wait until the studio.

Restore drill

  1. Pick a random file, not the one just copied; restore it from the backup to another machine.
  2. Open or relink it and confirm it plays and imports into the NLE. File size alone is not proof.
  3. Log restore time, path and checksum; have a different person run the next drill.

Drill quarterly, and at least once before a project delivery.

Fake backups

  1. RAID as backup: a second drive dies during rebuild and everything is gone. RAID is not version history.
  2. Sync as backup: delete locally and the cloud deletes too. Sync is not backup.
  3. Backing up only in the same building: fire or flood takes both. Offsite must be offsite.
  4. Copying without checksums: a bad file passes silently until someone opens it.

Backup acceptance log

  • Three copies, two media types and one offsite copy are identifiable; each has a checksum.
  • A random file restores on another machine and plays or relinks.
  • Restore time, steps and checksum are logged; another person can repeat it.
  • Two readable copies exist before card formatting; the backup log has no failed jobs.

Restore log

Every drill logs date, random file, source drive, checksum, target machine, open result, duration and operator. A drill without an open result does not pass.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Three copies, two media types, and one off-site copy can all be named.
  • 2. A random file restores on another machine and opens.
  • 3. Recovery time and steps are logged so the next test repeats them.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Three copies, two media types, and one off-sit…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“A random file restores on another machine and…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not copy without restoring; a failing drive does not warn you.

Extend

Check

  • Three copies, two media types, and one off-site copy can all be named.
  • A random file restores on another machine and opens.
  • Recovery time and steps are logged so the next test repeats them.

en.title: Weight: The Acceleration on Landing
en.summary: Weight is not a pose; it is acceleration in the landing frames. Without it, everything floats.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Weight: The Acceleration on Landing

Animation / Principles

Weight: The Acceleration on Landing

Weight is not a pose; it is acceleration in the landing frames. Without it, everything floats.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

Weight in animation is not a fatter character. Watch three things: feet pressing the ground, knees bending, delay at start and stop. Heavy objects start slow and stop slow; light objects start fast and stop abruptly.

Weight is support and delay

Test with a box: empty versus full changes lean, breath and step rate. Changing only box color does not convince.

Limits

Weight is not slow motion. Slowing everything looks underwater; weight lives in the acceleration and deceleration curves.

On set

Accelerate two frames before impact, hold two frames on contact, then settle for three. Add one or two frames of delay for heavy objects.

Do this

Weight is not a pose; it is the acceleration and deceleration at landing. Without it, everything floats.

  1. Accelerate for two frames before contact.
  2. Hold two frames after contact, then rebound for three.
  3. Add one or two frames of delay to heavy objects so weight lands after contact.

Avoid

Do not draw the pose without acceleration; even a heavy pose lands like a balloon.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The fall accelerates, then holds and rebounds after contact.
  • 2. Heavy objects lag one or two frames longer than light ones.
  • 3. Cover the pose and watch only the landing point; weight still reads.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The fall accelerates, then holds and rebounds…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Heavy objects lag one or two frames longer tha…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not draw the pose without acceleration; even a heavy pose lands like a balloon.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Hold two frames after contact, then rebound for”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • The fall accelerates, then holds and rebounds after contact.
  • Heavy objects lag one or two frames longer than light ones.
  • Cover the pose and watch only the landing point; weight still reads.

Deep dive

About 8 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: light object

A light object is not weightless; its weight is small enough that air, breath and fingers change it. Paper, a cup, a hem, hair drift before landing and stop after; animation needs a clear contact frame between drift and stop. Without contact, the object floats.

The key is a secondary action: after the main body lands, an edge moves once. Paper lifts at the corner, water in a cup ripples. The secondary action gives weight an after-wave instead of a hard stop.

Condition B: heavy object or character

Heavy is not “slow motion”; the body must bear the weight before it moves. A character lifting a heavy box bends the knees, grips, then rises; the weight passes over the feet before the box leaves the ground. Without a bearing frame, the box looks empty.

A heavy landing needs compression, rebound and settle: the foot contacts, the body sinks one frame, rebounds, then settles. Sink without rebound looks like sinking into the floor; rebound without sink looks like a spring.

Counterexample: bounce without contact

A ball falls from a table. The animation has a beautiful bounce curve, but the ball starts rising one frame before contact. The audience cannot say what is wrong, only that it feels fake. The curve is not the problem; the contact frame is missing.

The fix is not a lower bounce; add one or two compression frames at contact: the ball flattens, then rebounds. Compression makes the audience believe the floor exists; without a floor, a bounce is only up and down.

Reusable model

Anticipation → contact → compression → rebound → settle. Five frames decide weight. Anticipation tells the body to move, contact makes the ground exist, compression makes weight visible, rebound gives material elasticity, settle ends the action.

Watch with music off: if the silhouette alone tells how heavy the object is, the weight works; if it needs sound effects, the action is unfinished.
