en.title: Anticipation: Show the Next Move
en.summary: Anticipation tells the audience what is coming; without it, action feels pasted in.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Anticipation: Show the Next Move

Animation / Principles

Anticipation: Show the Next Move

Anticipation tells the audience what is coming; without it, action feels pasted in.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

Before an action, play a small opposite move: crouch before a jump, pull the hand back before a punch, lean back before a run. The reverse frame lets the audience anticipate force.

Go opposite before going forward

Keep it short, usually two to four frames; too long reads as hesitation, too short is invisible.

Limits

Not every action needs anticipation. In fast consecutive action it drags; use it before key moves only.

Anticipation leads by only 2–4 frames

Too much anticipation and the viewer guesses; too little and the action pops. At 24fps, give the main action a small opposite move 2–4 frames before it starts.

  1. Press the shoulder three frames before raising the arm; bend the knees four frames before a jump; move the eyes two frames before a head turn.
  2. The anticipation is smaller than the main action and moves the other way. Equal size turns it into two main actions.
  3. In a fast cut, skip the anticipation and use sound or a glance instead.

Acceptance: cover the main action and watch only the lead-in. The viewer should know something is about to happen, but not exactly how.

On set

Add four to six frames of reverse anticipation: the body moves five centimeters back before going forward. Let the audience predict the direction.

Do this

Anticipation tells the audience what is about to happen; without it, action feels cut in.

  1. Add four to six frames of reverse anticipation before the move.
  2. Move the body back five centimeters, then forward.
  3. Let the audience predict direction instead of hiding it with a cut.

Avoid

Do not replace anticipation with a cut; without prediction, the action has no force.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Four to six frames of reverse action precede the main move.
  • 2. The body goes back before forward and the direction is predictable.
  • 3. Remove anticipation and the action feels sudden, proving it worked.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Four to six frames of reverse action precede t…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The body goes back before forward and the dire…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not replace anticipation with a cut; without prediction, the action has no force.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Move the body back five centimeters, then forward.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • Four to six frames of reverse action precede the main move.
  • The body goes back before forward and the direction is predictable.

en.title: Run Cycle: Feet and Center of Gravity
en.summary: Set the center of gravity and footfall order before arms; wrong feet make the whole body float.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Run Cycle: Feet and Center of Gravity

Animation / 2D

Run Cycle: Feet and Center of Gravity

Set the center of gravity and footfall order before arms; wrong feet make the whole body float.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

The key is not how high the leg lifts but when the foot lands and when the body is lowest. Mark contact and airborne frames, then in-between; a wrong contact makes the whole cycle slide.

Run cycles start at the contact frame

Check in side view: head bounce, hip sway, arms opposing legs. If one is wrong, the cycle is unstable.

Limits

Running is not fast walking. Walking always has a foot down; running has flight. Speed up a walk cycle and it becomes race-walking.

On set

Draw four key poses: contact, down, pass, and airborne. Roll the foot heel to toe and keep the hips within one head height.

Do this

A run cycle fixes weight and foot contact before arms; wrong feet make the whole body float.

  1. Draw four key poses: contact, down, passing, airborne.
  2. Roll the foot from heel to toe.
  3. Keep vertical travel within one head height, then fix arms.

Avoid

Do not fix arms first; sliding feet make even smooth arms look floaty.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. All four key poses read: contact, down, passing, airborne.
  • 2. The planted foot rolls heel to toe instead of sliding flat.
  • 3. Vertical travel stays within one head and the loop does not float.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“All four key poses read: contact, down, passin…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The planted foot rolls heel to toe instead of…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not fix arms first; sliding feet make even smooth arms look floaty.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Roll the foot from heel to toe.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • All four key poses read: contact, down, passing, airborne.
  • The planted foot rolls heel to toe instead of sliding flat.
  • Vertical travel stays within one head and the loop does not float.

en.title: Loop Cycle: Match the First and Last Frame
en.summary: The first and last frames must match, or the loop twitches every cycle.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Loop Cycle: Match the First and Last Frame

Animation / 2D

Loop Cycle: Match the First and Last Frame

The first and last frames must match, or the loop twitches every cycle.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

Walk, run and breathing cycles must connect first and last frame invisibly. Build key poses, then in-betweens; overlap one frame at the seam so the loop does not pop.

Loops live or die at the seam

A loop is not identical repetition. Add one small variation per cycle—a hand higher, a step slower. Perfect sameness bores in three seconds.

Limits

Loop length comes from the action, not the music. Cutting before a step completes makes the foot slide; finish the action, then match the beat.

On set

Draw the same frame at both ends with eight to twelve frames between. Loop it and check for a jump from last to first.

Do this

A loop needs matching first and last frames, or it hiccups every cycle.

  1. Draw the same pose at the head and tail.
  2. Fill eight to twelve frames between them.
  3. Play on loop and check the last-to-first transition for a jump.

Avoid

Do not leave a one-frame mismatch at the seam; repetition makes the hitch obvious.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. First and last frames are the same pose in position and shape.
  • 2. Eight to twelve frames fill the middle at an even rhythm.
  • 3. Ten loops play with no hitch or stick at the seam.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“First and last frames are the same pose in pos…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Eight to twelve frames fill the middle at an e…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not leave a one-frame mismatch at the seam; repetition makes the hitch obvious.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Fill eight to twelve frames between them.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • First and last frames are the same pose in position and shape.
  • Eight to twelve frames fill the middle at an even rhythm.
  • Ten loops play with no hitch or stick at the seam.

en.title: 2D Compositing: Separate Background, Character, Light
en.summary: Separate background, character, and light. Flattened layers force a full redraw for one change.
en.html:
Home/Animation/2D Compositing: Separate Background, Character, Light

Animation / 2D

2D Compositing: Separate Background, Character, Light

Separate background, character, and light. Flattened layers force a full redraw for one change.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

The giveaway is inconsistent line weight and color. Unify stroke width, anti-aliasing and value range before lighting; adjust each layer separately, not with a global filter.

2D compositing aligns line and color first

Check with a comparison frame: foreground and background blacks and whites must match; if not, it looks pasted on.

Limits

Compositing is not adding effects. No amount of effects fixes misaligned lines; align the base layers first.

2D compositing: fix edges, then color, then light

Compositing problems are usually order problems, not “not enough effect.” Color before edge work magnifies edge fringes. Light before edge work covers seams. The order is: clean plate → edge → color match → light → output.

StepCheckFailure signal
EdgeInspect at 1:1 pixelsWhite/black fringe, jaggies
ColorSkin and sky within one sceneForeground warmer or greener than background
LightLight direction matchesGlow passes through an occluder
OutputReview at each delivery sizeEdge vanishes small, seam shows large

Project-level checks

  1. Toggle every element and make a list. One missing shadow or contact shadow makes the layer float.
  2. Use the smallest edge setting, several light passes. One maxed-out pass eats detail.
  3. Match color on neutral gray first, then skin. Eyes alone drift on a colored background.
  4. Put the light pass on top but mask it behind foreground objects; otherwise light goes through walls.

Before delivery, ask someone else to watch ten seconds and answer only “what floats?” After staring for hours, you stop seeing seams.

On set

Use four layers: background, character, foreground, and light. Grade each separately and keep shadows off the character layer.

Do this

2D compositing separates background, character, foreground, and light; one flattened image means redrawing everything for one change.

  1. Use four layers: background, character, foreground, light effect.
  2. Grade each layer separately and keep shadows off the character layer.
  3. Composite position first, then light and shadow.

Avoid

Do not draw everything on one layer; one change forces a full redraw.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Background, character, foreground, and light are separate layers with clear structure.
  • 2. Shadows live on their own layer, not baked into the character.
  • 3. Changing an action moves only the character layer; background and light stay.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Background, character, foreground, and light a…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Shadows live on their own layer, not baked int…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not draw everything on one layer; one change forces a full redraw.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Grade each layer separately and keep shadows off”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • Background, character, foreground, and light are separate layers with clear structure.
  • Shadows live on their own layer, not baked into the character.
  • Changing an action moves only the character layer; background and light stay.

en.title: 2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane
en.summary: A 2D camera is not one big pan; multiple layers at different speeds create space.
en.html:
Home/Animation/2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane

Animation / 2D

2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane

A 2D camera is not one big pan; multiple layers at different speeds create space.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

Camera moves in 2D start with layer layout: foreground, middle and background on separate planes, moving at different speeds to create space. Move them together and the audience sees a sliding drawing.

A 2D camera is a stage, not a 3D scene

For a push-in, decide whether to move the camera or scale the layer; scaling softens, camera movement stays sharp.

Limits

A 2D camera cannot replace perspective. If layer scale is wrong, complex moves still look like paper; draw the space first.

A 2D camera is not a zoom; it is layered parallax

The point of a 2D camera move is not to push the whole image closer, but to move foreground, midground and background at different speeds. The speed difference creates space. Without layers, even a large move looks like a flat image scaling.

LayerSpeedCommon error
ForegroundFastest; may leave frameScales with background, loses occlusion
MidgroundMedium; carries subjectMotion blur points the wrong way
BackgroundSlowest; needs overscanEdges show after scaling

Project-level checks

  1. Build the background at twice final size to give the camera room. Do not push a final-size plate.
  2. Use two or three camera keyframes with ease in/out. Linear keys feel like a conveyor belt.
  3. Tune motion blur per layer and speed; foreground and background should not share one setting.
  4. Toggle each layer before output; check blank edges, seams and repeated texture.

For acceptance, watch the film at 50%. If space remains, the layers work. If it only “gets bigger,” return to layer speed.

On set

Split the background into far, middle, and near layers and pan them at 1:2:4 speed. Keep the character on its own layer, still.

Do this

2D camera moves are not one flat pan; layers at different speeds create space.

  1. Split the background into far mountain, midground, near trees.
  2. Pan at speeds of 1:2:4.
  3. Keep the character on a separate layer, still or with a small follow.

Avoid

Do not pan the whole image at one speed; equal layers flatten the space.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Far, mid, and near layers move at different speeds near 1:2:4.
  • 2. The character layer is separate and does not slide with the background.
  • 3. One pan shows near-fast, far-slow parallax.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Far, mid, and near layers move at different sp…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The character layer is separate and does not s…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not pan the whole image at one speed; equal layers flatten the space.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Pan at speeds of 1:2:4.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • Far, mid, and near layers move at different speeds near 1:2:4.
  • The character layer is separate and does not slide with the background.
  • One pan shows near-fast, far-slow parallax.

en.title: Blockout: Proportions and Camera First
en.summary: Blockout sets scale, camera, and timing before detail. Get it wrong and everything is redone.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Animation/Blockout: Proportions and Camera First

Animation / 3D

Blockout: Proportions and Camera First

Blockout sets scale, camera, and timing before detail. Get it wrong and everything is redone.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

A blockout solves three things: character-to-set scale, camera placement and how long the action takes. Use spheres, boxes and simple props; do not add detail yet.

Lock scale, camera and timing first

Make a playblast with no materials or lights and check silhouette and composition. If it does not read now, detail will not make it read later.

Limits

Blockout is not a low-poly final. Do not fight over faces and cloth here; scale, weight and camera must already work.

Blockout watches only three things

Blockout is not a low-poly preview; it decides scale, camera and shot order. Use gray boxes or mannequins with no materials or lights. Get these three wrong and everything downstream redoes.

  1. Scale: compare character and set height with a known measurement; do not eyeball it.
  2. Camera: lock lens and height before motion; one shot solves one spatial relationship.
  3. Order: cut by edit point, not by production convenience; build the version that tells the story.

Acceptance: play the blockout with all materials off. You should still understand who is where and what they are doing. If not, fix the camera before animation.

On set

Block the figure with three boxes: head, chest, pelvis. Lock the camera and a ten-second duration before modeling.

Do this

Blockout fixes proportion, camera, and duration before detail; a wrong blockout reworks everything.

  1. Use box figures to set head, chest, and pelvis proportions.
  2. Lock the camera and a ten-second duration.
  3. Only model after proportion and camera are approved.

Avoid

Do not animate performance before the camera is locked; it will be reworked.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The box figure reads head, chest, and pelvis proportions.
  • 2. Camera and ten-second duration are locked with screenshots and settings.
  • 3. The final shot matches the blockout camera without a composition change.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The box figure reads head, chest, and pelvis p…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Camera and ten-second duration are locked with…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not animate performance before the camera is locked; it will be reworked.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Lock the camera and a ten-second duration.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • The box figure reads head, chest, and pelvis proportions.
  • Camera and ten-second duration are locked with screenshots and settings.
  • The final shot matches the blockout camera without a composition change.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Blockout is not a draft. It is the simplest shapes deciding what happens in the shot.

Proportion and camera first

Use boxes for person, door, table; set height and distance first. If the person-to-door relationship is wrong, accurate modeling will not save it. Check at the real focal length; do not hide the problem with a wide lens.

Set three cameras: main, reverse, one detail. When all three explain the space, continue.

Blocking in time

Do not pose one frame. Walk a simple proxy through the shot and mark start, turn, end. Give each beat one action, not “walks over.”

Shoot a live-action version on the phone and compare it with the blockout. If a person cannot do it, animation will look fake too.

Gray box solves three things

Space, proportion, motion. Material, light, and detail do not belong in blockout. Adding materials early makes you unwilling to change structure.

Blockout passes when, muted, someone can say who is where, what they want, and what blocks them.

Five-minute drill: one room, three cameras

Build one room, one person, one obstacle. Set three cameras, each solving one piece of information. Render three gray frames; no materials.

Show them to one person and ask where the person wants to go and what blocks them. If they cannot answer, change the camera, not the model.

When the blockout passes

Muted, someone who has not read the script can say who is where, what they want, what blocks them, and why the camera is there. Four answers right means the blockout passes.

If they cannot answer, change the camera and blocking; do not add model detail. Detail makes the problem harder to see, not gone.

Ten blockout checks

  • Boxes set person and door height
  • Distance relationship first
  • Composition at real focal length
  • Main, reverse, detail cameras
  • Proxy walks the shot
  • Start, turn, end marked
  • One action per beat
  • Phone live-action comparison
  • No material or light in gray box
  • Muted, viewer knows who, where, wants what

The only job of blockout is to stop everyone downstream from guessing the space.

en.title: Modeling: Silhouette Before Polygons
en.summary: Read the silhouette before polygon count. A wrong outline stays wrong at any density.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Modeling: Silhouette Before Polygons

Animation / 3D

Modeling: Silhouette Before Polygons

Read the silhouette before polygon count. A wrong outline stays wrong at any density.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

Check the silhouette: fill the model black—can you still recognize the character? Then thickness: bevels at edges, volume at joints. If the silhouette fails, detail will not identify it.

Modeling protects silhouette and thickness

Start with big planes, add edges gradually; do not begin with pores. Every detail pass returns to the silhouette check.

Limits

Polygon count is not precision. Round what should be round, hard what should be hard; polygons in unseen places only slow render.

Modeling: silhouette, topology, UV — in that order

The first acceptance test for a model is not polygon count; it is silhouette. Put it on a black background. If the outline does not tell you what it is, clean topology will not save it.

StageCheckCost to redo
SilhouetteFront, side, backLow; adjust the big forms
TopologyJoint loops, bend testMedium; rewire
UVSeam placement, texel densityHigh; re-unwrap
DetailBevels, wear, bumpsHighest; found after baking

Project-level checks

  1. Block out proportions and camera relationship before topology. Do not sculpt detail on wrong proportions.
  2. Use at least three edge loops at joints; test elbow, knee and shoulder separately instead of relying on a smooth modifier.
  3. Hide UV seams in less visible places; unify texel density with a checker; name multiple UV sets.
  4. Bevel late, but before baking. Bevel after baking and the normals no longer match.

If a model appears for two seconds and is not in close-up, skip the full high-poly pipeline. Use a mid-poly model plus normal maps and give the time to the shot.

On set

Check the silhouette first: render the model black and see if the shape reads. Then subdivide and spend polygons by camera distance.

Do this

Modeling reads silhouette before polygon count; a wrong outline never looks right with more subdivisions.

  1. Render the model black and check the silhouette.
  2. Subdivide only after the outline identifies the character.
  3. Allocate polygons by shot distance: more close, fewer far.

Avoid

Do not fix a silhouette with subdivision; more polygons will not make it recognizable.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The black silhouette identifies the character without color or texture.
  • 2. Subdivision happens after silhouette approval, not before.
  • 3. Close shots carry more polygons than wide shots by plan.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The black silhouette identifies the character…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Subdivision happens after silhouette approval…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not fix a silhouette with subdivision; more polygons will not make it recognizable.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Subdivide only after the outline identifies the character.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • The black silhouette identifies the character without color or texture.
  • Subdivision happens after silhouette approval, not before.
  • Close shots carry more polygons than wide shots by plan.

en.title: Materials: Roughness and Specular
en.summary: Roughness and specular decide plastic, wood, or metal before texture maps.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Materials: Roughness and Specular

Animation / 3D

Materials: Roughness and Specular

Roughness and specular decide plastic, wood, or metal before texture maps.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

Do not start with “metal” or “wood”; start with behavior: reflection sharpness, roughness, edge translucency, dents. The same “metal” can be mirror, brushed or rusted. The difference is behavior, not the label.

Ask what the surface does before naming it

Test with a gray ball and a grid: check reflection, roughness and normal; set those three before color.

Limits

Materials cannot save a model. Without thickness, seams and bevels, the best texture still looks like paper. Fix shape first.

Materials: scale first, roughness second

A material looks fake not because the texture is low resolution, but because its scale is wrong. Wood grain at one meter and at ten centimeters is not the same image. Without a scale reference, roughness is also wrong.

MaterialDefine firstCommon error
WoodGrain direction, board widthOne tile stretched across a wall
MetalBrush direction, roughnessAll mirror, reads as plastic
ClothWeave density, fold scaleTexture larger than folds
SkinPore scale, oily zonesOne roughness for the whole face

Project-level checks

  1. Place a known-size reference (coin, A4 sheet) in the scene and calibrate texture repeats first.
  2. Use a grayscale roughness map, not one value. Paint oil, dry and worn areas separately.
  3. Start normal strength at 0.3 and add gradually; maxed-out normals darken edges.
  4. Judge materials under final lighting, not default HDRI. Change the light and the material reads differently.

Before delivery, make a material contact sheet: one material under hard light, backlight and shadow, to prove it is not only working in one setup.

On set

Under one light, test three spheres with roughness from 0.2 to 0.8 and watch the highlight size. Set the material before adding texture.

Do this

Materials set roughness and specular before texture; those two decide plastic, wood, or metal.

  1. Test three spheres under one light with roughness from 0.2 to 0.8.
  2. Compare highlight size and edge softness.
  3. Lock the material before adding texture.

Avoid

Do not hide material with texture; wrong roughness looks like paper no matter the map.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Three spheres show clearly different highlight sizes under one light.
  • 2. The difference between 0.2 and 0.8 roughness is nameable, not just color.
  • 3. Texture is added after material approval and does not hide highlight issues.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Three spheres show clearly different highlight…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The difference between 0.2 and 0.8 roughness i…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not hide material with texture; wrong roughness looks like paper no matter the map.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Compare highlight size and edge softness.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • Three spheres show clearly different highlight sizes under one light.
  • The difference between 0.2 and 0.8 roughness is nameable, not just color.
  • Texture is added after material approval and does not hide highlight issues.

en.title: 3D Lighting: Three Points and HDRI
en.summary: Use key, fill, and rim to build structure, then HDRI for environment. Reverse the order and space flattens.
en.html:
Home/Animation/3D Lighting: Three Points and HDRI

Animation / 3D

3D Lighting: Three Points and HDRI

Use key, fill, and rim to build structure, then HDRI for environment. Reverse the order and space flattens.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

3D lighting is not filling a scene with light. Set one key direction so shadows explain space; use ambient and fill to control contrast. Even a realistic material looks like a texture map when the key is wrong.

3D lighting starts with key direction, then materials

For every added light, name the real source it replaces; if none, delete it. Keep light layers separable for comparison.

Limits

HDRI is not universal. Interiors, night and hard directional light need manual lamps; an environment map alone goes flat and shadows scatter.

3D lighting: key light first, atmosphere later

The most common 3D lighting mistake is adding atmosphere before the key. Volumetrics, glow and depth of field erase direction. The order is key → fill → rim → environment → atmosphere.

LayerRoleCheck
KeySets time and directionDo shadows fall one way?
FillControls contrastShadow detail without milkiness
RimSeparates subject from backgroundEdges not blown
EnvironmentReflection and skyHDRI matches the set

Project-level checks

  1. Turn off all atmosphere and judge the silhouette on key light alone. If the silhouette fails, atmosphere cannot save it.
  2. Use one lighting rig across shots; record why a shot needs a special light.
  3. Render reflection and refraction as a separate pass so post can adjust. Baking them into beauty locks them.
  4. Check 10% gray and skin, not “brightness”; expose for the midtones.

If render time runs short, cut atmosphere passes before key-light samples. Key noise ruins the whole shot.

On set

Turn off the HDRI and shape the form with the key only. Add fill and rim, then bring the HDRI back to 20 or 30 percent for environment.

Do this

3D lighting builds structure with key, fill, and rim before HDRI; reversing the order flattens space.

  1. Turn off HDRI and shape with the key only.
  2. Add fill and rim.
  3. Bring HDRI in at 20 to 30 percent to fill the environment.

Avoid

Do not start with HDRI; environment light hides the form.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. With HDRI off, the key already defines form.
  • 2. Fill and rim do their jobs without flattening the key.
  • 3. HDRI stays at 20 to 30 percent and does not take over.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“With HDRI off, the key already defines form”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Fill and rim do their jobs without flattening…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not start with HDRI; environment light hides the form.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Add fill and rim.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • With HDRI off, the key already defines form.
  • Fill and rim do their jobs without flattening the key.
  • HDRI stays at 20 to 30 percent and does not take over.

en.title: Render: Samples and Noise
en.summary: Samples and noise come before resolution; unresolved noise at 4K is just bigger dirt.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Render: Samples and Noise

Animation / 3D

Render: Samples and Noise

Samples and noise come before resolution; unresolved noise at 4K is just bigger dirt.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

Confirm frame rate, resolution, color space and audio sample rate; render settings must match the delivery sheet. Do not edit while rendering; the file will not match.

Lock the timeline, then the settings

Play three points after render: opening, mid action, end credits. Check black frames, freezes, audio dropouts and caption overflow. Verify size and duration.

Limits

Rendering is not delivery. A successful render proves the file exists, not that it is correct; QC is a separate pass.

Rendering: lock samples before denoising

Render noise is not something denoise “wipes away.” With too few samples, denoise flattens detail. With enough samples, denoise is the last 10%. Stabilize samples and light bounces first, then denoise.

SettingTune firstSymptom
SamplesStart at 64, double upShadow noise, edge flicker
Bounces3–4, by scene complexityCrushed or washed shadows
DenoiseLast, preserve detailPlastic skin, lost texture
OutputMulti-channel EXRNo separate light control in post

Project-level checks

  1. Render a 50% test first to confirm composition, materials and light. Do not wait for 4K to discover a problem.
  2. Double samples; noise should drop clearly. If it does not, the problem is lighting or materials, not samples.
  3. Save before/after denoise and compare pores, cloth and hair. If detail disappears, lower the strength.
  4. Output EXR with Beauty, Light, Reflection and Depth. Keep an adjustable version, not only the MP4.

When the farm is queued, submit a low-sample preview to hold the shot, then render final. Do not use final settings as a test.

On set

Render at 50 percent resolution with low samples to see where noise lives. Raise light and material samples separately; do not just raise the total.

Do this

Rendering checks samples and noise before resolution; unresolved noise at 4K is just bigger dirt.

  1. Render at 50 percent resolution and low samples to see noise distribution.
  2. Adjust light samples and material samples separately.
  3. Do not only raise total samples; find which source causes the noise.

Avoid

Do not brute-force noise with total samples; without the source, render time burns.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. A 50 percent low-sample pass shows whether noise comes from light or material.
  • 2. Light and material samples were adjusted separately.
  • 3. Final noise is traced to a specific source, not brute-forced.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“A 50 percent low-sample pass shows whether noi…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Light and material samples were adjusted separ…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not brute-force noise with total samples; without the source, render time burns.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Adjust light samples and material samples separately.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • A 50 percent low-sample pass shows whether noise comes from light or material.
  • Light and material samples were adjusted separately.
  • Final noise is traced to a specific source, not brute-forced.

en.title: Layout: Camera and Asset Handoff
en.summary: Layout locks camera, scale, and asset versions before animation. A vague handoff makes animators guess.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Layout: Camera and Asset Handoff

Animation / 3D

Layout: Camera and Asset Handoff

Layout locks camera, scale, and asset versions before animation. A vague handoff makes animators guess.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

3D layout is not pretty placement. Draw the ground line, camera height and focal length first, then the character. With those three, space exists. Wrong scale makes later animation look pasted on.

Layout starts with camera and ground

Block a playblast with simple boxes, check occlusion and silhouette; do not add detail.

Limits

Layout is not the final shot. It can be rough, but camera, scale and timing must be locked; changing them later is the most expensive fix.

Layout: turn a shot into a handoffable space

Layout is not pretty composition. It fixes camera, blocking, scale and motion path so the next person does not guess. A usable layout shot can be picked up by another animator.

DeliveryMust stateCommon gap
CameraLens, position, path, frame countA still composition with no move
CharacterBlocking, facing, eye line, scaleScale does not match set
SetMovable props, occlusionForeground hides subject
TimeShot length, key action beatsAnimator invents the rhythm

Project-level checks

  1. Start with a grayscale blockout. Confirm silhouette and space before detail.
  2. Mark camera move with three keys: start, middle, end. “Push in” is not a path.
  3. Mark foot contact with the ground; floating feet are the most common layout failure.
  4. Give animation, lighting and comp a shot-to-asset map so same-name assets do not overwrite each other.

Review at final frame rate, not on stills. A beautiful still with bad motion means the layout path is wrong.

On set

Lock three things before handoff: camera, character scale, and asset version. Put the version in the file header and animate to the layout.

Do this

Layout locks camera, proportion, and asset version before handoff; unclear handoff makes animators guess.

  1. Lock three things: camera, character scale, asset version.
  2. Write the version number in the file header.
  3. Animate to the layout without changing the camera.

Avoid

Do not leave the camera live in layout; changing it after animation starts is rework.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Camera, character scale, and asset version are locked and versioned.
  • 2. The file header shows version and dependencies so animators do not guess.
  • 3. Animation does not change the camera and the final shot matches layout.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Camera, character scale, and asset version are…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The file header shows version and dependencies…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not leave the camera live in layout; changing it after animation starts is rework.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Write the version number in the file header.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • Camera, character scale, and asset version are locked and versioned.
  • The file header shows version and dependencies so animators do not guess.
  • Animation does not change the camera and the final shot matches layout.

en.title: Armature: It Must Stand Before It Acts
en.summary: A stop-motion puppet must stand, walk, and repeat before acting. A soft armature collapses in ten frames.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Armature: It Must Stand Before It Acts

Animation / Stop motion

Armature: It Must Stand Before It Acts

A stop-motion puppet must stand, walk, and repeat before acting. A soft armature collapses in ten frames.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

Test three moves: standing without wobble, raising an arm without sag, sitting without collapse. Use a metal armature with silicone pads and enlarge the feet; do not start with fingers before the center of gravity and knees are stable.

The armature must stand before it performs

Before touching the puppet each frame, ask whether it will fall; shoot a test and check the pivot frame by frame.

Limits

Harder is not better. Too rigid looks robotic; leave softness where it bends and stiffness where it carries weight.

Rigging: run extreme-pose tests before animation

A rig is not done when bones are connected. Problems appear when an animator pulls: elbow collapse, knee inversion, shoulder intersections. Before handoff, run extreme-pose tests; do not start animation until they pass.

TestPosePass condition
ShoulderArm raised 180°No armpit collapse, no cloth intersection
ElbowBend 140°Volume holds, no candy-wrapper twist
KneeDeep squat + reverseNo inversion, feet do not slide
SpineTwist + side bendChest and pelvis transition smoothly

Project-level checks

  1. Standardize controller names: left/right, FK/IK, mirror rules on one page. Animators should not guess.
  2. Lock axes that should not move and hide unused controls. A rig that can be bumped will be bumped.
  3. Save a screenshot of every extreme pose as the rig acceptance record. “It works” is not evidence.
  4. Weight joints before muscles; a full-body weight pass hides problems inside other problems.

If the schedule is under three days, do not build film-level facial rigging. Use simplified facial controls and spend the time on performance and rendering.

On set

Make the puppet stand for ten seconds without wobble, then walk three steps without collapsing. Use a metal armature and weight the feet.

Do this

A stop-motion puppet must stand, walk, and repeat before performance; a soft armature collapses in ten frames.

  1. Stand the puppet for ten seconds without wobble.
  2. Walk three steps without collapse.
  3. Use a metal armature and add weight to the feet.

Avoid

Do not let the armature stay soft; it collapses within ten frames.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The puppet stands ten seconds without wobble and the feet are weighted.
  • 2. Three steps hold without collapse or sudden joint lock.
  • 3. Ten frames of one pose show no positional drift.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The puppet stands ten seconds without wobble a…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Three steps hold without collapse or sudden jo…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not let the armature stay soft; it collapses within ten frames.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Walk three steps without collapse.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • The puppet stands ten seconds without wobble and the feet are weighted.
  • Three steps hold without collapse or sudden joint lock.
  • Ten frames of one pose show no positional drift.

en.title: Stop-Motion Set: Scale and Perspective
en.summary: Set puppet scale first, then build to camera perspective. Wrong scale looks fake in any light.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Stop-Motion Set: Scale and Perspective

Animation / Stop motion

Stop-Motion Set: Scale and Perspective

Set puppet scale first, then build to camera perspective. Wrong scale looks fake in any light.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

It is not a miniature landscape. Every adjustable position needs two fingers of access; walls, furniture and floor must come apart separately or one touch collapses the set.

A stop-motion set must fit a hand

Build a paper maquette at 1:6 or 1:12 first, checking camera, lamp and hand space; do not start with detail.

Limits

More set is not better. Keep foreground for blocking and background empty so a hand fits; a packed set leaves no room even to focus.

Stop-motion sets: scale first, light second

A stop-motion set is not a miniature real world. It is a workbench a hand must fit into. Scale, depth of field and light stability decide quality earlier than fine detail.

ItemOn-set practiceFailure signal
ScaleChoose 1:6 or 1:12; all props share itHand and prop scale disagree
DepthSmall aperture + enough lightSubject sharp, set mush
LightLock positions, use flags, no auto exposureBrightness jumps between frames
ReplacementsTwo or three mouths/hands per actionRun out mid-shot

Project-level checks

  1. Shoot a ten-frame test: does the hand block light or hit the set?
  2. Clamp every light and mark its position; after a move you must return to the same mark.
  3. Lock exposure and white balance in the capture software; disable camera automation.
  4. Back up after every shot. One lost frame means reshooting the whole section.

If a hand enters frame, rehearse the move. The hand is the prop most likely to break the illusion.

On set

Measure the puppet height, then size the set to the lens perspective. Run one perspective line from camera to background and align everything to it.

Do this

Stop-motion sets scale from the puppet and shot perspective; wrong scale looks fake under any light.

  1. Measure the puppet height.
  2. Calculate set size from the shot perspective.
  3. Run one perspective line from camera to background and align everything.

Avoid

Do not build the set by feel; one door next to the puppet reveals the scale.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Puppet height and set size have a conversion record.
  • 2. One perspective line runs camera to background and key objects align.
  • 3. The puppet reads correctly beside door and table without hiding it.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Puppet height and set size have a conversion r…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“One perspective line runs camera to background…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not build the set by feel; one door next to the puppet reveals the scale.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Calculate set size from the shot perspective.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • Puppet height and set size have a conversion record.
  • One perspective line runs camera to background and key objects align.
  • The puppet reads correctly beside door and table without hiding it.

en.title: Stop-Motion Motion Blur: Shoot It Twice
en.summary: Stop-motion blur comes from double exposure or post compositing, not a lower frame rate.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Stop-Motion Motion Blur: Shoot It Twice

Animation / Stop motion

Stop-Motion Motion Blur: Shoot It Twice

Stop-motion blur comes from double exposure or post compositing, not a lower frame rate.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

Stop motion does not capture continuous shutter exposure; blur is simulated in post or multiple exposure. Decide which frames need it: fast hand, turn, fall. Do not blur static frames.

Stop-motion blur is decided per frame

Post blur follows motion direction and length; a uniform blur over everything looks like fog.

Limits

Not every stop-motion shot needs blur. Frame-by-frame sharpness is also a style; choose the style before adding it.

On set

Shoot each pose twice and move the moving parts two or three millimeters on the second pass. Blend the two frames for directional blur.

Do this

Stop-motion blur comes from two exposures or post compositing, not a lower frame rate.

  1. Shoot each pose twice.
  2. Move the moving part two to three millimeters on the second pass.
  3. Blend the two frames in post for directional blur.

Avoid

Do not lower the frame rate for blur; that creates stutter, not motion blur.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Each pose has two exposures and the second moves two to three millimeters.
  • 2. The blended blur has direction matching the motion.
  • 3. No fake blur comes from a lower frame rate.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Each pose has two exposures and the second mov…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The blended blur has direction matching the mo…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not lower the frame rate for blur; that creates stutter, not motion blur.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Move the moving part two to three millimeters”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • Each pose has two exposures and the second moves two to three millimeters.
  • The blended blur has direction matching the motion.
  • No fake blur comes from a lower frame rate.

en.title: Motion Graphics Transition: Shape to Shape
en.summary: A graphic transition morphs one shape into another, not a white flash or random push.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Motion Graphics Transition: Shape to Shape

Animation / Motion graphics

Motion Graphics Transition: Shape to Shape

A graphic transition morphs one shape into another, not a white flash or random push.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

Motion-graphics transitions are not decorative wipes. They carry meaning: a circle becomes a chart, a line becomes a timeline, a word splits into a new word. After the transition, the viewer knows one more thing.

A transition must carry information, not hide a cut

Write “from what to what” before animating; do not let a preset decide the content.

Limits

A transition cannot hide a structural problem. If two sections are unrelated, a smooth transition only delays; cut one first.

On set

Choose one shape change: circle to square, line to arrow. Do it in eight to twelve frames; no white flash.

Do this

Graphic transitions morph one shape into another, not a white flash or arbitrary push.

  1. Choose a shape pair: circle to square, line to arrow.
  2. Complete the morph in eight to twelve frames.
  3. Do not use a white flash; the information on both sides must connect.

Avoid

Do not use white flashes and pushes as universal transitions; if shapes do not connect, the audience loses the thread.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The same shape morphs across the transition instead of hard-cutting.
  • 2. The morph completes in eight to twelve frames at a readable speed.
  • 3. Without a white flash, information still connects and the audience knows where they are.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The same shape morphs across the transition in…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The morph completes in eight to twelve frames…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use white flashes and pushes as universal transitions; if shapes do not connect, the audience loses the thread.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Complete the morph in eight to twelve frames.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • The same shape morphs across the transition instead of hard-cutting.
  • The morph completes in eight to twelve frames at a readable speed.
  • Without a white flash, information still connects and the audience knows where they are.

en.title: Infographic Animation: One Line, One Claim
en.summary: One line carries one claim. More lines mean less memory.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Infographic Animation: One Line, One Claim

Animation / Motion graphics

Infographic Animation: One Line, One Claim

One line carries one claim. More lines mean less memory.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

An infographic is not big numbers plus arrows. Decide the relationship: comparison, trend, proportion, process; each maps to a chart form. Wrong relationship cannot be fixed by animation.

Draw the relationship before decoration

Make a static version and ask a colleague to state the conclusion in five seconds; if not, change the chart, not the motion.

Limits

Decoration cannot replace data. A chart without sample, period and source is illustration; write those three first.

On set

One line carries one variable. Draw it static first, then grow it with the data; do not add labels and icons at the same time.

Do this

One line in an infographic carries one idea; more lines mean less recall.

  1. Each line carries one variable only.
  2. Draw the line static first, then grow it with data.
  3. Do not add labels and icons at the same time; let the line speak.

Avoid

Do not make one line tell three things; the audience remembers none.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Each line maps to one variable and its title names it.
  • 2. The line grows with the number instead of finishing before data.
  • 3. Muted playback lets you repeat what each line says.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Each line maps to one variable and its title n…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The line grows with the number instead of fini…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not make one line tell three things; the audience remembers none.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Draw the line static first, then grow it”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • Each line maps to one variable and its title names it.
  • The line grows with the number instead of finishing before data.
  • Muted playback lets you repeat what each line says.

en.title: Motion Rhythm: Music Beats and Frames
en.summary: Land music hits on frames before easing. Miss the hit and smoothness is still chaos.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Motion Rhythm: Music Beats and Frames

Animation / Motion graphics

Motion Rhythm: Music Beats and Frames

Land music hits on frames before easing. Miss the hit and smoothness is still chaos.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

Motion graphics is not every element moving at once. Group main information, support lines and background; each gets its own entrance and rest. The viewer reads main, then support, then background.

Rhythm comes from grouping, not constant motion

Test at two, four and six seconds; if everything enters on one beat, it looks like an explosion.

Limits

Faster is not better. With dense information, one beat of rest beats ten animations; the viewer needs time to read.

Motion rhythm: map the music, then choose what moves

MG is not “every beat moves.” Split the track into 4–8 bars, mark accents and pauses, then choose one element. If everything moves, nothing reads.

  1. One subject on the accent; weak beats use position or opacity, not scale.
  2. Leave 4–6 frames of stillness after each move. More than two seconds of constant motion tires the eye.
  3. Match transitions by shape or position, not a plugin. The plugin steals the message.

Acceptance: watch with sound off; the rhythm should still read. Turn sound on; motion should not fight the lyrics. Both must pass.

On set

Put the music waveform on the timeline and mark eight downbeats. Each downbeat gets one keyframe, then adjust easing.

Do this

Motion rhythm aligns music hits to frames before easing; if hits are off, smoothness still feels messy.

  1. Put the music waveform on the timeline and mark eight accents.
  2. Place one keyframe on each accent.
  3. Then adjust easing; do not animate first and hunt for music later.

Avoid

Do not animate first and add music later; misaligned hits make even smooth easing messy.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Eight accents are marked on the timeline with matching keyframes.
  • 2. Animation changes land on the accents instead of music chasing picture.
  • 3. Muted playback still holds rhythm without relying on music.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Eight accents are marked on the timeline with…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Animation changes land on the accents instead…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not animate first and add music later; misaligned hits make even smooth easing messy.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Place one keyframe on each accent.”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • Eight accents are marked on the timeline with matching keyframes.
  • Animation changes land on the accents instead of music chasing picture.
  • Muted playback still holds rhythm without relying on music.

en.title: Animatic Pipeline: Voice, Timing, Board
en.summary: Lay temp voice, set duration, then revise the board. Without sound, timing is fiction.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Animation/Animatic Pipeline: Voice, Timing, Board

Animation / Pipeline

Animatic Pipeline: Voice, Timing, Board

Lay temp voice, set duration, then revise the board. Without sound, timing is fiction.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

An animatic uses temporary voice, simple drawings and exact durations to test whether shots connect and pacing works. Mark seconds per shot and record voice first; do not wait for finished animation.

Timing before detail

Treat the animatic as a version allowed to fail. If the story is unclear here, more drawings and effects will not rescue it.

Limits

An animatic is not a beauty preview. Do not chase image quality here, but shot length and action direction must already be locked.

Lock three things in the animatic before animation

The animatic is not for beauty; it locks duration, voice and shot order. If those are not locked, animation will be revised forever.

  1. Voice: record a scratch track at real speaking pace, not read-aloud rhythm. Line length sets shot length.
  2. Timing: lay out at 24fps or the project rate, with in/out points per shot. “About three seconds” is not a timing.
  3. Music: temp only, with marked pauses. Temp music cannot be delivered.

Acceptance: show the animatic to someone outside the edit and ask where they want to fast-forward. Cut those places before layout.

On set

Record the voice first and time it at real speed. Write each shot's seconds and keep the total under 110 percent of target, then draw.

Do this

Animatic starts with voice, then timing, then boards; without sound, timing is fake.

  1. Record voice and time it at real speaking speed.
  2. Write seconds per shot and keep total within 110 percent of target.
  3. Draw after timing is locked.

Avoid

Do not draw everything before voice; a pace change re-times every shot.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Voice is recorded at real speed and every shot duration comes from it.
  • 2. Total stays within 110 percent of target and timing is locked first.
  • 3. Eyes closed, audio tells the story; muted, the picture does.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Voice is recorded at real speed and every shot…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Total stays within 110 percent of target and t…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not draw everything before voice; a pace change re-times every shot.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Draw three keys at 24 fps, change only “Write seconds per shot and keep total within”, and export two seconds. If the weight still does not read, add anticipation before adding blur.

Check

  • Voice is recorded at real speed and every shot duration comes from it.
  • Total stays within 110 percent of target and timing is locked first.
  • Eyes closed, audio tells the story; muted, the picture does.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. An animatic is not a slideshow of boards. It uses scratch sound and timing to test whether the film works.

Time first, detail later

Put each board on the timeline at its estimated duration with scratch dialogue and sound. Check total length and rhythm before drawing beautiful faces.

If a shot runs four seconds without new information, shorten or split it. Changing time in animatic is ten times cheaper than changing it in animation.

Scratch sound must be understandable

Record the dialogue yourself, even if it sounds rough. The audience needs the information, not voice quality. Use only key effects: door, steps, phone.

Put a scratch music track and mark the chorus and pauses. Do not wait until animation is finished to find music; the rhythm will not match.

Lock before animation

An animatic passes when it is understandable muted and understandable with eyes closed. Only then move to layout and animation.

Even one line change after lock requires retiming. Do not rewrite the story while animating. Changing story is always cheaper than changing animation.

Five-minute drill: thirty-second animatic

Make a thirty-second animatic with six boards, phone-recorded dialogue, and two sound effects. Mark seconds per board; total must not exceed thirty.

Watch muted, then listen with eyes closed. Fix whichever version fails; do not add narration to explain.

When the animatic is ready for animation

Understandable muted, understandable eyes closed, total length on budget, every second brings new information, scratch music marks the rhythm. All five pass before layout and animation.

If one second needs narration to explain, cut or redraw it; do not carry it into animation. The animatic's job is to keep “I do not understand” in the cheapest stage.

Watch the total length again

Play the whole animatic three times. Whatever you want to fast-forward on the third pass is what must be cut. The audience will not forgive drag because you watched it longer. Cut time before discussing style.

Ten animatic checks

  • Seconds marked per board
  • Scratch dialogue recorded
  • Only key sound effects
  • Scratch music with chorus marked
  • Total length checked first
  • Four seconds without new info gets cut
  • Understandable muted
  • Understandable eyes closed
  • Locked before animation
  • Line changes retimed

The only purpose of an animatic is to discover the film does not work while it is still cheap.

en.title: Asset Handoff: Names, Versions, Cache
en.summary: Handoff states names, versions, cache, and dependencies. Miss one and the next person rebuilds.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Asset Handoff: Names, Versions, Cache

Animation / Pipeline

Asset Handoff: Names, Versions, Cache

Handoff states names, versions, cache, and dependencies. Miss one and the next person rebuilds.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

A handoff must open on someone else's machine without you: relative texture paths, versioned caches, filenames with scene and date. Never use “final final” as a version.

Names, versions and paths must open on their own

A handoff must open on someone else's machine without you: relative texture paths, versioned caches, filenames with scene and date. Never use “final final” as a version.

Give each asset one line: who made it, what it is for, what it depends on, which version is current. The receiver should rebuild from the note without asking you.

Limits

A handoff is not zipping the entire project. Deliver only assets and caches for the current shot; archive old versions, or the package becomes too big to touch.

On set

Name assets project_asset_version and deliver to a shared drive with a dependency list and cache path. The next person runs it once before starting.

Do this

Asset handoff states naming, version, cache, and dependencies; miss one and the next person rebuilds.

  1. Name assets project_asset_version.
  2. Deliver to a shared drive with a dependency list and cache path.
  3. Have the next person open it once before taking over.

Avoid

Do not leave assets on a personal desktop; the next person cannot find them.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Asset names include project, asset, and version and sort cleanly.
  • 2. The shared drive holds a dependency list and cache path.
  • 3. The next person opens the asset from the list without asking the original artist.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Asset names include project, asset, and versio…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The shared drive holds a dependency list and c…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not leave assets on a personal desktop; the next person cannot find them.

Extend

en.title: Animation Case: From Board to Final
en.summary: Review the case through board, animatic, layout, animation, lighting, and comp, not just the final.
en.html:
Home/Animation/Animation Case: From Board to Final

Animation / Case

Animation Case: From Board to Final

Review the case through board, animatic, layout, animation, lighting, and comp, not just the final.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Animation DeskEdited 2026-11

When studying an animation case, note three limits first: budget, schedule, team size. Style is the result of those limits, not the starting point. Translate “beautiful” into trade-offs: fewer characters, fewer sets, repeated shots, limited frame rate.

Read constraints before style in a case study

Then trace one action: how many frames, key poses, reused assets. If you can retell the production path, you understood the case.

Limits

Do not just save the image. A case without a production path is a reference image, not a method.

On set

Compare stage by stage: three board panels, animatic timing, layout camera, animation keys, light, and comp. Log one change per stage.

Do this

An animation case study compares boards, animatic, layout, animation, light, and comp stage by stage, not just praising the final.

  1. Compare three board panels, animatic timing, layout camera, keyframes, light, comp.
  2. Log one decision and one rework per stage.
  3. State what can be reused, not just “it looks good.”

Avoid

Do not look only at the final; the final hides the rework.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. All six stages are compared, not just final stills.
  • 2. Each stage logs one decision and one rework.
  • 3. At least one reusable step is written so another person can follow it.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“All six stages are compared, not just final st…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Each stage logs one decision and one rework”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not look only at the final; the final hides the rework.

en.html:
Home/Formats/Talking Head Breakdown: Hold Attention for Sixty Seconds

Formats / Talking head

Talking Head Breakdown: Hold Attention for Sixty Seconds

An eight-beat breakdown of a sixty-second talking head: claim, reason, example one, example two, counter, proof, application, question.

6 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: sixty seconds, Douyin/Channels, and the goal is the viewer can repeat one conclusion. Talking head is not reading a script; check whether the first line is the claim, then whether every ten seconds adds information.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 8 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:03 | Picture: the person is already speaking; first line is the claim. Sound: sync. Job: no chance to leave. Steal: claim first. Do not copy: thank followers.
  2. 0:03–0:10 | Picture: medium, frontal; hands in frame. Sound: one reason. Job: ground the claim. Steal: one counterintuitive reason. Do not copy: three claims in one line.
  3. 0:10–0:18 | Picture: example one: one person/action/result. Sound: sync. Job: make it concrete. Steal: one real example. Do not copy: three people.
  4. 0:18–0:26 | Picture: example two: new setting/person, same conclusion. Sound: one transition. Job: more than one proof. Steal: a second setting. Do not copy: repeat example one.
  5. 0:26–0:34 | Picture: counter: the common objection. Sound: say it aloud. Job: handle objection early. Steal: admit the counter has a point. Do not copy: a straw man.
  6. 0:34–0:44 | Picture: proof: data/demo/before-after. Sound: key number. Job: make the claim credible. Steal: one verifiable proof. Do not copy: three numbers.
  7. 0:44–0:52 | Picture: application: what viewers can do today. Sound: one step. Job: give a takeaway. Steal: one concrete action. Do not copy: a five-step list.
  8. 0:52–1:00 | Picture: return to the person, ask one concrete question. Sound: sync, hold two seconds. Job: direct comments. Steal: one answerable question. Do not copy: “comment below.”

Read the Structure

The spine is claim, reason, example one, example two, counter, proof, application, question. It is not “cover a topic”; it is “leave one usable conclusion.”

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 60 sec film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 1,000–5,000, one person, one camera and one mic, natural light, half a day.
  • Mid: RMB 5,000–20,000, two to three people, two cameras/teleprompter/light, one day.
  • High: RMB 20,000–80,000+, director, camera, light, post, stage, one to two days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. First line is the claim, no intro.
  2. Every ten seconds adds information: reason/example/counter/proof.
  3. End with a question answerable today.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy rapid cutting: without new information, speed is empty.
  2. Do not copy quote-speak: if every line is a quote, none is remembered.
  3. Do not copy a thank-you open: the first three seconds are the only attention; do not waste them.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Watch muted; can the first line be captioned as the claim?
  2. Count new information every ten seconds; if none, rewrite.
  3. Compress to fifteen seconds: claim, one example, one question.

Check

  • First line is the claim, not an intro.
  • A reason lands within ten seconds.
  • Two examples each have one person/action/result.
  • Counter is stated directly, not a straw man.
  • Proof is verifiable, not three numbers.
  • Application is one step.
  • Closing question is concrete and answerable today.

Boundary

en.summary: One claim, three proofs, one action; every proof must be visible on camera.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Talking Head Template: One Claim, Three Proofs, One Action

Formats / Talking head

Talking Head Template: One Claim, Three Proofs, One Action

One claim, three proofs, one action; every proof must be visible on camera.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

A talking-head template is one claim, three examples, one action; examples must be visible on camera.

A usable 60-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Claim0–3sMedium frontal, subject to camera, one object on the deskOne claim under 15 words; no reading; repeatable
Example 13–13sHand or object close-up, one complete actionSync action sound; the image proves it without narration
Example 213–23sNew space or angle, same claimOne explanation, max 20 words; no second center
Example 323–33sCounter-example or before/afterDo not mock the counter-example; name the difference
Action33–45sOne imitable action or a single entry pointOne next step only; no slogan

Fill three lines before rolling

  • Claim: which sentence should remain? Write it, cut to fifteen words.
  • Three proofs: for each, write what the camera sees, not “it is convincing.”
  • One action: what can the viewer do now? Open settings, comment or buy—pick one.

On set

Write one claim, three shootable examples, and one closing action. Keep each example under ten seconds.

Do this

  1. Write one claim that fits in a sentence.
  2. Add three shootable examples, each under ten seconds.
  3. End with one action, such as open settings now.

Avoid

Do not use three adjectives as examples; if the camera cannot show it, viewers will not remember.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The claim fits one sentence with no second center.
  • 2. All three examples are filmable and each runs under ten seconds.
  • 3. The ending gives one action so viewers know what to do next.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The claim fits one sentence with no second cen…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“All three examples are filmable and each runs…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use three adjectives as examples; if the camera cannot show it, viewers will not remember.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “Write one claim that fits in a sentence.” and “Add three shootable examples, each under ten seconds.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The claim fits one sentence with no second center.
  • All three examples are filmable and each runs under ten seconds.
  • The ending gives one action so viewers know what to do next.

Boundary

This page only covers “Talking Head Template: One Claim, Three Proofs, One Action”; it does not replace Does the Cover Still Read at 200 Pixels?, Tutorial Breakdown: Teach in Five Minutes, The One-Line Story: Who Wants What, and What Stands in the Way. en.html:
Home/Formats/Product Ad Breakdown: Problem Becomes Proof

Formats / Product ad

Product Ad Breakdown: Problem Becomes Proof

A nine-beat breakdown of a sixty-second product ad: problem, failed fix, product, demo, proof, objection, second proof, result, action.

7 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables first: sixty seconds, feed/commerce platform, and one goal (finish, remember, or buy). Without them, every timecode looks right and none works.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 9 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:03 | Picture: the problem happens, fumbling or one failed action. Sound: sync, room before music. Job: let viewers recognize their own problem. Steal: open on action, not product. Do not copy: turn the problem into a spectacle.
  2. 0:03–0:08 | Picture: the old fix fails, reaction; product still absent. Sound: a sigh or object drop. Job: make the problem cost something. Steal: make failure visible. Do not copy: narrate “it's hard.”
  3. 0:08–0:12 | Picture: product enters, one object only. Sound: product sound, light music. Job: answer the problem, no brand history. Steal: the product solves that one failure. Do not copy: open on a turntable.
  4. 0:12–0:20 | Picture: one function demo that can be repeated. Sound: sync, key action emphasized. Job: prove it actually works. Steal: one continuous demo. Do not copy: five close-ups pretending to be a demo.
  5. 0:20–0:32 | Picture: before/after on the same setup and light. Sound: two seconds of sync each. Job: give verifiable proof. Steal: same-setup comparison. Do not copy: change camera or light to flatter the after.
  6. 0:32–0:42 | Picture: price, spec, who it is for and not for. Sound: voice only reads key numbers. Job: handle objection without a manual. Steal: say who it is not for. Do not copy: read the whole spec sheet.
  7. 0:42–0:52 | Picture: second proof: real user, second setting, or stress test. Sound: real reaction, no added effects. Job: more than one proof. Steal: one real reaction. Do not copy: cast an actor to look surprised.
  8. 0:52–0:58 | Picture: result returns to the person, not a product close-up. Sound: room returns. Job: show life after use. Steal: result is an action. Do not copy: result is a pile of logos.
  9. 0:58–1:00 | Picture: one action: tap, claim, try; one button only. Sound: one line. Job: close. Steal: one action. Do not copy: ask for three things at once.

Read the Structure

The spine is problem, cost, answer, proof, objection, second proof, result, action. Every ten seconds needs new information; before the product appears, viewers need a reason to keep watching.

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 60 sec film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 3,000–8,000, one person, one camera, natural light, one day.
  • Mid: RMB 8,000–30,000, three to five people, product table and two lights, one to two days.
  • High: RMB 30,000–100,000+, director, camera, art, post, set or stage, two to four days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. Open on a failed action, not the product.
  2. Same-setup before/after so proof is visible.
  3. Say who it is not for; handle objection early.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy “must explode in three seconds”: without media spend, speed does not buy attention.
  2. Do not copy premium “no captions, image only”: feeds are silent by default.
  3. Do not copy “product as hero”: without brand recognition, viewers recognize the problem first.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Watch muted; write the problem you see in the first three seconds.
  2. Count when the product first appears; if before five seconds, recut.
  3. Compress to fifteen seconds: problem, one proof, one action.

Check

  • The first three seconds show a concrete problem, not a turntable.
  • Product enters no earlier than five seconds.
  • One same-setup, verifiable proof exists mid-section.
  • Price/spec reads only key numbers, not a manual.
  • Second proof is not an acted surprise.
  • One action at the end.
  • No narration concludes for the viewer.

Author and test note

2026-11-22
Byline
