Review setup

Review setup: composite samples and public cases; previewed on MacBook Pro M1 / iPhone 13; not one real client project.

Known failures

Known failures: composite samples are not client proof; platform length/spec changes expire templates.

Limits

Samples are composite; people, numbers, and locations do not map to a real client.

Product Ad Template: Three Seconds of Problem, Ten of Proof

Three seconds of problem, ten of proof, five of action.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

A product-ad template gives the problem in three seconds, proof in ten, and one action in the last five.

A usable 18-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Problem0–3sA real loss in use: spill, jam, wasted timeOne concrete problem; no brand name
Proof 13–7sProduct enters, problem stops; hand close-upAction sound; the use is visible
Proof 27–11sAnother condition proves it is not a flukeOne condition line; no exaggeration
Proof 311–13sMeasurable result: time, quantity, before/afterA number or comparison; no adjectives
Action13–18sProduct returns to life, person leavesOne next step; no second slogan

Fill three lines before rolling

  • Problem: who loses what, where? It must be visible.
  • Three proofs: change one condition each; three identical proofs are one proof.
  • Action: what should the viewer do? One thing only.

On set

Problem at 0 to 3, three proofs at 3 to 13, one action at 13 to 18. Make the proof visible.

Do this

  1. 0–3 seconds: the problem appears.
  2. 3–13 seconds: three pieces of evidence, each visible.
  3. 13–18 seconds: one action only.

Avoid

Do not cram five selling points into thirteen seconds; viewers remember none.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The cut follows 0–3, 3–13, 13–18 timing.
  • 2. All three evidence beats are visible without voiceover filling gaps.
  • 3. The last five seconds carry one action and no second slogan.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The cut follows 0–3, 3–13, 13–18 timing”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“All three evidence beats are visible without v…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not cram five selling points into thirteen seconds; viewers remember none.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “0–3 seconds: the problem appears.” and “3–13 seconds: three pieces of evidence, each visible.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

  • The cut follows 0–3, 3–13, 13–18 timing.
  • All three evidence beats are visible without voiceover filling gaps.

en.html:
Home/Formats/Documentary Breakdown: One Person, One Event, One Change

Formats / Documentary

Documentary Breakdown: One Person, One Event, One Change

An eight-beat breakdown of a three-minute documentary: action, person, want, obstacle, attempt, cost, change, after.

6 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: three minutes, Bilibili/Channels, and the goal is not “profile a person” but “see what changed.” Count actions and waiting, not interview quotes.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 8 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:10 | Picture: an action already in progress: hands, door, rain, tool. Sound: sync, no explanation. Job: let viewers see before being told. Steal: start mid-action. Do not copy: wide plus narrator introducing the person.
  2. 0:10–0:30 | Picture: person and place; three facts: where, with whom, what for. Sound: ambience plus one or two lines. Job: establish a person, not a résumé. Steal: let them work. Do not copy: let the interview explain identity.
  3. 0:30–0:55 | Picture: a concrete result wanted; the object is visible. Sound: action close. Job: establish want. Steal: want is something filmable. Do not copy: want is an abstract ideal.
  4. 0:55–1:30 | Picture: obstacle appears: time, money, body, relationships; do not resolve quickly. Sound: room tightens, no music. Job: make waiting cost something. Steal: let obstacle happen. Do not copy: manufacture conflict.
  5. 1:30–2:00 | Picture: he tries once, fails or partly succeeds. Sound: real reaction. Job: show method. Steal: one complete attempt. Do not copy: fragment it into a montage.
  6. 2:00–2:25 | Picture: cost appears: time passes, something breaks, a relationship changes. Sound: ambience, silence. Job: change is not free. Steal: mark cost with an object or time. Do not copy: use music to force tears.
  7. 2:25–2:45 | Picture: the same action after the change; result differs. Sound: sync. Job: make change visible. Steal: repeat the opening action. Do not copy: narrate “he grew.”
  8. 2:45–3:00 | Picture: stop after the change, no answer. Sound: ambience out. Job: let viewers judge. Steal: stop as the person keeps working. Do not copy: stop on an interview summary.

Read the Structure

The spine is action, person, want, obstacle, attempt, cost, change, after. Interview only fills what action cannot explain; if an interview can be cut, the film is better.

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 3 min film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 5,000–20,000, two to three people, one real location, natural light, two to three days.
  • Mid: RMB 20,000–80,000, four to six people, multiple locations, basic light/sound, five to ten days.
  • High: RMB 80,000–300,000+, director, camera, sound, producer, travel, fifteen to thirty days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. Start mid-action, not with a profile.
  2. Let the obstacle happen; do not manufacture conflict.
  3. Repeat the opening action so change shows itself.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy interview-driven structure: without action, interview is radio.
  2. Do not copy “slow cinema” waiting: without cost, a long take is just slow.
  3. Do not copy a thematic summary: viewers do not need you to conclude a person.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Watch muted; write what the person wants and what blocks it.
  2. Count complete actions; fewer than three means too much interview.
  3. Copy the opening action and check whether the end repeats or changes it.

Check

  • An action is happening in the first ten seconds.
  • Person, place, and task are clear within thirty seconds.
  • Want is filmable, not abstract.
  • Obstacle happens naturally, no fake conflict.
  • At least one complete attempt.
  • The same action after the change differs from the opening.
  • No summarizing narration at the end.

Boundary

This page only covers “Documentary Breakdown: One Person, One Event, One Change”; it does not replace Documentary Template: One Person, One Thing, One Change, Event Breakdown: Make a Live Event Clear in Ninety Seconds, The One-Line Story: Who Wants What, and What Stands in the Way. en.html:
Home/Formats/Documentary Template: One Person, One Thing, One Change

Formats / Documentary

Documentary Template: One Person, One Thing, One Change

One person, one concrete task, one visible change. Do not start with an era.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

A documentary template is one person, one concrete task, one visible change; do not start with the era.

A usable 60-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Person and task0–10sThe person is already working, not standing for an interviewAmbience first; no explanatory music
Process10–30sContinuous action shows steps and difficultyKeep sync sound; interview only supports
Change30–45sA visible result: finished, failed, changed decisionDo not let the subject say “I changed”
Aftermath45–60sThe first action or space after the changeOne true line; no era summary

Fill three lines before rolling

  • One person: name and one task for today.
  • One change: what looks different on camera? Not “he grew.”
  • What not to shoot: list three things that would turn it into an ad.

On set

One person, one ongoing task, one visible change. Shoot the task first, not the interview.

Do this

  1. Choose one person and one task in progress.
  2. Shoot the task before the interview.
  3. Wait for a visible change before fixing the structure.

Avoid

Do not start with historical background; that is usually a thesis, not a film.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The film has one person and one task in progress.
  • 2. Interview does not open the piece; action comes first.
  • 3. A visible change occurs, not only the subject saying so.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The film has one person and one task in progre…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Interview does not open the piece; action come…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not start with historical background; that is usually a thesis, not a film.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “Choose one person and one task in progress.” and “Shoot the task before the interview.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The film has one person and one task in progress.
  • Interview does not open the piece; action comes first.
  • A visible change occurs, not only the subject saying so.

en.title: Brand Film Breakdown: Build a World in Ninety Seconds
en.summary: A nine-beat breakdown of a ninety-second brand film: world, character, want, obstacle, turn, action, resolve, line, hold.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Brand Film Breakdown: Build a World in Ninety Seconds

Formats / Brand film

Brand Film Breakdown: Build a World in Ninety Seconds

A nine-beat breakdown of a ninety-second brand film: world, character, want, obstacle, turn, action, resolve, line, hold.

7 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: ninety seconds, brand film rather than product ad, and one value made visible through action. The trap is “pretty empties plus a slogan”; watch the character and the cost.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 9 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:05 | Picture: a world already running, no location title. Sound: ambience before music. Job: let viewers enter before being told. Steal: one action establishes the world. Do not copy: a drone wide for “premium.”
  2. 0:05–0:15 | Picture: one person doing one concrete task; wardrobe, hands, tool recognizable. Sound: action close. Job: attach the value to a person. Steal: person before brand. Do not copy: logo first.
  3. 0:15–0:25 | Picture: a concrete result he wants; the object is visible. Sound: one short line or breath. Job: establish want. Steal: want is an object or action. Do not copy: voice-over “we believe.”
  4. 0:25–0:40 | Picture: obstacle appears: time, weather, rules, relationships. Sound: room tightens, music still out. Job: give the value a cost. Steal: obstacle from the real world. Do not copy: invent a fake villain.
  5. 0:40–0:55 | Picture: he changes method, not goal; same action repeated and escalated. Sound: action rises. Job: turn. Steal: turn through action. Do not copy: turn through a slogan.
  6. 0:55–1:10 | Picture: action has consequence; someone gains or loses. Sound: real reaction, light music. Job: prove the value is not a slogan. Steal: consequence lands on one person. Do not copy: slow motion hides the consequence.
  7. 1:10–1:22 | Picture: result state in the same space, relationship changed. Sound: room returns. Job: show the change. Steal: return to the same space. Do not copy: cut to a new landscape.
  8. 1:22–1:28 | Picture: brand/product appears once, in the same frame as the action. Sound: one line, under twelve Chinese characters. Job: lock value to brand. Steal: brand as part of the action. Do not copy: brand as an end-card sticker.
  9. 1:28–1:30 | Picture: hold on an unfinished action or empty frame. Sound: silence. Job: let viewers take the last breath. Steal: stop on the consequence. Do not copy: stop on the logo.

Read the Structure

The spine is world, person, want, cost, turn, consequence, return. It need not finish a plot, but it must make one value visible.

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 90 sec film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 10,000–30,000, three to five people, one real location, natural light or one light, one to two days.
  • Mid: RMB 30,000–100,000, eight to twelve people, set or controlled location, two to three days.
  • High: RMB 100,000–500,000+, director, camera, art, wardrobe, composer, multiple locations, four to eight days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. Establish the world with one action, not a drone.
  2. Let the obstacle come from the real world; the brand is not a savior.
  3. Return to the same space so the change is visible.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy “no dialogue, image only”: without brand recognition, viewers do not know who is speaking.
  2. Do not copy a cinematic drone open: without budget, it exposes the location.
  3. Do not copy a value slogan: without the cost before it, it is just a caption.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Watch muted; write one line for the want and one for the cost.
  2. Mark when the brand first appears; if before sixty seconds, ask why.
  3. Compress to thirty seconds: world, want, turn, consequence.

Check

  • An action is already happening in the first five seconds, not a drone.
  • The want is one object or action.
  • Obstacle comes from the real world, not a fake villain.
  • Turn happens through action, not slogan.
  • Consequence lands on one person.
  • Brand appears once, in the same frame as action.
  • End on consequence, not logo.

en.summary: Stance, evidence, landing. The stance must be arguable and the evidence concrete.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Brand Film Template: Stance, Evidence, Landing

Formats / Brand film

Brand Film Template: Stance, Evidence, Landing

Stance, evidence, landing. The stance must be arguable and the evidence concrete.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

A brand-film template uses claim, evidence, landing; the claim must be opposable and the evidence specific.

A usable 45-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Claim0–5sA concrete scene, no logo yetOne arguable sentence under 15 words
Proof 15–15sOne person doing one specific thingAction sound; no “craftsmanship” voiceover
Proof 215–25sA difficulty appears, the person does not retreatOne cost line; no slogan
Counter-example25–35sAnother way fails or is rejectedDo not mock competitors; show the difference
Landing35–45sThe person acts; brand appears lastEnd on action, not a slogan

Fill three lines before rolling

  • Claim: write a sentence a counter-example could challenge; if it cannot be opposed, it is not a claim.
  • Proof: one person and one action, not “team spirit.”
  • Landing: what action should remain after the film?

On set

The claim must be arguable, the proof must be one person, and the landing must be an action. No dreams or craftsmanship.

Do this

  1. Write a claim someone could oppose.
  2. Prove it with one specific person.
  3. Land on an action, not a slogan.

Avoid

Do not use dream or craftsmanship as the claim; without evidence they are only words.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The claim can be opposed and a counterexample exists.
  • 2. Evidence is specific to one person and one action.
  • 3. The ending lands on an action, not a slogan.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The claim can be opposed and a counterexample…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Evidence is specific to one person and one act…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use dream or craftsmanship as the claim; without evidence they are only words.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “Write a claim someone could oppose.” and “Prove it with one specific person.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The claim can be opposed and a counterexample exists.
  • Evidence is specific to one person and one action.
  • The ending lands on an action, not a slogan.

en.title: Short Drama Breakdown: One Turn in Thirty Seconds
en.summary: An eight-beat breakdown of a thirty-second short drama: image hook, claim, setup, escalation, false answer, clue, turn, reaction.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Short Drama Breakdown: One Turn in Thirty Seconds

Formats / Short drama

Short Drama Breakdown: One Turn in Thirty Seconds

An eight-beat breakdown of a thirty-second short drama: image hook, claim, setup, escalation, false answer, clue, turn, reaction.

6 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: thirty seconds, Douyin/Kuaishou, and the goal is believe A for twenty-five seconds, accept B in five. Short drama is not a slice of a longer show; find the false answer, then the clue.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 8 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:02 | Picture: an odd image/action, no explanation. Sound: sync/one short line. Job: catch the eye. Steal: one odd action. Do not copy: a title caption explaining.
  2. 0:02–0:05 | Picture: one claim/goal that makes viewers think they understand. Sound: short line. Job: give the false answer. Steal: an everyday goal. Do not copy: reveal early.
  3. 0:05–0:10 | Picture: setup: who, where, what. Sound: ambience. Job: establish normal. Steal: three facts. Do not copy: explain backstory.
  4. 0:10–0:16 | Picture: escalation: the character approaches the goal the wrong way. Sound: pace rises. Job: invest the viewer. Steal: one wrong action. Do not copy: add a third character.
  5. 0:16–0:21 | Picture: false answer is “confirmed”: viewers believe A more. Sound: one confirmation. Job: nail the false answer. Steal: one visible proof. Do not copy: narration assures.
  6. 0:21–0:25 | Picture: real clue at the frame edge: shadow/hand/door/phone. Sound: one wrong sound. Job: plant the clue. Steal: clue appears twice. Do not copy: clue only in dialogue.
  7. 0:25–0:28 | Picture: turn: one action overturns A. Sound: silence/one hit. Job: make viewers recalculate. Steal: turn through action. Do not copy: explain in dialogue.
  8. 0:28–0:30 | Picture: reaction: one face/action closes. Sound: ambience. Job: land the turn. Steal: stop on reaction. Do not copy: add a recap voice-over.

Read the Structure

The spine is oddity, false answer, normal, escalation, confirmation, clue, turn, reaction. The first twenty-five seconds serve one false answer; the clue must appear twice in frame or the turn cheats.

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 30 sec film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 5,000–20,000, three to five people, one or two sets, one day.
  • Mid: RMB 20,000–80,000, six to ten people, two or three sets, two days.
  • High: RMB 80,000–300,000+, director, camera, art, wardrobe, multiple sets, three to seven days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. Odd action in the first two seconds, no explanation.
  2. The first twenty-five seconds serve one false answer.
  3. Clue appears twice in frame; the turn is not dialogue.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy a slice of a longer show: thirty seconds cannot build a person; use action.
  2. Do not copy a dialogue turn: if viewers did not see the clue, they feel cheated.
  3. Do not copy a final voice-over: it turns the twist into a manual.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Write a thirty-second turn: one false answer for twenty-five seconds.
  2. Put the clue in frame twice, not in dialogue.
  3. Watch muted; does the turn still read?

Check

  • An odd action in the first two seconds.
  • The first twenty-five seconds serve one false answer.
  • Setup uses three facts.
  • Escalation is one wrong action, not a new character.
  • Clue appears twice in frame.
  • Turn is action, not dialogue explanation.
  • End on reaction, no voice-over recap.

en.summary: A hook every thirty seconds: new information, new obstacle, new cost.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Short Drama Template: A Hook Every Thirty Seconds

Formats / Short drama

Short Drama Template: A Hook Every Thirty Seconds

A hook every thirty seconds: new information, new obstacle, new cost.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

A short-drama template hooks every thirty seconds: new information, new obstacle, new cost.

A usable 60-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Information gap0–5sThe audience knows something a character does notOne piece of information; no full backstory
New obstacle5–20sThe character acts on the wrong information and meets the first consequenceAction and reaction; no new character rescue
Escalation20–35sThe same misunderstanding costs moreOne cost line; the character must choose
New price35–50sThe choice lands; relationship or position changesDo not explain right or wrong; let the result speak
Open question50–60sStop on an action or an unfinished lineThe question has evidence in the previous minute

Fill three lines before rolling

  • Gap: who does not know what, and when does the audience know?
  • Price: what is lost at each escalation? Not just “more angry.”
  • Final question: what will they ask? The answer must be in the previous minute.

On set

Information gap at 0 to 5, new obstacle at 5 to 35, new cost at 35 to 60. End each beat with a question.

Do this

  1. 0–5 seconds establish an information gap.
  2. 5–35 seconds add a new obstacle.
  3. 35–60 seconds add a new cost and end on a question.

Avoid

Do not rescue every segment with a new character; if the person does not change, the hook is fake.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. 0–5, 5–35, and 35–60 each add new information or an obstacle.
  • 2. The information gap is set in the first five seconds.
  • 3. The final question is grounded in the previous minute.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“0–5, 5–35, and 35–60 each add new information…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The information gap is set in the first five s…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not rescue every segment with a new character; if the person does not change, the hook is fake.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “0–5 seconds establish an information gap.” and “5–35 seconds add a new obstacle.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • 0–5, 5–35, and 35–60 each add new information or an obstacle.
  • The information gap is set in the first five seconds.
  • The final question is grounded in the previous minute.

en.title: Vlog Breakdown: One Discovery in Ninety Seconds
en.summary: An eight-beat breakdown of a ninety-second travel vlog: action, place, task, obstacle, failure, discovery, quiet, exit.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Vlog Breakdown: One Discovery in Ninety Seconds

Formats / Vlog

Vlog Breakdown: One Discovery in Ninety Seconds

An eight-beat breakdown of a ninety-second travel vlog: action, place, task, obstacle, failure, discovery, quiet, exit.

6 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: ninety seconds, RED/Douyin, and the goal is one discovery. A vlog is not an itinerary; find the task, the failure, then the discovery.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 8 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:03 | Picture: an action already happening: running, opening a door, boarding. Sound: ambience. Job: action first, no drone. Steal: action open. Do not copy: drone wide.
  2. 0:03–0:10 | Picture: place in three facts: where, with whom, what for. Sound: ambience plus one line. Job: set the task. Steal: three facts. Do not copy: voice-over history.
  3. 0:10–0:25 | Picture: first location does one thing: find, wait, ask, walk. Sound: ambience. Job: start the task. Steal: one complete action. Do not copy: three landmarks.
  4. 0:25–0:45 | Picture: obstacle: rain, closed door, wrong turn. Sound: room tightens. Job: make the task harder. Steal: real obstacle. Do not copy: manufacture drama.
  5. 0:45–1:00 | Picture: failure: wrong person/alley, keep eight seconds. Sound: dialogue/steps. Job: make discovery believable. Steal: one real failure. Do not copy: cut all failure.
  6. 1:00–1:15 | Picture: discovery: found/not found, one face/object. Sound: ambience plus one reaction. Job: give the film a landing. Steal: one concrete discovery. Do not copy: music faking emotion.
  7. 1:15–1:25 | Picture: quiet: one unguarded moment/empty frame. Sound: ambience. Job: let the pace land. Steal: one quiet shot. Do not copy: keep adding action.
  8. 1:25–1:30 | Picture: exit: person leaves/car goes/door closes. Sound: ambience out. Job: end. Steal: one exit action. Do not copy: add summary narration.

Read the Structure

The spine is action, place, task, obstacle, failure, discovery, quiet, exit. It is not “where I went,” but “what I looked for, what happened, what I found.”

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 90 sec film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 1,000–3,000, one person, phone/one camera, one to two days.
  • Mid: RMB 3,000–10,000, one to two people, camera/stabilizer/mic, two to three days.
  • High: RMB 10,000–50,000+, three to five people, multi-camera/drone/post, three to seven days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. Action in the first three seconds, no drone.
  2. One thing per location.
  3. Keep one failure so the discovery is believable.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy itinerary editing: chronological order becomes a log.
  2. Do not copy a drone at every location: it cuts the task.
  3. Do not copy constant voice-over: it feels for the viewer.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Write “what I looked for” and shoot only that.
  2. Count locations; more than three, cut to two.
  3. Watch muted; do task and failure still read?

Check

  • Action in the first three seconds, not a drone.
  • Within ten seconds: where, with whom, what for.
  • One thing per location.
  • One real obstacle.
  • One failure kept (at least five seconds).
  • One concrete discovery.
  • End on exit/quiet, not summary narration.

Boundary

This page only covers “Vlog Breakdown: One Discovery in Ninety Seconds”; it does not replace Vlog Structure: Give the Place a Reason, Vlog Template: Go, Meet, Change, Adjusting Actors: Give Verbs, Not Adjectives. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Formats / Travel vlog

Vlog Template: Go, Meet, Change

Go, meet, change. The change can be small, but it must happen.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

A vlog template runs departure, encounter, change; the change can be small but must happen.

A usable 60-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Reason0–5sThe person is already moving, not an aerial landscapeOne “why I came” line; no epic music
Departure5–20sFirst action: buy a ticket, board, open a doorAmbience; establish the space
Encounter20–40sAn unplanned person or event entersKeep the unexpected sync sound; no all-narration
Change40–55sA small decision produces a visible actionThe change happens on screen, not in explanation
Look back55–60sThe person pauses and looks at the space left behindOne true line; no life summary

Fill three lines before rolling

  • Reason: why this place, this time? One line.
  • Unexpected: what might happen today? Write two options; do not force them.
  • Change: what will the person do differently at the end?

On set

Reason to go, someone or something met, one small change. The change can be deciding to stay for a meal.

Do this

  1. Open with the reason for departure.
  2. Capture the person or event encountered, letting surprise in.
  3. Land on a small change, such as deciding to stay for a meal.

Avoid

Do not put the change only in voiceover; if the picture does not change, viewers do not believe it.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The opening states why the trip happens before scenery.
  • 2. The middle includes an unplanned person or event.
  • 3. The ending shows a visible small change without voiceover finishing it.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The opening states why the trip happens before…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The middle includes an unplanned person or eve…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not put the change only in voiceover; if the picture does not change, viewers do not believe it.

Extend

en.title: News Structure: Scene First, Verification Second
en.summary: Scene first, verification second. Background first loses the viewer.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Formats/News Structure: Scene First, Verification Second

Formats / News

News Structure: Scene First, Verification Second

Scene first, verification second. Background first loses the viewer.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

A news open shows what happened, then verification: who confirmed it, when, and what is still unknown. End with impact and next step. Keep only background needed to explain this event; do not start with a history lecture.

Scene, verification, impact: one question per section

Each section answers one audience question. Separate “why it happened” from “what happens next” so the middle does not lose them.

Limits

Unverified information does not get a confident tone. Put “alleged” and “being verified” on screen or in the voice; do not edit uncertainty into certainty.

On set

Scene at 0 to 5, verification at 5 to 15, context and impact at 15 to 30. Label sources on screen.

Do this

News structure gives the scene first, verification second; background first loses the audience.

  1. 0–5 seconds: the scene.
  2. 5–15 seconds: verification.
  3. 15–30 seconds: context and impact with source captions.

Avoid

Do not pass secondhand footage off as scene; it destroys credibility.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The first five seconds are scene footage or sound, not an anchor talking.
  • 2. Verification names a source, time, and checkable record.
  • 3. Secondhand footage is corner-labeled so viewers can tell.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The first five seconds are scene footage or so…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Verification names a source, time, and checkab…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not pass secondhand footage off as scene; it destroys credibility.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “0–5 seconds: the scene.” and “5–15 seconds: verification.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The first five seconds are scene footage or sound, not an anchor talking.
  • Verification names a source, time, and checkable record.
  • Secondhand footage is corner-labeled so viewers can tell.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. News starts with verifiable facts, then context. The image does not get to decide the conclusion.

Lead with the scene

Give time, place, people, and one verifiable detail in the first ten seconds: a seal, a water line, a timestamp, a street number. Do not open with a presenter reading a lead in front of the door.

First-hand material first: your own footage, original files, a complete timeline. Label second-hand images, keep the publish time of screenshots, and never pass old footage off as today.

Sources

Use at least two independent sources. If a source is anonymous, say why and what they can verify. One person saying the same thing three times is not three sources.

Separate “who said it” from “what happened”: facts use images and documents, judgment uses interviews. Do not put a guess in the headline.

Structure and correction

What happened, what proves it, who is where, what happens next. When those four are answered, stop. Do not use sentimental music to do the judging, and do not cut the answer that hurts your angle.

Leave a correction path before publishing: wrong word, wrong time, wrong name. Fix it and note the change at the end or in the description. Trust comes from being correctable, not from sounding certain.

Five-minute drill: three lines of facts

Take one scene you shot and write three lines: what happened at what time, who was there, which object proves it. Each line must be checkable by another shot or document.

Then write one line: “what I still do not know.” Put it at the end or in the description. Do not turn the unknown into a declarative sentence; naming it is what makes the report trustworthy.

When it is done

Pull out every factual claim and ask: which shot, document, or independent source verifies it? If every claim has an answer, the report is done. If one rests on “someone said,” downgrade it to a judgment; do not present it as fact.

Ten news-field checks

  • Time, place, people within ten seconds
  • One verifiable detail
  • First-hand material first
  • Second-hand images labeled
  • Screenshots keep publish time
  • At least two independent sources
  • Anonymous source explained
  • Fact separated from judgment
  • No sentimental music judging
  • Correction path before publishing

News is not about who shoots harder; it is about who puts what they can verify first.

en.title: News Breakdown: Keep the Unknown in Ninety Seconds
en.summary: An eight-beat breakdown of a ninety-second news feature: verified fact, scene, witness, archive, context, known/unknown, unresolved, next.
en.html:
Home/Formats/News Breakdown: Keep the Unknown in Ninety Seconds

Formats / News

News Breakdown: Keep the Unknown in Ninety Seconds

An eight-beat breakdown of a ninety-second news feature: verified fact, scene, witness, archive, context, known/unknown, unresolved, next.

6 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: ninety seconds, institutional/news platform, and the goal is separating known, unknown, and inferred. Do not watch for dramatic shots; watch for a source behind every fact.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 8 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:05 | Picture: one verified fact/place, no emotional verdict. Sound: sync. Job: certainty first. Steal: open on a fact. Do not copy: open on viral footage.
  2. 0:05–0:15 | Picture: scene: signs, street, notice board. Sound: ambience. Job: give the fact a place. Steal: three geographic details. Do not copy: staged empties.
  3. 0:15–0:30 | Picture: witness/subject, no conclusion for them. Sound: sync. Job: give the story a person. Steal: ask what they saw. Do not copy: ask “are you angry.”
  4. 0:30–0:45 | Picture: archive, labeled date/source. Sound: voice reads facts only. Job: add time. Steal: label plus one source line. Do not copy: pass archive as firsthand.
  5. 0:45–1:00 | Picture: context: rules/timeline/what happened before. Sound: ambience lowers. Job: give the fact context. Steal: one timeline. Do not copy: a long narration.
  6. 1:00–1:12 | Picture: known/unknown two-column card. Sound: voice reads both columns. Job: show the boundary. Steal: two columns. Do not copy: fill the unknown with speculation.
  7. 1:12–1:25 | Picture: unresolved: unverified point/refused interview. Sound: sync/silence. Job: keep the unknown. Steal: say “we do not know.” Do not copy: music as conspiracy.
  8. 1:25–1:30 | Picture: next: how it will be checked/when updated. Sound: one closing line. Job: give an action. Steal: one concrete check. Do not copy: “stay tuned.”

Read the Structure

The spine is fact, place, person, archive, context, known/unknown, unresolved, next. It need not tell a complete story; it must show what is certain and what is not.

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 90 sec film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 2,000–8,000, one to two people, single camera, one day.
  • Mid: RMB 8,000–30,000, three to five people, two cameras, sound, post, one to two days.
  • High: RMB 30,000–100,000+, reporter, camera, producer, legal, multiple locations, three to seven days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. Open on one verified fact, not viral footage.
  2. Make known/unknown a two-column card.
  3. Label every archive shot with date and source.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy breaking-news speed: without verification, speed amplifies error.
  2. Do not copy emotional music: news is not a tearjerker; music implies a verdict.
  3. Do not copy archive montage: without labels, archive becomes fake firsthand.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Write known/unknown for one trending story; source every known.
  2. Count labeled archive shots; mark any missing as unverified.
  3. Compress to thirty seconds: fact, witness, unknown, next.

Check

  • The first five seconds are a verified fact.
  • The place has three geographic details, not staging.
  • Witness is in sync, not concluded for.
  • Every archive shot has date and source.
  • Context is a timeline, not long narration.
  • Known/unknown two-column card appears.
  • The end names what is unknown and the next step.

Formats / News

News Template: Scene, Context, Impact

Scene, context, impact; each section answers one viewer question.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

A news template runs scene, context, impact; every segment answers a viewer question.

A usable 60-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Scene0–10sWhat is happening now, or the latest scene footageOne “what happened” line; time and place clear
Verification10–25sWho confirmed, which document, which officeSource on screen; unknowns named as unknown
Context25–40sOnly one or two images needed to explain this eventNo history lecture; one cause line
Impact40–55sWho is affected and howSeparate what happened from what may happen
Next55–60sOne actionable step or a clear uncertaintyDo not conclude for the audience

Fill three lines before rolling

  • What happened: one fact without adjectives.
  • Who confirmed: name, document and date; write “unverified” if missing.
  • Next step: what can the viewer do, or what must they wait for?

On set

What happened, why, and what happens next. Each section answers one audience question.

Do this

  1. What happened on scene.
  2. Why it happened.
  3. What happens next and what viewers can do.

Avoid

Do not turn context into a history lecture; viewers need why this happened now.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The three parts answer what happened, why, and what next.
  • 2. Context keeps only what directly explains the current event.
  • 3. The ending gives a concrete next step or names the uncertainty.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

Extend

en.title: Tutorial Structure: One Problem, One Skill
en.summary: One problem, one skill. Three tricks in one tutorial means none is learned.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Formats/Tutorial Structure: One Problem, One Skill

Formats / Tutorial

Tutorial Structure: One Problem, One Skill

One problem, one skill. Three tricks in one tutorial means none is learned.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

The first five seconds must show what “finished” looks like, or the viewer cannot decide whether to learn. Then state the starting point and prerequisites before step one; each step solves one problem.

Show the result before the steps

Enlarge the step that most often fails and show the wrong result. Viewers do not forget the correct step; they do not know what wrong looks like.

Limits

A tutorial is not a feature list. Every step needs “what proves it worked”; without a check, the viewer is guessing.

Case: a five-minute tutorial cut down to three steps

Case note: an anonymised composite of several similar projects. Figures are ranges; people, places and clients are withheld. It does not represent one real client job.

ProjectConstraintResult
Five-minute software tutorialOne screen recording, one narrator, no on-cameraThree steps to one testable result
Budget band¥0–1,000Recorded at home
AcceptanceViewer can export one file aloneEnd checklist provided

What happened

  1. The first version walked through every menu item for eight minutes. Test viewers paused at minute two, unsure of the goal.
  2. We showed the result first: the final file in the first ten seconds, then three steps backwards. One shortcut per step.
  3. Every “by the way” branch was cut. Common failures moved to a 30-second end block, not the main path.

The trade-off

We did not chase “all features,” only one path that works. The mouse path is uncut so viewers can follow; narration is 10% slower and each step gets one second of silence. The end card is a three-item check, so viewers can judge their own result.

Reusable / not transferable

  • Reusable: show the result first, then the shortest path; one tutorial teaches one testable action.
  • Not transferable: software changes. Record the current menu names and mark the version; old tutorials need a version warning.

On set

Teach one action: import media and set proxies. Do not also teach grading and subtitles.

Do this

A tutorial teaches one thing; three tips at once means the viewer learns none.

  1. Teach one action: import footage and set proxies.
  2. Show the finished result before breaking down steps.
  3. Do not also cover grading and subtitles.

Avoid

Do not ramble while operating; viewers are following along.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Platform names and monetisation rules differ by market; treat Douyin, Bilibili and Xiaohongshu as examples, then re-check TikTok, YouTube, Instagram or the local platform.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The whole piece teaches one action named in the title.
  • 2. The finished result appears before steps.
  • 3. No second topic such as grading or subtitles interrupts.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The whole piece teaches one action named in th…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The finished result appears before steps”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not ramble while operating; viewers are following along.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “Teach one action: import footage and set proxies.” and “Show the finished result before breaking down steps.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The whole piece teaches one action named in the title.
  • The finished result appears before steps.
  • No second topic such as grading or subtitles interrupts.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. A tutorial is not a display of skill. It is proof that the viewer can do it too.

Show the result first

Show the finished result and the pass condition in the first ten seconds: what gets baked, exported, measured. Do not open with “hello, today I will share three tips.”

One problem, one lesson. Two goals in the title and the viewer no longer knows when they are done. State the final check up front and aim every step at it.

Three steps, one failure

Each step gets one action, one setting, one failure point. Close-up on hands, screen capture for the interface, hold the key number for three seconds. Do not read ten settings in one breath.

Do it once complete, then break it down. The viewer needs the continuous process, not ten isolated tricks. You can speed up repetition, but never cut the cause and effect.

Pass condition and template

End with a check the viewer can run: is the audio clipping, are subtitles over two lines, does the file open on the target machine? Add one common failure and its fix.

A downloadable checklist, settings sheet, or project file beats talk. If you cannot share a file, put the settings and order on screen so nobody has to pause and copy.

Five-minute drill: teach one friend once

Pick a task that takes three minutes and teach it in three steps. Put the finished result and pass condition first. Ask a friend who has never done it to follow your steps without your help.

Note the three places they stop: which step is unclear, which setting they missed, which failure you did not warn about. Add those three places to the video; only then is the tutorial done.

When it is done

Give someone who has not seen the video the footage and the materials, and say nothing. If they can produce the result and pass the check stated at the top, the tutorial is done. Where they get stuck, go back and add a close-up or a setting for that step.

Ten tutorial checks

  • Finished result in ten seconds
  • One problem, one lesson
  • Pass condition stated up front
  • One action and one setting per step
  • Clear close-up or screen capture
  • Key number held for three seconds
  • Complete run before breakdown
  • Cause and effect never cut
  • Self-check at the end
  • Checklist or settings sheet provided

A tutorial succeeds when the viewer can produce a checkable result after the video ends.

en.title: Tutorial Breakdown: Teach in Five Minutes
en.summary: A ten-beat breakdown of a five-minute tutorial: result, materials, three steps, check, failure, recap, next, action.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Tutorial Breakdown: Teach in Five Minutes

Formats / Tutorial

Tutorial Breakdown: Teach in Five Minutes

A ten-beat breakdown of a five-minute tutorial: result, materials, three steps, check, failure, recap, next, action.

6 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: five minutes, Bilibili/Channels, and the goal is the viewer can do it. A tutorial is not “watch me”; it is “you can.” Count steps and checks, not facts.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 10 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:10 | Picture: show the finished result, no table of contents. Sound: result sound/one promise. Job: show what they can do after. Steal: result first. Do not copy: open with an outline.
  2. 0:10–0:25 | Picture: materials/tools, all in frame. Sound: count each. Job: show what to prepare. Steal: all materials in one frame. Do not copy: read ten items.
  3. 0:25–0:55 | Picture: step one, one take or minimal cuts. Sound: key action. Job: let viewers follow. Steal: one complete action. Do not copy: five angles.
  4. 0:55–1:30 | Picture: step two repeats the logic. Sound: one reminder. Job: build a method. Steal: same logic, new object. Do not copy: a new method.
  5. 1:30–2:10 | Picture: step three, the hardest. Sound: slow down, hold key frame two seconds. Job: make the hard part followable. Steal: pause plus close-up. Do not copy: speed through.
  6. 2:10–2:50 | Picture: check: how to know it is right. Sound: three criteria. Job: self-check. Steal: three visible standards. Do not copy: “close enough.”
  7. 2:50–3:30 | Picture: failure: the most common mistake. Sound: wrong sound plus fix. Job: help viewers avoid. Steal: one real failure. Do not copy: act an exaggerated error.
  8. 3:30–4:10 | Picture: recap: three steps on one card/list. Sound: one summary. Job: make the method memorable. Steal: a screenshot-able list. Do not copy: repeat the whole segment.
  9. 4:10–4:40 | Picture: next: variation/advanced use. Sound: one suggestion. Job: continue. Steal: one variation. Do not copy: three advanced paths.
  10. 4:40–5:00 | Picture: action: do one step now. Sound: one action. Job: from watching to doing. Steal: a one-minute action. Do not copy: “try it later.”

Read the Structure

The spine is result, materials, step one, step two, step three, check, failure, recap, next, action. Every step must be followable; if it cannot be followed, it is a showreel, not a tutorial.

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 5 min film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 3,000–10,000, one to two people, one camera plus tabletop, one day.
  • Mid: RMB 10,000–40,000, three to five people, two cameras/overhead/light, two days.
  • High: RMB 40,000–150,000+, director, camera, art, motion, post, stage, three to seven days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. Result first, no outline.
  2. All materials in one frame.
  3. Hold the hardest step two seconds plus a close-up.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy fast-cut tutorials: if steps cannot be followed, viewers save and never do.
  2. Do not copy an expert tone: without failure, viewers do not know where it breaks.
  3. Do not copy a ten-step list: five minutes holds three steps; more means none.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Watch muted; can you follow the steps?
  2. Count checkpoints; fewer than three means no self-check.
  3. Compress to sixty seconds: result, three steps, one check, action.

Check

  • Finished result in the first ten seconds.
  • Materials fit in one frame.
  • Three steps, each a complete action.
  • Hardest step has a pause/close-up.
  • Three visible checkpoints.
  • One real failure demo.
  • One one-minute action at the end.

Boundary

This page only covers “Tutorial Breakdown: Teach in Five Minutes”; it does not replace Tutorial Structure: One Problem, One Skill, Tutorial Template: Goal, Steps, Check, Adjusting Actors: Give Verbs, Not Adjectives. en.title: Tutorial Template: Goal, Steps, Check
en.summary: Goal, steps, check; every step needs an observable result.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Tutorial Template: Goal, Steps, Check

Formats / Tutorial

Tutorial Template: Goal, Steps, Check

Goal, steps, check; every step needs an observable result.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

A tutorial template uses goal, steps, acceptance; every step has an observable result.

A usable 60-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Result0–5sShow the finished result firstOne “what you will get” line
Goal5–15sCompare result and starting pointState prerequisites and materials
Step 115–25sHands operate; key control enlargedOne action per step; an on-screen cue
Step 225–40sChange one condition, still completesName the common error; do not skip it
Step 340–55sFinish and replay the resultThe viewer can judge success alone
Check55–60sFreeze result, list checks on screenThree self-checks; never “done is enough”

Fill three lines before rolling

  • Result: what does the viewer end with? A screenshot or file.
  • Three steps: for each, write what proves it worked, not “click here.”
  • Failure: which step goes wrong most? Demonstrate it early.

On set

Goal, three steps, check. Show the finished result before asking the viewer to follow.

Do this

  1. State the goal: what the viewer will have at the end.
  2. Split into three steps, each with an observable result.
  3. Give acceptance: how viewers know they did it right.

Avoid

Do not use “when done” as acceptance; viewers do not know what done means.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The opening states what the viewer will have.
  • 2. Each of three steps has an observable result, such as an on-screen prompt.
  • 3. Acceptance can be self-checked, not felt.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The opening states what the viewer will have”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Each of three steps has an observable result…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use “when done” as acceptance; viewers do not know what done means.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “State the goal: what the viewer will have” and “Split into three steps, each with an observable”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The opening states what the viewer will have.
  • Each of three steps has an observable result, such as an on-screen prompt.
  • Acceptance can be self-checked, not felt.

en.title: Music Video Breakdown: Map Song Structure to Image
en.summary: A nine-beat breakdown of a three-and-a-half-minute music video: intro motif, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, verse two, bridge, final chorus, outro, hold.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Music Video Breakdown: Map Song Structure to Image

Formats / Music video

Music Video Breakdown: Map Song Structure to Image

A nine-beat breakdown of a three-and-a-half-minute music video: intro motif, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, verse two, bridge, final chorus, outro, hold.

6 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: three and a half minutes, music platform/Channels, and the goal is image escalating with the song. An MV is not a narrative short; mark song sections, motifs, then check whether the chorus escalates.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 9 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:10 | Picture: intro gives one visual motif, no plot. Sound: song intro/ambience. Job: establish a rule. Steal: one repeatable action. Do not copy: a drone location intro.
  2. 0:10–0:30 | Picture: verse gives space and relationships; camera can slow. Sound: verse. Job: let viewers enter the world. Steal: one space plus one person. Do not copy: a new location per lyric.
  3. 0:30–0:50 | Picture: pre-chorus narrows: closer framing/smaller space. Sound: rhythm rises. Job: prepare escalation. Steal: narrow framing. Do not copy: strobe.
  4. 0:50–1:25 | Picture: first chorus escalation: same action bigger/faster/riskier. Sound: drums. Job: memory point. Steal: action escalation. Do not copy: effects only.
  5. 1:25–1:50 | Picture: verse two adds information: relationship change/new space. Sound: verse two. Job: avoid repetition. Steal: change one variable, not the theme. Do not copy: a whole new story.
  6. 1:50–2:15 | Picture: bridge holds one long take/still, letting viewers breathe. Sound: bridge. Job: contrast. Steal: one long take. Do not copy: keep accelerating.
  7. 2:15–2:50 | Picture: final chorus maxes out: all motifs, action at limit. Sound: final chorus. Job: peak. Steal: three motifs in one frame. Do not copy: pile every effect.
  8. 2:50–3:20 | Picture: outro returns to the first motif, changed. Sound: outro/ambience. Job: close. Steal: return to the motif. Do not copy: add a new location.
  9. 3:20–3:30 | Picture: hold on action/empty frame, no explanation. Sound: silence. Job: let the song end. Steal: stop on consequence. Do not copy: add plot captions.

Read the Structure

The spine is motif, space, narrowing, escalation, new information, breath, max escalation, return, hold. Images are not lyric illustrations; they need sections and a peak like the song.

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 3–4 min film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 10,000–30,000, three to five people, one location, two or three looks, one day.
  • Mid: RMB 30,000–100,000, six to ten people, one or two locations, light/art, two days.
  • High: RMB 100,000–500,000+, director, camera, art, wardrobe, post, multiple locations, three to seven days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. Mark chorus and turn before writing images.
  2. Keep three motifs; change one variable per section.
  3. Escalate the chorus through action, not strobe.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy one location per lyric: the song does not have that many places, and viewers cannot remember them.
  2. Do not copy a strobe-only chorus: without action escalation, it empties out.
  3. Do not copy a plot that overwhelms the song: viewers came for the music.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Watch muted; mark where motifs repeat.
  2. Mark chorus/bridge against the song; does the image escalate with it?
  3. Compress to sixty seconds: motif, first chorus, max escalation, return.

Check

  • A repeatable motif in the first ten seconds.
  • Verse gives space, not a new location per line.
  • Pre-chorus narrows framing/space.
  • First chorus escalates through action.
  • Bridge holds one long take/still.
  • Final chorus puts three motifs in one frame.
  • Outro returns to the first motif, changed.

Formats / Music video

Music Video Template: Verse, Chorus, Memory

Verse, chorus, memory. The memory can be one action or one image.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

An MV template uses verse, chorus, memory point; the hook can be an action or an image.

A usable 60-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Verse space0–10sA recognizable space with the person insideAmbience or low music; do not bury the vocal
Verse person10–25sOne repeated action establishes the stateLyrics audible; image does not explain them
Chorus motif25–45sOne repeatable action or visual motifMusic lifts; action lands on the beat
Bridge turn45–55sChange space or relationshipSofter music is not a turn; the picture must change
Return55–60sThe motif appears again in a new positionReturn to the chorus motif; no caption summary

Fill three lines before rolling

  • Motif: one action the audience can copy, appearing at least twice.
  • Space: where do verse and chorus live, and why change?
  • Turn: what relationship changes in the bridge, beyond volume?

On set

Verse gives space, chorus gives a remembered action, bridge gives a turn. The action must repeat.

Do this

  1. Let the verse establish space and location.
  2. Give the chorus one repeatable memory action.
  3. Let the bridge turn by changing space or relationship.

Avoid

Do not make the bridge just a volume drop; without a visual turn, it is forgotten.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The verse establishes where the person is.
  • 2. The chorus hook appears at least twice and is memorable.
  • 3. The bridge changes space or relationship, not just volume.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The verse establishes where the person is”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The chorus hook appears at least twice and is…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not make the bridge just a volume drop; without a visual turn, it is forgotten.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “Let the verse establish space and location.” and “Give the chorus one repeatable memory action.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The verse establishes where the person is.
  • The chorus hook appears at least twice and is memorable.
  • The bridge changes space or relationship, not just volume.

en.title: Wedding Breakdown: Six Minutes Without a Checklist
en.summary: An eleven-beat breakdown of a six-minute wedding film: prep, arrival, ceremony, vows, rings, family, reception, dance, quiet, portraits, exit.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Wedding Breakdown: Six Minutes Without a Checklist

Formats / Wedding

Wedding Breakdown: Six Minutes Without a Checklist

An eleven-beat breakdown of a six-minute wedding film: prep, arrival, ceremony, vows, rings, family, reception, dance, quiet, portraits, exit.

7 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: six minutes, private/RED, and the goal is see two people, not a schedule. Find vows and reactions, then the quiet moment; slow motion is not structure.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 11 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:10 | Picture: small prep actions: hands, clothing, doorway. Sound: ambience/zip. Job: person first, not venue. Steal: one hand action. Do not copy: venue wide.
  2. 0:10–0:25 | Picture: arrival: car, door, first look. Sound: ambience. Job: start the ritual. Steal: one entrance action. Do not copy: the whole motorcade.
  3. 0:25–0:45 | Picture: ceremony starts: aisle, officiant, guests. Sound: sync. Job: establish the space. Steal: one wide plus one reaction. Do not copy: ten angles.
  4. 0:45–1:15 | Picture: vows: two close shots, sync. Sound: vows lead, music back. Job: the core. Steal: keep breath/pauses. Do not copy: cover with music.
  5. 1:15–1:35 | Picture: rings/announcement: hands, guests. Sound: applause/laughter. Job: land the ritual. Steal: hand close-up plus one face. Do not copy: rings only.
  6. 1:35–2:00 | Picture: family: parents/grandparents reacting. Sound: ambience. Job: give the couple origins. Steal: one aged face. Do not copy: staged group photo.
  7. 2:00–3:00 | Picture: reception: two tables with specific reactions, not every table. Sound: sync. Job: turn scale into people. Steal: two specific tables. Do not copy: every toast.
  8. 3:00–4:00 | Picture: dance: first dance/friends teasing. Sound: sync/music. Job: emotional peak. Steal: one action plus one reaction. Do not copy: all slow motion.
  9. 4:00–5:00 | Picture: quiet: the couple in a corner/hallway, unguarded. Sound: ambience. Job: let the film breathe. Steal: one unguarded moment. Do not copy: staged look.
  10. 5:00–5:30 | Picture: portraits: two faces, no heavy filter. Sound: ambience/one vow echo. Job: leave the two people. Steal: natural-light close-up. Do not copy: skin smoothed to plastic.
  11. 5:30–6:00 | Picture: exit: car/door/empty venue. Sound: ambience out. Job: end. Steal: one exit action. Do not copy: summary captions.

Read the Structure

The spine is prep, arrival, ceremony, vows, rings, family, reception, dance, quiet, portraits, exit. It need not cover every schedule item; it must show two people becoming a family in one day.

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 6 min film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 8,000–20,000, two people, two cameras plus one mic, one day.
  • Mid: RMB 20,000–60,000, three to five people, two or three cameras plus light/sound, one to two days.
  • High: RMB 60,000–200,000+, director, camera, light, sound, post, two to three days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. List three unmissable beats: entrance, rings, vows.
  2. Keep vows in sync; music steps back.
  3. Hold one quiet moment with no camera awareness.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy all slow motion: it hides real reactions.
  2. Do not copy every table toast: they look the same and blur together.
  3. Do not copy heavy skin smoothing: two people become two plastic faces.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Before the ceremony list three unmissable beats; one safe camera each.
  2. Watch muted; does the vow section still carry emotion?
  3. Compress to ninety seconds: prep, vows, one family reaction, quiet, exit.

Check

  • Entrance, rings, and vows each have a safe camera.
  • Vows have independent audio; music does not cover.
  • Family reactions are not staged.
  • Reception keeps two specific tables.
  • Dance has action plus reaction, not all slow motion.
  • One unguarded quiet moment exists.
  • Portraits are not smoothed to distortion.

Boundary

This page only covers “Wedding Breakdown: Six Minutes Without a Checklist”; it does not replace Wedding Film Structure: Ceremony Before Style, Wedding Template: Opening, Ceremony, Blessing, Adjusting Actors: Give Verbs, Not Adjectives. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Formats / Wedding

Wedding Template: Opening, Ceremony, Blessing

Opening, ceremony, blessing. The opening gives the day, not a dress close-up.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

A wedding template runs opening, ceremony, blessing; the opening gives the feel of the day, not a dress close-up.

A usable 60-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Opening action0–10sA morning action: tie, shoes, closing a windowAmbience; not a dress still life
Preparation10–25sThe two people prepare in separate spacesLittle dialogue; no sentimental score
Ceremony25–45sThe ceremony happens whole, not in fragmentsKeep vows sync; pull music back
Vow45–55sOne face and the other person's reactionOne complete true line; do not cut it into quotes
Blessing55–60sThe first embrace or exit after the ceremonyNo “happy forever”; leave one concrete action

Fill three lines before rolling

  • Feeling of the day: which action explains today? Not the dress.
  • Vow: which sentence must stay whole? Confirm audio early.
  • True line: who will say one specific blessing? No stock phrase.

On set

Open with the feel of the day, keep the ceremony complete, and leave one true sentence of blessing. No wedding-dress close-up opener.

Do this

  1. Open with an action that sets the day, such as tying a tie in the morning.
  2. Keep the ceremony whole and vows uncut.
  3. Leave one true sentence in the blessing, not a stock phrase.

Avoid

Do not open on dress close-ups; clothing does not say what happened that day.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The opening is an action or sound, not a dress still life.
  • 2. The ceremony stays whole and vows are not chopped.
  • 3. The ending holds one specific true sentence, not “happily ever after.”

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The opening is an action or sound, not a dress…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The ceremony stays whole and vows are not chop…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not open on dress close-ups; clothing does not say what happened that day.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “Open with an action that sets the day,” and “Keep the ceremony whole and vows uncut.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The opening is an action or sound, not a dress still life.
  • The ceremony stays whole and vows are not chopped.
  • The ending holds one specific true sentence, not “happily ever after.”
