Home/Formats/Event Film Structure: Result First, Process Second

Formats / Event

Event Film Structure: Result First, Process Second

Result first, process second; the viewer needs to know what the event became.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

The common event-film mistake is chronological coverage from check-in to load-out. The audience wants “what happened here,” so open on the hottest second or the finished room, then return to arrival and process.

Result first, process second

Pick three different highlights in the middle, one shot each. Do not give every guest speech equal time.

Limits

An event film is neither news nor a brand ad. It can move fast, but it cannot invent a result; do not use music and slow motion to fill what did not happen.

Case: a 90-second event recap that leads with the result

Case note: an anonymised composite of several similar projects. Figures are ranges; people, places and clients are withheld. It does not represent one real client job.

ProjectConstraintResult
90-second event recapOne venue, one shoot day, two peopleShot today, delivered tomorrow
Budget band¥2,000–6,000No rehearsal, no staged setups
PurposeTell absent people what happenedNot a full record of the program

What happened

  1. The opening did not show an empty hall. It showed the first sentence and first action of a guest arriving, so viewers knew what the day was about.
  2. The middle kept three highlights, no longer than eight seconds each. Executive speeches kept one sentence that could stand alone, not the full talk.
  3. The ending gave the next event's date and action, not a “success” title card.

The trade-off

We dropped the full program and multiple interviews for one result, three proofs and one next step. Location audio was unreliable, so key lines became subtitle cards, but two seconds of real room tone stayed so it still feels live.

Reusable / not transferable

  • Reusable: event films lead with the result, then the process; one visible action per highlight.
  • Not transferable: launches can involve unannounced products or guest likeness. Check the organizer's clearance list before publishing; “it happened live” is not consent.

On set

Give the result in ten seconds: attendance, deals, or closing. Then return to the process.

Do this

An event film gives the result before the process; viewers need to know what the event became.

  1. Give the result in the first ten seconds: attendance, sales, or closing.
  2. Then three on-site highlights.
  3. End with time, place, and action.

Avoid

Do not cut the event into a list of officials; viewers need to know what happened.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Platform names and monetisation rules differ by market; treat Douyin, Bilibili and Xiaohongshu as examples, then re-check TikTok, YouTube, Instagram or the local platform.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The first ten seconds give a measurable or visible result.
  • 2. The middle has three on-site highlights, not speeches.
  • 3. The ending states time, place, and how to join.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The first ten seconds give a measurable or vis…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The middle has three on-site highlights, not s…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not cut the event into a list of officials; viewers need to know what happened.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “Give the result in the first ten seconds:” and “Then three on-site highlights.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The first ten seconds give a measurable or visible result.
  • The middle has three on-site highlights, not speeches.
  • The ending states time, place, and how to join.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. An event film is not a record of the schedule. Give the result, three highlights, then how to join.

Lead with the result

Open with the busiest or most informative moment: a full room, lights up, a product raised, applause landing. Do not start at the registration desk and an empty hall.

The viewer must know what this is and whether it is worth watching before they invest in the schedule. One subtitle for time, place, attendance. No host introduction.

Three highlights

Pick one highlight each from people, action, and space: a face, a product being used, the scale of the room. Five to eight seconds each; do not divide the film evenly.

Give each highlight one piece of live sound or one interview line. No three-part narration. Keep the interview line that stands alone; do not run the full Q&A.

Close with the information

End with date, venue, registration, organizer. One piece of information per frame; do not squeeze four lines into a corner.

Fifteen to sixty seconds is enough. You can return to the opening moment so the viewer knows it will happen again. Do not replace the concrete result with “a complete success.”

Five-minute drill: a fifteen-second event cut

Cut fifteen seconds from existing footage: three seconds of result, three highlights at three seconds each, three seconds of information. No registration desk, no full executive speech.

Watch muted and ask: what event is this, when is it, how do I join? If any answer is missing, cut one highlight and make the information clear.

When it is done

Play it muted and ask someone who did not attend: what event is this, when is it, how do I register? If all three answers are clear, the promo is done. If one is missing, cut a highlight and put the information on screen.

Ten event-promo checks

  • Busiest moment within three seconds
  • No opening at registration
  • One subtitle for time, place, attendance
  • One highlight each for people, action, space
  • Five to eight seconds per highlight
  • Live sound or one interview line
  • Only one interview line
  • One information item per closing frame
  • Fifteen to sixty seconds
  • No “complete success” instead of a result

An event film does not finish the schedule; it helps the viewer decide whether to come next time.

en.title: Event Breakdown: Make a Live Event Clear in Ninety Seconds
en.summary: An eight-beat breakdown of a ninety-second event film: arrival, scale, key moment, detail, people, climax, aftermath, end card.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Event Breakdown: Make a Live Event Clear in Ninety Seconds

Formats / Event

Event Breakdown: Make a Live Event Clear in Ninety Seconds

An eight-beat breakdown of a ninety-second event film: arrival, scale, key moment, detail, people, climax, aftermath, end card.

6 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: ninety seconds, Channels/institutional, and the goal is “let people who were absent know what happened.” The trap is a schedule record; find the key moment, then reactions.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 8 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:05 | Picture: arrival: door, check-in, first look. Sound: event ambience. Job: bring viewers into the space. Steal: enter through an action. Do not copy: drone wide.
  2. 0:05–0:15 | Picture: scale: three things show crowd/set/theme. Sound: ambience plus one line. Job: how big, what is it. Steal: three details. Do not copy: a statistics caption.
  3. 0:15–0:30 | Picture: key moment: reveal, opening, first line. Sound: sync. Job: the main event. Steal: one action completes. Do not copy: five angles fragmented.
  4. 0:30–0:45 | Picture: detail: hands, props, screen, table. Sound: detail sound. Job: make the event believable. Steal: three touchable details. Do not copy: stage only.
  5. 0:45–1:00 | Picture: people: audience reaction, crew, guest. Sound: real talk/laughter. Job: turn scale into people. Steal: one reactive face. Do not copy: staged group photo.
  6. 1:00–1:15 | Picture: climax: award, signing, performance, applause. Sound: live peak, music later. Job: emotional peak. Steal: let sync peak first. Do not copy: push with music.
  7. 1:15–1:25 | Picture: aftermath: exit, cleanup, empty venue. Sound: ambience falls. Job: give the event an end. Steal: empty room/chairs/cups. Do not copy: cut straight to logo.
  8. 1:25–1:30 | Picture: end card: theme/date/host, once. Sound: one closing line. Job: land the information. Steal: same frame as the empty venue. Do not copy: three lines of titles.

Read the Structure

The spine is arrival, scale, key moment, detail, people, climax, aftermath, end card. It need not cover every schedule item; it must let absent viewers understand what happened and why it matters.

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 90 sec film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 3,000–10,000, one to two people, single camera, available light, one day.
  • Mid: RMB 10,000–40,000, three to five people, two cameras plus sound, one to two days.
  • High: RMB 40,000–150,000+, director, multi-camera, vision mixer, post, two to five days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. Open on an entrance action, not a drone.
  2. Three details show scale, not a statistics caption.
  3. Let live sound reach the peak before music.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy multi-camera switching without a vision mixer; five angles fragment.
  2. Do not copy a schedule film: covering every item means no focus.
  3. Do not copy “VIP first”: viewers recognize people, not titles.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. List three key moments and shoot only those.
  2. Watch muted; can the picture explain how big and what it is?
  3. Compress to thirty seconds: arrival, key moment, people, end card.

Check

  • An arrival action in the first five seconds, not a drone.
  • Scale/theme clear within fifteen seconds.
  • One complete key moment.
  • At least three touchable details.
  • One real reaction face, not staged.
  • Live sound peaks before music at the climax.
  • An aftermath/empty venue before the end card.

Boundary

This page only covers “Event Breakdown: Make a Live Event Clear in Ninety Seconds”; it does not replace Event Film Structure: Result First, Process Second, Event Template: Open, Live, Close, Adjusting Actors: Give Verbs, Not Adjectives. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Event Template: Open, Live, Close

Open, live, close. The live section needs ambience, not wall-to-wall music.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

An event template runs opening, site, close; the site section needs ambient sound, not wall-to-wall music.

A usable 60-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Result0–10sThe hottest second of the event, or the finished roomOne “what happened” line; not the host opening
Opening10–20sPeople enter, sign in, space establishedAmbience; time and place clear
Three highlights20–40sThree different highlights, one shot eachKeep event sound; no wall-to-wall music
Close40–50sThe crowd leaves or one final actionOne result line; no VIP list
Action50–60sTime, place or registration entryOne next step only

Fill three lines before rolling

  • Result: what happened by the end? One sentence.
  • Three highlights: write what the camera sees, not “good atmosphere.”
  • Action: how does the viewer join next time? Time, place, entry.

On set

Result, three live highlights, and a close with time, place, and action. No list of VIPs.

Do this

  1. Open with the result.
  2. Give three highlights with ambient sound.
  3. Close with time, place, and action, not an officials list.

Avoid

Do not score everything; without site sound, it feels like a promo.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The opening gives the result, not an emcee walking on.
  • 2. The site section has three highlights and audible ambience.
  • 3. The close states time, place, and how to join.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The opening gives the result, not an emcee wal…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The site section has three highlights and audi…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not score everything; without site sound, it feels like a promo.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “Open with the result.” and “Give three highlights with ambient sound.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The opening gives the result, not an emcee walking on.
  • The site section has three highlights and audible ambience.
  • The close states time, place, and how to join.

en.title: Interview Structure: The Question Matters More
en.summary: The question matters more than the camera; a vague question gets a vague answer.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Formats/Interview Structure: The Question Matters More

Formats / Interview

Interview Structure: The Question Matters More

The question matters more than the camera; a vague question gets a vague answer.

2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

The worst interview opens on a face reciting a résumé. Let the person complete one action in the real workplace so the audience sees the difficulty, then sit down and ask why that step is done that way.

Shoot the work before the talk

Questions circle the action, not a life story. Three are enough: what is hardest here, what failed before, what changes next time.

Limits

Do not cut the interview into quote confetti. Every line keeps its context; removing the question and keeping the answer can change the meaning.

Case: a five-minute interview that replaced the bio with a failure

Case note: an anonymised composite of several similar projects. Figures are ranges; people, places and clients are withheld. It does not represent one real client job.

ProjectConstraintResult
Five-minute portrait interviewOne founder, one afternoon, two camerasThree questions carry the film
Budget band¥3,000–8,000Office daylight + one fill
PurposeRemember one decisionNot a company CV

What happened

  1. The first 20 minutes asked for a company introduction; every answer was a pitch. We stopped and asked, “What was the last decision you got wrong?”
  2. The subject began naming a person, a date and a loss. The camera did not cut; four seconds of silence stayed so viewers wait for the end of the sentence.
  3. All company facts moved to end cards. The interview kept one decision and its cost.

The trade-off

We dropped the full “founder story plus milestones” arc and built around one failure. The second camera did not shoot reactions; it shot hands and the desk, giving the edit detail. Music only in the first five seconds; the rest is voice.

Reusable / not transferable

  • Reusable: ask for a specific experience, not an identity; let the guest do or remember an action, not read a bio.
  • Not transferable: undisclosed business decisions need clearance before publishing. Do not force “authenticity” into something the guest cannot say.

On set

Ask a question that makes them do something: show me how you do it. Do not ask about feelings.

Do this

In an interview, the question matters more than the camera; an empty question yields an empty answer.

  1. Ask a question that makes them do something: show me how you work.
  2. Shoot the actions and pauses in the answer.
  3. Add one environment shot.

Avoid

Do not ask “how do you feel”; feelings cannot be shown, actions can.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Platform names and monetisation rules differ by market; treat Douyin, Bilibili and Xiaohongshu as examples, then re-check TikTok, YouTube, Instagram or the local platform.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The first question makes the subject do something, not just answer.
  • 2. Actions or pauses are captured within the answer.
  • 3. An environment shot establishes where they are.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The first question makes the subject do someth…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Actions or pauses are captured within the answ…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not ask “how do you feel”; feelings cannot be shown, actions can.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “Ask a question that makes them do something:” and “Shoot the actions and pauses in the answer.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The first question makes the subject do something, not just answer.
  • Actions or pauses are captured within the answer.
  • An environment shot establishes where they are.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. An interview is not a recorded Q&A. Give the guest something to do and let the questions follow the action.

Questions that produce action

Do not ask “how did you feel?” Ask “what did you do first that day?” Do not ask “why did you persist?” Ask “when did you almost quit, and what happened the last time?”

Follow the detail: what time, where, who was there, what did you say, how did they answer. Detail brings emotion with it; do not force the guest to perform it.

The scene

Interview at the place where they work: hands busy, eyes not locked on the lens. Cooking, repairing, sorting papers beats a white wall.

Two cameras are nice; one works too: a medium and a hand or room detail. Without a second camera, shoot hand close-ups after the Q&A. Record thirty seconds of room tone separately.

Structure

One question, one story, one contradiction, one close. Do not run from childhood to today. Let the audience hear one concrete scene first, then add context.

Do not narrate “he is persistent.” Let the guest name the cost. Subtitles must be accurate; keep pauses and repetition where they carry meaning, do not rewrite everything into formal prose.

Five-minute drill: three action questions

Ask one person three questions only: what did you do first that day, who stopped you, what did you change in the end? No feelings, no “what do you think.”

Let them answer while doing something with their hands. Record sixty seconds and look for one concrete scene. If there is none, follow up: where were you, what time, who was nearby?

When it is done

Ask someone who has never met the guest to repeat one concrete scene: where they were, what their hands were doing, who blocked them. If they can, the interview is done. If all they retain is “he worked hard,” go back for action detail, not narration.

Ten interview checks

  • Questions ask actions, not feelings
  • At least three detail follow-ups
  • Guest is at the work site
  • Hands have something to do
  • Hand close-ups even with one camera
  • Thirty seconds of room tone
  • Concrete scene before context
  • One contradiction
  • No narration summarizing the person
  • Subtitles keep spoken texture

An interview does not get answers; it lets the viewer see the part of the person that appears while they work.

Review

Known failure

en.title: Interview Breakdown: Make a Person Land in Three Minutes
en.summary: A nine-beat breakdown of a three-minute interview: answer hook, person at work, question one, evidence, question two, turn, context, close, hold.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Interview Breakdown: Make a Person Land in Three Minutes

Formats / Interview

Interview Breakdown: Make a Person Land in Three Minutes

A nine-beat breakdown of a three-minute interview: answer hook, person at work, question one, evidence, question two, turn, context, close, hold.

7 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: three minutes, Bilibili/Channels, and the goal is the person stands on their own, not the host finishing questions. The trap is talking heads; count shots of the person working, not questions.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 9 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:08 | Picture: the person is already speaking; first line is an answer/conflict. Sound: sync. Job: hook first, no introduction. Steal: start mid-answer. Do not copy: host intro.
  2. 0:08–0:25 | Picture: the person works/walks/operates; interview continues. Sound: action plus interview. Job: give the person a body, not just a face. Steal: cover interview with work. Do not copy: cut faces throughout.
  3. 0:25–0:50 | Picture: question one, but keep the answer, not the question. Sound: answer. Job: let viewers listen to the person, not the reporter. Steal: cut the question. Do not copy: keep “what do you think.”
  4. 0:50–1:15 | Picture: evidence: hands, object, document, place. Sound: action. Job: make the claim verifiable. Steal: one touchable proof. Do not copy: repeat the answer in captions.
  5. 1:15–1:40 | Picture: question two; the answer contradicts or changes. Sound: answer slows/pauses. Job: give the person layers. Steal: keep the pause. Do not copy: fill with music.
  6. 1:40–2:05 | Picture: turn: the person does something and the answer becomes a decision. Sound: action. Job: turn interview into event. Steal: let action interrupt. Do not copy: keep the answer seated.
  7. 2:05–2:30 | Picture: context: place/time/rules/what happened before. Sound: ambience. Job: give the personal story a world. Steal: three environmental details. Do not copy: narrate history.
  8. 2:30–2:50 | Picture: close: the person returns to work, no summary. Sound: action plus one answer. Job: end on the person. Steal: return to the opening action. Do not copy: host summarizes.
  9. 2:50–3:00 | Picture: hold: a face or empty frame. Sound: ambience. Job: let viewers judge. Steal: stop unfinished. Do not copy: caption “this is…”.

Read the Structure

The spine is answer, body, question, evidence, contradiction, turn, context, return, hold. Fewer questions make a stronger person; every answer needs visible evidence.

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 3 min film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 2,000–8,000, two people, one camera and one mic, one location, half a day.
  • Mid: RMB 8,000–30,000, three to five people, two cameras, light, sound, one to two days.
  • High: RMB 30,000–100,000+, director, camera, sound, art, multiple locations, three to five days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. Start mid-answer; cut the introduction.
  2. Cover interview with work; give the person a body.
  3. Keep one pause/contradiction for layers.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy host/guest alternating cuts: without work shots, it is radio.
  2. Do not copy quote mining: if every line is a quote, the person feels fake.
  3. Do not copy historical narration: context comes from environmental detail, not a lecture.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Watch muted; can the picture say what the person does?
  2. Count work shots versus talking-head cuts; if talking heads exceed half, recut.
  3. Compress to sixty seconds: answer, evidence, turn.

Check

  • The first line within eight seconds is an answer/conflict, not an intro.
  • The person is working within twenty-five seconds.
  • Questions are cut; answers remain.
  • Every answer has one touchable proof.
  • One pause or contradiction is kept.
  • Context comes from environmental detail, not narration.
  • End returns to the person/work, not a host summary.

Formats / Interview

Interview Template: Person, Question, Scene

Person, question, scene. Shoot where they act before sitting them down.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

An interview template uses person, question, scene; shoot where they work before sitting down.

A usable 60-second segment table

SegmentTimePictureSound / pass line
Scene action0–10sThe person in the place where they actually work, hands busyAmbience; no résumé question first
Work10–25sOne complete work action shows difficultySync sound; interview does not cover the action
Question 125–40sSit-down interview, work traces still in the backgroundQuestion about the action just seen
Question 240–50sReaction shot and hand detailAsk about cost, not birthplace
Close50–60sThe person returns to work or looks at the spaceOne concrete line; no life summary

Fill three lines before rolling

  • Place: where do they really work? Why not a meeting room?
  • Action: what will you shoot first? It must be complete.
  • Questions: all three circle that action; delete résumé questions.

On set

Person, question, place. Shoot where they can work before sitting them down.

Do this

  1. Choose a place where they can do their work.
  2. Shoot the work first, then sit for the interview.
  3. Base questions on one concrete action, not a résumé.

Avoid

Do not let the subject read a résumé; a résumé has no images.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The scene is where they actually work, not an empty meeting room.
  • 2. One action is captured before the sit-down interview.
  • 3. Questions center on the action, not birthplace or résumé.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The scene is where they actually work, not an…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“One action is captured before the sit-down int…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not let the subject read a résumé; a résumé has no images.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “Choose a place where they can do their” and “Shoot the work first, then sit for the”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The scene is where they actually work, not an empty meeting room.
  • One action is captured before the sit-down interview.
  • Questions center on the action, not birthplace or résumé.

en.title: Experimental Structure: Rules Before Effects
en.summary: Set rules first: locked camera, repeated action, one color. Clear rules make stronger effects.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Formats/Experimental Structure: Rules Before Effects

Formats / Experimental

Experimental Structure: Rules Before Effects

Set rules first: locked camera, repeated action, one color. Clear rules make stronger effects.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

An experimental film is not random cutting. Write one rule first: fixed camera, fixed duration, fixed color, or one action per shot. The whole piece varies that rule so the strangeness has a logic.

Experimental can be strange, but it needs a traceable rule

Put the rule on paper and check after the shoot: which shot broke it, and was that intentional or loss of control? Those answers decide whether it stays.

Limits

Anti-narrative is not structureless. The viewer may not know the story, but something must accumulate or change, or after three minutes it is only noise.

Experimental film template: one rule, three repeats, one break

Experimental film is not “shoot whatever.” A usable template needs a rule the viewer can recognize, repetition to build expectation, and one controlled break to create change. Without a rule, the break means nothing.

SegmentDurationImageSoundViewer expectation
Rule0–15sLocked camera, one repeated actionLocation sound, no score“I know what this is”
Repeat 115–30sSame action, slight changeSame ambience“It will happen again”
Repeat 230–45sSame action, longer holdOne foreign sound“Something is off”
Break45–55sAction interrupted or reversedSound cuts, then returns“The rule failed”
Aftermath55–60sReturn to the rule, incompleteAmbience only“What just happened”
End card2sBlack or a still objectSilenceSpace

Rules for filling it in

  1. The rule must be one sentence: who, in what space, repeating what action. If it cannot be written, do not shoot.
  2. Repeat at least three times, changing one variable only: duration, sound, framing or action size.
  3. Break once. A second break exhausts the viewer.
  4. Aftermath returns to the rule without explanation. Explanation turns the experiment into a lecture.

Reusable Markdown template
Same segments as the table above; replace the brackets with your own shots.

Download .md

Acceptance: show it to someone who has not read the script, then ask “what was the rule, where did it break?” If they can answer, the template works. If not, cut a segment before adding an effect.

On set

Set one rule: a locked camera for ten minutes, one room, one color. Break it once.

Do this

Experimental film sets a rule first: fixed camera, repeated action, single color; the clearer the rule, the stronger the effect.

  1. Set one rule: locked camera for ten minutes, one room, one color.
  2. Break it once in the film.
  3. End on sound or black.

Avoid

Do not use “unintelligible” as depth; an unclear rule means no rule.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The whole film's rule fits one sentence.
  • 2. The rule breaks once at an identifiable point.
  • 3. The ending lands on sound or black, not an arbitrary stop.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The whole film's rule fits one sentence”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The rule breaks once at an identifiable point”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use “unintelligible” as depth; an unclear rule means no rule.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Break down one 30-second reference, mark the timecodes for “Set one rule: locked camera for ten minutes,” and “Break it once in the film.”, then answer: if one disappeared, would the film still hold?

Check

  • The whole film's rule fits one sentence.
  • The rule breaks once at an identifiable point.
  • The ending lands on sound or black, not an arbitrary stop.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Experimental film is not random. It sets one rule, then lets the image change inside that rule.

Set the rule first

The simpler the rule, the more visible the change: locked camera, one repeated action, one color, one duration. Do not juggle five effects; the viewer sees only noise.

Write the rule on one line and tape it to the monitor: “one window, once every ten minutes, twelve times.” With a rule, change means something.

Break one rule

Break the rule once in the whole film: the camera suddenly moves, color drops out, sound cuts. The fewer the breaks, the louder each one lands.

When the rule breaks, cut or sound must change with it. Do not pile on effects. Effects decorate; the rule structures.

Sound and length

Sound can carry the structure: a sustained room tone, one sudden silence, a repeated mechanical noise. Do not start with wall-to-wall music.

One to five minutes. The ending needs a reason to stop: the last action completes, the light dims, the sound disappears. No story is fine; no ending is not.

Five-minute drill: one rule, one break

Set a rule that can run sixty seconds: locked camera, one repeated action, one color. Shoot it three times; on the third, change one variable only: light, sound, or camera position.

Cut the three takes together and see whether the viewer can name which take changed. If not, the rule is not clear enough; if too much changed, you broke more than one rule.

When it is done

Ask the viewer what the rule was and where it broke. If they can answer both, the film is done. If they only say “good atmosphere,” the rule did not land. Cut half the effects and keep one change.

Ten experimental-film checks

  • The rule fits in one sentence
  • The rule is simple and repeatable
  • The rule breaks once
  • Sound or cut changes at the break
  • No pile of effects
  • Sound carries structure
  • Not wall-to-wall music
  • One to five minutes
  • The ending has a reason to stop
  • No story is fine, no ending is not

Experimental freedom is not “shoot anything.” It is setting one rule and daring to break it once.

en.title: Experimental Breakdown: Rule, Repetition, Break
en.summary: An eight-beat breakdown of a four-minute experimental film: pre-rule, rule, three repetitions, break, consequence, stop.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Experimental Breakdown: Rule, Repetition, Break

Formats / Experimental

Experimental Breakdown: Rule, Repetition, Break

An eight-beat breakdown of a four-minute experimental film: pre-rule, rule, three repetitions, break, consequence, stop.

6 min read · breakdown worksheetTVCN / 06Edited 2026-11

Fix Three Variables First

Fix three variables: four minutes, festival/art platform, and the goal is “the viewer can name the rule and the break.” Experimental is not random; it needs a rule more than narrative. Find the rule, then the variable in repetition.

Sample note: the timecodes below are a teaching sample for this format's usual length. They do not correspond to one specific film and are not frame-accurate analysis. Use the same positions on your own film; do not treat these beats as the only answer.

Timecode Breakdown: 8 Beats

Watch in order; do not read commentary first. For each beat record four things: picture, sound, job, and steal or do-not-copy.

  1. 0:00–0:10 | Picture: before the rule: an empty space, object, or preparation. Sound: ambience, no music. Job: quiet the viewer. Steal: open on a still frame. Do not copy: fast montage.
  2. 0:10–0:20 | Picture: rule established: locked frame, left to right, one action. Sound: the action sound complete for the first time. Job: signal repetition. Steal: first pass complete. Do not copy: fragment the first pass.
  3. 0:20–0:60 | Picture: repetition one: change one variable (light/slow/bright). Sound: same action sound. Job: build expectation. Steal: make the variable visible. Do not copy: change three variables.
  4. 1:00–1:40 | Picture: repetition two: the variable intensifies (heavy/fast/dark). Sound: action grows. Job: give repetition direction. Steal: use weight/speed. Do not copy: narrate it.
  5. 1:40–2:20 | Picture: repetition three: variable at limit; the person begins not to finish. Sound: breath close. Job: make expectation about to fail. Steal: almost complete the action. Do not copy: break immediately.
  6. 2:20–3:00 | Picture: break: camera still locked, action/person exits. Sound: remaining sound in the empty space. Job: make the rule fail. Steal: break once. Do not copy: break three times.
  7. 3:00–3:40 | Picture: consequence: empty space/object/trace remains. Sound: ambience. Job: the break costs something. Steal: stay on the consequence. Do not copy: cut to black.
  8. 3:40–4:00 | Picture: stop: no return to normal, no explanation. Sound: silence. Job: let viewers carry it out. Steal: stop unfinished. Do not copy: add a summary title.

Read the Structure

The spine is rule, repetition, variable, limit, break, consequence, stop. The clearer the rule, the more tension repetition creates; break once, and leave the consequence on screen.

Ask only three questions: what proof arrives in the first ten seconds; whether every ten to fifteen seconds adds information; whether the end lands one action, one change, or one question. If any is missing, a 4 min film falls apart.

Budget Order of Magnitude

Budget is a rough mainland-China production range, excluding media spend; it is an order of magnitude, not a quote. At the same length, a stage, cast, effects, or music rights can each double the cost.

  • Low: RMB 1,000–5,000, one to two people, one space, natural light, one day.
  • Mid: RMB 5,000–20,000, two to four people, controlled light/sound, two to three days.
  • High: RMB 20,000–80,000+, director, camera, sound, art, set or post, five to ten days.

Three Structures You Can Steal

Steal structure, not images. These three still work when you change the subject.

  1. Make the first pass complete so the rule is clear.
  2. Change one variable per repetition.
  3. Stay on the consequence after the break; do not cut to black.

Three Reasons Not to Copy

Not “bad,” but built on different conditions; copying exposes your budget, platform, and audience.

  1. Do not copy “long take equals experimental”: without a rule, long is just slow.
  2. Do not copy “no narrative equals high art”: without expectation, a break is an accident.
  3. Do not copy narration: explanation kills the viewer's own discovery.

Breakdown Exercises

Do them before shooting; do not just read. Do the three in order, and the third must become a fifteen-second file.

  1. Write the film's rule in one sentence.
  2. Count repetitions and variables; more than one variable per pass means recut.
  3. Watch muted; can the picture build expectation?

Check

  • The rule is established in the first twenty seconds.
  • The first repetition is complete, not fragmented.
  • One variable changes per repetition.
  • The third repetition brings expectation close to failure.
  • The break happens once.
  • The consequence holds for at least ten seconds.
  • No narration explains.

Home/Tools/Cine Camera: Sensor, Mount, Codec

Tools / Capability card

Cine Camera: Sensor, Mount, Codec

Cine cameras are sensor, mount, and codec first; the badge and body do not decide the job.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

With a limited budget, a crew under three or a need for a light single camera, a cinema camera is not required; a mirrorless with external recording may fit better. Do not substitute camera class for story.

What to compare first

  • Sensor and format: format, crop modes and high-frame-rate crops; do not buy by pixel count.
  • Mount and recording: mount ecosystem, internal ND, codec and monitoring output; these decide on-set speed.
  • Power and cooling: battery runtime, external power and fan noise; a paid shoot cannot rely on reboots.

On set

Bring your own PL or EF lens and card, record five minutes of 4K 60p, feel the mount temperature, and check rolling shutter and shadow noise.

Do this

A cinema camera is judged by sensor, mount, and recording format; the name and shape do not decide whether it shoots your project.

  1. Bring your own PL or EF lens and card, record five minutes of 4K 60p.
  2. Feel the mount temperature and play back for rolling shutter and shadow noise.
  3. Only discuss rental price after all three pass.

Avoid

Do not judge by the spec sheet alone; mount heat, rolling shutter, and shadow noise must show in your own footage.

Check

  • Five minutes of 4K 60p is recorded on your own lens and card and plays back.
  • Mount temperature is logged and not too hot to change lenses.
  • Playback shows rolling shutter and shadow noise levels, not just a demo reel.

en.summary: Check three things: overheating, rolling shutter, and whether video crops the frame.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Mirrorless for Video: Heat, Rolling Shutter, Crop

Tools / Capability card

Mirrorless for Video: Heat, Rolling Shutter, Crop

Check three things: overheating, rolling shutter, and whether video crops the frame.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For long interviews, extreme low light or professional audio, a mirrorless body is a compromise; use a actively cooled camera or camcorder. Do not hide overheating behind “cinematic.”

What to compare first

  • Heat and record limits: confirm real continuous runtime at room temperature, not the claim; summer and 4K high frame rates stop first.
  • Rolling shutter and readout: check whether fast pans and lateral motion skew; large sensors especially need readout speed.
  • Crop and ports: whether 4K crops, HDMI is clean, and external power works; these decide whether it fits a workflow.

On set

Record thirty minutes of 4K 25p and watch for a heat warning. Pan across a railing for rolling shutter, then switch to 4K 60p and check the crop.

Do this

A mirrorless video camera must answer three things: overheating, rolling shutter, and crop in video mode.

  1. Record thirty minutes of 4K 25p and watch for a heat warning.
  2. Pan across a railing to see rolling shutter.
  3. Switch to 4K 60p and check whether the angle narrows.

Avoid

Do not test for three minutes; overheating often appears around minute twenty.

Check

  • A thirty-minute 4K 25p run logs temperature or warnings.
  • Rolling shutter on the railing is visible and described.
  • The 4K 60p crop has a before-and-after angle comparison.

en.title: Prime Lens: Move Your Feet
en.summary: A prime forces you to step in, back, and change position; that is often better than turning a zoom ring.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Prime Lens: Move Your Feet

Tools / Capability card

Prime Lens: Move Your Feet

A prime forces you to step in, back, and change position; that is often better than turning a zoom ring.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For fast coverage of many shot sizes or tight spaces, a zoom is more practical; a prime is not “more professional,” only more constrained.

What to compare first

  • Focal length and working distance: choose from camera-to-subject distance, not “most popular”; a 50mm can be too tight indoors.
  • Aperture and breathing: fast glass gives shallow depth and harder focus; focus breathing affects the shot.
  • Mount and weight: confirm mount, flange distance and filter thread; a heavy prime needs gimbal rebalance.

On set

Shoot a half-body frame at 35mm and move two meters forward and back to find the composition. Get used to walking before choosing 24 or 50.

Do this

A prime lens does not forbid zooming; it forces you to walk, back up, and change position, which is often more useful than turning a zoom ring.

  1. Shoot the same half-body portrait on a 35mm.
  2. Walk two meters forward and back to find the frame.
  3. Get used to moving before deciding between 24 and 50.

Avoid

Do not stay glued to the tripod; the prime's value is making you change position.

Check

  • At least three positions cover the same person at one focal length.
  • The background and perspective change from two meters of walking is described.
  • The 24 vs 50 decision comes from walking, not review videos.

en.title: Zoom Lens: Convenience Has a Cost
en.summary: A zoom saves time but charges you in weight, aperture, and image; ask which one you can afford today.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Zoom Lens: Convenience Has a Cost

Tools / Capability card

Zoom Lens: Convenience Has a Cost

A zoom saves time but charges you in weight, aperture, and image; ask which one you can afford today.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For extreme shallow depth, low light or minimum weight, a prime is better. Zoom convenience is not free.

What to compare first

  • Range: choose from your common camera-to-subject distance; 24-70 is not universal, and the long end may be tight indoors.
  • Breathing and focus: does focus shift while zooming, and does the image breathe while focusing? Video is more sensitive than stills.
  • Aperture and weight: constant fast apertures are heavier; calculate total weight and balance before a gimbal.

On set

Take the camera to the shop and shoot a backlit window and a railing wide open. Check edges, distortion, and breathing, then lift the lens.

Do this

A zoom saves time but charges you in weight, aperture, and image quality; ask which you lack most today.

  1. Take the camera to a shop and shoot a backlit window and railing wide open.
  2. Check edges, distortion, and breathing.
  3. Weigh it and decide whether convenience is worth the price.

Avoid

Do not check center sharpness only; edges and backlight expose a zoom fastest.

Check

  • Wide-open backlit window and railing shots record edge performance.
  • Distortion and breathing are named, not just “good quality.”
  • Weight is measured and the saved step is stated.

en.title: Anamorphic: Wide Screen, Not a Crop
en.summary: Anamorphic is not a top-and-bottom crop; it squeezes the image horizontally and restores it, giving oval bokeh and specific distortion.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Anamorphic: Wide Screen, Not a Crop

Tools / Capability card

Anamorphic: Wide Screen, Not a Crop

Anamorphic is not a top-and-bottom crop; it squeezes the image horizontally and restores it, giving oval bokeh and specific distortion.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For wide, light, fast autofocus or clean images, do not use an anamorphic. It is a style choice with a cost.

What to compare first

  • Squeeze ratio: confirm 1.33x/1.5x/2x compatibility with sensor and desqueeze; a mismatch distorts.
  • Flare and distortion: flare is not the only selling point; edge distortion and close focus affect composition.
  • Focus and weight: manual focus, long throw and heavy front; a gimbal needs rebalancing.

On set

Shoot neon at night and look for oval bokeh and the horizontal blue flare. Then shoot a face and judge the horizontal stretch.

Do this

Anamorphic does not crop the top and bottom; it squeezes horizontally and expands back, producing oval bokeh and unique distortion.

  1. Shoot neon at night and look for oval bokeh and a horizontal blue line.
  2. Shoot a face and check whether horizontal stretch is acceptable.
  3. Keep anamorphic and cropping as separate ideas.

Avoid

Do not call cropping anamorphic; without oval bokeh and horizontal squeeze, it is only widescreen.

Check

  • Neon night footage shows oval bokeh or a horizontal blue line.
  • A face sample reveals horizontal stretch and whether it is acceptable.
  • Anamorphic and cropping are clearly distinguished.

en.title: Speed Booster: Wider Angle, Faster Aperture
en.summary: A speed booster squeezes a full-frame lens onto a smaller sensor: wider view, about one stop faster, softer edges.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Speed Booster: Wider Angle, Faster Aperture

Tools / Capability card

Speed Booster: Wider Angle, Faster Aperture

A speed booster squeezes a full-frame lens onto a smaller sensor: wider view, about one stop faster, softer edges.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For native autofocus, stabilization or low weight, buy the correct mount lens. A speed booster is an adapter solution, not a free upgrade.

What to compare first

  • Format and ratio: confirm the full-frame to APS-C/M43 ratio and sensor coverage; the wrong ratio vignettes.
  • Aperture and focus: the booster changes effective aperture and depth; test AF speed and compatibility.
  • Mount and clearance: check the lens rear does not hit the element; some wide lenses cannot be used.

On set

From the same position, shoot with and without the adapter. Compare angle, light gain, and corner sharpness; stop down if the edges soften.

Do this

A speed booster compresses a full-frame lens onto a smaller sensor, widening the angle and gaining about a stop, but edges may soften.

  1. Same position and lens, shoot with and without the adapter.
  2. Compare angle, exposure, and corner sharpness.
  3. If corners soften, stop down instead of forcing wide open.

Avoid

Do not treat a speed booster as free aperture; soft corners and vignetting are the bill.

Check

  • With and without the adapter are compared from the same position.
  • Wider angle and extra exposure are visible.
  • Corners are checked and a stopped-down comparison exists if soft.

en.title: Matte Box: Filters and Stray Light
en.summary: A matte box cuts stray light before holding filters; a cheap one can leak and ruin the frame.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Matte Box: Filters and Stray Light

Tools / Capability card

Matte Box: Filters and Stray Light

A matte box cuts stray light before holding filters; a cheap one can leak and ruin the frame.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For light travel, wide lenses or fast lens changes, a matte box adds bulk and steps; use a lens hood and light filters. Do not trade mobility for “professional look.”

What to compare first

  • Filter stages: how many slots, rotating polarizer and ND support; stage order affects vignetting.
  • Diameter and shading: a deep matte box clips wide lenses; test the widest focal length first.
  • Mount and light leaks: flags and top brow must lock; leaks show in long exposures and backlight.

On set

Shoot black velvet against the light and check for leaks at the matte box edge. Add a filter and rotate it to check vignetting.

Do this

A matte box blocks stray light before holding filters; a cheap one can leak and ruin the image.

  1. Shoot black velvet in backlight and check the matte box edges for leaks.
  2. Rotate the filter and check for vignetting.
  3. Seal leaks with black cloth or tape.

Avoid

Do not treat a matte box as a filter holder; check leaks before loading filters.

Check

  • A backlit black velvet test shows whether edges leak.
  • Filter rotation logs where vignetting appears.
  • Leaks are sealed with black cloth or tape, not ignored.

en.title: Follow Focus: One Hand Can Follow
en.summary: A follow focus gives marks and feel; autofocus is not reliable in darkness or fast motion.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Follow Focus: One Hand Can Follow

Tools / Capability card

Follow Focus: One Hand Can Follow

A follow focus gives marks and feel; autofocus is not reliable in darkness or fast motion.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

When autofocus is reliable, the subject is slow or the lens is wide with deep focus, a follow focus is extra weight. Do not give up usable AF for “cinematic.”

What to compare first

  • Gear ratio and throw: the lens focus throw decides the feel; too short jumps, too long lags fast action.
  • Mount and clearance: confirm lens diameter, gear position and matte-box clearance; if it does not fit on set, it is useless.
  • One-hand control: handle direction, drag and marking ring must work one-handed; two-handed focusing loses balance.

On set

Mark one, 1.5, and two meters on the floor. Have an assistant walk the marks and practice ten follows with less than five centimeters of error.

Do this

A follow focus gives focus changes marks and feel; autofocus is not reliable in darkness or fast motion.

  1. Mark one, 1.5, and two meters on the floor.
  2. Have an assistant walk while you pull focus ten times.
  3. Keep the error within five centimeters.

Avoid

Do not rely on autofocus alone; in darkness and fast blocking it hands focus to the background.

Check

  • Three distances are clearly marked on the floor.
  • At least eight of ten pulls stay within five centimeters.
  • The autofocus failure case is tied to a specific condition.

en.title: LED Panel: CRI and Brightness
en.summary: Check CRI and real output, not wattage on the box; green skin means the color is wrong.
en.html:
Home/Tools/LED Panel: CRI and Brightness

Tools / Capability card

LED Panel: CRI and Brightness

Check CRI and real output, not wattage on the box; green skin means the color is wrong.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For strong direction, long throws or large areas, a panel loses to a COB with a softbox. It is best for close, low-power and fast setups.

What to compare first

  • Color rendering: shoot skin, red cloth and green plants; check real performance beyond CRI/TLCI claims. Cheap panels often push green dirty.
  • Dimming: sweep from high to low and look for flicker, cast and steps; it shows most at low output.
  • Diffusion and control: is the built-in diffusion even, and can it take a grid? Edge spill shows when the panel is close to a face.

On set

Set the panel to 5600K at full power and shoot white paper and a hand. Check for green skin and measure the output at one meter.

Do this

An LED panel is judged by color rendering and actual output, not box wattage; green skin means bad color.

  1. Set the light to 5600K at 100 percent and shoot white paper and a hand.
  2. Check whether the hand turns green.
  3. Measure illuminance at one meter to see whether it can key.

Avoid

Do not buy by wattage; bad color rendering makes a bright light usable only as fill.

Check

  • White paper and hand are sampled at 5600K full power.
  • Green or magenta skin cast is named.
  • One-meter illuminance is measured and judged against key-light needs.

en.title: COB Light: One Source, One Soft Box
en.summary: A COB is a bare source; pair it with a soft box or lantern or the face gets hard shadows.
en.html:
Home/Tools/COB Light: One Source, One Soft Box

Tools / Capability card

COB Light: One Source, One Soft Box

A COB is a bare source; pair it with a soft box or lantern or the face gets hard shadows.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

In small rooms, close distance or when you need extreme softness, a COB and box may not fit; use a panel or reflector. Never point a bare COB at a face.

What to compare first

  • Output and color: check real illuminance, color range and low-output stability; wattage is not brightness.
  • Rendering and fan: shoot skin and red cloth, and listen to the fan; in a quiet interview the fan becomes a sound problem.
  • Mount and control: confirm Bowens mount, softbox and grid; a COB without modifiers is just hard light.

On set

Fit a 90-centimeter softbox, place it one meter from the face at 50 percent, and check the shadow edge. If it is still hard, add diffusion or move closer.

Do this

A COB is a bare source and needs a softbox or lantern; bare on a face, shadows turn unusable.

  1. Fit a 90 cm softbox, place one meter from the face at 50 percent.
  2. Watch the shadow edge.
  3. If it is still hard, add diffusion or move closer.

Avoid

Do not point a bare COB at a face; skipping the softbox makes shadows too hard to fix.

Check

  • The COB runs through a softbox, not bare.
  • A one-meter, 50 percent sample shows the shadow edge.
  • A diffusion or closer-position comparison exists if the edge stays hard.

en.title: Softbox: Size Decides Softness
en.summary: Bigger and closer means softer; move the box before changing the light.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Softbox: Size Decides Softness

Tools / Capability card

Softbox: Size Decides Softness

Bigger and closer means softer; move the box before changing the light.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For hard light, defined shadows or long throws, a softbox scatters the direction. Do not use it for every lighting problem.

What to compare first

  • Size: softness comes from area and distance, not brand; if a 120cm box will not fit, use a smaller one closer.
  • Mount and structure: confirm mount, quick release, grid and diffusion; a box that is hard to build will be used less on set.
  • Heat: a high-output COB in a small box traps heat; check vents and the fixture's cooling direction.

On set

With the same lamp, shoot at 0.8 and 1.5 meters. Compare the shadow edge and the size of the eye light.

Do this

The larger and closer the softbox, the softer the light; moving it closer beats changing the lamp.

  1. Same light, softbox at 0.8 and 1.5 meters.
  2. Shoot one frame at each distance.
  3. Compare shadow edges and the size of the eye light.

Avoid

Do not buy a pricier lamp for softness; moving the softbox closer works more directly.

Check

  • 0.8 m and 1.5 m samples use the same light.
  • The closer frame has visibly softer shadow edges.
  • Eye-light size changes with distance and is compared.

en.summary: The five surfaces are five fill strengths, not five styles; start white, not silver.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Reflector: Five Surfaces, One Job

Tools / Capability card

Reflector: Five Surfaces, One Job

The five surfaces are five fill strengths, not five styles; start white, not silver.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

When direction and intensity must be precise, a reflector is unpredictable; use a second light with a softbox. Do not fill a face into having no direction.

What to compare first

  • Size and distance: closer and larger is softer; a small board far away only adds a hot spot.
  • Surface: white is soft, silver is harder and brighter, gold shifts color; black is for negative fill, not reflection.
  • Mounting: confirm stand, clamp and wind resistance; an unsecured reflector outdoors becomes a kite.

On set

Start with the white side at 45 degrees on the shadow side. If it is not enough, switch to silver; do not start with gold.

Do this

A five-in-one reflector is five fill strengths, not five styles; start white, not silver.

  1. Place the white side at 45 degrees on the shadow side and shoot.
  2. Switch to silver only if more is needed.
  3. Use gold only for warmth, never by default.

Avoid

Do not start with gold; warm skin is hard to pull back to neutral later.

Check

  • A white-side 45-degree fill sample exists.
  • Silver is used only after white proves insufficient, with a comparison.
  • Gold is not default, or its warmth is justified.

en.title: Lighting Gel: CTO, CTB, ND
en.summary: Know CTO, CTB, and ND: warm, cool, and dim. The wrong gel changes the whole set.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Lighting Gel: CTO, CTB, ND

Tools / Capability card

Lighting Gel: CTO, CTB, ND

Know CTO, CTB, and ND: warm, cool, and dim. The wrong gel changes the whole set.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For precise, repeatable light reduction, use lens ND or electronic ND, not a guess with a gel. Gels are for color and atmosphere, not measurement.

Test the color shift

  • Density: shoot white paper and a gray card at the final light position with 1/4, 1/2 and full ND; compare color temperature and density.
  • Stacking: multiple ND gels add cast and vignetting; use one gel of the needed density where possible.
  • Heat: gels melt too close to a fixture; use a gel frame and distance, and check LED cooling too.

Do not stack more than two gels

CTO/CTB correct color temperature; ND lowers brightness. Stacking both shifts color, reduces sharpness and can add IR pollution. Decide whether you need a color shift before adding ND.

  1. Daylight too blue: 1/4 CTO. Tungsten too warm: 1/4 CTB. Add a quarter at a time.
  2. Put ND on the lens or window, not against the color gel. For deep cuts, use one strong ND, not three weak ones.
  3. Set LED color and brightness first; gels are for trim, not for fixing a bad lamp.

Acceptance: white-balance and check white paper and skin, not the lamp. Green cast or vignette means remove a layer.

On set

Put CTO on the window and CTB on the lamp, then check the color temperature. ND gel only cuts brightness; it does not shift color.

Do this

Lighting gels split into CTO, CTB, and ND: warm, cool, and dim; the wrong gel changes the whole set.

  1. CTO on a window, CTB on a lamp, shoot and read color temperature.
  2. ND gel only dims without shifting color.
  3. Label each gel with name and strength instead of judging by color.

Avoid

Do not sort gels by eye; CTO and ND can both look orange in the dark.

Check

  • CTO and CTB each have a comparable color-temperature sample.
  • ND changes brightness without shifting color temperature.
  • Each gel carries a name and strength label.

en.title: Practical Bulb: Color Temperature and Dimming
en.summary: A practical must dim and shift color temperature, or it is only a prop, not a source.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Practical Bulb: Color Temperature and Dimming

Tools / Capability card

Practical Bulb: Color Temperature and Dimming

A practical must dim and shift color temperature, or it is only a prop, not a source.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For repeatable output, long shoots or mixing with film lights, do not use an uncontrolled household bulb. It works as an in-frame practical, not as a key light.

Test three things

  • Dimming: take it from 100% to 10% and watch for flicker, color shift or steps; cheap LEDs often fail at low output.
  • Color temperature: compare with a gray card and camera white balance; confirm whether the claimed 3200K/5600K is real.
  • Color rendering: shoot skin and a red cloth, not only a white wall; poor rendering makes skin gray and red muddy.

Practical bulbs: dim first, then color

A table lamp or wall sconce is not “turn it on.” Mains bulbs flicker, drift in color and cannot be dimmed. Replace with dimmable LED or add a dimmer before the shoot.

  1. Look through the viewfinder for flicker; banding means change the bulb or set shutter to a multiple of local mains frequency.
  2. Use 2700K or 3200K, within half a stop of the key. A big mismatch reads as two rooms.
  3. Dim it below clipping; shape the pool with a flag, not with post.

Acceptance: shoot ten seconds and check flicker around the bulb and green skin. Flicker means change the lamp, not fix it in post.

On set

Use a tunable bulb at 3200K on a dimmer at 30 percent and check whether it still reads as the motive.

Do this

A practical bulb must dim and shift color, or the lamp in frame is only a prop, not a source.

  1. Use a tunable bulb and set it to 3200K.
  2. Put it on a dimmer at 30 percent.
  3. Shoot and see whether it still motivates the light in frame.

Avoid

Do not use a fixed household bulb; it blows out and becomes a prop only.

Check

  • The bulb reaches 3200K and runs on a dimmer.
  • At 30 percent the lamp in frame does not blow out.
  • It motivates the nearby key light.

en.title: Light Stand: Sandbag Everything
en.summary: Sandbag the stand before raising the light; an unweighted stand costs more than the lamp when it falls.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Light Stand: Sandbag Everything

Tools / Capability card

Light Stand: Sandbag Everything

Sandbag the stand before raising the light; an unweighted stand costs more than the lamp when it falls.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For a large softbox or height above a person's head, a small stand tips; use a heavy stand or truss. Do not use a backpack as a sandbag.

What to compare first

  • Payload and height: calculate light plus softbox plus sandbag, not the head alone; the center changes as it rises.
  • Legs and locks: legs lock without slipping and offer leveling; it must stand on uneven ground.
  • Sandbags and tie-downs: at least one sandbag per stand; outdoors it must take weight and rope, not rely on legs alone.

When not to use it

For a large softbox or height above a person's head, a small stand tips; use a heavy stand or truss. Do not use a backpack as a sandbag.

Light stand safety: sandbags at least twice the fixture weight

A falling stand is worse than a dim lamp. Put at least two sandbags on every stand, total weight at least twice the fixture. When a boom arm extends, counterweight the other side.

  1. Hang bags at the base tripod, not at the end of the arm; end weight increases tipping torque.
  2. Tie cables along the stand and leave a trip loop. Do not cross a walkway.
  3. Lock casters before raising, lock the arm after. At wrap, lower the lamp before removing bags.

Acceptance: push the stand lightly; it should spring back, not keep falling. If it keeps falling, add weight or lower it.

On set

Hang two sandbags on every stand and push it gently at full height. If it moves, lower it before rolling.

Do this

Sandbag the stand before raising the light; an unweighted stand costs more when it falls than the lamp did.

  1. Hang two sandbags on each stand.
  2. Raise to full height and push gently.
  3. Only power on if it does not wobble; otherwise lower it or add weight.

Avoid

Do not raise the light before finding sandbags; at full height it is already unmanageable.

Check

  • Each stand carries two sandbags with recorded weight.
  • A gentle push at full height does not wobble.
  • Any wobbling stand is lowered or weighted before power-on.

en.title: Shotgun Mic: Point It, Get Close
en.summary: A shotgun is directional; distance gives you room, not dialogue. Get close before denoising.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Shotgun Mic: Point It, Get Close

Tools / Capability card

Shotgun Mic: Point It, Get Close

A shotgun is directional; distance gives you room, not dialogue. Get close before denoising.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

In hard-wall rooms, seated groups or when the mic must be hidden, a lav beats a shotgun. Do not use one shotgun for every scene.

What to compare first

  • Pattern and off-axis: check pickup angle and off-axis rejection; too narrow misses movement, too wide collects the room.
  • Power and output: confirm phantom power, battery and output level; camera input gain may not be enough.
  • Wind protection and boom: a shotgun needs a blimp, furry cover and shock mount; without isolation, handling noise enters every line.

On set

Record the same line at one, two, and three meters. Check the directionality on playback; past two meters, switch to a lav or boom.

Do this

A shotgun is a directional tool; far away it only captures ambience. Move closer before discussing noise reduction.

  1. Record one line at one, two, and three meters.
  2. Play back for directionality and ambience ratio.
  3. Beyond two meters, switch to a lav or boom.

Avoid

Do not rescue a distant shotgun with noise reduction; dialogue is already buried in ambience.

Check

  • One line is recorded at one, two, and three meters.
  • Playback reveals dialogue buried past two meters.
  • Shots beyond two meters have a lav or boom alternative.

en.title: Wireless Lav: Frequency and Backup
en.summary: Check frequency and interference, and record a backup track; the set gives no second chance.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Wireless Lav: Frequency and Backup

Tools / Capability card

Wireless Lav: Frequency and Backup

Check frequency and interference, and record a backup track; the set gives no second chance.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

In heavy RF, long range or many simultaneous speakers, wireless lav is not the only answer. Add a shotgun, recorder or wired backup; one wireless link is not insurance.

What to compare first

  • Band and power: choose a band legal where you shoot; more power is not better, and crowded city bands drop more often.
  • Redundancy and monitoring: at least two channels or two systems; onboard recording and receiver monitoring are what make a backup.
  • Batteries and connectors: confirm battery type, runtime and locking connectors; a dead battery or loose plug is worse than average sound.

On set

Scan frequencies for two minutes and pick a clean band. Hide the transmitter at the back waist and record a 32-bit backup.

Do this

Wireless lavs need a frequency scan and a backup track; the set gives no second chance.

  1. Scan for two minutes and pick a clean frequency.
  2. Hide the transmitter at the lower back with the cable inside clothing.
  3. Record a 32-bit backup track.

Avoid

Do not record on the factory frequency; one interference hit ruins the whole take.

Check

  • A two-minute scan logs a clean frequency.
  • The transmitter sits at the lower back with no visible cable.
  • A 32-bit backup track exists and works independently.

en.title: Field Recorder: 32-Bit Is Not Magic
en.summary: 32-bit float can rescue clipping, not dialogue eaten by wind; mic and placement still come first.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Field Recorder: 32-Bit Is Not Magic

Tools / Capability card

Field Recorder: 32-Bit Is Not Magic

32-bit float can rescue clipping, not dialogue eaten by wind; mic and placement still come first.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

If one camera input is enough and sound is controlled, a separate recorder adds a sync step; solve mic distance and camera preamp first. Do not hide missing monitoring behind more gear.

What to compare first

  • Channels and preamps: how many independent inputs, phantom power and gain range; preamp noise matters more than a 32-bit claim.
  • Limits of 32-bit: it rescues a clipped peak, not a missing lav, a stopped record or wind in the capsule; still watch levels and monitor.
  • Media and power: card type, dual-card backup, battery runtime and external power; a card change must not stop recording.

On set

Record a quiet line with peaks at -12 dB, then clip it on purpose and see whether 32-bit float recovers it.

Do this

32-bit float can rescue clipping but not dialogue eaten by wind; microphone and position still come first.

  1. Record quiet dialogue with peaks at -12 dB.
  2. Deliberately clip once and see whether 32-bit recovers it.
  3. Test wind and confirm float cannot rescue it; do not treat it as insurance.

Avoid

Do not treat 32-bit as universal insurance; it cannot save wind noise or bad placement.

Check

  • Quiet dialogue peaks near -12 dB with audible noise floor.
  • Deliberate clipping is recovered to intelligibility in 32-bit.
  • A wind test proves float cannot rescue wind-eaten dialogue.

en.summary: Monitoring headphones must be closed, sealed, and honest; consumer cans are color grading with eyes shut.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Monitoring Headphones: Closed, Sealed, Honest

Tools / Capability card

Monitoring Headphones: Closed, Sealed, Honest

Monitoring headphones must be closed, sealed, and honest; consumer cans are color grading with eyes shut.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Headphones alone do not judge audio quality; they do not replace meters and a room test. Do not use bass-heavy consumer headphones to judge dialogue.

What to compare first

  • Closed-back and leakage: use closed-back on set so headphone sound does not enter the mic; open-back is for mixing only.
  • Impedance and sensitivity: direct from phone or camera needs low impedance and high sensitivity; high-impedance needs an amp.
  • Cable and backup: detachable cable, long cable and adapters; a broken cable on set must be replaceable.

On set

Wear closed headphones and listen to thirty seconds of room tone. If you hear your own breathing, the cups leak or the mic is too close.

Do this

Monitoring headphones must be closed, fit well, and not flatter; consumer headphones are like grading blindfolded.

  1. Wear closed headphones and listen to thirty seconds of ambience.
  2. If you hear your own breathing, the cups leak or the mic is too close.
  3. Refit the ear pads and listen again.

Avoid

Do not monitor on noise-canceling Bluetooth headphones; they flatter noise floor and sibilance.

Check

  • Monitoring uses closed-back headphones, not consumer Bluetooth.
  • Thirty seconds of ambience contains no own breathing or cup leak.
  • The seal holds and noise judgment stays stable when you move.

en.title: Timecode: Sync Without Guessing
en.summary: Timecode syncs cameras and recorders in the first minute of post; without it, sync is luck.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Timecode: Sync Without Guessing

Tools / Capability card

Timecode: Sync Without Guessing

Timecode syncs cameras and recorders in the first minute of post; without it, sync is luck.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For one camera, short clips or easy manual alignment in post, timecode is unnecessary. More devices make the sync chain more fragile.

What to compare first

  • Sync method: confirm jam sync, wireless sync or audio timecode; different cameras support different modes.
  • Drift: record 30 minutes and compare again; syncing only at start is not a test.
  • Backup: timecode does not replace a clap; cameras without timecode still need manual sync.

Multi-camera sync: jam before the shoot, compare after wrap

Timecode is not “set once.” Jam sync before the first take and compare before wrap; battery changes and sleep can drift.

  1. Choose one master camera and jam the others; log the jam time.
  2. Each camera films a clap or hand clap with timecode as a backup sync point.
  3. Before wrap, compare head and tail timecode. If drift exceeds one frame, align by clap in post, not by timecode.

Acceptance: put all cameras on one timeline and pick a random action; frame offset should be one frame or less. More means drift.

On set

Jam the recorder and camera to the same timecode and shoot ten seconds. Sync in post and check for less than one frame of drift.

Do this

Timecode aligns multicamera and recorder in the first minute of post; without it, syncing is luck.

  1. Jam the recorder and camera to the same timecode.
  2. Shoot a ten-second test.
  3. Sync in post and check drift under one frame.

Avoid

Do not jam once and shoot all day; drift shows up in the afternoon.

Check

  • Recorder and camera display the same timecode.
  • The ten-second test syncs under one frame in post.
  • A second jam is logged mid-shoot, not only one at the start.

en.title: Audio Interface: Inputs and Gain
en.summary: Check input count, gain range, and noise floor; a expensive interface with low gain cannot record a whisper.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Audio Interface: Inputs and Gain

Tools / Capability card

Audio Interface: Inputs and Gain

Check input count, gain range, and noise floor; a expensive interface with low gain cannot record a whisper.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

If you only need one lav into a camera, an interface is an extra link; solve mic distance and gain first. Do not replace recording basics with more boxes.

What to compare first

  • Inputs and gain: confirm the preamp has enough gain for your mic and the noise floor at maximum is acceptable.
  • Channels and monitoring: how many independent inputs, direct monitoring and headphone output; live work also needs a return.
  • Connection and power: is USB bus power stable, or does it need a supply? Will a long cable add noise?

On set

Connect a dynamic mic at 70 percent gain and record thirty seconds of silence. Listen to the noise floor and check the maximum gain.

Do this

An audio interface is judged by input count, gain range, and noise floor; a pricey box with too little gain cannot record quiet speech.

  1. Connect a dynamic mic and set gain to 70 percent.
  2. Record thirty seconds of silence and listen to the noise floor.
  3. Check whether maximum gain is enough for quiet dialogue.

Avoid

Do not count inputs only; without gain, quiet dialogue is all noise floor.

Check

  • A dynamic mic records thirty seconds of silence at 70 percent gain.
  • The noise floor is described, not just “fine.”
  • Maximum gain captures quiet dialogue with acceptable noise.

Failures

Three common failures all come from interface specs that never met the room:

  • 1. Trusting “24-bit / 192 kHz” without measuring the noise floor at maximum gain; quiet dialogue turns into hiss.
  • 2. Running a high-current condenser mic from USB bus power; the interface drops out or produces periodic crackle halfway through a take.
  • 3. Treating headphone monitoring as record monitoring and never watching input level; playback reveals a clipped left channel.

Extend

10-minute drill: connect a dynamic mic, start at 30 percent gain, and record thirty seconds of silence at each step while noting the noise floor. Raise gain until quiet dialogue one metre away is intelligible. With the same headphones, pick the highest step with acceptable noise and no clipping, and write it into the recording note.

en.summary: Check payload and head before max height; camera, lens, and accessories weigh more than the spec.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Tripod: Load and Head

Tools / Capability card

Tripod: Load and Head

Check payload and head before max height; camera, lens, and accessories weigh more than the spec.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For fast movement, tight spaces or low angles, a monopod, tabletop rig or gimbal beats a tripod. Do not trade “can shoot it” for “steady.”

What to compare first

  • Payload: calculate body, lens, battery, monitor and head, with at least 30% headroom.
  • Height and stability: do not buy by maximum height; raising it amplifies shake, test at your working height.
  • Legs and head: test leg locks, leveling and head return; a sandbag hook is more useful than a spec.

On set

Mount the body, lens, monitor, and battery and lock the head. Push it three times and check the legs and head for spring.

Do this

A tripod is judged by payload and head, not maximum height; body, lens, and accessories usually weigh more than the rating.

  1. Mount body, lens, monitor, and batteries.
  2. Lock the head and push three times.
  3. Check whether legs and head rebound.

Avoid

Do not size the tripod to a bare body; with lens and batteries the payload may already be over.

Check

  • Full rig weight is measured against the tripod rating.
  • Three pushes with the head locked show no leg slip or rebound.
  • Maximum height is not the main reason to buy; stability comes first.
