en.title: Fluid Head: Pan and Tilt Need Drag
en.summary: A fluid head is about drag: starts and stops must be smooth, not snappy.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Fluid Head: Pan and Tilt Need Drag

Tools / Capability card

Fluid Head: Pan and Tilt Need Drag

A fluid head is about drag: starts and stops must be smooth, not snappy.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For fast following, tight spaces or long handheld work, a fluid head is worse than a gimbal or body support. It is not a universal answer for “more stable.”

What to compare first

  • Payload and center of gravity: choose by the full rig, not the bare body; a long lens moves the center forward and needs more tilt range.
  • Counterbalance: let go at your working tilt angle; the head should hold or return slowly, not slam down.
  • Drag and locks: pan and tilt drag adjust separately, locks do not drift, and the plate returns to a repeatable position.

On set

Mount the full rig and set the drag. Do a three-second start, five-second pan, and three-second stop; check for a jerk.

Do this

A fluid head's value is damping: starts and stops must be smooth, not flying at a touch.

  1. Mount the full rig and set damping.
  2. Do a three-second start, five-second pan, three-second stop.
  3. Play back and check for jerks at start and stop.

Avoid

Do not back damping all the way out; a touch sends it flying and ruins starts and stops.

Check

  • A 3-5-3 second start-pan-stop runs with the full rig.
  • Playback shows no sudden jerk at start or stop.
  • Damping settings are logged and reproducible at a new position.

en.title: Gimbal: Balance Before Power
en.summary: Balance the gimbal before powering up; motors fighting imbalance cause shake and battery drain.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Gimbal: Balance Before Power

Tools / Capability card

Gimbal: Balance Before Power

Balance the gimbal before powering up; motors fighting imbalance cause shake and battery drain.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For locked-off shots, long lenses or repeatable motion, a tripod and slider beat a gimbal. Do not trade “can walk” for “can hold.”

What to compare first

  • Payload and balance: calculate the full rig; lens length changes tilt balance, and a payload rating is not a promise of balance.
  • Axis locks and plate: three axes lock and the plate returns repeatably; otherwise every lens change means rebalancing.
  • Follow and latency: check follow speed, deadband and motor noise; too responsive chases footsteps, too slow loses the subject.

On set

Balance all three axes and listen for motor noise. Walk ten meters straight and check for vertical bounce.

Do this

A gimbal must be balanced before power-on; motors constantly correcting imbalance cause shake and drain battery.

  1. Balance all three axes and listen for motor noise at power-on.
  2. Walk a ten-meter straight line.
  3. Play back and check vertical bounce.

Avoid

Do not let motors correct imbalance; constant effort makes the image shakier.

Check

  • Three axes balance and motors do not hum constantly at power-on.
  • A ten-meter walk shows no vertical bounce.
  • Footage exists before and after balancing for comparison.

en.summary: A slider exposes its start and stop; ease in, move evenly, ease out, and keep wheel noise off dialogue.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Slider: Start and Stop Quietly

Tools / Capability card

Slider: Start and Stop Quietly

A slider exposes its start and stop; ease in, move evenly, ease out, and keep wheel noise off dialogue.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For long distance, speed or uneven ground, a gimbal or vehicle rig beats a slider. Do not spend half an hour building a rail for one pan.

What to compare first

  • Length and payload: choose by the heaviest rig; longer rails are harder to level. Confirm the shot distance, do not buy the longest.
  • Start, stop and friction: it should start evenly and stop without shake; too much or too little drag makes the move look wrong.
  • Noise and setup: joints, wheels and legs must be quiet; on an interior dialogue scene, slider noise gets recorded.

On set

Put a cup of water on the slider and start and stop slowly. Listen for wheel noise; if it reaches dialogue, add a towel or silent wheels.

Do this

A slider exposes starts and stops; ease in, travel evenly, ease out, and keep wheel noise out of dialogue.

  1. Put a cup of water on the slider and start and stop slowly.
  2. Play back for wheel noise.
  3. If it reaches dialogue, lay a towel or switch to silent wheels.

Avoid

Do not shove the slider with your wrist; a sharp start moves both cup and frame.

Check

  • The cup test shows no spill or visible jolt at start and stop.
  • Playback reveals whether wheel noise reaches dialogue.
  • A towel or silent wheels are used with a comparison when noise exists.

en.title: Field Monitor: Brightness, Scopes, LUT
en.summary: A field monitor needs brightness, scopes, and LUT support; a pretty screen does not mean correct footage.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Field Monitor: Brightness, Scopes, LUT

Tools / Capability card

Field Monitor: Brightness, Scopes, LUT

A field monitor needs brightness, scopes, and LUT support; a pretty screen does not mean correct footage.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

If the delivery only needs the camera screen, do not add a monitor for “professional look.” It adds weight, cables and another power failure point.

What to compare first

  • Brightness: ask whether it is readable outdoors before resolution; 500–1000 nits is the divide, and a hood is still needed.
  • LUT and scopes: can it load a monitoring LUT and show waveform, zebra or false color? Do not judge by “pretty color” alone.
  • Latency and power: check HDMI/SDI delay, battery type and hot-swap support; losing monitoring is more common than losing recording.

On-set monitor: brightness, waveform, LUT — three checks

A monitor is not “brighter is better.” Set it to standard brightness first, then judge waveform and LUT. Otherwise you are grading the monitor, not the image.

  1. Brightness: use a built-in grayscale or hood; set it so 5% and 10% black are distinct. “Looks comfortable” is not a setting.
  2. Waveform: use it for midtones. When monitor and waveform disagree, trust the waveform.
  3. LUT: use the on-set LUT for style, not exposure. Judge exposure on the log waveform.

Acceptance: play the same clip on the monitor and the computer; brightness and skin should not differ a stop. If they do, calibrate the monitor.

On set

Set the monitor to 800 nits outdoors and load the LUT. Shoot a grey card and compare the waveform and skin with the monitor.

Do this

A field monitor is judged by brightness, waveform, and LUT; a pretty screen does not mean correct footage.

  1. Set 800 nits outdoors and load the LUT.
  2. Shoot a gray card.
  3. Check waveform and skin against the monitor.

Avoid

Do not trust a pretty monitor image; without waveform, brightness and color can lie.

Check

  • Outdoor brightness reaches 800 nits and stays readable.
  • The LUT is loaded and the gray card has a waveform reading.
  • Skin judgment matches waveform, not eye alone.

en.summary: Test latency and interference before sending to director or focus puller; a dropped signal stops the set.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Wireless Video: Latency and Interference

Tools / Capability card

Wireless Video: Latency and Interference

Test latency and interference before sending to director or focus puller; a dropped signal stops the set.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For critical live, long range or heavy RF, prefer wired or local recording; wireless video is convenience, not a reliability guarantee.

What to compare first

  • Latency: confirm end-to-end delay, not the “low latency” ad; follow focus and live broadcast have different limits.
  • Band and interference: check available bands, frequency hopping and antennas; on-site Wi-Fi and crowds compete.
  • Power and backup: both transmitter and receiver must hot-swap batteries; without a wired backup, do not use it for a critical live show.

On set

Walk the set and test latency and dropouts. Give the director and the focus puller separate signals; do not share one.

Do this

Wireless video needs latency and interference tests before deciding director or focus use; a dropout stops the set.

  1. Walk the set and measure latency and dropouts.
  2. Keep director and focus signals separate.
  3. Log dropout spots and add antennas or change channels.

Avoid

Do not share one wireless link between director and focus; one dropout stops both.

Check

  • Latency and dropouts are logged across the set.
  • Director and focus monitoring use two separate links.
  • Dropout spots have a response, such as antennas or channel change.

en.html:
Home/Tools/Video Assist: Playback on Set

Tools / Capability card

Video Assist: Playback on Set

Video assist handles playback, marks, and backup; instant review speeds the whole set.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

On a small crew with one camera and the director beside the monitor, a video assistant is an extra role; solve monitor position and communication first.

What to compare first

  • Latency and playback: confirm camera-to-monitor delay and instant playback; a three-second wait breaks the director's rhythm.
  • LUT and recording: LUT support, clean feed and backup recording; a pretty image is not enough.
  • Power and cable: long runs and strain relief; a loose connector is more common than a missing feature.

On set

Mark every take good or bad with scene and shot number, and back up the card so the director can replay without waiting.

Do this

Video assist handles playback, marking, and backup; when the director can see the last take immediately, the set moves faster.

  1. Mark good, bad, scene, and shot for every take.
  2. Back up the card.
  3. Playback reaches the right take without waiting.

Avoid

Do not back up without marking; when the director asks for playback, the set waits while you search.

Check

  • Every take carries good/bad, scene, and shot marks.
  • Cards are backed up between takes with verification.
  • A requested take plays within thirty seconds.

en.title: Scope Monitor: Exposure and Color Together
en.summary: A scope monitor shows exposure and color together; a histogram alone misses skin drift.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Scope Monitor: Exposure and Color Together

Tools / Capability card

Scope Monitor: Exposure and Color Together

A scope monitor shows exposure and color together; a histogram alone misses skin drift.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

A scope reads signal, not composition or performance. Treating the waveform as the only proof of “correct exposure” protects highlights while leaving the face without direction.

What to compare first

  • Waveform and vector: it must show luma waveform and vectorscope together; a histogram alone cannot judge skin or black level.
  • Inputs and zoom: confirm 3G/6G/12G SDI or HDMI version, and whether it can magnify a critical area to 1:1 pixels.
  • Power and brightness: it must run from mains or long batteries on set; screen brightness must survive exteriors, not only a dark room.

On set

Switch the scope to waveform and vectorscope and shoot a grey card. Black at 0, white at 100, skin line on target.

Do this

A scope monitor shows exposure and color together; a histogram alone misses skin shift.

  1. Switch the scope to waveform and vectorscope.
  2. Shoot a gray card.
  3. Black at 0, white at 100, skin on the target line.

Avoid

Do not read the histogram alone; skin can go green while the histogram looks perfect.

Check

  • Both waveform and vectorscope are used.
  • Gray card reads black at 0 and white at 100.
  • Skin sits near the target line and any shift is named.

en.title: CFexpress: Speed and Heat
en.summary: Check sustained write and heat, not peak speed; on long takes, thermal throttling hurts before capacity.
en.html:
Home/Tools/CFexpress: Speed and Heat

Tools / Capability card

CFexpress: Speed and Heat

Check sustained write and heat, not peak speed; on long takes, thermal throttling hurts before capacity.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For low-bitrate stills or short clips, do not pay for the fastest spec. Once the card exceeds the camera's write ceiling, extra speed does not become image quality.

What to compare first

  • Sustained write: look at sustained, not peak; a card that throttles after a few minutes will stop a long take.
  • Heat: cards and readers get hot; a reader that slows or disconnects during a long copy lacks cooling.
  • Capacity and backup: calculate from one day's footage and dual-card backup, not the advertised “record time.”

When not to use it

For low-bitrate stills or short clips, do not pay for the fastest spec. Once the card exceeds the camera's write ceiling, extra speed does not become image quality.

On set

Record ten minutes at the highest bitrate and feel the card temperature. Copy to an SSD and measure sustained write speed.

Do this

CFexpress cards are judged by sustained write and heat, not peak speed; on long takes, thermal throttling hurts more than capacity.

  1. Record ten minutes at maximum bitrate and feel the card temperature.
  2. Copy to SSD and measure sustained write for a drop.
  3. If it drops, change card or lower bitrate.

Avoid

Do not trust peak write; thermal throttling after ten minutes breaks long takes.

Check

  • A ten-minute maximum-bitrate take completes and card temperature is logged.
  • Sustained copy to SSD shows no sharp drop.
  • A card change or bitrate reduction is prepared if it drops.

With one array and no offline backup, do not make it the only media library. RAID solves speed or a single-drive failure, not “the whole project disappeared.”

Separate RAID from backup

  • RAID 0: speed stacks, risk stacks; one drive failure can make the whole set unreadable. Use it only for regenerable cache.
  • RAID 1/5/6: redundancy is still not backup; a controller failure, deletion or ransomware hits the whole array.
  • Interface and cooling: confirm Thunderbolt/USB version, sustained write and cooling; a hot editing array throttles.

On set

Use RAID 0 only for working media and keep a RAID 1 or NAS as backup. Run a full-disk test and watch for slowdown.

Do this

SSD RAID is a editing work disk, not an archive; when the array dies, rebuilding costs more than backup.

  1. Build RAID 0 for working media only.
  2. Set RAID 1 or NAS for backup.
  3. Fill the drive and measure the speed drop.

Avoid

Do not make RAID 0 the only storage; one drive failure takes all media.

Three causes

For “SSD RAID: Edit Array, Not Archive”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
RAID 0 as the only copyOne drive fails and all footage is goneUse RAID 0 as a working disk, never as backup
Interface too slowUSB 10Gbps cannot feed a multi-drive arrayMatch host port and cable
Poor coolingSustained writes throttle and the edit stuttersRun a thirty-minute sustained write test

On-set diagnosis

  1. Measure sustained read/write with AJA or Blackmagic, not peak burst only.
  2. Write for thirty minutes and log speed, temperature and dropout.
  3. Confirm an independent backup exists and a restore has been rehearsed.

Fix

RAID is an availability and speed tool, not a backup. Secure one independent copy before discussing an array.

  1. Use a two-drive RAID 0 as the working disk and a separate drive/NAS as backup.
  2. Use 10Gbps or faster; match cable and expansion card.
  3. Leave cooling space around the array; do not stack drives.
  4. Rehearse a restore monthly with a random file.

Failure cases

With “SSD RAID: Edit Array, Not Archive”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Keep the only footage on RAID 0One drive failure loses everythingIndependent backup
Judge peak speedSustained writes drop and the edit stallsThirty-minute test
Use a USB hubBandwidth is shared and speed halvesConnect directly

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
Sustained writeThirty minutes at twice the project bitrateSpeed log
BackupAt least one independent copyBackup list
RestoreA random file restoresDrill log
TemperatureNo thermal throttling under sustained writeTouch/sensor

One line for the set

RAID 0 is for speed; backup is for survival. They are not the same job.

Check

  • RAID 0 holds working media only and originals are backed up elsewhere.
  • A RAID 1 or NAS backup job runs.
  • A full-drive test logs the write-speed drop.

en.summary: NAS shares media, so set naming, permissions, and trash rules first; otherwise sharing means overwriting.
en.html:
Home/Tools/NAS: Shared Storage, Shared Rules

Tools / Capability card

NAS: Shared Storage, Shared Rules

NAS shares media, so set naming, permissions, and trash rules first; otherwise sharing means overwriting.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For one person and one project, power and management cost exceed a direct SSD. Do not buy complex storage early for a “team” feeling.

What to compare first

  • Bays and redundancy: at least two bays in mirror; a single-drive NAS is not backup, only a network disk.
  • Network: gigabit is enough for a small team; multicam editing needs 2.5G/10G NICs, switches and cabling.
  • Recovery: confirm rebuild after a failed drive and readability of old disks; RAID without a restore drill is reassurance only.

A NAS is a collaboration drive, not the only backup

A NAS solves sharing and versions, not fire, accidental deletion or ransomware. With a team NAS, add at least one offline drive and one offsite copy.

  1. Permissions by project: editors read/write, clients read-only; remove departing staff the same day.
  2. Enable snapshots for 7–30 days. Check a snapshot before deleting; do not empty the recycle bin first.
  3. Use at least 2.5GbE for multi-track editing; gigabit is enough for proxies only.

Acceptance: restore last week's version from a snapshot; unplug the NAS and confirm an offline copy opens. Both must pass before you call it a backup.

On set

Create user groups, read-only permissions, and a recycle bin. Have two people write the same file and test the conflict warning.

Do this

NAS shares media across the team, but naming, permissions, and recycle rules come first; otherwise sharing means overwriting.

  1. Create user groups and read-only permissions.
  2. Enable the recycle bin.
  3. Have two people write the same file and test the conflict warning.

Avoid

Do not give everyone read-write; two simultaneous edits erase a version.

Check

  • Groups and read-only permissions are set, not open write for all.
  • The recycle bin is on and deleted files are recoverable.
  • A two-writer test produces a conflict warning or lock.

en.summary: LTO is for cold archive, not same-day editing; calculate restore time before cost per TB.
en.html:
Home/Tools/LTO Archive: Cold, Cheap, Slow

Tools / Capability card

LTO Archive: Cold, Cheap, Slow

LTO is for cold archive, not same-day editing; calculate restore time before cost per TB.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For random access, frequent edits or projects under 10TB, LTO is not economical. Use drives plus cold cloud first; move to tape when the archive really grows.

What to compare first

  • Generation compatibility: confirm which LTO generation the drive and tapes read and write; a new drive usually reads one generation back, never forward.
  • Software and index: LTO without a catalog and checksums is just a tape; a restore needs to know which volume and partition holds the file.
  • Environment and rotation: tape dislikes humidity, dust and temperature swings; keep at least two copies off-site and plan migration to new media.

On set

Calculate restore time: how long to copy 1 TB from LTO to disk. If it exceeds the project window, do not use it as a working drive.

Do this

LTO suits long-term cold archive, not same-day editing; calculate restore time before cost per TB.

  1. Time a 1 TB restore from LTO to disk.
  2. If it exceeds the project cycle, it cannot be a work disk.
  3. Then calculate cost per TB and storage conditions.

Avoid

Do not use LTO as an editing disk; a 1 TB restore takes hours and today's cut will not finish.

Check

  • A 1 TB restore is timed.
  • Restore time is compared with the project cycle and a conclusion is stated.
  • Cost per TB and storage conditions are recorded.

en.summary: Nodes are not filter stacks; one node does one job, and disabling it reveals its effect.
en.html:
Home/Tools/DaVinci Nodes: Nodes Are Not Filters

Tools / Capability card

DaVinci Nodes: Nodes Are Not Filters

Nodes are not filter stacks; one node does one job, and disabling it reveals its effect.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

If the problem is camera white balance, exposure or lighting, more nodes only make it dirtier. Go back to the source before grading.

Basic node order

  • Balance then style: primary correction first, LUT and look later; reversing the order locks a cast into the LUT.
  • Local last: windows, tracking and local grades come after the global grade; local first breaks the overall relationship.
  • Cache and versions: more nodes cost performance; name key versions, do not rely on undo.

On set

Build five nodes: exposure, white balance, contrast, look, and output. Toggle each one to see its job; do not stack twenty.

Do this

Nodes are not a filter stack; each node does one job, and turning it off reveals what it did.

  1. Build five nodes: exposure, white balance, contrast, look, output.
  2. Toggle each node and watch the change.
  3. Do not stack twenty and lose track of the cause.

Avoid

Do not stack twenty nodes; when something breaks, you cannot tell which to disable.

Check

  • Five nodes each do one job with clear names.
  • Toggling each shows its specific change.
  • No more than ten nodes, and problems map to one node.

Tools / Capability card

AI Video Tool: Controllability First

Check controllability: can it lock character, camera, duration? Demo reels lie.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For real people, news scenes, precise dialogue or accountable footage, generation cannot replace live action. Shots without a rights chain do not enter delivery.

Control before demo

  • Shot control: can you specify size, angle, lens and motion? A tool that only offers “generate again” is not for paid work.
  • Consistency: character, wardrobe, light and set across shots; test three shots before batching.
  • Rights and output: commercial license, resolution, watermark and metadata; do not discover limits at delivery.

On set

Test one prompt for three things: character consistency, camera control, and usable duration. Pay only after all three pass.

Do this

An AI video tool is judged by control: can it lock character, camera, and duration; demo reels lie.

  1. Use one prompt to test character consistency, camera control, and duration.
  2. Pay only after all three pass.
  3. Save the failure cases too.

Avoid

Do not be fooled by demo reels; they show success, not character drift.

Check

  • The same prompt keeps the character consistent across three shots.
  • Camera motion and duration respond to specific controls.
  • Failure cases are saved and the boundary is known.

en.html:
Home/Tools/AI Audio Tool: Rights and Quality

Tools / Capability card

AI Audio Tool: Rights and Quality

Check rights and audio quality before features; a cloned voice's license matters more than timbre.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

News, documentary, testimony and real-person endorsement must not replace the original voice with a clone. Unlicensed voice does not enter delivery.

What to compare first

  • Rights: commercial license, voice-clone scope and output ownership; do not stop at “commercial use,” read the full terms.
  • Quality: test Chinese, English, numbers, names and emotional lines; a demo is not enough, use your own script.
  • Control: can it import your recording and control pauses and stress? A voice you cannot control does not enter dialogue editing.

On set

Have the tool read thirty seconds of dialogue and listen for sibilance, phrasing, and endings. Then check commercial rights and clone scope.

Do this

An AI audio tool is judged by license and quality before features; clone scope matters more than timbre.

  1. Have it read a thirty-second line.
  2. Listen for sibilance, pauses, and tails.
  3. Then check commercial license and clone scope.

Avoid

Do not judge timbre alone; a personal-use license still blocks commercial work.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Voltage, plug, warranty, import duty and radio certification differ by market; check the local spec sheet before ordering gear or batteries.

Check

  • Sibilance, pauses, and tails are assessed on a thirty-second line.
  • Commercial license and clone scope have written terms.
  • Output clears the current project without extra licensing.

Home/Tools/Cloud Render: Cost and Transfer

Tools / Capability card

Cloud Render: Cost and Transfer

Calculate upload time and output cost; with big media, upload is slower than render.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

With small media, short renders and a team in one city, a local machine is faster. Cloud rendering is for peak queues and temporary capacity, not a replacement for daily editing.

Do three calculations

  • Upload: total media times upstream bandwidth is often longer than the render; test real upload, not the plan's claim.
  • Render: priced by frame, node minute or GPU hour; run one ten-second test shot to get the real unit cost.
  • Download and rerun: failures, versions and final download all count; first-pass pricing underestimates.

On set

Upload 10 GB as a test and calculate the transfer time. Render 100 frames and compare local and cloud cost.

Do this

Cloud rendering starts with upload time and cost per frame; large media uploads slower than it renders.

  1. Upload 10 GB as a test and calculate upload time.
  2. Render 100 frames and compare local versus cloud cost.
  3. If upload exceeds render time, do not go cloud.

Avoid

Do not look at price per frame alone; uploading 10 GB can take longer than rendering.

Check

  • A 10 GB upload is timed.
  • Local and cloud costs are compared over 100 frames.
  • Upload time is compared with render time and a conclusion is stated.

Cap the lens, turn off all light, and black-balance at the shooting frame rate, shutter and gain. A balance made at other settings does not carry over. Shoot a black frame and zoom in for fixed bright dots or color patches.

Black balance in full dark, same settings

Redo after sensor temperature changes; on long shoots, warm up ten minutes first.

Limits

Black balance cannot fix dead pixels. Fixed dots are a sensor issue; black balance only suppresses dark current. Dead pixels need mapping or post.

On set

Cap the lens and run the camera's black balance. Shoot a dark area and check whether noise drops.

Do this

Camera black balance follows the manufacturer's procedure; do not call noise a style. Clean shadows give post room.

  1. Cap the lens and run black balance from the menu.
  2. Shoot a dark area afterward.
  3. Compare noise before and after to confirm cleanup.

Avoid

Do not skip black balance after conditions change; shadow noise drifts with temperature.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Black balance completes per the menu with the lens capped.
  • 2. Dark-area footage exists before and after for comparison.
  • 3. Shadow noise drops visibly instead of being kept as style.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Black balance completes per the menu with the…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Dark-area footage exists before and after for…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not skip black balance after conditions change; shadow noise drifts with temperature.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Cap the lens and run black balance from”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Black balance completes per the menu with the lens capped.
  • Dark-area footage exists before and after for comparison.
  • Shadow noise drops visibly instead of being kept as style.

Tools / Tutorial

Gray Card White Balance: Mixed Light

A gray card neutralizes mixed light; place it where the subject stands before reading.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

White balance is not clicking on sky or a white wall. Place the card at the face position, facing camera, in the same light as the subject. Under mixed light it represents one direction only.

Put the gray card where the subject is lit

Shoot one per light position or color temperature; calibrate in post, then fine-tune skin.

Limits

A gray card cannot turn two temperatures into one. With cool window and warm lamp, decide which to keep, then unify with fill or gel.

On set

Place the grey card where the subject stands and let the light hit it. Set manual white balance, then shoot and check skin.

Do this

Gray-card white balance solves neutrality under mixed light; put the card where the subject stands, then read it.

  1. Place the gray card at the subject position with light falling on it.

en.title: Follow Focus Practice: Mark, Watch, Breathe
en.summary: Three steps: mark the barrel, watch the chest, and keep breathing steady.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Follow Focus Practice: Mark, Watch, Breathe

Tools / Tutorial

Follow Focus Practice: Mark, Watch, Breathe

Three steps: mark the barrel, watch the chest, and keep breathing steady.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Start at a fixed distance: the subject walks a straight line while you only breathe and micro-adjust the wrist. Shoot ten seconds, play back and check whether focus stays on the eye, not whether the frame is steady.

Practice not losing focus before making it pretty

Then add curves and occlusion, changing one variable at a time. Three consecutive passes on the eye means the position is cleared.

Limits

One autofocus hit is not mastery. Manual follow focus is judged across the whole take; half a second lost is a wasted shot in the edit.

Follow focus in three steps: marks, rehearsal, edges

Follow focus is not “turn by feel.” Mark A/B focus positions on the floor, rehearse the walk, then judge the edge of the monitor, not the center.

  1. Mark start, middle and end with chalk or tape; each point maps to a lens mark.
  2. Rehearse by hand, watching the image, not the scale. On the take, trim by the marks.
  3. Watch edges: eyes and hairline tell the truth. The center can look sharp while the edge is soft.

Acceptance: shoot three takes and inspect a frame at 100%. Two of three should have sharp eyes; if not, stop down a stop or shorten the walk.

On set

Mark one, two, and three meters and have an assistant walk 1-2-3-2-1. Practice ten passes with less than five centimeters of focus error.

Do this

Follow-focus practice has three steps: make marks, watch the chest, and keep breathing from shaking the hand.

  1. Mark one, two, and three meters.
  2. Have the assistant walk 1-2-3-2-1.
  3. Do ten reps with focus error under five centimeters.

Avoid

Do not chase the mouth; it turns, while the chest does not disappear.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. One, two, and three meters are marked and walked 1-2-3-2-1.
  • 2. At least eight of ten reps stay within five centimeters.
  • 3. Focus follows the chest, not the mouth.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“One, two, and three meters are marked and walk…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“At least eight of ten reps stay within five ce…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not chase the mouth; it turns, while the chest does not disappear.

Extend

Check

  • At least eight of ten reps stay within five centimeters.
  • Focus follows the chest, not the mouth.

en.title: Handheld Brace: Three Contact Points
en.summary: Find three contact points: chest, shoulder, elbow; three points stabilize the frame.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Handheld Brace: Three Contact Points

Tools / Tutorial

Handheld Brace: Three Contact Points

Find three contact points: chest, shoulder, elbow; three points stabilize the frame.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Two hands on the camera, elbows against ribs, viewfinder to brow, feet shoulder-width, knees soft. Walk heel-first and move the body with the camera; do not let the arms swing alone.

Lock the elbows before discussing breath

Wide is steadier than long. With a long lens, brace on a wall, table or knee rather than muscle.

Limits

Handheld is not “as stable as possible.” A frozen frame looks like a tripod and loses presence; keep some breath, but no vertical bouncing.

Three contact points for handheld

Handheld instability is usually not arm strength; it is the absence of a triangle. Tuck both elbows against the ribs, rest the camera on the chest, and tension the strap as the third point.

  1. Feet shoulder-width, knees soft. When moving, step first and let the body follow; do not swing from the waist.
  2. Hold your breath for the first 3–5 seconds, not the whole take; breathe between actions on a long shot.
  3. Wide is steadier than long. Without stabilization, stay under 35mm and at 1/50 or faster.

Acceptance: shoot a 10-second locked subject and check the edges for breathing. If the frame jumps, check the third contact point before buying a gimbal.

On set

Use three contact points: the chest against the body, elbows into the ribs, the left hand under the lens. Hold ten seconds and check the breathing.

Do this

Handheld support finds three contact points: chest, shoulder, elbow; three points steady the frame.

  1. Press the chest against the camera back and tuck the elbow to the ribs.
  2. Support the lens with the left hand as the third point.
  3. Shoot ten static seconds and play back for breathing motion.

Avoid

Do not hold the camera at arm's length; two contact points fail within ten seconds.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Chest, elbow, and left hand all make contact.
  • 2. Ten static seconds show only slight breathing, no big sway.
  • 3. Arms are not extended and the center of gravity stays close.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Chest, elbow, and left hand all make contact”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Ten static seconds show only slight breathing…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not hold the camera at arm's length; two contact points fail within ten seconds.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Press the chest against the camera back and”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Chest, elbow, and left hand all make contact.
  • Ten static seconds show only slight breathing, no big sway.
  • Arms are not extended and the center of gravity stays close.

en.title: Gimbal Balance: Five Minutes Before Power
en.summary: Balance each axis with the others locked; five minutes before power saves half an hour on set.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Gimbal Balance: Five Minutes Before Power

Tools / Tutorial

Gimbal Balance: Five Minutes Before Power

Balance each axis with the others locked; five minutes before power saves half an hour on set.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Balance order: lock axes, mount camera, adjust fore-aft and left-right, check that all three axes rest at any angle. Rebalance after every lens or filter change; an unbalanced motor drains power, heats and jitters.

Power off, balance, then mount the lens

Walk a slow circle and listen for motor noise before fast follow.

Limits

Balance is not a substitute for walking. The gimbal saves only part of vertical bounce; practice heel-first, soft-knee steps.

Balance order: lock axes, then power on

Gimbal balance is not “turn it on and auto-calibrate.” Balance mechanically first, then power. Wrong order makes the motors fight and the image shake.

  1. Lock tilt, roll and pan. Adjust tilt front/back first, then roll left/right, then pan.
  2. Tilt each axis 45° by hand; the camera should stay. If it falls, move the center of gravity.
  3. Power on and auto-calibrate. Rebalance after a lens or battery change.

Acceptance: powered off, the camera should hold at any angle you release it. If it falls one way, do not let the motors hold it.

On set

Lock tilt to set roll, lock roll to set pan, and set pan last. Push the gimbal after each adjustment to check for centering.

Do this

Gimbal balance goes axis by axis, locking one before adjusting the next; five minutes before power-on saves half an hour on set.

  1. Lock pan and adjust tilt.
  2. Lock tilt and adjust roll.
  3. Finally adjust pan, nudging after each to check centering.

Avoid

Do not loosen all three axes at once; everything moves and never balances.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Axes are locked and adjusted in pan, tilt, roll order.
  • 2. Each axis returns to center after a nudge without drifting.
  • 3. Balance completes before power-on and motors do not constantly correct.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Axes are locked and adjusted in pan, tilt, rol…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Each axis returns to center after a nudge with…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not loosen all three axes at once; everything moves and never balances.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Lock pan and adjust tilt.”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Axes are locked and adjusted in pan, tilt, roll order.
  • Each axis returns to center after a nudge without drifting.
  • Balance completes before power-on and motors do not constantly correct.

Deep dive: balancing is about centre of gravity, not “level”

About 5 minutes. The three motors cancel shake; they do not hold the camera up. The goal of balancing is that the camera does not fall in any direction when the power is off and your hand is away. If the centre is off, the motors fight gravity, the image shakes, the head heats and the battery drains.

Three axes, three centres

Pitch: front-to-back. A heavier or further-forward lens makes the camera nod; move the plate until it stays put when you let go.

Roll: left-to-right. Battery, monitor and follow-focus all shift the side-to-side centre; check both sides, not one.

Yaw: up-down. The arm height sets the inverted-pendulum balance; too low is top-heavy, too high is bottom-heavy.

Two conditions, two methods

Light body + small lens (<1.5 kg): pitch first, roll second, yaw last; raise motor strength gradually, never start at maximum.

Heavy body + long lens (>2.5 kg): confirm the payload limit, support the lens, then run a 30-second power-off test to see whether it slowly tips.

Failure table

FailureWhy it happensFix first
Still shaky after balancingMotor strength too low, or the centre never actually zeroedLet go, see which way it drifts, return to that axis
Hot within a minuteOff-centre camera; motors fight gravityBalance with power off, then power on
Pitch nodsLens forward, plate too far backMove the plate 5–10 mm forward and lock it
Yaw driftsWrong arm height, or cable pullSet arm height, dress cables, run a 360° test

Ten checks

  1. With power off, the camera does not fall in pitch, roll or yaw.
  2. Let go for three seconds; the frame does not drift to either side.
  3. The plate is locked and the lens is supported.
  4. Battery, monitor and cables are mounted before balancing.
  5. Motor strength starts low; it does not lock at power-on.
  6. A 360° yaw turn does not pull or snag a cable.
  7. Thirty seconds of shooting needs no hand support and shows no low-frequency swing.
  8. A lens change triggers a fresh balance, not the old settings.
  9. You know the payload limit and do not exceed it.
  10. Motor strength is zeroed before packing, so it does not heat in transit.

Alternative

If it still shakes after balancing, do not keep raising motor strength. Use a lighter lens, add counterweight or switch to a shoulder rig. If the only option is handheld, turning the stabiliser off can be more reliable than half-stabilised footage. A gimbal is not a permit; it solves one kind of shake.

en.title: Slider Shot: Head, Body, Tail
en.summary: A slider shot needs a head, body, and tail: hold the start, move evenly, hold the end.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Slider Shot: Head, Body, Tail

Tools / Tutorial

Slider Shot: Head, Body, Tail

A slider shot needs a head, body, and tail: hold the start, move evenly, hold the end.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Ask what relationship the move reveals: foreground blocking giving way to a face, one person's back to another's face, an empty chair to a doorway. Without a change in relationship, the move is decoration.

A slider is a relationship shot, not a flourish

Ask what relationship the move reveals: foreground blocking giving way to a face, one person's back to another's face, an empty chair to a doorway. Without a change in relationship, the move is decoration.

Keep the travel 20–40 cm and slow enough to read the background; both start and end must compose on their own.

Limits

A slider is wrong for fast action and tight spaces. Uneven floors and cables cause shake; clear the path before laying track.

Slider start and stop: three frames of ease at each end

A slider looks fake when it starts and stops abruptly. For a manual move, ease in and out over three frames; for a motor, set start/stop to 10–20% of travel.

  1. Rehearse once and mark start and end. Do not look for the position after rolling.
  2. Match speed to shot length: one meter in three seconds is about 0.33m/s. Faster blurs, slower drags.
  3. Level the track with two boards on uneven ground; a tilted track tilts the frame.

Acceptance: playback for a “clunk” at the ends. If it knocks, add ease; do not fix it with warp stabilization.

On set

Hold one second at the start, move evenly for three, and hold one at the end. Watch the start and stop on the monitor; do not force it with the wrist.

Do this

A slider shot needs head, body, and tail: hold at the start, travel evenly, hold at the end.

  1. Hold one second at the start.
  2. Travel evenly for three seconds.
  3. Hold one second at the end and watch the monitor, not your wrist.

Avoid

Do not push the moment you roll; without a start hold, the editor cannot find an in-point.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Start hold, three-second travel, and end hold are timecoded.
  • 2. The monitor shows no sudden acceleration or stop.
  • 3. Movement comes from the slider, not a forced wrist.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Start hold, three-second travel, and end hold…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The monitor shows no sudden acceleration or st…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not push the moment you roll; without a start hold, the editor cannot find an in-point.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Hold one second at the start.”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Start hold, three-second travel, and end hold are timecoded.
  • The monitor shows no sudden acceleration or stop.
  • Movement comes from the slider, not a forced wrist.

en.title: Boom Swing: Follow the Chest
en.summary: Follow the chest, not the mouth; the mouth turns, the chest stays in range.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Boom Swing: Follow the Chest

Tools / Tutorial

Boom Swing: Follow the Chest

Follow the chest, not the mouth; the mouth turns, the chest stays in range.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

The operator must know where the actor goes next: watch rehearsal, listen for cues, track feet. Keep the tip 40–60 cm above and ahead, out of the shadow; move around outside frame, never across the head.

The boom follows action without crossing frame

Record a boom test before each setup to confirm it clears lamps and bounce boards.

Limits

Closer is not better. Too close captures breath and cloth; too far sounds empty. Protect the line before hiding the pole.

The boom follows lines, not bodies

The boom keeps the mic above the mouth; it does not chase the actor. Block the scene, mark the head position for each line, then plan the pole move.

  1. Keep the tip above frame and 30–60cm from the mouth. Too far is thin; too close enters frame.
  2. Move between lines, not during them. When the actor walks, reposition in the pause.
  3. Wear headphones and listen for clipping and wind. Use a windshield; do not rely on post denoise.

Acceptance: playback for level jumps and pole shadows. If they appear, fix blocking or pole position before compression.

On set

Keep the boom tip on the actor's chest at forty to sixty centimeters. When they turn, leave the tip above and outside the frame.

Do this

The boom follows the actor's chest, not the mouth; the mouth turns, the chest does not vanish.

  1. Track the boom head to the chest.
  2. Keep forty to sixty centimeters away.
  3. When the actor turns, keep the head above frame.

Avoid

Do not chase the mouth with the boom; one head turn brings it into frame.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The boom follows the chest, not the mouth.
  • 2. Distance stays between forty and sixty centimeters.
  • 3. On a turn, the boom head stays out of frame.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The boom follows the chest, not the mouth”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Distance stays between forty and sixty centime…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not chase the mouth with the boom; one head turn brings it into frame.

Extend

Check

en.html:
Home/Tools/Lav Hiding: Collar, Hair, Tape

Tools / Tutorial

Lav Hiding: Collar, Hair, Tape

Try collar, then hair, then medical tape; every wardrobe change needs a new hide.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

The enemy is cloth friction and muffling. Anchor the capsule inside a collar, tape the cable away from skin, keep jacket and buttons off the capsule. Do not bury it in hair or a scarf.

Hide the lav without rubbing

Record the actor turning, raising an arm and sitting; play back for rustle. If present, reposition rather than denoise later.

Limits

Invisible is not audible. Too deep sounds hollow and distant; let the capsule show a little rather than lose the line.

Hide a lav: 15–20cm below the mouth, protect against cloth first

Lavs fail from cloth rustle and occlusion. Do not center it at the collar; place it 15–20cm below the collarbone, with a small tape arch so the cable does not touch fabric.

  1. Mic head up, not under a button or zipper. Test sweaters and scarves for rustle first.
  2. Run the cable inside the clothes and leave a loose bend at the waist. A taut cable transmits cloth noise.
  3. Put a backup recorder in a pocket and sync the two devices.

Acceptance: have the actor turn, raise an arm and sit; listen for rustle and muffling. If present, move the mic before denoise.

On set

Try the collar first, then the hair. Use medical tape for strain relief; ordinary tape tears fabric.

Do this

Hide a lav at the collar first, then hair, then secure with medical tape; every wardrobe change needs a re-hide.

  1. Try the collar, then the hair.
  2. Use medical tape for shock isolation.
  3. Do not use ordinary tape; it tears clothing and leaves residue.

Avoid

Do not stuff the lav into a collar and stop; fabric rustle covers dialogue.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The lav tries collar then hair with positions logged.
  • 2. Medical tape secures it, not ordinary tape.
  • 3. After wardrobe changes the lav is re-hidden and rustle-tested.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The lav tries collar then hair with positions…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Medical tape secures it, not ordinary tape”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not stuff the lav into a collar and stop; fabric rustle covers dialogue.

en.title: Dual-System Sync: Clap and Timecode
en.summary: Clap first, then timecode; when both match, post does not have to listen to every take.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Dual-System Sync: Clap and Timecode

Tools / Tutorial

Dual-System Sync: Clap and Timecode

Clap first, then timecode; when both match, post does not have to listen to every take.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Dual-system sync claps first, then checks timecode; both must align before post stops listening shot by shot.

On set

Clap three times and record it on the recorder. Sync by waveform, then timecode, and keep drift under one frame.

Do this

  1. Clap three times while the recorder runs.
  2. Sync by waveform, then by timecode.
  3. Pass only under one frame of drift.

Avoid

Do not clap only once; if it misses, there is no second reference.

Three causes

For “Dual-System Sync: Clap and Timecode”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
No clapCamera and recorder share no marker, so sync is a guessClap before rolling; capture it in picture and sound
Timecode not syncedWrong jam or frame rate makes drift growJam once before the shoot
Wrong sample rate48kHz and 44.1kHz mixed together change pitchUse 48kHz throughout

On-set diagnosis

  1. Align the clap in the NLE and check whether the waveform peak meets the picture.
  2. Check frame rate and sample rate before aligning; unify first.
  3. Inspect the last section for drift; drift means timecode or clock trouble.

Fix

Dual-system sync does not rely on ears; it relies on a shared marker. A clap is the cheapest timecode; a timecode box is the steadier version.

  1. Clap for three seconds before every take and keep it in picture and sound.
  2. When using timecode, jam before the shoot and check again at wrap.
  3. Use 48kHz/24-bit and record a camera reference track.
  4. After syncing, check the whole take, especially the last section.

Failure cases

With “Dual-System Sync: Clap and Timecode”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Align by earTwo or three frames off reads as bad lip-syncClap/timecode
Check only the startThe head syncs and the tail driftsCheck the end
Ignore sample ratePitch rises or fallsUse 48kHz

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
ClapEvery take has a shared markerFootage check
TimecodeStart/end within one frameTimecode readout
Sample rateAll 48kHz/24-bitMediaInfo
Full lengthThe last section remains in syncPlay the end

One line for the set

No clap means no evidence; no timecode means no certainty.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Three claps are recorded by both camera and recorder.
  • 2. Waveform and timecode alignment are both performed.
  • 3. The two tracks drift under one frame.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Three claps are recorded by both camera and re…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Waveform and timecode alignment are both perfo…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not clap only once; if it misses, there is no second reference.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Clap three times while the recorder runs.”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Three claps are recorded by both camera and recorder.
  • Waveform and timecode alignment are both performed.
  • The two tracks drift under one frame.

en.title: Room Tone: Thirty Seconds per Location
en.summary: Record thirty seconds of room tone per location with everyone quiet; without it, dialogue cuts sound like a vacuum.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Room Tone: Thirty Seconds per Location

Tools / Tutorial

Room Tone: Thirty Seconds per Location

Record thirty seconds of room tone per location with everyone quiet; without it, dialogue cuts sound like a vacuum.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Room tone is not silence; it is the space's floor. At each main setup, record thirty seconds with everyone still and quiet, same mic, same gain. Use it to fill gaps between lines so the sound does not die.

Record thirty seconds of empty room per space

Room tone is not silence; it is the space's floor. At each main setup, record thirty seconds with everyone still and quiet, same mic, same gain. Use it to fill gaps between lines so the sound does not die.

Re-record after changing room, mic position or gain; tones from different conditions cannot be mixed.

Limits

Room tone cannot fix noise inside dialogue. It supplies continuous floor; wind, echo or hum on the line needs a re-record or separate repair.

On set

Record thirty seconds per scene with the crew still. Listen back for air conditioning and refrigerator noise.

Do this

Record thirty seconds of room tone per scene with the crew silent; without it, dialogue cuts sound like a vacuum.

  1. Record thirty seconds per scene.
  2. The whole crew stays still and silent.
  3. Play back and confirm no air conditioner or refrigerator hum.

Avoid

Do not grab room tone during a move; footsteps and chatter come with it.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Every scene has a thirty-second room-tone file.
  • 2. The crew stays still with no footsteps or chatter.
  • 3. Playback contains no sustained air-conditioner or fridge hum.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Every scene has a thirty-second room-tone file”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The crew stays still with no footsteps or chat…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not grab room tone during a move; footsteps and chatter come with it.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Record thirty seconds per scene.”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Every scene has a thirty-second room-tone file.
  • The crew stays still with no footsteps or chatter.
  • Playback contains no sustained air-conditioner or fridge hum.

en.title: One-Light Portrait: Direction First
en.summary: Set direction first: 45 degrees, side, or backlight; then softness and intensity.
en.html:
Home/Tools/One-Light Portrait: Direction First

Tools / Tutorial

One-Light Portrait: Direction First

Set direction first: 45 degrees, side, or backlight; then softness and intensity.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

With one lamp, decide where it comes from: side-back for a rim, side-front for the face, top for pressure. Wrong direction cannot be saved by ten more lamps. Fill with a white wall, foam board or reflector, not a second lamp from the same side.

One lamp sets direction; bounce fills

Shoot a test and read the nose and jaw shadow; the shape tells the audience the mood.

Limits

One light is not flat. Flag the other side to deepen contrast; do not shove the lamp straight on to save time, or the face goes flat.

One-light portrait: direction first, brightness second

One lamp can have depth if direction and distance are right. Place it 45° to the subject's side, 1–1.5 meters away; fill the other side with a white wall or bounce, keeping about 2:1.

  1. Turn off ambient light and use only the key. Check that nose and chin shadows fall the same way.
  2. Higher light deepens the eye sockets; do not go above the hairline or you get a ghost shadow.
  3. Soften with a box or white cloth; the closer the size to the face, the softer. Do not bare-bulb the face.

Acceptance: shadow should still hold skin texture. Dead black means not enough fill; flat means the key is too frontal. Shape lives between them.

On set

Place the light at 45 degrees, one meter from the face. Shoot one frame to see the nose shadow, then choose the softbox size.

Do this

One-light portraiture fixes direction first: 45 degrees, side, or back; then discuss softness and brightness.

  1. Place the light at 45 degrees, one meter from the face.
  2. Shoot one frame and watch the nose shadow.
  3. Then decide the softbox size.

Avoid

Do not change softboxes first; without direction, every size is a different wrong.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The light sits at 45 degrees, one meter away, with position logged.
  • 2. The nose shadow clearly shows light direction.
  • 3. Softbox size is chosen after direction is confirmed.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The light sits at 45 degrees, one meter away…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The nose shadow clearly shows light direction”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not change softboxes first; without direction, every size is a different wrong.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Place the light at 45 degrees, one meter”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • The light sits at 45 degrees, one meter away, with position logged.
  • The nose shadow clearly shows light direction.
  • Softbox size is chosen after direction is confirmed.

en.title: Window Light Fill: Reflector Placement
en.summary: Place the reflector on the shadow side, not by the window; it fills shadow, not adds light.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Window Light Fill: Reflector Placement

Tools / Tutorial

Window Light Fill: Reflector Placement

Place the reflector on the shadow side, not by the window; it fills shadow, not adds light.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Window light is not a fixed source; it cools, dims and moves. Lock the shooting window, then use sheer curtains, blinds or bounce to control hardness and direction. Do not mix morning and afternoon light in one scene.

Window light changes with time and direction

The closer the subject, the higher the contrast; to soften, move them back or add diffusion.

Limits

Window light is beautiful and unstable. For long interviews, prepare fill; a cloud passing breaks shot-to-shot continuity.

Window fill: where the bounce goes, and how far

With window light as key, closer is not better. Put the bounce 45° to the subject's side, 0.5–1 meter away. Too close flattens the shadow; too far does nothing.

  1. White is the general choice; silver is harder and useful for an eye light without adding a lamp.
  2. Keep the board below eye line so it does not light nostrils and chin. For softer fill, use a fabric surface or diffuser.
  3. Shoot one frame with window light only, then add the board. Compare whether shadow detail appears without milkiness.

Acceptance: shadow detail, highlights not clipped, skin not gray. If the image dies when the board is removed, the key is too weak; move closer to the window first.

On set

Put the reflector on the shadow side, one meter away at 45 degrees. Check that shadows lift without clipping.

Do this

Window fill puts the reflector on the shadow side, not by the window; it fills darkness, not adds brightness.

  1. Place the reflector on the shadow side, one meter from the face.
  2. Angle it at 45 degrees.
  3. Check that shadows lift without blowing out.

Avoid

Do not put the reflector by the window; it brightens the bright side and leaves shadows black.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The reflector sits on the shadow side, one meter away at about 45 degrees.
  • 2. Shadows lift without highlight clipping.
  • 3. Before-and-after shows more shadow detail.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The reflector sits on the shadow side, one met…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Shadows lift without highlight clipping”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not put the reflector by the window; it brightens the bright side and leaves shadows black.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Place the reflector on the shadow side, one”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • The reflector sits on the shadow side, one meter away at about 45 degrees.
  • Shadows lift without highlight clipping.
  • Before-and-after shows more shadow detail.

en.title: Night Practical: Balance the Lamp
en.summary: Make the lamp in frame believable, then add a small face light; a big ratio looks fake.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Night Practical: Balance the Lamp

Tools / Tutorial

Night Practical: Balance the Lamp

Make the lamp in frame believable, then add a small face light; a big ratio looks fake.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

In a practical-lit night scene, keep lamps and windows colored, not blown to white. Lift the face half a stop with a small fill or wall bounce and leave the rest to post; control noise on set rather than fixing it later.

Protect highlights, then lift the shadows

Play back a take and check shadows for blocks and flicker. If present, add ambient light or a higher-latitude mode; do not rely on lifting in post.

Limits

Night is not a brighter image. Blacks must stay black and lamps must read; a uniformly gray frame stops being night.

On set

Keep the practical in frame at 30 percent brightness. Add a small side light for the face and leave the background dark.

Do this

Night practicals first make the lamp in frame believable, then a small light fills the face; too much difference looks fake.

  1. Keep the practical in frame at 30 percent brightness.
  2. Fill the face from the side with a small light.
  3. Keep the background dark instead of lifting everything.

Avoid

Do not lift the whole street; a flat night kills the practical motivation.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The practical in frame sits near 30 percent without blowing out.
  • 2. The face is filled from the side, not flat frontal light.
  • 3. The background stays dark and does not become daytime.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The practical in frame sits near 30 percent wi…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The face is filled from the side, not flat fro…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not lift the whole street; a flat night kills the practical motivation.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Keep the practical in frame at 30 percent”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • The practical in frame sits near 30 percent without blowing out.
  • The face is filled from the side, not flat frontal light.
  • The background stays dark and does not become daytime.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: street or exterior

Street night starts with existing practicals: shop light boxes, street lamps, car lights, vending machines. Do not rig a lamp first; see what the location gives. Place the person where a practical reaches, then decide whether to fill. Practical direction is often bad but believable.

The biggest street problem is mixed colour: sodium orange, LED white, light-box green. Pick one key colour temperature and lock white balance; keep the other colours, do not neutralise everything. The “dirt” of night is sometimes information.

Condition B: interior or small space

Interior night practicals are usually a table lamp, a screen, a fridge, a hallway light. Decide which one is key and turn the rest off or down; do not leave every light on or the room looks like day. Put the key side-back for an outline; lift the front with a small reflector.

Interior night easily becomes one black mass: shadows have no layers and the person merges with the background. Leave one low-power practical in the background, or a narrow light behind the person to separate the outline. Separation does not need brightness, only an edge.

Counterexample: the practical is too bright

To “see clearly”, the team swaps the table lamp for a 100W bulb. The room brightens and the night disappears. The person looks in an office, the background looks like day. The audience does not say exposure is wrong; they say it does not look like night.

The fix is not dimming until invisible; use a lower-watt bulb, soften it, move it farther. Let the practical look bright in frame but hit the person only half a stop. A practical should look like life, not a photo lamp.

Reusable model

Practical → baseline → fill → separation. Find the location light, set exposure baseline, fill face or action, then separate the outline. Follow the order; do not rig a big lamp first.

Draw a light plot for every night scene: where the practical is, where the person is, where fill is, where separation is. The drawing outlasts memory when the camera moves.

en.title: Color Checker: Shoot It Before the Scene
en.summary: Shoot the chart under scene light before the take; after the first setup, the light has changed.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Color Checker: Shoot It Before the Scene

Tools / Tutorial

Color Checker: Shoot It Before the Scene

Shoot the chart under scene light before the take; after the first setup, the light has changed.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

The chart is not an opening ritual; it is an anchor for post. At each scene, lamp change or color-temperature change, fill one third of frame with the chart, sharp and correctly exposed. Do not shoot it only on take one.

Shoot a color chart every time the light changes

Use it to calibrate white balance and skin, then use scopes to match shots. The chart does not replace creative judgment.

Limits

A chart cannot fix mixed light. With two temperatures in one frame, it gives one reference; fix the light on set first, then shoot the chart.

A color chart is a coordinate, not a ceremony

Place the chart where the subject stands, in the same light, for 3–5 seconds. If the light changes, the chart is invalid. In post, use the neutral patch for white balance, then trim with skin.

  1. Shoot gray first, then the chart. Expose gray to 50–60% on the waveform, not clipped.
  2. Reshoot for every scene or color-temperature change; one chart cannot cover the day.
  3. Match cameras first, then add the look. The style LUT goes after the match.

Acceptance: compare chart frame and final; neutral gray should be neutral and skin natural. Green or magenta cast means check on-set white balance.

On set

Shoot the color chart at the head, filling a third of the frame. Match with the chart in post; do not grade from memory.

Do this

Shoot a color chart under the scene light for a post reference; shooting it later means the light has changed.

  1. Shoot the chart at the start.
  2. Fill about one third of the frame.
  3. Match in post from the chart, not memory.

Avoid

Do not shoot the chart at wrap; the light no longer matches the first take.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The chart is shot at the start under scene light.
  • 2. It fills about a third of frame with no glare on patches.
  • 3. Post matching uses the chart, not memory.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The chart is shot at the start under scene lig…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“It fills about a third of frame with no glare…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not shoot the chart at wrap; the light no longer matches the first take.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Shoot the chart at the start.”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • The chart is shot at the start under scene light.
  • It fills about a third of frame with no glare on patches.
  • Post matching uses the chart, not memory.

en.title: Proxy Creation: Match the Timeline
en.summary: Generate proxies to match timeline and delivery; full-res editing makes subtitles and framing wrong.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Proxy Creation: Match the Timeline

Tools / Tutorial

Proxy Creation: Match the Timeline

Generate proxies to match timeline and delivery; full-res editing makes subtitles and framing wrong.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Do not rename files or change folder structure when generating proxies. The editor relinks by original name and timecode; renaming turns relinking into manual hunting.

Proxies keep names, timecode and reel

Pick proxy resolution from timeline needs: multicam 4K can go to 1080p or 720p, but frame rate and color space must match the original.

Limits

A proxy is not delivery. Before the master, confirm the timeline points at originals; exporting from proxies loses a generation.

Proxy specs: editable, relinkable, never the master

A proxy is not “just a small file.” It must relink at the same timecode, frame rate and filename, or the cut shifts when you return to the original.

  1. Common: 1080p ProRes Proxy or high-bitrate H.264, same frame rate as source, audio kept.
  2. Add _proxy to the filename; do not change reel names. Relink against the original media path.
  3. Keep originals separate from the proxy project. Never grade the proxy as final.

Acceptance: pick a random cut point and relink to the original; the frame should not shift and audio should stay in sync. If it shifts, check frame rate and timecode.

On set

Make quarter-resolution ProRes Proxy files on a separate SSD. Relink and check timecode and framing.

Do this

Proxies follow timeline and delivery resolution; do not cut at full resolution. Wrong proxies misplace subtitles and framing.

  1. Generate quarter-resolution ProRes Proxy.
  2. Keep them on a separate SSD.
  3. On relink, check timecode and framing.

Avoid

Do not export from proxies; relinking to originals shifts every subtitle.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Proxies are quarter-resolution ProRes Proxy on a separate SSD.
  • 2. Timeline and proxy names map back to originals.
  • 3. After relink, timecode and framing match the proxy cut.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Proxies are quarter-resolution ProRes Proxy on…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Timeline and proxy names map back to originals”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not export from proxies; relinking to originals shifts every subtitle.

Extend

Check

  • Proxies are quarter-resolution ProRes Proxy on a separate SSD.
  • Timeline and proxy names map back to originals.
  • After relink, timecode and framing match the proxy cut.

en.title: Multicam Sync: Timecode and Clap
en.summary: Sync timecode first, clap as backup; with both, the edit can cut confidently.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Multicam Sync: Timecode and Clap

Tools / Tutorial

Multicam Sync: Timecode and Clap

Sync timecode first, clap as backup; with both, the edit can cut confidently.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Without timecode, use a clap, a line or a flash seen by every camera. Align by audio waveform in the edit; do not drag by “looks close.”

Give multicam one shared event

Match frame rate, shutter and audio sample rate before rolling. Mixed frame rates force speed changes that break sound sync.

Limits

Syncing once is not syncing forever. Long takes drift; re-sync every twenty to thirty minutes or use timecode.

Multi-camera sync: timecode first, clap as backup

The fear is “looks aligned but is two frames off.” Jam timecode if available; if not, clap on every camera. Align waveforms first, then trim frames.

  1. Set one frame rate and timecode before rolling. Do not mix frame rates on one timeline.
  2. Clap three times, one second apart, on every camera. Align on the first clap in post.
  3. After sync, pick a random action and check each camera. One frame is acceptable; two or more means drift.

Acceptance: all cameras film a stopwatch, pause on the same frame; readings should match. If not, return to timecode or frame rate.

On set

Sync timecode and clap once more. Build a multicam clip and switch using the camera map.

Do this

Multicam sync uses timecode first and a clap as backup; with both, the edit dares to cut.

  1. Sync timecode, then clap once more.
  2. Build a multicam clip in the edit.
  3. Switch by the camera map, not memory.

Avoid

Do not rely on timecode alone; one camera off-code throws the whole multicam group.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. All cameras share timecode with a clap backup.
  • 2. A multicam clip exists with the correct camera count.
  • 3. Switching follows the camera map and every shot's source is nameable.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“All cameras share timecode with a clap backup”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“A multicam clip exists with the correct camera…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not rely on timecode alone; one camera off-code throws the whole multicam group.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Sync timecode, then clap once more.”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check
