en.title: SRT Subtitles: Encoding, Timing, Punctuation
en.summary: SRT needs UTF-8, timing, and punctuation; wrong encoding shows garbage on platform.
en.html:
Home/Tools/SRT Subtitles: Encoding, Timing, Punctuation

Tools / Tutorial

SRT Subtitles: Encoding, Timing, Punctuation

SRT needs UTF-8, timing, and punctuation; wrong encoding shows garbage on platform.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

SRT subtitles protect UTF-8 encoding, timing, and punctuation; wrong encoding shows garbage on platforms.

On set

Save as UTF-8 with millisecond timing. Keep each subtitle under two lines and sixteen characters per line.

Do this

  1. Save as UTF-8.
  2. Time to the millisecond.
  3. No more than two lines per caption, sixteen characters per line.

Avoid

Do not save Chinese SRT as ANSI; platforms show question marks.

Three causes

For “SRT Subtitles: Encoding, Timing, Punctuation”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Wrong encodingUTF-8 saved as GBK shows garbage on the platformExport UTF-8 without BOM
Timeline driftWrong frame rate or start time makes later lines driftConvert by frame rate and check in a player
Line length/punctuationLong lines and mixed punctuation exhaust the reader12–16 characters per line, two lines max

On-set diagnosis

  1. Confirm UTF-8 in a text editor, not the system default.
  2. Watch the whole file in the target player and note the first drift.
  3. Measure the longest line; split anything over sixteen characters.

Fix

SRT is the simplest subtitle format and the easiest place to fail on encoding, frame rate and line length. Make it readable before translating it.

  1. Use UTF-8 without BOM; do not save from Word.
  2. Convert the timeline at the project frame rate and check first and last cues.
  3. Keep 12–16 characters per line, two lines max; never break mid-word.
  4. Use one punctuation system consistently, not a mix.

Failure cases

With “SRT Subtitles: Encoding, Timing, Punctuation”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Ship machine translationWord order and terms are wrong and the viewer cannot followDo at least one human pass
Fill one lineThe viewer cannot finish reading and the subtitle covers the imageSplit into two lines
Overlapping cuesTwo subtitles appear at onceCheck in/out times

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
EncodingUTF-8 without BOM; no garblingText editor
SyncFirst and last cue within one framePlayer check
Line lengthNo line over sixteen characters; two lines maxLongest-line count
PunctuationOne system throughoutRead-through

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Voltage, plug, warranty, import duty and radio certification differ by market; check the local spec sheet before ordering gear or batteries.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The file is UTF-8 and Chinese renders correctly.
  • 2. Timing is to the millisecond with no overlaps.
  • 3. Captions stay within two lines of sixteen characters with punctuation.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The file is UTF-8 and Chinese renders correctl…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Timing is to the millisecond with no overlaps”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not save Chinese SRT as ANSI; platforms show question marks.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Save as UTF-8.”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • The file is UTF-8 and Chinese renders correctly.
  • Timing is to the millisecond with no overlaps.
  • Captions stay within two lines of sixteen characters with punctuation.

en.title: H.264 Export: Bitrate and Compatibility
en.summary: Set platform and bitrate before two-pass encoding; low bitrate destroys motion first.
en.html:
Home/Tools/H.264 Export: Bitrate and Compatibility

Tools / Tutorial

H.264 Export: Bitrate and Compatibility

Set platform and bitrate before two-pass encoding; low bitrate destroys motion first.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

H.264 export fixes platform and bitrate first, then two-pass encoding; low bitrate destroys motion first.

On set

Use 10 to 16 Mbps for 1080p and 35 to 45 Mbps for 4K. Two-pass encode, AAC audio at 192 kbps.

Do this

  1. 1080p at 10 to 16 Mbps, 4K at 35 to 45 Mbps.
  2. Use two-pass encoding.
  3. Audio AAC at 192 kbps.

Avoid

Do not upload 4K at 5 Mbps; any motion turns into blocks.

Three causes

For “H.264 Export: Bitrate and Compatibility”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Bitrate too lowMotion and large detail block up, and platform recompression makes it worseTest 12/20/35Mbps on a two-second high-motion clip
Incompatible parametersColour, frame rate, pixel aspect and platform spec disagreeCheck MediaInfo against the delivery spec
Audio out of specWrong sample rate, channels or bitrate causes silence or distortionInspect the audio track separately

On-set diagnosis

  1. Use MediaInfo to read codec, profile, level, bitrate, colour tags and audio parameters.
  2. Upload a thirty-second test to the target platform and check clarity and colour.
  3. Compare the same frame in source and export for unintended crop or stretch.

Fix

H.264 is not about the smallest file; it is about correct playback on the target platform. Set the delivery spec first, then choose bitrate and profile.

  1. For web delivery use H.264 High Profile, 4:2:0 8-bit, AAC 48kHz.
  2. Use 12–20Mbps for 1080p and 35–60Mbps for 4K; go higher for heavy motion.
  3. Use two-pass or VBV limits so peaks do not blow the budget.
  4. After export, check first frame, last frame, audio sync and platform playback.

Failure cases

With “H.264 Export: Bitrate and Compatibility”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Watch file size onlyThe file is small and the detail and audio are brokenTest against platform spec
Deliver 4:4:4The platform does not support it and recompresses or rejectsDeliver 4:2:0
Ignore colour tagsColour looks grey or oversaturated on the platformWrite correct matrix/primaries

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
CodecH.264 High with a matching levelMediaInfo
BitrateNo blocking in high motionThirty-second upload
AudioAAC 48kHz, correct channels, no clippingListen separately
ColourPlatform playback matches the sourceCompare with source

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Resolution and bitrate sit in the recommended range.
  • 2. Encoding is two-pass, not single-pass rushed.
  • 3. Audio is AAC 192 kbps and stays in sync.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Resolution and bitrate sit in the recommended…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Encoding is two-pass, not single-pass rushed”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not upload 4K at 5 Mbps; any motion turns into blocks.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “1080p at 10 to 16 Mbps, 4K at”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Resolution and bitrate sit in the recommended range.
  • Encoding is two-pass, not single-pass rushed.
  • Audio is AAC 192 kbps and stays in sync.

en.html:
Home/Tools/ProRes Export: Archive and Delivery

Tools / Tutorial

ProRes Export: Archive and Delivery

ProRes is for archive and regrading, not direct upload everywhere; big files, but editable.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

ProRes is for archive and regrading, not direct upload to every platform; files are large but re-editable.

On set

Archive in ProRes 422 HQ and deliver 422. Do not upload ProRes to platforms; the files are too large.

Do this

  1. Archive in ProRes 422 HQ.
  2. Deliver in 422.
  3. Do not upload ProRes to platforms; the file is too large.

Avoid

Do not treat ProRes as a platform delivery format; it gets compressed back to H.264 anyway.

Three causes

For “ProRes Export: Archive and Delivery”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Wrong profileUsing ProRes 422 LT as a master leaves no room for gradingArchive with 422 HQ or 4444
Wrong colour spaceMislabeled Log/Rec.709 shifts colour downstreamFollow the project colour pipeline
Not enough storageProRes files are large and the write fails halfwayReserve twice the space and verify

On-set diagnosis

  1. Decide whether the file is an archive, a grading intermediate or a web deliverable.
  2. Use MediaInfo to check profile, colour tags and audio channels.
  3. Import into the target NLE and confirm no transcode and no colour shift.

Fix

ProRes is an intermediate/archive format, not a web delivery format. Decide its place in the pipeline before choosing a profile.

  1. Archive/grading: ProRes 422 HQ; alpha or maximum: 4444.
  2. Proxy/offline: ProRes Proxy or 422 LT; never use them as the final master.
  3. Keep source frame rate, colour space and audio channels; do not change them here.
  4. Checksum the export to confirm the file is complete.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Upload ProRes to a platformThe file is huge and gets rejected or transcodedMake a separate H.264 deliverable
Use LT as masterThere is too little room for grading and shadows breakUse HQ for the master
Ignore audioWrong audio channels are discovered in postCheck before export

en.html:
Home/Tools/3-2-1 Backup: Finish It Today

Tools / Tutorial

3-2-1 Backup: Finish It Today

Do 3-2-1 today: three copies, two media, one offsite; tomorrow the card may be gone.

2 min quick read + 5 min deep read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

3-2-1 is not “upload to cloud and done.” On a shoot day make at least three copies: card/camera, on-set drive, and another offline drive or cloud. One copy sits in a different building.

Three copies, two media, one off-site, same day

Every copy must read: randomly play one file and check name and duration. “Copy completed” is not a backup.

Limits

RAID is not backup, and a sync folder is not backup. A deletion syncs; ransomware encrypts the whole set. Keep at least one offline, read-only or versioned copy.

On set

Copy the card to an SSD, then to another drive, then to NAS or cloud. Format the card only after three copies exist.

Do this

3-2-1 backup finishes the same day: three copies, two media types, one offsite; wait until tomorrow and the media may be gone.

  1. Copy the card to SSD the same day.
  2. Copy to a second drive.
  3. Upload to NAS or cloud, and format the card only after three copies.

Avoid

Do not plan to back up tomorrow; if the card is lost, three copies never happen.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Three copies complete the same day with matching file counts.
  • 2. Two media types are used, one offsite or cloud.
  • 3. The card is formatted only after all three are confirmed.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Three copies complete the same day with matchi…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Two media types are used, one offsite or cloud”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not plan to back up tomorrow; if the card is lost, three copies never happen.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Copy the card to SSD the same day.”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Three copies complete the same day with matching file counts.
  • Two media types are used, one offsite or cloud.
  • The card is formatted only after all three are confirmed.

Deep dive

About 5 minutes. Backup is not dragging files to another drive. It is making sure tomorrow can still open and export them.

The same-day backup routine

Offload, verify, rename, make two media copies, and keep one away from the machine. Name files date_project_camera_card; never “final.” Open three random files after the copy instead of trusting the progress bar.

Skip it today and tomorrow starts from zero. Confirm both copies before formatting the card.

Run a restore drill

Once a month, pick a random project and open it from backup: find the original media and export one minute. Record how long it took and what was missing. An untested backup is only reassurance.

Put the restore steps on one page at the root of the project drive. In six months you will forget the password, the software version, and where the adapter went.

Cards, drives, and the cloud

A card is transport, not storage; the working drive is the copy being edited; backup drives and an offsite copy are insurance. Each has a job and none replaces another.

Cloud is for small files and final delivery, not hundreds of gigabytes of raw footage a day. Upload time is also a cost.

Naming and folders

A project root holds four things: media, projects, exports, documents. Media by date_camera, projects by version, exports by platform. Do not leave everything on the desktop.

Ban “final,” “final2,” and “really final.” Use date and version so three months later you still know what shipped.

Ten steps for every offload

  • Confirm the card plays back before copying
  • Copy to the first working drive
  • Verify file count and decode with a checksum tool
  • Rename date_project_camera_card
  • Copy to a second backup drive
  • Move one copy off this machine
  • Open three random files and play them
  • Confirm both copies before formatting the card
  • Put restore steps at the project root
  • Run one restore drill per month

Backup is not dragging files across; it is making sure tomorrow can still open, export, and deliver. Before formatting the card, open both copies once; open, play, and export is what makes a backup real.

en.title: Restore Test: Pick One Random File
en.summary: Restore one random file from backup; a backup that will not open does not exist.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Restore Test: Pick One Random File

Tools / Tutorial

Restore Test: Pick One Random File

Restore one random file from backup; a backup that will not open does not exist.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Once a month, restore one random project to a different drive, open it, relink media and export ten seconds. If restore fails, the backup is not there.

A backup passes when it restores, not when it exists

Record restore time and missing files; if every restore needs manual hunting, the structure or checksum is broken.

Limits

RAID and sync folders are not backup. They sync deletions and encryption. Keep one offline, read-only or versioned copy and test restore regularly.

Restore drill: pick a random file and actually restore it

A backup that has never been restored is not a backup. Run a 30-minute drill monthly: pick a random project file, restore to a clean disk, open it and compare the hash.

  1. Pick at random, not “the most important,” so you do not only rehearse the familiar path.
  2. Restore to a machine without the original; never overwrite in place.
  3. Check size, hash and that it opens. Log the time; over two hours means change the plan.

Acceptance: the file opens, the timeline has no offline media and the hash matches. Missing one means the backup plan is not proven.

On set

Restore one random file to another machine and play it. If it fails, redo the backup.

Do this

A restore drill pulls one random file from backup and opens it; a backup that will not open does not exist.

  1. Pick one file at random.
  2. Restore it to another machine.
  3. Open and play; if it fails, redo the backup.

Avoid

Do not trust a green check in backup software; without a restore, you do not know it opens.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. A random file is chosen, not the most familiar one.
  • 2. Restore goes to another machine, not the original path.
  • 3. The file opens and plays; failures trigger a redo log.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“A random file is chosen, not the most familiar…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Restore goes to another machine, not the origi…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not trust a green check in backup software; without a restore, you do not know it opens.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Pick one file at random.”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • A random file is chosen, not the most familiar one.
  • Restore goes to another machine, not the original path.
  • The file opens and plays; failures trigger a redo log.

en.title: ND Calculator: Change Filters Without Guessing
en.summary: The ND calculator puts shutter, aperture, ISO, and target exposure in one formula; calculate before swapping.
en.html:
Home/Tools/ND Calculator: Change Filters Without Guessing

Tools / Calculator

ND Calculator: Change Filters Without Guessing

The ND calculator puts shutter, aperture, ISO, and target exposure in one formula; calculate before swapping.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Fix aperture and ISO, then slow the shutter to the target; the needed reduction is ND stops = log2(current shutter ÷ target shutter) . From 1/50 to 1/200 is four times less light, so two stops.

Formula and stops

Fix aperture and ISO, then slow the shutter to the target; the needed reduction is ND stops = log2(current shutter ÷ target shutter). From 1/50 to 1/200 is four times less light, so two stops.

  • 1 stop = 1/2 light, 2 stops = 1/4, 3 stops = 1/8, 10 stops = 1/1024.
  • Common markings: ND0.3≈1 stop, ND0.6≈2, ND0.9≈3, ND1.8≈6, ND3.0≈10.
  • Stacked filters add stops, not factors; two 3-stop filters equal 6 stops.

A worked example

On a sunny day you want f/2.8, 1/50, ISO 100 for shallow depth, but the meter says 1/1600 to avoid clipping: 1/1600 ÷ 1/50 = 32, log2(32)=5, so you need 5 stops. Fit ND1.5 (5 stops), return to 1/50, and exposure is back.

Limits

The formula only covers exposure, not color cast, vignetting or long-exposure heat noise. Shoot a test clip after changing the filter; do not trust the calculator alone.

On set

Enter 1/50, f/2.8, ISO 100 and meter the scene EV. Calculate the ND stops before changing filters.

Do this

An ND calculator puts shutter, aperture, ISO, and target exposure into one formula; calculate before changing the filter.

  1. Enter 1/50, f/2.8, ISO 100.
  2. Meter ambient EV.
  3. Calculate ND stops, then fit the filter.

Avoid

Do not use defaults as the answer; they are not your project or light.

ND calculator

Enter current and target shutter denominators to get stops and the nearest standard ND.

ND —Between two densities, pick less ND and trim with aperture.

Formula: stops = log₂(current ÷ target); ND factor = 2^stops.

Boundary

It does not replace an on-set reading. The number is a starting point; the monitor, scope or actual recording decides.

Alternative

If “Enter 1/50, f/2.8, ISO 100.” is not the main problem, start with the basic move behind “Meter ambient EV.”. Upgrade only after both hold.

60-second test

Run a 60-second test with the gear you own, focused on “Enter 1/50, f/2.8, ISO 100.”, and record one number. If the number does not change, do not add budget.

Check

  • Shutter, aperture, and ISO match the on-set settings.
  • Ambient EV is measured, not guessed.
  • Calculated ND stops match the filter and exposure lands on target.

en.title: Depth of Field Calculator: Distance and Aperture
en.summary: Depth of field starts with subject distance, then aperture and focal length; move and everything changes.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Depth of Field Calculator: Distance and Aperture

Tools / Calculator

Depth of Field Calculator: Distance and Aperture

Depth of field starts with subject distance, then aperture and focal length; move and everything changes.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Hyperfocal H = f × f ÷ (N × c) + f , where f is focal length in mm, N is f-number and c is the circle of confusion (0.03mm for full frame). At focus distance s, near = H × s ÷ (H + s), far = H × s ÷ (H - s) when s is below H.

Formula

Hyperfocal H = f × f ÷ (N × c) + f, where f is focal length in mm, N is f-number and c is the circle of confusion (0.03mm for full frame). At focus distance s, near = H × s ÷ (H + s), far = H × s ÷ (H - s) when s is below H.

Example: full-frame 50mm at f/2, focused at 3m: H = 50×50 ÷ (2×0.03) + 50 ≈ 41,717mm (41.7m); near ≈ 2.8m, far ≈ 3.2m, about 0.4m of depth.

On set

  • To keep subject and background sharp, stop down or move back; do not only switch to wide.
  • To separate the subject, get closer, open up and move the background away.
  • The result is theoretical; lens aberrations and viewing size still matter.

Limits

Do not replace a monitor with a phone calculator; c changes with format, and crop modes change the result.

Enter the numbers

Enter focal length, aperture, and subject distance. Read the depth of field before deciding whether the actor moves.

Do this

A depth-of-field calculator starts with subject distance, then aperture and focal length; move the subject and everything changes.

  1. Enter focal length, aperture, and subject distance.
  2. Read the depth range.
  3. Then decide whether the actor can walk.

Avoid

Do not adjust aperture alone for depth; one meter of subject movement changes it.

Depth of field calculator

Estimated with a full-frame circle of confusion of 0.03mm; change it for other sensors.

DOF —Hyperfocal distance and near/far limits move with focal, aperture and distance.

Formula: H = f² ÷ (N × c) + f; near = H×s ÷ (H+s−f); far = H×s ÷ (H−s+f).

Boundary

It does not replace an on-set reading. The number is a starting point; the monitor, scope or actual recording decides.

Alternative

If “Enter focal length, aperture, and subject distance.” is not the main problem, start with the basic move behind “Read the depth range.”. Upgrade only after both hold.

60-second test

Run a 60-second test with the gear you own, focused on “Enter focal length, aperture, and subject distance.”, and record one number. If the number does not change, do not add budget.

Check

  • Focal length, aperture, and distance are measured values.
  • Near and far depth limits are numeric and show blocking room.
  • Blocking stays inside depth without desperate focus pulls.

en.summary: Calculate file size from minutes and Mbps; know if the drive fits before delivery.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Bitrate Calculator: How Big Is the File?

Tools / Calculator

Bitrate Calculator: How Big Is the File?

Calculate file size from minutes and Mbps; know if the drive fits before delivery.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

File size in GB ≈ bitrate in Mbps × duration in seconds ÷ 8 ÷ 1000 . Bitrate is megabits per second, storage counts bytes, so divide by 8; divide by 1000 for decimal GB.

Formula and units

File size in GB ≈ bitrate in Mbps × duration in seconds ÷ 8 ÷ 1000. Bitrate is megabits per second, storage counts bytes, so divide by 8; divide by 1000 for decimal GB.

Example: 4K at 100 Mbps for 10 minutes: 100 × 600 ÷ 8 ÷ 1000 = 7.5 GB. At 200 Mbps 4:2:2 10-bit, the same duration is 15 GB.

Three extras

  • Audio, proxies and metadata add 5–15%.
  • Cards and drives are sold in decimal capacity while the OS shows binary; “missing” gigabytes are normal.
  • Multiply by camera count for multicam, not just the A camera.

Limits

With variable bitrate this is an average, not every second. Card speed is sustained write; do not reverse this size formula into a card-speed claim.

On set

Enter minutes and Mbps to get GB. Add 20 percent headroom, then check the card and drive.

Do this

A bitrate calculator converts minutes and Mbps into file size; know whether the drive fits before delivery.

  1. Enter minutes and Mbps.
  2. Calculate GB and add 20 percent headroom.
  3. Compare with free space on card and drive.

Avoid

Do not read Mbps as MB; the factor of eight undercounts the drive.

Bitrate / file size calculator

Given duration and target size, estimate average bitrate; audio and container overhead excluded.

Bitrate —Leave 5%–10% headroom for audio and container on upload.

Formula: Mbps = sizeGB × 8000 ÷ durationSeconds.

Boundary

It does not replace an on-set reading. The number is a starting point; the monitor, scope or actual recording decides.

en.html:
Home/Tools/Budget Calculator: Four Buckets

Tools / Calculator

Budget Calculator: Four Buckets

Split the budget into people, gear, location, and post; keep ten percent buffer.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Split the total before quoting line items: shoot 50% / post 25% / gear and location 15% / contingency 10% . Contingency is not profit; it absorbs reschedules, pickups and overtime.

Four buckets

Split the total before quoting line items: shoot 50% / post 25% / gear and location 15% / contingency 10%. Contingency is not profit; it absorbs reschedules, pickups and overtime.

Example: a 20,000 budget gives 10,000 shoot, 5,000 post, 3,000 gear and location, 2,000 contingency. If the client adds a shoot day, move money from contingency and post; do not cut contingency to zero.

People before gear

  • Day rate × crew × days, plus travel and meals.
  • Post by finished minute × rate, plus revision rounds.
  • Gear at rental × days, plus insurance and wear.

Limits

This is a starting split for small commercial work, not large ads or features; tax, platform fees and financing costs sit outside the four buckets.

On set

Split the budget: people 40, gear 25, location 15, post 20. Keep 10 percent buffer in each.

Do this

A budget calculator splits production into four blocks: people, gear, location, post; each keeps 10 percent buffer.

  1. Split total: people 40, gear 25, location 15, post 20 percent.
  2. Keep 10 percent buffer in each block.
  3. Overspend moves within the same block, not across blocks.

Avoid

Do not merge four blocks into one total; you never see which block overspent.

Budget allocation calculator

Enter total and four percentages to get amounts and unallocated balance; keep the total at or below 100%.

Unallocated —Contingency is not profit; keep it on its own line.

Amount = total × percentage; unallocated = total − four amounts.

It does not replace an on-set reading. The number is a starting point; the monitor, scope or actual recording decides.

en.summary: Check characters per second; above reading speed, the viewer pauses and the film breaks.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Subtitle CPS: Can They Read It?

Tools / Calculator

Subtitle CPS: Can They Read It?

Check characters per second; above reading speed, the viewer pauses and the film breaks.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

CPS (characters per second) = characters ÷ display seconds . Chinese should stay under 9–12 CPS, English under 15–20; if over, split the line or hold it longer.

Formula

CPS (characters per second) = characters ÷ display seconds. Chinese should stay under 9–12 CPS, English under 15–20; if over, split the line or hold it longer.

Example: 24 Chinese characters for 2 seconds is 12 CPS, already at the limit; the same line for 3 seconds is 8 CPS and readable.

How to lower CPS

  • Cut filler first, then split into two lines; do not shrink the type.
  • Give key lines 0.3–0.5 extra seconds and remove “um” and “like.”
  • Do not show two long bilingual lines at once; protect the primary language.

Limits

CPS is an average; numbers, names and fast speech need a separate check. Watch it at phone size, not only on the timeline.

On set

Keep Chinese under nine characters per second and English under fifteen. If over, split the line or hold longer.

Do this

A subtitle CPS calculator checks characters per second; beyond reading speed, viewers pause and the film breaks.

  1. Chinese under nine characters per second, English under fifteen.
  2. Split the sentence if over.
  3. Or extend the duration; do not shrink it into two tiny lines.

Avoid

Do not shrink the font to fit; viewers cannot finish and will pause or quit.

Subtitle CPS calculator

Chinese subtitles should stay around 9–15 characters per second; above 15, split or hold longer.

CPS —When dialogue is dense, cut words before cutting duration.

Formula: CPS = characters ÷ seconds.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Voltage, plug, warranty, import duty and radio certification differ by market; check the local spec sheet before ordering gear or batteries.

Boundary

It does not replace an on-set reading. The number is a starting point; the monitor, scope or actual recording decides.

Alternative

If “Chinese under nine characters per second, English under” is not the main problem, start with the basic move behind “Split the sentence if over.”. Upgrade only after both hold.

60-second test

Run a 60-second test with the gear you own, focused on “Chinese under nine characters per second, English under”, and record one number. If the number does not change, do not add budget.

Check

  • Every caption stays under nine Chinese characters or fifteen English characters per second.
  • Over-limit lines are split or extended, not shrunk.
  • At playback speed, each caption reads in one pass without pausing.

Home/Tools/Aspect Ratio Calculator: Crop and Safe Area

Tools / Calculator

Aspect Ratio Calculator: Crop and Safe Area

Calculate effective pixels after crop, then safe area; vertical is not a horizontal crop.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Aspect ratio = width ÷ height . Cropping 16:9 to 9:16 keeps width = original height × 9 ÷ 16; a 3840×2160 frame becomes 1215×2160, losing about 1312 pixels on each side.

Formula and safe area

Aspect ratio = width ÷ height. Cropping 16:9 to 9:16 keeps width = original height × 9 ÷ 16; a 3840×2160 frame becomes 1215×2160, losing about 1312 pixels on each side.

Three common conversions

  • 16:9 → 1:1: keep 2160×2160, lose 840 pixels each side.
  • 16:9 → 4:5: keep 1728×2160, lose 1056 each side.
  • When shooting 9:16, keep the subject inside the central 1080-wide safe area.

Limits

A crop is not a recomposition; action and subtitles must stay inside the safe area. Platforms crop again, so check the platform preview before delivery.

On set

4K 16:9 cropped to 9:16 leaves about 1215×2160. Confirm the pixels are enough and redraw safe areas per platform.

Do this

An aspect-ratio calculator first computes effective pixels after crop, then the safe area; vertical is not just cropping the sides.

  1. 4K 16:9 cropped to 9:16 leaves about 1215×2160.
  2. Confirm the pixel count is enough.
  3. Redraw the safe area for the platform.

Avoid

Do not crop landscape into vertical blindly; effective pixels halve and close-ups soften.

Aspect-ratio crop calculator

Finds the largest crop at the target ratio and reports kept pixels and crop percentage.

Crop —Protect the subject first, then trim edges; do not center-crop blindly.

Compare source and target ratios: if wider, crop width; if taller, crop height. Keep the other axis.

Check

  • Cropped effective pixels are numeric, about 1215×2160.

en.title: Buying a Camera: Budget Before Body
en.summary: On a limited budget, the body is not first. Find whether you lack low light, autofocus, 10-bit, or audio. The wrong body forces every accessory to change with it.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Buying a Camera: Budget Before Body

Tools / Buying guide

Buying a Camera: Budget Before Body

On a limited budget, the body is not first. Find whether you lack low light, autofocus, 10-bit, or audio. The wrong body forces every accessory to change with it.

9 min read · Buying guideTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

If you already have a 4K body and one working lens, do not replace the body first. Ask which of your last three films was lost because the camera was not enough. Low light: fast lens and light first. Audio: microphone first. Autofocus: then the body. Under ¥10k, the body should not exceed half the budget.

Fits:

  • First paid work, ¥8,000–20,000
  • Interview, event, product, 4K delivery
  • 10-bit/Log for a simple grade

Does not fit:

  • 4K120 or global shutter
  • One hour without overheating
  • RAW and dual-card recording

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Bring your own Log footage and a 64GB card. Spend five minutes on each of the five checks. Do not just hold the body and listen to the shutter; a spec sheet will not show rolling shutter, heat, or AF breathing.

CheckPass lineReference/log
果冻效应快速横摇时直线可接受，不变成斜塔拍一段 2 秒横摇，回放
过热4K 30p 连续 30 分钟不报警室温 25°C，记录起始电量
自动对焦人眼/物体切换不呼吸、不拉风箱暗光 + 逆光各一次
电池实际录制 90 分钟以上原厂电池，关闭省电
音频有耳机监听、手动增益、底噪可控接一支动圈/领夹试录

Price bands: total cost of ownership first

Look beyond the sticker: cards, batteries, adapters, gimbal, stands, software subscriptions, and repair. Bands describe the minimum kit for a real project type, not toy pricing.

TierReferenceIncludesWatch
Entry¥4,000–8,000APS-C + kit lens + one card/batteryLimited low light/AF
Main¥8,000–20,000Full-frame/APS-C video body + prime + spareLens/storage extra
Advanced¥20,000–50,00010-bit/RAW, dual card, monitor, audioAccessories may exceed body

Prices are China mainland channel references as of November 2026; tax and quotes vary. Not buying advice.

Alternatives and upgrades: do not add money on the wrong axis

  • A fast prime first
  • An audio kit first
  • A used previous-gen flagship

Buying steps: bring footage, not spec sheets

Run these in order before paying. If one fails, do not tell yourself post will fix it.

  1. Rent one day in your usual scene
  2. Test adapters and AF with your lenses
  3. Confirm HDMI, monitoring, and power
  4. Price cards, batteries, cage, monitor
  5. Check warranty and repair turnaround

Check

  • Body is at most half the total budget.
  • Five tests have footage logs.
  • Total includes cards, batteries, monitor, adapters.
  • At least one lens covers the main scene.
  • Heat and rolling shutter are acceptable.
  • Warranty and repair turnaround are known.

Decision tree: project first, body second

Do not start with “which body is best”. Start with what the project cannot lose. Interviews need continuous recording, autofocus and audio; products need resolution, colour and close focus; narrative needs dynamic range, Log and cooling. Pick the wrong project and no body can buy it back.

  1. Write the project type, delivery platform and longest single take.
  2. Choose three pass lines: autofocus, 10-bit, cooling, audio or low light.
  3. Then choose the mount; existing lenses decide the body, not the reverse.
  4. Finally total the cards, batteries, monitor, adapter and repair cost.

Eight comparisons the spec sheet omits

ItemPass lineFitsDoes not fit
Mount and lens poolExisting lenses cover the main range; adapter keeps autofocusExisting lens inventoryBuilding from zero on a tight budget
AutofocusEye/object transitions do not hunt; works in low lightInterview, event, one-person followManual narrative only
Low lightSkin is usable at ISO 3200; shadows show no obvious blockingNight, unlit interiorLit studio
10-bit/Log10-bit 4:2:2 or RAW with a correct transformGradingStraight-out meeting records
Cooling4K 30p for 30 minutes without warningLong interview, eventShort takes
StorageDual card or external record; card cost acceptableCommercial deliveryShort single-card work
Power90 minutes per battery; external power supportedFull-day shootFixed studio
Total costCards, batteries, monitor, adapter and repair includedEvery projectSticker price only

Test scope: measured and not measured

Bring your own Log footage, a 64GB card and a common lens. Run five minutes on each of five checks: rolling shutter, overheating, autofocus, battery and audio. Record room temperature, battery level, card type and firmware. Not measured: integrating sphere, noise meter, lab-grade dynamic range. Those numbers are not printed here.

Continue: camera and lens hub

Read the body, then lenses and support. These ten links follow buying order, not popularity.

  • Buy lenses first: range, aperture, breathing
  • Buying a zoom: parfocal, breathing, servo
  • Buying a cinema camera: shootable is not deliverable
  • Buying used gear: shutter, sensor, repair
  • Buy audio first: mic, noise floor, gain
  • Buying a light kit: soft before bright
  • Buying project storage: speed, capacity, backup
  • Exposure check: waveform, zebra, false colour
  • Frame rate: action and slow motion
  • Budget and quote: price the risk

Verification and price date

Verified 2026-11-23. Prices are China mainland channel references; tax and stock depend on the quote. Only public specs and short samples were checked; no lab measurement. Not buying advice.

Buying order: rent before buying

Do not let a spec sheet choose the body. Rent once, shoot the project you actually want, then total the cost.

  1. Rent the target body and a common lens once; shoot a real project.
  2. Confirm mount, adapter, autofocus and power.
  3. Total the cards, batteries, monitor, storage and repair.
  4. Keep 10% for surprises and consumables.
  5. Buy the second lens after the first delivery.

Add: failure cases

These three buying moves are common and all spend the budget on the wrong axis.

MoveResultReplace with
Buy a body for 4K120 with no light/lens budgetHigh frame rate is unusable without lightRent the body; keep money for light and lens
Judge a sample, not firmware/warrantyRetail units focus or overheat differentlyBring your own card and run 30 minutes
Buy a niche mount firstSmall lens pool and adapters sacrifice autofocusChoose the mount from existing lenses

en.html:
Home/Tools/Renting a Camera: Insurance, Deposit, Check

Tools / Buying & fixes

Renting a Camera: Insurance, Deposit, Check

Insurance, deposit, and a hands-on check; film scratches and dead pixels as evidence.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

A cheap day rate with no backup, a long pickup and no insurance can cost more than the rental when the camera stops. Ask: same-model backup, early pickup, damage liability, tech support hours.

Rent by downtime cost, not day rate

Test card slots, sensor, audio and battery at pickup; do not discover it on set.

Limits

Do not save rent by taking an unfamiliar body. Learning the menu on set spends the crew's money on your lesson.

On set

Shoot a 4K video at pickup: six sides, mount, sensor, shutter. Repeat before returning it.

Do this

Renting a camera: buy insurance, pay the deposit, and inspect it in person. Record scratches and dead pixels.

  1. At pickup, shoot 4K video of all six sides, mount, sensor, shutter, and screen.
  2. Test recording, autofocus, stabilization, ports, and batteries one by one.
  3. Shoot the same pass before returning and compare it with the pickup video.

Avoid

Do not rely on stills; video proves whether a mark was pre-existing or new.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Pickup video covers six sides, mount, sensor, shutter, and screen in 4K.
  • 2. Recording, autofocus, stabilization, ports, and batteries were tested.
  • 3. The same pass is shot before return and compared.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Pickup video covers six sides, mount, sensor…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Recording, autofocus, stabilization, ports, an…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not rely on stills; video proves whether a mark was pre-existing or new.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “At pickup, shoot 4K video of all six”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Pickup video covers six sides, mount, sensor, shutter, and screen in 4K.
  • Recording, autofocus, stabilization, ports, and batteries were tested.
  • The same pass is shot before return and compared.

en.title: Buy the Lens First: Focal Length, Aperture, Breathing
en.summary: The lens decides half the image and holds value better than a body. Buy one focal length that covers 70% of your work, then a second; do not start with three cheap zooms.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Buy the Lens First: Focal Length, Aperture, Breathing

Tools / Buying guide

Buy the Lens First: Focal Length, Aperture, Breathing

The lens decides half the image and holds value better than a body. Buy one focal length that covers 70% of your work, then a second; do not start with three cheap zooms.

3 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

List the focal lengths in your last 20 films. If 35mm and 50mm dominate, buy a fast 35 or 50 first. If you shoot events and cannot move, consider a 24-70 zoom. The first lens should not exceed 60% of the budget; leave money for a second lens or light.

Fits:

  • Portrait/interview, shallow depth
  • Low-light interiors, no light
  • One lens to build a look

Does not fit:

  • Events/sports needing fast zoom
  • Product macro at 1:1
  • One ultra-wide for everything

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Bring the body and shoot three frames: a face, a hand detail, and a backlit window. Check edges, chromatic aberration, focus breathing, and vignetting—not only centre sharpness.

en.title: Buy Audio First: Mic, Noise Floor, and Gain
en.summary: Audiences forgive a plain image; they do not forgive unclear sound. On a limited budget, put money into a microphone and recorder before a second lens.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Buy Audio First: Mic, Noise Floor, and Gain

Tools / Buying guide

Buy Audio First: Mic, Noise Floor, and Gain

Audiences forgive a plain image; they do not forgive unclear sound. On a limited budget, put money into a microphone and recorder before a second lens.

8 min read · Buying guideTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Decide whether you lack clear speech or clean ambience. For interior interviews, a dynamic/shotgun mic plus recorder is steadier than a lav; for moving exteriors, a lav with wind protection is more useful. Do not buy an expensive mic and feed it through a camera’s auto gain.

Fits:

  • Interview/voiceover, clear speech
  • Controlled interior, close to talent
  • Limited budget, intelligibility first

Does not fit:

  • Distant multi-person events
  • Windy exterior without protection
  • Multi-channel sync recording

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Record 30 seconds of room tone in a quiet room, then normal speech and a close shout. Listen for noise, clipping, sibilance, and plosives—on headphones and once on a speaker.

CheckPass lineReference/log
底噪增益 50% 时安静房间无明显嘶声30 秒房间声
最大声压正常喊话不削波近距 30cm
离轴侧后方 30° 仍可懂侧向说话
手持走动无摩擦/线噪手持绕圈
供电续航与幻象供电明确电池/48V

Price bands: total cost of ownership first

Look beyond the sticker: cards, batteries, adapters, gimbal, stands, software subscriptions, and repair. Bands describe the minimum kit for a real project type, not toy pricing.

TierReferenceIncludesWatch
Entry¥800–2,500Lav + portable recorder/phone adapterNoise and wireless range limited
Main¥2,500–8,000Shotgun/dynamic + 2-channel recorder + monitoringWind/line extra
Advanced¥8,000–20,000Multichannel recorder, timecode, pro wirelessBattery/accessory cost

Prices are China mainland channel references as of November 2026; tax and quotes vary. Not buying advice.

Alternatives and upgrades: do not add money on the wrong axis

  • Phone + lav first
  • Rent a wireless lav kit
  • Add a dynamic mic for interiors

Buying steps: bring footage, not spec sheets

Run these in order before paying. If one fails, do not tell yourself post will fix it.

  1. Record room tone
  2. Test normal/shout clipping
  3. Test 30° off-axis
  4. Handheld walk for cable noise
  5. Confirm power and runtime

Check

  • Quiet-room noise is acceptable.
  • Normal speech does not clip.
  • 30° off-axis stays intelligible.
  • Handling has no rub/line noise.
  • Headphone monitoring and manual gain exist.
  • Runtime covers the shoot day.

Decision tree: say what you are recording

Interior interview, moving exterior and multi-person scene are three different answers. Interior interview favors a dynamic/shotgun mic plus recorder; moving exterior favors lavs with wind protection; multi-person favors a multichannel recorder and timecode. Do not force one kit to cover all three.

  1. Write the distance: fixed under 1m, moving under 3m, multi-person under 10m.
  2. Interior: directional mic; exterior: lav/wireless; multi-person: multichannel.
  3. Confirm manual gain, headphone monitoring and 48V/plug-in power.
  4. Total the batteries, cards, wind protection and backup recording.

Eight comparisons: expensive is not the same as suitable

ItemPass lineFitsDoes not fit
Mic typeDynamic/shotgun/lav matches the sceneInterior/moving/multiOne mic for everything
Self-noiseNo obvious hiss at 50% gain in a quiet roomQuiet interviewHigh SPL event
Max SPLNormal shout does not clipPerformance, eventWhispers only
Off-axis30° off-axis stays intelligibleRoundtableSingle fixed subject
HandlingNo rub or cable noise while walkingMoving shootFixed camera
Wireless range30m line of sight, recoverable dropoutExterior movementFixed interview
PowerBattery covers the shoot dayAll-day exteriorStudio mains
Total costMic + recorder + wind + backupEvery projectMic only

Test scope: room tone and dialogue separately

Record 30 seconds of room tone, 30 seconds of normal speech and one close shout. Listen on headphones for noise, clipping, sibilance and plosives, then play it once at low speaker volume. Not measured: frequency response, THD, lab isolation. Those numbers are not printed here.

en.summary: The first light kit is not the brightest; it is the easiest to control skin and shadow. Soft area, consistent color, and dimmability matter more than peak output.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Buying a Light Kit: Soft Before Bright

Tools / Buying guide

Buying a Light Kit: Soft Before Bright

The first light kit is not the brightest; it is the easiest to control skin and shadow. Soft area, consistent color, and dimmability matter more than peak output.

8 min read · Buying guideTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Buy one large soft source plus a reflector/diffusion, then a second light. The first light must dim, hold color, and run quiet. On a budget, solve direction and softness on a face before buying color effects.

Fits:

  • Interview/voiceover, one or two
  • Indoor product, controlled ratio
  • Small crew, fast setup

Does not fit:

  • Large events needing high output
  • Bright exteriors needing power
  • Complex color effects

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Put the light through a softbox on a face. Shoot normal skin, shadow side, and highlight. Record 30 seconds of sync sound for fan noise. Put two lights at the same temperature on one wall and compare.

CheckPass lineReference/log
显色肤色自然，不偏绿/品人脸 4K 回放
输出柔光后 ISO 800 可用测光表/波形
色温两灯同场景无跳色双灯对比
噪声1 米录音无风扇声30 秒同期
控光能做出 2:1–4:1 光比柔光/旗板

Price bands: total cost of ownership first

Look beyond the sticker: cards, batteries, adapters, gimbal, stands, software subscriptions, and repair. Bands describe the minimum kit for a real project type, not toy pricing.

TierReferenceIncludesWatch
Entry¥1,000–3,000One COB + softbox + standLimited output/color
Main¥3,000–8,000Two COBs + softbox/grid + reflectorBattery/control extra
Advanced¥8,000–20,000Three lights, RGB, pro control, wirelessWeight and power

Prices are China mainland channel references as of November 2026; tax and quotes vary. Not buying advice.

Alternatives and upgrades: do not add money on the wrong axis

  • One light + reflector
  • Rent two COBs
  • Window light + diffusion

Buying steps: bring footage, not spec sheets

Run these in order before paying. If one fails, do not tell yourself post will fix it.

  1. Softbox on face in 4K
  2. Meter ISO 800 through diffusion
  3. Two-light color match
  4. Record fan at 1m
  5. Build 2:1/4:1 ratio

Check

  • First light is soft and dimmable.
  • Skin is not green/magenta.
  • ISO 800 works through diffusion.
  • Two lights match color.
  • No fan noise at 1m.
  • Softbox/flag can build ratio.

Decision tree: soft or hard, power, then power supply

More light is not better light. Close portraits need soft; product detail needs hard; night exteriors need spill control. Decide soft/hard first, choose power by distance, then battery or mains.

  1. Write the subject distance: 0.5m, 1.5m, 3m.
  2. Close portrait: softbox/lantern; product: bare head plus control.
  3. Estimate power from distance and aperture, not wattage alone.
  4. Mains for fixed interior, battery for exterior; budget runtime and weight.

Eight comparisons: brightness is not the only metric

ItemPass lineFitsDoes not fit
OutputAt 1.5m through a softbox, ISO 800/1/50 reaches f/4Single interviewLarge daylight exterior
ColourCRI/TLCI public; skin not greenPeople, productRim only
Beam angleSoft and spot attachmentsMultiple scenesFixed soft only
Colour temp2700–6500K, bi-colour without shiftMixed lightSingle temp
FlickerNo banding at 1/50VideoHigh-speed
Fan noiseInaudible at 1mSync soundSilent set
PowerBattery covers half a day; hot-swapExteriorFixed studio
Total costHead + softbox + stand + sandbag + batteryEvery projectHead only

Test scope: white wall, grey card, flicker, fan noise

At 1.5m, shoot a white wall at three levels and check centre-to-edge falloff; place a grey card to see skin shift; shoot a fan/tube at 1/50 for banding; record 30 seconds of room tone for fan noise. Not measured: integrating sphere, spectrometer, lab flicker.

Continue: lighting hub

Read the fixture, then control and exposure.

  • Buying LED: output, flicker, power
  • Softbox: size decides softness
  • COB light: one head plus softbox
  • LED panel: colour and output
  • Light gels: CTO, CTB, ND
  • One-light portrait: direction first
  • Window fill: reflector position
  • Stands and sandbags: safety first
  • Exposure check: waveform, zebra, false colour
  • Night practicals: balance exposure

Verification and price date

Verified 2026-11-23. Prices are China mainland channel references; only white-wall and grey-card short tests were done, not integrating-sphere or spectrometer measurement.

Buying order: rent before buying

Rent one head and softbox for a close-up; confirm output, colour and fan noise before buying a second.

  1. Rent the target body and a common lens once; shoot a real project.
  2. Confirm mount, adapter, autofocus and power.
  3. Total the cards, batteries, monitor, storage and repair.
  4. Keep 10% for surprises and consumables.
  5. Buy the second lens after the first delivery.

Add: failure cases

The common lighting mistake is buying wattage instead of distance and softness.

MoveResultReplace with
Judge wattage without a softboxClose-ups go hard and skin shinesTest with the softbox
Bare head with no controlSpill flattens the backgroundBuy diffusion/flags first
Ignore fan noiseSync dialogue is full of humRecord 30 seconds before deciding

Add: pre-purchase checklist

A light is bought to make a face clean at 1.5m, not to look good in a shop. Pay only after four checks.

CheckPass lineLog
SoftboxEven pool at 1.5m; edge not hardWhite-wall test
FlickerNo banding at 1/50Fan/tube shot
Fan noiseInaudible at 1mThirty-second recording
PowerBattery covers half a dayDischarge test

One line for the set

Give the face a direction before giving it more output; wrong direction plus power only looks faker.

Boundary: brighter is not better

Too much output flattens the room and makes the subject squint. Give the face direction, then match power to aperture and distance; do not use power to solve a small-light problem.

en.title: Buying Project Storage: Speed, Capacity, and Backup
en.summary: Storage is not “bigger is better.” It is “the shoot does not stop, the offload does not lose data, and the project is findable later.” Calculate a real shoot day before buying.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Buying Project Storage: Speed, Capacity, and Backup

Tools / Buying guide

Buying Project Storage: Speed, Capacity, and Backup

Storage is not “bigger is better.” It is “the shoot does not stop, the offload does not lose data, and the project is findable later.” Calculate a real shoot day before buying.

8 min read · Buying guideTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Calculate a shoot day: camera bitrate × hours × cameras × copies. 4K 10-bit 422 is roughly 100–200 GB/hour; three cameras for eight hours is 2.4–4.8 TB before copies. Size for the worst day, not “enough this year.”

Fits:

  • Multicam/high-bitrate projects
  • On-set offload and backup
  • Long-term project archive

Does not fit:

  • Single-camera 1080p lightweight work
  • One drive for everything
  • Using NAS as an on-set drive

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Record 30 minutes at the project bitrate or copy a 100GB file and log real write speed and throttling. Do not trust the interface label: USB-C is not Thunderbolt, and a spinning drive cannot saturate 10GbE.

CheckPass lineReference/log
持续写入项目码率 2 倍以上，30 分钟不降满盘/大文件
容量最坏拍摄日 2 份仍有余量项目日计算
接口实际拷贝速度达标100GB 计时
散热连续工作不烫手/不降速30 分钟
保修3–5 年，可换盘/可恢复发票/序列

Price bands: total cost of ownership first

Look beyond the sticker: cards, batteries, adapters, gimbal, stands, software subscriptions, and repair. Bands describe the minimum kit for a real project type, not toy pricing.

TierReferenceIncludesWatch
Entry¥1,000–3,0002–4TB portable SSD + backup driveLimited capacity/sustained write
Main¥3,000–8,0004–8TB fast SSD + two backupsInterface and heat
Advanced¥8,000–25,000NAS/array + 10GbE + offsiteOps and power

Prices are China mainland channel references as of November 2026; tax and quotes vary. Not buying advice.

Alternatives and upgrades: do not add money on the wrong axis

  • Two ordinary SSDs for double backup
  • Rent an on-set DIT
  • Existing drives + cloud backup

Buying steps: bring footage, not spec sheets

Run these in order before paying. If one fails, do not tell yourself post will fix it.

  1. Calculate worst shoot day
  2. Record 30 min at project bitrate
  3. Time a 100GB copy
  4. Confirm interface and power
  5. Check warranty/data recovery

Check

  • Two copies of the worst day fit.
  • Sustained write is 2× bitrate.
  • Copy speed meets the real need.
  • No throttle in 30 minutes.
  • At least two copies on separate media/site.
  • Warranty and recovery are known.

Decision tree: working disk, backup, archive

Most people treat storage as one drive, then lose the working disk with no backup or keep an archive too slow to use. Split three layers: working fast, backup independent, archive readable in ten years.

  1. Working: SSD/RAID 0, capacity covers the current project, speed at least twice the project bitrate.
  2. Backup: independent HDD/NAS, at least one offline copy.
  3. Archive: LTO or cold drive, verifiable and restorable.
  4. Name, checksum and retention for every layer.

Eight comparisons: capacity, speed and redundancy cannot all win

ItemPass lineFitsDoes not fit
Working diskSustained write at twice project bitrateEditingLong archive
RAID 0Two-drive speed with a separate backupWorking diskOnly copy
RAID 1/5Rebuilds after one drive failureTeam shareExtreme writes
NAS10GbE reaches about 500MB/sMulti-userSingle mobile
Portable driveStable USB 10GbpsOn-set backupLong cold archive
LTOOffline, verifiable, long lifeArchiveFrequent access
CloudRestore time acceptableOff-site backupDaily edit of large projects
Total costWorking + backup + archive + restore drillEvery projectPrice per TB only

Test scope: sustained write and restore drill

Write for thirty minutes and log speed, temperature and dropout; restore a random file from backup and time it; compare checksums. Not measured: lab IOPS or long-term aging.

Continue: storage and backup hub

Cards first, then arrays and backup.

  • Buying cards: VPG, sustained write, heat
  • Buying NAS/RAID: throughput, rebuild, noise
  • SSD RAID: editing array
  • 3-2-1 backup: finish it today
  • Restore drill: pick one random file
  • Media management: back up today, name for search
  • Media cart: offload and naming on set
  • LTO archive: long-term cold storage
  • ProRes export: archive and delivery
  • Proxy creation: edit without stutter

Verification and price date

Verified 2026-11-23. Prices are China mainland channel references; sustained write and restore times are local short tests, not lab scores.

Buying order: rent before buying

Borrow a card/SSD for one real project; log sustained write and offload time before choosing capacity and redundancy.

  1. Rent the target body and a common lens once; shoot a real project.
  2. Confirm mount, adapter, autofocus and power.
  3. Total the cards, batteries, monitor, storage and repair.
  4. Keep 10% for surprises and consumables.
  5. Buy the second lens after the first delivery.

Add: failure cases

The most common storage error is treating RAID 0 as the only copy.

MoveResultReplace with
Keep the only footage on RAID 0One drive failure loses the projectIndependent backup
Test peak speed onlySustained writes drop and the edit stallsThirty-minute write
Use a USB hubShared bandwidth halves speedConnect directly

Add: pre-purchase checklist

Storage fails on the project day. Run a restore drill before buying.

CheckPass lineLog
Sustained writeThirty minutes at twice project bitrateSpeed screenshot
BackupAt least one independent copyBackup list
RestoreA random file restoresRestore timing
ChecksumMatchesVerification tool

One line for the set

The working disk may fail; the backup must not fail with it. That is the whole point of three layers.

en.html:
Home/Tools/Buying a Monitor: Brightness, Gamut, and Latency

Tools / Buying guide

Buying a Monitor: Brightness, Gamut, and Latency

A monitor is not a bigger screen. It must be bright enough outdoors, calibratable, and low-latency for focus; if one fails, the camera screen is better.

3 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

500 nits is enough indoors; outdoors needs 1000+ or a hood. Do not buy on specs: bring the camera, your Log footage, load a LUT, and shoot a moving object to check latency.

Fits:

  • Exterior/high light, high nits
  • Grade/multicam, LUT and calibration
  • Focus pulling, low latency

Does not fit:

  • Indoor locked-off, camera screen is enough
  • Client viewing only, no calibration
  • Very low budget, buy light/audio first

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Take the monitor to a window/outdoors and see whether shadows remain visible at 1000 nits. Connect the camera, load the project LUT, compare with the camera screen. Shoot a moving object and check smear/lag.

en.html:
Home/Tools/Buying a Tripod: Payload, Torsion, and Height

Tools / Buying guide

Buying a Tripod: Payload, Torsion, and Height

A tripod’s payload rating is not a safety line. Leg stiffness, head lock, torsional rigidity, and centre of gravity decide stability; a flexy tripod rated 20kg still shakes in wind.

3 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Weigh the real rig: body + lens + monitor + battery + head. Payload should be at least 2×, but leg diameter and locking matter more. For video, prioritize eye-level height without raising the centre column; for stills, folded length matters.

Fits:

  • Interview/locked-off
  • Long lens/time-lapse
  • Windy exterior, stability

Does not fit:

  • Frequent travel
  • Handheld only
  • Extreme low-angle macro

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Mount your heaviest rig at eye level and lock the head. Push lightly and watch rebound. Shoot a 2-second exposure at the longest focal length. Shoot a 30-second time-lapse and check head sag.

CheckPass lineReference/log

扭转轻推后无持续晃动手推回弹

云台漂移锁紧 30 秒不下垂延时
高度不升中轴到眼平现场站位

Run these in order before paying. If one fails, do not tell yourself post will fix it.

  1. Weigh the real rig
  2. Eye level without column
  3. Long lens 2-sec exposure
  4. 30-sec time-lapse drift
  5. Check locks and feet

Check

  • Payload at least 2× rig weight.
  • Eye level without centre column.

  • Leg locks do not slip.

Home/Tools/Renting Lighting: List and Damage

Tools / Buying & fixes

Renting Lighting: List and Damage

List, test, and photograph the gear; one missing soft box costs an hour on set.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Draw the positions: key, fill, rim, background. For each, decide size, color temperature and diffusion. Rent by position, not “more is better.”

Rent by lighting roles, not lamp count

Test each lamp at pickup for color, output, flicker and accessories; shoot a phone clip for banding.

Limits

More lamps is not better light. Two fighting from one position lose to one lamp and a diffusion frame. Get direction right, then quantity.

On set

List every light, softbox, stand, sandbag, and cable. Test each at pickup and video the condition.

Do this

Light rental: list every item, test every unit, and record damage. One missing softbox costs an hour on set.

  1. List lights, softboxes, stands, sandbags, cables, and gels.
  2. Power up each unit and test color temperature and output.
  3. Video the condition and accessories; compare before returning.

Avoid

Do not count heads only; one missing softbox or mount stops the shoot.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. The list covers lights, softboxes, stands, sandbags, cables, and gels.
  • 2. Every unit was powered up and tested for color temperature and output.
  • 3. Condition and accessories are videoed and checked before return.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“The list covers lights, softboxes, stands, san…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Every unit was powered up and tested for color…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not count heads only; one missing softbox or mount stops the shoot.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “List lights, softboxes, stands, sandbags, cables, and gels.”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • The list covers lights, softboxes, stands, sandbags, cables, and gels.
  • Every unit was powered up and tested for color temperature and output.
  • Condition and accessories are videoed and checked before return.

en.title: Used Gear Check: Shutter, Mount, Sensor
en.summary: Check shutter count, mount play, and sensor dead pixels before paying.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Used Gear Check: Shutter, Mount, Sensor

Tools / Buying & fixes

Used Gear Check: Shutter, Mount, Sensor

Check shutter count, mount play, and sensor dead pixels before paying.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Body: shutter count, sensor dead pixels, card slots, ports, screw marks. Lens: fungus, haze, scratches, aperture blades, autofocus. Audio: battery corrosion and XLR locks. Test each in person.

Check whether used gear was repaired before whether it is cheap

Record serial number, boot screen and test results before paying; do not rely on seller photos.

Limits

Too far below market usually has a reason. Do not bargain-hunt past the tests; one motherboard repair erases the savings.

On set

Check shutter count, mount play, and sensor spots. Shoot a white wall and the sky and inspect the files.

Do this

Used gear: check shutter, mount, and sensor. Pay only after all three pass.

  1. Check shutter count or hours and ask for repair history.
  2. Mount a lens and wiggle the mount; check play and contacts.
  3. Shoot a white wall and the sky, then review for dead pixels and vignetting.

Avoid

Do not judge by cosmetics; shutter and sensor are the real cost.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Shutter count, hours, and repair history are known.
  • 2. Mount play and contacts are checked.
  • 3. White-wall and sky frames show no dead pixels or vignetting.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Shutter count, hours, and repair history are k…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Mount play and contacts are checked”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not judge by cosmetics; shutter and sensor are the real cost.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Check shutter count or hours and ask for”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Shutter count, hours, and repair history are known.
  • Mount play and contacts are checked.
  • White-wall and sky frames show no dead pixels or vignetting.

en.title: Overheating Fix: Cool, Segment, Lower Bitrate
en.summary: Cool it, shoot in segments, lower bitrate; do not put a wet towel on the body.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Overheating Fix: Cool, Segment, Lower Bitrate

Tools / Buying & fixes

Overheating Fix: Cool, Segment, Lower Bitrate

Cool it, shoot in segments, lower bitrate; do not put a wet towel on the body.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

For long takes, lower resolution, frame rate, bitrate and screen brightness to a stable setting; disable IBIS and wireless, remove the battery to cool. Check temperature every twenty to thirty minutes and swap cards early.

Drop specs before the camera dies

Do not blow a fan directly at the sensor; it adds vibration and dust. Use vents and shade.

Limits

Overheating is not “broken.” It appears with heat, direct sun and high bitrate together; change conditions before blaming the body.

On set

Lower the bitrate, turn off stabilization, open the battery door, and shoot in shorter takes. Never put a wet towel on the body.

Do this

Overheating: cool it, shoot in blocks, lower the bitrate. Do not put a wet towel on the body.

  1. Lower resolution or bitrate and turn off in-body stabilization and long monitoring.
  2. Open the battery door or add a heat sink; keep the body out of direct sun.
  3. Stop for five minutes every twenty and shoot in shorter blocks.

Avoid

Do not use a wet towel or ice pack directly; condensation shorts the camera.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Resolution or bitrate is lower and stabilization and long monitoring are off.
  • 2. The battery door or heat sink is handled and the body is out of direct sun.
  • 3. The camera stops five minutes every twenty and shoots in blocks.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Resolution or bitrate is lower and stabilizati…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“The battery door or heat sink is handled and t…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not use a wet towel or ice pack directly; condensation shorts the camera.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Lower resolution or bitrate and turn off in-body”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Resolution or bitrate is lower and stabilization and long monitoring are off.
  • The battery door or heat sink is handled and the body is out of direct sun.
  • The camera stops five minutes every twenty and shoots in blocks.

en.title: Jelly Effect Fix: Read Speed and Shutter
en.summary: Rolling shutter comes from slow readout and fast motion; change body or shutter before blaming the lens.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Jelly Effect Fix: Read Speed and Shutter

Tools / Buying & fixes

Jelly Effect Fix: Read Speed and Shutter

Rolling shutter comes from slow readout and fast motion; change body or shutter before blaming the lens.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Rolling shutter shows most in fast lateral moves: poles lean, faces narrow, hands bend. Avoid fast pans, use a wider lens and steadier support; stabilization can crop but cannot restore shape.

Read the direction of motion for rolling shutter

For fast action, use a global-shutter camera or slow the action; do not “fix” heavy skew in post.

Limits

Mild skew is acceptable. The audience does not freeze-frame poles; if the action reads, do not reshoot everything.

On set

Pan fast across a railing and check for bent lines. Change the camera or use a global shutter; post cannot fix it.

Do this

Rolling shutter comes from slow readout plus fast motion. Change the camera or use a global shutter before touching shutter speed.

  1. Pan across a railing or window and review whether straight lines bend.
  2. Use a faster-readout camera or a global shutter.
  3. Reduce fast whips; use locked-off shots and slow pans.

Avoid

Do not blame the lens; CMOS readout speed is the cause.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. A pan across a railing or window was shot and straight lines reviewed.
  • 2. A faster-readout camera or global shutter is used.
  • 3. Fast whips are reduced; locked-off shots and slow pans replace them.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“A pan across a railing or window was shot and…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“A faster-readout camera or global shutter is u…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not blame the lens; CMOS readout speed is the cause.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Pan across a railing or window and review”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • A pan across a railing or window was shot and straight lines reviewed.
  • A faster-readout camera or global shutter is used.
  • Fast whips are reduced; locked-off shots and slow pans replace them.

en.title: Audio Noise Fix: Start With the Room
en.summary: Start with the room: air conditioning, lights, outlet, cable; blame the mic last.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Audio Noise Fix: Start With the Room

Tools / Buying & fixes

Audio Noise Fix: Start With the Room

Start with the room: air conditioning, lights, outlet, cable; blame the mic last.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Three kinds: constant floor (AC, fan), intermittent (door, car), voice flaws (sibilance, plosives). Constant floor can be reduced; intermittent must be cut or re-recorded; sibilance uses EQ and de-essing, not global denoise.

Classify noise before choosing a tool

Keep an untouched track; after processing, listen for muffled or metallic dialogue. A little floor is better than a robot voice.

Limits

Denoise cannot rescue unintelligible dialogue. If speech is mushy, re-record or dub; denoise makes mush more obvious.

On set

Turn off air conditioning, lights, and fans, then change outlets and cables. Record a comparison on a phone to find the source.

Do this

Noise starts in the room: turn off AC, change outlets and cables, blame the mic last.

  1. Turn off AC, fridge, and lights; record thirty seconds of silence.
  2. Change outlets and cables, and put gain on the recorder.
  3. Move the subject closer and record room tone for a bed.

Avoid

Do not buy a new mic first; the noise may be power or the room.

Judge

This page passes on three observable checks, not slogans:

  • 1. Thirty seconds of silence was recorded with AC, fridge, and lights off.
  • 2. Outlets and cables were changed and gain sits on the recorder.
  • 3. The subject is close to the mic and room tone exists.

Failures

Any one of these means stop and fix it before post:

  • 1. Check 1 is only staged (“Thirty seconds of silence was recorded with AC…”); another camera position or location exposes it.
  • 2. Check 2 is left to post or a verbal explanation (“Outlets and cables were changed and gain sits…”); nothing on set can be rechecked.
  • 3. Do not buy a new mic first; the noise may be power or the room.

Extend

10-minute exercise: Run a 60-second test with the gear you already own, measuring only “Turn off AC, fridge, and lights; record thirty”. Record two numbers: what you need and what the gear actually gives.

Check

  • Thirty seconds of silence was recorded with AC, fridge, and lights off.
  • Outlets and cables were changed and gain sits on the recorder.
  • The subject is close to the mic and room tone exists.
