en.title: 14-Day Live-Action Short
en.summary: Take a 3–8 minute live-action short from scope to delivery in fourteen days with two to four people, one camera, and one mic.
en.html:
Home/Main/14-Day Live-Action Short

Main / Learning path

14-Day Live-Action Short

Take a 3–8 minute live-action short from scope to delivery in fourteen days with two to four people, one camera, and one mic.

6 min read · Intermediate · 6 nodesTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Confirm a crew of two to four for two weeks, a camera that shoots 4K or 1080p, one working mic, one controllable location, and a backup for cast and location.

How the path runs

Fourteen days split into six stages: the first eight are paper and prep, days nine to twelve shoot, the last two are post and delivery. Do not move on without the stage deliverable.

  1. Days 1–2: Set scope: Write who wants what and what blocks them. List three things you cannot afford: crowds, children, animals, rain at night, underwater, multiple locations. Delete three. Set a three-to-eight minute target; if it runs longer, cut scenes before cutting sound. Output: One-line story, three limits, runtime target.
  2. Days 3–4: Script and board: One change per scene: who gains or loses what. Board action before framing; one main action per shot. Draw a camera plan per scene with the axis, window light, and a backup position. Output: Three to five scenes, twelve to twenty shots, one camera plan per scene.
  3. Days 5–6: Crew, location, permits: Confirm cast to the hour, not just the day. Confirm load-in, noise limits, load-out, and the nearest hospital. Ask for permits before shooting in public spaces, shops, transit, or parks. Every critical resource gets a backup and a contact. Output: Cast and location confirmations, permit list, backup contacts.
  4. Days 7–8: Budget and call sheet: Split the budget into people, gear, location, post, and contingency; contingency at least ten percent. Build the schedule backward from the shoot days: fittings, tech scout, and recce. The call sheet lists time, address, contact, parking, meals, nearest hospital, and load-out; send it a day early. Output: A five-block budget, a reverse schedule, a call sheet.
  5. Days 9–12: Shoot: Start each day with a wide and a master so the edit has coverage. On every new setup, check axis and light continuity. Record thirty seconds of room tone before dialogue scenes. Back up and reconcile the shot log before wrap; do not fix yesterday's gap today. Output: Daily media backup, shot log, and a safe master.
  6. Days 13–14: Post and delivery: Cut structure, then clean dialogue, then grade; do not polish effects while the cut is moving. Lock one master: resolution, bitrate, subtitles, loudness, and filename on one delivery sheet. Check the export on a computer, a phone, and a speaker. Output: A finished film, a delivery sheet, a project backup.

Three exercises

  1. Exercise 1: Scout twice: Visit the same location at midday and dusk. Take three photos and write three risks: noise, neighbors, load-out. Output: Three scout photos and three risks.
  2. Exercise 2: One-page call sheet: Write one page for a six-person crew: time, address, contact, parking, meals, hospital, load-out. Output: A call sheet ready to send.
  3. Exercise 3: Three-minute assembly: Cut three minutes from existing footage, keeping only story-moving shots; no music yet. Output: A three-minute v1.

Deliverables

  • One-line story and three limits
  • Three to five scenes and twelve to twenty shots
  • Cast/location confirmations and permit list
  • Five-block budget, reverse schedule, call sheet
  • Daily backups and shot logs
  • A finished film, delivery sheet, and project backup

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating a full pipeline as a big crew: two people can finish if every stage has a deliverable.
  • Shooting an unlocked script: every on-set rewrite resets the board, call sheet, and budget.
  • Skipping backup: one lost card erases the fourteen days.

Next step

Next, take path-producing to make reusable budget, schedule, and risk sheets, or path-post to deepen sound and delivery.

Check

  • The film runs three to eight minutes and has one clear change.
  • Every shoot day has a safe master and a Plan B.
  • Dialogue is audible without subtitles and ambience is continuous.
  • Media has two copies and the project opens offline.
  • Permits, insurance, and contacts are on the call sheet.
  • The master matches the delivery sheet: frame, loudness, captions, filename.

en.title: Story, Script & Storyboard
en.summary: Turn an idea into a repeatable line, three scenes that change, eight to twelve executable shots, and one table read that removes explanation.
en.html:
Home/Main/Story, Script & Storyboard

Main / Learning path

Story, Script & Storyboard

Turn an idea into a repeatable line, three scenes that change, eight to twelve executable shots, and one table read that removes explanation.

5 min read · Learning path · 6 nodesTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Bring three things: a real location you can shoot, a person you can cast, and a real action you have seen. Do not start from a theme; start from what someone wants.

How the path runs

Six steps only: one line, want and stakes, three scenes, eight to twelve shots, table read, rewrite. Every step lands on paper.

  1. One line: who wants what: Each line under forty Chinese characters with one concrete action and one obstacle. Not “a man is lonely,” but “a night guard wants to be seen, but the camera only catches him dozing.” Circle the one that gives you three shots immediately. Output: One logline and three shootable images.
  2. Want and stakes: what losing costs: The want must be concrete: a job, a room, a person turning around. The loss must be visible: money, housing, a relationship, dignity. The price must be an action: lie, borrow, quit, walk ten kilometers. The columns cannot substitute for each other. Output: A three-column character sheet.
  3. Three scenes: one change each: Scene one sets the want, scene two raises the same obstacle, scene three changes the approach. Each scene must end different from it began: relationship, information, or decision. Cut scenes that only explain backstory. Output: Three scenes, one page each maximum.
  4. Eight to twelve shots: break the scene: Write what the audience must see, then choose framing. One main action per shot; every scene needs a wide, a close, and an insert. The sheet lists shot number, framing, action, line, and duration. Output: An eight-to-twelve-shot sheet and one camera plan per scene.
  5. Table read: only three questions: Do not explain or defend during the read. Ask readers to mark three places: unclear, boring, unbelievable. After the read, ask only those three questions, never “is it good?” Output: Three marks and a one-page rewrite list.
  6. Rewrite: cut explanation, add action: Delete “because… therefore…” sentences and replace them with what someone does. Replace “he is angry” with “he puts the cup back; the base clicks.” Read again and confirm every scene still changes. Output: A rewrite with three cuts marked.

Three exercises

  1. Exercise 1: Ten openings: Write ten first lines for the same story; every one is an action already happening. Output: Choose one opening.
  2. Exercise 2: Three scenes on one page: One line each for want, obstacle, turn, and end state. Output: A shootable three-scene sheet.
  3. Exercise 3: Rewrite three places: Have two people read and change only their first three marks. Output: A v2 draft.

Deliverables

  • One logline
  • A want/loss/price sheet
  • Three scenes, one page each
  • An eight-to-twelve-shot sheet
  • One table-read record
  • One rewrite

Where it goes wrong

  • Starting from a theme: “I want to say loneliness” produces explanation; “what does he want” produces action.
  • Two changes in one scene: the audience cannot absorb them and the edit cannot connect them.
  • Boarding as art: the shot sheet is an execution file; framing, action, and duration matter more than drawing.

Next step

Next, take path-live-film to turn the script into a fourteen-day shoot, or path-post to make the three scenes work in the edit.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Contracts, tax, insurance and consent rules differ by market; use the local currency and local counsel before signing or invoicing.

Check

  • The line is repeatable and ends on an action.
  • Every scene changes; removing one breaks the story.
  • One main action per shot.
  • The table read found at least three places needing explanation.
  • The rewrite has less explanation and more action.
  • The eight to twelve shots can be shot with what you have.

en.title: Edit, Grade & Sound
en.summary: A reusable post pipeline from ingest to delivery: structure first, sound second, grade last, then a technical check.
en.html:
Home/Main/Edit, Grade & Sound

Main / Learning path

Edit, Grade & Sound

A reusable post pipeline from ingest to delivery: structure first, sound second, grade last, then a technical check.

6 min read · Learning path · 7 nodesTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Confirm all media is offloaded, a drive twice the media size is free, the editor opens the project, and you know the final platform.

How the path runs

The trap is polishing while the cut is still moving. Seven steps in order: ingest, assembly, rough cut, sound, grade, QC, delivery. Do not skip.

  1. Step 1: Ingest and back up: Name folders date_scene and keep original filenames. Verify copies with checksums, not a progress bar. Keep proxies in a separate folder and treat camera originals as read-only. Back up to a second drive and one offsite copy. Output: Two source copies, proxies, and a media list.
  2. Step 2: Assembly: Lay the safe takes on the timeline by scene and shot number; confirm every shot exists. Mark the best take from the log in the filename. Assembly answers “is it there,” not “is it good.” Output: A complete assembly and best-take marks.
  3. Step 3: Rough cut: Every twenty minutes ask what the viewer knows and what the next shot adds. Three same-length shots in a row need a rhythm change. Trim one or two seconds from each shot. Show the rough cut to a stranger and ask who wants what. Output: A clear rough cut and a problem list.
  4. Step 4: Sound: Clean noise, level, and intelligibility on every line; lay ambience so cuts do not live in a vacuum; add music last. If music covers dialogue, drop it six dB or cut it. Output: A sound-clean mix and a music/ambience list.
  5. Step 5: Grade: Unify exposure and white balance so every shot feels like the same day; then secondary work on skin, sky, and product color. Style comes last; a LUT is not a correction. Calibrate monitor brightness first. Output: A primary-corrected version and a styled version.
  6. Step 6: QC: Run the delivery sheet: runtime, frame, resolution, bitrate, frame rate, loudness, true peak, captions, filename. Listen on headphones and a speaker; watch the vertical cut on a phone; mute it and look for black frames. Output: A QC sheet and a fixed master.
  7. Step 7: Deliver: Keep one master with fixed resolution, bitrate, audio, and captions. Platform cuts derive from it; the master never changes. Name files title_platform_version_date; delivery notes state what is included, excluded, and how many revisions remain. Output: Master, platform cuts, delivery notes, project backup.

Three exercises

  1. Exercise 1: Three-minute assembly: Assemble one scene by shot number for three minutes; do not fix pacing, just confirm coverage. Output: One assembly.
  2. Exercise 2: Sound-only pass: Turn off picture and listen for three minutes; log unclear, broken, or repeated sound. Output: A sound problem list.
  3. Exercise 3: Ten-point QC: Check ten items: runtime, frame, resolution, bitrate, frame rate, loudness, peak, captions, black frames, filename. Output: A QC sheet.

Deliverables

  • Two source copies and proxies
  • An assembly
  • A clear rough cut
  • A sound-clean mix
  • Primary and styled versions
  • A QC sheet
  • Master, platform cuts, delivery notes

Where it goes wrong

  • Grading before structure: every structural change wastes the grade.
  • Covering dialogue with music: viewers forgive ordinary images, not unintelligible words.
  • Naming files “final for real”: version chaos loses the master.

Next step

Next, take path-distribution for platform cuts, titles, covers, and review, or return to path-live-film to improve coverage.

Check

  • Two source copies exist and the project opens offline.
  • A stranger can say who wants what.
  • Every line is audible without subtitles.
  • No color jumps between shots and skin is neutral.
  • All ten QC items have pass/fail.
  • One master exists; platform cuts derive from it.

en.title: Image History
en.summary: Use four timelines to see which old problem each image technology solved: photography, cinema, sound, TV, digital, and generation.
en.html:
Home/Main/Image History

Main / Learning path

Image History

Use four timelines to see which old problem each image technology solved: photography, cinema, sound, TV, digital, and generation.

5 min read · Learning path · 6 nodesTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Pick four works: a nineteenth-century photograph, a 1920s silent film, a 1950s TV segment, and a 2020s generated video. Watch five minutes each, no notes.

How the path runs

No date memorization. Each node answers two questions: what old method did it replace, and what new limit did it add?

  1. 1839: Photography makes reality copyable: Photography brought a claim of evidence: someone can say “this was there then.” It also brought new problems: exposure time, framing, who is photographed, who is absent. Ask who stood before the camera, then who did not. Output: One note on what photography replaced.
  2. 1895: Cinema starts charging: Cinema turned images from solo viewing into a public event: screen, seats, darkness, collective reaction. Editing followed because an audience had to follow multiple places within an hour. Film history is the history of how audiences are organized, not just gear. Output: One note on what public viewing changed.
  3. 1927: Sound enters the frame: Synchronized dialogue stopped actors from explaining everything with the body, and cuts could not be arbitrary because sound had to continue. Recording gear constrained camera positions and forced new blocking. Technology rewrote performance and editing. Output: Two comparison notes: performance and editing.
  4. 1950s: TV moves cinema home: Smaller screens brought viewers closer and pushed framing closer. Slots, ads, and seasons cut content into fixed durations. TV was not “small cinema”; it invented its own time units: thirty minutes, sixty seconds, the same hour every week. Output: One note on TV's time units.
  5. 2000s: Digital cuts the cost: Digital shooting made takes cheap, editing moved from suites to laptops, and distribution moved from cinemas and TV to the web. Cost did not vanish; it moved to storage, backup, version control, and attention. Digital is not free; the bill moved. Output: An old-cost/new-cost table.
  6. 2020s: Images start being generated: Generation turns shooting into sampling: a shot need not exist first; it can be described. The old problems were sets, cast, weather, and budget. The new ones are consistency, provenance, rights, disclosure, and whether the shot ever happened. The more it looks real, the harder evidence becomes. Output: One note on what generation adds.

Three exercises

  1. Exercise 1: Four timelines on one page: Draw four lines: photography, cinema, sound/TV, digital/generation; five nodes each. Output: One page of timelines.
  2. Exercise 2: Before and after one work: Pick one work and write how people solved the same problem before and after it. Output: Two paragraphs, two hundred characters each.
  3. Exercise 3: Three limits of a technology: Pick a technology you use and write three things it cannot do. Output: Three limits.

Deliverables

  • One page of four timelines
  • Three work analyses
  • One old-problem/new-problem table
  • One technology-limit list

Where it goes wrong

  • Memorizing a timeline: forgetting years is fine; naming what replaced what is not.
  • Only directors and masterpieces: technical history is also workers, audiences, distribution, and censorship.
  • Technological determinism: technology offers possibilities; people decide use and exclusion.

Next step

Next, take path-literacy to turn history into source and context judgment, or read the specific nodes on the context site.

Check

  • Each node names the old method it replaced.
  • Each node also names a new limit.
  • At least one work is analyzed, not just dated.
  • “New” is not treated as “good.”
  • Dates may be approximate, but causality is clear.
  • You can name a limit of a technology you use.

en.title: Media Literacy
en.summary: Judge a video in a fixed order: source, edit, context, money, AI traces, charts, rights. Pause before concluding.
en.html:
Home/Main/Media Literacy

Main / Learning path

Media Literacy

Judge a video in a fixed order: source, edit, context, money, AI traces, charts, rights. Pause before concluding.

5 min read · Learning path · 7 nodesTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Pick three recent videos: one that made you angry, one that moved you, one you thought was fake. Do not verify yet; write your first reaction.

How the path runs

Media literacy is not “believe nothing”; it is a repeatable order: source, edit, context, then money and rights.

  1. Step 1: Source: Start from the earliest version, not the share chain. Check account history, first post time, cross-platform versions, and visual geography. Find at least two pieces of evidence before naming who. If there is no first post, write “source unknown”; do not fill the gap. Output: A source table: account, time, first link.
  2. Step 2: Edit: The emotional peak is often the densest edit. Look for action cuts, sound cuts, and reaction shots: which step is missing between two shots? Reverse the order and test whether the conclusion still holds. Output: Three cuts and three “what was removed.”
  3. Step 3: Context: Three common cuts: head cut, tail cut, reframing. Return to the original, restore the lines before and after, then check title, cover, and music. Context decides whether a line is a statement, a joke, or irony. Output: Original context and a title/music change table.
  4. Step 4: Money: Look for ad labels, sponsorship, affiliate links, paid promotion, and account ownership. No label does not mean no commercial relationship. Money does not automatically make content false, but it explains why it appears now and why it says this. Output: A money-relationship map.
  5. Step 5: AI traces: A trace shows a tool failed; it does not settle truth alone. Log all five checks, then weigh the source. A generated video can tell a true story; live footage can be edited into a lie. Output: A five-point check table.
  6. Step 6: Charts: Does the axis start at zero? Who is the sample? Which period was chosen? What is the denominator? Correlation is not causation. Charts lie less through numbers than through what is left out. Output: Four chart checks.
  7. Step 7: Rights: “Downloadable” is not “commercial use.” Music, fonts, footage, likeness, and location: missing one can take a film down. For your own work, keep releases in the project folder; for others, ask whether rights are cleared. Output: A five-item rights list.

Three exercises

  1. Exercise 1: Source table for one video: Find first post, account history, cross-platform versions, visual geography; mark unknown if missing. Output: A source table.
  2. Exercise 2: Reverse the order: Take a causal video, swap two shots, and test the conclusion. Output: A two-hundred-character analysis.
  3. Exercise 3: Five-item rights list: List music, font, footage, likeness, and location for your next film. Output: An actionable list.

Deliverables

  • A source table
  • Three cut analyses
  • Original context
  • A money map
  • A five-point AI check
  • Four chart checks
  • A five-item rights list

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating an AI artifact as proof of a fake: it shows a tool failed, not what happened.
  • Concluding from one source: use two independent sources or mark unknown.
  • Treating “downloadable” as “commercial”: rights are five items, not one image.

Next step

Next, take path-history to see where the technology came from, or read platform rules, copyright, and ethics on the context site.

Check

  • Find the first post before commenting.
  • Name the step a cut removed.
  • Restore at least one truncated context.
  • Name a beneficiary or write “not found.”
  • An AI trace is not a truth verdict by itself.
  • Chart check finds at least one omission.

en.title: Producing & Management
en.summary: Producing is not ordering lunch; it locks scope, money, people, time, permits, and risk into one table, and knows which overrun stops the shoot.
en.meta: 5 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Learning path · 7 nodes
en.html:
Home/Main/Producing & Management

Main / Learning path

Producing & Management

Producing is not ordering lunch; it locks scope, money, people, time, permits, and risk into one table, and knows which overrun stops the shoot.

5 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Learning path · 7 nodesTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Bring a real project with cast, location, gear, budget, and a delivery date. If none, use a film you will actually shoot in the next three months, not a hypothetical.

How the path runs

Producing works backward: define the stop line, build the schedule backward, then fill the budget. Do not start with a gear list and discover the money is short.

  1. Step 1: Scope: Three columns: deliverables, non-deliverables, revisions. Put “one more cut” and “one more subtitle language” under out of scope or a separate quote. Scope is a contract exhibit, not a wish list. Output: A one-page scope sheet.
  2. Step 2: Budget: Each block has a cap and cannot borrow from another. Contingency sits before the shoot, not at the end. The budget must answer “if one day disappears, which block is cut?” If not, it is numbers, not a decision tool. Rights, insurance, and transport get their own rows. Output: A five-block budget and one “cut first” answer.
  3. Step 3: Schedule: Lock delivery, then reserve thirty percent for post, forty for shoot, thirty for prep. Shoot the same location on the same day; shoot difficult light and children first. Leave a pickup window each day. Put a latest-decision date for cast, location, and gear. Output: A reverse schedule and three latest-decision dates.
  4. Step 4: People: Director, camera, sound, light, producing, post: who does it, who backs up, who to call. Do not write “we'll figure it out.” A key role without a backup is project risk. Output: A crew table: role/primary/backup/contact.
  5. Step 5: Permits and risk: Ask for permits for public space, shops, transit, and parks; confirm insurance covers gear and third parties. Risk sheet: who can get hurt, what can fall, who owns it, nearest hospital. The whole crew reads it; producing does not sign alone. Output: Permit list, risk sheet, nearest hospital.
  6. Step 6: Shoot day: Send the call sheet a day early with time, address, contact, parking, meals, hospital, load-out. Ten minutes before roll, the crew names the three must-get shots. Before wrap, confirm backup, log, prop return, and tomorrow's call sheet. Output: Daily call sheet, three must-get shots, wrap checklist.
  7. Step 7: Delivery and close: Lock one master with resolution, bitrate, captions, loudness, and filename. Archive releases by project for at least three years. Close with a review: where the budget overran, where the schedule failed, what changes next time. Output: Master, delivery sheet, rights archive, review.

Three exercises

  1. Exercise 1: One-page scope: Write deliverables/non-deliverables/revisions; show it to someone outside the project. Output: A one-page scope.
  2. Exercise 2: Reverse schedule: Build fourteen days backward from delivery and mark three latest-decision dates. Output: A reverse schedule.
  3. Exercise 3: Risk sheet: List weather, gear, people, and rights risks with one owner each. Output: A four-row risk sheet.

Deliverables

  • One-page scope
  • Five-block budget
  • Reverse schedule and three latest-decision dates
  • Crew table with backups
  • Permit list and risk sheet
  • Daily call sheet and wrap checklist
  • Master, delivery sheet, rights archive, review

Where it goes wrong

  • Starting with a gear list: gear is a result, not a starting point; lock scope and delivery first.
  • Expanding scope with “we'll do it first”: if money and time do not change, the project ends badly.
  • A risk sheet only producing reads: if the crew does not read it, it does not exist.

Next step

Next, take path-distribution to release, or return to path-live-film to tighten shoot execution.

Check

  • Scope states exclusions and revision count.
  • Contingency is at least ten percent; every block is capped.
  • Every key role has a backup and a contact.
  • Every shoot day has a Plan B.
  • Permits, insurance, noise, load-out, and hospital sit on one sheet.
  • One master, archived rights, and one concrete review change.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. Producing is not managing people. It is keeping money, time, crew, and permission on the same sheet.

Four budget blocks

Prep, shoot, post, contingency. Each block has a cap; do not borrow across them. Contingency is at least ten percent, held before the shoot, not at the end. Talent, location, music, and font licenses get their own line.

The budget must answer “if we lose a day, which block gets cut?” If it cannot, it is a list of numbers, not a decision tool.

Schedule and call sheet

Break the script into strips: scene, pages, cast, props, camera. Shoot the same location on the same day; schedule the difficult light and children first. Leave one pickup window each day; do not fill every hour.

The call sheet states time, address, contact, parking, meals, nearest hospital. Send it the day before, not the morning of. Everyone should know when to arrive and what they are doing.

Risk, permits, delivery

Before rolling, fill one risk page: who can get hurt, what can fall, who is responsible, nearest hospital. Read it to the crew. For public space, shops, subway, parks, ask permission first; do not shoot and apologize later.

Before delivery, define one master: resolution, bitrate, subtitles, loudness, naming. Keep three backups, one off-site. Producing does not end at wrap; it ends when the next person can find the files and the rights.

Five-minute drill: one-page production sheet

Take a small project and write one page: four budget blocks, two shoot days, five scenes, three names, three permits, one delivery spec. Every row gets an owner and a date.

Show it to someone outside the project and ask, “if it rains tomorrow, which row changes first?” If they can answer, the sheet works. If not, add priorities.

Ten producing checks

  • Budget in four blocks
  • Contingency at least ten percent
  • Licenses on their own line
  • Budget answers what gets cut first
  • Script broken into strips
  • Same location, same day
  • Pickup window each day
  • Call sheet sent the day before
  • Risk page read to crew
  • One master and three backups

Producing is not making everyone listen. It is making everyone know, on the same day, where the money is, where the time is, and who does the next thing.

en.title: Release & Distribution
en.summary: Release is a pipeline, not an upload: master, platform specs, title and cover, captions, SEO, launch, and a forty-eight-hour review.
en.html:
Home/Main/Release & Distribution

Main / Learning path

Release & Distribution

Release is a pipeline, not an upload: master, platform specs, title and cover, captions, SEO, launch, and a forty-eight-hour review.

5 min read · Learning path · 7 nodesTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Confirm a locked master, one primary and two distribution platforms, the platform specs for frame, runtime, captions, and cover, and time to check data forty-eight hours after launch.

How the path runs

Lock the master, derive platform cuts, then write titles and covers. Do not design a cover before the master is locked.

  1. Step 1: Master: The master never changes; every platform cut derives from it. Name it title_master_date and keep a read-only copy. The master holds the fullest captions and highest quality; platform cuts only reframe, compress, and adjust captions. Output: One read-only master and a master spec sheet.
  2. Step 2: Platform specs: Do not rely on memory; check the platform help page before publishing. Vertical is not a center crop: subject, captions, and safe area are redrawn. Give each platform a column and tick it off. Output: A platform spec table.
  3. Step 3: Title and cover: The title promises only what the film delivers: who, what happens, what result. The cover shows an action, not just a pretty face. Title and cover answer the same question; do not pair emotion with information. Output: Five titles, three covers, one reason for the choice.
  4. Step 4: Captions and access: Place platform captions inside the safe area, off faces and hands. Open captions are burned in for silent viewing; SDH labels sound events, not just dialogue. Keep Chinese under sixteen characters and English under forty-two per line. Output: Three caption files and a caption check sheet.
  5. Step 5: Upload and search: Search is not keyword stuffing; it is making the problem obvious. Put the topic in the title, the result and audience in the first two description lines, and format, tool, and setting in tags. After upload, search one keyword yourself. Output: Title, description, tags.
  6. Step 6: Launch: Post one tease before launch; do not give the film away. Watch comments and completion for the first two hours and log specific questions, not just “thanks.” Do not change title, cover, and description on launch day; you will not know which variable worked. Output: A launch checklist, one tease, and a comment-question log.
  7. Step 7: Forty-eight-hour review: Within forty-eight hours log four numbers: completion, three-second retention, traffic source, and repeated comment questions. Do not judge the film from one launch; find one change for next time, such as “open on a person's action instead of scenery.” Output: A review sheet and one next change.

Three exercises

  1. Exercise 1: Five titles, three covers: Write five titles and make three covers for one film; ask someone to choose and explain. Output: Five titles, three covers, one reason.
  2. Exercise 2: One platform cut: Make one vertical cut from the master; redraw subject, captions, and safe area instead of center-cropping. Output: One platform cut.
  3. Exercise 3: Forty-eight-hour review: Forty-eight hours after release, log four numbers and write one concrete change. Output: A review sheet.

Deliverables

  • Read-only master and spec sheet
  • Platform spec table
  • Five titles and three covers
  • Three caption files
  • Title, description, tags
  • Launch checklist and tease
  • Forty-eight-hour review sheet

Where it goes wrong

  • Posting one master everywhere: platforms are not pipes; viewing differs.
  • Making the cover on launch day: a rushed cover gets no clicks.
  • Changing title, cover, and description on the same day: you cannot tell what worked.

Next step

Next, take path-career to turn release results into a portfolio and quotes, or return to path-post to improve delivery quality.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Contracts, tax, insurance and consent rules differ by market; use the local currency and local counsel before signing or invoicing.

Check

  • One master; platform cuts trace back.
  • Each platform has its own spec.
  • The title promises only what the film delivers.
  • Captions clear the subject; SDH includes sound events.
  • One keyword search finds it.
  • Only one variable changes on launch day.
  • Review has four numbers and one concrete change.

en.title: Career & Clients
en.summary: From portfolio, showreel, quote, contract, and delivery to repeat work: turn craft into a sustainable client practice.
en.html:
Home/Main/Career & Clients

Main / Learning path

Career & Clients

From portfolio, showreel, quote, contract, and delivery to repeat work: turn craft into a sustainable client practice.

6 min read · Learning path · 7 nodesTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Bring one to three films you can show, a real role description for each, one target client type, and your minimum acceptable quote.

How the path runs

Client work is not “I can do everything”; it is making one target client see which problem you solve in thirty seconds. Order: target, portfolio, showreel, quote, contract, delivery, repeat.

  1. Step 1: Target client: Not “brands” or “all companies.” Write “a local coffee-shop owner who needs three vertical videos a month and has no shoot time.” Then three problems: no script, no on-camera comfort, no ad plan. The narrower the target, the easier the portfolio. Output: One client profile and three problems.
  2. Step 2: Portfolio: A portfolio is not a pile; it is three proofs of “I solve this problem.” For each: client problem, your approach, your role, result. Do not include films you cannot show or roles you inflate. Output: Three pieces and three role notes.
  3. Step 3: Showreel: A showreel is proof, not a trailer. Put the strongest action in the first ten seconds, then group by skill: people, product, space, motion. Label camera/edit/grade per shot; do not claim all the credit. Output: A sixty-second showreel and a role sheet.
  4. Step 4: Quote: A quote is not one number; it shows where money goes. Days: how many people, how many days. Gear: rented or owned. Post: edit, grade, captions, mix. Licensing: scope, term, platform. Revisions are a number, not “reasonable revisions.” Output: A four-part quote and a revision count.
  5. Step 5: Contract: Six clauses at minimum: scope, rights/term, payment, revisions, delivery format, cancellation/postponement. Payment at thirty/forty/thirty or fifty/fifty; never shoot with zero deposit. Rights state where, how long, and whether the client can sublicense. Output: A six-clause contract skeleton.
  6. Step 6: Delivery: Deliver to the sheet: files, formats, captions, loudness, filenames, releases. The delivery email states what is included, excluded, and how many revisions were used. Archive after sign-off; new requests outside scope get a new quote, not free work. Output: Delivery pack, sign-off email, archive.
  7. Step 7: Repeat and referral: Seven days after delivery, ask three questions: what worked, what fell short, what the next film should solve. Do not just say “let me know.” Offer one concrete next plan: holiday, product launch, monthly package. Repeat work comes from remembering their next step, not a mass message. Output: One follow-up and one next plan.

Three exercises

  1. Exercise 1: Three-piece portfolio: Choose three pieces closest to the target; write problem, approach, role, result. Output: A one-page portfolio.
  2. Exercise 2: Four-part quote: Quote a real project across days, gear, post, and licensing, plus revisions. Output: A quote.
  3. Exercise 3: Six-clause contract: Write scope, rights, payment, revisions, delivery, cancellation; three lines each. Output: A one-page contract skeleton.

Deliverables

  • A client profile and three problems
  • Three portfolio pieces with roles
  • A sixty-second showreel
  • A four-part quote
  • A six-clause contract skeleton
  • A delivery pack and sign-off email
  • One follow-up and next plan

Where it goes wrong

  • Selling “I can do everything”: clients remember the specific problem you solved, not range.
  • Shooting with zero deposit: without payment milestones, the client can vanish.
  • Unlimited free revisions: without a number, the relationship ends badly.

Next step

Next, return to path-distribution to update the portfolio with release data, or path-producing to turn quotes and schedules into reusable templates.

Check

  • The client profile names industry, budget range, and cadence.
  • The portfolio reads in thirty seconds.
  • The showreel uses only your shots and does not inflate roles.
  • The quote has four parts and a numeric revision count.
  • The contract has six clauses and payment dates.
  • Every delivery item is ticked; out-of-scope work is re-quoted.
  • The follow-up asks specific questions; the next plan has timing and scope.

en.title: You Only Have a Vague Idea
en.summary: Do not write a script from a vague idea; write three lines: who wants what, what blocks them, what losing costs.
en.html:
Home/Main/You Only Have a Vague Idea

Main / Method card

You Only Have a Vague Idea

Do not write a script from a vague idea; write three lines: who wants what, what blocks them, what losing costs.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Do not write a script yet. Fill one page with three lines: who, what they want, what blocks them. If any line is an abstract noun (“growth,” “warmth,” “connection”), replace it with a filmable action.

Turn a vague idea into a 30-second test

  1. Find three references: one for the person's state, one for the space, one for the light. Do not collect films in the same genre; collect the sources of the feeling.
  2. Record a 30-second spoken pitch on your phone, unedited. Play it for three uninvolved people and ask what they remember. If they remember different things, the idea is not focused.
  3. Turn the most-questioned sentence into the first scene. If you cannot write an action, keep asking “what is he doing?”

Acceptance: within 30 seconds a listener can repeat “who wants what, and what blocks them.” Only then move to a storyboard; do not discuss gear or style first.

On set

Write three sentences: who wants what, what blocks them, what they lose. If they join into one logline, start the script.

Do this

Write one sentence you can actually shoot: who wants what, what blocks them, and what they lose if they fail. Then compress it into three shots: a person, an action, a result.

  1. Write three sentences, twenty words or fewer, each with a verb and a concrete object.
  2. Pick the one you can finish in one room or one street; cut what needs a built set.
  3. Shoot three tests: a wide for context, a medium for action, a close-up for the result. If they cut together, write scene two.

Avoid

Do not start with backstory and world-building; a setting you cannot shoot is not a story.

Boundary

This page only covers “You Only Have a Vague Idea”; it does not replace The Image Looks Flat, The Lines Sound Read, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “One sentence names who wants what and what blocks them” is not the main problem, start with “The three test shots cut together without voice-over”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: One sentence names who wants what and what blocks them. If check 2 (The three test shots cut together without voice-over) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • One sentence names who wants what and what blocks them.
  • The three test shots cut together without voice-over.
  • Unshootable settings are gone; what remains fits one location.

en.title: You Cannot Write a Script
en.summary: If you cannot write a script, board eight shots with one action each; action will force the lines.
en.html:
Home/Main/You Cannot Write a Script

Main / Method card

You Cannot Write a Script

If you cannot write a script, board eight shots with one action each; action will force the lines.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Turn the three lines into three beats: opening, conflict, ending; one action per beat. Read it to someone who has not seen it and ask them to retell it. If they cannot, the structure is unclear, not the actor.

Write three lines, not ten pages

  • Who: a specific person with a job, an age or an action already in progress.
  • Want: a goal that can be completed today and seen on screen.
  • Blocked by: a specific person, rule, deadline or their own fear.

When not to improvise

Do not improvise without an ending. Improvisation works inside a clear goal and obstacle; it cannot replace structure. Write one page first, then let actors move inside it.

On set

Draw eight panels, one action each, no dialogue. Tell it in order; if it does not flow, change a panel.

Do this

If you cannot write a script, write an eight-panel shot board, one action per panel. Action forces dialogue, not the other way around.

  1. For each panel write “who does what,” with no emotion or explanation.
  2. Give each panel a shootable location, prop, and time.
  3. Read the eight panels in order, cut repeated information, and add one action wherever cause and effect are missing.

Avoid

Do not start with pages of dialogue; lines without action play like a reading on set.

Boundary

This page only covers “You Cannot Write a Script”; it does not replace You Only Have One Room, The Highlights Are Gone, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “Each of the eight panels has one action and no emotion adjectives” is not the main problem, start with “Every panel has a location, prop, and time you can shoot”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Each of the eight panels has one action and no emotion adjectives. If check 2 (Every panel has a location, prop, and time you can shoot) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • Each of the eight panels has one action and no emotion adjectives.
  • Every panel has a location, prop, and time you can shoot.
  • Read in order, cause and effect are clear and repeats are gone.

en.title: You Cannot Find Actors
en.summary: No actors? Shoot hands, backs, objects, and sound; a person can be complete without a face.
en.html:
Home/Main/You Cannot Find Actors

Main / Method card

You Cannot Find Actors

No actors? Shoot hands, backs, objects, and sound; a person can be complete without a face.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Ask for three actions: enter, look for something, hear bad news. Give verbs, not adjectives. Watch whether the response is natural and repeatable. Someone who cannot repeat it will consume the whole day on set.

Do you need “real” or “trained”?

  • Real: job, age, physicality. Casting an actual worker often reads truer than casting an actor.
  • Trained: sustained emotion and dialogue. Untrained performers do better with actions and short lines; do not hand them a long monologue.
  • Controllable: time, consent, availability. A friend is easier to talk to, but familiarity does not replace a release form.

When not to cast a non-actor

Complex crying, long speeches, precise blocking or intimacy carry high risk with an untrained performer. Rewrite the scene or cast someone trained; do not force it on set.

On set

Shoot hands, backs, objects, and sound. Use voice-over or titles; a character can exist without a face.

Do this

If you cannot cast an actor, shoot hands, backs, objects, and sound. Give a real person a real task instead of asking for emotion.

  1. Break the character into four shootable parts: hands, back, profile, shadow.
  2. Find someone willing to do a real task: cook, repair, walk. Give them a concrete job.
  3. Record breath, footsteps, and room tone while they work; let sound fill in the person.

Avoid

Do not ask a non-actor to “play sad.” Ask them to find keys or wait for water to boil; emotion arrives on its own.

Boundary

This page only covers “You Cannot Find Actors”; it does not replace Your Budget Is Zero, You Have No Coverage, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “You have hands, back, profile, and shadow shots” is not the main problem, start with “The non-actor performs a real task, not an emotion at the lens”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: You have hands, back, profile, and shadow shots. If check 2 (The non-actor performs a real task, not an emotion at the lens) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • You have hands, back, profile, and shadow shots.
  • The non-actor performs a real task, not an emotion at the lens.

en.summary: One room works if it changes once during the film: messier, emptier, darker.
en.html:
Home/Main/You Only Have One Room

Main / Method card

You Only Have One Room

One room works if it changes once during the film: messier, emptier, darker.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Shoot six different sizes and angles in one room without repeating a setup: wide, medium, close, low, high and an off-screen sound. Cut 30 seconds and see whether it tells a change. Do not hide flat blocking behind a new location.

Break one room into six shots

  • Blocking: from door to table, table to window; a change in position is a change in scene.
  • Off-screen: sound, a phone, a neighbor, the corridor can double the room.
  • Inserts: hands, a cup, a screen, the gap under a door replace a new location.
  • Light: one lamp or one curtain changes the time of day in the same room.

When not to add a location

If the relationship is not established inside one room, a new location only adds cost. Stage the power relationship in the room first.

On set

Shoot the same room in three states: tidy, messy, empty. Change the space with light and props.

Do this

One room must change on screen: tidy to messy, day to dusk, full to empty. When the space changes, the story moves.

  1. Shoot three empty frames from the same camera position, noting light and props.
  2. Change the space with three actions: open a box, draw the curtain, move the chair away.
  3. Add one close-up detail per stage so the audience sees the change.

Avoid

Do not only change camera positions; the audience will feel the film is circling in place.

Boundary

This page only covers “You Only Have One Room”; it does not replace The Highlights Are Gone, The Pacing Is Flat, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “Three empty frames from one position show light and prop changes” is not the main problem, start with “Three actions leave the space in different states: full, messy, empty”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Three empty frames from one position show light and prop changes. If check 2 (Three actions leave the space in different states: full, messy, empty) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • Three empty frames from one position show light and prop changes.
  • Three actions leave the space in different states: full, messy, empty.
  • One close-up per stage proves the change.

en.title: You Have No Lights
en.summary: Use window, white wall, reflector, and phone light; find direction before intensity.
en.html:
Home/Main/You Have No Lights

Main / Method card

You Have No Lights

Use window, white wall, reflector, and phone light; find direction before intensity.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Place the same person by the window, one meter away, and with their back to it; shoot each. Choose the frame with shadow detail and a clear direction on the face. Do not use an on-camera light; it flattens every space.

Use the light you already have

  • Window: turn the subject sideways to the window, not toward it; it is a free large softbox.
  • Bounce: a white wall, paper or foam board fills the shadow; try reflection before buying a light.
  • Black flag: a dark shirt or card darkens the background and separates the subject.
  • Practicals: a lamp, screen or torch can be in frame, but check color temperature and flicker first.

When not to force it

If the room has only mixed practicals and cannot be changed, shoot silhouette or atmosphere instead of forcing a lit face. Having no light is not a crime; pretending you do ruins the film.

On set

Find a window at 45 degrees, use a white wall as fill, and diffuse a phone light with tissue. Shoot half-body first.

Do this

With no lights, find direction first: window, white wall, reflector, phone light. Shape comes before brightness.

  1. Turn the subject forty-five degrees to the window and drop the background one stop.
  2. Use a white wall or paper as a reflector to lift the shadow a little, not to flatten it.
  3. Diffuse a phone light with tissue and use it only for an eye light or edge; never hit the face straight on.

Avoid

Do not turn on every room light; light from all sides flattens the face.

Boundary

This page only covers “You Have No Lights”; it does not replace You Cannot Write a Script, You Only Have One Room, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “Turn the subject forty-five degrees to the window and drop the background one stop” is not the main problem, start with “Use a white wall or paper as a reflector to lift the shadow a little, not to flatten it”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: The subject faces the window at an angle, the nose casts a shadow, and the background is a stop darker. If check 2 (The shadow is lifted slightly but fabric texture is still visible) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • The subject faces the window at an angle, the nose casts a shadow, and the background is a stop darker.
  • The shadow is lifted slightly but fabric texture is still visible.
  • Phone light only makes an eye light or edge; no flat bright patch on the face.

en.title: Your Budget Is Zero
en.summary: Cut scale, not structure; a simple film you can finish beats a better one you cannot.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Main/Your Budget Is Zero

Main / Method card

Your Budget Is Zero

Cut scale, not structure; a simple film you can finish beats a better one you cannot.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Zero budget can shoot a small space, few characters, natural light, short runtime. Compress the script to one room, two people, one afternoon; do not keep five locations and call it low budget.

With no budget, change scale, not standards

Spend on what the audience feels most: sound, actors, one key prop. Do not spread it evenly across gear.

Limits

Low cost is not roughness. The image can be simple, but sound must be audible and the story must change. Those are the floor, not budget lines.

Zero-budget projects start with what you will not do

Zero budget is not “free filming.” It is trading existing resources for a presentable result. Before starting, write three boundaries: no gear rental, no paid talent, no exterior; or keep only one. Clear boundaries make completion possible.

ResourceWhat it trades forCost
Your skillA 30-second film for the other sideTime, not cash
Their location or productA free set and propsA usable film in return
Platform or communityReach, cross-promotion, feedbackNot guaranteed clients

The right goal for zero budget

Not “a big film,” but “one complete process.” Cut scope to one location, one camera, one finished piece, one revision. Use a phone or the camera you own; do not chase specs. Spend the time on script, location sound and edit rhythm.

Three zero-budget jobs to refuse

  • A commercial brand that says “show us the result, then we'll talk money.” That is a spec pitch, not a collaboration.
  • A project that asks you to front location, gear or talent costs. Zero budget is not zero cost.
  • Client owns all rights and asks for unlimited revisions. With no budget, lock scope even harder.

If you do it, sign a one-page memo: who contributes what, where the film can be used, how credit reads, and when it ends. A zero-budget project still needs a delivery date, or it never ends.

On set

Cut crowds, night exteriors, and vehicles. Rewrite with one room, two people, one prop.

Do this

With zero budget, cut scale, not structure. A simple story you can finish beats a better story you cannot afford to shoot.

  1. Reduce the script to one or two locations and one or two characters.
  2. Use available light, existing rooms, a phone, or borrowed gear.
  3. Spend what is left on sound and a meal for the crew; finishing is the priority.

Avoid

Do not hide behind “we will shoot it when we have money.” Make a version you can deliver now.

Boundary

This page only covers “Your Budget Is Zero”; it does not replace pricing, contract review, or the creative brief. If the problem belongs to another page in the related list, use that page first.

Alternative

If “Locations and characters are reduced to one or two” is not the main problem, start with “The film is finished with available light, existing rooms, a phone, or borrowed gear”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Locations and characters are reduced to one or two. If check 2 (The film is finished with available light, existing rooms, a phone, or borrowed gear) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

When not to use

This page only covers “Your Budget Is Zero”; it does not replace You Have No Coverage, You Have No Lights, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Check

  • Locations and characters are reduced to one or two.
  • The film is finished with available light, existing rooms, a phone, or borrowed gear.
  • Sound is clean, the crew ate, and the film can be delivered.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Zero budget is not waiting for money. It is turning constraints into rules so the film works without gear.

Cut what you cannot afford

List three things you cannot afford: a dolly, lights, actors, a location. Cut them from the script; do not replace them with fake shots. If you cannot cut it, move the scene into a behavior that can happen in one room.

Keep three things that cost nothing: a window, a wall, a person, an action. Write every scene around them. Ask only: what can this person do in this room right now?

Use the light and hours you have

Use window light by day and one practical at night. Schedule the stable two hours of light. Do not buy a lamp; learn to block and bounce: black cloth on the window, a white wall as bounce, one sheet of paper as diffusion.

Use a phone or the camera you have: lock white balance, set exposure manually. Record with a wired headset mic, or put the phone close to the person. Clear sound first; style second.

Make the limit the form

Shoot three days in one room, separated by three times of day, three shirts, three actions. Black and white, a locked camera, repeated composition can become the style. Clear limits look intentional, not poor.

The worst zero-budget film pretends to be rich. Admit the small room, the few people, the hard light; the audience trusts it more. Spend the little you have on one visible thing: a prop, a meal, a sound detail.

Five-minute drill: one film in twenty-four hours

Choose one location, one person, one action. Shoot thirty seconds within twenty-four hours. No new gear, no narration, only available light and live sound.

After the cut, ask which three unaffordable things you removed made the story clearer. Write the answer into the rules for the next film.

Ten zero-budget checks

  • Three unaffordable things cut first
  • Scenes written around the room
  • One window or one practical only
  • Shoot in the stable light window
  • Block and bounce instead of buying
  • White balance and exposure locked
  • Wired mic or phone close to subject
  • Three times of day separate the room
  • The limit becomes visible style
  • Savings spent on one visible detail

Zero budget is not no conditions. It is writing the conditions into the script so the film admits what it is from the first second.

en.title: You Are Shooting Alone
en.summary: Use a locked camera and continuous action; do not act, operate, and pull focus at once.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Main/You Are Shooting Alone

Main / Method card

You Are Shooting Alone

Use a locked camera and continuous action; do not act, operate, and pull focus at once.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

The time goes into moving the camera, pulling focus and recording sound. Design fixed positions, preset focus and continuous action. If a tripod and auto exposure solve it, do not do it manually on the day.

Shooting alone starts with shots that need no second pair of hands

One action per shot, play back immediately. Do not shoot ten and discover at home that none work.

Limits

Do not attempt complex follow-focus and tracking alone. It is not impossible; it is unrecoverable when it fails. Save complexity for a crew.

On set

Lock the camera, shoot your blocking and action, then shoot the empty frame. Do not act and pull focus at once.

Do this

Shooting alone means locked-off camera and continuous action. Do not act, operate, and pull focus at the same time.

  1. Shoot the empty frame and the wide first, then lock the camera down.
  2. Check framing on a monitor, pre-focus, then walk into position and do the action.
  3. Shoot the same action three times: wide, medium, close-up. Cut them together later.

Avoid

Do not handhold and follow yourself; focus and framing will drift.

Boundary

This page only covers “You Are Shooting Alone”; it does not replace pricing, contract review, or the creative brief. If the problem belongs to another page in the related list, use that page first.

Alternative

If “The camera is locked and the empty frame and wide are shot first” is not the main problem, start with “Each action has a wide, medium, and close-up take”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: The camera is locked and the empty frame and wide are shot first. If check 2 (Each action has a wide, medium, and close-up take) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

When not to use

This page only covers “You Are Shooting Alone”; it does not replace The Opening Is Too Slow, The Subtitles Are Hard to Read, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Check

  • The camera is locked and the empty frame and wide are shot first.
  • Each action has a wide, medium, and close-up take.
  • Focus is set before the walk; the lens does not hunt.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Shooting alone is not doing three jobs at once. It is cutting the shots down to what one person can control.

Fewer setups, fewer actions

One camera, one action, one take. Do not combine a move, a zoom, and blocking in the same shot. Each shot delivers one piece of information: space, relationship, reaction, or detail.

Shoot for the edit: wide for space, medium for action, close for reaction, insert for hands or prop. Get at least two takes per size; do not move on after one.

Separate monitoring from sound

Use a tripod and a phone as monitor; do not hold the camera and the script at once. Record sound separately, clap at the head, and listen for ten seconds after the take. One person can run dual-system.

If you only have the camera mic, get the camera close, turn off the air conditioner and close the window. Do not plan to save dialogue with noise reduction; what you cannot hear on set will not come back in post.

Shoot enough coverage

Shoot the same action three ways: normal speed, slower, hands only. That gives the edit choices. Do not shoot one perfect take; the perfect one is often unusable.

After each take check three things: focus, exposure, sound. If one is broken, reshoot immediately. For a solo shooter, the most expensive mistake is coming back for pickups.

Five-minute drill: one person, three shots

On a tripod, shoot three shots: a wide, a hand detail, a reaction. One action each, no zoom. Cut them into fifteen seconds on the phone and check for space, action, and reaction.

Add whichever is missing, then put the person in frame. When shooting alone, make sure it can be cut before making it beautiful.

When the solo shoot is done

Done does not mean every shot is perfect. It means every shot can cut: the wide establishes space, the medium shows action, the close reads reaction, the insert connects detail. If one size is missing, shoot it; do not force the same take to do the job.

Before wrapping, play the material back by scene: dialogue clear, focus holding, every take backed up. When all three pass, the shoot is done. For a solo shooter, the wrap check is worth more than ten extra takes.

Ten solo-shoot checks

  • One camera, one piece of information
  • At least two takes per size
  • Wide, medium, close, insert covered
  • Tripod plus phone monitor
  • Sound recorded separately
  • Clap at the head
  • Listen for ten seconds
  • Same action shot three ways
  • Focus, exposure, sound checked
  • Cuttable first, beautiful second

Shooting alone is not heroics. It is reducing every shot to what one person can actually control at once.

en.title: You Only Have a Phone
en.summary: Lock exposure and white balance, then stabilize the phone; steady image and sound beat lenses.
en.html:
Home/Main/You Only Have a Phone

Main / Method card

You Only Have a Phone

Lock exposure and white balance, then stabilize the phone; steady image and sound beat lenses.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Record 30 seconds at the final position: lock exposure for one take, have someone speak normally, then play back for sound. If highlights clip, dialogue is hollow or the frame shakes, fix one cause before adding filters and transitions.

Turn the phone into a controllable camera

  • Exposure: lock AE/AF so the image does not pulse with the face; protect highlights and leave shadow detail for post.
  • Sound: the built-in mic is too far away. Use a lav or shotgun; even one lav doubles intelligibility.
  • Stability: tuck your elbows, or brace against a wall, table or bag. Do not walk with the phone held out; electronic stabilization crops and jitters.
  • Lens: use the main camera, not digital zoom. Need a longer lens? Walk closer, do not magnify.

When not to use a phone

For very shallow depth of field, clean low light, telephoto compression or professional sound, a phone is not a cheaper cinema camera; it is a different medium. Do not force it to imitate one.

On set

Lock exposure and white balance, use a tripod or wall, and add a lav mic. Protect sound first.

Do this

On a phone, lock exposure and white balance first, then stabilize the body. Stability and sound matter more than the lens.

  1. Long-press to lock auto exposure and focus, then pull exposure down to protect highlights.
  2. Use a tripod, wall, or backpack; turn off stabilization modes that crop the frame.
  3. Add a lav mic or recorder fifteen to twenty centimeters from the mouth, and record room tone separately.

Avoid

Do not walk and handhold; the shake makes the audience dizzy before the story starts.

Boundary

This page only covers “You Only Have a Phone”; it does not replace The Platform Rejected It, You Have No Portfolio, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Exposure and white balance are locked and highlights are not blown out. If check 2 (The frame is stable; no walking shake) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • Exposure and white balance are locked and highlights are not blown out.
  • The frame is stable; no walking shake.
  • Dialogue is clean and there is a separate room-tone track.

en.title: The Image Looks Flat
en.summary: Flat images usually lack directional light and separated layers, not a better camera.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Image Looks Flat

Main / Method card

The Image Looks Flat

Flat images usually lack directional light and separated layers, not a better camera.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Draw three horizontal lines on the monitor: foreground, subject, background. If all three land on one plane, move the camera or add a foreground object. Do not add a filter; a filter does not create space. When not to chase depth Documentary, surveillance and some graphic compositions are meant to be flat. Decide whether you want space or graphic tension; do not turn every frame into the same “cinematic” look.

Does the frame have three planes?

  • Foreground: is there anything in front? Without it, the subject looks pasted onto a backdrop.
  • Angle: is the camera at eye height? Move lower, higher or to the side and space appears.
  • Light: are subject and background equally bright? Take one down a stop and the subject separates.
  • Lens: too wide or too compressed? Change position before changing the lens.

A three-plane test

Draw three horizontal lines on the monitor: foreground, subject, background. If all three land on one plane, move the camera or add a foreground object. Do not add a filter; a filter does not create space.

When not to chase depth

Documentary, surveillance and some graphic compositions are meant to be flat. Decide whether you want space or graphic tension; do not turn every frame into the same “cinematic” look.

On set

Add side light, foreground, and background layers. Move the subject one meter off the wall for depth.

Do this

A flat image is usually not the camera. Light has no direction and foreground and background are not separated. Add side light, then a foreground layer.

  1. Move the key from the front to forty-five degrees to one side so the nose casts a shadow.
  2. Put a soft foreground object near the lens: a cup, door frame, shoulder.
  3. Move the subject at least 1.5 meters from the background so it falls out of focus.

Avoid

Do not fix it with contrast and sharpening; flatness is a spatial problem.

Boundary

This page only covers “The Image Looks Flat”; it does not replace The Lines Sound Read, Music Covers the Dialogue, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: The key is to one side and the nose casts a shadow. If check 2 (A soft foreground object separates the subject from the background) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • The key is to one side and the nose casts a shadow.
  • A soft foreground object separates the subject from the background.
  • The subject stands at least 1.5 meters from the background.

en.title: The Shadows Are Dirty
en.summary: Lower ISO, add ambient light, and do not lift shadows hard; lifted black is noise.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Shadows Are Dirty

Main / Method card

The Shadows Are Dirty

Lower ISO, add ambient light, and do not lift shadows hard; lifted black is noise.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Noisy shadows: lower ISO, add a little ambient light, and do not force the shadows up. Lifted blacks are noise.

On set

Drop to native ISO, add a small ambient light, and do not lift the shadows hard. Let some black stay.

Do this

  1. Set ISO to its native base; accept a slightly darker image.
  2. Add a quarter stop to the shadow with a small lamp or reflector; do not light the face straight on.
  3. Lift shadows only slightly in post and keep blacks black; do not excavate the noise.

Avoid

Do not use “cinematic” as an excuse for underexposure; crushed shadows do not come back.

Three causes

For “The Shadows Are Dirty”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Underexposure + high ISOLifting shadows reveals noise and grey colourDrop ISO one stop and add face light
Log not transformedThe image is flat and black is not blackApply the correct colour transform first
Heavy compressionShadow blocking and smearing appearUse a higher bitrate or a ProRes intermediate

On-set diagnosis

  1. Open the waveform: check black level and whether shadows hold more than 5% detail.
  2. Judge after transforming Log, not on the flat image.
  3. Compare high and low bitrate versions to see whether blocking is compression or noise.

Fix

Dirty shadows usually mean too little light on set and too much lifting in post. Expose skin first, then decide how black the shadows should be.

  1. Add soft light to the face; let the background go dark before underexposing skin.
  2. Drop to native ISO and use ND to control highlights.
  3. Apply the correct LUT/transform before judging black level.
  4. Denoise shadows only until blocking disappears; keep some grain.

Failure cases

With “The Shadows Are Dirty”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with

en.title: The Highlights Are Gone
en.summary: Stop down, add ND, kill unnecessary practicals; clipped pixels do not come back.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Highlights Are Gone

Main / Method card

The Highlights Are Gone

Stop down, add ND, kill unnecessary practicals; clipped pixels do not come back.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Clipped highlights: stop down a stop, add ND, and kill unnecessary practicals. Blown pixels do not return.

On set

Cut a stop, add ND, and turn off practicals in frame. Clipped highlights cannot be saved.

Do this

  1. Use ND or close the iris until highlights sit inside the waveform.
  2. Turn off unneeded bulbs or windows in frame to reduce the ratio.
  3. Check faces and sky with zebras or false color before rolling.

Avoid

Do not expect post to recover highlights; pure white has no detail.

Three causes

For “The Highlights Are Gone”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
No NDAt a wide aperture in daylight the shutter is maxed and highlights clipAdd 2–4 stops of ND
Specular highlightsLamps, windows and metal reflect straight into the lensChange the angle or diffuse/polarize
Overexposed Log“Expose right” without a ceiling leaves no highlight detailKeep highlights below 95%

On-set diagnosis

  1. Turn on 95% zebras and look for large blinking areas; confirm with false colour.
  2. Check whether the histogram is pinned at the right edge; clipped areas cannot be recovered.
  3. Shoot the same shot one stop down and compare highlight texture with shadow noise.

Fix

Clipped highlights are not a post fix. Cut light first, then decide which highlight must survive; you cannot keep all of them.

  1. Add ND or stop down; keep the shutter near 1/50 at 25p.
  2. Change the angle on windows, tubes and metal, or diffuse the source.
  3. Expose to the right with a third-stop margin; keep peaks below 95%.
  4. If the highlight is the subject, underexpose the shadows a little and keep the texture.

Failure cases

With “The Highlights Are Gone”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Pull highlights in postThey turn dead white with halosReduce light on set
Darken the whole imageMidtones die and the frame looks muddyLower highlights only
Add contrastHighlights get harder and detail disappearsRecover highlights before contrast

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
HighlightsLamps and windows have texture, not pure whiteZebra/false colour
ShutterMotion blur is natural, no flicker25p at 1/50
SkinThe face is not overexposedWaveform 60–75%
ShadowsUsable detail remainsReview the shadow side

en.title: The Color Is Off
en.summary: Fix white balance and mixed light before color wheels; grading a bad source gets dirtier.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Color Is Off

Main / Method card

The Color Is Off

Fix white balance and mixed light before color wheels; grading a bad source gets dirtier.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Have a person hold a gray card at the subject position, shoot one frame; move the card to the background, shoot another. Use the same white balance. If the card differs, fix the light before grading.

Find where the cast comes from

  • White balance: white paper is not white in the same scene. Shoot a gray card, then match camera and lights.
  • Mixed light: window light is blue, practicals are yellow, and the face is half cool and half warm. Choose the dominant side, then gel or flag the other.
  • Log/monitoring: the monitor LUT and output LUT differ; it looks right on set and green on export. Use one color pipeline; do not switch LUTs between monitoring and output.

When not to hide it with a LUT

If the cast comes from the source or white balance, a LUT only makes skin dirtier. Match the capture side first, then add style in post. Do not call bad skin “cinematic.”

On set

Check white balance and mixed light first. Neutralize with a grey card, then grade.

Do this

A color cast starts with white balance and mixed light, not the color wheels. Fix the source or every correction gets dirtier.

  1. Shoot a gray card or white paper under each light position to confirm white balance.
  2. Turn off or unify mixed sources; gel windows with CTO or CTB so warm and cool stop fighting.
  3. Balance to the gray card first, then grade; correct the cast, do not invent a style.

Avoid

Do not grade over mixed light; the face will go green in one patch and yellow in another.

Boundary

This page only covers “The Color Is Off”; it does not replace Continuity Broke, The Crew Is Fighting, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “A gray card or white paper was shot under every light position” is not the main problem, start with “Mixed sources are unified or turned off; warm and cool no longer fight”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: A gray card or white paper was shot under every light position. If check 2 (Mixed sources are unified or turned off; warm and cool no longer fight) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • A gray card or white paper was shot under every light position.
  • Mixed sources are unified or turned off; warm and cool no longer fight.
  • Post balances to the card and skin is not green in one patch and yellow in another.

en.title: The Audio Has Hiss
en.summary: Check room, air conditioning, cables, and gain; replace the mic last.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Audio Has Hiss

Main / Method card

The Audio Has Hiss

Check room, air conditioning, cables, and gain; replace the mic last.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Hiss starts with the room, air conditioning, cables, and gain. The microphone is the last thing to replace.

On set

Turn off the air conditioning, change cables, and lower gain to -12 dB. Change the mic last.

Do this

  1. Turn off AC, fridge, and lights; record thirty seconds of silence and listen for the source.
  2. Change outlets and cables; put gain on the recorder, not the microphone.
  3. Move the subject closer to the mic and record room tone for a post bed.

Avoid

Do not buy a new mic first; the noise may be the room.

Three causes

For “The Audio Has Hiss”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Gain structureThe mic gain is high and the noise floor rises with itLower gain until peaks sit near -12dBFS and listen again
Room reflectionsA persistent hum or ring stays when the mic movesRecord 30 seconds of room tone and move the mic
Cable or inputNoise changes with a cable swap; a loose connector clicksSwap cable, input and battery one at a time

On-set diagnosis

  1. Record 30 seconds of a quiet room with no speech and listen to the noise alone.
  2. Solo the dialogue track and classify the noise: hiss, low hum, or intermittent clicks.
  3. Swap cable, input and power one by one to see which stage carries the noise.

Fix

Noise floor is not solved by one denoise preset. Move the mic closer, stage the gain in two steps, and remove constant room sources.

  1. Keep the mic 15–20 cm from the mouth; tape the lav inside the collar away from fabric rub.
  2. Stage gain: recorder input to about -18dBFS, then trim; keep dialogue peaks near -12dBFS.
  3. Turn off air conditioning, fridges and projector fans; if you cannot, record room tone for matching.
  4. Route cables away from power adapters; keep wireless receiver and transmitter in line of sight.
  5. In post, denoise only until the processing is inaudible; do not chase absolute silence.

Failure cases

With “The Audio Has Hiss”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Maximum denoiseDialogue becomes hollow; consonants and tails disappearLimit reduction to 6–10dB and keep room tone
Auto gainNoise breathes between lines and jumps in the editSet manual gain and lock it before rolling
Swap only the micThe noise is in the room or cable, so the new mic changes nothingCheck room, cable and input in order

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
Room tone30 seconds loops without sudden HVAC eventsKeep the original file
Dialogue peaksNormal speech peaks around -12dBFS, no clippingRecorder meter
Noise floorQuiet gaps stay steady, not pumping between linesSolo dialogue
IntelligibilityEvery word is clear without guessing from subtitlesOne headphone pass

Boundary
