Alternative

If “Turn off AC, fridge, and lights; record thirty seconds of silence and listen for the source” is not the main problem, start with “Change outlets and cables; put gain on the recorder, not the microphone”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Thirty seconds of silence was recorded with AC, fridge, and lights off. If check 2 (Outlets and cables were changed and gain sits on the recorder) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • Thirty seconds of silence was recorded with AC, fridge, and lights off.
  • Outlets and cables were changed and gain sits on the recorder.
  • The subject is close to the mic, dialogue is clear, and room tone exists.

en.title: Wind Noise Outside
en.summary: Use a windshield and find shelter; post cannot recover words eaten by wind.
en.html:
Home/Main/Wind Noise Outside

Main / Method card

Wind Noise Outside

Use a windshield and find shelter; post cannot recover words eaten by wind.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Have the host say one sentence in the open, beside a wall, and with a body blocking the wind; record ten seconds in each. Compare on headphones and choose the position with the clearest consonants. Record ten seconds of ambience as a reference for post.

Find where the wind comes from

  • Steady crosswind: a furry windshield is not enough; move to a blimp or add a second cover, and do not point the capsule into the gust.
  • Gusts: lavs suffer first. Add a windshield and hide the capsule inside the collar.
  • Low-frequency rumble: usually wind hitting the capsule or boom, not a noisy floor. Move the boom and add protection before denoise.

When not to rely on post

Once wind eats the consonants, denoise only makes the voice duller. Move, shorten the mic distance and add protection on set; it is always cheaper. If dialogue already has wind, do not cover it with music.

On set

Use a wind screen, find shelter, and block the wind with your body. Post cannot recover words the wind ate.

Do this

Outdoor wind: put a windshield on the mic first, then find shelter. Post noise reduction cannot recover words the wind ate.

  1. Fit a furry windshield or cage on the shotgun; add a wind cover to lavs.
  2. Use your body, a backpack, or a wall as a barrier, and move the mic closer to the mouth.
  3. Record a sheltered reference track and use only light noise reduction later.

Avoid

Do not tell yourself post will fix it; wind takes consonants first.

Boundary

This page only covers “Wind Noise Outside”; it does not replace Career & Clients, Release & Distribution, Media Literacy: Five Questions for Any Video. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “The shotgun has a windshield and the lav has a furry cover” is not the main problem, start with “A body, backpack, or wall blocks the wind at the shooting spot”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: The shotgun has a windshield and the lav has a furry cover. If check 2 (A body, backpack, or wall blocks the wind at the shooting spot) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • The shotgun has a windshield and the lav has a furry cover.
  • A body, backpack, or wall blocks the wind at the shooting spot.
  • Consonants survive the wind and post uses only light noise reduction.

en.title: The Actor Is Stiff
en.summary: Give a concrete task and make them walk; movement loosens lines.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Actor Is Stiff

Main / Method card

The Actor Is Stiff

Give a concrete task and make them walk; movement loosens lines.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

A stiff actor needs a concrete task and a reason to move. Once the body works, the lines loosen.

On set

Give a task: put the cup on the table, then turn. Make them walk one step and the lines loosen.

Do this

  1. Turn the line into an action: look for someone, open a door, hand something over.
  2. Have them actually do it, not perform the idea of doing it.
  3. Walk it twice before rolling and shoot the most natural rhythm.

Avoid

Do not tell them to relax; the more you say it, the stiffer they get.

Three causes

For “The Actor Is Stiff”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Lines before actionThe actor stands still and only moves the mouth; the hands have no jobRemove the lines and give one physical task
Abstract direction“Just relax” makes the body stifferReplace it with a verb: open, hand over, find
Camera fearThe eyes hunt for the lens and the action lands half a beat lateAsk for one take facing away, then turn back

On-set diagnosis

  1. Shoot one silent action take and watch whether hands and feet do the same job.
  2. Then add the lines after the action and compare breathing and pauses.
  3. Shoot one wide and one close. If only the close works, the action has not built a space.

Fix

Replace “play the feeling” with “finish the task”. The actor does not need to feel relaxed first; he needs something that must be done.

  1. Turn lines into actions: find someone, open a door, hand over an object, hide something.
  2. Give the action an obstacle: a stuck door, an overfull cup, a missing key.
  3. Walk it twice before rolling: first silent, then with lines.
  4. Shoot a wide for space, then a close for reaction; do not start with faces only.

Failure cases

With “The Actor Is Stiff”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Repeat “relax”The actor performs relaxation; shoulders and hands become less believableName a concrete action and obstacle
Ask for “nervous”Shaking hands and shoulders become a generic trickGive a real deadline or consequence
Ten takes in a rowEnergy drops and the last takes repeatStop at two different rhythms and review

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
Body taskHands and feet do one job, not a poseReview the silent take
Line placementLines follow the action instead of replacing itCheck take two
SpaceThe wide shows who is where and what they doKeep one wide
RhythmTwo takes have different pauses and both are usableLog the difference

Alternative

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: The line is now a concrete action. If check 2 (The actor actually does it rather than performing the idea) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • The line is now a concrete action.
  • The actor actually does it rather than performing the idea.
  • Two walk-throughs happened before rolling and the rhythm is natural.

en.title: The Lines Sound Read
en.summary: Cut explanation, add action, and give them a listener; more adjectives make it worse.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Lines Sound Read

Main / Method card

The Lines Sound Read

Cut explanation, add action, and give them a listener; more adjectives make it worse.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Flat lines: cut explanation, add action, and have the actor speak to a person. More adjectives will not help.

On set

Cut explanation, add action, and have the actor speak to one person. Do not add adjectives.

Do this

  1. Delete lines that explain; keep only want and obstacle.
  2. Give every line an action or object: look at someone, pick something up, walk somewhere.
  3. Play the line to a real person, not to the air or the lens.

Avoid

Do not replace subtext with volume or a crying voice.

Three causes

For “The Lines Sound Read”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Written languageComplete sentences carry too much information and sound like an essayBreak into short spoken lines; allow half-sentences
No intentionEvery word is correct but the actor does not know what the line should change in the other personGive one subtext: stay, leave, admit
No obstacleThe other character agrees immediately, so the line has nothing to push againstLet them refuse, stay silent or challenge

On-set diagnosis

  1. Ask the actor to say the line in their own words; check whether the meaning survives.
  2. Ask what the line wants from the other person. If the actor cannot answer, intention is missing.
  3. Play the action without lines; if it works, add the lines back.

Fix

Flat lines are usually not a pronunciation problem; the line has no task. Make every sentence try to change the other person, then work on rhythm and stress.

  1. Split long sentences and remove explanatory clauses.
  2. Give every line an action: ask, probe, threaten, conceal.
  3. Let the scene partner provide real resistance; do not feed the next line early.
  4. Allow pauses and overlaps; do not wait for a clean end every time.

Failure cases

With “The Lines Sound Read”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Add more emotionEvery line pushes and sounds less trueSet intention first, then decide delivery
Tell them to be naturalNatural toward what?Give an action and an object
Rewrite word by wordThe sentence flows but the intention is still emptyWrite what each line wants to change

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
SpokenThe line runs in one breath and does not sound like an essayActor paraphrase
IntentionEach line names what it wants from the other personAnnotate line by line
ResistanceThe partner reacts instead of waitingWatch the exchange

en.title: A Scene Has No Change
en.summary: If a scene changes nothing, cut it or let someone gain or lose something.
en.html:
Home/Main/A Scene Has No Change

Main / Method card

A Scene Has No Change

If a scene changes nothing, cut it or let someone gain or lose something.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Write three sentences: what they want at the start, what blocks them, what they do by the end. If the third sentence does not exist, the scene has no event. Do not rescue it with more angles and music.

Does the scene change anything?

  • Goal: what does the character want in this scene? If you cannot say it, the scene is a transition.
  • Obstacle: who or what blocks them? The obstacle must be present, not only in dialogue.
  • Turn: by the end, what the character knows, where they are or who they are to someone must change. If nothing changes, cut or merge it.

When not to add a scene

If the scene changes neither character nor information, deleting it is stronger than adding action. In a short film, every scene carries one turn.

On set

Make someone gain or lose something. If nothing changes, cut the scene.

Do this

If a scene does not change, cut it, or let someone gain or lose something.

  1. Write the state at the start and the state at the end; they must differ.
  2. Take an object away, close a door, or say the line that changes the relationship.
  3. If the state is unchanged, cut the scene and fold its information into the next one.

Avoid

Do not keep a static scene alive with “mood.”

Boundary

This page only covers “A Scene Has No Change”; it does not replace You Are Shooting Alone, The Opening Is Too Slow, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “Write the state at the start and the state at the end; they must differ” is not the main problem, start with “Take an object away, close a door, or say the line that changes the relationship”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

en.title: The Opening Is Too Slow
en.summary: Cut the first thirty seconds and start where someone is already acting; context can wait.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Opening Is Too Slow

Main / Method card

The Opening Is Too Slow

Cut the first thirty seconds and start where someone is already acting; context can wait.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Show only the first eight seconds to someone who has not seen it, muted, then ask: who did you see, what did they want, what blocked them? If they cannot answer, the opening has not started. Do not use music or titles to supply the answer.

What happens in the first eight seconds?

  • Only atmosphere: the opening is a wide shot, titles and music, and nobody wants anything yet. Move the first person with a goal earlier.
  • Only explanation: narration explains backstory while nothing happens. Delete it and replace it with a visible action.
  • Late conflict: the character meets the obstacle after 30 seconds. Put the obstacle in the first shot.

When not to speed up

If the character is not established, speeding up only makes it less clear. Add an action or one informative line before discussing pace.

On set

Cut the first thirty seconds and start where the character is already doing something. Add context later.

Do this

A slow opening: cut the first thirty seconds and start where the character is already doing something. Backstory can come later.

  1. Find the first shot where the character must act, and start there.
  2. Split the backstory into two or three beats and hide them inside later actions.
  3. Keep only one question and one action in the first thirty seconds; no world-building.

Avoid

Do not narrate the backstory in voice-over or titles; the audience came to watch action.

en.title: The Ending Has No Force
en.summary: Weak endings usually mean no cost; make the character choose, then stop.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Ending Has No Force

Main / Method card

The Ending Has No Force

Weak endings usually mean no cost; make the character choose, then stop.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

A weak ending usually means the character paid no price. Make them choose, then stop.

On set

Make the character pay a price, choose, and stop on the action after the choice.

Do this

  1. Turn the ending into a choice where both options cost something.
  2. Let them make the choice; do not let someone else solve it.
  3. End on a concrete action: close the door, put down the key, walk away. Do not explain.

Avoid

Do not push emotion with crying or music; the cost must be visible.

Three causes

For “The Ending Has No Force”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Too much explanationVoice-over summarises the theme and leaves nothing for the audienceRemove the summary and end on action
Ending on the answerThe character already has the result and the film explains itEnd at the moment of choice
No costNothing is lost, so the emotion has nowhere to landMake the choice carry a visible cost

On-set diagnosis

  1. Find the last choice in the film: what the character decides to do or not do.
  2. See whether the last shot sits before, during or after the choice; if it sits too long after, shorten it.
  3. Watch the last ten seconds with sound off; does the picture still work?

Fix

An ending does not exhaust the story; it leaves the character inside a choice. The audience should leave with a question, not a summary.

  1. Hold one or two seconds after the choice; do not add an explanation shot.
  2. Put the theme in an action: close a door, set down keys, turn away.
  3. Remove voice-over summaries and title cards; put any necessary note outside the film.
  4. Leave the last shot unfinished: a hand in mid-air, a door not fully closed.

Failure cases

With “The Ending Has No Force”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Add a montage summaryThe emotion repeats and the audience waits for creditsKeep one action
Add voice-overThe theme is stated and the image loses weightLet the image end itself
End on the answerOnce the character has the result, the scene is overEnd on the choice, not the result

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
Last choiceThe ending contains an identifiable choiceMark the timecode
DurationNo more than two seconds after the choiceWatch the last ten seconds
ExplanationNo voice-over or card summarises the themeInspect the tail
AftertasteThe last shot holds an unfinished actionPlay it back

Boundary

Check

  • The character makes the choice; nobody solves it for them.
  • It ends on a concrete action, with no explanatory voice-over.

en.title: The Film Is Too Long
en.summary: Find repetition: if one idea appears twice, cut the weaker instance.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Film Is Too Long

Main / Method card

The Film Is Too Long

Find repetition: if one idea appears twice, cut the weaker instance.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Watch the whole cut without looking at the timeline, holding only a sheet of paper. Every time you reach for your phone or drift, note the time. See which scene those points share; cut that scene before changing speed.

Is the story long or the edit long?

  • Story: the goal arrives late or there are too many subplots. Remove a subplot before speeding anything up.
  • Edit: every shot holds two seconds too long, or transitions repeat. Trim six frames from both ends of each shot and watch again.
  • Structure: the same information appears twice. Merge the scenes and keep the more specific one.

When not to cut shorter

If removing it breaks the character's motivation, the problem is structure, not length. Add an action or a line instead of forcing the platform runtime.

On set

Find repeated information and cut the weaker one. One change per scene.

Do this

A long cut: find repetition. If the same information appears twice, keep the stronger version.

  1. Label what new information each scene provides; cut the scenes that provide none.
  2. Merge characters and locations that do the same job.
  3. Run a test screening, note where attention drops, and cut thirty more seconds from there.

Avoid

Do not speed up or quick-cut your way through it; repeated information does not disappear when cut faster.

Boundary

This page only covers “The Film Is Too Long”; it does not replace The Transition Is Jarring, Wind Noise Outside, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “Label what new information each scene provides; cut the scenes that provide none” is not the main problem, start with “Merge characters and locations that do the same job”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Every scene is labeled with its new information; scenes without any are cut. If check 2 (Characters and locations that do the same job are merged) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • Every scene is labeled with its new information; scenes without any are cut.
  • Characters and locations that do the same job are merged.
  • Thirty more seconds came out after the test-screening attention dip.

Deep dive

About 8 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: narrative short

A narrative short is usually too long not because shots are long, but because the change arrives late. Budget by act: first quarter setup, half development, quarter turn; each act needs a visible change. Without change, the audience feels slow even when shots are short.

Do not cut from the end first; cut the scene that repeats information. If two scenes both say “he is lonely”, remove the second; if two both say “the client is difficult”, remove the explanation. Keep change, remove repetition.

Condition B: platform version

A platform cut is too long because of the entry, not the story. The feed version removes setup and puts the person or problem in the first three seconds; the site version can keep setup but must give information in the first ten; the channel version follows the slot, not patience. Three lengths, not three stories.

Do not solve a platform cut with speed: 1.1x makes the audience breathless. Removing one complete passage works better than speeding the whole film.

Counterexample: trimming pauses, not scenes

A twelve-minute short needs to become eight. The editor trims one second from the head and tail of every shot and removes four minutes. It is shorter but still slow because two repeated scenes remain. The audience feels faster pacing but no movement.

The fix is not more trimming. Make a scene-information-change table: any scene with no new information goes entirely; any scene with change stays. Cutting scenes hurts, but it works better than speeding the film.

Reusable model

Length budget → scene table → remove repetition → test screening. Allocate acts by length, list each scene's information and change, remove repeats, then screen and watch where attention drops. The drop is not impatience; it is repeated information.

Remove one scene at a time and watch. Remove three and the audience loses the thread. The test is “does the rest still work without it?” If yes, cut; if no, keep.

en.title: You Have No Coverage
en.summary: Coverage fails when every shot is one size; add wide, close, and insert.
en.html:
Home/Main/You Have No Coverage

Main / Method card

You Have No Coverage

Coverage fails when every shot is one size; add wide, close, and insert.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

You cannot cut because every setup has only one shot size. Add wides, close-ups, and inserts.

On set

Add a wide, a close, an insert, and a reverse. Get at least two takes of each.

Do this

  1. For each action, shoot at least a wide, a medium, and a close-up.
  2. Add inserts: hands, feet, props, the gap in a door.
  3. Leave three seconds of handle at the head and tail of every take.

Avoid

Do not shoot one long take and wrap; you will have no alternatives in the edit.

Three causes

For “You Have No Coverage”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Master onlyOne wide runs from start to finish; by the second line there is nothing to cut toSplit every dialogue beat into two angles
No insertsAction detail lives only in performance and cannot be cutShoot hands, doors, cups, phone screens
No reactionsThe cut only shows the speaker, never the listenerAdd one reaction per exchange

On-set diagnosis

  1. List every line as a cut point: who speaks, who listens, what the hands do.
  2. Play the scene on a timeline and count usable angles per dialogue beat.
  3. Write the gaps as a pickup list: missing wide, insert or reaction.

Fix

Coverage is not more footage; it is one shot for each relationship, action and reaction the cut needs. Secure two angles per beat before chasing beauty.

  1. Shoot one wide per scene to hold positions and spatial relations.
  2. Shoot two mediums per dialogue beat: one favoring the speaker, one the listener.
  3. Add three inserts: hands, prop, environment; one action each.
  4. Add one reaction per exchange with two seconds of handle before and after.
  5. Shoot two clean seconds of tail and head for every transition.

Failure cases

With “You Have No Coverage”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Repeat the wideTime stops advancing; the audience sees the same faceCut on inserts and reactions
Cross the line for coverageSpace flips and the audience loses directionDraw the axis before pickups
Pretty empty shotsNo action, so the shot reads as a pausePut one recognizable action in every insert

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
Angles per beatEvery beat has a usable wide and mediumMark the timeline
InsertsEach action detail has its own shotPickup list
ReactionsEvery exchange has a listener reactionReview dialogue block
HandlesTwo clean seconds around each transitionInspect tail/head

Boundary

This page only covers “You Have No Coverage”; it does not replace You Have No Lights, You Cannot Write a Script, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “For each action, shoot at least a wide, a medium, and a close-up” is not the main problem, start with “Add inserts: hands, feet, props, the gap in a door”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Each action has a wide, a medium, and a close-up. If check 2 (Inserts cover hands, feet, props, and door gaps) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • Each action has a wide, a medium, and a close-up.
  • Inserts cover hands, feet, props, and door gaps.
  • Every take has three seconds of handle and the edit has alternatives.

Deep dive

About 8 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: narrative scene

Coverage in a narrative scene is not “shoot every angle”; it is “every piece of information has an alternative”. List the cut points first: who speaks, who listens, what the hands do, what the environment gives. Each cut point needs at least two choices: a master and a reaction or insert. A scene without reactions breaks at the second line.

Draw the coverage sheet before the shoot, not from memory on set. Put shot number, size, action, duration and whether it crosses the axis; tick each after shooting. The more specific the sheet, the less pick-up work.

Condition B: action or ensemble

Action coverage follows direction and consequence: who comes from where, goes where, hits what. Shoot three things per action: the wide relationship, the body detail and the result reaction. Pretty angles alone lose space; the audience cannot tell who hit whom.

Ensemble adds allocation: everyone gets a small action instead of standing around the lead. Give each person a reaction so the edit has choices. The more people, the more the master goes first; by the time you shoot details, the light may have changed.

Counterexample: five angles, no reaction

A dialogue scene is shot from five angles: wide, over-shoulder, close, low and high. In the edit every angle is on the speaker; nobody is listening. Five angles sound like a lot but carry one piece of information: who talks. By the third line the editor is reusing the same close-up.

The fix is not another angle; it is the listener. For each exchange, shoot the listener's face with two seconds before and after. A reaction does not need to be beautiful, only to change.

Reusable model

Cut point → information → alternative → tick. List cut points, write the information each carries, decide the alternative, then tick on set. Coverage is not quantity; it is a fallback for every point.

Run an empty-timeline test that day: lay the usable shots against the cut points and fill the missing point tomorrow, not at rough cut.

en.title: You Crossed the Axis
en.summary: Return to a wide or add a neutral shot; do not hard-cut reversed faces.
en.html:
Home/Main/You Crossed the Axis

Main / Method card

You Crossed the Axis

Return to a wide or add a neutral shot; do not hard-cut reversed faces.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

A line jump: return to a wide or add a neutral shot. Do not hard-cut two faces looking in opposite directions.

On set

Return to a wide or add a neutral shot. Do not cut between two opposite-facing faces.

Do this

  1. Shoot a wide or neutral shot between the two people to re-establish the line.
  2. Keep the next setup on the same side; do not cross to the other side.
  3. If you already crossed, bridge with an insert or a moving shot.

Avoid

Do not gamble that the audience will not notice; once direction breaks, the space falls apart.

Three causes

For “You Crossed the Axis”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Camera crosses the lineTwo cameras sit on opposite sides of the actor axisDraw the axis and keep all cameras on one side
Opposite screen directionThe actor exits left and enters right in the next shotKeep direction or add a neutral shot
No masterThe audience cannot tell who shares the spaceShoot a wide to establish relations first

On-set diagnosis

  1. Draw actor and camera positions on paper and mark the 180-degree line.
  2. Check screen direction and gaze continuity shot by shot.
  3. Play the two conflicting shots together and ask whether you still know who is left and right.

Fix

A line break is not fixed by flipping the image. Return to the same side of the axis, or use a neutral shot to rebuild the space.

  1. Keep all cameras on one side; shoot the wide before mediums and closes.
  2. If you must cross, insert a frontal neutral shot or a move that carries the audience across.
  3. Preserve screen direction: exit left, enter left; do not reverse without a reason.
  4. Add an action match at the cut so the audience crosses with the movement.

Failure cases

With “You Crossed the Axis”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Flip horizontallyText, hair and wardrobe reverseReturn and shoot a neutral
Hard cut acrossThe audience loses orientationAdd an establishing wide
Judge single framesEvery frame looks fine but the sequence reversesPlay in order

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
AxisAll cameras on one side or a neutral transition existsPaper axis map
GazeScreen direction is continuousCompare shots
MovementExit and entry directions matchWatch the action
SpaceA viewer can say who is left and rightAsk someone who has not seen it

en.summary: Photograph the set and match props, wardrobe, hands, and table; continuity is records, not memory.
en.html:
Home/Main/Continuity Broke

Main / Method card

Continuity Broke

Photograph the set and match props, wardrobe, hands, and table; continuity is records, not memory.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Before each camera move, have the script supervisor take three frames: wide, prop detail, hands. Compare them with the last frame of the previous setup before deciding whether to reshoot.

Check four continuity classes

  • Props: cup position, cigarette length, phone screen. Photograph the prop before and after every shot.
  • Wardrobe: collar, cuffs, sweat, buttons. Keep the actor in the same garment; do not fix it in post.
  • Blocking: a character exits left and enters right in the next shot. Mark positions and use landmarks.
  • Light: the window turns from day to night, shadows change direction. Shoot coverage before close-ups.

When not to reshoot

If the break sits at the edge of frame and carries no story information, use an insert or sound to move attention; do not reshoot a whole scene for a cup. A break on the hero's face must be reshot.

On set

Photograph the table, hands, and wardrobe before rolling. Compare before wrap.

Do this

A continuity break: take a set photo, then check props, wardrobe, hands, and table. Continuity lives in records, not memory.

  1. Every time you change the camera or wardrobe, shoot a wide and a detail photo.
  2. Assign one person to track props, collar, watch, and how much drink is left.
  3. Check photos by scene before the edit; fix breaks with pickups or inserts.

Avoid

Do not match from memory; memory keeps the big shape, not the details.

60-second test

Check

en.title: The Transition Is Jarring
en.summary: Find an action, sound, or shape match; white flashes and pushes work once.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Transition Is Jarring

Main / Method card

The Transition Is Jarring

Find an action, sound, or shape match; white flashes and pushes work once.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

A hard transition: find an action, sound, or shape to bridge it. White flashes and whip pans only work once.

On set

Find an action, sound, or shape match. A white flash works once.

Do this

  1. Leave an action unfinished at the end of one shot and pick it up in the next.
  2. Bring sound in early or let it linger to connect the two spaces.
  3. Match a shape, color, or composition across the cut.

Avoid

Do not use white flashes or spin wipes as universal glue; repeated, they pull the audience out.

Three causes

For “The Transition Is Jarring”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Hard cuts onlyEvery transition is a cut with no time or space bridgeAdd an action or sound bridge
No shared informationScene A ends on one idea and scene B starts somewhere unrelatedGive the end and start a shared object
Music cuts hardThe picture changes but the score stays in the old sectionResolve or carry the music

On-set diagnosis

  1. Play three seconds either side of each transition and list what the audience knows and does not know.
  2. Check whether the cut shares an action, object or sound.
  3. Turn off music and see whether the picture still transitions.

Fix

A transition does not hide time; it explains time. Find a shared anchor: action, object, sound or gaze.

  1. Match action: a door closes in one scene and opens in the next.
  2. Bridge with sound: the room tone of the previous scene continues into the next.
  3. Match gaze: a character looks at an object and the next shot shows it.
  4. Keep two seconds of tail and head; do not add an effect to every cut.

Failure cases

With “The Transition Is Jarring”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Overuse dissolvesDissolves slow time and fight the scene’s paceUse them only for time jumps
Add a whooshThe effect hides the logic; the audience still does not know where they areBuild the spatial/time anchor first
Fade every sceneThe film feels like a slide deckKeep hard cuts and fix only information gaps

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
AnchorEvery transition has a shared action, object or soundMark scene by scene
TimeThe audience knows how much time passedAsk a fresh viewer
SpaceThe audience knows where they areCheck the establishing shot
HandlesTwo clean seconds around the transitionInspect tail/head

Alternative

If “Leave an action unfinished at the end of one shot and pick it up in the next” is not the main problem, start with “Bring sound in early or let it linger to connect the two spaces”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: An unfinished action ends one shot and continues in the next. If check 2 (Sound arrives early or lingers to connect the spaces) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • An unfinished action ends one shot and continues in the next.
  • Sound arrives early or lingers to connect the spaces.
  • The cut uses a shape, color, or composition match, not a white flash.

en.title: The Pacing Is Flat
en.summary: Vary shot length; three same-length shots in a row lose attention.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Pacing Is Flat

Main / Method card

The Pacing Is Flat

Vary shot length; three same-length shots in a row lose attention.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Flat pacing: change shot lengths. Three shots of the same length in a row lose the audience.

On set

If three shots run the same length, change one: long, short, long. Give the audience air.

Do this

  1. List the shot lengths in a scene and avoid three identical ones in a row.
  2. Shorten before information, hold longer after a reaction.
  3. Build rhythm from action and sound, not a cut on every music beat.

Avoid

Do not quick-cut the whole film; without breathing room, the audience tires.

Three causes

For “The Pacing Is Flat”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Equal shot lengthsThe scene feels like a slideshowMark the information change every ten seconds
No reactionsAction happens without anyone’s attitude toward itAdd a reaction after each action
Constant musicThe score stays at one level and the cut never breathesLet music enter and leave at turns

On-set diagnosis

  1. Watch without music and mark what the audience learns every ten seconds.
  2. Count shots and average length per scene; identical lengths flatten rhythm.
  3. Find three places that can hold for one second: action completion, line landing, reaction.

Fix

Rhythm is not shorter shots; it is information increasing and decreasing. Cut on action first, then let a pause carry pressure.

  1. Cut on action: a door opens, a cup lands, a body turns; the completion point is the cut.
  2. Shorten empty shots to the one second that carries information; never use them as filler.
  3. Hold one pause before each turn so the audience expects the next line.
  4. Bring music in or out at turns; do not wallpaper the whole scene.

Failure cases

With “The Pacing Is Flat”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Speed everything upThe audience cannot read the frame and feels dizzyOnly shorten shots with no information
Cut every lineThe performance breaks into fragmentsLet one action span two shots
Push with musicThe score peaks but the picture has not changedChange the information first, then add music

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
First 30 secondsAt least three information changesMark each block
Shot lengthsNot every shot is the same lengthTimeline statistics
PauseAt least one one-second pause carries pressureReview the turn
MusicMusic enters and exits; it is not continuousSolo the music track

Boundary

This page only covers “The Pacing Is Flat”; it does not replace You Only Have a Phone, The Platform Rejected It, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: No three consecutive shots share the same length. If check 2 (Shots shorten before information and hold after a reaction) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • No three consecutive shots share the same length.
  • Shots shorten before information and hold after a reaction.
  • Rhythm comes from action and sound, not a cut on every beat.

en.title: Music Covers the Dialogue
en.summary: Drop music six dB, then ask whether the scene needs it at all.
en.html:
Home/Main/Music Covers the Dialogue

Main / Method card

Music Covers the Dialogue

Drop music six dB, then ask whether the scene needs it at all.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Music over dialogue: drop the music six dB first, then ask whether the scene needs it at all.

On set

Lower the music by 6 dB and ask whether it is needed at all. Dialogue first.

Do this

  1. Solo the dialogue and confirm every word is audible.
  2. Lower the music six to ten dB under dialogue, or use sidechain and automation.
  3. If it still masks words, cut the music and let room tone carry the scene.

Avoid

Do not fill every silence with music; quiet is also rhythm.

Three causes

For “Music Covers the Dialogue”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Music too fullThe score stays at one level and dialogue has no spaceDrop music 6dB between lines
Frequency collisionMusic midrange overlaps speech and blurs wordsClear 1–4kHz for dialogue
No automationThe whole cue sits at one level, so climax and quiet hit the sameDraw a level curve per scene

On-set diagnosis

  1. Solo dialogue and confirm every word is clear without subtitles.
  2. Solo music and check whether it keeps pushing between lines.
  3. Play both and listen for buildup around 1–4kHz.

Fix

Music supports emotion; it does not cover lines. Make dialogue intelligible first, then decide where the cue enters and leaves.

  1. Automate music down 3–6dB under dialogue and let it return between lines.
  2. Make a broad, shallow EQ dip around 1–4kHz to clear space for speech.
  3. Keep ambience; do not fill the location with music.
  4. Leave a no-music gap before the climax so the entrance has force.

Failure cases

With “Music Covers the Dialogue”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
Lower the whole cueThe music loses shape and the emotion flattensAutomate instead of a single static cut
Mute the musicThe scene dries out and the audience hears the techniqueDrop to -18dB rather than silence
Only change levelThe frequency collision remainsUse EQ and level together

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
DialogueEvery word is clear without subtitlesSolo dialogue
MusicIt yields between lines and enters at the climaxInspect automation
FrequencyNo pile-up at 1–4kHzSolo and full mix
AmbienceThe room is not completely covered by musicListen for space

One line for the set

Solo the dialogue first; music only earns its place when every word is clear.

Check

  • Music under dialogue is down six to ten dB.
  • If it still masks words, the music is cut and room tone carries the scene.

en.title: The Subtitles Are Hard to Read
en.summary: Cut words, raise contrast, avoid mouth and hands; thicker strokes do not fix it.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Subtitles Are Hard to Read

Main / Method card

The Subtitles Are Hard to Read

Cut words, raise contrast, avoid mouth and hands; thicker strokes do not fix it.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Shrink the cut to phone width, set brightness to 50%, and watch muted for 30 seconds. Can you read without pausing? Then switch to the brightest shot and confirm the captions still hold.

Check four things

  • Line length: over 18 Chinese characters, or two languages on one line. Split the sentence; do not shrink the type.
  • Contrast: white type over sky, a white wall or a bright face. Add a translucent plate, outline or shadow; readability first.
  • Duration: one sentence held for 0.8 seconds. Target 4–6 Chinese characters per second and split long lines.
  • Safe area: captions on the bottom edge get covered by platform UI. Move them inside the lower 10% of frame height.

When not to ship auto-captions

Names, technical terms, dialect, numbers and negation are where auto-captions fail. Without human review, do not deliver. One wrong character makes viewers doubt the whole film.

On set

Cut words, raise contrast, and avoid mouths and hands. Keep each line under 16 characters.

Do this

Hard-to-read subtitles: cut words, raise contrast, and keep them off mouths and hands. Heavy outlines are not the fix.

  1. Keep each line to twelve to sixteen Chinese characters or thirty-two to forty-two English characters, two lines maximum.
  2. Place subtitles above the safe area, clear of mouths, hands, and platform UI.
  3. Use a subtle background or light shadow for contrast; do not outline until the text blurs.

Avoid

Do not transcribe every word; subtitles are a guardrail, not a transcript.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Contracts, tax, insurance and consent rules differ by market; use the local currency and local counsel before signing or invoicing.

Alternative

If “Line length: over 18 Chinese characters, or two languages on one line. Split the sentence; do not shrink the type” is not the main problem, start with “Contrast: white type over sky, a white wall or a bright face. Add a translucent plate, outline or shadow; readability first”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Each line is twelve to sixteen Chinese characters or thirty-two to forty-two English characters, two lines maximum. If check 2 (Subtitles sit above the safe area, clear of mouths, hands, and platform UI) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • Each line is twelve to sixteen Chinese characters or thirty-two to forty-two English characters, two lines maximum.
  • Subtitles sit above the safe area, clear of mouths, hands, and platform UI.
  • A subtle background or light shadow adds contrast without blurring the type.

en.title: The Thumbnail Gets No Clicks
en.summary: Weak thumbnails usually lack an action; show a face doing something.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Thumbnail Gets No Clicks

Main / Method card

The Thumbnail Gets No Clicks

Weak thumbnails usually lack an action; show a face doing something.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Place three candidates side by side at phone width, cover the titles, and look only at the images: can you say what it is about in three seconds? Then reveal the title and check that image and words tell the same story. Pick the one that needs no explanation. When not to bait A thumbnail can be specific, but must not promise what the video lacks. One bait click buys long-term distrust, and platforms punish it through retention and negative feedback.

Is it unseen or unclicked?

  • Distribution: the platform did not show it to the right audience. Check publish time, title terms and first frame before redesigning the image.
  • Legibility: at 120px wide the subject disappears. Crop out the background; keep one face, one object or one action.
  • Mismatch: the thumbnail promises something the video does not deliver. Viewers leave immediately and the damage compounds.
  • Contrast: face and background share a tone, or type sits on a busy pattern. Use a solid block or vignette to separate the subject.

A phone-size test

Place three candidates side by side at phone width, cover the titles, and look only at the images: can you say what it is about in three seconds? Then reveal the title and check that image and words tell the same story. Pick the one that needs no explanation.

When not to bait

A thumbnail can be specific, but must not promise what the video lacks. One bait click buys long-term distrust, and platforms punish it through retention and negative feedback.

On set

Show a face in action: who is doing what, with what result. It must read at 200 pixels.

Do this

A weak thumbnail is usually unclear, not ugly. Show a face doing something.

  1. Choose a frame with a person, an action, and contrast; no empty scenery.
  2. Scale the subject to at least a third of the frame and darken the background.
  3. Shrink it to phone size and check in three seconds: can you say who is doing what?

Avoid

Do not pile on giant text and arrows; the thumbnail tells a story before it shows style.

Boundary

This page only covers “The Thumbnail Gets No Clicks”; it does not replace The Title Says Nothing, The Film Is Too Long, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: The thumbnail has a person, an action, and contrast; it is not empty scenery. If check 2 (The subject fills at least a third and the background is darker) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • The thumbnail has a person, an action, and contrast; it is not empty scenery.
  • The subject fills at least a third and the background is darker.
  • At phone size, three seconds is enough to say who is doing what.

en.title: The Title Says Nothing
en.summary: Write who meets what result; more adjectives, fewer clicks.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Title Says Nothing

Main / Method card

The Title Says Nothing

Write who meets what result; more adjectives, fewer clicks.

4 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

A title with no information: write “who hits what result.” More adjectives means fewer clicks.

On set

Write who meets what result. Fewer adjectives. The title and body must be the same story.

Do this

  1. Write three titles using person plus action plus result or cost.
  2. Cut empty words such as “shocking,” “premium,” and “must-see.”
  3. Choose one that matches the body exactly; do not bait.

Avoid

Do not trade an exaggerated promise for clicks; when the body cannot cash it, the audience leaves.

Three causes

For “The Title Says Nothing”, check three directions first. Change one variable, record a 30-second comparison, and see which link the change follows.

CauseSignal on setFive-minute test
Abstract nouns only“Growth”, “choice” and “goodbye” have no object, so nothing seems to happenReplace the noun with a person and an action
No conflictThe title gives the conclusion and the piece has no questionAdd a concrete obstacle or cost
Keyword stuffingThe title reads like a search box and never says whose story it isRemove two keywords and keep one action

On-set diagnosis

  1. Read the title to someone who has not seen the piece and ask what they think will happen.
  2. If they can only repeat abstract words, the title is under-specified.
  3. Compare title and first scene: does the promised action appear?

Fix

A good title is not a summary of theme; it is a person, an action and a cost. It should predict the first scene, not explain the film.

  1. Write “who + wants what + what blocks it”, then cut to twelve words or fewer.
  2. Put the most specific prop in the title: the cat, the old coat, the last delivery.
  3. Keep one unknown: do not reveal the result, only the price.
  4. If it sounds like a paper, rewrite it as something a character would say.

Failure cases

With “The Title Says Nothing”, these three moves make it worse. Pick one replacement action and do not change three variables at once.

FailureWhy it gets worseReplace with
ClickbaitThe piece cannot pay off the title and the audience leavesPromise only an action the first scene can deliver
RestatementTitle and summary say the same thingTitle gives action; summary gives conditions
Keyword pileIt reads like a tag listKeep at most one search phrase

Acceptance table

Acceptance is not “it feels better”; all four must be identifiable, playable and logged.

CheckPass lineLog
Concrete subjectA person or object, not only an abstract nounCircle the nouns
ActionThe title answers what happensAsk a stranger to retell it
CostThe title implies what may be lostWrite one cost line
PayoffThe first scene contains the promised actionCompare with the body

Check

en.summary: Check images, text, music, and claims; fix one cause, not the whole film.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Platform Rejected It

Main / Method card

The Platform Rejected It

Check images, text, music, and claims; fix one cause, not the whole film.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Watch the cut muted for visual risk; then listen with eyes closed for sound and claims. Compare each item with the current rule and write three columns: issue, evidence, fix.

Check four categories first

  • Content class: violence, medical, financial, minors, politics and news each carry extra documentation. Read the platform's current rule, not last year's experience.
  • Claims and proof: efficacy, price, comparison, expert identity. Delete absolute claims without evidence.
  • Music and assets: commercial license or platform-only use? “Others use it” is not a license.
  • People and privacy: likeness, voice, address, plate, minors. Get consent, or obscure and remove.

When not to re-upload repeatedly

Uploading the same version again does not change the result and may trigger risk controls. Get the specific reason, add evidence or change the frame, then appeal. “I think it's fine” is not a fix.

On set

Check images, text, music, and claims. Fix one item, not the whole film.

Do this

A platform rejection: check image, text, music, and claims. Change one thing; do not rebuild the film.

  1. List four likely triggers: sensitive imagery, absolute claims, unlicensed music, engagement bait.
  2. Change one item at a time and re-upload to test.
  3. Keep the rejection notice and screenshots; appeal with evidence if needed.

Avoid

Do not delete the whole film at once; locate the trigger first.

en.title: The Client Keeps Revising
en.summary: Write the objective in one sentence and test every revision against it.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Main/The Client Keeps Revising

Main / Method card

The Client Keeps Revising

Write the objective in one sentence and test every revision against it.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

When the client says “one more version,” ask which problem it solves: pacing, information or emotion. Then offer two options with their costs. Let them choose rather than redefine at the next meeting.

Turn revisions into options, not infinity

The contract states revision rounds and scope per round; new requests outside scope get a separate quote.

Limits

Do not hide scope creep behind “the client is always right.” Professionalism is showing the cost of each choice, not unlimited compliance.

Write revisions as enforceable terms, not feelings

When a client says “it doesn't feel right,” it is usually not taste. It is the absence of a shared test. Revision terms must answer three things: what changes, how many rounds, and when it is done.

StageCan changeCannot changeApproval
Script / storyboardStructure, lines, shot orderApproved locations and budgetEmail reply “approved”
Rough cutPace, shot selection, subtitle positionPickups, recasting, script rewriteTimecoded notes
Final cutTypos, levels, end-card detailsStructural change, new musicWritten approval on watermarked cut

After two rounds, quote new work

The contract includes two revision rounds; round three bills by hour or extra edit day. This is not punishment; it makes cost visible. If round three introduces a structural change, stop, rewrite the script, then decide whether to continue.

Notes need a timecode and an action

Do not accept “make it more premium.” Ask for “00:12 subtitle is too fast, hold two seconds” or “00:20 music is too full, bring it to -18 LUFS.” One note solves one point, so nobody guesses.

Three signals of scope creep

  • “By the way” requests: an extra product close-up, an English version, a BTS cut.
  • The decision-maker changes: the original contact no longer approves; a new leader restarts notes.
  • Deliverables multiply: one film becomes three ratios, two languages and a social cut.

When any appears, send a one-page change order: new scope, new schedule, new cost. Start only after written approval.

On set

Write the goal in one sentence and check every revision against it. Quote separately for scope creep.

Do this

Endless client revisions: write the goal in one sentence, then judge every change against it.

  1. Put one line in the brief: “this film makes whom do what,” and get both sides to confirm.
  2. Collect notes in rounds, one category per round; quote extra rounds beyond the contract.
  3. After each change, ask whether it makes the goal clearer or fuzzier.

Avoid

Do not accept every note under “the client is always right”; unlimited revisions sink the project.

Boundary

This page only covers “The Client Keeps Revising”; it does not replace pricing, contract review, or the creative brief. If the problem belongs to another page in the related list, use that page first.

Alternative

If “Put one line in the brief: “this film makes whom do what,” and get both sides to confirm” is not the main problem, start with “Collect notes in rounds, one category per round; quote extra rounds beyond the contract”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: The brief contains one line: “makes whom do what,” confirmed by both sides. If check 2 (Notes arrive in rounds, one category per round) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

When not to use

This page only covers “The Client Keeps Revising”; it does not replace The Color Is Off, Continuity Broke, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Check

  • The brief contains one line: “makes whom do what,” confirmed by both sides.
  • Notes arrive in rounds, one category per round.
  • Extra rounds are quoted; revisions are not unlimited.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Endless revisions are usually an unlocked brief, not a bad client. Turn spoken opinions into one page.

Lock the brief

Write five things: who watches, what they do after, what must appear, what must never appear, three reference films. Get confirmation on that page, not a “sure” in a chat thread.

Mark each reference “structure” or “style.” Without that, the client wants every strength of all three, and nobody can deliver it.

Three kinds of changes

Bug fixes are free: a typo, a black frame, out-of-sync audio. Scope changes are billed: a new scene, a new version, a different actor. Taste changes use the included round: color, music, pacing. Track the three separately so the client sees what they are asking for.

Give every revision a version number and a cutoff. Past the cutoff, it moves to the next round. Do not edit while chatting; otherwise nobody knows which version is current.

Protect the edit

Do not let clients into the timeline. Have them comment on a timecoded review link. Each note says minute, second, what to change, and why. “It feels off” is not a note.

If notes contradict each other, go back to the brief: which goal changed? If the goal is the same, keep the original plan. If the goal changed, it is a new project; quote again.

Five-minute drill: translate three notes

Take three client lines and translate each into one executable action: add a close-up, change the music to no drums, move the ending five seconds earlier. If you cannot translate it, book ten minutes on the phone; do not guess.

Put the three translations on the change sheet and ask the client to confirm “this is what I mean.” One confirmation can save three rounds.

When a revision is finished

A revision is done when the client confirms the latest version is deliverable, every note on the change sheet has an answer, and the version number stops moving. Do not end a round with “should be fine.”

Archive the final version with the change sheet. When someone later asks why this changed, the sheet answers. Unrecorded changes become new arguments.

Ten client-revision checks

  • Brief has five items
  • Client confirms on paper
  • References marked structure or style
  • Bug fixes free
  • Scope changes quoted
  • Taste changes use the round
  • Every revision numbered
  • Clear cutoff time
  • Timecoded review link
  • Contradictions return to the brief

Revisions are not a fight. They are proof that two people still lack the same one-page answer to “what is this film.”

en.title: There Is No Time
en.summary: Cut shots and locations, not sound or backup; post can be lean, media cannot.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Main/There Is No Time

Main / Method card

There Is No Time

Cut shots and locations, not sound or backup; post can be lean, media cannot.

2 min quick read + 6 min deep read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Fix the delivery date and immovable gates: client review, platform launch, event date. Then count back through post, shoot, prep and recce, leaving rework time—not “probably enough.”

Schedule backward from delivery, not forward from the shoot

Write latest decision dates: if the location is not locked by then, switch; if cast is not confirmed, rewrite.

Limits

Rushing does not mean cutting sound and QC. When time is short, cut scope, not acceptance; a film without sound and QC is not delivered.

Back-planning is not squeezing the schedule; it is finding the critical path

“Next week” is usually not a date; it is anxiety. Ask for three dates: internal review, platform launch and the latest acceptable delivery. Once those exist, plan backwards; do not count days from today.

Back-planned milestoneMinimum reserveCost of compressing it
Final delivery2 days before launchNo revision or transcode buffer
Client final review1 day before deliveryNotes cannot be fixed; errors ship
Rough cut2 days before final reviewStructural problems surface at the end
Shoot1 day before rough cutNo backup; edit starts with damaged media
Script / storyboard lock2 days before shootOn-set rewrites; crew and location idle

There is only one critical path

Write the prerequisites for every task; the longest chain is the critical path. Compressing a non-critical task does not finish the project earlier; it only creates a longer wait. If the shoot on the critical path is one day, do not spend the budget on a second camera; protect that day first.

Name three buffers

  • Shoot buffer: weather, location, late talent, two hours.
  • Post buffer: software crash, media re-transcode, one day.
  • Client buffer: approval delay, one day.

A buffer is not “if there is time.” Put it on the calendar and tell the client, “these days are protected; no new tasks.” An unnamed buffer will always be eaten by another meeting.

On set

Cut shots and scenes, not sound and backup. Post can be lean; media cannot be missing.

Do this

Short on time: cut shots and locations, not sound or backup. Post can be leaner; footage cannot be missing.

  1. Split the shot list into must-have and nice-to-have; shoot must-have first.
  2. Merge locations and camera setups to cut moves.
  3. Protect fixed time for backup, meals, and wrap; do not squeeze them.

Avoid

Do not trade sleep or backup for time; a failure costs more.

Boundary

This page only covers “There Is No Time”; it does not replace pricing, contract review, or the creative brief. If the problem belongs to another page in the related list, use that page first.

Alternative

If “Split the shot list into must-have and nice-to-have; shoot must-have first” is not the main problem, start with “Merge locations and camera setups to cut moves”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: The shot list is split into must-have and nice-to-have; must-have is shot first. If check 2 (Locations and setups are merged and moves reduced) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

When not to use

This page only covers “There Is No Time”; it does not replace The Ending Has No Force, How to Get the First Client, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Check

  • The shot list is split into must-have and nice-to-have; must-have is shot first.
  • Locations and setups are merged and moves reduced.
  • Time for backup, meals, and wrap is protected.

Deep dive

About 6 minutes. Not enough time is not a reason to work late. It is a reason to schedule backward and cut scope first.

Schedule backward from delivery

Write the delivery date first, then work backward: final export, client review, mix, fine cut, assembly, shoot, prep. Give every stage a twenty percent buffer; do not save the buffer for the end.

The shoot day is not “finished shooting”; it is “material can enter the edit.” If you cannot back up and transcode that day, everything downstream slips.

Cut scope first

When time halves, cut locations, cameras, and versions, not sleep. One location, one camera, one version can still hold quality; three locations, two cuts, four aspect ratios will all be mediocre.

Split “must have” and “nice to have” into two columns. If there is only time for the first, delete the second. Do not add while working.

A visible deliverable every day

Break the project into daily deliverables: selects today, assembly tomorrow, sound the day after. End every day with a file someone can open. “Working on it” is not progress.

If a day slips, the next day restores the deliverable before optimizing images. Polish can move later; structure cannot.

Five-minute drill: backward schedule

Take a real delivery date and write seven rows backward: export, review, mix, fine cut, assembly, shoot, prep. Give each row a date and a name. No name means it is not scheduled.

Write the buffer as its own row before the shoot, not at the end. Circle every row without an owner in red and resolve it today.

When the deadline is met

Met does not mean exported. It means the client can open it, play it, download it, and publish it. Export is half. Upload, review, subtitles, and cover all passing is the other half.

The day before delivery, do a full pass: open it on another device, watch muted, listen with headphones, click every link. When the pass clears, the deadline is actually safe.

Ten deadline checks

  • Schedule backward from delivery
  • Seven stages with dates
  • Twenty percent buffer each
  • Buffer before the shoot
  • Shoot day means material can enter edit
  • Cut locations, cameras, versions first
  • Must-have and nice-to-have separated
  • Visible deliverable every day
  • Restore structure before polish
  • Every row has an owner

A deadline is not for staying up late. It is for deciding what does not get made this time.

en.title: The Budget Is Over
en.summary: Stop nonessential gear first; overruns usually come from scope, not unit price.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Budget Is Over

Main / Method card

The Budget Is Over

Stop nonessential gear first; overruns usually come from scope, not unit price.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Split the budget into prep, shoot, post and contingency. Keep at least 10% buffer in each. List actual and forecast overruns in two columns, then work only the top three forecast items. Do not hide the gap with “we'll figure it out.”

Find which bucket is over

  • Prep: gear, location or crew days grew. Cut scope, never insurance or safety.
  • Shoot: losing one shot a day for three days sinks post. Re-rank the remaining shots by “can we deliver without it?”
  • Post: unlimited revisions or more footage than budgeted. Put revision rounds in the contract and price them.

A ten-minute table

Split the budget into prep, shoot, post and contingency. Keep at least 10% buffer in each. List actual and forecast overruns in two columns, then work only the top three forecast items. Do not hide the gap with “we'll figure it out.”

When to stop

When an overrun threatens safety, insurance or delivery quality, stop and renegotiate scope. That is more professional than pushing to a film nobody can use. A client can accept one missing shot; not an unusable master.

When the budget overruns, start with three sheets

Overruns are rarely one expensive item. They are missing line items, changes and cash timing. Split the budget into cost, cash flow and change sheets. If the three do not reconcile, an unwritten assumption is still hiding.

SheetWhat goes inCommon omissions
CostShoot days, post days, gear, locations, travel, taxTransport, insurance, overtime, backups, platform fees
Cash flowWhen money arrives, when it leavesClient approval cycles, invoice mail, deposit returns
ChangeScope, schedule and cost of each additionVerbal promises, free pickups, late script changes

Contingency is not profit

Keep 10–15% contingency on total cost, on its own line, outside margin. It has three uses: pickups, delays and gear replacement. Record every spend. If unused, do not distribute it early as a bonus; the next overrun will have no buffer.

The order of response after an overrun

  1. Stop new purchases and confirm what is already owed.
  2. Classify change-sheet items as client-caused, self-caused or force majeure.
  3. Client-caused gets a change order; self-caused comes from contingency; force majeure follows the contract.
  4. Do not hide it as “the next job will make it up.” The next job has its own costs.

Run a 30-minute close-out: which line exceeded 10%, why, and which sheet it enters next time. “Control the budget” is not an action; write the specific move.

On set

Stop nonessential gear and change scope. Overruns usually come from scope, not unit price.

Do this

Over budget: stop optional gear first, then talk about people. Overruns usually come from scope, not unit price.

  1. List spending as incurred and pending; cut pending nonessentials first.
  2. Compare with the original budget and name the scope change: extra locations, days, revision rounds.
  3. Quote the addition to the client; do not absorb it silently.

Avoid

Do not fill the hole with a lower price; the next job gets harder.

Boundary

This page only covers “The Budget Is Over”; it does not replace The Client Keeps Revising, The Color Is Off, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “List spending as incurred and pending; cut pending nonessentials first” is not the main problem, start with “Compare with the original budget and name the scope change: extra locations, days, revision rounds”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Spending is split into incurred and pending; pending nonessentials are cut. If check 2 (The scope change is named: locations, days, or revision rounds) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • Spending is split into incurred and pending; pending nonessentials are cut.
  • The scope change is named: locations, days, or revision rounds.
  • The addition is quoted to the client, not absorbed.

en.title: The Crew Is Fighting
en.summary: Stop for ten minutes and write who is waiting on whom; do not assign blame in public.
en.html:
Home/Main/The Crew Is Fighting

Main / Method card

The Crew Is Fighting

Stop for ten minutes and write who is waiting on whom; do not assign blame in public.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Before rolling, each lead states the most important shot, the most likely failure and who they need. Record actions only, not judgments. In a conflict, repeat the other person's request first, then offer one executable option.

Name the conflict type

  • Unclear ownership: two people direct the camera. Write final authority for each department into the call sheet; keep one decision-maker on set.
  • Schedule pressure: falling behind turns into blame. Cut shots or change the plan; do not fix a schedule with overtime and temper.
  • Safety: someone sees a hazard but stays quiet. Safety veto outranks director and producer; anyone can call stop.

A five-minute stand-up

Before rolling, each lead states the most important shot, the most likely failure and who they need. Record actions only, not judgments. In a conflict, repeat the other person's request first, then offer one executable option.

Do not

Do not call someone out in a group chat, do not pressure with “everyone does it,” and do not continue while a hazard is unresolved. On-set shouting is not a creative style; it is a management failure.

On-set conflict starts with unclear decision rights

Most set conflicts are not temperament. They are unclear authority: the director wants a shot, the client wants the product, the DP wants light, the producer wants time, and all four are deciding. A one-page decision chain before the shoot beats mediation after.

ItemFinal sayMust be consulted
Script and shotsDirectorClient, DP
Product presentationClientDirector, editor
Lighting and cameraDPDirector
Time and budgetProducerDirector, client
SafetyAnyone can stopEveryone

Three set rules

  1. One question goes to one decision-maker. Two approvers means no decision.
  2. A new client idea goes on a change sheet, not into the shot, unless it is safety or legal.
  3. When director and DP disagree, shoot both, play back, then decide. Do not argue theory on set.

Escalating a conflict

Stop for five minutes and write three lines: what happened, what it affects, who decides. Do not blame a person in front of the crew. If client and director are stuck, the producer ranks options by time, budget and safety, then lets the client choose; do not choose for them.

Ten minutes after wrap, review: which decision was overturned, why, and which rule it becomes. “Poor communication” is not a lesson; “product close-ups are the client's call; the director does not change them on set” is.

On set

Stop for ten minutes and write who is waiting on whom. Do not assign blame in front of the crew.

Do this

On-set conflict: stop for ten minutes and write the problem as “who is waiting for whom.” Do not judge right and wrong in front of the crew.

  1. Have each side write one line: what I am waiting for, where I am stuck.
  2. Turn it into tasks and order: who goes first, who follows, by what time.
  3. Name one decision maker; everyone else executes. Review after wrap, not in the moment.

Avoid

Do not smooth it over with “we all want the film to be good”; unresolved waiting starts the fight again.

Boundary

This page only covers “The Crew Is Fighting”; it does not replace The Shadows Are Dirty, There Is No Time, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “Each side wrote “what I am waiting for, where I am stuck.”” is not the main problem, start with “The problem became tasks and an order”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Each side wrote “what I am waiting for, where I am stuck.”. If check 2 (The problem became tasks and an order) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • Each side wrote “what I am waiting for, where I am stuck.”
  • The problem became tasks and an order.
  • One decision maker is named and the review happens after wrap.

en.title: AI Looks Uncanny
en.summary: Check eyes, hands, lip sync, and motion; any one breaks the illusion.
en.html:
Home/Main/AI Looks Uncanny

Main / Method card

AI Looks Uncanny

Check eyes, hands, lip sync, and motion; any one breaks the illusion.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Take the frame closest to the face and place it beside a live-action frame from the same scene on a phone. If you notice skin or catchlights before performance, it is not usable. Then watch the clip muted and check whether the motion gives it away.

Identify which kind of “fake”

  • Skin and light: too-clean skin, catchlights in the wrong place, background and subject lit from different directions. Fix the source first, not with more smoothing.
  • Motion: knees bending backwards, fingers merging, clothes without inertia. Shorten the action or shoot it live.
  • Detail: garbled text, asymmetric earrings, the wrong number of teeth. Hide it wide; replace it close.

When not to use it

Do not replace a hero close-up, long dialogue, a real interview or a news scene with generated images. Use AI for inserts, backgrounds, concept frames and pickups that cannot be shot.

On set

Check eyes, hands, lips, and motion. If any one breaks, regenerate or change the shot.

Do this

An AI image feels fake: check eyes, hands, lip sync, and motion. When one of these breaks, the audience leaves.

  1. Zoom into eye highlights, finger joints, teeth, and ears.
  2. Check lip closure and motion direction, especially turns and walks.
  3. Reframe the failure: hands out of frame, face in profile, shorter shot.

Avoid

Do not hide it with filters or skin smoothing; the more you polish, the faker it gets.

Boundary

This page only covers “AI Looks Uncanny”; it does not replace The Audio Has Hiss, You Crossed the Axis, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “Zoom into eye highlights, finger joints, teeth, and ears” is not the main problem, start with “Check lip closure and motion direction, especially turns and walks”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Eye highlights, finger joints, teeth, and ears were checked at full size. If check 2 (Lip closure and motion direction were checked) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • Eye highlights, finger joints, teeth, and ears were checked at full size.
  • Lip closure and motion direction were checked.
  • Failures were reframed: hands out, profile, or a shorter shot.
