en.title: AI Characters Drift
en.summary: Build a character sheet and carry one reference into every shot.
en.html:
Home/Main/AI Characters Drift

Main / Method card

AI Characters Drift

Build a character sheet and carry one reference into every shot.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Generate front, profile and looking-down views and compare them in one image. If cheekbones, nose bridge, hairline and wardrobe do not align, do not start batch generation. Fix the references, then the prompt. When not to force it For long dialogue, complex expressions or sharing the frame with a real actor, shoot a live reference first and use generation for wides and inserts. Do not hide drift with “we'll match it in post.”

Lock four things

  • Face: one front, one profile and one three-quarter reference; fix hair and brow shape. Do not rely on a text description each time.
  • Wardrobe: material, color, collar and buttons in the character sheet; do not switch to a near-match color in the same scene.
  • Light: key direction, color temperature and softness in the shot card; change the light before changing the face.
  • Lens: focal length and shot size change the face. The same character on a wide and a tele looks like two people; lock the lens first.

Three-angle test

Generate front, profile and looking-down views and compare them in one image. If cheekbones, nose bridge, hairline and wardrobe do not align, do not start batch generation. Fix the references, then the prompt.

When not to force it

For long dialogue, complex expressions or sharing the frame with a real actor, shoot a live reference first and use generation for wides and inserts. Do not hide drift with “we'll match it in post.”

On set

Use a character sheet, three views, and one reference. Compare face, wardrobe, and hair shot by shot.

Do this

AI character drift: build a character sheet and three views, then carry the same reference into every shot.

  1. Lock ten traits: age, hair, face shape, brows, nose, wardrobe, shoes, accessories, build, skin tone.
  2. Generate front, side, and back views; choose one as the master.
  3. Every shot carries the same reference and the same description; change only action and camera.

Avoid

Do not rewrite the adjectives for every shot; each one grows a different person.

Boundary

This page only covers “AI Characters Drift”; it does not replace AI Rights Are Unclear, AI Looks Uncanny, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Alternative

If “Lock ten traits: age, hair, face shape, brows, nose, wardrobe, shoes, accessories, build, skin tone” is not the main problem, start with “Generate front, side, and back views; choose one as the master”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Ten traits are locked and one three-view master is chosen. If check 2 (Every shot carries the same reference and the same description) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

Check

  • Ten traits are locked and one three-view master is chosen.
  • Every shot carries the same reference and the same description.
  • Only action and camera change; the adjectives are not rewritten.

Home/Main/AI Rights Are Unclear

Main / Method card

AI Rights Are Unclear

Check training source, commercial terms, and likeness consent; if unclear, do not deliver.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

For every generated asset, log model and version, prompt, input references, output file, rights source and where it is used. Without all six, it does not go into a paid delivery. When not to use it News, documentary, testimony, real-person endorsement and projects that explicitly require live action must not use generated images. Never publish an uncleared asset and fix the rights later.

Separate four rights

  • Model terms: commercial use, output ownership, whether training a derivative is allowed. Read the current version and save a dated screenshot.
  • Input assets: do you have the right to use reference images, video or voice for generation? Do not use a client's uncleared asset as a style reference.
  • Personality: real face, voice, name and likeness. AI generation does not bypass consent.
  • Output similarity: existing characters, trademarks, music or artwork. Run a similarity check before delivery.

A five-minute record

For every generated asset, log model and version, prompt, input references, output file, rights source and where it is used. Without all six, it does not go into a paid delivery.

When not to use it

News, documentary, testimony, real-person endorsement and projects that explicitly require live action must not use generated images. Never publish an uncleared asset and fix the rights later.

On set

Check training sources, commercial terms, and likeness permission. If unclear, do not deliver.

Do this

Unclear AI rights: check training source, commercial terms, and likeness permission. If it is unclear, do not deliver.

  1. Read the model terms: commercial use, modification, credit, prohibited uses.
  2. Get written permission for real people, celebrities, or brands.
  3. Keep prompts, references, generation logs, and licenses; label the AI content on delivery.

Avoid

Do not gamble on “nobody will sue”; rights problems travel with the work.

60-second test

Check

en.title: You Have No Portfolio
en.summary: Make three 30-second proof films: a person, an object, a story.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Main/You Have No Portfolio

Main / Method card

You Have No Portfolio

Make three 30-second proof films: a person, an object, a story.

2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Do not wait for a big project. Choose three films you can actually finish: a 60-second portrait, a 30-second product, a 15-second event. For each, state your role, gear and deliverable.

With no portfolio, make three small signed deliverables

A portfolio is not a pile of films; it is three lines: problem, action, result. Clients want to see whether you solve their problem.

Limits

Do not label exercises as commercial cases. Invented clients, fake data or claiming others' shots invalidates the whole portfolio once noticed.

A credible portfolio without clients

A portfolio is not a client list; it is evidence of the problems you can solve. Without commercial work, fill it with three types: self-initiated films, shot reconstructions and process records. Each proves a different capability.

TypeProvesMinimum delivery
Self-initiated shortStory, directing, editingOne 60-second film + one-page intent
Shot reconstructionPrecision in camera, light, gradeOriginal frame + rebuilt frame + difference notes
Process recordReliability, communication, deliveryOne-page timeline + risk sheet + finished film

Four blocks per project

  1. Problem: who hit what specific problem, in one sentence.
  2. Constraint: budget, time, location, crew; at least two.
  3. Action: the trade-off you made, not “I shot it.”
  4. Result: a verifiable change, or an honest “not launched / not tested.”

What not to include

  • Client films without permission, clear faces of passersby, uncleared music.
  • A duty list that says “shot and edited” with no judgment.
  • Team work presented as solo; naming your role is more credible, not less.

Put three strongest projects on the first page, not twenty. Give each a reason to watch: a 30-second cut, a technical breakdown or a one-page review. Label self-initiated work as self-initiated; never imply a commercial commission.

On set

Make three thirty-second films: people, objects, and one story. One skill per film.

Do this

No portfolio: make three thirty-second proof films. Show you can shoot a person, an object, and a story.

  1. Each film proves one skill: portrait interview, product texture, or narrative turn.
  2. Shoot with the same settings to show consistent quality.
  3. Add one page per film: goal, method, result, failure.

Avoid

Do not use a travel montage as a portfolio; the client cannot see what you can do.

Boundary

This page only covers “You Have No Portfolio”; it does not replace pricing, contract review, or the creative brief. If the problem belongs to another page in the related list, use that page first.

Alternative

If “Each film proves one skill: portrait interview, product texture, or narrative turn” is not the main problem, start with “Shoot with the same settings to show consistent quality”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Three thirty-second proof films: a person, an object, and a story. If check 2 (They share one setting so quality is consistent) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

When not to use

This page only covers “You Have No Portfolio”; it does not replace Your Quote Is Too Low, A Scene Has No Change, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Check

  • Three thirty-second proof films: a person, an object, and a story.
  • They share one setting so quality is consistent.
  • Each has a one-page breakdown: goal, method, result, failure.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. An empty portfolio is not a lack of clients. It is a lack of three complete cases that prove you can deliver.

Make three complete films

Do not make a one-minute reel. Make three complete films, sixty to ninety seconds each, each proving one ability: people, product, space. A reel proves you can cut; a complete film proves you can deliver.

Point all three at one niche, not weddings today and AI tomorrow. Clients do not remember “does everything”; they remember “call him for this kind of film.”

One page per case

One page, five things: brief, constraint, key decision, result, one mistake. Do not write “the client was happy”; write what you changed and why.

Include two comparison images: before and after, or option A and B. When the client can see your judgment, they trust you to judge their project.

Publish and reuse

Turn each case into three formats: a landscape site version, a vertical social version, and a one-page proposal PDF. Title it with the result, not “Project X.” Use one readable image on the cover.

After every new project, replace the weakest piece; do not keep adding forever. A portfolio is not a warehouse; it is how you want to be remembered.

Five-minute drill: three-film list

Write three films you can shoot starting tomorrow: one person, one product, one space. For each, write one line: “after watching, you will believe I can do what.” If you cannot afford it, make the phone version; do not wait for gear.

Until the three exist, do not take a job that needs a fourth ability. A portfolio is not waited for; it is shot.

When the portfolio exists

The portfolio exists when three films play end to end, each has a one-page case, the site opens, and the PDF sends. Footage and drafts do not count.

One more test: after three films, a stranger can say what you are good at and why they would call you. If not, the three still point in different directions. Keep cutting, not adding.

Ten portfolio checks

  • Three complete films, not a reel
  • One ability per film
  • All three point at one niche
  • One page, five items per case
  • Brief and constraint written
  • Key decision written
  • Result written
  • One mistake written
  • Two comparison images
  • Three formats per case

A portfolio does not prove how much you shot; it proves you can finish three films inside constraints.

en.title: Your Quote Is Too Low
en.summary: Price days, gear, post, and revisions; low quotes repel good clients.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Main/Your Quote Is Too Low

Main / Method card

Your Quote Is Too Low

Price days, gear, post, and revisions; low quotes repel good clients.

2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Split the quote into four: days, gear, post, licensing. Low quotes count only the shoot day, missing prep, revisions, delivery and archiving—plus gear depreciation and software subscriptions.

Low quotes usually miss three costs

Calculate the break-even line before profit. A job below break-even costs more to take than refuse.

Limits

Do not comfort yourself with “I will raise prices later.” The first client locks expectations at the low price; raising it later requires explaining value again, not sending a message.

A quote is not a number; it is three levels of risk

The difference between ¥3,000 and ¥30,000 for the same 60-second film is not “expensive or cheap.” It is who absorbs changes, delays and rights. Split the quote into three tiers so the client knows what the money buys.

TierFitsIncludesExcludes
ExecutionLocked script, one location, one shootOne shoot day, one edit, basic subtitlesScript changes, pickups, voice-over, music rights
StandardNeeds a proposal, two locations, two revisionsTreatment, storyboard, two shoot days, two revisionsTalent, location fees, specialty gear
Full packageBrand needs multi-platform delivery in one goConcept to delivery, rights clearance, three aspect ratiosMedia spend, creators, platform fees

Find the break-even line before any discount

Add shoot days, post days, gear rental, travel, tax and a 10% contingency, then divide by deliverable days. That is the minimum you must recover per day. Below it, a discount is not generosity; it is borrowing from a future job. A discount can come out of profit, never out of cost.

Put payment milestones in the quote

  1. 50% after script or storyboard approval, before the shoot. No money, no camera.
  2. 30% after rough-cut approval, 20% before final delivery. Final files leave only after the watermarked cut is approved.
  3. Client-caused delays bill as extra shoot days; weather and force majeure are separate, not hidden inside “revisions.”

    4. End the quote with one line: “Based on one script, two locations and two revisions; additional work is quoted separately.” That sentence does more than any verbal promise.

On set

Price days, gear, post, and revisions. Low rates drive good clients away.

Do this

A quote that is too low: count days, gear, post, and revisions. Low prices drive good clients away.

  1. Calculate break-even: days times day rate plus gear, location, post, and tax.
  2. Add ten to twenty percent risk, and state revision rounds and overtime.
  3. Offer three tiers: basic, standard, rush. Let the client choose scope, not cut the rate.

Avoid

Do not say “let me win it first”; the low price becomes the new standard.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Contracts, tax, insurance and consent rules differ by market; use the local currency and local counsel before signing or invoicing.

Boundary

This page only covers “Your Quote Is Too Low”; it does not replace pricing, contract review, or the creative brief. If the problem belongs to another page in the related list, use that page first.

Alternative

If “Calculate break-even: days times day rate plus gear, location, post, and tax” is not the main problem, start with “Add ten to twenty percent risk, and state revision rounds and overtime”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Break-even is calculated: days times day rate plus gear, location, post, and tax. If check 2 (Ten to twenty percent risk is added, with revision rounds and overtime stated) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

When not to use

This page only covers “Your Quote Is Too Low”; it does not replace A Scene Has No Change, You Are Shooting Alone, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Check

  • Break-even is calculated: days times day rate plus gear, location, post, and tax.
  • Ten to twenty percent risk is added, with revision rounds and overtime stated.
  • Three tiers let the client choose scope; the rate is not cut.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. A low quote is not competitiveness. It is giving away your future revisions, gear, and hours for free.

Find the cost floor

Write the real cost of one day: shoot days, gear depreciation or rental, software, insurance, transport, tax, contingency. Add profit after that. A quote without profit is not cheap; it is borrowing money to do the job.

Do not use “what others charge” as the only reference; their crew, gear, and scope differ. First count how many days your scope actually takes.

Price the usage

Organic, paid media, territory, term, exclusivity: five separate lines. The client buys usage, not just shoot days. One year of media and one month are not the same price.

Revision rounds, rush, extra aspect ratios, and source files each get a line. Do not hide them inside “included,” or every add-on eats your margin.

Negotiate scope, not rate

If the budget is low, remove locations, cameras, versions, shoot days. Do not halve the day rate. Cutting the rate teaches every future client that this is your price.

Put deposit, balance, and cancellation in the contract; cancellation pays for time already spent. A low quote collected late is worse than a fair quote collected on time.

Five-minute drill: one cost sheet

Write a three-day project: people per day, gear, post hours, tax, insurance. Get a floor price, add twenty percent profit, and compare it with your old quote.

Turn the difference into a scope note; do not nervously delete it. The client can decline, but you should not buy an unfinished project with a low price.

Ten quoting checks

  • Cost floor includes gear, software, insurance, tax
  • Profit added separately
  • Workload counted in shoot days
  • Five usage lines separated
  • Organic and paid media priced differently
  • Revision rounds itemized
  • Rush and extra ratios itemized
  • Source files itemized
  • Negotiate scope, not day rate
  • Deposit, balance, cancellation in contract

A low price buys a one-time client. A fair price buys someone who comes back.

en.title: How to Get the First Client
en.summary: Start with acquaintances, community, and small shops; send a specific proposal, not a portfolio blast.
en.meta: 2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Field note
en.html:
Home/Main/How to Get the First Client

Main / Method card

How to Get the First Client

Start with acquaintances, community, and small shops; send a specific proposal, not a portfolio blast.

2 min quick read + 7 min deep read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Do not start with “who will pay me.” Start with “whose specific problem have I solved?” List three real outcomes: time saved, rework reduced, a process that now runs. The first client usually resembles the people in those three stories.

Find the first client in a problem you already solved

Keep the first engagement to one deliverable; do not sell a yearly content plan.

Limits

A low price is not a ticket in. Below cost, the first client becomes the first unfinished project. Trade clear scope for trust, not free work.

The first client comes from a testable small delivery, not a contact list

Without clients, the useful move is not a DM saying “I can shoot.” It is a 30–60 second sample aimed at one specific problem for one type of buyer. The sample must be understood in ten seconds and must make them say, “that's us.”

Three sources, ranked by conversion

  1. Communities you already belong to: industry groups, alumni, former colleagues. Solve one small problem for one person in under an hour, free, and leave a reusable file behind.
  2. Local small businesses: cafés, barbers, pet shops. Bring one 30-second sample and ask what their current photos or videos lack; do not start with gear.
  3. Open calls: brand collaborations and platform briefs. Use them to practice quoting and delivery, not to fund your month.

Make the first scope small enough to close

Take one location, one finished piece and two revisions, under seven days. The first job is not for profit. It is for three assets: one complete process, one publishable case and one client willing to write two sentences. Mention future work in the email, not in the quote.

Ask four questions at the first meeting

  • Who watches this?
  • What should they do after watching?
  • What do you lose without this film?
  • Which is tighter, budget or launch date?

If the four answers do not exist, the project is not ready. Sell a one-page treatment or a one-day consultation first; do not promise a finished film.

On set

Start with friends, community, and small shops. Send one concrete proposal, not a poster.

Do this

Your first client comes from people you know, your community, and small businesses. Send a specific plan, not a portfolio poster.

  1. List ten people or shops you might know; pick one with a real need.
  2. Give them a one-page plan: what, how long, what they get, what it costs.
  3. Do one small job, deliver on time, then ask for a quote or referral.

Avoid

Do not mass-message “I make videos”; a specific plan beats a self-introduction.

Boundary

This page only covers “How to Get the First Client”; it does not replace pricing, contract review, or the creative brief. If the problem belongs to another page in the related list, use that page first.

Alternative

If “Ten people or shops were listed and one with a real need was chosen” is not the main problem, start with “A one-page plan states what, how long, what they get, and the price”; only upgrade after both hold.

60-second test

Run one 60-second test against check 1: Ten people or shops were listed and one with a real need was chosen. If check 2 (A one-page plan states what, how long, what they get, and the price) does not change, do not add gear or budget.

When not to use

This page only covers “How to Get the First Client”; it does not replace You Only Have a Vague Idea, The Image Looks Flat, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Check

  • Ten people or shops were listed and one with a real need was chosen.
  • A one-page plan states what, how long, what they get, and the price.
  • The small job was delivered on time and earned a quote or referral.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. Your first client does not wait for a perfect portfolio. You write scope, price, and delivery clearly and trade a small project for trust.

Sell one small, clear job

Do not pitch a brand film for your first job. Pitch one thirty- or sixty-second product video: one location, one person, one deliverable. The smaller the scope, the more likely you deliver on time and the client tries you.

Ask three questions: who watches it, what should they do after, when is it needed? If the answers are unclear, do not quote yet; every later revision will come from those three blanks.

Quote in four lines

Scope, deliverables, revision rounds, rights and payment milestones. Four lines on one page. Deposit at least half; balance before the source files leave. Never write “pay what you think.”

Price by time and usage, not by runtime. Thirty seconds is not necessarily cheaper than three minutes; shoot days, cameras, talent, and post decide the cost.

Delivery and the relationship

Include one revision round in the quote; extra rounds are billed hourly or per version. Collect feedback once, in one link, not as a stream of voice messages.

Deliver three files: a platform-compressed version, a high-quality master, and a cover image, plus one page of notes. A case study one week after delivery is worth more than dinner with the client.

Five-minute drill: one-page quote

Take a real small request and write one page: scope, deliverables, revisions, rights, payment, schedule. No company introduction, no “we are professional.”

Send the page to a peer and ask which line a client could misread. Fix that line, then send it. The first job is not to earn the most; it is to deliver one complete project without rework.

When the first job is delivered

The job is delivered when the client has three files, has confirmed they play, the balance has arrived, and the usage range is written down. Sending files is not delivery. Leave a twenty-four-hour confirmation window so a broken file is found now, not next week.

The delivery email states which version is final, which files are for platforms, which are for archive, and how the next revision is billed. Four lines save ten explanation emails later.

Ten first-client checks

  • First job is small
  • One location, one person, one deliverable
  • Audience and action asked first
  • Delivery date written
  • Four-line quote on one page
  • Deposit at least half
  • Balance before source files
  • One revision round included
  • Feedback collected once
  • Three files plus one page of notes

Your first client is not buying your talent. They are buying whether you can finish one small thing on time, in scope, at the price.

en.title: Minimum Kit
en.summary: Minimum kit: a camera, one standard zoom, a tripod, and a mic that works.
en.html:
Home/Main/Minimum Kit

Main / Tool card

Minimum Kit

Minimum kit: a camera, one standard zoom, a tripod, and a mic that works.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Sound first, light second, lenses last. Viewers forgive a flat image; they do not forgive dialogue they cannot hear. The body sets the ceiling; sound and lighting set the floor.

Build backwards from the job

  • Minimum: one camera with manual exposure, one 24–70mm-equivalent lens, one lav or on-camera mic, one dimmable light, two cards, one portable drive. Finish a 30-second dialogue scene and ten shots first.
  • Working: add a prime, a shotgun mic and recorder, ND filters, and a monitor. Independent sound and exposure are the entry ticket to style.
  • Backup: a second body, a second audio chain, spare batteries, and a separate backup drive. A paid shoot should survive one failed link.

Three tests before you shoot

  1. Record 30 seconds of dialogue, listen on headphones for noise and sibilance, then play it back without monitoring.
  2. Shoot a frame with a bright window: check that highlights hold and shadows still carry detail.
  3. Copy the test clip to the drive, eject the card, and play it back from the drive only.

When not to upgrade

If the bottleneck is script, blocking or editing, a fourth lens will not help. Finish three complete short films with the current kit, then buy against a recorded failure.

On set

A body, standard zoom, tripod, and lav. Keep 20 percent of the budget for storage and batteries.

Avoid

Do not pick a camera body first; write the four jobs it must do.

Check

  • Each of four items maps to one named capability.
  • Storage and batteries take about 20 percent of budget.

en.title: Audio Starter Kit
en.summary: Audio starter: shotgun, lav, recorder, headphones; dialogue first.
en.html:
Home/Main/Audio Starter Kit

Main / Tool card

Audio Starter Kit

Audio starter: shotgun, lav, recorder, headphones; dialogue first.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

A shotgun carries the main dialogue, a lav is the backup, a recorder keeps the tracks separate, and headphones catch noise on the spot. Missing one of the four turns the shoot into guesswork.

One chain that can stand alone

  • Minimum: shotgun into camera, lav backed up on a phone or second body; only for a quiet interior and one speaker.
  • Working: shotgun into a 4-channel recorder, lav on its own track, headphones live; enough for two-person interviews and exteriors.
  • Insured: add a second lav, a backup recorder and timecode; one broken chain does not end the shoot.

Levels and redundancy

Keep dialogue peaks around -12 to -6 dBFS. Do not treat 32-bit float as insurance: it can rescue a clipped peak, not a missing lav, a stopped recorder, or wind inside the capsule. Every camera position needs at least one independent audio track.

Thirty-second acceptance

  1. Have one person speak normally while shotgun and lav record; each track must be intelligible alone.
  2. Record 30 seconds of a quiet room at the gain you will actually use; listen for an acceptable noise floor.
  3. Record 10 seconds outdoors in wind; confirm the blimp and shelter work and consonants survive.

Do not hide it in post

Denoise removes steady hiss, not wind, clothing rustle or room reflection. Change position, mic distance or wind protection on set; it is always cheaper than repair.

On set

Shotgun, lav, recorder, and headphones. Record thirty seconds of dialogue and check the noise floor.

Avoid

Do not bring only a shotgun; indoor dialogue without a lav backup dies in a draft.

Check

  • Shotgun and lav record simultaneously and each works alone.
  • A thirty-second dialogue test reveals the noise floor.
  • Someone wears headphones during recording, not just watching meters.

en.title: One-Light Kit
en.summary: One light: COB, soft box, reflector, two sandbags; one direction first.
en.html:
Home/Main/One-Light Kit

Main / Tool card

One-Light Kit

One light: COB, soft box, reflector, two sandbags; one direction first.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

One light and one softbox establish where the light comes from; a reflector then opens the shadow side. Multiple lights without direction only flatten the face.

Direction first, softness second

  • Minimum: one dimmable COB, one 60–90cm softbox, one stand, two sandbags. Enough for a single interior interview.
  • Working: add a 5-in-1 reflector, a black flag and a small background light; now you can separate face, background and edge.
  • Insured: a second matched light for backup or fill, plus extension cables and independent power; one missing outlet does not stop the shoot.

Match color temperature first

Write down the color temperature of window light, practicals and fixtures, then confirm with a gray card. Mixed light is not “atmosphere” most of the time; it is a white balance problem.

Startup test

  1. Place the light 45° to the side, shoot one frame; move it to the front, shoot another; compare nose shadow and catchlight.
  2. Move the softbox from 1.5m to 0.8m and shoot both; the shadow edge should visibly soften.
  3. Film the fixture with a phone to check for flicker; test at 1/50 and 1/100 shutter.

When not to add a light

If window light already has a direction, add a reflector or black flag before a second fixture. In night and documentary scenes, preserving the existing direction matters more than filling every shadow.

On set

One COB, a 90-centimeter softbox, a reflector, and two sandbags. Shoot half-body before adding a second light.

Avoid

Do not buy a second light first; without one direction, the second only fights it.

Check

  • One light and softbox produce a usable half-body setup.
  • Shadows are filled with a reflector before a second light.
  • Two sandbags keep the stand stable when nudged.

en.title: Travel Kit
en.summary: Travel light: one body, one lens, small stabilizer, two batteries, one ND, one pouch.
en.html:
Home/Main/Travel Kit

Main / Tool card

Travel Kit

Travel light: one body, one lens, small stabilizer, two batteries, one ND, one pouch.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

The first constraint on a travel shoot is the bag and the walk, not the number of lenses. If body, two lenses, audio and tripod exceed what you can lift after an hour, you start missing shots.

Weight budget before focal length

  • Light: one body, one 24–70mm-equivalent zoom, one small shotgun or lav, one ND, two cards, one SSD, one lightweight reversing tripod.
  • Full: add one wide or tele, spare batteries and a small fill light; everything fits one carry-on.
  • Leave behind: a drone with no shot plan, a third duplicate focal length, and lights the location cannot power.

Three things at the end of each day

  1. Copy the day to the SSD, then play back from the card to confirm the files are not empty.
  2. Charge batteries; format a card only after the backup is verified.
  3. Write tomorrow's first location and light time; do not decide at the location.

Field test

Before leaving, wear the final bag, walk ten minutes and climb one floor, then shoot 30 seconds. If a strap cuts, the tripod wobbles or an audio cable is missing, remove gear at the table, not at the destination.

On set

One body, one lens, a small gimbal, two batteries, ND, and a waist bag. Weigh it and walk a day before going.

Avoid

Do not carry three lenses “just in case”; after half a day you cannot shoot anything.

Check

  • Total weight is measured and survives a full-day walk.
  • One body and one lens only, no extra optics.
  • Batteries, ND, and gimbal sit in the waist bag for one-hand access.

en.title: Interview Two-Camera Kit
en.summary: Interview kit: A camera medium, B close, shotgun, backup lav; the edit gets choices.
en.html:
Home/Main/Interview Two-Camera Kit

Main / Tool card

Interview Two-Camera Kit

Interview kit: A camera medium, B close, shotgun, backup lav; the edit gets choices.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

One wide camera holds body and hands; one medium-close camera holds the face. Both share the same audio so the edit has choices. Two identical angles only give you the same footage twice.

Two cameras, not two copies

  • Minimum: main camera on a medium shot, second camera on a wide; lav into the main, on-camera mic on the second as reference only.
  • Working: two manual-exposure bodies, two primes, two lavs plus a shotgun, two lights, timecode or a clap sync.
  • Insured: separate recorder, third lav, spare batteries and a spare card; a main-camera failure does not stop the interview.

Ten minutes before rolling

  1. Have the subject speak normally; confirm both angles are in focus and neither audio channel clips.
  2. Clap or jam timecode, then play back one sync check.
  3. Shoot an empty frame and a frame with hands to confirm subtitle safe area.

Do not

Do not pair two different camera brands and expect a one-click match; do not give the subject only one lav; do not change a battery mid-interview without stopping. Continuity is the value of an interview, not the number of angles.

On set

A camera for the medium, B for the close, a shotgun, and a backup lav. Test two-camera sync first.

Avoid

Do not set both cameras to the same framing; the edit has no choices.

Check

  • A is mid-shot, B is close-up, clearly different.
  • Shotgun and lav each record a usable track.
  • The two-camera test syncs and framings do not duplicate.

en.title: Live Streaming Kit
en.summary: Live kit: camera, capture card, wired network, hotspot backup, local recording; uptime first.
en.html:
Home/Main/Live Streaming Kit

Main / Tool card

Live Streaming Kit

Live kit: camera, capture card, wired network, hotspot backup, local recording; uptime first.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

If the stream drops, viewers do not wait; if audio clips, a sharp image does not save it. The order is network, audio, backup recording, cameras, lighting.

Network and audio before image

  • Minimum: one camera, one capture card, one laptop, wired network, one lav or console feed; run a 15-minute private test first.
  • Working: a second network path (hotspot or router), independent audio, backup recording, headphones and a waveform display; you can see drops and clipping.
  • Insured: hardware encoder, UPS, second camera and independent backup recorder; a failed primary path can be switched.

Pre-broadcast test

  1. Push a private stream for 15 minutes at the real bitrate; log dropped frames, latency and upload variation.
  2. Have the host speak normally; confirm both the live feed and backup recording do not clip or drift.
  3. Unplug the primary network, confirm the backup takes over, then plug it back and confirm no duplicate stream.

Do not gamble on wireless

Use Ethernet whenever possible; wireless is backup only. Do not discover insufficient upload at showtime, and do not put backup recording on the same machine without independent power.

On set

Camera, capture card, wired network, hotspot backup, and local recording. Rehearse one network drop.

Avoid

Do not rely on venue Wi-Fi alone; one drop erases the stream.

Check

  • The stream runs wired and the backup hotspot is speed-tested.
  • A complete local recording exists alongside the stream.
  • The disconnect drill logs switchover and recovers within ten seconds.

Boundary

This page only covers “Live Streaming Kit”; it does not replace Backup Three-Piece Kit, Travel Kit, 16mm: Cinema Left the Theater. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

en.summary: Backup kit: reader, SSD, hard drive; offload, verify, and move offsite the same day.
en.html:
Home/Main/Backup Three-Piece Kit

Main / Tool card

Backup Three-Piece Kit

Backup kit: reader, SSD, hard drive; offload, verify, and move offsite the same day.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Three copies, two media types, one off-site. RAID is not backup; a sync folder is not backup either. Deletion syncs, and ransomware encrypts the sync target too.

3-2-1 is the floor, not a slogan

  • Minimum: one working SSD, one on-set drive, one drive or cloud copy taken away after the shoot.
  • Working: SSD working disk, NAS or two-drive backup, offline drive; add LTO or cold cloud for critical projects.
  • Team: checksums, version naming, restore log, media rotation; anyone can find and open the original footage a month later.

Three things after a copy

  1. Name by project/date/camera; do not carry “New Folder” into post.
  2. Generate checksums or at least compare file count and total size; do not trust a progress bar.
  3. Pick one random file, open it from the backup media and play ten seconds.

Restore drill

Once a month, restore one random project to an empty machine and record the time and failure points. A backup without a restore drill is only reassurance.

On set

Card reader, SSD, and hard drive. Copy, verify, and move offsite the same day. Confirm three copies before formatting.

Avoid

Do not format the card after one copy; at that moment you have no backup.

Check

  • SSD and hard drive each hold a copy with matching file counts.
  • Verification happens the same day and is logged.
  • Three copies exist before formatting, one offsite.

en.summary: AI workflow: script, reference, generator, upscale, comp, disclosure; every step reversible.
en.html:
Home/Main/AI Workflow Kit

Main / Tool card

AI Workflow Kit

AI workflow: script, reference, generator, upscale, comp, disclosure; every step reversible.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

An AI workflow is not “one prompt and a finished film.” Lock the script, character bible, shot list, rights scope and delivery specs before deciding which shots to generate.

Lock what must not change

  • Minimum: one usable generator, a set of character references, an upscale/repair tool, an editor and a rights log.
  • Working: character sheet, shot-prompt template, generated-asset IDs, compositing and grade, human check list.
  • Insured: local backups, model/version records and a live-action fallback; a failed generation does not stop the project.

Use it where it is controllable

Start with inserts, backgrounds, concept frames and pickups; do not start with a hero close-up and long dialogue. Hands, text, fast motion, mirrors and complex occlusion remain high-risk.

Three checks

  1. The same character across three angles keeps face, hair, wardrobe and light direction.
  2. A continuous five-second move shows no warping, flicker or limb fusion.
  3. Output files, model version, prompts and rights sources are all findable in the project record.

When not to use it

News, documentary, testimony, real-person endorsement and projects requiring clear authorship must not use generated images as on-set evidence. Assets without a rights chain do not enter delivery.

On set

Script, reference, generator, upscale, comp, and label. Keep a rollback version at every step.

Avoid

Do not keep rerolling generations; without script and references, a good roll is still unusable.

Check

  • Script and references exist before the first generation.
  • Generation, upscale, and comp each carry a rollback version.
  • The delivered version has an AI label and a traceable version chain.

en.summary: Accessibility check: captions, contrast, audio description, loudness, flicker; one by one before delivery.
en.html:
Home/Main/Accessibility Check Kit

Main / Tool card

Accessibility Check Kit

Accessibility check: captions, contrast, audio description, loudness, flicker; one by one before delivery.

2 min read · Field noteTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Captions, contrast, audio description and a flash check. Contrast and description are the ones most often skipped, and they decide whether low-vision viewers can follow.

Four things first

  • Minimum: an accurate caption file, readable caption styling, text for essential information.
  • Working: SDH captions (sound effects and speakers), an audio-description script, contrast checks, keyboard-operable pages.
  • Insured: multilingual captions, described audio mix, flash testing, tests with real users.

Captions are not just dialogue

Keep each line under roughly 16–18 Chinese characters, one or two lines. Mark speakers and key sounds. Keep captions inside the safe area, not on the bottom edge. Split fast speech instead of shrinking type.

Three checks

  1. Watch muted: you still know who speaks, what happens and which sounds matter.
  2. Shrink the frame to phone size: captions remain readable and contrast with the background.
  3. Tab through the page: focus is visible and every link and button is reachable.

Do not fake accessibility

Unedited auto-captions, description that only narrates the image, and contrast judged by eye do not count. Accessibility is a delivery spec, not a favor.

On set

Subtitles, contrast, audio description, loudness, and flicker. Check each before delivery.

Avoid

Do not check captions only; failed contrast and flashing make the picture unwatchable.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Contracts, tax, insurance and consent rules differ by market; use the local currency and local counsel before signing or invoicing.

Check

  • Captions name speakers and key sounds at a compliant rate.
  • Text contrast, audio description, and loudness all pass.
  • Flashing is compliant and all five items are ticked before delivery.

en.summary: A ninety-second travel vlog: one person, two days, one town, one rainstorm; not a drone reel, but “looking for one thing.”
en.html:
Home/Main/Travel Vlog Case: One Discovery Only

Main / Project review

Travel Vlog Case: One Discovery Only

A ninety-second travel vlog: one person, two days, one town, one rainstorm; not a drone reel, but “looking for one thing.”

4 min read · Project reviewTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

This is an anonymized composite review. It merges constraints, decisions, and consequences that recurred across three similar projects into one checkable timeline. Budgets and schedules are ranges, not one client's ledger, and no client is named. Use it to test your own project, not as a single job's diary.

How to read this review

This is an anonymized composite review. It merges constraints, decisions, and consequences that recurred across three similar projects into one checkable timeline. Budgets and schedules are ranges, not one client's ledger, and no client is named. Use it to test your own project, not as a single job's diary.

Project card

  • Format: ninety-second travel vlog
  • Crew: one (shoot + on camera)
  • Schedule: two shoot days plus one post day
  • Budget range: RMB 1,000–3,000
  • Platform: RED / Douyin
  • Limits: rain, no drone, one backpack

Timeline

  1. 第 1 天 07:30: Arrive in town; the first shot is a person entering, not a drone.
  2. 第 1 天 09:00: First shop; shoot “how he asks,” not a sign montage.
  3. 第 1 天 11:00: Rain; move to the market; rain becomes the through-line.
  4. 第 1 天 14:00: Wrong alley; keep eight seconds of failure.
  5. 第 2 天 08:00: Second location; the shop is closed, the task gets harder.
  6. 第 2 天 11:00: Find it or not; close on a face or an empty frame.
  7. 后期: Cut three pretty empties; music only at three seconds open and eight seconds close.

Constraints

Rain was forecast both days; the sunset and drone plans were dead. One thirty-five millimeter lens, one phone, one tripod, no second person to carry, no reshoot budget.

Pre-production decisions

  1. Replace “place” with “task”: not “how beautiful this town is,” but “find the old shop that sells one kind of noodle.” One action per location.
  2. Person before place: every scene opens on a person entering, then the environment; scenery without action lasts two seconds at most.
  3. Cut on ambience: rain, umbrella ribs, and the wok first; music enters last and never covers the place.

What changed on set

Afternoon rain killed the riverside shot and broke the umbrella. We did not wait for sun; we moved to the market and shot the asking. Rain became the through-line and made “not finding it” more believable.

Post choices

  1. Cut three pretty empties: they did not move “find the shop” and turned the film into a scenery reel.
  2. Keep one failure: eight seconds of asking the wrong way and walking the wrong alley; the discovery needs it.
  3. Music enters twice: three seconds at the open, eight at the close; the middle runs on rain and dialogue.

Result

In internal preview, viewers could retell “he looked for a noodle shop, it rained, he found it or did not,” not just recall drone shots. There was no sunset, but “looking in the rain” became the one memory.

Three reusable lessons

  1. Give the trip a task before a location: travel without a task is moving scenery.
  2. Keep the failure: wrong turns, wrong alleys, and rain are the cost of a discovery.
  3. Ambience is the transition: let the place speak; music is punctuation.

One failure

Day one scheduled four locations and delivered two; transit broke the “find the shop” continuity. Next time schedule two locations a day and put travel time in the plan.

Regional note for US / UK / EU readers

This English page keeps mainland-China examples where they are part of the method. Read platform names as examples, not as the only market: Douyin ↔ TikTok/Reels, Bilibili ↔ YouTube, Xiaohongshu ↔ Instagram/Pinterest; RMB figures are not converted here. Contracts, tax, insurance and consent rules differ by market; use the local currency and local counsel before signing or invoicing.

Check

  • Is there one clear “looking for”?
  • One action per location?
  • Does scenery run over two seconds without a person?
  • Is one failure kept?
  • Can ambience carry the transitions alone?
  • Does music cover the place?
  • How many locations were planned versus finished?

Project card

  • Format: ninety-second news feature
  • Crew: two (reporter + camera)
  • Schedule: one shoot day plus one post day
  • Budget range: RMB 3,000–8,000
  • Platform: institutional / news
  • Limits: six-hour window, one official source, one witness

Timeline

  1. 08:00: The official statement lands; the reporter checks first-post time by phone while the camera shoots signs and the street.
  2. 09:30: Arrive; record thirty seconds of ambience before waiting.
  3. 10:00: Twelve-minute witness interview; ask what was seen, not how it felt.
  4. 10:40: The witness leaves; shoot the empty chair, wind in the doorway, notice board.
  5. 12:00: Clear archive rights; the unlicensed clip becomes a three-second blurred background.
  6. 15:00: Rough cut; cut “may be linked,” replace with “still unclear.”
  7. 16:00: Legal and editor review; deliver.

Constraints

Before the shoot only three facts were fixed: time, place, and one official statement. The witness gave twenty minutes, archive came from two sources, and one was not licensed for commercial use. The film was due at 4 p.m. with no reshoot.

Pre-production decisions

  1. Verify before shooting: the reporter spent ninety minutes checking the official statement, first-post time, and address; the camera shot signs, the street, and the notice board, not emotional empty frames.
  2. Two columns, known and unknown: every known fact carried a source, every unknown was marked “to verify”; the film ended on one unknown instead of speculation.
  3. Label every archive shot: the unlicensed clip became a three-second blurred background, never the main image; each carried “archive / date / source.”

What changed on set

Forty minutes in, the witness took a call and had to leave. The plan was three lines pointing at the spot; instead we got a twelve-minute interview and one shot of his back. We did not ask him to reenact. We shot the empty chair, the wind in the doorway, and the notice board, leaving “the person left, the event remains” in frame.

Post choices

  1. No music: sync sound, footsteps, wind, and paper on the notice board carried the feeling; music would tell viewers what to conclude.
  2. Cut one speculation: the rough cut said “this may be linked to…”; after legal and editor review it became “it is still unclear.”
  3. Make the unknown a graphic: a two-column known/unknown card ran from 1:10 to 1:22 instead of repeating it in narration.

Result

The piece passed internal review with no correction. It did not get the most dramatic shot, but every key fact had a source on screen; the empty chair after the witness left became the only emotional image, not a substitute for evidence.

Three reusable lessons

  1. Verification is production: the ninety minutes on the phone decided what the ninety seconds could say.
  2. Put “we do not know” on screen: viewers accept an unknown, not a fake certainty.
  3. Archive is not free footage: source, date, and rights; if one is missing, keep it out of the main image.

One failure

Waiting for the witness cost us the location's room tone; post used library street sound and the space felt thinner. Next time record thirty seconds of ambience before the interview, not after.

Music Video Case: Three Motifs Hold the Song

A three-and-a-half-minute music video with five people, one day, one warehouse: no plot, three visual motifs escalating with the song.

5 min read · Project reviewTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

This is an anonymized composite review. It merges constraints, decisions, and consequences that recurred across three similar projects into one checkable timeline. How to read this review

This is an anonymized composite review. It merges constraints, decisions, and consequences that recurred across three similar projects into one checkable timeline. Budgets and schedules are ranges, not one client's ledger, and no client is named. Use it to test your own project, not as a single job's diary.

Project card

  • Format: three-and-a-half-minute music video
  • Crew: five (director/camera/light/art/producer)
  • Schedule: one shoot day plus three post days
  • Budget range: RMB 10,000–30,000
  • Platform: music / Channels
  • Limits: artist for six hours, one warehouse, three looks

Timeline

  1. 08:00: Light the warehouse; lock three motifs: shutter door, white beam, mirror.
  2. 09:00: Artist arrives; the first two hours go to chorus and bridge.
  3. 11:00: Change look; shoot verse space and narrowing pre-chorus.
  4. 13:00: Projector flickers; slow shutter, make it texture, switch key to hard light.
  5. 15:00: Add a riskier chorus action; keep a safe take.
  6. 16:00: Wrap; sync every performance shot to playback.
  7. 后期: Cut to song structure; remove the “door into another world” story.

Constraints

The artist had six hours, the warehouse could not be held overnight, and there was no second lighting day. The song had four sections: verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge; no narrative budget and no second location.

Pre-production decisions

  1. Keep three motifs: a rolling shutter door, a moving white beam, a mirror; each section changes one variable.
  2. Escalate the chorus through action, not flashes: same move bigger, faster, riskier; cut on the drum, not the lyric.
  3. Performance first, empties later: the artist's best two hours go to chorus and bridge; inserts wait for the break.

What changed on set

The warehouse's old projector started flickering on the third chorus and caused banding. We did not swap the light; we slowed the shutter, made the projector background texture, and used one hard key. The flicker became the chorus rhythm.

Post choices

  1. Cut to song structure, not shoot order: verse gives space, pre-chorus narrows, chorus cuts action, bridge holds one long take.
  2. Cut a “story”: the original had the artist opening a door into another world; it fought the song, so it went.
  3. Sync first: every performance shot goes back to playback, cut two frames before the drum so action and sound land together.

Result

The artist's team approved on the first pass and did not ask for a plot. Viewers remembered the shutter door, the moving beam, and one turn into the mirror; the chorus needed no explanation because the action escalated.

Three reusable lessons

  1. Motifs before looks: motifs decide shots; wardrobe is a variable.
  2. Escalate the chorus through action, not flashes: same move bigger, faster, riskier beats ten effects.
  3. Performance first: do not spend the artist's best two hours on inserts.

One failure

We shot too many empties and missed a close-up of hands on the instrument; post used a wide instead, and the chorus lost a visible action detail. Next time put three must-get details on the shot list.

Main / Project review

Wedding Case: Vows Cannot Be Reshot

A six-minute wedding film with two cameras, twelve hours, and low light: cover three ritual beats before emotion or slow motion.

4 min read · Project reviewTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

This is an anonymized composite review. It merges constraints, decisions, and consequences that recurred across three similar projects into one checkable timeline. Budgets and schedules are ranges, not one client's ledger, and no client is named. Use it to test your own project, not as a single job's diary.

How to read this review

This is an anonymized composite review. It merges constraints, decisions, and consequences that recurred across three similar projects into one checkable timeline. Budgets and schedules are ranges, not one client's ledger, and no client is named. Use it to test your own project, not as a single job's diary.

Project card

  • Format: six-minute wedding film
  • Crew: two (two cameras + sound)
  • Schedule: one shoot day plus four post days
  • Budget range: RMB 8,000–20,000
  • Platform: private / RED
  • Limits: ceremony cannot repeat, low light, 120 guests

Timeline

  1. 07:00: Prep; shoot hands, clothing, doorway, no staging.
  2. 10:00: Confirm three unmissable beats; check lav and independent recorder.
  3. 10:30: Entrance; A holds the aisle wide, B holds faces close.
  4. 10:45: Vows; the lav is knocked off, the recorder saves the whole passage.
  5. 11:00: Rings and announcement; A holds hands, B holds guests.
  6. 12:00: Reception; keep two tables with specific reactions.
  7. 16:00: Back up before wrap; confirm vow track syncs.

Constraints

The ceremony happens once; vows cannot be reshot. The hall has only ceiling light and two warm wall fixtures; no big light. One hundred twenty guests; cameras cannot block the aisle. Two people: A camera holds the wide, B holds close and sound.

Pre-production decisions

  1. List three unmissable beats: entrance, rings, vows; each gets a safe camera, no improvisation.
  2. Two audio sources: B camera takes the lav, a separate recorder sits near the officiant; vows lead, music steps back.
  3. No big light: use the warm practicals plus one small LED for faces; keep the hall dark. Dark is fine; a black face is not.

What changed on set

Thirty seconds before the vows, the lav was knocked off by the dress strap and the signal dropped. B camera kept rolling close; the nearby recorder saved the whole vow. Post replaced the track from the recorder; lip sync held.

Post choices

  1. No music under the vows: sync, breath, and guests' small laughter; music only before the entrance and after the exit.
  2. Cut four minutes of table shots: every table's toast looked the same; keep two with specific reactions.
  3. Grade for consistent temperature only: keep the warm hall, do not cool faces to white; do not lift shadows hard.

Result

The couple could point to the grandparents' reaction and one line from the vows, not just the schedule. No reshoot, no slow motion hiding a missed moment; the lav failure did not become the film's failure.

Three reusable lessons

  1. Ritual before emotion: entrance, rings, vows; slow motion only matters after coverage.
  2. Two audio sources are not backup; one is the master: a lav falls, a recorder does not.
  3. Dark is fine; a black face is not: practicals first, a small light for faces, not the whole hall.

One failure

We forgot a dedicated mic for the officiant and relied on the room mic; a few opening lines were buried by guests. Next time put the officiant's mic on the ritual checklist beside rings and vows.

A four-minute experimental film: locked frame, one action, three repetitions, one break; sound carries structure, no narration.

Project card

  • Format: four-minute experimental short
  • Crew: two (director/camera + sound)
  • Schedule: one shoot day plus two post days
  • Budget range: RMB 2,000–5,000
  • Platform: festival / art
  • Limits: locked frame, no dialogue, one action, one location

Timeline

  1. 13:00: Light; lock the camera and shoot the empty table to establish the rule.
  2. 14:00: Take one: light box, light steps, wide ambience.
  3. 15:00: Clouds cover the window; no fill, wait twenty minutes.
  4. 16:00: Take two: heavy box, heavy steps, loud landing.
  5. 17:00: Take three: the person does not put it down; breath gets close.
  6. 17:30: Break: the person exits, camera stays, sound remains on the empty table.
  7. 后期: Cut opening title; no music; place the break after the third repetition.

Constraints

One rule for the whole film: the camera does not move; a person walks left to right and puts a box on a table. No dialogue, no music budget, one afternoon of light.

Pre-production decisions

  1. Put the rule in the first shot: within fifteen seconds the viewer knows the camera will not move and the action will repeat.
  2. Three repetitions change one variable: light box, heavy box, and the person does not put it down.
  3. Sound builds structure: footsteps, the box landing, and breath each own a section; no narration explaining “what it means.”

What changed on set

On the third take, clouds covered the window and the image dropped a stop. We did not add light; we waited. The twenty-minute wait was cut into the opening and became part of “time.”

Post choices

  1. No music: the location sound already had three sections; music would turn it into a “soundtrack short.”
  2. Cut the opening title: a conceptual line was planned, but the rule itself already explained enough.
  3. Put the break after the third repetition: the first cut broke too early, before expectation existed.

Result

Preview viewers could name the rule and the break without the director explaining. No plot, no narration, but “the box gets heavier” gave repetition a direction.

Three reusable lessons

  1. Write the rule first: the clearer the rule, the more tension repetition creates; more rules mean less attention.
  2. Change one variable per repetition: weight, speed, light, or sound, one at a time.
  3. Sound can carry structure: footsteps and a box landing can mark sections without narration.

One failure

The first cut broke after the second repetition; without expectation, the break felt like an accident. Recutting after the third made the rule land.

en.title: Multicam and Live: Lock Timecode, Return, and Recording First
en.summary: Multicam is not more cameras. It is three cameras on one timeline, one return, and one audio plan. If any link lacks a backup, directing turns into guessing.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/Multicam and Live: Lock Timecode, Return, and Recording First

Shooting / Multicam & live

Multicam and Live: Lock Timecode, Return, and Recording First

Multicam is not more cameras. It is three cameras on one timeline, one return, and one audio plan. If any link lacks a backup, directing turns into guessing.

5 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tech DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: when multicam is worth it

Use multicam only when something happens once and cannot be repeated: a ceremony, a match, a performance; when a continuous take matters; or when someone must switch live for an audience. An interview that merely wants another angle is cheaper and safer shot twice with one camera.

Write a camera-role sheet: A holds the wide and the main action, B holds reactions and close-ups, C holds inserts, hands, or roams. Each camera answers one question so the director knows when to cut. Three medium shots are one camera.

Signal chain: draw the interfaces before the frames

Draw the chain on one page: where each camera leaves, which switcher it enters, where it records, and which monitor gets return. Consumer HDMI connectors have no lock and fail when bumped; use SDI where possible, and add a locking sleeve plus a spare HDMI cable where not. Test any run over 15 metres before dressing the set.

Keep program and ISO recording separate: program is what the audience sees; clean ISO is what post can rescue. Program only leaves no second choice; ISO only means no one sees the finished show. Two recorders, two cards—not one card counted twice.

Timecode and sync: put three cameras on one timeline

The most expensive multicam error is not composition; it is three tracks that do not align. Use one timecode generator when possible. If not, clap in front of every camera and align by audio waveform in post. That is a rescue, not a workflow.

Lock frame rate, shutter, and white balance before rolling. Mixed frame rates confuse switchers and recorders; mixed white balance makes skin jump on every cut. Shoot ten seconds of the same grey card on every camera so post has one manual anchor.

On set: rehearsal, return, and failure drills

Run one full rehearsal before recording: the director calls “camera three standby,” every operator answers, tally lights, and return appears. Without this, everyone hunts for their own frame when the show starts. Put return where the operator can see it without turning away from the lens.

Prepare three failure plans: which cable replaces a dead one, who takes over a dead camera, and what covers a lost audio feed. Put names on the plan, not “everyone watch out.” Live has no retake, only cuts.

Failure case: three cameras became three separate films

A two-hour industry forum used three cameras with no timecode and audio only on A. The show looked fine on set; in post, B and C drifted twelve seconds, applause no longer matched, and every cut was off. The fix was to rebuild on A audio and discard most of B and C.

The real cost was not one timecode cable; it was three people aligning waveforms for two days. Put “sync test” in the multicam budget, or the saved cable money returns double in post.

Cost and acceptance

Low: one switcher, two cameras, camera audio, ¥3,000–8,000/day for an internal stream. Mid: three cameras, SDI, timecode, separate audio, ISO record, ¥8,000–20,000/day. High: four-plus cameras, director team, comms, return, dual recorders, ¥20,000–60,000/day. Excludes venue, dedicated network, and travel.

Check

  • Every camera has one role, and at least one holds the wide.
  • All cameras share frame rate, shutter, and white balance.
  • Timecode or clap sync is proven in rehearsal.
  • Program and ISO record separately, with two cards or recorders.
  • Tally, return, and comms are rehearsed at least once.
  • Failure plan names people and replacement cables.

Boundary

This page only covers “Multicam and Live: Lock Timecode, Return, and Recording First”; it does not replace Multicam Sync: Timecode and a Camera Map, ND Filter: Wide Open in Daylight, Color: Match First, Style Second. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

en.title: LED Virtual Production: Wall, Tracking, Sync, and Color
en.summary: LED virtual production is not swapping a backdrop for a screen. It binds practical light, camera tracking, panel refresh, and color into one chain; if one link is loose, the light on the actor separates from the background.
en.html:
Home/Shooting/LED Virtual Production: Wall, Tracking, Sync, and Color

Shooting / LED virtual production

LED Virtual Production: Wall, Tracking, Sync, and Color

LED virtual production is not swapping a backdrop for a screen. It binds practical light, camera tracking, panel refresh, and color into one chain; if one link is loose, the light on the actor separates from the background.

5 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tech DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: wall or green screen

A wall suits scenes the actor can see and the light can hit: car windows, interior windows, distant ridges, interactive screens. It gives real eyelines and ambient light. Green screen suits heavy set changes, added characters, or close-ups where wall resolution is not enough; post is freer, but the set has no reference.

If the film has many close-up faces, transparent materials, or fine hair, do not use a wall just to save post. Wall resolution and moiré amplify those problems. Ask: what does the actor need to see, and is it worth building a wall for?

Wall and tracking: turn seeing into coordinates

Tracking needs camera position, focal length, and lens distortion. Camera only makes the background slide when you push in; lens only makes it drift when the camera moves. Markers cannot sit where the actor blocks them, and too many markers turn the frame into dots.

Walk a test chart through the full path before rolling: near, mid, far, tilt down, tilt up. Check the relative position of background and actor. If one position fails, the actor will break the illusion there, and post cannot recover it.

Sync and latency: the actor sees the past

The wall image takes time from engine to light, and tracking takes time to reach the engine. The actor sees a world tens of milliseconds old. With high latency, eyelines lag and blocking chases the background. Measure it: have the actor watch a moving object on the wall, shoot a take, and check lip sync and eyeline.

Wall refresh and camera shutter must match. Too fast a shutter catches scan lines; too slow smears. Start at 1/50 or 1/60, then match local mains frequency. LED refresh differs by region; do not copy a setting from another country.

Color: the wall is a light, not a monitor

Wall color temperature, brightness, and spectrum all hit the actor. Set the wall to the same white as practical light before styling the background. A blue wall makes a blue face; a bright wall becomes the key light. Meter the face, not just the monitor.

Lock the color pipeline before rolling: camera Log or RAW, engine output, wall calibration LUT, post ACES/Rec.709. Each stage needs a transform; do not put one LUT on everything. Shoot a grey card and a skin reference so post shares an anchor.

Failure case: bright wall, dark face, pasted background

A car ad set the wall bright for the background but did not fill the actor. On set the background looked rich; in post the face was three stops darker, and lifting it destroyed noise and skin. Tracking followed only the camera, so the background scaled on the push-in and the window edge looked pasted.

The fix was two stops down on the wall, a soft fill on the actor, and a re-shoot of the push-in. The extra cost was not a light; it was rebuilding the wall and rebooking the actor. Wall brightness serves the face first, the background second.

Cost and acceptance

Low: small-pitch wall, locked camera, 2D background, ¥15,000–40,000/day. Mid: tracking, real-time engine, sync, color management, ¥40,000–100,000/day. High: multicam, complex interaction, on-set comp team, ¥100,000–300,000/day. Excludes content, cast, and venue.

Check

  • The background the actor must see is worth a wall.
  • Tracking records camera, focal length, and distortion.
  • Latency is tested with a moving object and lip sync.
  • Wall refresh matches shutter with no scan lines.
  • Wall color and brightness serve the face first.
  • Each color stage has a transform, with grey-card and skin references.

Boundary

This page only covers “LED Virtual Production: Wall, Tracking, Sync, and Color”; it does not replace LED Volume: Track First, Light Second, Focal Length: Decide How Close the Audience Stands, Color: Match First, Style Second. en.title: HDR End to End: Do Not Just Brighten at the End
en.summary: HDR is not brightening SDR. It preserves one luminance relationship from capture through monitoring, grading, and delivery. Guess in SDR at any stage and the result is bright but flat.
en.html:
Home/Post/HDR End to End: Do Not Just Brighten at the End

Post / HDR

HDR End to End: Do Not Just Brighten at the End

HDR is not brightening SDR. It preserves one luminance relationship from capture through monitoring, grading, and delivery. Guess in SDR at any stage and the result is bright but flat.

4 min read · AdvancedTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: does this film need HDR

HDR usually needs usable highlight detail: windows, neon, fire, metal reflections, plus a platform that supports HDR. A film with no highlight information, watched mostly on a phone, often just gets brighter midtones.

Ask delivery first: PQ or HLG, is an SDR version required, which standard for the master. If you cannot answer, do not grade HDR first; the SDR trim will cost another pass.

Capture and monitoring: protect highlights before brightness

Shoot Log or RAW and expose to protect highlights; do not crush white to make the monitor look like SDR. On-set monitors can load an HDR transform LUT, but that LUT is for framing and exposure, not the final grade.

Anchor with an 18% grey card and a white card: grey sets midtones, white sets headroom. Shoot both at every scene change so post knows where each section starts.

Grade: HDR first, then the SDR trim

Set the HDR white point first: SDR white is not 100% in HDR and usually sits lower; then shape the highlight roll-off so windows and lamps have layers instead of clipping. Read skin on scopes, not by “brightness.”

Lock the HDR master, then trim SDR: do not just compress the curve. Check midtone relationships per scene, then lift highlights separately. SDR is not a smaller HDR; it needs its own contrast judgment.

Delivery: platform, master, captions, and QC

Write a delivery sheet: PQ or HLG for HDR, what peak, Rec.709 for SDR, subtitle luminance, platform transcode rules. Do not use 100% white for HDR subtitles; they glare in dark scenes. Check SDR subtitles separately.

QC at least three times: HDR reference monitor, SDR reference monitor, and a normal phone. Each pass checks clipped highlights, skin shift, shadow detail, and subtitle readability.

Failure case: brightening SDR and calling it HDR

A city night piece was shot for SDR with blown windows, then brightened and contrasted and called HDR. Neon had no color, the sky had no layers, and faces were too bright. After platform transcode, highlights clipped and HDR looked like SDR.

The only fix is the source: no highlight information means no HDR. Re-shoot the windows or make the best SDR contrast; do not hide capture limits behind an HDR label.

Cost and acceptance

Low: borrowed HDR monitor, one HDR grade, one SDR trim, ¥5,000–15,000. Mid: HDR suite for two to three days, SDR version, QC, ¥15,000–40,000. High: multi-platform delivery, Dolby Vision/HLG dual masters, ¥40,000–100,000+.

Check

  • Platform and HDR standard are written down.
  • Highlights are protected; grey and white cards exist per scene.
  • HDR grade sets white point before highlight roll-off.
  • SDR trim happens after the HDR master is locked.
  • HDR and SDR subtitles are checked separately.
  • QC runs on three viewing devices.

en.title: Conform and Online: Relink, Round-Trip, and Master
en.summary: Conform is not opening the edit in another app. It verifies every cut returns to the original media, every clip has enough handles, and every version traces to one master.
en.html:
Home/Post/Conform and Online: Relink, Round-Trip, and Master

Post / Conform

Conform and Online: Relink, Round-Trip, and Master

Conform is not opening the edit in another app. It verifies every cut returns to the original media, every clip has enough handles, and every version traces to one master.

4 min read · AdvancedTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: when Online is needed

Online is needed when the film gets a grade, VFX, or multiple platform versions. A straight cut with no grade can finish in the NLE. The test is not runtime; it is whether the timeline returns to original media.

If the edit used proxies, transcodes, speed changes, or nests, Online must rebuild from source. Grading a proxy timeline is judging at low resolution.

Round-trip: EDL/XML is an address, not media

When exporting EDL/XML/AAF, confirm reel name, timecode, frame rate, and clip name. Filenames can change; timecode cannot. Leave at least 12–24 frames of handles at every cut for transitions, stabilization, denoise, and grading.

Check shot by shot after relink: source file, in point, out point, speed, transform, audio sync. Total duration matching does not mean every cut matches.

Order of grade and VFX

Do VFX before the final grade unless the VFX needs a graded background as reference. VFX before grade gives the compositor neutral footage; after grade means chasing a locked look and repeating notes.

Build separate versions for VFX shots instead of editing the master timeline. Label each version with VFX on/off, captions on/off, titles on/off. One master, many versions.

Master and versions: naming beats software

Keep one master: highest quality, no captions, no titles, no platform compression. Platform versions derive from it and never modify it. Filenames carry project, date, version, status; no final/final2.

Watch the master end to end before delivery: no black frames, offline media, wrong captions, or drift. Archive LUTs, fonts, music licenses, and output presets with the project.

Failure case: the round-trip opened, every cut was wrong

An ad edit used 120% speed changes and heavy nesting. The XML opened in the grade with the right duration, but every speed change pulled the wrong frames and transitions stretched. Two days of grading were wasted when the client saw the action was wrong.

The problem was not the software; speed and nests were not flattened and handles were missing. Conform starts with whether the timeline can be reconstructed, not whether it opens.

Cost and acceptance

Low: single-seat relink and basic check, ¥2,000–5,000. Mid: full conform, grade, VFX round-trip, version outputs, ¥5,000–20,000. High: multicam, multiple versions, HDR, separate captions/titles, ¥20,000–60,000+.

Check

  • EDL/XML timecode, frame rate, and reel match.
  • Every cut has at least 12 frames of handles.
  • Shot check covers source, in/out, speed, and transform.
  • VFX versions are separate from the master.
  • One master; platform versions trace back.
  • Watch the master end to end before delivery.

Boundary

This page only covers “Conform and Online: Relink, Round-Trip, and Master”; it does not replace Cut Points: Action, Eye Line, Sound, Asset management: structure, proxies, versions, Composition: Tell the Eye Where to Look.
