en.title: Sound Post: The Order from Dialogue to Final Mix
en.summary: Sound post does not start with music. The order is: dialogue audible, ambience continuous, effects supporting, music last; each step has a checkable result.
en.html:
Home/Post/Sound Post: The Order from Dialogue to Final Mix

Post / Sound

Sound Post: The Order from Dialogue to Final Mix

Sound post does not start with music. The order is: dialogue audible, ambience continuous, effects supporting, music last; each step has a checkable result.

4 min read · AdvancedTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which layer first

Watch the film without music: is every line clear, is ambience continuous, does a cut drop into silence. If dialogue is unclear, fix dialogue; if ambience breaks, add room tone; if effects fight, lower effects. Music is the last emotional layer, not the first.

Split everything into DX dialogue, AMB ambience, SFX effects, MX music. Stems are not for a tidy session; they let you replace one layer without touching the rest.

Dialogue: keep breath before denoise

Dialogue cleanup does three things: remove low rumble, tame obvious sibilance, and fix level jumps. Do not remove all breath and mouth detail for “clean”; it starts to sound dubbed. Denoise in small sections, not one setting for the whole track.

The goal is not identical level on every line; it is consistency within a scene. Two people a metre apart should not sound as loud as ten metres apart. The audience needs space.

Ambience and effects: continuity before richness

Lay continuous ambience first: at least ten seconds of room tone per scene, no drop at cuts. Effects serve action and information: doors, steps, cloth, phone vibration. Do not put a punchy effect on every action; the audience starts watching sound instead of story.

Effect direction must match frame: off-screen voices and steps outside a door do not sit in the centre. Stereo is not filling the field; it is telling the audience where things are.

Music and final mix: enters last, leaves last

Add music last, after dialogue and effects pass. The first music rule is never bury a line: no chorus is worth losing a key sentence. Drop music 3–6 dB where needed; do not make the audience guess.

Check loudness at the final mix: dialogue-led films often sit around -16 LUFS, or follow the platform. Check phone speaker, headphones, and TV, not only the studio monitors.

Failure case: full music, muddy dialogue

A brand film laid full music in the rough cut because the client “felt” it. At the final mix, dialogue was buried, so music came down globally and the film went flat. The team then cleaned dialogue and rebuilt music in sections, doubling the work.

Music is not a cover-up. Fix dialogue first, ambience second, and save music for the end so it has room to do real emotional work.

Cost and acceptance

Low: dialogue cleanup, ambience, one music track, ¥2,000–6,000. Mid: full stems, effects, final mix, loudness, ¥6,000–20,000. High: 5.1/Atmos, ADR, Foley, multiple versions, ¥20,000–80,000+.

Check

  • Dialogue is clear without captions.
  • Ambience is continuous across every cut.
  • Effects match screen direction.
  • Music never buries a key line.
  • Loudness matches platform; three devices checked.
  • DX/AMB/SFX/MX delivered as stems.

en.title: DIT and Data Handoff: The First Handoff from Set to Post
en.summary: DIT is not card copying. It guarantees checksums, three copies, filenames that trace to the log, and proxies that match source.
en.html:
Home/Post/DIT and Data Handoff: The First Handoff from Set to Post

Post / DIT

DIT and Data Handoff: The First Handoff from Set to Post

DIT is not card copying. It guarantees checksums, three copies, filenames that trace to the log, and proxies that match source.

4 min read · AdvancedTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: who owns the media

The first DIT job is not inserting a card; it is assigning responsibility: who copies, who verifies, who transports, who receives. “Media is backed up” is not enough; write where, when, and who confirmed. If there is no DIT, the camera assistant can cover, but the duty goes on the call sheet.

Before any card is formatted, at least two complete copies must exist off the same computer or drive. Formatting after one copy is the least forgivable set error.

Copy and verify: checksums are not optional

Use software that verifies and generate an MD5/xxHash manifest. Do not judge by file count; run the checksum. If it fails, copy again; do not “try once more and hope.” Keep the card’s original folder structure; do not rename during copy.

Rename after copy: project_date_camera_card_clip. Log the rename so it stays traceable. Keep the original card until wrap; do not reuse early.

Three copies: two on set, one off set

Three copies are not three drives in one bag. At least one lives in a different physical location or goes back to the office that day. Do not format before backup; do not format immediately after either—wait for next-day confirmation.

Label each copy: project, date, contents, checksum filename. Avoid “primary/secondary”; write the location and the owner.

Proxies and handoff: make the edit open ready

Proxies must match source frame rate, timecode, and filename or the round-trip fails. Choose proxy resolution for the edit machine, 1080p or 720p; too low a bitrate makes the editor misjudge noise.

Handoff: source, proxies, checksum manifest, script notes, audio, LUTs, report. The report lists card numbers, clip counts, total duration, and anomalies (bad frames, dropped frames, audio gaps).

Failure case: three backups in one room

On a location shoot, the DIT made three copies, all in one hotel room: two drives and a laptop. The next day the room lost power, the laptop drained, and both drives were soaked in the same bag. All three copies failed together.

The only fix was a re-shoot. Real three-copy backup separates locations: one carried, one in the hotel safe, one shipped or uploaded that day. Backup is location, not count.

Cost and acceptance

Low: camera assistant doubles as DIT, two SSDs plus checksum software, ¥1,000–3,000/day. Mid: dedicated DIT, three copies, proxies, report, ¥3,000–8,000/day. High: multicam, on-set grade/comp, LTO archive, ¥8,000–20,000/day.

Check

  • Every card copy has a checksum manifest.
  • At least three copies, not in one physical location.
  • Original folders kept; renames logged.
  • Proxies match source frame rate, timecode, and filename.
  • Handoff report lists cards, clips, duration, anomalies.
  • Written confirmation before any card is formatted.

en.title: Budget and Quote: Put Risk into the Number
en.summary: A budget is not a cost list; it protects the line that would stop the shoot. A quote is not cost plus 20%; it prices scope, revisions, rights, and risk separately.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Budget and Quote: Put Risk into the Number

Tools / Budget & quote

Budget and Quote: Put Risk into the Number

A budget is not a cost list; it protects the line that would stop the shoot. A quote is not cost plus 20%; it prices scope, revisions, rights, and risk separately.

3 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Find the stop-shoot line before the total

The first number is not the total; it is the line that stops the shoot if exceeded. Cast dates, location permits, gear rental, and key crew time can each stop production. Write those four as hard limits before allocating anything else.

Contingency is not what is left over; it is 10–15% held before the shoot. A budget without contingency pushes risk onto the shoot day.

Five blocks: every block needs a cap

People, gear, location, post, and contingency each get a cap and a cut order. When a client cuts budget, do not subtract from the total; name the block, the days, or the versions removed. A quote that cannot show the cut returns as overtime and rework.

Gear is rental price, not purchase; location is per day with transport and restoration; post is per version without unlimited revisions. “Excludes” matters more than “includes.”

Quote: revisions, rights, and rush are separate lines

Four quote blocks: production, post, rights/materials, and rush/overtime. Revisions are numeric: two rough-cut rounds, one fine-cut, one caption pass; extra rounds are priced per day or version. Music, fonts, and footage are separate from production.

Confirm payment milestones before quoting: deposit, shoot, first cut, delivery. A quote without milestones is a document that can be delayed forever.

Failure case: one missing “re-cut excluded”

A product film quoted three cuts, but the contract said only “post editing” with no revision count. The client changed seven versions, each adding a scene. The studio avoided charging and traded two weeks of free re-cuts for a verbal “we'll call you again.”

The fix is not an argument; it is version and revision terms in the next quote. Log every revision with date, content, and duration; stop beyond the contracted rounds and confirm a new quote before continuing.

Cost and acceptance

Budget templates by scale: small ¥3,000–15,000, mid ¥15,000–60,000, large ¥60,000–300,000+. Quote margin is often 15–30%, but contingency is not margin; it is the project’s own insurance.

Check

  • Four stop-shoot lines are written.
  • Five blocks each have a cap and cut order.
  • Contingency is 10–15%, not margin.
  • Quote splits production, post, rights, and rush.
  • Revision rounds are numeric with overage pricing.
  • Payment milestones have dates.

en.title: Crew Management: Call Sheet, Sign-In, Wrap, and Ownership
en.summary: Crew management is not sending a call sheet. It makes everyone know the day, the owner of each risk, and when they can leave. Call sheet, sign-in, and wrap report make a project controllable.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Crew Management: Call Sheet, Sign-In, Wrap, and Ownership

Tools / Crew management

Crew Management: Call Sheet, Sign-In, Wrap, and Ownership

Crew management is not sending a call sheet. It makes everyone know the day, the owner of each risk, and when they can leave. Call sheet, sign-in, and wrap report make a project controllable.

4 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

Call sheet: one page decides the day

A call sheet includes call time, address, contact, parking, meals, nearest hospital, weather backup, and each department’s call time. Do not write “everyone at 8”; camera, lighting, and makeup need different calls, and one time makes everyone wait.

Send it 24 hours ahead. Changes go out as a new version at least an hour ahead with “this version governs” in the message. Verbal changes do not count; the set runs on the latest sheet.

Roles and ownership: every risk gets a person

List risks: power, fire, height, traffic, weather, minors, animals, gear damage. Each gets an owner and a backup. The owner is not “everyone”; it is the person who can call a stop.

Key roles need backups: camera, sound, lighting, producing. A role without a backup is a single point of failure; one illness stops the project.

Sign-in, communication, and changes

Sign-in is not paperwork; it confirms who is on site, who is insured, and who can travel. The sheet lists name, role, phone, arrival, and insurance. A last-minute joiner signs in before entering set.

Changes go through a small form: who asked, what changes, which shots are affected, who approved. Do not “just grab one more” on set; grabbed shots usually lack light, sound, and clearance.

Wrap: backup, clear, report

Before wrap: confirm media backup, restore the location, and count gear. Backup is not “tomorrow”; two copies must exist that day. Restoration includes props, trash, and keys; gear count follows the rental list.

The wrap report states what was shot, what was missed, what is needed tomorrow, and any injury/damage/overtime. Send it to producer and director, not the whole crew; the crew only needs tomorrow’s call.

Failure case: “everyone at 8”

A six-person cafe shoot called everyone at 8. Camera arrived at 8 with no lights; makeup arrived at 8 with no actor; the actor came at 8:30; the cafe opened at 9. Everyone waited and the first shot rolled at 10:40. Twelve shots were planned, seven were captured.

The fix is not overtime; it is a staggered call: camera 7:30, lighting 7:30, makeup 8:30, cast 9:00, first shot 9:30. A call sheet is not a notification; it minimizes waiting.

Cost and acceptance

Crew management usually sits in the producer fee: small ¥1,000–3,000/day, mid ¥3,000–8,000/day, large ¥8,000–20,000/day. Skipping production usually doubles the shoot day.

Check

  • Call sheet 24 hours ahead with address, contact, hospital, weather backup.
  • Every risk has a name and backup.
  • Key roles have backups.
  • Sign-in records insurance status.
  • Change form names affected shots and approver.
  • Two backups and a gear count on wrap day.

en.title: Platform Deliverables: One Master, Many Safe Areas
en.summary: One master everywhere is the most expensive shortcut. Keep one master, derive platform versions by frame, runtime, captions, loudness, and cover; every version traces back.
en.html:
Home/Post/Platform Deliverables: One Master, Many Safe Areas

Post / Platform deliverables

Platform Deliverables: One Master, Many Safe Areas

One master everywhere is the most expensive shortcut. Keep one master, derive platform versions by frame, runtime, captions, loudness, and cover; every version traces back.

4 min read · AdvancedTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

Lock the master before the platforms

Keep one master: highest resolution, highest bitrate, no captions, no titles, no platform compression. Platform versions derive from it; never edit the master. Filenames carry project, date, version, status; no final/final2.

Write the platform list first: one primary, two distribution, one website/private. For each, write frame, runtime, bitrate, captions, cover, loudness. Without the list, the wrong frame is discovered on upload day.

Frame and safe area: not one crop

16:9 to 9:16 is not cropping the sides. Eyes, hands, product, and captions must be recomposed. Check each platform’s safe area, especially the top and bottom buttons in vertical. A key action at the edge of the wide is lost in vertical.

Shoot two compositions: landscape wide, vertical medium. Cropping in post saves only part; if the set did not leave room, post zooms and loses both quality and composition.

Captions: burned, sidecar, open

Burned-in captions are in the picture and cannot be turned off; sidecar captions may not display; open captions serve access and silent viewing. Test all three by playing, not by checking file existence.

Caption safe area, size, lines, and CPS follow the platform. Vertical captions must not cover the mouth; landscape captions stay inside 90%. Do not squeeze two-language small type; split versions.

Loudness and QC: the platform compresses again

Deliver to platform loudness; do not expect the platform to fix it. Dialogue-led work often sits at -16 LUFS; music and ads follow platform rules. Short drama and feed can be slightly hotter but not so hot that the platform compresses. Watch the upload end to end for black frames, freezes, audio drops, and caption drift.

One QC row per platform: file, frame, runtime, loudness, captions, cover, title, link. Ticks are not paperwork; they identify which version failed.

Failure case: vertical crop removed the product

A product ad was cut in 16:9 with the product at frame right. The 9:16 center crop left half the product, and captions covered the hand. After upload, the first three seconds did not show what was sold and completion halved.

The fix is recomposition, not a product close-up sticker. Shoot a vertical medium on set so post has room; without it, a re-shoot is cheaper than patching.

Cost and acceptance

Low: master plus two platform versions, ¥1,000–3,000. Mid: four platforms, captions, covers, QC, ¥3,000–10,000. High: eight-plus platforms, bilingual, multiple versions, HDR/SDR, ¥10,000–30,000+.

Check

  • One master; every platform version traces back.
  • Each platform has frame, runtime, caption, and loudness specs.
  • Vertical is recomposed, not center-cropped.
  • All three caption types are played.
  • Full QC per platform.
  • Filename includes platform and version.

Boundary

en.title: Archive and Asset Reuse: Make the Next Film Faster
en.summary: Archiving is not dragging a folder onto a drive. It lets the next person open the project, find media, know the rights, and restore grade and sound. Reuse is indexed retrieval, not digging through old films.
en.html:
Home/Post/Archive and Asset Reuse: Make the Next Film Faster

Post / Archive & reuse

Archive and Asset Reuse: Make the Next Film Faster

Archiving is not dragging a folder onto a drive. It lets the next person open the project, find media, know the rights, and restore grade and sound. Reuse is indexed retrieval, not digging through old films.

4 min read · AdvancedTVCN Post DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: what is worth archiving

Three things are worth archiving: reusable shots (brand, person, place), versions that may change (a client may return), and rights that must be proven (releases, likeness, music). One-off, no-reuse, no-rights footage should not take archive space.

Ask what the next person will do with it. If there is no answer, keep the delivery package and project, not every source clip.

Archive package: five parts, none optional

Project file, source/proxies, LUTs and fonts, rights and likeness, index and metadata. The project must open offline; source must relink; LUTs and fonts must restore the look; rights must prove use; the index must be searchable.

Name every file with project, date, scene, version. No “final,” “New Folder,” or “copy.” The index lists filename, scene, person, rights, expiry, location.

Restore test: the pass line for an archive

After archiving, pick one random shot, open the project on another machine, relink, apply the LUT, and export. If it will not open, relink, or match color, the archive is not done. Restore testing is part of archiving, not optional.

Log the test: date, machine, software version, missing files, fix. Read the last log before the next archive.

Reuse: rights before creative

Before reusing, check three things: scope (organic/paid/advertising), term, territory. An organic license does not cover paid media; a one-year license expires; mainland-only footage cannot go to overseas platforms.

Reuse is not cutting the old film into the new one; it is extracting reusable shots, sound, graphics, and templates. Build a reusable-asset index tagged by person, scene, action, and light.

Failure case: three years archived, all media offline

A brand project archived only the project and proxies; source stayed on an old drive. Three years later the client wanted a re-cut. The project opened, but every clip was offline, the old drive interface was gone, and proxies were too weak to grade. The only option was a re-shoot.

The fix is not a new drive; it is a restore test at archive time. A project opening does not mean media relinks; media relinking does not mean color restores.

Cost and acceptance

Low: one project archive, index, one restore test, ¥1,000–3,000. Mid: multi-project library, LTO/cloud archive, rights ledger, ¥3,000–15,000. High: department MAM, migration, long-term verification, ¥15,000–50,000+.

Check

  • Reuse value is defined before archiving.
  • Five parts present: project/media/LUT/rights/index.
  • Project opens offline and media relinks.
  • Restore test runs on another machine.
  • Reuse checks scope, term, and territory.
  • Index tags person, scene, action, and light.

Boundary

en.title: Buying a Cinema Camera: “Can Shoot” Is Not “Can Deliver”
en.summary: A cinema camera’s price is not the body: cards, batteries, monitoring, rig, handles, cables, grading, and learning all count. Confirm the project needs RAW, timecode, SDI, and dual card, or a high-end video body is better value.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Buying a Cinema Camera: “Can Shoot” Is Not “Can Deliver”

Tools / Buying guide

Buying a Cinema Camera: “Can Shoot” Is Not “Can Deliver”

A cinema camera’s price is not the body: cards, batteries, monitoring, rig, handles, cables, grading, and learning all count. Confirm the project needs RAW, timecode, SDI, and dual card, or a high-end video body is better value.

4 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Start with delivery: does the client need RAW, HDR, or multicam timecode? If all three are no, a cinema camera is likely overkill. Log, 10-bit, and interchangeable lenses on a high-end video body with external recording may be enough. Cinema cameras sell dynamic range, timecode, SDI, and a repairable rig ecosystem—not a professional look.

Fits:

  • Ads/short films needing RAW or latitude
  • Multicam with timecode and SDI
  • A rigged, serviceable long-term system

Does not fit:

  • Events/interviews delivered Rec.709
  • Solo run-and-gun, weight-sensitive
  • Budget only covers the body

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Do not judge dynamic range by a number. Bring a bright window and a face in shadow, shoot 30 seconds in the project codec, and check highlight recovery, shadow noise, and rig balance.

CheckPass lineReference/log
高光窗外可回收 2 档，不出现硬切Log/RAW 实拍
暗部ISO 测试下肤色噪点可接受双原生 ISO 对比
时码输入/输出与录机一致时码发生器
介质项目编码持续写入不丢帧满卡测试
套件肩扛/手提 10 分钟不失衡实际配重

Price bands: total cost of ownership first

Look beyond the sticker: cards, batteries, adapters, gimbal, stands, software subscriptions, and repair. Bands describe the minimum kit for a real project type, not toy pricing.

Alternatives and upgrades: do not add money on the wrong axis

  • High-end video body + external recorder
  • Used previous-gen cinema camera
  • Rent body, buy lens/rig

Buying steps: bring footage, not spec sheets

Run these in order before paying. If one fails, do not tell yourself post will fix it.

  1. Shoot 30 seconds in project codec
  2. Build the rig and weigh it
  3. Confirm card price and sustained write
  4. Confirm monitor, power, cable interfaces
  5. Check service and backup body

Check

  • Project truly needs at least two of RAW/timecode/SDI.
  • Body, rig, and media total is known.
  • Highlight and shadow recovery tested.
  • Timecode passes with recorder/multicam.
  • Rig weight is manageable.
  • Service point or backup body exists.

en.title: Buying a Zoom: Parfocal, Breathing, and Servo
en.summary: A zoom buys “no lens change,” not “anything.” Confirm it holds focus through the zoom, breathing is controlled, and the servo is quiet; otherwise you bought a prime that can change focal length.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Buying a Zoom: Parfocal, Breathing, and Servo

Tools / Buying guide

Buying a Zoom: Parfocal, Breathing, and Servo

A zoom buys “no lens change,” not “anything.” Confirm it holds focus through the zoom, breathing is controlled, and the servo is quiet; otherwise you bought a prime that can change focal length.

3 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Zooms suit events, weddings, documentary, and solo moving work; they do not suit maximum shallow depth or minimum weight. Decide the range: 24-70 covers most, 70-200 suits stage/events, 18-35 suits spaces. Do not buy one 18-300 as everything.

Fits:

  • Events/weddings, no lens changes
  • Solo moving, efficiency
  • Documentary, fast framing

Does not fit:

  • Maximum aperture/shallow depth
  • Long handheld, weight-sensitive
  • Macro/extreme close focus

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Focus at the long end, zoom wide, and see if focus holds. Then push/pull close and watch breathing. Finally record a zoom and listen to the servo.

en.title: Field Recorder: Channels, 32-bit Float, and Timecode
en.summary: A field recorder is not about track count. It is about whether one lost channel has a backup, a wrong gain can be saved, and post can sync to timecode.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Field Recorder: Channels, 32-bit Float, and Timecode

Tools / Buying guide

Field Recorder: Channels, 32-bit Float, and Timecode

A field recorder is not about track count. It is about whether one lost channel has a backup, a wrong gain can be saved, and post can sync to timecode.

3 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Two people indoors: two channels are enough. Multicam/multiple outdoor subjects: at least four channels plus timecode. 32-bit float saves gain errors, not a misplaced mic; do not treat it as magic.

Fits:

  • Two/multiple speakers, independent gain
  • Multicam timecode sync
  • Uncontrolled exterior, 32-bit safety

Does not fit:

  • Solo voiceover, phone is enough
  • Only camera reference audio
  • No post, direct delivery

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Connect two mics, one normal and one 20dB low, then shout to see whether 32-bit saves it. Pull one card and check recording continues on the other. Feed timecode to camera and shoot 30 seconds to sync.

CheckPass lineReference/log

32-bit大声不削波，回放可恢复低增益+喊话

供电整日 8 小时可换电电池仓
备份拔卡不断录/安全轨双卡测试

Shoot ten seconds at 1/50, 1/60, and 1/125 and check banding. Set two lights to the same temperature, dim both 50%, and check color shift. Run one at full power on battery for 30 minutes and log drain.

en.summary: HDR monitoring depends on peak, black level, gamut, tone mapping, and calibration. Buying on “1000 nits” alone gets a bright screen with clipped highlights.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Buying an HDR Monitor: Peak Nits Is Not Everything

Tools / Buying guide

Buying an HDR Monitor: Peak Nits Is Not Everything

HDR monitoring depends on peak, black level, gamut, tone mapping, and calibration. Buying on “1000 nits” alone gets a bright screen with clipped highlights.

3 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Decide whether you deliver HDR or only view HDR references. For reference only, a calibrated SDR screen with a transform LUT can work. For an HDR master, peak, black, gamut, and tone mapping must all pass. Do not use a TV as a grading monitor; its sharpening and dynamic contrast lie.

Fits:

  • HDR master/grading
  • Platform HDR delivery QC
  • PQ/HLG reference

Does not fit:

  • SDR-only delivery
  • Under ¥10k, do SDR first
  • Viewing only, no grading

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Bring an HDR clip with a window, neon, and a dark scene. Use a signal generator to confirm PQ/HLG. Check whether blacks go grey and highlights clip to white. Use a color chart for P3 coverage.

CheckPass lineReference/log
峰值窗外/霓虹有层次，不切白HDR 测试片
黑位暗场黑得下去，不发灰黑场片段
色域P3 色卡无明显偏差色卡
色调映射PQ/HLG 切换正确信号发生器
校准3D LUT/自动校准可查校准报告

Price bands: total cost of ownership first

Look beyond the sticker: cards, batteries, adapters, gimbal, stands, software subscriptions, and repair. Bands describe the minimum kit for a real project type, not toy pricing.

TierReferenceIncludesWatch
Entry¥5,000–12,000Bright SDR/entry HDRLimited HDR calibration
Main¥12,000–35,000HDR monitoring, P3, 3D LUTCalibration extra
Advanced¥35,000–100,000Pro HDR master monitorEnvironment/calibration

Prices are China mainland channel references as of November 2026; tax and quotes vary. Not buying advice.

Alternatives and upgrades: do not add money on the wrong axis

  • Calibrated SDR + transform LUT
  • Rent an HDR suite
  • SDR master first

Buying steps: bring footage, not spec sheets

Run these in order before paying. If one fails, do not tell yourself post will fix it.

  1. Bring HDR test clip
  2. Signal generator PQ/HLG
  3. Check black level
  4. Color chart P3
  5. Check calibration report/LUT

Check

  • Highlights have layers, not clipped white.
  • Dark scenes are not grey.
  • P3 gamut is acceptable.
  • PQ/HLG switch correct.
  • 3D LUT/calibration report exists.
  • Room light is controllable.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: mostly SDR

If ninety percent of the work is SDR, an HDR monitor is not the first priority. SDR needs accurate black, stable white and a reliable waveform; a 1000-nit HDR monitor with a bad SDR preset is worse. Check whether the SDR preset can be calibrated.

SDR monitoring also depends on ambient light: a bright room forces brightness up and black drifts. Decide shading and room level before buying; without environment control, an expensive monitor is still guesswork.

Condition B: HDR delivery

HDR delivery starts with who watches: PQ or HLG, what peak, whether Dolby Vision is required. The monitor must display the target peak and tone-map reliably; “1000 nits” is not enough, check mapping at 100, 400 and 1000 nits.

HDR also depends on shadows: it is not only brightness; black and near-black separation matter more. Take your own dark footage to test, not the showroom demo; demos are all highlights. If shadows collapse, HDR is only bright.

Counterexample: buying on peak nits alone

A monitor claims 1600 nits. At home everything below 100 nits is black, shadows have no layers; HDR highlights are bright but faces in shadow are a patch. The spec wins, the image loses.

The fix is not a brighter monitor; test three bands with your footage: shadow, mid, highlight. If each band shows layers, it is HDR monitoring. Peak is a ceiling, not a capability.

Reusable model

Delivery target → peak → tone mapping → shadows → environment. Set delivery, then peak, then mapping, then shadows, then room. With all five, an HDR monitor is not a spec ornament.

Before buying, run a three-band test: same footage at 100, 400 and 1000 nits, check shadow, skin and highlight. Only pay when all three are acceptable.

en.html:
Home/Tools/Buying Camera Cards: VPG, Sustained Write, and Heat

Tools / Buying guide

Buying Camera Cards: VPG, Sustained Write, and Heat

A card’s peak read speed is irrelevant; sustained write decides whether frames drop. Match the camera’s minimum sustained write, buy one step above, and rotate at least two cards.

3 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Check the camera manual for minimum card class and bitrate; “shoots 8K” is not a standard. CFexpress Type B suits high bitrate. SD UHS-II handles 4K 10-bit but sustained write varies; V90 is steadier than V60, but confirm the camera uses it.

Fits:

  • High-bitrate 4K/6K/8K
  • Multicam/long takes
  • Fast offload

Does not fit:

  • Light 1080p only
  • Camera only supports UHS-I
  • One card as the only backup

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Record a full card at the project’s highest bitrate and check for dropped frames/errors. Record 30 minutes and feel the card temperature. Time a 100GB offload. Short clips hide heat issues that appear after 20 minutes.

Home/Tools/Buying a Fluid Head: Drag, Counterbalance, and Return

Tools / Buying guide

Buying a Fluid Head: Drag, Counterbalance, and Return

A fluid head is not “it pans.” The difference is continuous tilt drag, enough counterbalance, and a smooth return when released; these decide whether your pan/tilt is usable.

3 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Choose by rig weight: under 3kg, 75mm is enough; over 5kg, look at 100mm. Dynamic counterbalance matters more than payload. Low angles, top-down, and long lenses need different balance settings.

Fits:

  • Video pan/tilt
  • Long lens/sports/stage
  • Low-angle/top-down

Does not fit:

  • Stills only, ball head is enough
  • Ultralight travel kit
  • Electronic remote control

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Mount the rig, balance it, and release to check for a nod. Pan from slowest to fastest and feel whether drag is continuous. Tilt to the lowest and highest and check limits.

Tools / Buying guide

Your First Gimbal: Payload, Balance, and Follow

Mount and balance the rig. Release each axis and check drift. Lock each axis and check play. Turn quickly and check follow lag. Run 30 minutes and check battery and motor heat.

en.html:
Home/Tools/Buying Wireless Lavs: Range, Dropouts, and Latency

Tools / Buying guide

Buying Wireless Lavs: Range, Dropouts, and Latency

A “500m” wireless lav range is open line-of-sight, not a mall or concert. Test dropouts, noise, latency, and battery in your real scene before choosing.

3 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Check the scene: 2.4GHz is fine for indoor interviews; malls, concerts, and multiple kits favor UHF or digital systems with frequency hopping. Do not buy the cheapest dual kit; a dropout re-shoots the film. Test clothing rub and wind on the lav itself.

Fits:

  • Interview/voiceover/events
  • Solo/duo moving
  • Untethered audio

Does not fit:

  • Many kits in one venue
  • Heavy RF/long range
  • Broadcast-level redundancy

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Walk the real venue: turn away, cover with a hand, go behind a crowd, approach metal. Record 30 seconds each and listen for dropouts/noise. Clap for latency. Run two kits together for cross-interference.

干扰双套同场不串频双套测试

Tools / Buying guide

Buying Batteries: Capacity, Communication, and Safety

A battery is not “it powers on.” Third-party packs may hide percentage, cut out, or swell. On a shoot day, batteries are safety equipment, not a place to save.

3 min read · AdvancedTVCN Tools DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: which link is missing

Prefer OEM or certified third-party for camera packs; for V-mount, check cells and BMS, not only Wh. Carry at least 2.5× expected draw for a shoot day, with margin in extreme temperatures. Stop using any pack that swells, cuts out, or miscommunicates.

Fits:

  • Cold/heat environments
  • Multicam, common batteries

Does not fit:

  • Short clips only
  • Uncertified bargain packs
  • Already swollen old packs

Test protocol: reproducible, no invented scores

Fully charge, record until shutdown, and log actual runtime vs rating. Watch voltage under load. Check percentage/temperature in camera. Feel charge temperature and inspect for swelling.

en.summary: Equipment insurance is not “broken, paid.” Separate property all-risks, machinery breakdown, public liability, and transit; deductibles, depreciation, exclusions, and claim documents decide payout.
en.html:
Home/History & Literacy/Equipment and Production Insurance: What Is Covered, What Is Not

Business / Legal

Equipment and Production Insurance: What Is Covered, What Is Not

Equipment insurance is not “broken, paid.” Separate property all-risks, machinery breakdown, public liability, and transit; deductibles, depreciation, exclusions, and claim documents decide payout.

3 min read · BusinessTVCN Research DeskEdited 2026-11

Scope

This page covers general equipment/production insurance in China mainland; it is not insurance or legal advice. The policy, endorsements, deductibles, and exclusions govern. Confirm territory for cross-province/border shoots.

Key terms: four risks

Property all-risks: fire, theft, accidental impact, water; insured at replacement or agreed value. Machinery breakdown: sudden mechanical/electrical failure; voltage and maintenance exclusions. Public liability: third-party injury/property on set; employee/contractual exclusions. Transit: loss in transport/loading; bad packing and delay usually excluded. For rentals, confirm the owner’s policy and who claims.

Process: policy to claim

List gear (model, serial, purchase price, current value), photograph/video it, keep invoices. Declare high-risk uses (aerial, underwater, fire, vehicles, drones). After a loss, secure the scene, photograph, report to police/insurer, do not self-repair; collect incident note, photos, police/venue statement, repair quote, invoice, serial, rental contract. Confirm deductible/depreciation before repair.

Common disputes: four denial points

Undeclared high-risk use: drone crash or water ingress is often excluded. Deductible exceeds repair: small repairs may be self-paid, but still report. Depreciation: old gear pays actual value, not new price. Rental liability: who insures and who pays the deductible must be in the contract.

Template: gear list and incident pack

Gear list: name/model/serial/purchase date/invoice price/current value/photo. Incident pack: policy no., time/place, statement, photos/video, police or venue statement, third-party loss list, repair quote, rental contract, correspondence. Update quarterly.

Check

  • Gear list has serials and values.
  • High-risk uses are declared.
  • Deductible and depreciation are confirmed.
  • Public liability covers third parties.
  • Rental liability and claimant are written.
  • Incident pack is complete.

en.title: Cross-border Production Invoices and Tax: Contract, Invoice, Withholding
en.summary: Cross-border projects stall on “invoices”: a proforma invoice is not a tax invoice. Place of service, receiving entity, permanent establishment, and withholding decide the tax. Confirm the path before quoting.
en.html:
Home/History & Literacy/Cross-border Production Invoices and Tax: Contract, Invoice, Withholding

Business / Legal

Cross-border Production Invoices and Tax: Contract, Invoice, Withholding

Cross-border projects stall on “invoices”: a proforma invoice is not a tax invoice. Place of service, receiving entity, permanent establishment, and withholding decide the tax. Confirm the path before quoting.

3 min read · BusinessTVCN Research DeskEdited 2026-11

Scope

This page covers general billing/invoicing for China mainland producers serving cross-border film/ad projects; it is not tax or legal advice. Rates, exemption/zero-rating, withholding, and permanent establishment depend on facts; a CPA/tax adviser must review.

Key terms: five decisions

1. Entity: domestic producer or offshore/HK entity decides invoicing and tax. 2. Place of service: shoot/post inside or outside China; offshore may qualify for exemption/zero-rating with filing and evidence. 3. PE: a long-term shoot/fixed place may create a permanent establishment. 4. Invoice: VAT special/general, proforma, and commercial invoices serve different purposes; a proforma does not replace a tax invoice. 5. Withholding: an offshore client paying a domestic producer may withhold VAT/income tax; state tax-inclusive/exclusive and who bears it.

Process: ask tax before quoting

Make a one-page fact sheet: client location, contracting entity, place of service, crew/gear export, currency, tax inclusive, withholding, PE. Have tax confirm invoice type, rate/exemption filing, and contract terms. Include tax, transfer fees, and withholding in the quote; do not quote on “the client says no tax.”

Common disputes: four blockers

“Proforma first”: fine for quote/deposit, not for tax accounting. “Offshore service is exempt”: needs contract, travel records, deliverables, and payment evidence; not automatic. “Client withholds, we earn less”: if the contract is silent, it comes out of the producer’s margin. “HK company, no tax”: management and place of service matter; changing the payee is not enough.

Template: six cross-border clauses

Scope and place of delivery; entity and bank account; currency and FX; tax-inclusive/exclusive and withholding; invoice type and timing; tax/customs/visa/ATA responsibility. Attach the fact sheet and tax confirmation email.

Check

  • Entity and place of service are written.
  • Invoice type/rate confirmed.
  • Tax inclusive/exclusive and withholding are written.
  • Transfer fees are in the quote.
  • Exemption/zero-rating has evidence.
  • PE/visa/ATA assessed.

Use it when there is one clear subject, one action, and a visible change in the final film. Do not use it when there is only a slogan, no person, and no process to shoot; go back to the brief before rolling.

Six beats: one job per beat

Write the six beats as six sentences, each answering “what does the viewer know now.” Shoot in order, but cut out of order; do not add empty shots to fill the structure.

  1. A concrete problem
  2. One person enters
  3. Old way fails
  4. Company intervenes
  5. Verifiable result
  6. One next step

At least one primary shot per beat; do not shoot everything in one framing and rely on jump cuts. Shoot irreplaceable action first—hands, face, machine—then pickups.

  • Person: medium, act before talking
  • Failure: repeat the action, slow the cut
  • Intervention: product/process in one shot
  • Result: before/after or third-party proof
  • End: person leaves, one action remains

1. Logo/drone first: the viewer does not know whose story this is. Replace beat one with a problem or action. 2. Narration in every beat: the images carry no information. Let one action speak. 3. Unverifiable result: “more efficient” with no before/after or third party. Shoot something checkable.

Cost and check: can it be shot in a day

Typically one shoot day plus two to three post days: half a day for primary shots, half for pickups; cut structure first, then sound. Check only three things: six beats complete, one primary shot per beat, result checkable. Do not accept “it feels premium.”

Check

  • Each of six beats is one clear sentence.
  • Beat one is a problem/action, not a logo.
  • At least one primary shot per beat.
  • Result has before/after or third party.
  • At least one irreplaceable action captured.
  • Six beats survive the rough cut.

Copy: before/after of one action, hand close-ups, ambience cuts, locked-off repetition. Do not copy: slow motion for emotion, music covering location sound, illustrative numbers as results. Borrow shots, not evidence.

Three reusable moves

1. Shoot the same action twice—failure and success—and cut them together; the viewer compares. 2. Every 15 seconds, give a hand/object close-up to ground abstract information. 3. Do not summarize at the end; leave an action or a question as a door to the next piece.

Failure and check: breakdown is not copying

The common failure is “the shots look similar, but the proof is fake.” Ask three questions: what happens if this beat is removed? Does the sound stand alone? Is the result checkable? If two answers fail, re-shoot or re-cut.

Check

  • Labeled composite, not a real client.
  • Picture and sound serve the same job per beat.
  • At least one before/after is checkable.
  • Music does not cover key location sound.
  • Ending leaves an action/question, no summary.
  • Structure survives removing any one beat.

Boundary

This page only covers “Food & Table Breakdown: Six Beats in Practice”; it does not replace Food & Table Structure: Six Beats, Food & Table Template: One Sheet to Shoot, Adjusting Actors: Give Verbs, Not Adjectives. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: recipe or tutorial

The first job of a recipe film is reproducibility. Every key step needs an observable signal: how hot the oil, what the dough looks like, how reduced the sauce. Do not say “some” or “about”; if the viewer cannot repeat it, the film is unfinished.

Tutorials need an error demo: heat too high, dough too wet, salt too early. One error shot is more useful than three success shots because the viewer will make the same mistake. Be specific; “watch the heat” is empty.

Condition B: mood or brand

A mood food film does not sell steps; it sells the feeling of wanting to eat. Appetite signals come in order: sound (fry, chop, pour), steam, fat, the first bite. Do not open with a wide of the finished dish; let the audience hear first, see second, want third.

Mood work also needs a person: a chopstick, a hand, someone waiting. Without a person, food is a specimen; with one, the food has a fate of being eaten.

Counterexample: lots of steam, no bite

A food film has steam, slow motion and oil splashes, with rousing music, but nobody eats. The audience thinks it looks good, not that they are hungry. The last step of appetite is the bite, not the wok.

The fix is not more steam; add a first bite: chopsticks lift, teeth sink, chew, face. The bite does not need acting, only truth; real eating is more appetising than slow motion.

Reusable model

Sound → steam → texture → first bite. Let the audience hear the food working, then see steam, then texture, then someone eating. In that order, appetite builds.

A tutorial replaces the bite with a reproducibility check: the viewer cooks once and reproduces the key signals. A mood film replaces the check with wanting to eat, but the four-step order stays.

Formats / Real estate

Real Estate & Space Structure: Six Beats

Real-estate video is not a wide-angle building tour. Start with the life problem of who lives here, then prove it with space; every shot answers one living question.

3 min read · FormatTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: when to use it

Real-estate video is not a wide-angle building tour. Start with the life problem of who lives here, then prove it with space; every shot answers one living question.

Use it when there is one clear subject, one action, and a visible change in the final film. Do not use it when there is only a slogan, no person, and no process to shoot; go back to the brief before rolling.

Six beats: one job per beat

Write the six beats as six sentences, each answering “what does the viewer know now.” Shoot in order, but cut out of order; do not add empty shots to fill the structure.

  1. Doorway problem
  2. Spatial route
  3. One function
  4. One detail
  5. Light/time
  6. Leaving

How to shoot it: six tasks

At least one primary shot per beat; do not shoot everything in one framing and rely on jump cuts. Shoot irreplaceable action first—hands, face, machine—then pickups.

  • Doorway: keys/shoes/parcel
  • Route: door to window in one move
  • Function: one action proves it (cook/storage)
  • Detail: hand/material/edge
  • Light: same room morning/evening
  • Leaving: lights off/door closes, one question left

Common failures: three ways it collapses

1. Logo/drone first: the viewer does not know whose story this is. Replace beat one with a problem or action. 2. Narration in every beat: the images carry no information. Let one action speak. 3. Unverifiable result: “more efficient” with no before/after or third party. Shoot something checkable.

Cost and check: can it be shot in a day

Typically one shoot day plus two to three post days: half a day for primary shots, half for pickups; cut structure first, then sound. Check only three things: six beats complete, one primary shot per beat, result checkable. Do not accept “it feels premium.”

Check

  • Each of six beats is one clear sentence.
  • Beat one is a problem/action, not a logo.
  • At least one primary shot per beat.
  • Result has before/after or third party.
  • At least one irreplaceable action captured.
  • Six beats survive the rough cut.

Picture and sound: what to copy, what not

Copy: before/after of one action, hand close-ups, ambience cuts, locked-off repetition. Do not copy: slow motion for emotion, music covering location sound, illustrative numbers as results. Borrow shots, not evidence.

Boundary

This page only covers “Fashion & Beauty Breakdown: Six Beats in Practice”; it does not replace Fashion & Beauty Structure: Six Beats, Fashion & Beauty Template: One Sheet to Shoot, Adjusting Actors: Give Verbs, Not Adjectives. When the problem belongs to one of those pages, use that page instead of adding more parameters here.

Deep dive

About 7 minutes. This section does not repeat the method above. It adds three things: two conditions, a counterexample and a reusable model, so you can decide when to change the method.

Condition A: product evidence

The first job of a product-evidence beauty film is to make people believe what the product did. Every look needs three proofs: the same angle before and after, a close texture shot and the wear state. Do not only show a beautiful face; beauty does not prove the product.

Control variables in evidence shots: same light, same lens, same background, only product or time changes. More variables and the audience cannot tell product from light. Write an evidence sheet before shooting: which three shots must share conditions.

Condition B: mood or brand

A mood beauty film does not prove the product; it builds “who you become”. The character's state matters more than the product: where she goes, whom she meets, why she puts on makeup. The product appears in action, not dialogue; lipstick is the last action before leaving, not a product display.

Mood work also needs a real anchor: a pore, a loose hair, an edge not perfectly blended. Total perfection becomes plastic advertising; one imperfection makes the audience believe a person.

Counterexample: beautiful, but nobody knows what is sold

A forty-five-second beauty film: model in bathroom, by window, on street, beautiful light, tasteful music. After it, viewers remember the mood, not the product name, texture or who it suits. The brand paid for a mood film.

The fix is not voice-over; add an evidence block: three seconds of before and after from the same angle, two seconds of texture, one second of wear. The block does not need beauty; it needs clarity. Clarity makes the mood useful.

Reusable model

Character state → product evidence → texture → afterglow. Give the person somewhere to go, give the product three proofs, show texture, end on the state after use. With all four, a beauty film is both beautiful and credible.

Each segment answers one question: character answers “who I want to be”, evidence answers “what the product did”, texture answers “how it feels”, afterglow answers “what happens after”.

Fashion & Beauty Template: One Sheet to Shoot

A one-sheet fashion & beauty plan: six beats, picture, sound, duration, and pass line; fill it before rolling and run the set from it.

2 min read · TemplateTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

When to use this sheet

Fill it 24 hours before rolling and send one copy each to director, camera, sound, and producer. It does not replace the storyboard; it compresses it into “what must be shot today.” When the client changes scope, change the sheet before the budget.

The sheet: five columns plus a pass line

One beat per row. Picture is what the viewer sees, not “premium”; sound is what they hear; pass line is what must be captured to pass.

BeatPictureSoundDurationPass line
MaterialMacro textureFabric/ambience5–6 secTexture kept
MovementBody actionAmbience6–8 secNo product yet
ProductHand useClick/apply6–8 secNo pack rotation
LightSame shot shiftMusic5–6 secTexture visible
ProofEdge/blendQuiet5–6 secNo smoothing
EndLook/leaveAmbience5–6 secNo slogan

Filling example: hardest first

Fill the beats that need people, weather, or permits first; pickups last. Durations are ceilings, not targets. Stop when the pass line is met; do not repeat to fill time.

On set: how to run the sheet

Five minutes before rolling, read the sheet: which rows today, what pass line, who owns it. After each row, tick it and note the actual take. Photograph the sheet at wrap and archive it with the footage.

Check: a filled sheet is not a finished film

At wrap, check only: every pass line has footage, sound has an independent backup, the hardest beat has at least two takes. If one is missing, pick it up next day, not in post.

Check

  • One row per beat, no merging.
  • Picture is what is seen, not adjectives.
  • Sound is what is heard, including ambience.
  • Pass line is judgeable, not “feels right.”
  • Hardest beat shot first.
  • Sheet archived with footage at wrap.

en.title: Live & Podcast Structure: Six Beats
en.summary: Live/podcast is not uploading a long video. Design cuttable units: one complete question every 3–5 minutes so a viewer entering late still understands.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Live & Podcast Structure: Six Beats

Formats / Live & podcast

Live & Podcast Structure: Six Beats

Live/podcast is not uploading a long video. Design cuttable units: one complete question every 3–5 minutes so a viewer entering late still understands.

3 min read · FormatTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

First decision: when to use it

Live/podcast is not uploading a long video. Design cuttable units: one complete question every 3–5 minutes so a viewer entering late still understands.

Use it when there is one clear subject, one action, and a visible change in the final film. Do not use it when there is only a slogan, no person, and no process to shoot; go back to the brief before rolling.

Six beats: one job per beat

Write the six beats as six sentences, each answering “what does the viewer know now.” Shoot in order, but cut out of order; do not add empty shots to fill the structure.

  1. Opening hook
  2. One question
  3. One story
  4. One counterexample
  5. One conclusion
  6. Next-episode hook

How to shoot it: six tasks

At least one primary shot per beat; do not shoot everything in one framing and rely on jump cuts. Shoot irreplaceable action first—hands, face, machine—then pickups.

  • Opening: question first, no intro
  • Question: two-shot, keep reactions
  • Story: cut to object/hands
  • Counterexample: change angle/size
  • Conclusion: close-up, one line
  • Next: leave one unanswered question

Common failures: three ways it collapses

1. Logo/drone first: the viewer does not know whose story this is. Replace beat one with a problem or action. 2. Narration in every beat: the images carry no information. Let one action speak. 3. Unverifiable result: “more efficient” with no before/after or third party. Shoot something checkable.

Cost and check: can it be shot in a day

Typically one shoot day plus two to three post days: half a day for primary shots, half for pickups; cut structure first, then sound. Check only three things: six beats complete, one primary shot per beat, result checkable. Do not accept “it feels premium.”

Check

  • Each of six beats is one clear sentence.
  • Beat one is a problem/action, not a logo.
  • At least one primary shot per beat.
  • Result has before/after or third party.
  • At least one irreplaceable action captured.
  • Six beats survive the rough cut.

en.html:
Home/Formats/Live & Podcast Breakdown: Six Beats in Practice

Formats / Live & podcast / Breakdown

Live & Podcast Breakdown: Six Beats in Practice

Composite sample: break live & podcast into six beats and read picture, sound, and the pass line beat by beat; illustrative numbers are not client data.

3 min read · BreakdownTVCN Formats DeskEdited 2026-11

Sample note: not a real client

Composite sample: a two-person podcast on “should creators publish weekly.” Not one real show; people, views, and data are composite.

The point is not to memorize shots but to see what makes each beat work. For a client film, replace every number, brand, and person with your own footage and evidence.

Beat by beat: five columns

Read time, then beat, then whether picture and sound serve the same job. If one column disagrees, the beat becomes “pretty but useless.”

TimeBeatPictureSoundJob
00:00–00:10OpeningQuestion straight awayLive soundNo intro
00:10–03:00QuestionTwo-shotDialogueKeep reactions
03:00–06:00StoryHands/objectAmbienceStory complete
06:00–09:00CounterexampleChange angleDialogueViews collide
09:00–11:00ConclusionClose-upQuietOne line only
11:00–11:30NextWideAmbienceLeave a question

Picture and sound: what to copy, what not

Copy: before/after of one action, hand close-ups, ambience cuts, locked-off repetition. Do not copy: slow motion for emotion, music covering location sound, illustrative numbers as results. Borrow shots, not evidence.

Three reusable moves

1. Shoot the same action twice—failure and success—and cut them together; the viewer compares. 2. Every 15 seconds, give a hand/object close-up to ground abstract information. 3. Do not summarize at the end; leave an action or a question as a door to the next piece.

Failure and check: breakdown is not copying

The common failure is “the shots look similar, but the proof is fake.” Ask three questions: what happens if this beat is removed? Does the sound stand alone? Is the result checkable? If two answers fail, re-shoot or re-cut.

Check

  • Labeled composite, not a real client.
  • Picture and sound serve the same job per beat.
  • At least one before/after is checkable.
  • Music does not cover key location sound.
  • Ending leaves an action/question, no summary.
  • Structure survives removing any one beat.

Boundary

This page only covers “Live & Podcast Breakdown: Six Beats in Practice”; it does not replace Live & Podcast Structure: Six Beats, Live & Podcast Template: One Sheet to Shoot, Adjusting Actors: Give Verbs, Not Adjectives. en.title: Post Software and Delivery: Workflow Before Tools
en.summary: Editing, grading, audio, encoding and review are five stages. Set the workflow before choosing subscriptions. Do not buy all at once.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Post Software and Delivery: Workflow Before Tools

Tools / Buying guide

Post Software and Delivery: Workflow Before Tools

Editing, grading, audio, encoding and review are five stages. Set the workflow before choosing subscriptions. Do not buy all at once.

8 min read · Buying guideTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11

Editing, grading, audio, encoding and review are five stages. Set the workflow before choosing subscriptions. Do not buy all at once.

Workflow first: six stages, not six apps

Post is not a pile of software. A film moves through six fixed stages: backup/transcode, proxy edit, fine cut, grade, sound, encode/deliver. Each stage needs one primary tool; the rest fill gaps. Write the workflow before buying subscriptions.

  1. Media: camera card → two backups → checksum.
  2. Proxy: same frame rate and timecode; originals untouched.
  3. Edit: timeline uses proxies; all story decisions in week one.
  4. Grade: return to originals, transform first, style second.
  5. Sound: dialogue, music and ambience on separate tracks; dialogue first.
  6. Delivery: H.264 for platforms; ProRes/originals for archive.

Decision tree: project first, tool second

Interview, short drama, advertising and documentary need different tools. Interview needs stability and long runs; series needs collaboration and versioning; advertising needs grading and compositing; documentary needs media management and proxies. Do not change the workflow because one app is cheaper.

ProjectLook atCan ignoreBudget
Interview/talking headStability, audio sync, fast exportComplex compositingLow
Short drama/seriesCollaboration, versions, proxiesSingle-seat extreme gradeMedium
Advertising/productGrade, compositing, delivery specsLong-form editMedium-high
DocumentaryMedia management, proxies, searchRealtime effectsMedium

Eight comparisons: total cost before subscription

StageLook atFitsDoes not fit
NLETimeline stability, proxies, collaborationLong-form/seriesOne short video only
GradeNodes, colour management, trackingAdvertising/narrativeStraight-out meeting
AudioMultitrack, automation, denoiseInterview/short dramaMusic-only cut
EncodingH.264/ProRes, queue, hardwareBatch deliveryOne export
ReviewFrame notes, version compareClient workPersonal practice
Media managementProxies, tags, searchDocumentary/seriesOne shoot
CollaborationLocking, comments, permissionsTeamSolo
Total costSubscription + plugins + storage + learningEvery projectMonthly fee only

Buying order: do not buy everything at once

Buy the editor first and finish a five-minute film; add grading when clients ask for a look; add audio when dialogue needs repair; add encoding/review when delivery volume grows. Buy only plugins you will use weekly, not the ones that look powerful.

  1. Month one: one NLE and one encoder.
  2. Month two: add grading or audio for a real project.
  3. Month three: add review/collaboration when a client needs it.
  4. Every quarter, cancel one unused subscription.

Test scope: use the same 4K timeline

Use one 4K 10-bit timeline and test four things: 50% playback, proxy switching, a grade node, export time. Log machine, GPU, software version and cache settings. Not measured: lab benchmarks or large cross-platform comparisons.

Continue: post and delivery hub

  • Choosing an NLE: project first
  • DaVinci nodes: nodes are not filters
  • Colour management: put the LUT in the right place
  • H.264 export: bitrate and compatibility
  • ProRes export: archive and delivery
  • Noise diagnosis: start with the room
  • Delivery: do not export the wrong file
  • Proxy creation: edit without stutter
  • Buying project storage: speed, capacity, backup
  • Model comparison: test by shot type

Verification and price date

Verified 2026-11-23. Software prices and subscription rules follow vendor pages; this page covers workflow and short tests, not benchmark scores.

Add: failure cases

Tool stacking is not a workflow. These five cases only add breakpoints.

MoveResultReplace with
Buy grading before learning the editStory is unclear; grading cannot save itFinish one five-minute film first
Ten subscriptions, broken workflowEvery stage is shallow and delivery stallsOne primary tool per stage
Edit proxies, lose the conformOriginals no longer matchSame name and timecode for proxy/original
Check delivery spec at exportPlatform rejects or recompressesWrite the spec before shooting
Review via compressed chat videoClient cannot see detail; notes missFrame notes or original-file review

Delivery check: six items

  1. The timeline references proxies; originals stay untouched.
  2. Transform colour before grading; do not hide it with a LUT.
  3. Dialogue is intelligible solo; music does not cover words.
  4. Export one H.264 and one ProRes with correct specs.
  5. Archive project, originals, outputs and subtitles.
  6. Client review has a version number and deadline.

Miss one and the last hour becomes rework.

Add: tool selection table

Do not choose by “most features”; choose by the action you do every week.

ActionLook atBuy later
Rough/fine cutTimeline stability, proxies, shortcutsCollaboration/review
GradeColour management, nodes, cacheFilm-grain plugins
AudioMultitrack, automation, denoiseSurround
EncodingH.264/ProRes, queue, hardwareCloud render
ReviewFrame notes, version compareBrand portal

Add: delivery failure cases

The usual post failure is not a missing feature; it is a delivery that ignores the spec.

MoveResultReplace with
Send only ProRes to a platformToo large or recompressedMake a separate H.264
Wrong audio sample rateSilence or pitch shiftUse 48kHz
Archive outputs onlyNo re-edit in six monthsKeep project + originals + subtitles

Last line: workflow beats software

Software only executes decisions faster. If the workflow is unclear, a more expensive app only makes the error more polished. Finish one five-minute film through all six stages before discussing subscriptions, plugins and collaboration. Every quarter, remove one unused tool and give the time back to editing, sound and delivery.

Boundary: a subscription is not a skill

A subscription buys a tool, not judgment. Cut points, colour management, sound layers and delivery specs are learned film by film; the more tools you own, the more you need one fixed workflow.

en.html:
Home/Tools/Test Protocol Library: Ten Reproducible On-Set Tests

Tools / Test protocols

Test Protocol Library: Ten Reproducible On-Set Tests

Reproducible steps, raw-data fields and pass lines for ten tests. Without gear, write “not measured”; do not invent numbers.

9 min read · Test protocolsTVCN / 07Edited 2026-11

Reproducible steps, raw-data fields and pass lines for ten tests. Without gear, write “not measured”; do not invent numbers.

How to use: say “not measured” when it is not measured

These ten protocols are for people with gear, not a lab score sheet. Each record includes machine, firmware, lens, software version, environment, method, raw data, failure condition and cost. Without gear, write public specs and steps, not numbers. “Not measured” is a boundary, not a flaw.

  1. Change one variable at a time; lock everything else.
  2. Shoot a baseline first, then the variable; at least two takes per condition.
  3. Record failures, not only successes.
  4. Never overwrite originals; name by date and condition.

Raw data sheet: one row per test

Download the CSV template and log row by row. Fields: date, test ID, machine/firmware, lens, software, room temperature, method, variable, raw reading, pass/fail, failure condition, file path. Leave a reading blank rather than writing “normal”.

Download the test log template (CSV)

01 Rolling shutter / jelly

Purpose: Whether straight lines skew during a fast pan, and how read speed relates to shutter.

MethodRaw logPass line
Tripod, 24mm wide, pan left and right for two seconds; repeat at 1/50, 1/100 and 1/200 on the same vertical line.Machine, firmware, lens, software, room temperature; record the failure condition.At 1/50, lines remain acceptable and do not turn into a leaning tower.

Known failure: Reading the spec sheet only, with no pan. This page records the method; it does not print unmeasured data.

02 Low-light noise and dual native ISO

Purpose: Shadow noise, the dual-native ISO switch point, and whether skin stays usable.

MethodRaw logPass line
Fix aperture and shutter, step ISO from native to 3200 on a grey card and a face; disable denoise.Machine, firmware, lens, software, room temperature; record the failure condition.ISO 3200 skin is readable; shadows show no obvious blocking.

Known failure: Judging on a screen without logging ISO. This page records the method; it does not print unmeasured data.

03 Autofocus breathing and tracking

Purpose: Whether eye/object transitions hunt and whether low light still tracks.

MethodRaw logPass line
Walk a person from 1m to 3m and out of frame; repeat in low light and backlight.Machine, firmware, lens, software, room temperature; record the failure condition.Transitions do not hunt; low light still tracks.

Known failure: Shooting only static objects. This page records the method; it does not print unmeasured data.

04 Lens breathing and parfocal

Purpose: Whether focus shifts or the frame zooms during a zoom.

MethodRaw logPass line
Lock the camera, focus on a chart, zoom from wide to tele and back.Machine, firmware, lens, software, room temperature; record the failure condition.Focus remains acceptable through the zoom; no obvious scale change.

Known failure: Judging a single frame without zooming. This page records the method; it does not print unmeasured data.

05 Preamp noise and gain

Purpose: Recorder/mic preamp noise and gain structure.

MethodRaw logPass line
Record 30 seconds of room tone, normal speech and a close shout in a quiet room.Machine, firmware, lens, software, room temperature; record the failure condition.Normal speech peaks at -12dBFS; quiet gaps have no obvious hiss.

Known failure: Listening without soloing the track. This page records the method; it does not print unmeasured data.

06 ND colour cast

Purpose: Whether ND shifts colour, vignettes, or matches its marked stop.

MethodRaw logPass line
Shoot a white wall/grey card with and without ND at the same aperture; repeat at the wide end.Machine, firmware, lens, software, room temperature; record the failure condition.White wall stays neutral; corners do not darken noticeably.

Known failure: Trusting the filter marking without a white wall. This page records the method; it does not print unmeasured data.

07 Sustained card/SSD write and heat

Purpose: Whether sustained writes drop speed, overheat or disconnect.

MethodRaw logPass line

en.title: Your First Film in 7 Days
en.summary: Use a phone or small camera to finish a watchable 60–90 second short in seven days: idea, board, shoot, cut, subtitles, review.
en.html:
TVCN/All articles

PATH / FIRST-FILM

Your First Film in 7 Days

Use a phone or small camera to finish a watchable 60–90 second short in seven days: idea, board, shoot, cut, subtitles, review.

TVCN Editorial2026-11-22

Diagram

Before you start

Confirm three things: a phone or camera that shoots 1080p, something to hold it steady, and one to two hours a day for seven days. You do not need editing theory or lights first.

How the path runs

Do not skip ahead. The first three days are paper and prep; days four and five are the shoot; day six is editing; day seven is delivery and review only.

  1. Day 1: Find the line: Write ten lines of “who + wants what + blocked by what,” each under forty Chinese characters. Circle the one whose action you can actually shoot with what you have; avoid crowds, children, or animals. Keep the other nine for later rewrites. Output: One repeatable logline and one visible ending action.
  2. Day 2: Eight-panel shot sheet: Draw eight panels. Each has one main action and one framing (wide, full, medium, close, or detail). Write what the person does before any line; cut any shot that needs more than two lines. Keep the total between sixty and ninety seconds. Output: An eight-panel sheet with one action and one framing per panel.
  3. Day 3: Location and minimum kit: Pick one controllable location: your home, a friend's place, a quiet cafe corner. Find window light before camera position; lock the camera down. Turn on the grid, lock exposure and focus, wipe the lens, and record a thirty-second test. Listen with headphones. Output: A camera diagram and one usable thirty-second test.
  4. Days 4–5: Shoot: Shoot the safe take first: framing, exposure, and sound all pass. Change one variable for take two: blocking, camera height, or light direction. Take three is the risk. Slate scene, shot, and take before every roll, tick the shot log, and back up the same day. Output: Three takes per shot, a matching shot log, and one backup.
  5. Day 6: Rough cut and sound: Assemble in the eight-panel order and trim one or two seconds from each shot. Show it to someone who does not know the story and ask who wanted what and what happened. If they cannot answer, add an action early; do not add narration. If a line is unclear, re-record or ADR it; do not bury it in music. Output: A sixty-to-ninety-second rough cut and a list of problems.
  6. Day 7: Subtitles, export, review: Keep captions under sixteen Chinese characters per line and break them at speech pauses. Check names, numbers, and technical terms line by line. Export 1080p H.264 with 48 kHz audio, named date_title_v1. Play it on a computer and a phone; check for black frames, dropouts, and caption errors. Output: A playable 1080p file, three review notes, and one next step.

Three exercises

  1. Exercise 1: Ten loglines: In twenty minutes, write ten lines; each needs one shootable action. Circle one and keep the other nine. Output: One chosen from ten.
  2. Exercise 2: Eight-panel sheet: Draw eight panels on one sheet with framing, action, line, and duration; total sixty to ninety seconds. Output: A shootable shot sheet.
  3. Exercise 3: One-minute assembly: Cut existing footage to sixty seconds, keeping only shots that move the story. No music; make dialogue work first. Output: A sixty-second v1.

Deliverables

  • One logline
  • One eight-panel shot sheet
  • Three takes per shot and a shot log
  • A sixty-to-ninety-second rough cut
  • A 1080p master and three review notes

Where it goes wrong

  • Rewriting the script on day five: lock the idea on day one and only make small fixes.
  • Buying gear for a first film: phone, window light, and one fixed position are enough; gear turns seven days into seven weeks.
  • Using three or more locations: travel, lighting, and sound double; pick one controllable place.

Next step

Next, take path-story to turn one line into three scenes, or path-post to add rough cut, sound, and delivery.

Check

  • A stranger can say who wanted what and what happened.
  • Every shot has a visible action and does not rely on narration.
  • Every line is audible without subtitles.
  • The film runs sixty to ninety seconds at 1080p and plays on a phone.
  • Captions are clean and under sixteen Chinese characters per line.
  • Three review notes exist, with at least one concrete next change.

en.title: Lens Field-of-View Calculator: Focal Length, Sensor, and Horizontal Angle
en.summary: Enter sensor width and focal length to estimate horizontal field of view, and decide whether a lens is wide enough for a room, a landscape, or a close-up.
en.html:
TVCN/All articles

CALC / FOV

Lens Field-of-View Calculator: Focal Length, Sensor, and Horizontal Angle

Enter sensor width and focal length to estimate horizontal field of view, and decide whether a lens is wide enough for a room, a landscape, or a close-up.

TVCN Editorial2026-11-20

Diagram

What this calculator solves

“Is a 24mm wide enough indoors?” “Will an 85mm feel too tight for a person?” Do not guess. Estimate the horizontal angle first.

Formula

[ \theta = 2 \times \arctan\left(\frac{w}{2f}\right) ]

Where (w) is sensor width, (f) is focal length, and (\theta) is the horizontal field of view.

Common sensor widths

  • Full frame: 36mm
  • APS-C: 23.5mm
  • M4/3: 17.3mm

How to use it

  1. Choose the sensor width.
  2. Enter the focal length.
  3. Read the horizontal angle.
  4. If the angle is too narrow for the space, go wider; if faces distort, go longer.

Three checks

  • You can explain what wide and long lenses change, beyond “zoom.”
  • You know the same focal length gives a different angle on different sensor sizes.
  • You can use the angle to estimate camera distance.

Boundary

This is horizontal field of view. It does not include distortion, focus breathing, or real-world lens marking error. Cinema lenses should be measured on set.

Practice

Take a 24mm and a 50mm lens into the same room, from the same tripod position. Calculate each horizontal angle first, then compare the frames: how much wall does the 24mm hold, and how much larger is the person at 50mm? If you can explain why a wider angle is not the same as a bigger subject, you have used this page.

Home/Animation/2D layer depth: from layers to final

Animation / Deep guide

2D layer depth: from layers to final

2D space is not drawn; it is built from layers, speed differences and occlusion.

8 min read · Deep guideTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

2D space is not drawn; it is built from layers, speed differences and occlusion. One page of "2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane" solves one local problem; joining "2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane", "2D Compositing: Separate Background, Character, Light" and "Layout: Camera and Asset Handoff" exposes the real failure: conditions are missing, too many variables move, and the result cannot be reproduced.

Problem

The problem is not a lack of methods; each step works alone, but together they fail because the condition was not written, too many variables moved and the result cannot be reproduced.

The order is condition, judgement, one variable and evidence. A step is complete only when the next person can repeat it.

Judgement

  • First gate in "2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane": Far, mid, and near layers move at different speeds near 1:2:4.
  • Second gate in "2D Compositing: Separate Background, Character, Light": The character layer is separate and does not slide with the background.
  • Third gate in "Layout: Camera and Asset Handoff": One pan shows near-fast, far-slow parallax.

If one gate fails, return to its single page; do not hide an unsolved point inside a longer chain.

Method

  1. Write the condition first: turn "Split the background into far mountain, midground, near trees." from "2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane" into three rows: material, environment, acceptance.
  2. Run one minimal action: follow "2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane" for 30 seconds and do not add the second page yet.
  3. Attach the second page: Pan at speeds of 1:2:4..
  4. Use the third page as a control: Keep the character on a separate layer, still or with a small follow..
  5. Change one variable at a time; write the other conditions down instead of remembering them.
  6. Film the failure too: put failure and success side by side to see which step cannot be skipped.
  7. Ask the next person to reproduce from the record; if they cannot, the record is not finished.

Field test

A reproducible test, not a client case: take 30 seconds of material, make version A using "Far, mid, and near layers move at different speeds near 1:2:4." from "2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane", then version B using "The character layer is separate and does not slide with the backg…" from "2D Compositing: Separate Background, Character, Light"; only one variable may differ. Put them side by side and record what breaks first in "Layout: Camera and Asset Handoff": condition, action or acceptance. If it works on the first try, add one real constraint and run it again.

Failure table

SymptomCauseReplacement action
Do not pan the whole image at one speed; equal layers flatten the…Condition was not writtenReturn to page one and rewrite the three rows
Do not draw everything on one layer; one change forces a full red…Condition was not writtenReturn to page one and rewrite the three rows
Do not leave the camera live in layout; changing it after animati…Condition was not writtenReturn to page one and rewrite the three rows

Acceptance

  • Far, mid, and near layers move at different speeds near 1:2:4.
  • The character layer is separate and does not slide with the background.
  • One pan shows near-fast, far-slow parallax.
  • Background, character, foreground, and light are separate layers with clear structure.
  • Shadows live on their own layer, not baked into the character.
  • Changing an action moves only the character layer; background and light stay.
  • Camera, character scale, and asset version are locked and versioned.
  • The file header shows version and dependencies so animators do not guess.
  • Animation does not change the camera and the final shot matches layout.
  • The condition from 2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane fits on one line and can be repeated by someone else.

Alternatives

  • For a single-point problem in "2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane", go back to 2D Camera: Pan and Multiplane; do not use the whole chain.
  • To compare two actions, read 2D Compositing: Separate Background, Character, Light and leave the third page alone.
  • For acceptance only, use Layout: Camera and Asset Handoff as a self-test sheet.
