en.title: Real Estate Video: Turn a Floor Plan into a Route
en.summary: A real estate video is not a room sweep. It shows a route through daily life: from the entry to the chair, how the space is used.
en.html:
Home/Formats/Real Estate Video: Turn a Floor Plan into a Route

Formats / Real Estate

Real Estate Video: Turn a Floor Plan into a Route

A real estate video is not a room sweep. It shows a route through daily life: from the entry to the chair, how the space is used.

8 min read · IntermediateTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Real estate video easily becomes a wide-angle sweep: every room appears, and after it the viewer still does not know what living there feels like. The problem is not a wide enough lens; there is no route. The viewer sees square metres, not life.

On location

A ninety-square-metre three-bedroom with good light and a long corridor. The client asks for “high-end”; the previous video sweeps from the entry to the main bedroom with a wide lens and piano music. The owner says it looks like a hotel, not a home. The agent says buyers cannot remember which room faces south.

What to look for

  • Clear route: the viewer can repeat entry, shoes, living room, kitchen, bedroom in order.
  • Credible scale: a person or a piece of furniture gives reference; wide angle alone makes rooms look falsely large.
  • Visible function: each space has at least one use action: sit, boil water, open a cabinet, look out.
  • Directional light: the viewer knows where light comes from; not every room is equally bright.

What to do

  1. Draw a route: start at the entry and walk in real living order; do not shoot by room number.
  2. Set the entry first: the first shot is the first look through the door, at 24–28mm, not ultra-wide; the viewer must know where they are.
  3. Move with a person: gimbal or slider at walking speed; each space is crossed once, not swept repeatedly.
  4. Give function an action: sit, turn on a light, put down a bag, boil water; action turns space into life.
  5. End on a decision: window, balcony or dining table; make the viewer ask whether they would sit here.

Failure modes

  • Wide sweep: every room appears, the viewer remembers “big” and not the layout.
  • Too fast: three seconds per room; the viewer cannot see before the cut. It feels like a listing app, not a viewing.
  • Empty rooms only: no person, no furniture in use; the space has no scale and no life.

Limits

A property video cannot replace listing facts: area, orientation, title and price come from text and the agent, not from images. It is not for commercial leasing or architectural documentary, which need fuller spatial analysis. Get owner or tenant permission before shooting, and do not show house numbers, plates or private photos.

Check

  • After one viewing the viewer can sketch the route without rewinding.
  • Each space has one use action, not an empty shot.
  • A person or furniture gives scale reference.
  • The ending lands on a specific life scene, not a logo.

Deep dive

About 8 minutes. This section places the same judgement in two different conditions, then gives a counterexample and a reusable model. It does not repeat the page; it decides when to change the method.

Condition A: owner-occupier

Owner-occupiers care how they will live daily, not how big the property is. The route starts from repeated actions: bedroom to kitchen in the morning, living room to balcony at night, where a guest sits. Shoot each repeated action once; the viewer connects the day.

Leave room for imperfection: a long corridor, little storage, a small second bedroom can be shown, not hidden. Buyers trust the advantages when they see the limits. Hiding defects leads to disappointment at the viewing and a slower sale.

Condition B: investment or rental

Investors care who will use it, for how long and whether it can change, not whether they like it. Show functional combinations: can it work from home, can a second room be partitioned, can the balcony be used. Do not only show finish. Prove each function with an action: open a laptop at the dining table, air bedding on the balcony.

Label visible and invisible: which finishes, furniture and styling are included, which are staging. Do not let a show flat imply the handover standard. The prettier the frame, the clearer the caption: “for display, not included in the price”.

Counterexample: beautiful but the layout is unreadable

A property film uses drone, slider and slow motion with car-commercial music. After it, viewers remember a big living room and a bright kitchen but cannot say how the two bedrooms connect or where the bathroom is. There is no route, only shot display.

The fix is not a caption saying “master bedroom 18 sqm”. Have a person walk from the entry to the master, passing the bathroom and second bedroom; the camera follows and the order sticks. Put the number in the caption and the relationship in the body.

Reusable model

Entry → route → function → decision. Entry tells the viewer where they are; route fixes the order; function shows life; decision asks whether they would live here. With all four, the film is not a room slideshow.

Before shooting, ask the agent to say in one sentence who this property suits. If they cannot, the film becomes generic. Define the person before the route; different buyers should get a different order in the same property.

en.title: Gear Maintenance: Before Call, After Wrap, In Storage
en.summary: Most gear failures are not sudden. They come from long neglect. Make inspection, cleaning, storage and records fixed habits instead of luck.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Gear Maintenance: Before Call, After Wrap, In Storage

Tools / Maintenance

Gear Maintenance: Before Call, After Wrap, In Storage

Most gear failures are not sudden. They come from long neglect. Make inspection, cleaning, storage and records fixed habits instead of luck.

8 min read · IntermediateTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

A camera that fails at call time usually did not break at that moment. The mount has been loose for months, the sensor has dust, the battery sits full, salt mist was never wiped after a beach shoot. The fault was there; the call only revealed it. Maintenance is not repair; it is making faults show up early.

On location

A three-year-old body: before the shoot the mount has a slight wobble, there is a fixed dust spot in the upper right of the sensor, and the battery reads 100% but drops to 40% at start. The team wipes the lens with a shirttail, swaps a battery and keeps shooting. Three months later the mount fails completely; the repair quote is close to half the used price.

What to look for

  • Mount and lens seat: does the lens wobble up and down after mounting? If yes, stop shooting; do not tape it.
  • Sensor: shoot a white wall at f/16 and look for fixed spots; a spot that does not move with the lens is on the sensor.
  • Battery: a full battery that drops over 20% at start, or two batteries with a big voltage difference, are ageing.
  • Firmware and storage: firmware version, card health and dropped frames; do not discover a card error on set.

What to do

  1. Ten checks before call: mount, sensor dust, front and rear lens groups, battery voltage, card space, firmware, record test, timecode, vents, strap lugs.
  2. Three things after wrap: blow the sensor and lens, wipe salt or rain off the body, let the body cool ten minutes before packing.
  3. Store batteries at 40–60%, not full; run a full charge-discharge every three months and log health.
  4. Use a dry cabinet at 40–50% humidity; keep lens and body separate, cap the mount, do not seal in a plastic bag.
  5. Keep a maintenance log: date, project, problem found, action, next check. The log travels with the body, not with the person.

Failure modes

  • Wiping a lens with a shirttail: fibres and sand leave fine scratches; the more you wipe, the worse it gets.
  • Storing batteries full: full storage accelerates ageing, and they drop faster than expected on set.
  • No cleaning after the coast: salt stays on the mount and screws and starts corroding within weeks.

Limits

This covers digital bodies, lenses, batteries and cards. It does not replace manufacturer service and is not for film or vintage mechanical cameras. If you are not confident with sensor cleaning, do not try it; a sensor costs far more than a cleaning. A body that has been wet or dropped goes straight to repair; do not power it on to test.

Check

  • The ten pre-call checks fit on one sheet and take under five minutes.
  • The sensor dust test is logged, with the last cleaning date.
  • Batteries are stored at 40–60%, with health recorded.
  • Body, lens and cards have unique IDs that match the maintenance log.

Deep dive

About 8 minutes. This section places the same judgement in two different conditions, then gives a counterexample and a reusable model. It does not repeat the page; it decides when to change the method.

Condition A: rented body

For a rental, maintenance is handover evidence. On pickup, shoot a thirty-second video: body exterior, mount, sensor against a white wall, every button, a record test and the accessory list. Do not rely on stills. Before returning, shoot the same sequence and compare for new scratches, spots or errors. A time-stamped video beats a verbal description.

Do not deep-clean a rental on set, especially not the sensor; contact the rental house first and keep a record. For a short rental, spend ten extra minutes on handover rather than lose the deposit on return.

Condition B: owned body

For an owned body, maintenance is a lifetime account. Track shutter count, recording hours, battery cycles and cleaning count; every six months compare repair cost to depreciation. If a year's repair exceeds 20% of the used value, consider replacing instead of reinvesting.

An owned kit can carry a spares pack: one battery of the same model, one backup card, a mount cap and a cleaning swab. Spares are not hoarding; they keep one failure from stopping a shoot. Log the spares too, or the backup battery will be old when you need it.

Counterexample: cleaning the lens, missing the mount

One corner is always soft. The team cleans the lens, swaps the lens, and the problem stays. Finally the mount screws are loose and the lens is not parallel to the sensor. Three days of lens cleaning, no mount check.

Reverse the order: mount and sensor first, lens second. A wobbling mount is visible to the eye; sensor dust shows on a white wall at f/16; lens problems are the rarest. Check the cheapest, most ignored link first.

Reusable model

Inspect → clean → store → log. Inspection makes faults appear early; cleaning stops accumulation; storage keeps gear from failing while idle; the log gives the next inspection a baseline. None of the four needs deep expertise; all four need repetition.

Put maintenance on a five-minute card inside the case; follow it before every call instead of trusting memory. The card is more reliable than experience, especially when you are in a hurry.

en.title: Lighting Safety: Power, Heat, Falls, Load
en.summary: Lighting safety is not “be careful”. It is calculating power, heat, falls and load. If any one exceeds the limit, the lamp should not go on.
en.html:
Home/Tools/Lighting Safety: Power, Heat, Falls, Load

Tools / Safety

Lighting Safety: Power, Heat, Falls, Load

Lighting safety is not “be careful”. It is calculating power, heat, falls and load. If any one exceeds the limit, the lamp should not go on.

8 min read · IntermediateTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Low-budget sets cut safety first: three lamps on one strip, a stand with no sandbag, cables across a walkway. Nothing happens and the shoot wraps, but that does not make it right; it only means nothing fell this time. Safety is not luck; it is lowering probability.

On location

A small room, three 300W LEDs on one power strip, stands by the door, a carpet on the floor. No sandbags, an arm extended 1.2 metres, cables running from the door to the window. Mid-shoot someone trips on a cable; the stand wobbles and does not fall. The team laughs and keeps shooting.

What to look for

  • Power and circuits: three 300W lamps plus other gear exceed the safe margin of one 10A/220V circuit; a warm power strip is a signal.
  • Heat: the lamp head, softbox and cable connectors feel hot; LEDs heat too, do not assume otherwise.
  • Fall: the longer the arm, the more counterweight; no sandbag, uneven floor and foot traffic are all fall conditions.
  • Load: arm rating, rigging point and stand legs locked; nobody stands under the arm.

What to do

  1. Calculate total power: add every lamp's rating, keep 20% headroom; if it exceeds one circuit, split across circuits, do not chain strips.
  2. Check heat: after ten minutes touch the lamp head, softbox and cable connectors; if hot, lower power, increase distance or move.
  3. Counterweight: at least two sandbags per stand, more for a longer arm; hang them at the centre of the legs, not the end of the arm.
  4. Cable management: run cables along walls or in cable ramps; no cable across a walkway; connectors face down, not up.
  5. Power down at wrap: lamps off, then strip, then cables; do not pack a hot lamp.

Failure modes

  • Everything on one strip: the strip overheats and connectors melt; it only feels “a bit warm” at first.
  • No counterweight: the arm extends and the base is light; a passer-by touches it and the lamp falls.
  • Cables trip people: a line across a walkway is invisible to someone carrying a camera; the person falls and the gear falls.

Limits

This checklist is for small interior and exterior shoots. It does not replace a licensed electrician, a studio safety officer or a large rigging plan. Above 5kW, overhead work, generators or wet conditions require a professional. A fallen stand, damaged cable or burnt plug is retired, not repaired and reused.

Check

  • Total power is calculated and split across circuits, not chained on one strip.
  • Each stand has at least two sandbags and nobody stands under the arm.
  • No cable crosses a walkway and connectors face down.
  • Power-down order is followed and lamps cool before packing.

Deep dive

About 8 minutes. This section places the same judgement in two different conditions, then gives a counterexample and a reusable model. It does not repeat the page; it decides when to change the method.

Condition A: small indoor power

The main danger in small indoor power is not shock but heat and tripping. LEDs draw little, but power adapters and cable connectors get hot; keep adapters ventilated, not under a carpet. Put stands against walls, open the legs fully and hang sandbags at the centre; do not narrow the legs to save space.

In a small interview room there are many lamps, many cables and few people. Keep all cables on one side and leave the actor a clean walking path; tape stand positions on the floor so a camera move does not kick them. At wrap, lamps off before cables, never unplug live.

Condition B: outdoor or high power

The first problem outdoors is where the power comes from. A generator needs grounding, distance from people and rain protection; cables need waterproof connectors, not household strips. A stand in wind becomes a sail, and a longer arm is more dangerous; counterweight by wind, not by indoor experience.

Outdoors also calculate the fall direction: which way the stand goes, and whether there are people, cars or glass there. Put stands on the low-traffic side and point the arm at open space, not at the actor. Check the forecast at wrap; do not hang a large softbox above force 5 wind.

Counterexample: the stand falls and nobody steadies it

A stand by the door, arm over the walkway, no sandbag. Three people pass, the stand wobbles three times, nobody steadies it because everyone is busy. The fourth time it falls, hits the monitor, injures nobody, and stops the shoot for two hours.

The problem is not the fourth time; it is the first three. Make a rule that anyone can stop: if you see a wobbling stand, a cable across the path or a hot strip, call stop without the director's approval. Safety is not one person's job; it is a system that can be stopped.

Reusable model

Power → heat → fall → load. Power decides whether it can go on; heat decides how long; fall decides who it hits; load decides whether it holds. Do them in order: power first, then hang. Do not hang first and look for power after.

Walk the set for sixty seconds before call: strips, cables, stands, sandbags, people under arms. If any item is uncertain, stop; do not “finish the shot first”. Safety is not the opposite of efficiency; it is the precondition.

en.title: Platform History: From Channels to Feeds
en.summary: Platforms are not neutral containers. From channels to feeds, the entry, attention and duration changed, and so did the grammar of images.
en.html:
Home/History & Literacy/Platform History: From Channels to Feeds

History / Platform

Platform History: From Channels to Feeds

Platforms are not neutral containers. From channels to feeds, the entry, attention and duration changed, and so did the grammar of images.

8 min read · IntermediateTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

The same three-minute film should open differently on a TV channel, a video site and a feed. The audience did not change; the entry did. A channel relies on a schedule, a site on search and lists, a feed on the first three seconds. Platform history is not interface history; it is the history of viewing conditions.

On location

A director puts the same three-minute short in three places: a late-night TV slot, a video-site front page and a short-video feed. The TV cut opens with twenty seconds of black and titles; the site cut opens with ten seconds of logo; the feed cut has no person in the first three seconds and completion is very low. The director says the film did not change; the platform says the audience did not wait.

What to look for

  • Where the entry is: does the viewer open a channel, search a title or get pushed by a feed? The entry decides the opening.
  • What sets duration: a schedule gives a fixed slot, a site gives a progress bar, a feed gives the cost of swiping away.
  • Person or problem in the first three seconds: a feed with no person leaves the viewer unsure who they are watching.
  • Whether the ending loops: a feed replays and the ending meets the opening; a channel does not.

What to do

  1. List the platform stages: channel, site, feed, and write one sentence for how the viewer finds the film in each.
  2. Compare openings for the same subject: channel can be slow, site needs information, feed needs a person or conflict; do not use one opening everywhere.
  3. Mark grammar changes: shot length, subtitle position, vertical safe area, sound-first or picture-first.
  4. Treat platform rules as conditions, not aesthetics: “first three seconds” does not mean “explode in three seconds”.
  5. Make two endings: a channel ending that closes, a feed ending with a loopable action or question.

Failure modes

  • Treating the algorithm as the work: cutting the film into a reversal every three seconds for completion, until the story is gone.
  • Only seeing interfaces: mistaking app redesigns for platform history, missing the change in entry, attention and distribution.
  • Ignoring distribution: releasing only in the feed, with no channel or site version, so long-tail viewers cannot find it.

Limits

This is a framework for viewing conditions, not an industry study, and it does not replace the platform's current rules. Regions and platforms do not move in sync; the channel, site and feed timelines differ across China, the US and Europe. Mark region and period when writing platform history; do not flatten the world into one line.

Check

  • Can name the entry for each of the three stages.
  • The same subject has three different openings, driven by entry, not showing off.
  • Platform rules are written as conditions, not as style.
  • At least one long-tail version exists, not only the feed cut.

Deep dive

About 8 minutes. This section places the same judgement in two different conditions, then gives a counterexample and a reusable model. It does not repeat the page; it decides when to change the method.

Condition A: the channel era

In the channel era the entry is the schedule: the viewer chooses a channel first, then whether to watch this film. The opening can be slow because the viewer is already seated; the ending must be on time because the next programme will not wait. Duration is set by the slot, not the content; the director completes a change inside a fixed length.

The grammar is segment-based: a film is several self-contained passages so a viewer who joins late can follow. Subtitles carry who is speaking because screens are small and sound is poor; music carries emotional continuity because it cannot stop. The feed changed both.

Condition B: the feed era

The feed entry is the cost of swiping: the viewer does not know you and has made no commitment; without a person, problem or conflict in three seconds, they leave. The opening is not background; it is the character wanting something first. Background can arrive at second eight, second twenty, or never. Duration is set by retention, not by story.

The grammar is hook, payoff, hook: a small payoff every ten to twenty seconds, and a loopable action or question at the end. Not every subject fits; slow documentary, long takes and mood pieces get shredded in a feed and should return to the site or channel cut.

Counterexample: the platform changed, the opening did not

A director uploads a TV documentary straight to a feed, keeping forty seconds of drone and voice-over at the opening. The TV cut completes normally; the feed cut loses more than half in three seconds. The director says the content is good and the audience has no taste; the platform says the audience never reached the content.

The problem is the entry, not the content. The fix is not deleting the drone; move it later. Give a person one line or one action in the first three seconds; the drone becomes a breath at second fifteen. Same material, two entries, two openings.

Reusable model

Entry → attention → duration → feedback. Entry decides how the viewer arrives; attention decides what the first seconds give; duration decides how the story closes; feedback decides whether the ending loops. The four change by platform stage, not by director preference.

Make a platform version sheet: one row each for channel, site and feed, with entry, first three seconds, duration, ending and subtitle position. One film can have three versions but only one core change. Versions change the entry, not the theme.

History / Ethics

Archive Ethics: Restoration, Alteration, Credit

Archives are not neutral material. Restoration, alteration and credit all rewrite history; keep the original, the scope and the permission record.

8 min read · IntermediateTVCN EditorialEdited 2026-11

Old footage is restored, graded, subtitled and scored, then placed in a new film, and the audience assumes they are seeing “the image of the time”. But restoration is already an edit: scratches removed, time removed; speed changed, motion changed. Archive ethics is not refusing to restore; it is letting the audience know what was restored.

On location

A 16mm home movie from 1968: scratched, red cast, no sound. A new film wants it for a story about a family moving. The family agrees but asks to remove an argument. The producers restore the image, add music and use subtitles for narration, but do not label restoration or removal. The audience believes they saw the complete original.

What to look for

  • Is the original preserved: was an unprocessed scan or file kept before restoration? Without the original, restoration cannot be checked.
  • Is restoration scope stated: scratches only, or also speed, colour, framing and sound? The larger the scope, the more it needs explanation.
  • Is alteration labelled: removing an argument is an ethical decision and a historical edit; without a label, the audience misreads.
  • Is credit complete: shooter, archive, restorer and licensor; missing one breaks the chain.

What to do

  1. Preserve the original first: keep an unprocessed scan or transfer in a separate place with source, date, format and hash; restore from a copy.
  2. Keep a restoration log: what was done at each step, which tools, how much changed; keep before and after frames.
  3. Get three-way approval for alteration: family or rights holder, director, archive; write what was removed, why and who approved.
  4. Label on screen: restoration, alteration, reconstruction, dubbing or subtitles, in one line, not buried in end credits.
  5. Credit fully: shooter, archive, restorer, licence number; if anonymous, state why.

Failure modes

  • Treating restoration as the original: scratches removed, colour changed, frames interpolated, no note; the audience thinks history looked like this.
  • Silent alteration: an argument removed without a label; family history becomes a “harmonious version” and the audience does not know.
  • No source: archive footage labelled only “file”; author, archive and licence all missing.

Limits

This is an editorial ethics framework, not a substitute for copyright, privacy or archive licence terms. Permission for home archives must separate use from alteration; agreeing to use is not agreeing to change. News archives are more public, but that does not mean free editing; with minors, victims or privacy, protect the person before completeness.

Check

  • Original, restoration copy and restoration log all exist.
  • The film has one clear on-screen note for restoration or alteration.
  • Credit includes shooter, archive, restorer and licence number.
  • Alteration has written approval from at least two parties, traceable to a date.

Deep dive

About 8 minutes. This section places the same judgement in two different conditions, then gives a counterexample and a reusable model. It does not repeat the page; it decides when to change the method.

Condition A: family or private archive

The first rights holder in a family archive is the person on screen, not the director. Ask three things before use: who is in the frame, who can consent, and to what degree. If the family says “you can use it”, ask separately whether you can cut, change speed or add music; do not package it as one “permission”.

Alteration needs extra care: removing an argument may protect one person and erase another's experience. Do not refuse to cut; write the cut into the opening or closing note and keep the pre-cut version in the archive. The audience has a right to know this is “selected memory”.

Condition B: news or public archive

News archive ethics balances public knowledge against personal harm. Public figures in public places have wider use; minors, victims, patients and private homes need blurring or exclusion. Do not use “historical completeness” as an excuse to expose a face that should not be public.

Restoration of news archive should be conservative: no frame interpolation, no speed change, no generative upscaling; these alter evidence. Dust and scratch removal is acceptable with a note: “cleaning only; timing, order and sound unchanged”. The restorer is not the author and cannot decide for history.

Counterexample: over-restoration becomes a new film

A 1960s street scene is restored with AI interpolation, colourisation and upscaling. Scratches are gone, colours are vivid, faces are sharp. The audience says “the past looked great”. But the original is 18 fps, black and white, visibly grainy; the restored image no longer has the colour or motion of that era.

The fix is not no restoration. Make two versions: a cleaning restoration that only removes dust and scratches and stabilises, keeping the original frame rate and black and white; an interpretive restoration that may colourise or interpolate but must be labelled “reconstruction, not original”. Show both and let the audience choose.

Reusable model

Original → restoration → alteration → credit. The original is evidence, restoration is editing, alteration is selection, credit is responsibility. Keep all four records and archive use is not “take and run”.

For every archive use, write one A4 sheet: source, permission, restoration scope, alterations, credit and contact. The sheet travels with the film, not the project; if someone questions it three years later, you can produce the paper.
